Lantern v0 — query_volume_delta event envelope (experimental, dogfood-only)

Status: experimental. NOT part of the stable PM-facing v0 contract.
Iris 7/11: data_quality must be exposed explicitly (UI chip on the demo tile).
Theo 7/11: internal dogfood-only is fine as long as demo still shows the signal (raw-envelope expand-on-click covers this).


Top-level shape

  {
    "signal_name": "query_volume_delta",
    "schema_version": "lantern.v0.experimental",
    "timestamp": "2023-07-11T11:05:00-04:00",
    "service": "ingest-edge",
    "environment": "prod",
    "emitted_by": "metrics-router@<sha>",
    "query_volume_delta": { ... },
    "provenance": { ... },
    "data_quality": { ... }
  }


Stable fields (universal across all v0 Lantern signals)

  signal_name       string   "query_volume_delta"
  schema_version    string   "lantern.v0.experimental"  — bumped to .stable only when this signal graduates
  timestamp         string   ISO 8601, emission time
  service           string   emitting service, e.g. "ingest-edge"
  environment       string   dev | staging | canary | prod
  emitted_by        string   emitter build identity, e.g. "metrics-router@1f4a2c7"


Experimental fields (dogfood-only — may shift between v0 minor revs; PM/UI do not pin to these)

  query_volume_delta:
    baseline_window    string   ISO 8601 duration, e.g. "P7D"
    current_window     string   ISO 8601 duration, e.g. "P1D"
    delta_pct          number   signed, vs. matched baseline period
    absolute_delta     number   count, signed
    query_class        string   "cardinality_bound" | "label_join" | "ad_hoc" | ...
    tenant_id_hash     string   optional, SHA-256 prefix (16 chars) — hash, do not emit raw


Provenance (always populated — Iris 7/11 ask, lets UI label the demo honestly)

  provenance:
    source             string   origin dataset, e.g. "shard-keeper.query_log"
    computation        string   one-line human description, e.g.
                              "sum(qps) over current_window / sum(qps) over baseline_window - 1"
    sampled            boolean
    sample_rate        number   0.0–1.0; present only when sampled=true
    computed_at        string   ISO 8601
    computed_by        string   build identity of the compactor that produced this value


Data quality (Iris 7/11 ask — must be exposed explicitly; UI renders as a chip)

  data_quality:
    tier               string   "high" | "medium" | "low" | "experimental"
    coverage_pct       number   0–100, fraction of expected samples present in current_window
    known_gaps         string[] e.g. ["rollup-service backfill replay (post 7/10)"]
    staleness_tolerance string  ISO 8601 duration, e.g. "PT10M"
    last_full_window   boolean  true iff both baseline_window and current_window are complete
    caveats            string[] e.g. ["dogfood-only signal", "schema_version may change"]


Contract notes for the doc

  - v0 PM-facing contract reads only signal_name + data_quality.tier. Everything under
    query_volume_delta.* and provenance.* is experimental and may change without a
    PM-facing changelog entry.
  - For the Theo demo: the tile shows delta_pct with a data_quality.tier badge;
    experimental payload is reachable via a "raw envelope" expand-on-click so the
    signal lands without pinning PM/UI to the experimental shape.
  - Graduation criteria from .experimental to .stable: two consecutive v0 minor revs
    with no field changes AND data_quality.tier="high" or "medium" in prod for ≥14d.

Schema's deliberate — emitting_adapter + provenance_url together are the anti-git-tax scaffolding landing exactly right. A few things worth pushing on:

1. baseline_window is under-specified. One field name doesn't tell consumers the actual period the delta is compared against. Split into baseline_window_start + baseline_window_end (or a nested {start, end}). Otherwise when the demo audience asks "compared to when?", Iris/Theo can't reproduce the number without reverse-engineering the adapter.

2. Missing schema_version. Cheap now, expensive to retrofit. Bake it in from day one — you'll want to evolve delta_percent units, add fields, deprecate experimental handling, etc.

3. experimental vs visibility are different jobs; spell it out so Iris's UI logic doesn't conflate them:
   - data_quality = data trustworthiness (complete|estimated|partial)
   - experimental = methodology stability (treat as dogfood)
   - visibility = audience (internal|public)
   Three orthogonal axes. Worth a one-paragraph note on the contract doc so the frontend doesn't branch on the wrong one.

4. delta_percent: signed float, units = percent. For Theo's "demo still shows query movement" ask — does Iris also need absolute volume change in the same event? If yes, add delta_abs now and avoid a second adapter/event later. If no, leave it.

5. Keep source_system and emitting_adapter distinct:
   - source_system = upstream truth (shard-keeper rollups, rollup-service, etc.)
   - emitting_adapter = dotted code path that produced this event (e.g. lantern-adapters/query-volume-delta)
   Git-tax value of emitting_adapter is highest when it's a real grep-able path, not a free-form string.

6. Trim candidates if you want to actually resist git tax:
   - event_type — redundant if query_volume_delta is its own stream/topic. Drop unless you're multiplexing event types on one topic.
   - experimental — fold into visibility (dogfood|internal|public) unless there's a real near-term case for "experimental but public" or "stable but internal-only". Probably not for v0.
   Net: -1 or -2 fields, no signal loss.

7. Type/lock-down:
   - event_id: ULID string
   - service, source_system: controlled vocab — cross-check against the owner map (locked 5/22). Don't let these drift.
   - all timestamps: RFC3339 with offset
   - data_quality, visibility: enums, not free strings
   - delta_percent: signed float, document units in contract

  1. READ
     Job: Show you actually looked at the system as it sits today, not as it should sit. One paragraph. Name 2–3 things you noticed — a pattern that works, a pattern that's inconsistent, a place where the "system" is really just tribal knowledge wearing a token-name costume.
     Don't overdo: Don't prescribe a fix here. Don't list five observations. Don't open with "I'm excited about…" — read first, react later. No org-chart inferences from a one-hour interview.

  2. SEAMS
     Job: This is the section that earns "can own a system." Show you see where decisions actually happen — the spots where the system bends (handoff to eng, exception flow, when someone goes off-token, the Slack thread that decides what ships). Name 2–3 seams. A seam is a place where two things meet and the design judgment has to live somewhere.
     Don't overdo: Don't draw a diagram. Don't use the word "stakeholders" more than once. Don't pretend you saw the seams — frame them as "where I'd want to look first."

  3. ONE TENSION
     Job: Pick a single tension you'd hold out loud as a design lead — the kind that doesn't have a right answer (consistency vs. shipping speed, system purity vs. team autonomy, documented decision vs. made-the-call-myself). Name it, name what each side is optimizing for, name where you'd land by default and why. This is the "she has a point of view" section.
     Don't overdo: Don't pick a tension that's actually fake-balanced (e.g. "quality vs. speed" — boring). Don't resolve it cleanly — a real tension stays live. Don't make it abstract; ground it in something concrete from the interview or from the system she read in section 1.

  4. 90 DAYS
     Job: One thing you'd move in the first 90 days, and one thing you'd deliberately not touch. The "not touch" half is what separates a designer-with-judgment from a designer-with-a-plan. Both should be short — a sentence or two each.
     Don't overdo: Don't propose a process overhaul. Don't say "I'd hire" or "I'd restructure." Don't make the "move" something that needs permission from three VPs. The "not touch" should be a real thing she's tempted to fix, not a softball ("I wouldn't change the culture").

  5. THE SIGNAL
     Job: One signal — not a dashboard, not three KPIs — that would tell you in six months whether the system is healthier than it is today. A sentence. Optional: what would make you wrong about that signal.
     Don't overdo: Don't measure design output ("number of components shipped"). Don't measure sentiment ("team feels aligned"). SUBJECT: Re: Follow-up — design-system pattern ownership

Hi [First name],

Thanks for the thoughtful prompt. Short answer: treat v1 as the start of a stewardship loop, not a finished spec. A few principles I'd lean on:

1. Steward, not owner. Name 1–2 stewards accountable for consistency, accessibility, and evolution — but consumption rights belong to product teams. Stewards propose and approve; they don't ship unilaterally.

2. Versioned adoption, never forced migration. v1 ships with a documented deprecation path and a public roadmap. Teams upgrade on their own cadence. Forced cutovers are where rigidity lives.

3. Open contribution, light review. Any product team can propose a change via a short RFC (use case, proposed delta, a11y/consistency impact). Stewards approve on fit, not preference. Edge-case teams can fork locally — escape hatches exist on purpose.

4. Fitness signals over rigid specs. Track usage, friction reports, and accessibility/consistency outcomes — not "did everyone adopt." If a pattern is widely forked or worked around, the pattern is the problem, not the teams.

5. Quarterly check-in, not a council. Two or three product-team reps, one steward, one hour. Catch divergence early; sunset patterns that aren't earning their keep.

6. Documented escape hatches. "If your case is X, you can extend or substitute Y" — written into the pattern itself. Rigidity is the absence of an exit, not the presence of a rule.

Through-line: patterns earn their authority by being useful, not by being enforced. Stewardship is mostly about keeping the feedback loop short.

Happy to go deeper on any of these.

Best,
Anya

```
Hi Mara,

Thanks for the prompt. Here's how I'd approach it.

WHAT I NOTICED
The system reads as more consistent at the surface than underneath it. Component tokens are well-named and the primitives get reused, but the harder calls — when a team goes off-token, when accessibility gets traded for shipping speed, when a pattern needs to bend for one product — live in a Slack thread or one designer's memory. The pattern is documented; the decisions aren't.

WHERE THE SYSTEM BENDS
Three seams I'd want to look at first:
  - The handoff between a pattern going from v1 to v1.1 and engineering picking it up. That's where consistency either holds or quietly erodes.
  - The exception path. When a product team needs to extend or substitute a pattern, where does that ask land and who decides?
  - Onboarding. What does a new designer need to know before they ship without a senior in the room?

I'd rather name these as places to look than as conclusions I've already drawn.

ONE TENSION I'D HOLD OUT LOUD
When the system says no to a product team — for consistency, for accessibility, for long-term coherence — and the team's deadline says yes, where does that call live? I don't think it has a clean answer. My default would be: the design lead makes the call, writes down the reason, and revisits it at the next review. The pattern protects itself by being argued about out loud, not by being enforced.

FIRST 90 DAYS
Move: shorten the path between a pattern proposal and a decision. A short RFC template, a standing review slot, a written outcome — so a team isn't waiting on a hallway conversation.
Don't touch: the token taxonomy itself. It's load-bearing and it isn't broken. Reshaping it would cost six months of goodwill for no clear gain.

THE SIGNAL
In six months, I'd want to see new designers shipping patterns without me in the room — and I'd want the off-token asks to slow down, not the on-token ones to speed up. I'd be wrong about this signal if the asks slowed because the path got harder, not because the patterns got better.

Best,
Anya
```

Looks like Anya's draft — 4 days post-North-Pier, fits the agency backstory. The substance is solid. Quick take:

Strongest line is "making the pattern easy to use correctly, not controlling every use of it." That's the move — it frames her as not-a-gatekeeper without sliding into anything-goes. Most pattern-owner candidates land on one of those two poles, and the productive middle is exactly where she's pointing.

Naming those two layers explicitly makes the "what can change" question answerable when a request lands, instead of something she has to argue from scratch each time.

2. The revisit trigger is the most important question she asked and the one she answered least concretely. Cleaner version: "If we have three one-off variants solving the same underlying problem, that's a signal the pattern is under-abstracted — not the time to add a fourth." Or: "If a variant has to fork the stable primitives to work, the pattern needs to grow, not bend." Either gives her a concrete trigger instead of a vibe.

3. The owner role ends abstract. "Keeps the pattern understandable" is a goal; "writes the change log, runs the review, ships the example updates" is a job. Two or three specific recurring activities would land harder than the explainer framing alone, because it tells the interviewer what her week actually looks like.

Tight hamstring with no pop, no swelling, walk-normal but stairs-noticeable — most likely a Grade I strain (microtears) or right on the edge of one. Not a tear, not dramatic, but stairs are the provocation test for this muscle and "noticeable on stairs" means it's genuinely complaining, not just post-soccer stiffness.

Tomorrow's plan (the day you'd be tempted to climb)

Morning self-check, before you decide anything:
  - Walk across the room: any pull?
  - Slow bodyweight squat: clean or pulling?
  - Single-leg stand on the affected leg, knee slightly bent: any sensation behind the thigh?

If all three are clean, you're in the green zone and bouldering becomes possible-but-constrained (below). If any of them pulls, you're in the yellow zone: rest day, no climbing.

If you rest:
  1. Gentle isometrics, 3x across the day: stand and press your heel into the floor as if bending the knee, 30-45 second holds, 4-5 reps. The leg should feel like it's working, not hurting. Early isometric load has better evidence for hamstring recovery than pure rest.
  2. Walk flat-ground, short distances. Avoid stairs.
  3. No forward folds with straight legs, no straight-leg kicks, no lunges, no running.
  4. Ice 15-20 min if there's heat or sharpness. Skip NSAIDs unless pain is real — they blunt early healing.
  5. Hydrate, protein, sleep.

If you climb:
  - Warm up longer than usual, submaximal only.
  - Avoid dynos, drop knees, heel hooks, high flags, anything that loads the hamstring at length.
  - Stop at the first hint of the same sensation, not after it.
  - No max-effort attempts. Treat it as movement quality only.

Practical recommendation: skip it.

Here's why, plainly. Bouldering has exactly the failure modes a complaining hamstring doesn't tolerate well. High steps put the hamstring in a deep stretch under load. Heel hooks load the distal tendon. Dynos fire it eccentrically on the catch. Bailing off a problem can plant you in a sudden split. The math is bad: a Grade I you push through today is a Grade II that benches you 3-6 weeks, and a Grade III that takes months. You asked for the voice that counters your "dumb version" — this is it.

If you want to honor the invite without being the person who flakes, go watch. Climb with the group the week after, when you're clean.

Red flags that change this (not drama, just threshold):
  - Swelling or bruising showing up tonight or tomorrow.
  - Sudden snap or sharp pain.
  - Pain at rest or at night.
  - Can't bear weight.

If any of those show up, that's a "see someone" event.

Return-to-play test (cleaner than waffling day-to-day): when you can sprint, do a single-leg Romanian deadlift to full depth, and bound up a flight of stairs fast — all without that same sensation — you're back. Until then, pickup soccer and bouldering are both off.

Acceptance criteria — Iris's refresh-staleness fix (Lantern v0)

Data model
- Two distinct persisted fields: `worker_heartbeat_at` and `latest_source_event_at`. No shared field, no shared write path.
- `worker_heartbeat_at` is updated only by a successful worker tick. Source-event ingestion, backfills, and replays MUST NOT touch it.
- `latest_source_event_at` continues to reflect the most recent observed source event. Heartbeat writes MUST NOT touch it.

UI behavior
- Deploy-movement card displays "last source event at <timestamp>" sourced from `latest_source_event_at`, unchanged in label.
- Card enters a stale state when `now() - worker_heartbeat_at > 300s`. Threshold is exact (5 min), not a fuzzy band.
- Stale state and a current source-event timestamp are not contradictory: stale means the worker is lagging, not that the data is old. Both are surfaced.
- When the worker resumes and `worker_heartbeat_at` advances, stale state clears within one poll cycle. No manual refresh required.

Scope guardrails (v0 boundary — must hold)
- No inferred ownership changes. Provenance-backed ownership renders identically on fresh and stale cards. Heartbeat absence MUST NOT trigger any owner-flip heuristic.
- No raw incident detail. Card surface area is unchanged: summary + timestamps + stale indicator only. No incident text, comment snippets, or payload bodies added to "explain" the stale label.
- No new signals introduced. No query-volume deltas, code-movement inference, or unpermissioned status fields. If implementation needs any of these to function, stop and flag — do not silently expand v0.

Test coverage (must exist and pass pre-merge)
- Paused-worker test: worker heartbeat frozen at T-6m while `latest_source_event_at` advances to T-1m → card MUST render stale.
- Resume test: same setup, then worker heartbeat advances to T → card MUST clear stale within one poll cycle.
- Replay/backfill test: replaying source events MUST NOT move `worker_heartbeat_at`.
- Owner-stability test: with heartbeat frozen, the card's displayed owner MUST match the owner shown when fresh.

Out-of-scope reminder (do not fold in)
Query-volume deltas, code-movement inference, unpermissioned status, raw incident text. If Iris's implementation requires any of these, surface before merge — the omission is the v0 contract, not a backlog item.

Recommended (one line, two clauses, no new surface):

  Incident summary not available in this view. The source may require permissioned access, or no summary has been published.

Why it lands:
- "in this view" is the load-bearing word — it forecloses the "no incident load" misread by framing the empty state as scope, not signal.
- "Incident summary" anchors what the empty state is *about*, so the two reasons after it are read as explanations of the summary, not of incident activity.
- "may require … or … has been published" keeps both boundary cases without privileging either, and "may" / "has been" stay neutral on whether anything actually exists underneath.

Two tighter variants if you want to A/B:

  Summary not available in this view. May require permissioned source access, or no summary is published yet.

  Incident summary unavailable here. Source may need permissioned access, or no summary is published.

If testers still read it as a status signal, the next cheap fix is moving the "or no summary has been published" clause to the end and inverting the connector (e.g., "either the source needs permissioned access, or no summary has been published") so the access clause lands first and sets the frame — but try the one-liner first, it usually clears it without a structural change.

Quick read: what you're describing — walk fine, no pop, no swelling at 20 min, tender only on pivot — is the picture of a very mild lateral-ligament tweak (or just a soft-tissue bump). It's probably nothing serious, but the classic trap is that it can look fine at 20 min and stiffen up overnight, so don't trust today's read until you've seen the morning.

For the next 24 hours:
- Ice 15-20 min on / 40+ min off, a few cycles today. Compression sleeve or wrap if you've got one. Elevate when you're sitting.
- No pivoting, cutting, or jumping today. Walking is fine; soccer is not.
- OTC anti-inflammatory (ibuprofen 400 mg with food, if you tolerate it) is reasonable today and tomorrow morning — it also helps you tell real pain from stiff soreness, since the swelling-suppression is mild at that dose.
- Reassess first thing tomorrow, before the friend pressure starts.

On bouldering: skip it. The climbing itself is mostly fine, but bouldering lands you on the mat from height and asks for occasional one-foot push-offs and barn-door moves — exactly the lateral loading a tender ankle does not need, especially when you're tired. The cost of skipping one session is basically zero. The cost of re-rolling a freshly-grumpy ATFL on a bad landing is weeks. Take the rain check, tell your friend you'll be back next weekend.

Actually worry (and go get it looked at) if any of these show up by tomorrow:
- Swelling that shows up overnight, especially on the outside of the ankle or in front of the lateral malleolus
- Bruising anywhere along the foot or lateral ankle
- Can't bear weight at all in the morning, or it gives out when you try to step down stairs
- Pain that's localized on the bone rather than the soft tissue, or tenderness right on the lateral malleolus itself

If morning looks boring — just mild residual tenderness on a forced pivot — you're probably fine to do easy stuff in a week and back to full soccer in 2-3. If anything on the worry list shows up, that's when a clinic visit earns its keep.

Short version: probably nothing, don't boulder tomorrow, reassess in the morning.

Here is a short answer you can hand her. Three blocks matching her three questions, each with one quotable line.

Token ownership — where the line is
  Design owns: the token's name, semantic intent, the value itself, the usage rule (when this token is right vs. alternatives), and the pairings it composes into.
  Engineering owns: resolution mechanism (CSS vars / Sass / build-time / JS), distribution (Style Dictionary, Token Studio, in-house), theme + SSR mechanics, fallback chains, component-API shape, and every rename / deprecation / migration decision.
  Clean line she can quote: "If the question is answered by opening the design spec or the value space, it's design's. If it's answered by opening the codebase, it's engineering's."

Handoff document — what belongs
  Token definition with the WHY (semantic role, what it replaces conceptually), not just a value.
  Decision criteria: when to use it / when not to, with a concrete anti-example.
  Composition rules: which tokens travel together.
  State coverage the token promises — dark, dense, RTL, interaction states.
  Accessibility floor baked in (contrast target, motion preference).
  Acceptance criteria for design-layer "done."
  Explicit non-goals: what this handoff is NOT deciding.

Handoff document — what does not belong
  Framework-specific code patterns, version numbers, codemods, deprecation windows, or anything that needs to know the consumer codebase's reach or blast radius.

Saying design owns semantics + usage without owning migration
  Frame tokens as a contract — input to output semantics — not an implementation.
  Phrasing that holds up in review: "Design owns the meaning of this token and the rule for picking it. Engineering owns the code that consumes it, including how it gets renamed, replaced, and removed." That line works because migration choices depend on codebase reach, blast radius, and consumer commitments — things design has no authoritative view into.
  Publishing usage guidance ("use this token when…") is fine. Guidance is a contribution to a decision, not ownership of the decision. The moment a question requires opening a file in the consumer repo, it has left design.

Kibo walk-incident checklist — Sat 2023-09-23

INSPECT KIBS (do this in the next hour, calmly, with treats)
- Paw pads: lift each paw, press gently between toes and across the pad. Look for a hot spot, blood, or him pulling back. Curb clips often show on the side that took the impact.
- Legs + shoulders: run your hand down each front leg from shoulder to paw, press the pads. Watch his face, not just whether he pulls away — dogs mask.
- Chest / ribcage / armpits: where the harness webbing sits. Look for red streaks, missing hair, or a wet patch. Even a partial slip can shear skin if the webbing caught.
- Neck / throat: lightly feel the trachea and the area under the jaw. Brief leash catch can irritate.
- Behavior over the next 12–24h: appetite, willingness to jump on the couch, going up stairs. Any of those dropping = vet, not "let's wait."
- Vet threshold: any of the above off, or you just can't shake a gut feeling. A same-day walk-in for "I'm probably being paranoid" is the right call; trust that.

CHECK HARNESS FIT (the two-finger rule, everywhere)
- Chest strap (between front legs): two fingers flat under the webbing, snug not tight. Most backing-out comes from this strap being loose.
- Neck opening: should NOT be possible to back over the ears. If it is, the harness is the wrong shape for his build.
- Back / girth strap: two fingers again; you should not be able to twist the webbing more than a quarter turn.
- D-ring / leash clip point: dead-center on the back for a calm walker. If he pulls or backs out, a front-clip (chest) attachment or a Y-front harness fixes ~80% of slip-outs.
- Try the "lean-back test" indoors: have him walk forward while you apply gentle backward leash pressure. If the harness rides up toward his neck or shifts sideways, it's not the right harness.

WHAT TO REPLACE / REFIT BEFORE THE NEXT WALK
Pick one:
1. Refit the current one (free, do today)
   - Re-tighten every strap to the two-finger rule with him standing, not sitting.
   - Re-position the chest strap so it sits at the sternum, not behind the armpits.
   - If the webbing is stretched, buckles cracked, or stitches frayed → stop, do not reuse. A stressed-out dog on a half-failed harness is worse than no harness.
2. Replace with a better-fitting style (today, before evening walk)
   - For dogs that back out: Y-front harness (Ruffwear Front Range, Kurgo Tru-Fit, etc.) or a harness with both front and back clip points used together.
   - Skip "step-in" styles if the backing-out was sudden — they shift the easiest.
   - Measure his chest girth at the widest point (just behind the front legs) before you go; pet store staff will size off that number.
3. Backup plan for the next few days while you decide
   - A properly-fitted martingale collar with a front-clip harness attached to the same leash, so if one fails the other holds. Sounds overbuilt; isn't, given the week ahead.

TEXT TO DEVIKA (short, calm, action-confirming, not dismissive)

"Hey — he's okay. I caught the leash the second the harness slipped, no limp, no cut, no sign he's hurt. I checked him over and I'm watching him through the day. I'm refitting or replacing the harness this afternoon so tonight's walk is on a different setup. I'll tell you everything when you're home. Love you."

Why it's worded that way: "he's okay" + the concrete detail ("caught the leash the second it slipped") is the reassurance without saying "it was nothing." Naming the next action (refit/replace today) is the "it's handled" part. The "tell you everything when you're home" gives her the conversation she actually wants without forcing it over text mid-shift.

Read on Yuki's diff:

  Goal coherence: the changes mostly line up with "reduce exporter retry noise":
    - Longer batch timeout (10s) + larger send_batch_size (8192) -> fewer export calls/sec -> fewer retry triggers.
    - Higher memory_limiter thresholds (82% / 25%) -> fewer backpressure drops -> fewer queue-full retries cascading to the exporter.
    - Explicit retry_on_failure with bounded backoff (1s -> 15s, 5m max) -> transient blips absorbed instead of bubbling up as failures.

  But the framing is loose. retry_on_failure ENABLES retries where before there were presumably fewer or none. The "noise" reduction comes from retries succeeding (no failure events), not from fewer retry attempts. Worth confirming alerting fires on retry-exhaustion, not just immediate failure -- otherwise a 5-minute upstream hiccup becomes silent.

  Concerns:

  1. memory_limiter at 82 / 25: OTel collector defaults are 80 / 20. At 82% you're two percentage points from the GC cliff on a high-throughput service. Combined with 25% spike_limit, a transient burst can easily push into drop territory. Staging tests should include burst patterns (not just steady-state load), and the success criterion should be explicit: what drop rate is acceptable? On ingest-edge, drops = data loss -- needs to be measured, not assumed.

  2. batch.timeout 10s + send_batch_size 8192: this sets a 10-second floor on data latency, on top of whatever retry budget ends up being used. Fine for metrics. If ingest-edge is also carrying traces or anything latency-sensitive downstream, sanity-check with the consumer team.

  3. "staging first, then prod if quiet": the missing piece is the definition of quiet. Concrete go/no-go criteria (p99 latency, retry-exhaustion count, memory_limiter drop count over a defined window) would make the prod decision less subjective. Otherwise "quiet" becomes whatever the loudest voice in the room calls it.

  4. The retry numbers (1s initial, 15s max, 5m elapsed) -- is this aligned with anything in the ingest-edge runbook, or Yuki's call? Worth checking against documented policy before approval.

Short read on it first: no pop, can walk, no real swelling = almost certainly a Grade 1 calf strain (gastrocs/soleus micro-tear) or protective spasm. Annoying, not alarming.

Decision on bouldering tomorrow

If it's still tight tomorrow: skip it. A tight calf under explosive load (heel hooks, dynos, jump-downs) is the textbook path from Grade 1 to Grade 2, and Grade 2 is weeks not days. One session isn't worth that trade.

If it's clearly gone by morning — no tightness on stairs, painless single-leg calf raise, symmetric squeeze vs. the other side — an easy session is okay. But still avoid heel hooks (they load the calf in a stretched position, which is the worst angle for an acute strain) and skip dynos/jump-downs. Downclimb instead of jumping.

If you're somewhere in between, default to skipping. Bouldering will be there next week; a strain escalation won't be.

Next 48 hours, conservative

Walking is fine. Pain is the guide — if a step makes it talk, slow down.

Ice 15-20 min, 3-4x/day, for the first 24-36 hours. Don't ice constantly.

Calf compression sleeve if you have one. Surprisingly helpful for this exact thing.

Avoid for 48h: sprinting, jumping, plyos, deep calf stretching (no pushing into the stretch in the first 24h), foam-rolling directly on the tender spot, and any loaded heel-hook work.

After ~36h, start gentle progressive loading: seated heel raises → standing heel raises → single-leg heel raises. If a set leaves it tighter an hour later, you went too hard.

Hydration, normal protein, sleep — boring but does more than any gadget.

Red flags, briefly (not spiraling): sudden sharp increase in pain, expanding bruise, can't toe-walk on that leg, or swelling that gets worse after day 2. Any of those is a real medical eval, not "push through it."

Return-to-bouldering checkpoint (Mon or Tue): pain-free single-leg calf raise 3x15, no tightness on stairs, symmetric squeeze. All three and you're cleared for an easy session, still no heel hooks. If any of the three are still off, give it another 48h.

The practical summary: treat tomorrow as rest, use the 48h to load progressively, and only go back to bouldering when the calf squeeze matches the other side. Tightness under load is the thing you're protecting against — pain-free at rest isn't enough.

Four questions, each pointed at the seam where design and engineering meet rather than at the design choices themselves. The point is to let her describe what the handoff actually felt like from her side, not to push her toward any framing.

1. When the build came out differently than the spec implied, who actually owned the call? Did she keep the pen, did engineering push back with a counter, or did it move to a PM?

2. What did "ready for engineering" mean as a moment? Agency decks have an approval gate; product handoffs need a buildable definition of done. Was there an artifact state, a review sign-off, or a written line that said this is ready to build?

3. When engineering hit a constraint mid-build — cost, scale, a platform limit — how did that loop work? Formal re-spec, async comment thread, hallway conversation?

4. Did she get to see the engineering constraints (latency, accessibility, data shape, platform limits) while she was still designing, or did they show up at handoff? The agency world rarely surfaces those; product work does, and it's the most concrete difference from a campaign deck.

If you want one of them to lead with, #4 is the one that usually opens the most honest answer — it's the kind of question a designer can answer without performing anything.

Title and P1 are doing the real work here. "Shared handoff surface" is the load-bearing concept, and P1 names the actual move: separating customer-facing readiness from internal engineering checks. That's a sharp distinction, not a vague one — it shows up in the prose as a clean split between what the dashboard *said* and who was allowed to *act* on each color of state. The owner-notes-as-provenance line in P2 is the same move at smaller scale. Also good.

  1.  "My role was not just to make another dashboard screen" reads slightly defensive. In case-study prose the work usually shows the scope without you disclaiming it. If the audience might wonder why an engineer is writing about UX, the line earns its keep. If not, it sounds like bracing for a question that wasn't asked. Cut it, or move it to a context note above the body.

  2.  P2 is carrying two beats at once: the design-system moves (status names, empty states, owner notes) and the outcome (PMs self-serve, tech checks stay in engineering). Right now they're fused. If you split — moves in P2, outcome / takeaway in a P3 — the second beat lands harder. As written, "pretending the UI had answered them" closes on the *what* of the design, not the *so what*, which buries the strongest line you wrote.

The trick is that none of these can be "does the user do the right thing on first try" surveys — those favor articulate users and tell you nothing about whether the surface itself is doing the work. Each signal below is behavioral, in-product, and answers one comprehension question without rewarding the scope creep.

1. Provenance — provenance-check-before-share rate
Of cards a user copies or pastes out of Lantern (into Slack, a doc, a ticket), what fraction had the provenance strip expanded or hovered in the prior 30 seconds. If the rate is high, users treat source + last-refreshed + ownership anchor as load-bearing context to verify before forwarding. If it's low, cards get shared on face value — which is exactly the provenance-blindness we're trying to prevent. This is a comprehension signal, not a feature-existence signal: a present-but-ignored provenance line is the failure mode, and this catches it.

2. Permission wording — boundary self-resolution rate
When a user lands on a card with a permission marker (internal-only, owner-only, not-shareable), fraction of encounters that resolve without (a) opening a why-can't-I-share help link, (b) attempting a share that gets blocked at the boundary, or (c) pinging Theo, you, or Iris with a question. The wording is doing its job when the marker carries on its own. Note this is the inverse of how a permissions cop would frame the metric — you don't want to minimize blocked shares, you want to minimize *unsupported* shares and lookups. A user who reads the marker and walks away is a success, even though nothing visible happened.

3. Empty states — re-query shape after an empty result
When a user gets an empty result, the direction of their next query is diagnostic. Narrowing the filter (shorter window, specific service) means they understood "no deploy movement in this window." Broadening or requesting access means they understood "not visible to you at this scope." Re-querying identically or abandoning means the empty state didn't communicate — that's the failure you measure against. You want the first two outcomes to dominate, not the third. Crucially, you do not measure empty-state frequency. That pushes you toward fewer empties, which pushes you toward showing more, which is scope-broadening wearing a UX hat.

Why each one sidesteps Iris's instinct: signal 1 measures whether users verify before they forward, not whether Lantern shows up in more conversations. Signal 2 measures silent correctness, not engagement with permission docs. Signal 3 measures interpretation, not the rate at which empty states get filled in by widening scope. None of them turn into a release-readiness number, none of them surface raw incident text, and none of them require anyone to override or hand-edit an owner card. I'm not a clinician and can't diagnose what you're dealing with — sounds like a low-grade calf strain (soleus more likely than gastroc if stairs were the trigger and it feels like a tight band rather than a pinpoint). General conservative return-to-activity guidance below; treat it as a framework, not a prescription.

Where you are

Improving, not cleared. Stairs no longer grabbing is a real win — that means end-range loaded dorsiflexion is tolerable. A faint tight spot on a long stride means the muscle-tendon unit still isn't tolerating full lengthening under load. That's the line you're walking this weekend.

Bike vs walk

Both are reasonable. The bike is the lower-load option for a first session back:

  Easy bike spin (today)
    - Flat route, low resistance, cadence ~85-95, 30-40 min
    - Calf is mostly isometric under the pedal; minimal stretch, low force per rep
    - If the tight spot shows up, you're done for the day — don't push through

  Flat easy walk (Sunday, only if Saturday went clean)
    - Short stride, conversational pace, flat surface, 30-45 min
    - Soft ground (grass, dirt) preferred over concrete if you have it
    - Drop the "long walk" framing this week — volume is the variable to control, not intensity

Why bike first: it loads the calf in a shortened, low-force range. Walking at any pace loads it through a full stride cycle and accumulates more stretch-reps over the same time. Reintroduce walking after the bike session confirms no next-day flare.

What to avoid this weekend

  - Soccer, sprinting, hill repeats, plyos, jumping rope
  - Bouldering that involves heel hooks, drop-offs, or dynamic moves — easy traverse only if at all
  - Deep calf stretching or aggressive foam rolling on the spot
  - Stair-running, even casual
  - Barefoot time on hard floors for long stretches
  - Stretching the spot "to see if it's still there" — that's reloading it, not testing it

Symptoms that mean back off that same session

  - Tight spot sharpens or localizes during the activity
  - Discomfort that climbs over the first 10-15 min instead of fading
  - Any grabbing, catching, or feeling like the calf wants to cramp
  - Next-morning soreness that's worse than the day before, or hasn't settled within 24-48 h

Red flags — don't just back off, get evaluated

  - Sudden snap, pop, or sharp stabbing mid-activity
  - New swelling, warmth, or a tender cord in the calf (DVT worth ruling out, especially after a week of relative rest)
  - Calf pain at rest, night pain, or any color/temp change in the foot

Return-to-sprint gate (so improvement doesn't get read as clearance)

Three sessions in a row — easy bike, easy walk, then a short easy jog on flat ground (10-15 min, all easy) — without next-day regression. THEN you can think about strides: 4-6 x 20 m on flat grass, full rest between, only if the jog was clean. No pickup soccer, no hard bouldering, no hill sprint until that's gone two weeks without flare.

If the faint tight spot is still showing up on a long stride at the end of this weekend, that's a signal it needs another week of easy cycling and walking before jogging — not a signal to push through it.

Your remaining signal (dull tightness on lengthening, fine elsewhere) is exactly where a healing calf is weakest — eccentric load at long muscle length. Bouldering can either stay out of that lane or end your day. The plan below keeps it out.

Hard yes today if: single-leg raises are clean, easy flat warmup walk had zero grab, you slept and ate reasonably, and you commit to the avoid list.

WARMUP (before any climbing)

  1. 5 min easy cardio on a bike or flat walk. No jumping rope, no running.
  2. Single-leg calf raises: 2 × 15 straight knee. If clean, 2 × 15 bent knee. These double as your readiness test — if the dull tightness shows up here, do not climb; do the rehab option below instead.
  3. 5 min easy traverse on jugs and big feet. Flat feet, slow, deliberate. No high steps.
  4. 1–2 problems well below your flash grade, focused on footwork. Both feet on, smooth.

MOVES TO AVOID

  - Dynos. Non-negotiable — that's exactly the "push off quickly" move.
  - Heel hooks. They load the gastroc at long length under tension.
  - Drop-and-stick onto one foot. If you fall, absorb on two feet, knees bent.
  - High steps that put the calf in deep dorsiflexion under load.
  - Powerful toe-off on small footholds — if the foot leaves the wall and comes back, that's the move you're avoiding.
  - Long, reachy sequences where the last foot is the push-off point.
  - Mantles requiring push.
  - Anything your brain labels a "push" — that mental cue is your calf telling you something.

WHAT IS FINE

  - Compression, crack-style, slab, technical footwork on big feet.
  - Sit-starts, static sequencing on big holds.
  - Traverses.
  - Anything where heels stay low and weight stays on full feet.
  - Keep session cap at maybe 60% of normal volume — fewer problems, more rest between.

STOP CRITERIA (any one means you're done)

  - Sharp or "grabbing" pain at any moment. That's a different signal than the dull tightness — stop.
  - Dull tightness that sharpens under load, even briefly.
  - Pain above 3/10, or pain that lingers 5+ minutes between attempts.
  - Single-leg calf raise at the wall starts reproducing the dull tightness.
  - Loss of confidence pushing off — if you're hesitating on moves you wouldn't normally, that's your calf talking.
  - Tomorrow morning: if first steps out of bed feel worse than yesterday morning's first steps, you overdid it today.

AFTER

  5 min easy walk or bike cool-down. Note how the calf feels 1 hour later and again tonight. If it's tighter tonight than yesterday at the same time, you crossed the line.

IF YOU SKIP — three useful options, not "do nothing"

  1. Social climb: go to the gym, spot and beta for your friend, do upper-body pulls on a hangboard or bar, stay off the wall. Keeps the routine and the friendship intact.
  2. Active rehab: 3 × 15 single-leg calf raises off a step, 3-second eccentric on the way down, straight knee then bent knee. If pain-free, this is the most useful thing you can do for climbing next weekend.

Alex, your concern is well-placed and I'd push back on the shape before Cyrus touches it. The core issue isn't "is the ID useful" — it's "is this label value a bounded family."

Why `replay_source_id` is high-risk as a label

- A label in Prometheus should index a *bounded, enumerable* set of values: a low single-digit to low-double-digit cardinality is the sweet spot, and a handful of dozen is usually the ceiling.
- A raw replay source ID, by construction, identifies one specific source/replay run. That's effectively a per-execution identifier. Even if you have ten "regular" replay sources, the moment a one-off backfill, a one-time validation chunk, or a tenant-specific replay shows up, every unique value becomes a new time series — and you keep them for the retention window.
- Mismatches are rare by definition (a well-behaved validation pipeline is mostly `match`). So the metric is dominated by the `mismatch` series, and each new replay source adds a new `mismatch` series with no upper bound. That's the worst case for cardinality: high churn, no natural cap, low per-series volume.

The "but the ID is already in metadata" argument doesn't help

That's true, and it's actually the reason putting it on the metric is *redundant*, not necessary. If the ID is in the replay metadata that produced the counter increment, then:
- Logs already group by it cheaply (you can find "which source produced this mismatch" by joining metric scrape to log).
- Dashboards that aggregate mismatches by source can be built from logs or from a separate, properly-bounded join.

What "bounded family" means in practice for this metric

The debugging need Roman is describing is: "during a replay-validation investigation, I want to know which source is contributing mismatches." That's a real need, but there are a few bounded ways to serve it:

1. **Use a bounded category, not the raw ID.** "Source class" — e.g. `validation_chunk` / `routine_replay` / `backfill` / `tenant_replay` — gives dashboards a useful breakdown with a cardinality of ~5.
2. **Use the raw ID, but only on the log side.** Keep the counter bounded (`validation_result` only), and join on `(timestamp, source_id)` from the log when investigating a specific incident.
3. **Use the raw ID on a *sample* or *exemplar* attached to the counter.** Prometheus exemplars let you attach a reference to a higher-cardinality trace/log without exploding the series count. That's the "show me one example of which source caused this mismatch spike" use case, without "give me a time series per source forever."

How I'd frame the response to Roman

Something like: "I'm not against exposing the source identity — the debugging need is real. But before we put `replay_source_id` on the metric, I'd like to know:
  1. How many distinct values have we observed in the last 90 days? (rough cardinality now)
  2. What's the upper bound on new values per month? (backfills, tenant replays, etc.)
  3. Is the typical debugging question "which source caused *this spike*" (exemplar-shaped) or "which source has been misbehaving over the last week" (label-shaped)?

If (1) is unbounded or (3) is exemplar-shaped, I'd rather keep the metric with `validation_result` only and either (a) add a bounded `source_class` label, or (b) attach the raw ID as an exemplar pointing to the log line. That keeps the dashboards cheap and the debuggability intact."

That gives Cyrus a clean thing to cost-model: the proposal in its current form (raw unbounded label) vs. the bounded-counter + exemplar alternative. The latter usually wins on cost without losing the actual debugging value Roman is after.

The short read: **Iris's instinct is right**, and the clean rule is worth naming explicitly so future versions of this question don't relitigate it.

**The clean rule**
Lantern can show incident *signals* (status, severity, owner, affected service) sourced from systems other than the incident body — that's already in scope under "provenance-backed ownership" and "empty states." Lantern cannot show incident *content* (what happened, the timeline, the customer impact, the technical specifics) in any form — raw, paraphrased, summarized, or AI-digested — because it originates from the excluded source. Format doesn't change scope; "AI digest of an excluded body" is still excluded-body content.

**Why the digest isn't the right shape, even though the need is real**
- People at a glance usually want status + severity + owner + service, not the narrative — so the click cost is mostly about wanting *signals*, not *content*.
- A digest surface creates a new path where people consume incident context without going through the access-controlled path. That's exactly what the boundary was drawn to prevent, and it's the same posture as the 11/2 PE pushback (Captain/readiness stays on the release-process surface, not the Lantern card).
- "Permission-safe summary" was written for things like deploy movement and ownership — content that's already in-scope to surface, just shaped carefully. Pulling it out of an out-of-scope source is a different move.

**What solves the click without stretching scope**
Show incident-card signals from non-note sources (alerting system status, owner map, severity tag) with an empty state when the user doesn't have access. "View incident" link when they do, nothing when they don't. That's the design "empty states on missing/unpermissioned data" was written for, and it gets Iris most of what she actually wants.

**Wording for Iris that doesn't read as blocking**

> "We can definitely cut the click cost. The thing I'd push back on is the digest itself — the underlying note is out of scope for Lantern regardless of format, since that's where the boundary was drawn. What we *can* show in-place is the metadata we already have from other sources (status, severity, owner), with a view-incident link for people who have access and an empty state for people who don't. Want me to sketch what that looks like on the incident card?"

That names the constraint, offers the path, and asks for the next step rather than just declining.

If you want, I can draft a slightly tighter version, or sketch what the in-scope "signals only" card would actually contain.

DEFAULT RECOMMENDATION: SKIP.

Reasoning in one line: the exact movement that still pulls (push-off, longer strides) is what soccer primarily loads. A faint pull there, on a calf that's been recovering for two weeks, during a packed holiday week, is the textbook setup for turning a 2-week recovery into a 6-week one. The fact that you're asking for a conservative plan rather than just going is already the answer.

But if you genuinely want data instead of just defaulting, run the gates below. Any single fail = skip, no debate.

---

WARMUP DECISION TREE (run only if you mean it):

Gate 1 — at home, before you leave:
  - Walk downstairs normally, both legs.
  - 10 slow single-leg calf raises each side, body weight.
  - PASS=*** pull, equal both sides.
  - FAIL = any pull, or one side clearly different → SKIP.

Gate 2 — at the field, after 5 min easy walk/light jog:
  - 4 × 20m at ~60% (jog, not sprint). Note how the calf feels on each rep.
  - PASS=*** pull, equal bilaterally.
  - FAIL = pull on any rep → SKIP.

Gate 3 — at the field, after Gate 2:
  - 3 × 20m at ~80% with a longer stride, one push-off per rep.
  - PASS=*** pull, calf feels the same or looser than at end of Gate 2.
  - FAIL = pull, or any sharp/tight sensation → SKIP.

Only if all 3 gates pass: play, under the rules below.

---

RULES DURING PLAY (only if all 3 gates passed):
  - First 10–15 min: stay in low/mid intensity positions. Don't be the one sprinting onto every ball.
  - No max-effort sprints in the first 20 min total.
  - Re-check every ~15 min: does the calf still feel like it did at end of warmup? If any pull returns → off.

---

HARD STOP CONDITIONS (any one = off the field immediately, no negotiation):
  - Sharp or pinching pain (different from the dull pull you've had).
  - Pull that gets worse as you play, instead of staying flat or fading.
  - Tightness that limits normal stride length.
  - Compensating gait — you notice yourself limping or shifting weight.
  - The "just one more point" feeling. That is the trap. Off.

---

SHORT TEXTS (pick one based on the decision):

Skip entirely (Text A):
  "Hey — calf's still not 100%, sitting this one out. Have fun, save me a spot next week."

Downgrade — show up but don't play hard, or play 15 min and sub out (Text B):
  "Hey — calf's about 80%, want to play it safe this week. Can I come watch / sub in for 15? If not, next week for sure."

Both are short, don't invite a back-and-forth, and don't require you to explain the calf in detail. Send and move on.

SLIDE 2 — Five questions that make a handoff honest
────────────────────────────────────────
Presenter notes (one beat per bullet, slow down here — this is the teachable part):
  • What does the receiving team need to have *seen* before we call this a handoff? Not "do you have the ticket" — what have they actually walked through?
  • Which decision is still unmade that will block them mid-build? Get it in writing; not in a DM.
  • What's the smallest thing that, if it's wrong, makes everything after it wrong? That's the thing to validate first.
  • Who owns the answer when a blocker shows up two weeks in? Name a person, not a team.
  • Where will the unresolved list live, and who reads it Monday morning? Visibility beats resolution speed.

────────────────────────────────────────
SLIDE 3 — Readiness is a state you declare, not a vibe
────────────────────────────────────────
Presenter notes:
"Ready" should be a sentence you can say out loud: scope is locked, decisions are made or named, the receiving team has read it, the blocker list has an owner. If you can't say the sentence, it's not ready. Saying "not ready" in the room is the whole skill. The cost of an early "not yet" is one meeting. The cost of a late one is a rebuild.

────────────────────────────────────────
SLIDE 4 — The dashboard was a symptom, not the goal
────────────────────────────────────────
Presenter notes:
The dashboard existed because we didn't have a shared, current place to see unresolved blockers. It was a side effect of the handoff being undersupported. If your handoff already has a visible blocker list and named owners, you probably don't need the dashboard — and that's a good outcome, not a missing deliverable. Don't copy the artifact; copy the gap it filled.

────────────────────────────────────────
Presenter notes — say this part deliberately, don't rush:
My role was to keep the readiness conversation honest and keep the unresolved-blocker list accurate and visible. Engineering owned delivery. I did not coordinate implementation. Drawing that line cleanly is what makes the handoff land — if the receiving team thinks you also own the build, they stop raising blockers to you because they assume you already know.

Plan for Kibo's paw — keep it boring and consistent.

Tonight
  - Visual recheck with good light: each pad, the webbing between toes, around the nail beds, and the top of the paw. You're looking for a cut, a cracked pad, a dark speck wedged between toes, redness, or any swelling. Salt irritation usually shows as pinkness between the toes or on the pad edges.
  - Second rinse with lukewarm water, gentle. A quick wipe *between* each toe with a damp cloth catches grit the paw dip misses. Pat dry — damp paws in a cold apartment just keep the irritation going.
  - Walk to water and back: watch the first steps. A brief head-turn is curiosity; a repeated hitch or carrying the paw is a real sign.
  - Baseline note: eating normally, settling, no panting or restlessness. If he sleeps through the night, that's a strong "irritation, not injury" signal.

Tomorrow morning
  - Same 30-second visual before the leash goes on.
  - On the walk, watch the first block and any curb step. Front-clip harness + short leash is already the right rig; just keep him off the freshest salt lines where you can.
  - After the walk: rinse again, same routine. If the sidewalks are still heavily salted, smear a thin layer of paw balm or plain petroleum jelly on the pads and between the toes *before* the next outing — it keeps the salt off the skin. Booties are fine if he'll tolerate them; most Prospect Park dogs won't.
  - Licking check: a few licks at bedtime is normal grooming. Repeated licking that persists after the rinse, or licking that starts up the moment you stop watching, means the paw is bothering him.

Call the vet tonight or in the morning if you see any of these — these are the "don't wait" signs, not just "watch closer":
  - Visible cut, crack, bleeding, or a foreign body (grit, ice fragment) you can't easily wipe out.
  - Swelling, heat, or any discharge, especially between the toes.
  - Limping that lasts more than a handful of steps, gets worse through the walk, or shows up the next morning.
  - Refusing to put the paw down at all, or repeatedly holding it up.
  - Behavior change alongside the paw: stopped eating, panting, restless, snapping when you touch the paw.

If none of those show up and the licking fades after tonight's rinse + tomorrow's pre-walk balm, this was almost certainly salt irritation. That's the boring, expected outcome of a cold-snap walk on a Prospect Park curb.

One small thing worth doing regardless: note which block or curb he was on when you first noticed the licking. If it happens again on the same stretch, the salt mix on that block is harsher than the rest and you can route around it.

TOMORROW (Sun) — Bouldering Go/No-Go Plan
Default = no. "Yes" requires passing every gate below.

1. Morning check (at home, ~60-90 min before you'd leave)
   - Single-leg calf raises, both sides, 15 reps slow. Compare L vs R.
   - Single-leg hops in place, ~10 each side, low amplitude. Note sharp vs dull vs nothing.
   - Eccentric calf load: walk down a flight slowly, toe-heel, both sides.
   - 5 min brisk walk, then sit 10 min. Re-check calf: any tightness, grab, after-ache?
   - Gate: any sharp pain, asymmetric weakness, or after-ache = no-go, full stop.

2. Decision gate (after morning check)
   - All clear + no after-effects = lite session allowed.
   - Anything off = skip. Don't negotiate. Walking-fine is not the bar.

3. At-gym warmup (before any real attempt)
   - 8-10 min easy traverse on jugs, flat feet, no reach.
   - 2 easy problems, 2-3 grades below your normal flash, static-only footwork.
   - One slow downclimb off a low problem, controlled. (This IS the downclimb test.)
   - Gate: any guarded feeling, calf weaker than this morning, ankle hesitant = call it.

4. What to climb
   - Vertical or mild overhang, large positive feet, static movement.
   - Crimpy/techy with secure footholds (less calf-dominant).
   - Problems short enough you can downclimb carefully, not jump.

5. What to AVOID (hard list)
   - Dynos, deadpoints, dynamic lunges off the foot.
   - Steeps requiring big pull + push-off.
   - Slab with poor/small feet (precision push-off).
   - Anything you'd have to jump down from — even small.
   - Slopers needing micro foot-adjustments.
   - Highballs / sketchy falls. No "just one more go."

6. Hard stop conditions (any one = done)
   - Any sharp calf sensation, ever.
   - Calf feels tight, grabby, weaker, or "off" vs morning.
   - You catch yourself reaching for a dynamic move — auto-stop.
   - Cap: 3-4 problems total, ~30-40 min, then walk out.
   - 24-hr rule: nothing that leaves you worse by Monday.

7. Texts

Skip entirely (recommended default):
   "Sitting this one out — calf's flat-walk ok but I haven't tested push-off / dyno / jump / downclimb yet, and walking tolerance isn't the same as climbing tolerance. Rain check next week?"

Downgrade to lite (30 min, easy stuff, walk-out only):
   "In, but going lite — easy vertical only, no dynos or jump-downs, capped at 30. If anything feels off in the warmup I'm bailing."

Tell your friend the second one up front so the expectation is set before you arrive, not when you're tempted mid-session.

Bottom line first: you're at about four days out and Kibo is eating, drinking, and behaving normally. That's genuinely reassuring — most short ribbon pieces either pass through or declare themselves within the first 72 hours. The odds are now in your favor. A short watch window still makes sense, not because you're in a crisis, but because linear foreign bodies are the slow-burn category and you've already done the hard part by noticing.

WHAT TO ACTUALLY DO — NEXT 24–48 HOURS

  1. Normal meals, normal routine. Don't withhold food; don't switch to rich or unfamiliar stuff. His regular food is fine.
  2. When he poops, glance at it (glove or bag — you're not excavating). Looking for: the ribbon itself, bright red blood, black/tarry stool, or mucus.
  3. Once a day, a quick relaxed hands-on check of his belly while he's standing or lying on his side. You're feeling for a hard or distended loop, wincing when touched, or guarding (tensing the abdominal wall).
  4. Register his baseline energy and appetite at his normal rhythm — you already know him, so you don't need to obsess, just notice if something is genuinely off.

That's it. No hourly checks, no temperature taking, no forcing anything.

WHAT NOT TO DO

  - Do NOT induce vomiting. With linear objects this is worse than the original problem — a ribbon coming back up can lacerate the esophagus and mouth. Hydrogen peroxide without vet direction is a no.
  - Do NOT pull on a ribbon end if you ever see one dangling from his anus. One end can be anchored in the intestine; pulling can saw through tissue. Cut it short at the skin and call the vet.
  - Do NOT feed a giant bulky meal to "push it through." It can worsen a partial obstruction.
  - Do NOT add laxatives, fiber bombs, or supplements without talking to your vet.

RED FLAGS — VET OR URGENT CARE NOW

  - Repeated vomiting or dry heaving, especially if he can't keep water down
  - Refusing food for more than one meal when he'd normally take it
  - A real change in energy — withdrawn, won't get up, won't engage
  - Abdominal pain signs: "praying position" (front down, rear up, holding it), hunched/tucked posture, groaning when you touch his belly, or a visibly tense belly
  - Straining to poop with nothing coming out, or repeated unproductive squatting
  - Any blood in vomit or stool (bright red or black/tarry)
  - Sudden drooling or pawing at the mouth (could mean it's lodged in mouth or esophagus after all)
  - Restlessness — pacing, can't get comfortable, getting up and down

YELLOW FLAGS — CALL YOUR VET SAME DAY

  - One vomit, then back to normal (could be nothing; worth a quick call)
  - One bout of softer stool or diarrhea
  - Slight appetite dip for a single meal
  - Any behavior you're second-guessing

If in doubt, call. Vets would rather take a "false alarm" call than meet you at 2 a.m. with an obstruction. If your regular clinic is closed, the ER line will triage by phone.

ONE THING WORTH DOING TODAY

  Call your regular vet or send a portal message: "Four days ago he may have swallowed a 1–2 inch curling ribbon; currently asymptomatic, eating and drinking normally — anything you want me to do or watch for, given his size and history?" Most clinics will say "keep watching, here's what to look for, come in if X." It puts you on their radar if you do need to bring him in, and it gives you a number you've already touched today if things shift overnight.

Recommend running the 4-worker comparison. The 6-worker result only tells you that one specific config violates the memory budget — it doesn't characterize the scaling curve. Concluding "no value" from a single constrained-out data point is an inference, not an answer.

If 6 workers at 3x scaling bought 28s, 4 workers at 2x will probably land around 12-20s. Whether that's meaningful depends on your baseline (which you didn't share) — 15s on a 10-minute job is noise, 15s on a 2-minute job is real. But the question isn't really "is 4 better than 6" — it's "does any point on the curve fit both constraints?" 4 workers is the cheapest way to find out. Two data points (2-worker baseline + 4-worker if-it-fits) draws a line; one data point plus a violation doesn't.

Cost framing: this is a one-off benchmark on a representative replay, not a production change. The marginal expense of one more run should be low, and the downside of skipping is committing to a "no value" conclusion that might be off by ~15s and one config point. If 4 workers also blows the budget, you've cleanly confirmed the constraint is binding and the conclusion holds. If it fits, you have a real candidate.

One caveat where I'd reverse: if spinning up 4-worker is non-trivially more setup than 6 (custom config, manual coordination) AND the expected gain is bounded below ~10% of baseline, skip it. But for a routine benchmark run, just do it.

Verdict: 6-worker run fails the budget.

  Memory: 86% vs <75% ceiling → 11pp over (not borderline)
  Time:   14m12s vs 14m40s → 28s saved, ~3.2%
  Trade:  +18pp memory for ~3% time. Bad ratio.

2-worker is the only config that clears the gate. If cutting completion time matters, before raising worker count again:

  1. Sweep 3 and 4 workers — memory-vs-worker curve usually bends before 6; one intermediate data point tells you if 6 was overshoot or if the slope is genuinely steep.
  2. Profile what inflates at 6 — per-worker heap vs shared buffers vs shard-cache retention. That tells you whether more workers can ever be safe, or whether per-shard footprint has to come down first.
  3. Cut per-shard footprint before scaling workers. Otherwise you're trading a budget breach for a marginal win.

Recommend: hold at 2 workers; do a 3/4-worker pass and a memory profile before any 6-worker rerun. If 3/4 also busts 75%, the path forward is footprint reduction, not parallelism.

The current query won't run against histogram-only data — there's no `quantile="0.99"` label on the `_bucket` metric. Use `histogram_quantile()` over a rate of the bucket series:

    histogram_quantile(
      0.99,
      sum by (route, le) (
        rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="metrics-router", source="live"}[5m])
      )
    )

Two things that matter here:

1. `le` must stay in the `by` clause. `histogram_quantile()` interpolates across the bucket boundary set, so stripping `le` before it gets called silently breaks the result (you'll get either NaN or a nonsense value). `route` stays because it's the required grouping.

2. `sum by (route, le) (...)` before `histogram_quantile()` is the statistically correct shape — it aggregates the bucket counts across all other dimensions (instance/pod/etc.) first, then interpolates the quantile on the combined distribution. The original `avg by (route)` pattern was actually wrong even when the summary metric existed: averaging per-series quantiles is not the same as the quantile of the aggregate. So this rewrite isn't just a compatibility fix, it's a correctness improvement.

Notes on the rest of the panel:
- Window matches your `[5m]` rate range. If the panel's display step is coarser than the rate window (e.g. 1m points from a 5m rate), that's fine — just keep them consistent if you tune later.
- `source="live"` filter is preserved; mirror/replay traffic stays excluded from the release panel.
- No alert wiring touched, per your scope note.

Invalid pattern (the panel averages the `quantile` value, which is the bug):
```
avg by (job) (<metric_name>{quantile="0.99"})
```

Why averaging per-instance summary quantiles is invalid:
A Prometheus `Summary`'s `quantile` value is computed per-instance over a local sliding window — each value is an estimate with its own error. Averaging those estimates doesn't produce a percentile, a mean, or a max of the merged stream; it yields a number with no statistical meaning, and it consistently understates tail latency.

Corrected query — requires the metric to be a `Histogram` (summaries cannot be aggregated correctly, period):
```
histogram_quantile(
  0.99,
  sum by (le) (rate(<metric_name>_bucket[5m]))
)
```

If the underlying metric is still a `Summary` and migration isn't on the table, the panel must not call its output "p99". Acceptable interim options: plot per-instance p99 lines each labeled with its instance, or show `max by (job) (<metric_name>{quantile="0.99"})` and relabel the panel as a worst-case envelope.

Hi Yuki —

Thanks for running the benchmark and putting the memory number on the table. I want to be clear that I'm not arguing with the memory result; I'm arguing that the benchmark doesn't yet cover the case the dedup window is actually responsible for holding, so the two numbers shouldn't be weighed against each other as if they were comparable.

**The two numbers are answering different questions.**
- 5 min vs 15 min on memory is a measurement of how long a stale dedup key stays resident in the staging dedup store. That's real, and it's the only thing the benchmark shows.
- 15 min vs 5 min on safety is a measurement of whether a legitimate retry that arrived after the dedup window expired gets processed or silently dropped. The benchmark as described doesn't measure that.

**Why 5 min is unsafe by default, not by suspicion.**
A retry-dedup window has to be longer than the worst-case legitimate retry gap, not the median one. The median of the sample can show clean arrivals under 5 min while the tail — slow network paths, queued retries behind a transient exporter flush stall, retries that piggyback on the next periodic flush — sits out beyond it. Those tail retries aren't noise; they're the ones the dedup window is *for*, and dropping them is the failure mode the window exists to prevent. Cutting the window without seeing the tail is the same shape of mistake as cutting a timeout below p99 latency.

**What I need before revisiting 15 → 5:**
1. The full retry-gap distribution from prod, not just the staging sample — at minimum p50, p95, p99, p99.9 and the count of retries arriving after each of 1m, 2m, 5m, 10m, 15m. If the prod p99.9 is comfortably under 5 min, the conversation changes.

Thresholds for the jitter rerun (100 clients, injected 503, full jitter [0, 2s]):

1. Peak concurrent retries: ≤ 20 in any 100ms window. The fixed-1s baseline shows ~100 retries piling on the same tick; we need ≥5x reduction to actually call it smoothed. Anything in the 20–50 range is partial — the herd is still showing up, just shorter.

2. Staging p99: no regression. Preferred absolute: p99 ≤ 2.5s end-to-end per client (one retry cycle fits inside the 2s jitter window plus a small processing budget). If you have a fresh fixed-retry baseline from this same run, also require p99_jitter ≤ p99_fixed — the absolute bound is the floor, the relative bound is the proof.

3. Completion-time tradeoff: jitter adds per-client wait, so don't let it get hidden as batch cost.
   - Total batch wall-clock (time when the 100th client finishes) ≤ 0.8x the fixed-retry baseline. This is the headline smoothing win — fewer cycles, last finisher comes in sooner.
   - Per-client tolerated regression vs fixed-retry baseline: median +0.5s, p99 +1.0s. Beyond that, jitter is buying headroom by stealing latency we shouldn't quietly accept.

4. Data integrity: zero tolerance. All 100 points accepted exactly once. Any drop or duplicate-accept fails the run outright, regardless of how clean the retry curve looks — a beautiful sawtooth with lost points is not a win.

Pass = all four. If any single metric is ambiguous (e.g., baseline p99 wasn't captured cleanly), default to fail and rerun rather than declaring smoothing from a partial result. Solo-safe per the staging rollback-drill scope, so this can run without pairing.

Your diagnosis matches the data: 94/100 retrying together with a fixed delay is the synchronization signature, not a coincidence. p99 of 470ms on the success path means the service itself is healthy - the sawtooth is purely a client-side retry pileup, and 0 dropped / 0 dup-accepted confirms nothing is actually failing under load, just bunching.

Full jitter 0–2s is a reasonable rerun. Expected shift: those 94 concurrent retries spread roughly uniformly across the 2s window, so peak concurrent retries drops to ~45–50 (Poisson-ish) and the sawtooth flattens into a low-amplitude ripple. Same harness, same 503 injection - apples to apples.

Two things worth deciding before the rerun:

1. Upper bound of 2s: worst-case a retried point lands ~2s + 470ms ≈ 2.5s after the original attempt. Is that inside the ingest-edge tail SLO? If we're tight, equal jitter (0.5–1.5s) gives less smoothing but bounds the added latency harder. Full jitter is the better de-sync tool; equal jitter is the better latency-bounded tool. Pick based on which axis the SLO cares about more.

2. Worth instrumenting the rerun for max-window concurrent retries (not just peak instant) - that tells you the actual herd footprint, which is what the canary review will want to see when this becomes a rollout case.

Here's a compact rubric. Designed to be read off in 30 seconds during the interview and to fit on one page if you print it. No trivia scoring, no "correct architecture" assumption — only how the candidate reasons under the constraints you've named.

================================================================
45-MIN PLATFORM SYSTEMS INTERVIEW RUBRIC
Multi-tenant metrics ingestion under bursty load
================================================================

OPENING FRAME (state verbatim, ~2 min)
"There is no canonical architecture. I'm scoring how you reason
through load, fairness, and ownership — not whether you pick a
specific stack. Take the first few minutes to ask clarifying
questions before you sketch."

TIME BUDGET
  ~5 min  clarify requirements
 ~25 min  design walk-through (interrupt with questions, fine)
  ~5 min  rollout / observability / ownership
  ~5 min  candidate questions

SCORING BANDS (use the same four across every dimension)
  Strong     — names the constraint, proposes a concrete
               mechanism, and identifies a failure mode the
               mechanism does NOT solve.
  Adequate   — addresses the constraint with a workable
               mechanism but leaves a failure mode implicit.
  Weak       — names the constraint without a mechanism, or
               proposes a mechanism that ignores the constraint.
  Not raised — fine if the dimension is genuinely irrelevant
               to their design; never a default penalty.

DO NOT SCORE
  Language or framework recall.
  Naming a specific product unless they picked it as their
  choice and can defend it.
  Speaking style, pace, or confidence.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. REQUIREMENT CLARIFICATION
----------------------------------------------------------------
  Signal
    - Asks about tenant count and skew before sizing anything.
    - Asks about SLOs: write success, end-to-end freshness,
      query latency, retention.
    - Asks about read patterns (who queries, how often,
      per-tenant vs aggregate).
    - Asks about the failure-domain boundary: per-tenant
      isolation target, blast radius of a bad tenant.
    - Asks about cost ceiling (storage, egress, compute).
  Anti-signal
    - Opens with a diagram or a stack list.
    - Treats "multi-tenant" as one uniform tier.
    - Skips straight to "we'd use Kafka" without numbers.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. BOUNDED BACKPRESSURE
----------------------------------------------------------------
  Signal
    - Distinguishes queue depth, memory pressure, and
      downstream service rate as separate limits.
    - Names what gets shed first (samples vs whole tenants
      vs oldest-N-per-tenant) and the boundary it sheds at.
    - Gives the receiver a way to signal the sender
      (credit-based, RPC backpressure, 429 with budget).
    - States the bounded-resource budget, not "we'll scale."
  Anti-signal
    - "Just add a bigger queue."
    - Unbounded buffers anywhere in the path.
    - No shedding policy, or shedding that's silently lossy
      without the sender knowing.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. TENANT FAIRNESS
----------------------------------------------------------------
  Signal
    - Per-tenant budget (rate, bytes, cardinality) named
      explicitly, with an enforcement point.
    - Defines the degraded mode when a tenant exceeds budget
      (degrade quality, isolate, shed) and what other tenants
      experience during that.
    - Acknowledges that full isolation has a cost and picks
      a point on the curve.
  Anti-signal
    - "We'll rate-limit per tenant" with no budget, no
      enforcement point, no degraded mode.
    - Noisy-neighbor treated as a config knob, not a design
      constraint.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. IDEMPOTENCY
----------------------------------------------------------------
  Signal
    - Names the unit of dedup: request / sample / series-write.
    - Defines the key shape, the dedup window, and where it
      lives (sender, broker, storage).
    - Addresses retry, partial failure, and split-brain
      between ingest path and storage path.
    - Names the storage cost of dedup state.
  Anti-signal

Q1 — design-vs-engineering ownership after a component enters the codebase:

What it reveals is whether "design owns the system" stops being true the moment code gets written. Three signals worth listening for in the answer:

  - Is there a documented contribution model — PR template, code owners on the lib repo, design review required on contributions — or is it "we just talk about it"?
  - Does design retain approval rights on *changes* after the first version, or only on the initial build? If design can't veto the fifth refactor, the system is engineering's in practice even if the org chart says otherwise.
  - Who signs off "done" — design, engineering, or both in a defined order? "Engineering, with design notified" is drift waiting to happen.

Q2 — exception documentation and removal ownership:

This is the harder question and the real maturity test. Most orgs can answer Q1 cleanly. Far fewer can answer Q2. Listen for:

  - Is the exception tracked somewhere durable (ticket with link, code comment referencing ticket, design-spec annotation) or is it folklore? Folklore exceptions become permanent.
  - Does removal have a *named* owner, and is it the original feature team or a design-system steward? Original-team-owns-removal almost never works (people rotate off). A steward who owns cleanup is the healthier model.
  - Is there a sunset trigger — "remove when X lands," "remove by Q3" — or is it "we'll get to it"? The latter is a debt time bomb.
  - Does design have approval on the exception itself, or can engineering ship one under deadline pressure without check? If engineering self-approves, the system will quietly fragment.

Read together: clean answers to both = real design-system practice. Q1 clean + Q2 hand-wavy = slow drift toward entropy — exceptions will accumulate with no cleanup loop. Both vague = the "design system" is probably a folder of components, not a system.
