Both positions captured. The wording problem is real: the current draft elides two distinct durability boundaries under a uniform "2xx is success" framing, which leaks the retry contract between services.

Proposed replacement language for the cross-service retry-invariant section:

    A 2xx response indicates that the caller may stop retrying only
    against the durability boundary owned by the responding service.
    The two services in scope acknowledge at different points, and
    treating either 2xx as a uniform durability signal is incorrect.

      - ingest-edge: returns 2xx after the batch is durably appended
        to the local WAL. Downstream processing may still be pending
        at that point. WAL retention and replay are operated by the
        ingest-edge owner.

      - rollup-service: returns 2xx only after the aggregate is
        committed to durable object storage. Work before that commit
        point remains retryable. Commit behavior and retry handling
        are operated by the rollup-service owner.

    The cross-service invariant is not "a 2xx means the same thing
    everywhere." It is: the caller's retry obligation ends at the
    durability boundary the responding service owns, and not before.

Three things this version does that the current draft doesn't:

  1. Names the durability boundary as the unit of correctness, not the
     status code.
  2. Keeps owner scope explicit on each side (WAL/replay vs.
     commit/retry), so no one reads the invariant as authorizing
     cross-boundary retry behavior.
  3. Reframes the invariant as an end-of-obligation statement, which
     is what retry logic actually consumes.

One-sentence version of the open problem, if you want it for your notes: the draft treats 2xx as a single durability signal, but ingest-edge's 2xx is a WAL-append guarantee and rollup-service's 2xx is a committed-aggregate guarantee — those are not interchangeable, and the cross-service language has to say so.

  - Can't keep water down — if sipping water reliably triggers vomiting, that's a real red flag (persistent nausea or something more going on).

  - Any new diarrhea, especially if it's bloody, black/tarry, or watery and frequent.
  - You find evidence he got into something — medication (human or pet), chocolate, grapes/raisins, xylitol (gum, peanut butter, baked goods), trash, bones, cooked bones, socks, small toys, ribbon/string, or anything else he shouldn't have.

  - A short phone video of any concerning behavior (retching, gait, posture) is genuinely useful if you end up calling.
  - Trust your read of him. You know his normal; if something feels off even before a checklist item is triggered, a call is the right move.

Here's a compact invariant paragraph that captures the agreement without naming either service or pinning specific status codes:

  A service that accepts input before its durability boundary must report pending state on success, not committed completion. Success is returned only after the write has crossed that service's durability boundary. Failures occurring before the boundary are retryable, and each service must make its supported retry horizon discoverable to clients.

It encodes the four points in order — pre-boundary success signals pending, post-boundary success means crossed, pre-boundary failures are retryable, and the retry horizon is a discoverable contract — while leaving each service free to choose how it expresses "pending" (202 vs other) and how it advertises the horizon (header, documented contract, etc.).

Yogurt sauce first — it benefits from sitting while everything else cooks. Then chickpeas carry the timing, and pita warms at the very end.

YOGURT SAUCE (make first, 5 min)
  1 cup Greek yogurt
  1 small garlic clove, grated on a microplane (or minced very fine)
  Juice of half the lemon
  Pinch of salt
  Drizzle of olive oil
  Pinch of smoked paprika on top
  Stir, taste, adjust salt/lemon. Cover and leave on the counter.

SKILLET (30 min total, one pan)
  1. Heat 3 tbsp olive oil over medium heat. Add 3 sliced garlic cloves, cook 30-60 sec until fragrant, don't brown.
  2. Drain and rinse both cans of chickpeas. Pat dry with a towel — drier = better crust.
  3. Add chickpeas to the skillet with 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp smoked paprika. Stir to coat.
  4. Cook 12-15 min, stirring every few minutes, until chickpeas are golden and a few are popping/crisping on the outside. Salt lightly partway through.
  5. Halve a generous cup of cherry tomatoes while chickpeas cook. Add them in around minute 10, stir, let them burst and release juice.
  6. Add a few big handfuls of spinach at minute 13-14. Stir until just wilted, 60-90 sec. Pull off heat. Squeeze the other lemon half over the top.

PITA (last 3-5 min)
  Right before serving: stack pitas, wrap in a slightly damp towel, microwave 60-90 sec. Or warm directly over a gas burner with tongs, 20 sec per side. Cut into wedges.

PLATE
  Pile chickpeas in a bowl or on a plate, tuck pita around the side, spoon yogurt sauce over or serve alongside for dipping. A pinch of smoked paprika on the yogurt if you want it pretty.

Order of operations recap: sauce → chickpeas alone → tomatoes → spinach → pita → eat. The sauce rests the whole cook, the pita lands when the chickpeas do, and the greens go in last so they don't overcook while you finish plating.

The rejection pattern points to clock skew on that one collector host, not a problem with shared ingest-edge. The ~11m42s offset matches a host clock running that far ahead of real time — ingest rejects samples whose timestamps fall outside the accepted time window, which is why that host's batches fail while the others pass. Since your other collectors are ingesting normally and our shared ingest-edge metrics (error rate, latency, queue depth) are clean, the issue is isolated to that host's clock, not the ingest path.

Before sending more samples, please correct time synchronization on that host (NTP, chrony, or your platform's equivalent) and confirm the host clock is within a few seconds of real time. Once it's corrected, verify recovery by sending a small test batch and checking that:

  - the sample timestamps in the collector's logs match the actual send time (no longer in the future),
  - those samples are accepted by ingest without rejection, and
  - the host's clock offset against your reference time source is stable and near zero.

One thing to avoid: don't rewrite sample timestamps to mask the skew. That hides the underlying problem and breaks time-series ordering — the fix is the clock, not the data. If you resync and rejections continue, send us the host's time-sync status and we'll look further into the configuration.

---

Covers: diagnosis (clock-skew on the one host, ingest healthy), the fix (correct time sync before more sends), three concrete verification steps, and an explicit "don't rewrite timestamps" with the practical reason. Length is roughly one screen — concise but gives the customer enough to act without a back-and-forth.

Diagnosis: single-host clock skew (+11:42). That is the cause of the rejection — the sample timestamp is genuinely ahead of true wall clock by ~12 minutes, which trips whatever forward-tolerance window ingest-edge enforces. Other hosts normal, ingest-edge normal: confirms it's host-local, not a service bug.

First action — fix the clock on that host, not the timestamps.

Why "fix the clock" beats "rewrite timestamps":

  - Rewriting collector-side timestamps silently shifts samples away from their true wall-clock association. Any cross-host join, aggregation, or freshness check on those samples now lies. You trade a visible ingest rejection for invisible data corruption.
  - It also masks the root cause. A drift of +11:42 on one host is not random jitter — something changed for that host (chrony source loss, NTP reachability, a VM migration, a stale hwclock). If you paper over it, the same drift comes back on the next sampling interval and you fight it again.
  - The forward-tolerance window on ingest-edge is a safety check, not a knob to negotiate with. Working around it in the collector means the safety check is no longer doing its job for any host that drifts.

Concrete sequence for the affected host:

  1. Quarantine: stop the collector process (or drop its traffic at the load balancer) so it stops emitting more rejected samples. One host, cheap to isolate.
  2. Inspect time sync: `chronyc tracking` / `chronyc sources` / `ntpq -p`. Confirm the upstream source state, last reach, offset, stratum. Note the root cause (source unreachable? huge offset step refused by slewing?).
  3. Force a step if needed: `chronyc makestep` after verifying the upstream is healthy, or restart chrony against a known-good source. Do not run makestep if the upstream is itself wrong — fix the source first.
  4. Confirm: host clock within tolerance (sub-second vs. true time), then re-enable the collector.
  5. Verify at ingest-edge: error rate for that host's sample stream returns to baseline, rejection counter stops incrementing.

After it's back: audit the gap window. The samples that *were* rejected can be replayed from the collector's local buffer with the corrected clock — they were never written, so you are not "rewriting," you are re-emitting with accurate timestamps. Do not bulk-edit already-stored samples.

One follow-up worth filing regardless: why did only this host drift? If chrony is the configured path on all collectors, a single-host drift usually points at something local (network path, VM clock source, firewall rule on NTP egress). Worth a runbook note so the next on-call doesn't re-debug it from scratch.

Staging, 128/128 shards restored, three manifests flagged on checksum, nothing touching prod. Goal is to rerun the rehearsal against the real cause, not papering over the symptom. Three hypotheses to disambiguate, in the order that gets you to a decision fastest.

1. Recompute-from-bytes on the three failing manifests. Pair: you run, Wes observes and records, no manifest writes.
   - Pull the raw restored bytes for each manifest, recompute the checksum using the verifier's library, and compare against the stored checksum on the manifest.
   - If recomputed == stored: bytes are intact, ruling out an actual restore defect (C is out). Whatever's wrong is in how the checksum got recorded — proceed to step 2.
   - If recomputed != stored but bytes match the expected manifest content: either the stored checksum was computed under a different library version (B) or it was never regenerated when fixtures moved (A). Step 2 disambiguates.
   - If recomputed != stored and bytes don't match expected content: real restore defect (C confirmed). Stop. Do not repair the manifests. Page the restore-path owner, engage Cyrus-team backup, treat this as a real defect signal, not a fixture problem.

2. Diff the checksum-library version between writer and verifier. You can run this solo; it's read-only against images and lockfiles.
   - Compactor image's checksum-lib version vs verifier image's version. If they differ, that's B — pin both to the same version and rerun verification only, not the full rehearsal. If they match, B is out.

3. Check fixture provenance for the three manifests. Solo is fine.
   - For each failing manifest: fixture generation timestamp, which checksum-algo version produced the recorded checksum, and whether a known library bump post-dates the fixture. If all three predate the bump and step 2 showed no skew, that's A — regenerate fixtures from the current producer, then rerun the rehearsal cleanly.

Why this order: step 1 is the single test that separates "the system thinks the bytes are wrong" from "the bytes actually are wrong," and everything downstream depends on knowing which world you're in. Step 2 is a binary config diff that cheaply picks B out of {A, B}. Step 3 only matters once C is gone and B is either gone or fixed.

Rerun gate: only proceed to a full rerun after step 1 has ruled out C. If step 1 lands on C, there is no rerun yet — there's an incident.

Reading this as engineer-flavored prep (not a script to memorize):

BOUNDING THE EXCEPTION

Three axes, all named up front:
- Scope: which component(s), which states, which props. Anything not in the contract is out. If you can't write a failing test for "outside this scope," it isn't bounded.
- Time: pinned to the deadline + a named review trigger (DS PR lands, product sunset, quarter boundary — pick one, don't leave it open).
- Contract: intended behavior and states documented once, in one place, design-signed. Eng implements the contract; they don't redefine it.

The interviewer's trap on this one is letting "scope" become "this general area." Force it down to: name the props, name the states, name the trigger.

DOCUMENTING OWNERSHIP

"Owns" splits cleanly:
- Design owns the spec — intent, states, acceptance criteria, the *what* and *why*.
- Eng owns the implementation and tests — the *how*, the bugs, the test coverage.
- One artifact. Pick: exception register entry, ADRFC, or a header section in the component README. It links spec → impl → known gap → retirement trigger. Don't scatter this across Slack threads.
- One named approver per side, named at filing time. Not "the design team." A person who has the call when a state is ambiguous.
- One line in the doc that matters most: "Do not extend without refiling." Exceptions drift by default; that line is the only thing that stops it.

The usual failure mode: ownership gets blurred when eng starts making spec calls under deadline pressure, or design starts dictating implementation. The doc makes the seam explicit.

RETIREMENT

Named at creation, in the same doc. Three legitimate triggers:
1. DS ships the supported behavior
2. The product need disappears (feature sunset, pivot)
3. Calendar-certain (launch + 90 days, end of quarter, whatever)

Default state: not auto-extended. At each review, someone actively chooses to renew, or it retires. Owner of the retirement work is named at creation, not at sunset — last-minute handoffs are where exceptions live forever.

WHAT THEY'LL PROBE

- "Eng pushes back on retirement timing" → answer is: the doc named the trigger; the conversation is about the trigger, not the work.
- "A third use case shows up" → it's a new exception, filed separately. Don't retrofit the first one.
- "Design and eng disagree on a state mid-build" → spec owner decides; eng's job is to implement what's specified, not relitigate.

Verdict: don't ship as-is. This will page on routine deploy churn and re-purposes a metric the owning side already classified as validation-only. The underlying concern (a build the router can't classify is in production) is real, but this expression doesn't catch it — it catches config-reload noise.

On the four gaps you flagged:

  1. No user-impact condition. `build_channel="unknown"` is a closed-set legitimate value, not corruption. It appears during canary rollouts, fresh deploys before the channel tag is set, and internal/dogfood builds. None of those are user-impact events by themselves. The right user-impact condition is *unknown-channel traffic being served with non-trivial share*, e.g.
     sum(rate(router_request_total{build_channel="unknown"}[5m]))
       / sum(rate(router_request_total[5m])) > 0.01
     not a reload counter.

  2. No expected baseline. Steady-state yes, ~0. During any canary rollout or config push that touches channel classification, non-zero is the *expected* baseline. `for: 5m` with no carve-out for active deploy windows fires on routine work. Either gate by "no active rollup tag / no in-flight canary," or extend `for:` to 30m so it catches stuck states only, not transitional ones.

  3. No severity rationale. `platform-page` is a page. Blast radius of an `unknown` config reload with no traffic context is near-zero. If the actual worry is "an unknown build might be routing live traffic incorrectly," page on the *served-traffic* metric (#1), not the reload counter, and the runbook should describe how to identify and roll back. If the worry is just "something in the pipeline isn't labeled," that's a warn or Slack-notify, not a page.

  4. No responder runbook action. First thing the on-call will do is check whether a deploy is in flight. If "is there a deploy?" is the right first action, the alert is detecting the deploy, not the incident. The runbook should answer: what does the responder *change*? If the answer is "nothing, file a ticket for Nadia," that's not a page.

Reframe: if the real concern is "a build is in prod that the router can't classify," the alert that catches it is on `router_request_total{build_channel="unknown"}` share above threshold during a quiet window (no active rollup tag, no in-flight canary), warn at >1%, page only at >10% sustained, runbook = identify source host/build via the `source` label, page the deploy owner to confirm or roll back. That preserves Nadia's validation-panel use of `router_config_reload_total` and points the paging signal at the metric that actually maps to user-facing risk.

The 415s line up with the encoding change in SDK 4.7.1, not with anything on the ingest side. Our remote-write endpoint advertises gzip and snappy; it does not accept zstd. If 4.7.1 changed the default compression on upgrade, every request gets rejected before the body is parsed.

What to change:

One operational note worth pinning in the retest plan: when you re-run, also verify the canary's histogram buckets are an exact superset/subset match against stable before reading the number — just having "both emit histograms" isn't enough, the bucket *boundaries* have to match for the merged `le` series to aggregate correctly through `histogram_quantile`.

Diagnosis is right — that's a real bug, and the comparison numbers can't be trusted as shown.

Why the query is wrong

`sum by (le, route)` drops `build_channel`. When stable has a bucket at `le=500` and canary has none, the combined series carries only stable's count at `le=500`. When canary has a bucket at `le=750` and stable has none, the combined series carries only canary's count at `le=750`. The resulting "histogram" interleaves the two boundary sets as if they were the same axis.

`histogram_quantile` then does linear interpolation assuming the buckets are contiguous on a shared axis. With stable's last sub-500 bucket being 500 and canary's first post-250 bucket being 750, the function sees:

  combined(le=250)  = stable + canary  (counts ≤ 250ms on both)
  combined(le=500)  = stable only       (canary contributes 0 — wrong)
  combined(le=750)  = canary only       (stable contributes 0 — wrong)
  combined(le=1000) = stable + canary

Between 500 and 750, the combined bucket jump is interpreted as "lots of requests landed in 500–750ms" — but in reality all of that mass is canary and stable has *no* bucket there at all. The interpolation produces a number that is neither stable's p99 nor canary's.

The canary's actual p99 is almost certainly not 740ms — that value lives at the broken-query artifact layer, not the canary-isolated quantile. The 410ms stable figure looks more plausible because stable's bucket layout happens to match the implied axis better at the p99 region, but it's still computed off a series that has been polluted by canary's le=750 and le=1000 mass.

Fix

Preserve `build_channel` in the `by` clause:

  histogram_quantile(
    0.99,
    sum by (le, route, build_channel) (
      rate(router_request_duration_ms_bucket[5m])
    )
  )

`histogram_quantile` will then be evaluated per build_channel, against each channel's own bucket layout. That gives you an honest stable p99 and an honest canary p99.

Recommendation before any release call

Don't act on the 740ms figure. Re-run with `build_channel` preserved, then compare. If the corrected canary p99 still lands in the 500–750ms range and stable is genuinely near 410ms, the regression is real and the bucket-boundary mismatch is a separate issue (likely an exporter change in the canary build). If it drops back into the 250–500ms band, the release panel was lying and the canary is fine.

Worth a follow-up either way: the fact that the two histogram layouts differ at all means the canary build is exporting a different bucket definition than stable. That's its own debugging thread — could be a default-config drift, a feature flag, or a build-time override. Worth pinning before this comparison gets re-run next release.

1. PROBE: "Did engineering build it as designed, or what changed?"

   - State the design intent in one line (what it was meant to do for the user).
   - Name what was handed off (spec, states, tolerances, edge-case behavior).
   - Defer the engineering confirmation: "engineering confirmed the build lands within X" or "I can't speak to the exact implementation, but what I specified was Y."
   The line: she owns intent and handoff, not the build.

2. PROBE: "What did engineering push back on, and how did you resolve it?"
   What they're testing: whether she was a real collaborator in the handoff, not a designer who threw specs over the wall.
   Structure:
   - Name one real friction point in user-impact terms (e.g., "the loading state went from skeleton to inline because the data window was too tight").
   - What was preserved from the design intent.
   - What was traded or deferred, framed as collaborative — not as her making engineering calls.
   If she wasn't in the loop on the negotiation, say so once and move on: "I wasn't in the engineering conversations directly, but the design rationale was X and the team landed on Y." Honest, not weak.

3. PROBE: "Where will this break, or what would you want engineering to follow up on?"
   What they're testing: system thinking and whether she understands the design's limits.
   Structure:
   - Name the failure mode in user terms, not stack terms ("if the network is slow, the user sees a half-loaded state").
   - What the design does about it (state, fallback, microcopy).
   - What she'd want engineering to look at next — framed as a follow-up, not a guarantee she made.
   The line: behavioral intent and known limits, not engineering decisions.

General line to hold across all three:
- "Designed for" / "the design intent was" / "what I specified" = her side.
- "Engineering confirmed" / "engineering can speak to" = their side.
- If a probe lands in pure engineering territory (timing guarantees, framework choice, performance budgets), one honest redirect is fine: "That's an engineering call — I can describe what the design needed, but the implementation details aren't mine."

Here's the prep, written as conversational notes rather than a deck. The throughline I'd hold across all three areas: convergence is a decision-making discipline, not a structural one. Whoever decides, on what evidence, with what visibility — that's the actual topic.

---

**Opening (~3 min)**

The three areas aren't separate. They're one question with three faces: how do we converge a set of local variants without losing what each one earned, and how do we keep the convergence honest once it ships? The component work, the sequencing shifts, and the temporary exceptions are all instances of the same underlying question — who's deciding, on what evidence, with what visibility.

Two things I want to set up front. First, all three of us see different surfaces of the same system. The design director sees intent and user need. The engineering manager sees feasibility, sequencing, and team load. I see both, plus the operational surface that doesn't always make it into either view. The value of this conversation is that all three vantage points get stress-tested, not that we each defend our own. Second, none of this works as one-discipline work. If the design director's call on user need is something I have to reconstruct from telemetry, we've already lost. If the engineering manager's call on team load is something I have to infer from the code, we've already lost.

---

**Area 1: Variants toward a shared component (~15 min)**

The first move I'd push back on is starting from the component. Starting from the component makes the conversation about structure, and structure is the easiest thing to argue about and the hardest thing to verify. Start from the contract: what does the user need this thing to do, and what observable behaviors does each variant deliver today?

Before I draw a component diagram, I want three artifacts in front of us.

A behavior map. Not features, behaviors. "On submit, if X, then Y." Across every variant. Where the same intent shows up with different mechanics, that's candidate commonality. Where different intents show up with the same mechanic, that's a coincidence, not a pattern. The second one is the trap — it looks like convergence but isn't.

An exception ledger. Every place a variant deviates from the others, with a reason and a name. "We do this because regulatory in EU." "We do this because the legacy data shape forces it." "We do this because the original PM asked and nobody said no." The last category is the one that needs a defender in the room. If nobody can defend it, it doesn't migrate.

A usage profile. Telemetry on what people actually do, not what they were intended to do. A variant's most-touched code path is its most-defended, regardless of whether that path is what we'd choose to keep.

The exception ledger is the part most teams skip and then regret. If you migrate without cataloging exceptions, you either smuggle them in via config flags — and you've just built the old system in a new shape — or you drop them, and you've broken someone. Neither is OK. The ledger forces the conversation: is this exception still earning its keep?

On sequencing: I'd start with the variant that has the lowest user-facing risk and exercises the most of the common contract. Not the highest-traffic one. The one that, if it goes wrong, hurts the fewest people and teaches us the most. Highest-traffic migrations become easy once a low-risk migration has flushed out the assumptions baked into the contract.

Cutover pattern: dual-render behind a flag, then three classes of parity check before flipping default. Visual diff. Behavioral diff — same inputs produce same outputs. Telemetry diff — no error rate, no perf regression, no support-ticket movement. All three. Visual-only is how you ship a regression dressed as a refactor.

The piece I want the design director's read on: which of the existing exceptions are you willing to defend as user need, and which are you willing to let retire? That's not an engineering question and I shouldn't be the one to answer it. The piece I want the engineering manager's read on: which variant can the team actually stand up behind a flag without losing velocity on the next commitment? That's a load question, not a code question.

---

**Area 2: Feasibility shifts the sequence (~12 min)**

The mental move that helps here is to separate intent from sequence. The intent is the user outcome and the design language. The sequence is the order we land things. Feasibility changes sequence. It shouldn't change intent without an explicit conversation, and it shouldn't change intent silently.

When feasibility pushes back — and it will, every time — the question isn't "what do we cut." It's three questions:

1. What's the smallest core that delivers the intended outcome in this slice?
2. What does that leave for later slices, and is the later slice still coherent, or does it quietly become something else?
3. Are we revising the sequence, or are we discovering that the original sequence assumed something about the system that isn't true?

The third one is the question we underweight. A feasibility shift is information about the design. Sometimes the right answer is to revise the intent — to discover that two things we thought were independent are actually coupled, or that a state we thought was transient turns out to be permanent. That's not a failure of the original plan, that's learning. The failure mode is noticing it six weeks late.

The conversation I want to have with the engineering manager: when you bring me a feasibility constraint, bring it with the dependency it implies, not just the date. "We can't ship A by Q2 because B is still in flight and B blocks the shared component A needs" is more useful than "A is at risk." The first lets me re-route. The second just makes me anxious and doesn't change the picture.

The conversation I want to have with the design director: when the sequence shifts, here's what stays safe (the intent), here's what changes shape (the path to the intent), and here's what we don't yet know. The thing I don't want is to discover six weeks into a shifted sequence that the design assumed an ordering we've already passed. Surface the assumption early, surface it again when it changes.

One pattern that helps on my side: build the plan as a dependency graph with named blockers, not as a timeline. Timelines lie about what's possible — they make independent things look sequential and coupled things look parallel. A dependency graph lets you re-route when one node slips. When the engineering manager and I are looking at the same dependency graph, we can argue about the same thing.

---

**Area 3: Temporary exceptions (~12 min)**

The reason this matters operationally: temporary exceptions are how systems rot. Not because the exception is wrong, but because nobody decided it was right. It just kept being there.

Evidence for "standardize or retire":

- Usage telemetry. Is anyone using it, and if so, who, and for what? A temporary exception with no usage is a retirement waiting for paperwork.
- Cost. Maintenance load, support tickets, on-call pages, cognitive load for new engineers reading the code. An exception that costs more than it returns is already retired in everything but name.
- Alternative. Is the new world good enough that nobody would choose the old behavior given the choice? If yes, retire. If no, the new world isn't done — the exception is doing work the new system isn't.
- Original reason. Is the constraint it worked around still true? Sometimes the constraint is gone and nobody noticed.

The decision is rarely binary. It's usually "keep with a sunset," "rebuild properly in the new system," or "retire." The middle option is the dangerous one if it doesn't come with a date.

Ownership needs three properties. It's a name, not a team — "the platform team owns it" is not ownership, it's a hint. The named person has authority to deprecate — they can pull the trigger without escalating to a committee. The named person has on-call context for the blast radius — if the exception breaks at 2am, the owner is the one who understands why.

Visibility: every temporary exception lives in the runbook with its owner, its introduction date, its review date, and the evidence that will be on the table at review. The review date is the load-bearing piece. Without it, "temporary" means "permanent until someone gets tired."

The piece I want this conversation to actually land: design and engineering agree, before the exception ships, on the review date and what evidence will be on the table. Bake it into the shipping decision, not the follow-up. A temporary exception without a pre-agreed review is a permanent exception we haven't admitted to yet.

---

**Close (~3 min)**

What I want out of this conversation: shared language for what a temporary exception is and how it dies; agreement on how feasibility shifts get surfaced early and with the dependency they imply; a sequencing principle for the next consolidation round so we're not negotiating from scratch each time.

The thing I'd push back on if it comes up: treating any of these as one-discipline work. The convergence only works if all three of us are in the room for the hard calls, and the hard calls aren't the ones where we agree.

That pattern matches exactly. With identical external labels on the remote_write path, both collectors are writing into the same logical series, and offset 15s scrape schedules mean samples land out of order relative to each other. The 20-minute burst of out-of-order rejects plus flat shared ingest-edge metrics and unaffected peer targets confirms this is isolated to that target's scrape topology, not a backend issue.

Immediate mitigation (safe, reversible):
Pick one collector as the active writer for that target and stop the other from remote-writing to ingest-edge. Keep the writer whose external label set is already canonical in your dashboards and alerts, so rule-eval keeps working without a relabel churn. This removes the competing-writer effect at the source and stops the reject growth within a minute. Do not try to dedup at the receiver under load — at 3.3k rejects in 20 min you are already pushing the out-of-order window.

Supported HA pattern when you bring the second writer back:
Both collectors need distinct, stable, bounded cluster and replica labels (e.g. replica: replica-a and replica: replica-b, plus your cluster value), and ingest-edge's dedup config has to be tuned for that replica set. The replica label set has to be finite and known ahead of time — that is what makes dedup tractable.

What not to use as a replica label:
Pod UIDs, container IDs, request IDs, or any high-cardinality or restart-volatile value. Those make the replica set unbounded and churn on every restart, so dedup silently breaks and you trade one problem for a worse one. On Kubernetes, a StatefulSet ordinal or a fixed replica name is the right shape.

Recovery checks after disabling one writer:
  - cortex_discarded_samples_total{reason="out-of-order"} for that tenant flattens within ~1m and returns to baseline.
  - Active writer count for the target is 1 (verify on the kept writer via its remote-write writer gauge or equivalent).
  - Single series per metric for the target on the rule side — a count by __name__ against the rule-eval store confirms no stale entries from the disabled writer are still being indexed.
  - 5m and 1h rate panels on the target return to their expected band.
  - If the disabled writer was the only one scraping some intervals, decide whether to backfill from the kept writer's TSDB or accept the gap against your SLO.

Happy to review the relabel config on the kept writer and to confirm the replica label set before you re-enable the second one.

A few notes on the choices in this draft, in case you want to adjust:

- I led with the diagnosis-confirmation sentence because support escalations tend to land with stakeholders who need to see that the responder has actually looked at the signal, not just guessed.
- I named the Mimir/Cortex metric name for out-of-order rejects since your stack is on that side; if the affected tenant is on a different backend, swap in that backend's discard counter.
- The "do not use pod UIDs" warning is stated as a flat rule rather than as a justification chain, because the typical reason it gets pushed back on is "but Kubernetes gives us a UID for free" — naming the failure mode (unbounded set, restart churn) in one line is enough to head that off without lecturing.
- Recovery checks are in the order an oncall would actually run them: external symptom first, internal state second, panel sanity last, backfill decision last because it is the only one that can wait.

Root cause

Both collectors are producing samples for the same series with identical external + target labels. The tenant cannot distinguish writer A from writer B — it sees them as one source. With offset schedules, writer B's samples arrive at the tenant with timestamps that are sometimes older than writer A's already-ingested timestamp for the same series. The tenant rejects those as out-of-order. This is the standard Prometheus HA duplicate-write pattern: with N writers and identical labels, roughly (N−1)/N of samples are out-of-order on arrival.

Why scope is one target

Only that target sits in the intersection of what both collectors scrape. Other targets are single-sourced — that's why shared ingest-edge error/latency/queue are all normal and no other target shows OOO. The 3,284 / 20 min rate (~2.7/s) is consistent with a 15s dual-scrape where the offset window puts a stable fraction of B's samples behind A's.

Immediate mitigation (allowed by constraint)

Take one writer offline for the affected target — either flip remote-write off on collector B for that job, or drop the duplicate scrape config from one of them. Cost: loses HA on that target until the proper fix lands. Expect OOO on that target to drop to zero within one scrape cycle.

Proper fix: HA deduplication with a stable replica label

Two changes, both required:

1. Receiver side: turn on HA deduplication and tell it which label is the replica label.
   - Cortex / Mimir: `ha_tracker.enable_ha_deduplication: true`, with `cluster_replica` as the replica label (or whatever the deployment's convention is).
   - Thanos: configure the receive side with `replica` as the replica label for dedup.

2. Writer side: give each collector a stable, bounded value for that label.
   - Hardcoded per-collector in agent config (e.g. `external_labels: { replica: "0" }` and `{ replica: "1" }` for an HA pair).
   - StatefulSet ordinal parsed from the pod name.
   - Per-replica value from a mounted ConfigMap / Secret.

Required properties of the label value:

- Stable across restarts, deploys, and config reloads — the same collector must always emit the same value.
- Bounded — fixed small set (2 for an HA pair, never growing with cluster size). The set itself is the cardinality budget.

Once both sides are in place, re-enable the second writer. The tenant will group samples by all labels minus the replica label, dedup by timestamp, and stop rejecting.

Stable label sources that work: hardcoded string, StatefulSet ordinal, ConfigMap value, node label on a dedicated collector node.

What NOT to use (per constraint)

- Pod UID: changes on every restart, so every restart re-labels every series and the dedup window loses continuity.
- Request IDs / trace IDs / span IDs: unbounded cardinality, no use as series identity, will blow up the index.
- Random suffixes, timestamps, hashes: defeat dedup entirely; every sample looks like a new replica.
- Per-scrape or per-request values: unbounded cardinality.
- Different replica values per target (e.g. `{target="api", replica="a"}` / `{target="api", replica="b"}`): breaks dedup across the pair — both writers must use the same label name and value scheme on the same target.

Verification

- OOO error count on the affected target returns to the same baseline as other targets within one or two scrape cycles after both writers are back.
- A query like `up{...}` grouped appropriately returns one series per (cluster, replica), not two with the same identity.
- HA drill: stop collector A, confirm continuous samples from B with no scrape gap; bring A back, confirm no OOO spike during re-convergence.

If the deployment does not run HA deduplication on the receiver, the only correct steady state is one writer per target — the constraint permits it as mitigation and there is no alternative until the receiver side is enabled.

WHAT YOU'RE LIKELY LOOKING AT

The summary page of a 1099-DIV lists box totals. The supplemental detail page breaks Box 1a (total ordinary dividends) out by security and payment date. The supplemental sums TO Box 1a — it is not added on top of it. So your read is structurally the default: $1,284.37 is one amount on the return (the ordinary-dividends line), and the supplemental rows are supporting detail.

"Structurally normal" and "your numbers actually reconcile" are still two different things, though. To verify, I'd need:

  - the Box 1a total on the summary page
  - the supplemental rows (security, pay date, amount, and which box each row maps to)
  - whether any other boxes are non-zero (1b qualified, 2a cap gain, 5 §199A, 7 foreign tax, etc.)

QUICK SELF-RECONCILIATION

  1. Sum every row on the supplemental that is an ordinary dividend. The total must equal Box 1a to the cent.
  2. If the supplemental lists qualified dividends separately, sum those — they should be LESS THAN OR EQUAL TO the ordinary total. Qualified is a subset of ordinary, never in addition.
  3. Confirm that rows labeled return of capital, capital gain distribution, §199A dividends, or foreign tax paid are NOT folded into the ordinary-dividend sum — those belong to other boxes (3, 2a, 5, 7 respectively).

FLAG WITH THE BROKERAGE IF YOU SEE ANY OF THESE

  - Supplemental total differs from Box 1a by even a few cents
  - A "qualified" amount that exceeds the ordinary total (structurally impossible)
  - Foreign tax paid (Box 7) reported with no foreign-source rows visible on the supplemental
  - A row you can't identify or assign to a box
  - An amount for a security you didn't hold that year, or a missing expected position
  - A corrected 1099-DIV was issued after the original (the brokerage should have notified you; if you didn't get a notice, ask)
  - Any year-end or year-start reinvestment that doesn't appear as a cash dividend row but was treated as one

WHAT I'LL DO ONCE YOU PASTE THE FIGURES

Triage plan: monitoring-agent image rollout vs. rollup-service scrape failure

Premise (from your signals): rollup-service is healthy by every customer- and SLO-facing signal; scrape failures are confined to the 3 agents on the new image, all returning x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. The new monitoring-agent image is the suspect, not the service. The plan below keeps that framing intact and does not let "dashboards have gaps" get re-read as "rollup-service is down."

Order:

1. Lock the scope before touching anything.
   - Confirm the failing-scrapes set is exactly the 3 agents on the new image, and zero from agents still on the prior image.
   - Confirm timestamps: scrape failures began within minutes of the rollout, no lead/lag.
   - Purpose: stops the incident from being widened to "rollup-service observability is broken." It is "the new monitoring image broke its own scrapes."

2. Snapshot the independent service-health evidence first.
   - Capture, with timestamps: rollup-service query latency p50/p95/p99, rollup completion rate, error rate, processed-points counter.
   - Pull these from a path that does not depend on the new agent image (the service's own /metrics scraped by an unrelated path, or a blackbox/probe check). The SLO dashboard for rollup-service is the thing showing gaps — do not use it as your evidence of health.
   - Save as a single named artifact (link + filename) you can point at later. This is the artifact that proves rollup-service was never in an outage, so it must exist before any rollback discussion.

3. Pull both images and extract their CA bundles (the load-bearing step).
   - Pull the prior (known-good) tag and the new tag into a sandbox; do not run them, just inspect.
   - Extract the bundle the agent uses for outbound TLS. Common locations to check, in order:
     - /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt (Debian/Ubuntu base)
     - /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt (RHEL base)
     - the file pointed to by the agent's --ca-file, tls-ca-file, or equivalent Prometheus flag
     - a CA file baked into the image's Prometheus/web config
   - Also note whether the new image changed any TLS-flag default or scrape config, not just the bundle. You want to rule out "bundle is fine, flag changed" before attributing to the bundle.

4. Diff the bundles and inspect the failing target's chain.
   - Clean diff: sorted list of subjects plus sha256 of each PEM block. Look for added, removed, or truncated entries — specifically the CA that signs rollup-service's scrape target cert.
   - Independently, capture the cert chain rollup-service presents (openssl s_client -showcerts from a host that scrapes successfully and, if reachable, from one that fails). Identify the issuing CA and root.
   - Expected finding given the symptom: the issuing root is present in the old bundle and absent (or replaced) in the new bundle.

5. Decide on rollback with one explicit criterion.
   - Roll back the monitoring-agent image on the 3 affected hosts if and only if:
     (a) step 4 shows the new bundle is missing a CA the old bundle had, and that CA is in rollup-service's chain, AND
     (b) the independent service-health snapshot from step 2 is clean (latency, errors, completion, points all within SLO).
   - Do not roll back if the bundle diff is benign — fix forward on the monitoring side (rebuild the image with the right bundle, or restore the prior TLS flag) rather than churn the fleet on an unrelated image.
   - Do not open, escalate, or page a rollup-service incident. The service is not in an outage. If anyone in the channel is treating it as one, point them at the snapshot from step 2.

6. Roll back narrowly and verify.
   - Revert only the 3 affected agents to the prior image tag. The rest of the fleet is already on the prior image, so this is a 3-host revert, not a fleet change. Coordinate with whoever owns the monitoring image (this is not a rollup-service change), and stay within the weekday deploy window.
   - Watch scrape success return to ~99.9% within a few minutes on those 3 hosts; confirm the other agents are unaffected and rollup-service's independent health signals are unchanged.

7. Close out the misclassification risk in writing.
   - In the incident note / handoff, state plainly: rollup-service was healthy throughout; dashboards had gaps because the new monitoring-agent image shipped without the CA bundle needed to validate rollup-service's scrape target cert; customer-facing signals were never degraded.
   - Follow-up for the monitoring image pipeline: add a pre-deploy smoke test that scrapes a known internal target with the new image before rollout, so a CA-bundle drift fails the rollout instead of failing scrapes in prod.

Stop conditions (what would change the plan):
- If step 4 shows the bundles are identical, the cause is not the CA bundle. Stop the rollback path, look at TLS flags / Prometheus config in the new image, or at a recent cert rotation on the rollup-service side, and re-decide. Do not roll back on a hypothesis the diff does not support.
- If step 2 shows rollup-service is genuinely degraded on any independent signal, the picture changes — investigate rollup-service separately, but still do not attribute it to the monitoring rollout without evidence.
- If more than the 3 agents are failing, scope is wider than the image rollout and the rollback decision needs a wider look before acting.

KEEP-OR-DISCARD PLAN (assumes your 28°F reading is accurate — see calibration note below)

THE THRESHOLD THAT MATTERS
  USDA/FDA guidance: food is safe to refreeze if a freezer thermometer reads 40°F or below,
  OR if the food still contains visible ice crystals. You're at 28°F, so by the official
  rule, everything still in the freezer is technically safe to keep. The discard calls
  below are QUALITY decisions, not safety ones.

ITEM-BY-ITEM

  1) Ice cream (soft)
       Verdict: DISCARD for quality, keep only if you'll bake with it.
       Reasoning: Soft means it warmed past scoopable but almost certainly stayed under
       40°F given your thermometer reading. Not a safety hazard. But once you refreeze
       it, the texture turns icy and grainy — it's not really ice cream anymore. If you
       want to use it, fold it into a milkshake, ice-cream cake, or baked good before
       it fully re-melts. Otherwise toss.

  2) Berries (partly thawed, still icy)
       Verdict: KEEP, refreeze. Plan to cook, not eat fresh.
       Reasoning: Ice crystals present = the safe-to-refreeze signal. They will lose a
       lot of structure and come out mushy. Best uses after re-freezing: jam, sauce,
       compote, pancake/waffle topping, smoothie, baked into muffins or pie. Don't try
       to serve them as "fresh" berries — disappointment and wasted fruit.

  3) Packaged chicken (hard, ice crystals visible, no leaked juices)
       Verdict: KEEP, refreeze, no action needed.
       Reasoning: This is the best-case item. Still hard and no juice purge = it never
       meaningfully thawed. Refreeze as-is, use within a normal timeframe. You can
       also cook it now from its current partially-frozen state if your meal plan
       allows — that just shortens the path.

GENERAL RULE FOR ANYTHING ELSE YOU HAVEN'T MENTIONED
       Hard with ice crystals AND no liquid purge → keep.
       Any soft/wet items where you're not sure → cook thoroughly now (heat kills
       what a freezer thaw cannot), then decide on quality.

RECHECK SCHEDULE
  Don't keep opening the door — each open slows recovery.

    Now     : door is closed, hands off. Don't peek for 1 hour.
    +1 hour : first recheck. Expected: temp has dropped a few degrees (still nowhere
              near 0°F, that's fine — thermal mass is large).
    +2 hours: should be dropping further, trending toward setpoint.
    +4 hours: clear downward trend expected.
    +24 hrs : should be at or very near normal operating temp (typically 0°F).

WHAT POINTS TO AN APPLIANCE PROBLEM (NOT JUST THE DOOR)

  Door-was-ajar signature (this is what you should see):
    - Steady downward trend starting within 1–2 hours of closing.
    - Returns to normal setpoint within ~12–24 hours.
    - No warm spikes after recovery.

  Appliance-problem signature — call a tech if you see any of these:
    - +1 hour reading is NOT lower than 28°F (compressor may not be running).
    - +2 to +4 hours reading is flat or still rising (cooling system not engaging
      or not holding temp).
    - +24 hour reading is still above ~10°F.
    - You hear the compressor rarely or never cycling.
    - Heavy frost on the back wall or around the seal, or a wet floor under the unit
      (defrost drain clogged, evaporator leak).
    - The door closes but doesn't "seal" — run a dollar-bill test: close a bill
      half-in/half-out at several points around the gasket; if it slides out with
      no resistance, the seal is bad and that IS your root cause (cheaper fix than
      a compressor).

ONE CALIBRATION CHECK BEFORE YOU TRUST ANY OF THIS
  Cheap freezer thermometers drift. Quick test: make an ice-water slurry (50/50
  ice and water, stir, let sit 2 min), insert thermometer — should read 32°F.
  If it reads 33–34°F, your "28°F" was actually ~29–30°F in reality (still fine).
  If it reads 30°F or lower, your thermometer is reading cold and your actual
  freezer temp may have been higher than 28°F at the moment you checked — in
  that case, still OK because the chicken is clearly still hard and icy, but it
  does weaken the thermometer-only argument for items on the margin.

BOTTOM LINE
  Door ajar ~3h at an internal reading of 28°F with chicken still hard and icy =
  nothing to throw out on safety grounds. Toss the ice cream on quality, keep the
  berries and the chicken, cook the berries, and recheck in one hour to confirm
  recovery.

The deadlock is hold-lock-across-wait. Coordinator holds `manifestMu` while blocked in `wg.Wait()`. Workers need `manifestMu` to record completion (which is the path that ends in `wg.Done()`). Neither side can make progress — the coordinator will never release the lock because it's blocked on the very `Done()` calls that need the lock.

812 is just where the lock-window closed. Some earlier phase let workers acquire `manifestMu` long enough to record and `Done()` — by 812, the coordinator entered a phase (probably the shown one, or a prior iteration of it) where the lock spans the wait, and after that no worker can ever get in. Not load-related, not bound-related — purely structural.

Fix is the obvious one: release before waiting.

```
manifestMu.Lock()
enqueueRemaining(manifests)
manifestMu.Unlock()    // <-- before wg.Wait()
wg.Wait()
```

The worker path doesn't need to change. `wg.Done()` is already outside the lock, so once the coordinator releases, a worker acquires `manifestMu`, writes `completed[id]`, releases, calls `Done()`, and `wg.Wait()` unblocks when the counter hits zero. `enqueueRemaining` is safe under the lock — it just has to finish before the unlock.

One follow-on worth considering while you're in there: the `completed` map needs a mutex only if something reads it concurrently with worker writes. If the only reader is the coordinator *after* `wg.Wait()` returns, the mutex on writes is redundant — the happens-before from `wg.Done()` → `wg.Wait()` return guarantees the coordinator sees the writes. Drop the lock on writes in that case (just `completed[id] = true; wg.Done()`). If `completed` is hot, this matters; if it's diagnostic, the readability cost probably isn't worth it.

**Numbers**

  Renewal: $238/yr, $25,000 personal property, $500 deductible, $300,000 liability
  Other:   $211/yr, $25,000 personal property, $1,000 deductible, $300,000 liability, excludes pet-caused damage to the unit
  Annual savings: $238 − $211 = $27
  Deductible gap: $1,000 − $500 = $500
  Breakeven: $500 / $27 ≈ 18.5 years

**The narrow tradeoff, given that you have Kibo**

  The savings are too small to justify swapping on deductible alone. To come out ahead on the deductible change alone, you'd have to file roughly one claim every ~18 years, which is not how renters claims work in practice — most years you file zero, and in a bad year the claim size is what matters, not how often you file. So the deductible difference is a tail risk, not a recurring cost.

  The deductible bump is the smaller of the two issues. The pet-damage exclusion is the binding one for your household. "Damage to the unit" means the dwelling itself — chewed door frames, scratched floors, urine-soaked subfloor, carpet padding pulled up. None of that is covered under the other policy, and none of it would be covered under your own contents coverage either, because contents is *your* property, not the landlord's structure. So a pet-caused incident to the unit lands entirely on you out of pocket against the other quote, with no deductible offset and no liability cap protecting you — your landlord can still pursue repair costs above your security deposit.

  Kibo's profile matters here. He's a dog who startles briefly at skateboards near the curb but recovers and doesn't keep pulling. Startle-recover behavior and any chew/scratch history are the relevant inputs, not size or breed. If there's been a prior incident in this unit, or he's in a teething/chewing phase, the exclusion has real expected value. If not, the exclusion is a low-probability but high-severity gap rather than a routine one.

Here's a draft you can adapt:

The per-pod p99 values you're seeing are each the 99th percentile of that pod's own request distribution. A quantile is a positional statistic on a single distribution and is not additive across partitions: the average of six per-pod p99s is not equal to the 99th percentile of the combined request stream, and weighting by request count does not change that. You're averaging positional statistics from disjoint subsets, not recombining the underlying distributions.

A concrete reason the math breaks: imagine the slow traffic in the customer's environment is not evenly spread — say, one pod sees a non-trivial share of slow requests while the other five see only fast traffic. That one pod's p99 sits in its own slow tail, while the other five report small p99s. Simple or request-count-weighted averaging across the six will, in general, not equal the 99th percentile of the combined traffic — the answer depends on how the slow tail happens to be partitioned across pods, which is incidental to the question being asked. Depending on the partition, averaging can overstate, understate, or coincidentally match the true combined p99. It is not a repairable approximation; it discards the cross-pod information needed to position the combined quantile.

The fix is to emit histogram buckets (counts of requests in each latency range) from each pod instead of pre-computed summary quantiles. Bucket counts are additive: summing them across the six pods reconstructs the combined distribution. `histogram_quantile` applied to the aggregated series then gives a mathematically correct service-wide p99 — and the same aggregated series supports p50, p95, p99.9, and any other quantile, with no further work.

About 240 words. The three points you wanted land in order: why averaging fails, why weighted averaging fails for the same reason, and the histogram → aggregate → `histogram_quantile` path. Let me know if you'd like a shorter version, a version that omits the worked example, or one tuned for a specific channel (email vs. support ticket reply).

- Validator, running after download, computes `sha256(compressed_tar_zst_bytes)` and compares.

Smallest fix — pick one side, not both
The principle: hash what actually travels through the pipeline. The artifact on disk and on the wire is `.tar.zst`; the uncompressed stream only exists transiently inside the generator. Hashing the compressed file on both sides is the natural contract. (Hashing the tar stream on both sides would also work, but it requires decompressing during validation on every consumer, which is strictly more work for no extra safety.)

1. Generator (manifest writer)

- Unit, generator: given a fixed input directory, the emitted checksum equals `sha256` of the `.tar.zst` file the generator just wrote to disk. Assert against a known-answer vector so a future "hash the tar stream again" regression fails loudly.
- Unit, validator: given a manifest checksum and a `.tar.zst` on disk, accept when they match; reject when the file is mutated by even one byte at the tail (catches "hash the wrong buffer" bugs).

Diagnosis: manifest/validator contract mismatch on what `sha256` names. The artifact itself is fine; the pipeline is rejecting it by design.

What you have:
- Manifest `sha256` = hash of the canonical tar stream (uncompressed)
- Validator hashes the `.tar.zst` bytes and compares against that field
- These will never match for any valid artifact, since zstd changes the bytes

What this is not:
- Not tampering — decompressed tar stream hash matches the manifest exactly
- Not corruption — decompression produced the canonical stream the manifest claims
- Not a deployment issue — per your note, nothing reached staging or prod

The generator wrote the inner-stream hash into a field the validator interprets as the outer-archive hash. That's a contract bug, not a release bug.

Where to fix:

Option A (recommended) — generator side
- Hash the `.tar.zst` file before upload and write that into manifest `sha256`.
- Validator stays as-is. Smallest change, matches the conventional reading of `sha256` on a downloadable artifact (hash of bytes as transmitted). zstd is deterministic at fixed level/threads, so the compressed hash is a stable content identifier.

Option B — validator side
- Decompress, hash the canonical tar stream, compare. Generator stays. Cost: decompression + canonical-tar guarantees on the validator path.

Option C — both, explicit
- Two fields: `sha256_archive` (compressed) and `sha256_tar_stream` (inner). Validator compares `sha256_archive`; inner hash is available for downstream tooling that consumes the tar directly. Most explicit, slight schema change.

Recommendation: Option A unless there is a documented reason `sha256` was meant to name the inner stream — in which case rename it to `sha256_tar_stream` and add `sha256_archive` per Option C. Don't leave it ambiguous; whichever side wins, the other tool needs to be updated in the same change.

Process notes:
- This blocks every release going through the current generator, not just 1.44.3. Worth checking whether anything shipped between the generator change that introduced this and today, and if so, whether the validator was bypassed or the manifest was hand-corrected.
- Catching it pre-release is the right time. No rollback or hotfix needed; nothing deployed.
- After the fix, re-run 1.44.3 through the corrected generator and validator end-to-end before tagging the release.

Good — that's a clean fix shape. A few things worth calling out, in case it helps when the next reviewer looks at it:

  - Hash is taken over the final `.tar.zst` bytes after compression, not over the uncompressed tar. That's the right invariant — anything earlier lets compression nondeterminism or wrapper tooling quietly change the bytes you sign.
  - Naming the field `archive_sha256` explicitly (rather than overloading a generic `sha256` or reusing the per-file field name) keeps archive-level and per-file hashes from being interchangeable in consumer code. Easy bug to introduce later otherwise.
  - Validator compares before unpacking. That's what closes the bad-archive-reaches-prod path; the per-file hashes alone wouldn't have, since they only see post-unpack contents.
  - Byte-flip regression test is the right one to keep — it pins down the failure mode that mattered, not just a "hashes match" smoke test.

On the superglue question — yes, it can get in the way of a proper repair, and not for the obvious reason. Cyanoacrylate cures rigid, and a rigid bond inside a flex zone (the toe rand area sees a lot of flex) tends to crack and re-fail within a handful of sessions. The bigger problem is what it does to a future repair: resolers want clean rubber surfaces to bond to, and CA residue is annoying to remove — the solvents that break it down (acetone, nitromethane) also swell or attack the rubber and the rand adhesive. A resoler who sees superglue in there may quote you a worse repair or tell you the rand area is now compromised. Ren's instinct (something flexible) is right; the specific product is just wrong.

On flexible adhesive for 8mm — reasonable, yes. This is a standard DIY fix at this size, given what you've described (rand intact, no fabric exposed):

  - Clean both faces with isopropyl alcohol, let dry fully
  - Lightly scuff both surfaces (very fine sandpaper or a careful knife scratch) so the adhesive has tooth — go easy, the rubber is thin at the edge
  - Use a flexible shoe adhesive: Shoe Goo is the common pick, Gear Aid Aquaseal / Shoe & Boot Glue works, or a contact cement like Barge. Climbing-specific adhesives (Tenaya, a few resoler brands) are fine but overkill at this scale
  - Press the two faces back together — clamp it, wrap with athletic tape, or wedge a shoe tree in overnight. Cure 24h before climbing
  - Thin continuous film, not a thick bead. The faces do the work; thick glue is a weak bond

On signs to stop using and take it to a resoler:

  - Fabric or mesh exposed anywhere — rand has failed, not just edge rubber
  - The rand itself is lifting or delaminating from the upper (different failure mode than the sole-edge gap)
  - Separation spreads, or re-opens at the same spot after your repair — usually means the rand underneath has lost its structural role or the rubber has thinned past useful life
  - Toe box lost shape when unweighted (crumples instead of holding form) — rand is no longer doing its job, an edge re-bond won't hold
  - Sole delaminating across a wider area, not just the 8mm edge — that's a resole, not a patch

For your current state — 8mm, rand intact, no fabric — the DIY flexible-adhesive fix is the right scope. If any of those escalation signs show up, a climbing-shoe resoler is worth the visit over a general cobbler; most handle edge re-bonds and rand repairs for roughly $20-40 depending on brand, and they understand climbing shoe construction in a way a shoe-repair shop usually doesn't.

KB search didn't surface a security-scanner playbook (v2 stub), and the ingest-edge runbook doesn't cover scanner false positives — so the following is grounded in the artifact side of the question, not a templated classification. Adapt the exact digests/paths to what CI hands you.

VERIFICATION ORDER

Do these in sequence. Capture each output; don't skip ahead — the classification at the end only holds if every step checks out.

1. Identify the published release digest, not a local rebuild.
   - Get the exact runtime image digest CI scanned: e.g. `crane manifest <registry>/ingest-edge:v2.19.0@sha256:<digest>` and the digest of v2.19.0 (`crane digest <registry>/ingest-edge:v2.19.0`). Record both. This is the artifact you are clearing the finding against.

2. List the runtime image's actual layers.
   - `crane export <registry>/ingest-edge:v2.19.0@sha256:<release-digest> - | tar -tvf - | head` and/or `crane config <release-digest>` for the diff IDs. Capture the full layer list — this is the ancestry the scanner should be matching against.

3. Compare the reported layer digest against that list.
   - The finding names a specific layer digest. If it does not appear in step 2's layer list, it is not in the shipped image. If it does appear, stop — the finding is real and the rest of the order doesn't help.

4. Pull the SBOM attached to the release image, not the builder image or an aggregate.
   - `cosign verify-attestation --key <key> --type spdxjson <registry>/ingest-edge:v2.19.0@sha256:<release-digest>` (or cyclonedx, depending on your attestation type), or `crane get <release-digest>`-side manifest for the SBOM reference. Grep for `libxml2`. The runtime SBOM must not list libxml2. If it does, stop.

5. Confirm the shipped binary has no dynamic linkage to libxml2.
   - Export the binary out of the runtime image: `crane export <release-digest> - --platform linux/amd64 | tar -xO ./usr/local/bin/ingest-edge > /tmp/ingest-edge`. Run `file /tmp/ingest-edge` (expect `statically linked` or note the dynamic libs) and `readelf -d /tmp/ingest-edge | grep -i NEEDED`. No `libxml2.so` / `libxml2.so.2` in NEEDED. If you want a belt-and-suspenders pass: `ldd /tmp/ingest-edge` on a sandbox host with the same arch. If libxml2 appears, stop.

6. Confirm the builder base's *current* libxml2 version.
   - On a fresh pull of the builder base (not the cached layer): `docker run --rm <builder-base> apk -v info libxml2 2>/dev/null` or `dpkg -s libxml2 | grep -E '^(Package|Version)'`. If the current builder base carries a patched libxml2, the cached layer carrying 2.10.3 is doubly stale and isn't pulled forward on the next clean build.

Before I draft, one honesty note: the runbook I pulled for `ingest-edge` only contains operational playbooks (cutover, deploy surface, canary stop rule, ownership). It doesn't document the actual rejection path for `time_unix_nano`, so what follows is grounded in the OTLP specification and standard exporter behaviour, not a quoted rule from ingest-edge. If you need a citation phrased as "per our runbook," that's a gap I'd want to close first — flag if so.

Draft below, ready to paste to support / the customer.

---

**Why `time_unix_nano` rejections are almost always a unit bug, not clock skew**

ingest-edge evaluates OTLP metric points against a staleness window using the `time_unix_nano` field, which the OTLP spec defines as **nanoseconds since the Unix epoch**. If the exporter (or an SDK on the host) writes that field in a different unit, the value parses as correct-unit nanoseconds and therefore lands in the deep past — and gets rejected as `sample timestamp too old`. The exporter host's wall clock can be perfectly healthy and the points still get rejected, because the field is being read in the wrong unit.

This is distinguishable from genuine clock skew in a couple of seconds:

**Verify-and-retry sequence (do steps 1–3 before any replay):**

1. Capture one rejected point's raw `time_unix_nano` from the exporter's debug/diagnostic log or the raw payload — before any unit conversion in your pipeline.
2. **Magnitude check** — the only diagnostic that cleanly separates unit-bug from skew:
   - ~1.78 × 10^18 (≈ 18 digits) → correct, nanoseconds
   - ~1.78 × 10^15 (≈ 15 digits) → SDK wrote microseconds
   - ~1.78 × 10^12 (≈ 12 digits) → SDK wrote milliseconds ← most common
   - ~1.78 × 10^9  (≈ 10 digits) → SDK wrote seconds
3. **Only if the magnitude is correct**, check host clock sync: `chronyc tracking` / `w32tm /query /status` / `ntpq -p`. An offset of minutes or more will also push `time_unix_nano` into the past. If NTP is unsynced or offset is large, that's real skew, not a unit bug.
4. **Then** fix the root cause (SDK/exporter unit config, or NTP) before replaying the buffer — replaying before the fix will just re-reject.

The two failure modes are not mutually exclusive, but step 2 alone resolves the majority of these cases.

---

If you want, I can also tighten this into a 3-line reply for the support ticket, or post it as a doc/runbook entry so the next occurrence has a known-good sequence to point at.

Diagnosis: unit confusion. The exporter is writing a Unix-millisecond value into OTLP's `time_unix_nano` field, which expects Unix nanoseconds.

  1709908205123 as ms  = 2024-03-08 14:10:05 UTC  (current, matches your note)
  1709908205123 as ns  = 1.7 s past epoch         (~56 years stale)

ingest-edge's freshness check sees a near-zero ns timestamp, fails the "too old" gate, and rejects. The rejection is accurate but diagnostically useless — it points the exporter at a clock problem when the actual problem is the field's unit.

Fix lives on the customer side, not in ingest-edge:

  - Multiply by 1e6 before assigning to `time_unix_nano`, or
  - Reconfigure the exporter to emit ns natively (preferred — fixes the same bug class for any other field, e.g. `start_time_unix_nano`).

Do not auto-convert in ingest-edge. A silent ms->ns lift would mask the same mistake for every future exporter and quietly change what gets stored — exactly the kind of "helpful" scope-widen that bites later.

Still reject, still no auto-fix — just a clearer breadcrumb so the customer's next debug cycle is minutes instead of hours. Why (tenant_id, batch_id) is wrong:
  - A batch is an *attempt* unit, not a commit unit. The 12 segments commit independently, and retry/reassignment operates on unacked segments, not whole batches. So the batch boundary has no transactional meaning at the output store.
  - A batch-level key either double-writes on reassignment or drops segments on partial commit. Either way it lies about what is durable.

Idempotency invariant (precise):
  For each (tenant_id, segment_id), the rollup output store contains at most one committed write of that segment's payload. A subsequent write with the same key and an identical payload hash is a no-op. A write with the same key but a different payload hash is a conflict and must be surfaced, never silently overwritten.

Smallest safe dedupe key:
  (tenant_id, segment_id)
  - segment_id is producer-assigned at submission time, globally unique per tenant (UUIDv4 or producer-monotonic), and stable across every retry and reassignment of that segment. It must be minted at submission, not at attempt time — otherwise it isn't stable across retries.
  - batch_id is a retry-grouping hint only; it is NOT part of the dedupe key. segment_index is unnecessary if segment_id is unique.
  - Fallback if the producer cannot mint segment_ids: (tenant_id, batch_id, segment_index), with the constraint that batch_id is stable across retries and segment_index is assigned deterministically within the batch. Weaker — only use it if segment_id is unavailable.

Commit ordering (the only rule that matters):
  1. Upsert FIRST, ack SECOND.
  2. Worker performs a conditional upsert keyed by (tenant_id, segment_id), recording the segment payload hash. The upsert must be atomic at the row/key level — no read-modify-write.
  3. Only on upsert success does the worker ack that segment to the producer.
  4. Producer marks segment_id acked. On retry, producer omits acked segment_ids from the batch the reassigned worker receives.
  5. Batch "done" = every segment_id in the batch is acked or producer-aborted.
  6. Every side effect of a segment commit (output store, index, derived tables, audit log) must be gated by the same (tenant_id, segment_id) check. If side effects span multiple stores, wrap them in a per-segment outbox keyed by segment_id or a transactional coordinator — no side effect may commit before the dedupe-key check passes.

  Lease/epoch can fence the worker's intermediate state but is NOT needed in the dedupe key. (tenant_id, segment_id) alone is sufficient if the upsert is atomic.

Failure tests to require before merge:

  T1. Worker reassignment mid-batch.
       12 segments; W1 acks 1–3, starts 4, lease expires or W1 is killed. W2 picks up the batch, sees 1–3 acked and omitted, processes 4–12.
       Assert: exactly one record per (tenant_id, segment_id) for all 12. Final output state byte-equal to a clean single-worker run.

  T2. Crash after write, before ack (the headline failure mode).
       W writes segment S (upsert commits). W is killed before ack. Producer retries; W2 attempts S.
       Assert: W2's upsert is a no-op (same key, same payload hash). W2 then acks. Output store has exactly one record for S. Downstream rollup readers see S exactly once.

  T3. Conflicting payload (regression guard for T2).
       W1 writes S with payload hash H1, crashes before ack. W2 is given the same segment_id but payload hash H2 (corrupted input or wrong fetch).
       Assert: W2's upsert fails with a conflict error, NOT a silent overwrite. Conflict surfaces via the standard retry-exhaustion / paging path. Output store still holds H1.

  T4. Lease expiry during upsert (split-brain).
       W1 begins upsert of S, lease expires mid-call. W2 takes the segment and upserts.
       Assert: exactly one of (W1, W2)'s writes commits. The loser detects the existing record and stops. Producer acks S exactly once.

  T5. Replay of a fully-acked batch.
       Operator or producer retry replays a batch where all 12 segments are already acked.
       Assert: zero new writes; all upserts are no-ops; the batch is recognized as already-done and is not re-acked.

Push-back items if any are missing in the diff:
  - Producer mints segment_ids at submission time, not at attempt time. (Critical for stability across retries.)
  - Output-store upsert is atomic at the row/key level. No read-modify-write, no separate existence check followed by insert.
  - The dedupe key gates every side effect of a segment commit, not just the primary write.
  - Lease/epoch handling is for intermediate state only; it does not appear in the dedupe key.

Two structural defects in the current shape; all three required failure cases hit them.

  1. The seen-key is at batch granularity: key := (tenantID, batchID)
     Any segment write that reaches markSeen marks the entire batch as seen.

       Case 1: the first segment commits and marks seen. The other 11
               then check seen(tenant, batch), see true, return success.
               11 of 12 segments are never written. Silent data loss.

       Case 3: when the unacked segment is reassigned, its new worker
               checks seen(tenant, batch). If any other segment of the
               batch has marked seen in the meantime, the new worker
               returns success — that segment is never written or acked.
               The loss is shared across the batch, not isolated to the
               reassigned one.

  2. markSeen and ack are sequenced, and ack fires only on the fresh path.

       Case 2, sub-case A: crash between writeSegment and markSeen.
               Segment is durable, but retry doesn't see "seen" and calls
               writeSegment again. Duplicate unless the write itself is
               idempotent on (tenant, batch, segment).

       Case 2, sub-case B: crash between markSeen and ack.
               Retry sees "seen", returns success, ack never fires.
               Upstream hangs on a segment that is actually written.

Fix — the only meaningful change is widening the key to per-segment, and
re-firing ack on the early-return path:

  key := (tenantID, batchID, segmentID)
  if seen(key) {
      ack(segment)            // re-fire on retry; idempotent upstream
      return success
  }
  writeSegment(segment)       // must be idempotent on key
  markSeen(key)
  ack(segment)

For that to actually be safe end-to-end:

  - seen and markSeen share a durable store (already true in the current
    shape — fine).

  - writeSegment is idempotent on (tenant, batch, segment). Otherwise
    sub-case A still double-writes on every retry. CAS / insert-if-absent
    at the storage layer, or dedup-on-key at ingest.

  - ack is idempotent upstream. If it isn't, you cannot just re-fire it
    on the retry path — the alternative is to fold ack into the same
    durable operation as markSeen, so that "seen" implies "acked" and
    the early-return branch no longer needs to know about ack at all.

Good closure. The clean tell was that the buffered 11 minutes went through on retry with no too-old rejections — that's the proof that ingest-edge's threshold logic was correct and the fault really was on the producer side. Nothing left dangling on our end.

Got it — backfill idempotency is settled on Cyrus's side: atomic dedup key `(tenant_id, batch_id, segment_id)` written with the segment, twelve unique commits under crash + reassignment, Cyrus owns. Eggs on wilted spinach with feta and warm pita, plus a garlicky yogurt sauce on the side.

The shape: yogurt sauce made first so it sits and mellows, spinach wilted and held warm, then eggs are the final 3–4 minutes so they hit the plate hot instead of overcooking on the stove. One wide skillet does almost everything.

Start at 6:35, eat at 7:

  6:35  Yogurt sauce. In a small bowl whisk about 3/4 cup yogurt, 1 small garlic clove grated on the fine side of a box grater (no mincing needed), a squeeze of lemon, pinch of salt, and a glug of olive oil. Loosely cover and leave on the counter.

  6:35  Oven to 400°F.

  6:45  Spinach. Wide skillet, medium heat, generous pour of olive oil. Thinly slice 1 garlic clove into the oil and stir 30 seconds — pale gold, not brown.
