Pattern matches classic aerator blockage — debris in the screen, flow restored with the aerator off, no leak, kitchen fine. Safe to service yourself. Here is the sequence.

PREP

1. Plug the sink drain with a rag. Aerator parts are small and chrome-finished; one drop into the P-trap means a trip to the hardware store.
2. Lay a folded towel on the counter next to the faucet. You will set parts on it in the order they come off.
3. Close both shutoff valves under the sink — clockwise until they stop. Do not force past the stop; if they don't fully close, stop and call the building, do not proceed (see below).
4. Open the faucet to drain residual pressure and confirm the shutoffs actually shut off the flow. If water keeps flowing after a few seconds, the shutoff is broken — stop and call the building.

REMOVAL

5. Unscrew the aerator by hand, counterclockwise as you face the spout. Most come off without tools. If it is stuck, wrap the aerator (not the spout) in a rag and use soft-jaw pliers gently. Do not grip the spout itself with pliers — the chrome will mar and the brass will deform.
6. If it will not budge with moderate hand pressure plus one gentle pliers nudge, stop. The spout threads can be damaged or the spout cracked. Apply a drop of penetrating oil, wait 10 minutes, retry. Still stuck → building/plumber.

The aerator comes apart as a stack. Typical order, top to bottom:
  - outer cap / housing
  - rubber washer or O-ring
  - flow restrictor disc (plastic; sometimes absent)
  - fine mesh screen — one or sometimes two
  - sometimes a second rubber washer at the base

Set each piece on the towel in the exact order you removed them. Reverse order on reassembly matters — wrong order means leak from the spout tip or no flow.

CLEANING

Use:
  - warm water
  - old soft toothbrush
  - white vinegar, soak 15–30 min for mineral crust
  - mild dish soap

Do NOT use:
  - steel wool, Scotch-Brite, sandpaper, or any abrasive pad — tears the mesh and scratches chrome
  - toothpicks, pins, needles, wire to poke the screen — stretches/tears the weave and creates a permanent weak spot
  - compressed air or high-pressure back-flush — same reason
  - muriatic acid, sulfuric drain cleaner, or any strong acid — eats brass and attacks chrome; residues are not appropriate for a drinking-water line
  - undiluted CLR / Lime-A-Way on rubber gaskets or plastic restrictors — degrades them. If you use it on metal parts only, rinse thoroughly before putting the rubber parts back
  - bleach — not necessary, degrades rubber over time

For the mesh: soak in vinegar until the white crust softens, then brush gently with the toothbrush from both sides. Most flakes will lift off without poking.

REASSEMBLY

7. Stack the parts back in the exact reverse order. Do not forget the rubber washer(s) — without them the aerator will not seal against the spout and you'll get a constant drip from the tip.
8. Thread the aerator back on hand-tight. Snug plus a tiny nudge is enough; the gasket does the sealing. Do not use pliers to tighten — over-tightening cracks the housing or the spout.
9. Open the shutoff valves slowly, counterclockwise. If a valve is stiff, do not force it — open it the small amount you can and call building if you cannot restore full flow.
10. Run the faucet for 30–60 seconds to flush loosened debris into the sink (not back into the cartridge). Check flow on both hot and cold.

STOP AND CALL THE BUILDING IF YOU SEE ANY OF THESE

  - The aerator still leaks from the spout tip after you have confirmed the rubber washer is in place and the housing is hand-snug. Usually a cartridge or seat issue, not solved by tightening the aerator further — forcing it cracks the housing.
  - Water appears under the sink, around the shutoff valves, supply lines, or the faucet base at any point during or after the work. Supply-side problem, not aerator.
  - Pressure stays weak with the aerator removed entirely. That points to the cartridge, supply line, or building riser — not the aerator, and not something to chase further on your own.
  - Water hammer (banging in the walls) when you open or close the faucet after the work.
  - Brown, yellow, or rust-colored water that does not clear after running for a minute or two.
  - The aerator or spout threads look corroded, cracked, or chewed up. Do not keep threading — you will cross-thread the spout and need a faucet replacement. (If the housing is bad, bring the old one to the hardware store to match the thread — common sizes are M22x1 and M24x1 female, and 55/64"-27 / 15/16"-27 male, but they vary.)
  - Shutoff valve will not close fully, or will not open fully without forcing.
  - Visible crust / green / white deposits on the shutoff valves or supply lines — sign of a slow leak that has been getting worse; let building maintenance handle it.

If everything is clean and reassembled and flow is restored, you're done. The grit and flakes are normal in older buildings with galvanized or partially-galvanized risers, especially after any upstream work in the building — worth mentioning to building maintenance next time you have a chance, but not an emergency.

Good — vinegar soak plus a no-overtighten reassembly is usually all it takes. Nice that you ran the ten-minute check on the shutoffs too; that's the part most people skip and the one that bites later if it was going to. Enjoy the even stream.

Two flavors of the same bug, both worth naming for Yuki so the fix covers both:

  a) Wall-clock arithmetic on naive datetimes. If `issued_at` is naive and `expires_at = issued_at + timedelta(minutes=30)` is also naive, the +30 lands inside the missing hour (02:00–03:00 on Mar 10). The persisted string is a wall-clock value that never existed.

  b) Round-trip with implicit zone. Even with a tz-aware datetime, if the serializer drops the offset and the parser reattaches *today's* local zone, the same wall-clock string means two different UTC instants before vs after the transition.

In both flavors the math is right and storage drops the offset.

Smallest unambiguous fix

  On issue:

    record["expires_at"] = expires_at.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
    # epoch seconds (int) is equally valid and slightly more foolproof;
    # ISO-Z is more debuggable. Same code path decodes either.

  On recovery:
    s   = record["expires_at"]
    exp = datetime.strptime(s, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ").replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    if datetime.now(timezone.utc) >= exp:
        expire()

  1. The serializer never emits a naive or local-time string for any field that participates in lease math — issued_at, last_renewed_at, fencing tokens, anything whose meaning depends on an absolute instant.
  2. The parser pins to UTC on read. A single grep-able helper (parse_utc(s)) at the storage boundary makes the contract unmissable for future contributors.
  3. Every "now" side of a comparison is datetime.now(timezone.utc). Mixing naive and aware is how 1-hour bugs sneak back in.

If Yuki wants the cleanest single diff: switch the lease record's time fields to epoch seconds (int), keep the +30 calculation in UTC, and add one parse_utc_record_exp helper at the recovery boundary.     (b) restart at 07:05 UTC (03:05 EDT wall) — lease must be expired.

Summary of the four fail-closed gates I called out:
1. Reauthorize before every source-page fetch — no page against a stale snapshot, retries included.
2. Reauthorize again right before publication — in-flight auth does not carry to publish.

The snapshot model is the root problem, and the current draft permits the failure sequence you walked through: pages 1–4 succeed under the original snapshot, access is revoked before page 5, the worker fails, and the retry resumes at page 5 with the cached snapshot — reads continue and (worse) publish occurs before the next sweep runs.

Authorization is not a job-scoped property. It can be revoked at any time, and partial success under a revoked grant is still a leak. Required changes:

1. Reauthorize before every source-page fetch. No page is read under a snapshot taken earlier in the job. The revocation between page 4 and page 5 must be visible to page 5's read.

2. Reauthorize immediately before publication. A grant that existed at fetch time is not a grant at publish time. The write is a separate authorization decision and must be re-checked at the moment of publish.

3. Fail closed on any denial and invalidate partial imported material. If authorization fails on a fetch or on the pre-publish check, the job stops and the partial room content is discarded. This replaces the "complete the import and let the next sweep hide it" path: a revoked grant must not produce a room that exists at all, even briefly.

4. Retries begin with a fresh authorization context. A retry must not reuse the original snapshot. It re-establishes authorization from current state and re-derives the resume point; it does not inherit the prior job's grant.

Net effect: revocation is observed at the next fetch (or at publish, whichever comes first), and the import cannot outrun a revoked grant.

# Review: smallest alert correction for canary-aware queue-age signal

## What the bug is, in runbook-language

The current rule averages queue age across the whole metrics-router service. During a canary that means the canary slice — which is small by design — gets diluted under a much larger stable slice, and a real canary regression never crosses the threshold. This is the same structural footgun the Yuki `histogram_quantile` entry already documented for the release panel, except it's happening at the alert-aggregation layer instead of the panel-query layer.

The previous runbook framing matters here: alerting+dashboards lives with Nadia, metrics-router ownership stays with you (Alex primary / Wes backup), and the Cardinality Guardrails addendum specifically keeps "alert-source semantics" review in Nadia's lane. So this stays in her lane; I'm only commenting on whether the fix is minimal and preserves rollout separation.

## The smallest correction that preserves rollout separation

**Scope-narrow rule.** The fix is one expression change in the alert rule, no instrumentation, no panel changes, no threshold change:

- Keep the existing metric and existing threshold.
- Add `rollout_stage` as a required group label on the alert query, so each rollout stage is evaluated independently. The service-wide average goes away; the alert becomes a per-stage evaluation.
- Keep `severity` and `for:` exactly as they are. Threshold and timing are Nadia's call, not part of this review.

Why this is the minimum:

1. **Preserves rollout separation by construction.** A canary slice is no longer summed into the stable baseline — each `rollout_stage` value (canary / stable / etc.) is its own series, and the threshold applies per series.
2. **No alert rewrite.** Same metric, same threshold, same `for:` window, same severity routing. Only the aggregation grouping changes.
3. **No cardinality explosion.** `rollout_stage` is a small bounded enum that's already on the emit side; it doesn't add a new high-cardinality dimension.
4. **No ownership movement.** Nadia keeps alert semantics; you keep the service. The runbook owner map is unchanged.

What to be explicit about in the rule comment so the next reader doesn't re-introduce the bug:

- "Do not average or `sum`-collapse across `rollout_stage` — the canary slice is intentionally small and must be evaluated independently of the stable slice."
- A one-line cross-reference to the Yuki `histogram_quantile` entry, so future reviewers see both "averaging quantiles" and "averaging across rollout stages" treated as the same class of mistake.

## Synthetic test expectations

These are the cases Nadia should cover in the canary test fixture. Positive = rule fires when it should; negative = rule stays silent when it shouldn't.

### Positive (must fire)

1. **Canary slice bad, stable slice clean.** Set the canary `rollout_stage` queue age above threshold for the full `for:` window; keep stable slice well below. Expect: alert fires, labels show `rollout_stage="canary"`, stable slice produces no alert. This is the exact regression Nadia's test surfaced and the one the current rule misses.
2. **Stable slice bad, canary slice clean.** Mirror of #1. Expect: alert fires with `rollout_stage="stable"`. Confirms the grouping doesn't accidentally suppress the stable path.
3. **Both slices bad simultaneously.** Expect: two distinct alert instances, one per `rollout_stage`. Confirms there's no silent dedup that would mask the canary under the stable.

### Negative (must not fire)

4. **Both slices clean, including realistic canary fraction.** Set the canary slice at, say, 5% of total traffic with queue age comfortably below threshold; stable slice also clean. Expect: no alert. This is the steady-state case the current rule passes and the new rule must not regress.
5. **Canary slice briefly above threshold but inside `for:` window.** Spike the canary queue age for less than the full `for:` duration, then let it recover. Expect: no alert. Confirms the `for:` window is still doing its job and the grouping change didn't accidentally turn every canary blip into a page.
6. **Missing `rollout_stage` label on a tiny fraction of traffic.** A handful of series with the label absent should not produce an alert, and should not be silently merged into either rollout stage. Expect: either no alert (if the missing-label traffic is below threshold on its own) or a clearly-labeled alert that is not attributed to either rollout stage. This is the "don't paper over label hygiene with aggregation" case.
7. **Canary slice entirely absent (no rollout in progress).** Only `rollout_stage="stable"` traffic present, all clean. Expect: no alert. Confirms the rule doesn't depend on a canary slice existing to evaluate correctly.

### One case worth flagging to Nadia before she merges

8. **Threshold interaction with `for:` under per-stage evaluation.** Because per-stage evaluation can be stricter than the old service-wide average, an existing canary that was previously masked could now legitimately cross the threshold on its first deploy after this change. That's the intended behavior, but it would be worth Nadia either (a) running the synthetic test against current prod canary data to confirm no immediate page, or (b) calling it out in the PR description so on-call isn't surprised. This is a communication note, not a design change.

## Things I am *not* asking Nadia to change

- Threshold value, `for:` window, severity, page routing — all hers.
- Dashboard/panel display — out of scope for an alert fix.
- Cardinality Guardrails preflight — unrelated to this rule change; `rollout_stage` is already a known label.
- Owner map — unchanged.

## One question for you before this goes further

Do you want the rule comment to cross-reference the Yuki `histogram_quantile` entry directly, or keep the alert fix self-contained and let the conceptual link live only in review comments? I'd lean toward a short cross-ref in the rule comment — it's one line and it stops the next person from re-introducing either averaging footgun — but it's your call since it lives on your runbook.

Root cause (confirming what `lsof` already tells you): every successful reload leaks exactly one inotify FD — the retired watcher's FD is never closed. The validation-failure path also leaks the candidate FD if you ever do hit it, but your soak is dominated by the swap-without-close case.

Minimal safe lifecycle — five steps, in this order, every reload:

  1. Construct  — `candidate = build(new_config)`          (allocates FD)
  2. Validate   — exercise the candidate end-to-end          (sees the file)
       if validate fails:
           `candidate.close()`                              (free the FD we just allocated)
           return error; active watcher untouched
  3. Swap       — under the same lock the event loop uses to
                  read `self.active`, do a single pointer
                  assignment: `self.active = candidate`
  4. Retired    — `old.close()`                              (free the stale FD)
  5. (optional) — bump a `reload_count` gauge + the
                  `inotify_fds_open` gauge you're already
                  emitting; cheap and makes this regression
                  self-alarming in the future.

Invariants that make this "safe":
  * At every instant, at least one watcher is live on the config path
    (during validation only `old` exists; after step 3 only `candidate`
    exists; between 3 and 4 both exist, which is fine because they're
    independent inotify instances and step 3 is what the reader sees).
  * A failed reload cannot leave two watchers allocated, and cannot
    retire the active one.
  * Step 3 must be under the lock the event reader uses. If your loop
    is `select/poll` over `self.active.fd`, the lock must guard both
    the `fd` lookup and the assignment, otherwise the reader can be
    inside `read()` on the old FD when you `close()` it in step 4 and
    come back with EBADF / lost edge events. Holding the lock for
    steps 3+4 keeps that window at one critical section.

What step 2 ("validate") should actually do — pick the cheapest check
that proves the candidate FD is wired up:
  * Confirm `inotify_init()` returned >= 0 and the watch was added.
  * Touch the config file once, do a `read(fd, IN_NONBLOCK)`, assert
    you got the `IN_MODIFY`. That single round-trip is the strongest
    proof and is the one I'd push for — it costs ~one syscall and
    catches the "FD allocated but watch path wrong" class of bug
    that "looks valid" checks miss.

Focused tests (the three you named):

  T1 — repeated successful reloads do not grow FD count
    Loop reload N=100 (or higher; the soak reached 60 so 200 is a
    comfortable margin) on a real config file in a temp dir.
    Sample `/proc/self/fd` count (or wrap a `lsof -p $PID | wc -l`)
    before and after. Assert the delta is bounded by a small constant
    (e.g., <= 3 to absorb unrelated growth in test-runner FDs).
    Tighter assertion: filter to inotify FDs only and assert that
    count is exactly 1 — that's the regression assertion. This test
    fails today and will pass after the patch.

  T2 — failed validation leaves the active watcher intact and
       leaks no FDs
    Construct a config that fails schema validation (or one that
    fails the touch-and-read check in step 2 — e.g., point at a
    path you can't watch). Call reload. Assert three things:
      (a) `loader.active_watcher is old_watcher`  — pointer unchanged
      (b) inotify FD count is unchanged from before the call
      (c) the old watcher still receives a subsequent edit you make
          to the original config path. (c) is the test that proves
          step 1 didn't accidentally retire `old` early.

  T3 — uninterrupted file watching across the swap
    Pre-condition: an edit-to-handler pipeline is wired through
    `loader.active_watcher`. Concurrently: a writer thread mutates
    the config file on a tight loop (~1ms cadence) while the main
    thread fires reloads at ~10ms cadence for ~1s.
    Post-condition: every writer iteration `i` that the filesystem
    observed must be delivered to the handler, modulo inotify's
    coalescing on rapid same-file writes. Assert:
      - the sequence of received versions is monotonically
        non-decreasing (no out-of-order; proves a single owner)
      - the largest gap between consecutive received versions is
        below a coalescing threshold you calibrate once (e.g., <10)
      - the final received version equals the last writer iteration
        (proves no edit was permanently dropped during a swap)
    A simpler variant if concurrent is annoying: between
    `loader.reload()` start and return, do N writes to the file.
    Assert all N reached the handler. That directly tests the
    "swap window" without needing threads.

For Nadia's patch, the only mechanical changes are: add the
`candidate.close()` on the validation-failure path, add the
`old.close()` after the pointer swap (under the same lock), and
wrap the swap+close in a single critical section. The reload loop
itself doesn't change shape — just the cleanup that was missing.

Why the current rule misses the case

`rate(batch_completed_total{job="nightly"}[5m]) == 0` only matches when samples are present and the per-second rate is zero — i.e., the counter is alive but not advancing. When the exporter disappears, the series goes stale and `rate()` returns no vector at all. The `== 0` comparison never gets a left-hand side, so the alert never enters pending. That is the bug.

Customer-facing distinction (present-but-flat vs. absent):

  - Present counter, zero increase — samples are arriving, the exporter is scraping, the job is just not producing work. `rate(...) == 0` catches this case.

  - Absent series — no samples at all in the window. The exporter may be down, the scrape target may have been removed from service discovery, or the job may have stopped emitting entirely. `rate(...)` cannot see this case at all; only `absent_over_time` can.

In other words: `rate(...) == 0` answers "is the counter moving?" and `absent_over_time(...) == 1` answers "is anything being scraped at all?" The customer wants the second question.

The fix

  expr: absent_over_time(batch_completed_total{job="nightly"}[15m]) == 1
  for: 0m

`absent_over_time(metric[15m])` returns a vector with value 1 when no samples landed in the last 15 minutes for a given label set, and an empty vector otherwise. `for: 0m` is correct here because the 15-minute detection window is already encoded in the expression; adding `for: 15m` on top would push effective detection out to roughly 30 minutes. If they want a small debounce against a single missed scrape, `for: 1m` or `for: 2m` is a normal choice — but `for: 0m` is the baseline that matches "alert after 15 minutes of silence."

Test expectations

  Positive — alert SHOULD fire:

    - No samples in the last 15 minutes (exporter absent, or last scrape older than 15m). `absent_over_time` evaluates to 1; alert fires within one evaluation cycle after the window has been empty for the full 15 minutes.

  Negative — alert SHOULD NOT fire:

    - A recent sample (e.g., one scraped 30 seconds ago). `absent_over_time` returns an empty vector; no fire. This confirms the rule does not flap on healthy targets.

    - A continuously scraped counter that stays flat — samples arriving every scrape interval, value unchanged. Same outcome: samples exist in the window, function returns an empty vector, no fire. This is the case the original `rate(...) == 0` rule was meant to catch, and worth calling out for the customer: under the new rule, "alive but not advancing" is intentionally NOT a paging condition. If they also want to alert on a flat-but-present counter, that should be a separate alert using the original `rate(...) == 0` pattern, not folded into the absent-data rule.

The picture you describe — a slow FOOSH-type mechanism, mild (2/10) soreness, no swelling, no deformity, full motion and grip, and a negative snuffbox — is reassuring and most consistent with a wrist sprain/contusion. Conservative care is reasonable today, but wrist injuries (notably scaphoid-related ones) can evolve over 24-72 hours, so monitor for the flags below.

TODAY'S CARE (rest of the day):

 1. Activity: stop the aggravating motion. No more soccer today, and avoid heavy lifting, push-ups, hard gripping, or weight-bearing through that hand.
 2. Ice: 15-20 minutes on the sore spot, then 40+ minutes off. Repeat every 2-3 hours while awake. Use a thin cloth between the ice and your skin.
 3. Compression: a snug elastic bandage or store-bought wrist sleeve. It should feel supportive, not tight — remove it if your fingers feel cold, numb, or tingly.
 4. Elevation: when sitting, rest the hand on a pillow above heart level to limit swelling.
 5. OTC analgesia: ibuprofen 400-600 mg with food every 6-8 hours (max ~1200 mg/day OTC) OR naproxen 220 mg every 8-12 hours with food. If NSAIDs are rough on your stomach, or you have any reason to avoid them (kidney issues, ulcers, blood thinners, etc.), acetaminophen 500-1000 mg every 6 hours is the alternative. Ibuprofen plus ice tends to help this kind of soft-tissue soreness best.
 6. Optional night-time support: a removable drugstore wrist splint in a neutral position for comfort while you sleep. Not a hard cast. Take it off to ice and to gently flex/extend the fingers a few times so they don't stiffen up.

Recheck tomorrow morning. If it's trending better, you can gradually resume light activity. If it's unchanged or worse after 3-5 days, get it looked at.

GET URGENT (same-day) IN-PERSON EVALUATION IF:

 - Visible deformity, bump, or a wrist that just looks "off"
 - Rapid or significant new swelling
 - Spreading bruising or any skin color change over the wrist/hand
 - Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the fingers or thumb
 - Fingers going cold, pale, or blue
 - Pain clearly worse than today's 2/10, or pain that wakes you from sleep
 - Sudden loss of grip, or inability to bear any weight through the hand
 - An open wound near the sore area, or any sign of infection (red streaks, fever, pus)

GET TIMELY (WITHIN A FEW DAYS) IN-PERSON EVALUATION IF:

 - Tenderness develops in the thumb-side anatomical snuffbox — the small hollow between the two thumb tendons at the base of your thumb when you extend it. Scaphoid injuries sometimes declare themselves this way over 24-72 hours, even when the initial check feels fine.
 - Pain when you push along the thumb toward the wrist (axial compression), or pain resisting thumb extension
 - Clicking, catching, snapping, or locking in the wrist
 - Soreness or stiffness persisting past 3-5 days without clear improvement
 - Pain that returns or worsens as you resume activity
 - Loss of range of motion that doesn't recover

Practical note: if you'd like a same-day hands-on read rather than waiting, urgent care or a walk-in orthopedic/sports-medicine clinic can examine it and decide whether an x-ray is warranted. The ER is fine but is overkill for this presentation.

  The contract isn't Figma-vs-repo — it's that there is exactly one machine-readable canonical source, every other representation is generated from it, every change is versioned through the same review path as code, and an automated drift check fails the build the moment a generated artifact diverges from its source. Whether the source lives in Figma Variables or in the repo JSON is your team's authoring call; the engineering guarantees are the same either way.

If you want a slightly more concrete framing for a design audience:

  Whichever surface your team authors in, the rest of the system treats it as derived — tokens flow one way out of the source, not back and forth. The hard requirements are: one authoritative file, generation as the only path downstream, version control and review on every change, and a CI check that catches drift before anyone ships it. The choice of authoring surface is workflow, not architecture.

Both leave the surface decision to her and her team, and neither restructures her proposal — they only pin down the engineering contract she can hang the rest on.

**Subject: How ingest-edge enforces the 10 MiB body limit (and how to stay safely under it)**

Hi [name],

Thanks for sending the payload details — that helps explain exactly what happened. Here is what's going on and how to get past it cleanly.

**Which size is enforced: decoded, not compressed**

ingest-edge counts the **decompressed (decoded) body** against the 10 MiB limit, not the bytes you put on the wire. The 10 MiB cap — 10,485,760 bytes — is a ceiling on the size of the request **after** gzip has been expanded. We have to enforce it there because every downstream consumer (parser, schema check, persistence) works on the decoded bytes. gzip is just a transport optimization; it does not change how large a logical request we're willing to accept.

This is why your 1.86 MiB compressed upload was rejected. On the wire it looked well within 10 MiB, but it decompressed to 14,889,779 bytes — about **4.2 MiB over** the decoded limit. The expansion ratio on your payload (≈7.6×) is on the high side, but gzip ratio depends entirely on the data, so we can't promise a fixed "X MiB on the wire is always safe."

**A conservative batching-and-retry procedure**

We're not raising the 10 MiB limit — that's a platform-wide ceiling — but you can comfortably fit under it by sizing your batches against the *decoded* size, not the compressed size. Concretely:

1. **Build and encode locally, then measure the decoded size** before sending (e.g. decompress your payload and check the byte count of the JSON body itself). Use that number as the truth.
2. **Target a batch whose decoded size is at or below 8 MiB** (8,388,608 bytes), and never exceed **9 MiB** (9,437,184 bytes) per request. The 9 MiB ceiling gives you roughly 1 MiB of headroom against the limit; the 8 MiB target gives you a comfortable safety margin for small variations in expansion across runs.
3. **If your batch is over 9 MiB decoded, split it.** A simple split-and-stagger (half, then the remainder, or several smaller groups) is fine — there's no minimum batch size and smaller batches don't change the contract.
4. **Retry only after the buffer drains.** The rejected payload is still buffered on your side; don't just resend the same 14.9 MiB-of-decoded payload. Once you've split it, send the smaller pieces and confirm each gets a 2xx before moving on.
5. **Leave gzip on.** Smaller payloads gzip even smaller, so compression is still a net win — just don't *rely* on it to get under the cap.

If you'd like, send us one of your typical decoded payloads' sizes and we can sanity-check it against this procedure before you retry. Happy to jump on a quick call if it's easier to walk through the splitting on your end.

Best,
[Engineer name]

The customer's intuition is reading off Content-Length, but that's the *compressed* (gzip) wire size — not the decoded payload size. The gateway enforces the limit on the decoded body, and it logs that explicitly:

- decoded_body_bytes: 14,889,779 bytes ≈ 14.2 MB
- max_decoded_body_bytes: 10,485,760 bytes = 10 MB exactly
- decision: reject, status 413, reason: "decoded body exceeds limit"

So the request was rejected because the decoded protobuf is ~14.2 MB, which is over the 10 MB cap. The wire size is irrelevant once the body is `Content-Encoding: gzip` — gzip is for transport efficiency, and applying a small limit to inflated data would be a trivial DoS (a few KB of zip-bomb would pass). The gateway is behaving correctly.

For the customer, the actionable question is what is making the decoded payload ~14 MB. A few usual suspects for protobuf ingestion:

- A batch/aggregate endpoint being used as a single-call bulk write when it should be chunked.
- Unbounded repeated fields — large lists, large maps, or many nested messages without pagination.
- Repeated embedding of whole sub-trees that should be referenced by id.
- Per-record fields that should be normalized (e.g. long repeated string fields that compress extremely well because they're highly repetitive — that's why gzip made 14.2 MB look like 1.86 MB on the wire).

Concrete next steps for the customer:

1. Confirm the endpoint and schema: which collection/table, and which repeated field is dominating the decoded size.
2. Chunk the submission so each request's decoded body stays under the 10 MB cap (with headroom).
3. If the data is inherently large per record, move to a streaming or upload-then-reference pattern rather than a single request body.

And a separate operational note: the request is still buffered on the client side and hasn't been retried. If retries are blind, the client will keep producing 413s; it needs to chunk before retry, or the same payload will fail the same way. The buffer should be drained/replayed only after the client is changed to send smaller batches.

DECISION: Accept the shape (pool is the right call - 34% alloc reduction is real value on a hot path). Reject the current implementation. Don't let it merge until there's a bound and eviction. The benchmark already proved the failure mode.

MEMORY-RISK EVIDENCE

  - Pod limit: 1 GiB. Steady-state observed: 910 MiB. That's ~87% utilization with no headroom for GC pause spikes, JIT/compiler transients, request-scoped allocations, or a traffic burst. OOM under realistic prod conditions is the expected outcome, not a tail risk.
  - The "doesn't fall back after idle" line is the load-bearing finding in the benchmark. Without eviction, worst-case pool size is bounded only by the cardinality of distinct buffers ever returned over the pod's lifetime. Today's cap is "process death."
  - The growth math: 910 - 420 = 490 MiB of retained growth, at 8 MiB per buffer = ~61 distinct entries. For a fixed-size pool that's far above what concurrency would justify. Open question for Wes: what keys the pool? If it's single-size 8 MiB, 61 retained entries means reuse isn't actually happening - that changes the bound. If it's size-class keyed, 61 distinct classes is the cardinality we have to budget for.
  - 90 minutes wasn't long enough. The trace shows a climb but doesn't show a plateau. We don't yet know if 910 MiB is steady-state or just a snapshot on the way up. The current benchmark can't answer its own question.

THE BOUND

  Two-layer cap, memory as the primary ceiling:

  1. Hard memory ceiling: 512 MiB for the pool. Leaves ~500 MiB for heap, GC metadata, runtime overhead, and request-scoped allocations. Real margin against a doubling of non-pool memory before we hit the OOM threshold.
  2. Soft eviction trigger: at ~384 MiB (75% of ceiling), start evicting cold entries. Eviction on access, not on insertion - LRU keeps hot buffers hot without forcing re-allocation churn on the working set.

  Why 512, not 768: 768 leaves 256 MiB headroom, which feels comfortable until the first GC-mark-phase spike or a traffic surge that doubles working-set memory. 512 leaves enough room that the OOM killer doesn't get a vote.

  Defense in depth: cap also by entry count (96 entries OR 512 MiB, whichever fires first). This protects against the case where a variable-size pool accumulates many smaller-than-8-MiB buffers.

  If the pool is actually variable-size, Wes needs to come back with the size distribution before the cap can be tight. The 61-entry count hints it might not be single-size.

THE TESTS

  1. Steady-load soak, extended
     - 8 hours minimum at p50 prod-shaped load.
     - Capture: pool MiB, entry count, GC pause distribution, p99/p999 latency, RSS.
     - Pass: pool plateaus within 30 min and holds; max RSS < 750 MiB; GC pause p99 within 10% of current baseline.
     - 90 min was insufficient. Need a trace long enough to see the plateau or prove there isn't one.

  2. Burst-and-idle
     - 5 min at p99 burst, then 10 min at zero load. Repeat 10 cycles.
     - Capture: pool size after each idle window, time to baseline.
     - Pass: pool returns to baseline within 5 min of idle. This is the test the current benchmark already failed. It's the gating test.

  3. Concurrency
     - Drive 2x p99 concurrent requests for 30 min.
     - Capture: lock contention on pool check path, p99/p999 latency, eviction-during-load behavior.
     - Race test: many workers get/return the same buffer slot simultaneously - verify no double-free, no use-after-evict, no torn read on the LRU pointer.
     - Pass: p99 latency under contention within 20% of single-thread; eviction during load doesn't cause a >2x p99 cliff.

Gate on burst-and-idle. That's the test that has to pass before this moves forward. The steady-load soak and concurrency tests are needed before merge; the burst-and-idle test is needed before the design is even worth another review cycle.

The shared parity fixture (added 3/6 per Hema) is the required prod-review gate for covered cross-service metric label renames. For a shard-keeper / rollup-service rename, it works like this:

  Before the production review can proceed, the affected engineering owners each run the shared parity fixture against their service's view of the label being renamed:
    - Producer side (shard-keeper owner) runs the fixture to confirm values emitted under the new label match what consumers currently key on.
    - Consumer side (metric-rollup / rollup-service owner) runs the fixture to confirm their read path still resolves correctly under the rename.
    - Each owner signs off on the run individually. Sign-off lands in the prod-review thread before the cross-service reviewer takes the change further.

  This is owner-driven by design — the cross-service reviewer (Alex, per the 2/23 gate corrected 2/27) covers invariants, failure modes, ownership seams, and escalation boundaries, but does not become a per-service approver. Service owners keep impl, telemetry, op-readiness, release, and go/no-go. The parity fixture is what they must clear.

Executable evidence (what "ran and passed" looks like)

  - Parity-fixture run output: the matched / mismatched label-value pairs across producer and consumer, for the affected label.
  - Owner-by-owner sign-off comment in the prod-review thread, tied to that specific fixture run (not a generic PR approval click).
  - A reference back to the fixture's known-good baseline so reviewers can reproduce locally rather than trusting the summary.

  The bar is both sign-offs present in the prod-review thread. If either is missing, the change is blocked at the prod-review gate — not "approved anyway with a note."

Additional pre-production checks (complements, does not replace)

  - Label-cardinality preflight — catches label-explosion risk on the new label before the rename ships. Still required.
  - Alert-source classification — confirms alerts routing or deduping on the old label either resolve under the rename or have been explicitly migrated. Still required.
  - Owner-map freshness on the affected services — so the fixture sign-off actually comes from the named maintainer.

Concrete shape, applied to the case in question (e.g. `shard_region` → `storage_region`)

  1. Parity fixture run on shard-keeper producer side → signed off by shard-keeper owner.
  2. Parity fixture run on rollup-service consumer side → signed off by metric-rollup owner.

  4. Any of the three checks missing or ambiguous → blocked; surfaces to the owners (and Alex only if the seam itself is unclear), not scope-widened.

The control is narrow on purpose: it covers cross-service label renames, not every metric change. Sounds textbook for seasonal allergic rhinitis + allergic conjunctivitis — clear drainage and itching (not pain) in both eyes are the hallmark allergy pattern, and your negatives rule out the usual look-alikes (no fever/body aches → not viral; no facial pain → not sinusitis; no SOB/wheeze → not asthma/anaphylaxis; no eye pain, normal vision → not serious eye pathology).

TONIGHT
- Shower + wash hair/face as soon as you're in. Pollen on skin, lashes, and pillow fuels the cycle all night.
- Saline nasal rinse (neti pot or squeeze bottle with distilled/boiled water, or saline spray). Flushes allergens out of the nasal mucosa.
- Cool compress over closed eyes, 5-10 min, for the itch.
- Don't rub your eyes. Mechanical irritation amplifies the histamine response and can worsen swelling.
- Take a non-sedating antihistamine now: loratadine 10 mg OR fexofenadine 180 mg. With water, not juice — grapefruit/apple/orange juice cuts fexofenadine absorption significantly.
- If eyes are the dominant complaint: ketotifen 0.025% (Zaditor / Alaway), 1 drop each eye twice daily. OTC, no sedation.
- Bedroom: windows closed, A/C or fan on a clean filter if you have one. Don't dry the day's clothes/sheets outside.
- Skip pseudoephedrine tonight. It's non-sedating but it's a stimulant — easier to use tomorrow morning only if you actually need a decongestant.

TOMORROW MORNING
- Same non-sedating antihistamine, daily. Daily dosing beats PRN for allergic rhinitis.
- Add an intranasal corticosteroid: fluticasone (Flonase) or mometasone (Nasacort), 2 sprays each nostril. First-line, no sedation. It won't help much today but starting now matters because full effect takes a few days.
- Saline rinse before you head out.
- Sunglasses outdoors — physical barrier against pollen hitting the conjunctiva.
- Ketotifen drops again in the morning if the itch persists.
- Shower when you get home to remove pollen before it migrates to your pillow.

OTC OPTIONS, RANKED BY SEDATION RISK AT WORK
  Lowest (essentially none)
    Fexofenadine (Allegra) 180 mg qd — with water, not juice
    Loratadine (Claritin) 10 mg qd
  Low for most people
    Cetirizine (Zyrtec) 10 mg qd — slightly more sedating than the above two; fine for many, but if you're sensitive to it, swap to fexofenadine
    Intranasal fluticasone or mometasone — first-line, no sedation
    Intranasal azelastine (Astepro) — fast-acting antihistamine spray; occasional bitter taste, rare somnolence
    Ketotifen or olopatadine eye drops — for the eyes, no sedation
  Avoid before/during work
    Diphenhydramine (Benadryl), doxylamine, hydroxyzine, chlorpheniramine — first-generation, cross the blood-brain barrier heavily, impair alertness and reaction time even if you "feel fine"

WARNING SIGNS — WORTH PROMPT MEDICAL ATTENTION
Respiratory
  - Wheezing, chest tightness, new cough, shortness of breath
  - Throat tightness, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, drooling
  - Stridor (high-pitched sound on inhale)
  - Fever >100.4 F / 38 C, chills — argues for sinus or respiratory infection
  - Severe facial pain / pressure or thick yellow-green nasal discharge persisting >10 days (acute bacterial sinusitis)
  - Coughing up blood

Eye
  - Eye pain — anything beyond itch or scratchiness
  - Vision change: blur, decrease, halos, double vision
  - Light sensitivity (photophobia)
  - Marked redness with thick discharge, or feeling of something stuck in the eye
  - Pupil looks different size or shape than usual

Systemic / allergic emergency
  - Hives or a spreading rash
  - Swelling of lips, tongue, face, or throat (angioedema)
  - Dizziness, near-fainting, sense of dread
  - Nausea/vomiting together with any of the above
  - Any cluster of these after a known or suspected trigger = anaphylaxis — use epinephrine if available and call 911

If symptoms are still daily and bothersome after 2 weeks of OTC treatment, or if they keep flaring, see a clinician — there are prescription antihistamine doses, leukotriene modifiers, and allergy testing / immunotherapy that can change the trajectory. Minimal deterministic behavior: reject any config that sets both keys. Check presence, not value agreement — the rule is about authoring state ("the operator hasn't finished migrating off the legacy key") rather than whether the values happen to coincide, and a value-equality rule would still leave map-iteration coupling lurking in the code.

Why not the alternatives:
  - "Replacement wins if both set" silently masks the migration gap. The staging config is exactly the bug surface you want loud.
  - "Legacy wins if both set" preserves the bug shape with a different arbitrary winner.
  - "Error only when values disagree" lets coexistence pass silently when they match, which is the same nondeterministic design wearing a thin disguise.

Error message should name both keys and say which to remove. Keep the deprecation warning on legacy-only configs intact — that's the migration pressure you want.

Startup tests (parser unit, deterministic, no map-iteration dependence):

  dual-key rejected (different values): `max_batch_bytes=8388608` + `max_request_bytes=12582912` → error mentions both key names. Use the staging values verbatim so the test reads as the actual bug.
  dual-key rejected (same values): both keys present, both set to the same number → still error. Guards against a reviewer "simplifying" the rule to value-equality later.
  legacy-only accepted: `max_batch_bytes=8388608`, no replacement → parses, effective limit is 8388608, deprecation warning emitted. Assert on the warning so a refactor can't silently drop it.
  replacement-only accepted: `max_request_bytes=12582912`, no legacy → parses, effective limit is 12582912, no warning.
  neither key: falls through to default; assert the default value, not just success.

Live-reload tests (loader + reload transaction, integration-level):

  failed reload preserves active (the operational test): load replacement-only A, assert active. Attempt dual-key reload → returns error. Assert effective config still equals A — not zero, not partial, not the rejected config. Then load legacy-only B and assert it takes effect. This is what stops a bad config push during rollout from blanking the service.
  successful legacy-only reload: from replacement-active state, load legacy-only; assert deprecation warning and the new effective value.
  successful replacement-only reload: happy-path replacement → replacement.
  reload is atomic on failure: assert that validation runs before any in-memory swap. Easiest form: after the failed dual-key reload above, no field of the active config has changed beyond what the previous successful load set.
  reload idempotent on bad input: same dual-key config parsed twice returns the same error both times. Guards against any residual map-iteration coupling in the validator itself.

Two small things worth pinning in the patch:
  - The check is presence-based, not value-based — make the "same value, still error" test explicit so it isn't softened later.
  - Capture the legacy deprecation warning in a test assertion, not just a log line, so it can't quietly disappear in a future refactor.

   - Do not force food or water.
   - Do not give milk, yogurt, butter, or any food remedy.
   - Do not give activated charcoal at home — wrong tool for a local irritant, aspiration risk.
   - Do not scrub or rinse the mouth forcefully; inflamed tissue tears easily.
   - Do not assume "he's fine" and walk away. Oral swelling can develop over several hours even when initial signs are mild.

5. Go to an emergency vet immediately if you see any of these
   - Noisy breathing, stridor (high-pitched sound on inhale), or any visible effort to breathe.
   - Swelling of the tongue, lips, face, or throat — even mild.
   - Persistent drooling that doesn't ease within 30–60 minutes, or refusal to swallow.
   - Repeated vomiting, gagging, or retching.
   - Pawing at the face or rubbing the mouth on the floor without stopping.
   - Hives, sudden itch, red/flushed skin.
   - Weakness, wobbliness, collapse, pale or blue gums, loss of consciousness.

Plan for the next few hours: keep Kibo with you, no food for 30 minutes, cool water available if he wants it, recheck inside of mouth and breathing every 30–60 minutes for the next 4–6 hours. The poison line will tell you if tonight needs an overnight watch too.

  3. The current draft of your 2023 return in the software
  4. Confirmations for any other 2023 estimated payments (Q1/Q2/

----------------------------------
Jan 15, 2024 was MLK Day; the Q4 2023 estimated tax deadline
slid to Tuesday Jan 16, 2024. Your Jan 15 payment was one day

says for tax year and tax type. Three cases:

  - Tax year 2024, type 1040-ES -> you accidentally paid your

  - Tax year 2023, type Balance Due -> you paid it as if

PHASE 2: ENTER IT INTO THE SOFTWARE (5 min)
-------------------------------------------
Open the federal "Estimated tax payments" section:

  1. Add a payment (do NOT replace anything; add)

The 200 indicates the transport outcome, not the data outcome of every record inside the payload. In OTLP/HTTP, a 200 response with a `partialSuccess` field in the body means the server received the request, inspected it end-to-end, accepted some records, and rejected the rest. The HTTP status covers the request; `partialSuccess` covers the contents.

  - `partialSuccess.rejectedDataPoints: 487` is the count of records the backend refused to persist. Everything *not* in that count is already in the backend's storage and is durable.
  - `errorMessage` ("exponential histogram scale 25 exceeds supported range [-10,20]") describes why those 487 were rejected. Here the cause is structural: the rejected records carry an exponential-histogram scale value that the receiver will not accept. Per the OTLP spec, the supported range for scale is currently [-10, 20], so scale=25 is spec-invalid; the receiver is enforcing the spec range, not a narrower custom range.

Resending the entire batch is the wrong move, for two independent reasons:

  1. It duplicates the accepted records. The non-rejected records are already stored. Re-sending them produces double-counted metrics and broken aggregations on the customer's side, and the receiver does not know which records were already accepted, so it cannot de-dup them.
  2. The 487 will be rejected again with the same error. The scale value is a property of the histogram data itself, not a transient condition. There is no recovery by retry.

One nuance the customer is likely to ask about: the `partialSuccess` body only reports a count, not an enumeration of which specific records were rejected. The protocol deliberately omits per-record identification (it would be expensive at scale). So even "retry only the rejected ones" is not a viable operation — they can't be picked out of the original batch.

Safe replay guidance for this specific batch:

  - Do NOT resend the original batch. The accepted portion is already stored; the rejected portion will fail again.
  - Pinpoint the source of the scale-25 histograms. Current OpenTelemetry SDKs cap maximum scale at the spec limit (20) by default, so scale=25 means either a non-conformant SDK/instrumentation library, a custom aggregator that bypasses the default cap, or an exporter rewriting bucket boundaries into an invalid scale. The customer needs to identify the offending metric stream and code path.
  - Fix at the source. Three viable options, in rough order of preference:
      1. Upgrade/downgrade the SDK or instrumentation library to a version that respects the spec cap on maximum scale.
      2. Configure the exporter's aggregation to clamp maximum scale to a value the receiver accepts (some SDKs expose this as a reader/aggregation option).
      3. Switch the affected instruments to explicit-bucket histograms. Explicit buckets have no scale-range issue at all.
  - Verify with a fresh batch after the fix lands. The response should have no `partialSuccess` (or an empty one). Do not use the original batch as the verification probe.

Short paragraph Support can paste or adapt into the ticket:

    The 200 you saw confirms the request was received and fully inspected; it does not mean every record was accepted. Your response body reports 487 rejected data points with the reason "exponential histogram scale 25 exceeds supported range [-10,20]". The other records in the batch have already been stored on our side, so we recommend against resending the full batch — re-sending would duplicate the accepted records, and the 487 will be rejected again for the same reason, since the scale value is a property of the histogram data itself. To resolve, the SDK or aggregation producing these histograms needs to respect the maximum scale of 20 (the OpenTelemetry spec limit). If you can share which SDK/instrumentation version produced these and which metric stream they came from, we can help narrow down the fix.

Two facts to land if the customer pushes back on the "don't resend" guidance: (a) the accepted records are already in storage and resending duplicates them, and (b) the rejected 487 will fail on every retry until the histogram source is corrected, so resending is pure cost with zero recovery.

Plan for two — warm lemon-garlic chickpeas over couscous with yogurt sauce. ~25 min active, holds cleanly for an hour-plus if her shift slips.

Quantities (for 2 with a little leftover)

- Couscous: 1 cup dry
- Canned chickpeas: 1 can (15 oz), drained and rinsed
- Cherry tomatoes: 1 pint (~2 cups), halved
- Baby spinach: 4 oz (about 3 generous handfuls)
- Garlic: 4 cloves total — 2 sliced thin for the pan, 1 grated for yogurt sauce, 1 minced for finishing
- Lemon: 1 whole
- Yogurt: 1/2 cup plain (whole milk if you have it)
- Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper, ground cumin, smoked or sweet paprika

Timing math
Start at 8:05 PM, dinner ready at 8:30 PM. If she walks in at 9:30 PM, that's a 60-min gap — covered in the hold section below. If she slips past 9:45, push the spinach step to her actual ETA so it stays bright.

Sequence (active cooking ~22 min)

1. Pot: 1 1/4 cups water + 1 tbsp olive oil + 1/2 tsp salt. Bring to a boil. Stir in couscous, return to a boil, cover, kill the heat. Set a timer for 5 min — do not peek.

2. Pan, medium heat, 3 tbsp olive oil. Add the 2 sliced garlic cloves, 3/4 tsp cumin, 1/2 tsp paprika. Stir 30 sec — just fragrant, not brown.

3. Add the drained chickpeas and a generous pinch of salt. Toss 3 min until warmed through and the edges look slightly dry/crisp.

4. Add the halved cherry tomatoes and another pinch of salt. Toss 3-4 min until they soften and a few start to burst and jammy-up. Splash in 2 tbsp water and scrape any brown bits.

5. Couscous timer should be done. Fluff with a fork — should be tender with no white core. If still raw, re-cover for 1-2 min. Cover the pot again and turn off the burner.

6. Yogurt sauce (small bowl): 1/2 cup yogurt + juice of half the lemon + the grated garlic clove + pinch of salt. Stir, taste, add more lemon if flat.

7. Kill the heat under the chickpea pan. Fold the minced garlic clove and the spinach in — residual heat wilts it in 30-45 sec. Squeeze in the other lemon half. Taste for salt.

8. Plate: couscous base, chickpea-spinach-tomato on top, big dollop of yogurt sauce. Optional: drizzle of olive oil, pinch of paprika.

Hold strategy if her departure slips (the important part)

- Couscous: covered off-heat holds 60 min no problem. Fluff again at the 30-min mark and at serving. If it looks dry, stir in 2-3 tbsp hot water and re-cover.
- Chickpea-tomato pan: covered on the lowest burner setting (or off-heat with the lid on) holds 30-45 min well. Tomatoes break down more but the flavor gets better, not worse.
- Hold the spinach OUT of the pan until 5 min before she walks in. Wilted spinach that sits covered turns gray and watery — that is the only thing in this recipe that does not forgive waiting.
- Yogurt sauce: cover and park in the fridge. Take it out 5 min before serving so it isn't cold.

Quick finish at her ETA (~5 min)

1. Crank the chickpea pan to medium, splash in 1 tbsp water to re-loosen, toss 1 min.
2. Off heat — fold in the spinach and minced garlic, wilt 30 sec, squeeze of lemon.
3. Fluff couscous (add a splash of hot water if tight), plate, dollop yogurt.

If she ends up much later than 9:45 PM, the couscous and chickpea pan will both still be fine; just refresh with the water trick and wilt fresh spinach at the end. The lemon-garlic-yogurt contrast is what makes this feel light rather than heavy, so don't skip the sauce or skip the lemon squeeze at the end.

Quick assessment: the missing items (no SSN, no bank info, no fee, no coercion) rule out the worst-case scenarios. But "photo ID + two pay stubs + current address" before you've even walked through the door is genuinely overreach — that's application-stage paperwork, not viewing-stage paperwork. "Pre-registration" isn't a recognized term in NYC rentals; legitimate brokers either call it a pre-qualification or just confirm attendance. So the picture is: non-standard request, not necessarily a scam, but the right move is to provide less now and reserve the actual documents for when you actually apply.

Reasonable to provide NOW (the minimum):
  - Just your name, phone, and email to confirm the slot — that's it.
  - Optionally, a one-line pre-qual statement ("two adults, combined gross ~$X, target move-in Y date") if they refuse to confirm attendance without one. This is a soft pre-qual, not a document.
  - Photo ID only if they explicitly justify it for a private showing (some private listings do require ID confirmation at the door — fine to ask why).

Wait until you actually choose to apply:
  - Color copies of photo IDs (front and back).
  - Two recent pay stubs.
  - Proof of current address (utility bill, bank statement, or lease — whichever you have).
  - SSN — only via their secure application portal, only after you've seen the unit and decided to apply.
  - Bank statements and credit-check authorization — only if requested during application.

Why the line matters even though they didn't ask for the worst stuff:
  Pay stubs alone disclose employer, pay period, deductions, and partial routing/account numbers — enough for a determined actor to start an identity-reconstruction attempt. A color scan of a driver's license is enough to defeat a lot of account-recovery flows. None of this is theoretical; it's the typical Phase 1 of rental-themed phishing. The fact that they were polite and didn't ask for SSN doesn't change that — you're still emailing PII to a recipient you haven't verified.

Red flags worth pulling the thread on if they appear:
  - Insisting on documents before the viewing after you push back.
  - Asking later for SSN, bank login, or any fee (application, "credit check," "hold deposit").
  - Won't meet you at the actual unit, or wants you to wire money to an out-of-state account.
  - Email domain doesn't match the brokerage on the listing.

Recommended next step — short reply you can send:

Diagnosis: attestation-subject mismatch. Not artifact substitution.

Reasoning:
- Expected subject `sha256:9f41d8c0...` is the registry manifest list — the multi-arch index that resolves when the tag is pulled. That's what the release pipeline has nominated as the promoted artifact.
- Attested subject `sha256:21b77a6e...` is the linux/amd64 image manifest — a single-platform object that the build actually signed during the per-platform build step.
- A manifest list and a platform image are structurally distinct OCI objects. They will never share a digest by design. The build produced both; the verifier is comparing apples to the basket.
- There is no substitution indicator here (no second digest, no pulled-vs-pushed divergence in the record). Both digests are legitimate outputs of the same build — the attestation just names the wrong layer.

Why it is not artifact substitution:
- In a substitution case, the artifact you intend to deploy is replaced by something else after attestation. Here the promoted digest and the attested digest refer to different layers of the same OCI content tree — not to a swap. The promoted artifact is still the manifest list the pipeline produced.
- A substitution would normally be caught by a *matching* attestation whose subject disagrees with what was actually pulled at deploy time, not by a *non-matching* attestation that names a legitimate but different object from the same build.

Safe release correction (no verification bypass):
1. Keep the promoted artifact as the manifest list `sha256:9f41d8c0...`. Do not repoint staging to the linux/amd64 digest silently — that would be a scope change masquerading as a fix and would forfeit multi-arch for the release.
2. Regenerate the provenance attestation so its subject is the manifest list digest, with the per-platform attestation (subject `sha256:21b77a6e...`) carried as related material / evidence chain. This is the canonical SLSA pattern for multi-arch: attest the index after the index exists, not the platform image in isolation.
3. Re-run the verifier. With the new attestation, the equality check on `promoted artifact digest == attestation subject digest` should pass on the manifest-list subject.

If your build system cannot emit an index-level attestation in the current Lantern permission scope (the prov + perm-bounded constraint in your notes), the tactical alternative that still doesn't bypass verification is: for this single release only, promote the linux/amd64 image by digest and document the scope narrowing (single-arch staging, multi-arch restored at the next index-level attestation). That is a deliberate narrowing, not an exception.

- Don't add a policy exception or a "skip if attestation exists" carve-out to clear this — that would be the bypass to avoid, and it would also undermine the Lantern evidence chain for the next drill.

The failure is on the exemplar's label set, not on the series labels. ingest-edge validates series labels and exemplar labels as two separate passes against two separate rule sets. The series labels and timestamps for series_index=17 passed (the error names no series-side field), and the only thing that failed is the exemplar attached to that sample — specifically the `trace_id` label inside that exemplar, which is 142 bytes against the 128-byte per-label-value cap that ingest-edge enforces for exemplar labels.

Shortening an ordinary sample label will not help. The 128-byte cap is checked against each label value in the exemplar's own label set. The series label set is in a different validation scope and isn't even examined when the exemplar fails. Reducing the size of a series label (`job`, `instance`, anything on the metric) does not affect the length of the exemplar's `trace_id`, so the exemplar still fails the same way. The series labels are already valid; they are not the problem.

The unchanged request cannot be retried. The 400 is deterministic on the byte content of the exemplar. Resending the exact same payload produces the same `exemplar label value exceeds 128 bytes` failure on the same `trace_id`. The customer only burns 4xx budget.

What the customer must change before retrying: shorten the exemplar's `trace_id` to ≤128 bytes. Nothing else in the request needs to change — the series labels, timestamps, and the rest of the exemplar are already valid. Three practical paths:

  - Switch to a tracing scheme whose IDs fit. W3C trace-context 128-bit IDs hex-encode to 32 chars; OpenTelemetry-compatible IDs are 16 or 32 hex chars. A 142-char `trace_id` strongly suggests they're using either a non-standard ID format, a namespace prefix (`trace-svc-...`, vendor prefixes, etc.), or a tracing backend that packs extra context into the ID string itself.
  - Strip any prefix or wrapper from the `trace_id` value so the bare ID fits.
  - Truncating is not recommended — it breaks trace correlation in whatever backend the exemplars point at.

One caveat for Support: if the customer's underlying ask is to raise the cap rather than shorten their IDs, that's a tenant-side ingest-edge config change, not a payload change. That is a separate request and Support should not promise it can be granted on the same 400.

Logged. Full rollout retained on Wes's independent read — retry peaks, p99, 5xx, throughput, and post-429 burst behavior all within the agreed bounds, no remediation loops opened. Nothing pending on my end.

Decision: keep 429 admission rejection. Do not switch to evict-oldest.

The eviction model doesn't reduce lost work, it relocates it from a visible place (caller sees 429, sheds load) to an invisible one (caller sees 200, has no idea the oldest items were dropped). The freshness improvement Wes measured is real but comes from hiding loss rather than reducing it, and hidden loss is harder to operate against than visible loss. Specific reasons:

1. Honest back-pressure is the only signal path that lets upstream producers react. With 429 + Retry-After, the producer can shed load, retry on a sane cadence, or tag the gap in its own telemetry. With eviction, the producer sees success and has no reason to compensate.

2. Eviction is non-deterministic under correlated load. Wes's test is synthetic; real load arrives in bursts driven by downstream blips. Evict-oldest in that regime tends to evict the same retrying client repeatedly - the one already over capacity. FIFO and fairness don't agree.

3. Partial-state ambiguity at eviction. A queued item has had parse, route lookup, and fan-out prep. Whether it's safe to drop depends on what downstream consumers can already see. For metrics-router's multi-destination fan-out, the answer is "not safe without an explicit cancel we don't have."

4. Recovery gets worse. After the queue drops below cap, eviction has to reconcile "we returned 200 but didn't deliver X oldest items." Downstream observability sees X missing with no marker. With 429, the producer knows immediately and chooses re-emit or skip.

5. Freshness is the wrong metric to chase. If the load test shows rejection at steady state, the question is whether the SLO permits that rejection rate, not how to hide it. Eviction can lower admission-time queue depth without lowering mean staleness - it shifts which requests get delayed.

If freshness is actually the constraint, the right moves are: a separate fast-lane queue for time-sensitive items (liveness, heartbeats) with its own cap and rejection signal; tune Retry-After against observed drain rate rather than a fixed value; if the steady-state rejection rate breaches the SLO, that's a capacity or sharding question, not an eviction question.

Focused tests required:

Retry signaling
- 429 is returned before any state mutation: no admitted counter increment, no log line implying "received," no fan-out prep started.
- 429 carries Retry-After whose value is bounded by observed drain time and tracks current queue depth, not a static config.
- A single caller under sustained overload sees a stable reject ratio across a request burst - no accept/reject oscillation within a burst.
- 429 body or headers carry reason="queue_full" so the caller can branch behavior.
- Retry-After is never zero or negative (would cause immediate retry storms) and never exceeds a configurable ceiling.

Ordering
- Across the full 0 to cap range, FIFO order is preserved for admitted items.
- An admitted request never appears before an earlier-arriving admitted request on any fan-out leg, including cross-tenant fan-out.
- tenant_size_class and build_channel routing decisions for an admitted item are stable regardless of current queue depth - no depth-dependent routing drift.

Accounting
- admitted_total + rejected_total{reason="queue_full"} == received_total. No silent gaps.
- Downstream send counters reconcile: per tenant per window, sent_to_destination equals admitted_for_tenant. No admitted-but-not-sent drift.
- Reject counter carries tenant_size_class and build_channel labels so pressure is attributable to a tenant or channel, not only visible in aggregate.
- Per the existing convention: the below-threshold slice of any new reject counter stays a release-validation / validation-fixture annotation only - no alert, threshold, or page wired off it.

Recovery after queue falls below cap
- New admissions resume within one drain interval after depth drops below cap. No artificial hold or hysteresis.
- Retry-After value decays monotonically as depth drops.
- No thundering herd: clients holding back via Retry-After do not all retry at the same instant when capacity returns. Jitter or token-bucket pacing on the client side is in scope; the server-side test verifies that admission rate at recovery doesn't exceed processing rate by more than a small bounded factor.
- In-flight items at the moment of recovery complete cleanly. Fan-out is not interrupted or duplicated for them.
- Steady-state behavior after recovery is identical to behavior before the saturation event. No leaked state, no degraded routing, no stuck connections in the rejected path.

If Wes wants eviction retained as a configurable behavior for a specific subset of metrics where freshness genuinely beats completeness, the tests above are still the bar - silent partial success should not ship without each of those passing under sustained overload with realistic retry patterns, not just synthetic load.

The skate tells you the smear is being pulled, not pressed. On a polished slab hold, any horizontal component of force blows it out. Two things to change: how the sidepull is loaded, and which body part initiates the reach.

Try this sequence on the next attempt:

  1. Foot before hand. Set the left smear with the pad of your big toe pressed into the dimple, knee bent so the shin angles toward the wall. Before the right hand does any work, drive the left foot straight down into the slab. You should feel the smear load up — if it doesn't, the foot is too flat or the knee is too straight.

  2. Straighten the right arm. The shallow sidepull is a stabilizer, not a pull hold. Bend the arm to set it, then straighten it and drop the right hip a few inches. This shifts your body weight off the sidepull and onto the left foot. If you feel the smear start to compress, you're in the right position.

  3. Shift hips before reaching. With the right arm straight and the left foot pressing, drive the hips left and up — toward the wall, not out from it. The high left edge should feel close before your hand leaves the sidepull.

  4. Reach last. The left hand floats up to the edge from hip movement, not from a hard pull. Think of it as placing, not grabbing.

A few specifics on the right foot: "low and outside" is pulling your center of mass away from the wall, which is what's loading the smear in shear. Options:

  - Flag the right foot out to the right (toe pointed) and use it as a counterweight, not a base. This frees the hips to track straight up.
  - Bring the right foot up to a heel hook on whatever volume is near the sidepull if one exists.
  - Step the right foot onto the same plane as the left smear to make a narrow stacked base — narrower is usually better on slabs.

One more: exhaling hard on the press helps the core brace, and a quick scuff of the shoe rubber on the wall (or on your thigh) before stepping on the smear resets the grip on a polished hold.

Support guidance for the customer's 429 handling against ingest-edge:

The 1-3 second Retry-After values they are seeing are the expected production behavior. The server-side randomization was deployed in v2.19.4 specifically to break the synchronized retry bursts seen with the pre-v2.19.4 baseline. It is not a hint that something is wrong, and the values are not expected to be constant.

Direct answers to their three questions:

1. Can they cache the first Retry-After and reuse it for all later retries? No. Each 429 response carries its own value. The server does not promise, and should not be assumed, to return the same value on the next 429. Treat each response's header as a fresh signal for that retry.

2. Should they add their own jitter on top? Yes, in addition to (not instead of) honoring the header. The server-side randomization breaks synchronization across the whole client population; client-side jitter breaks synchronization across the customer's own workers / replicas / processes. Both layers serve different purposes, and the customer's layer still matters even though the server is now randomizing.

3. Does a successful retry mean later 429s can be ignored? No. A successful retry only confirms that one request cleared at that moment. It says nothing about the conditions that produced the 429, and it does not authorize the client to skip Retry-After on subsequent 429s. Each 429 should be honored on its own header.

Specific client behaviors Support should recommend:

- Read Retry-After on every 429 individually; treat that value as the minimum delay before that specific retry attempt.
- Do not assume the value is constant across responses, including across responses to identical requests.
- Add a small client-side random delay on top of the header's minimum.
- Preserve an overall retry budget (cap on total elapsed time, cap on total attempts) independent of any single Retry-After value. A long Retry-After is not authorization to retry forever.
- Avoid synchronized immediate retries across workers — even when the header value is identical, stagger the actual send time.
- After any retry attempt succeeds, do not relax 429 handling for subsequent requests on the same workload.

What Support should NOT say to the customer:

- That a retry is guaranteed to succeed. The 429 communicates load state, not a reservation.
- That the server-side change removes the need for client-side backoff. The server-side change reduces cross-client synchronization; per-client backoff, jitter, and a retry budget are still required.
