Quick read: the sputtering + cloudiness is almost certainly trapped air and loose sediment stirred up in the service line and riser — normal after a shutdown, and consistent with the kitchen cold clearing on its own. The yellow tint confined to the hot side after 30 seconds is almost certainly sediment from the water heater tank getting pulled when the tank refilled and you drew from it. No smell, no sediment, no boil notice all point to "stirred-up sediment," not a contamination event. The plan below assumes that; the reporting criteria tell you when to abandon that assumption.

Flushing order
  Aim: clear the service line first (cold), then the water heater (hot), working from highest-flow to lowest-flow fixtures, and clearing aerators so you can actually see when each fixture is clean.

  1. Confirm the main shutoff is fully open (apartment valve, not building). Open it slowly if you closed it for the shutdown.
  2. Remove aerators from the kitchen cold, bathroom hot, and any other faucet you'll flush. Sediment clogs the screen and will keep tinting the stream even after the line is clear.
  3. Cold side first, fixture by fixture:
     - Start at the fixture closest to the entry point and work outward.
     - Run each cold tap at a steady moderate flow — volume, not pressure.
     - Stop when the stream runs visually clear and stays clear for 1-2 minutes.
     - The kitchen cold already did most of this; flush another 1-2 minutes to confirm stable.
  4. Hot side, full flush:
     - Pick one fixture (bathtub is ideal — high flow, no aerator) and run hot continuously for 10-15 minutes.
     - The first minute or two will look worst; it should taper to clear.
     - If after 15 minutes the yellow tint is still visible, the heater itself probably needs a longer drain-and-flush — that's a building-management item, not yours.
  5. Walk every other hot fixture (kitchen, bathroom sink, shower) and run each for 2-3 minutes until clear.
  6. Reinstall aerators only after each tap has run clear — flushing with the aerator in place is far less effective.

Drinking water
  No boil-water notice means no mandatory advisory, and your symptoms don't match a contamination event. Practical rule of thumb:

  - Use the kitchen cold tap as your drinking source.
  - Run it 30-60 seconds before each use for the first 24 hours as a precaution; after that, normal use.
  - Don't drink from the hot tap — even when clear, hot-water lines aren't a designed potable source, and the heater tank is the sediment reservoir.
  - If any discoloration, sediment, or off smell reappears at any point, stop drinking from the tap and switch to bottled until the building clears it.

Appliance return to service
  Don't run either until both supply lines at the nearest tap are fully clear. Sediment in a dishwasher inlet valve or washing machine solenoid is a cheap way to break an expensive appliance.

  Washing machine:
    - Wait until both hot and cold run clear for several minutes at the nearest laundry or bathroom tap.
    - Run one empty cycle on cold only to flush the hoses and any sediment in the valve body.
    - Then a normal load is fine. Check the inlet filter screens on the hoses once after the first real cycle — small debris can collect there even after a clean flush.

  Dishwasher:
    - Same precondition: hot and cold clear.
    - Run an empty rinse cycle with no detergent to flush the supply line and the internal.
    - If you want to be thorough, follow with a normal cycle using a dishwasher cleaner (citric-acid based) to clear sediment from the spray arms and filter.
    - Then normal use.

When to report to management
  Treat this as "stirred-up sediment" for now, but escalate if any of these show up:

  - Yellow or brown tint persists in hot water past 15-20 minutes of full-flow flushing.
  - Tint appears in the cold side after the initial clearing — that points to the service line or building main, not the heater.
  - Any visible particles, not just tint.
  - Any smell: sewage, sulfur/rotten egg, chlorine, or chemical.
  - Low or uneven pressure that doesn't resolve after flushing.
  - Discoloration reappears the next morning or after the next heavy draw — that's the heater resettling sediment and likely needs a full drain-and-flush by building staff.

  When you do report, the phrase to use is "post-maintenance sediment flushing," not "dirty water" — building management will recognize the procedure and won't reflexively escalate it to a boil notice. Ask specifically whether the building main was depressurized during the shutdown and whether they ran a building-side flush; if they didn't, the cloudiness and tinting you're seeing at the apartment level is the expected downstream effect.

The shape of the proposal is sound — coordinated upgrade, branch isolation, hold the 0.8.4 baseline, and bake in negative tests (steps 5 and 6) rather than relying on green-path only. The risks below are mostly gaps where the proposal asserts protections without naming the mechanism that enforces them. I'll group by your two named concerns, then list cross-cutting items.

PARTIAL-PUBLICATION RISKS

Step 1 (schema 2 -> 3)
  - "Canonical" needs a defined home. If the schema file lives in a path that's read by both this branch and shared CI (e.g., a monorepo root), a fast-forward or accidental merge publishes schema 3 to consumers still pinned at 0.8.x. Worth confirming the schema is branch-local or vendored into the isolated branch with no symlinks/hot-reload into shared state.
  - Schema 3 should be required to reject schema 2 documents (not just "accept with new defaults"). Otherwise step 6's "validation failure" is a no-op against inputs that pass either way.

Step 2 (pin together at 0.9.0)
  - "Pin together" needs to be a single atomic operation, not two commits in sequence. A window where consumer=0.9.0 and generator=0.9.0-rc1 (or local cache of 0.9.0) re-creates the prior mismatch the proposal is trying to prevent.
  - The shared CI generator is only pinned if shared CI actually reads the version from this branch. If shared CI has its own version source (lockfile in its own repo, baked image), this pin is decorative. Need to name the shared CI repo and confirm it consumes the pin.
  - iOS/Android toolchains (Xcodebuild, Gradle) often have their own snapshot or codegen caches. Pinning the generator at 0.9.0 doesn't help if those caches serve 0.8.x artifacts. Cache invalidation needs to be in the matrix.

Step 3 (generate all four targets)
  - Generation must write to a branch-isolated output path, not the published artifact location. Confirm explicitly. Even scratch writes to a shared scratch bucket count as partial publication if downstream tooling watches that bucket.
  - iOS/Android generators sometimes feed off a shared types output that's generated first. If one target fails silently and the rest compare against stale shared types, the "compare to fixtures" in step 4 passes for the wrong reason.
  - Documentation is often treated as advisory. If docs are in-scope for the matrix, they need the same gating rigor as CSS; if they're not, they should be excluded by name so a doc-only regression can't be waved through.

Step 7 (hold 0.8.4 published)
  - "Published" is multi-channel: package registry, CDN, docs site, release tag, internal artifact bucket. Holding one open while another updates is still partial publication. Enumerate the channels and the holder for each.
  - Docs site auto-deploy from main is the most common silent-leak vector here. If the isolated branch is forked from main, any docs-only update on main during this work deploys. Either freeze docs deploys for the matrix window or branch docs off the isolated branch too.
  - "Until the complete matrix passes" needs a named decision-maker and an explicit cutover step, not a rolling green. A human sign-off between "matrix green" and "publish 0.9.0" is the natural place to lose the 0.8.4 baseline.

MISLEADING-COMPARISON RISKS

Step 4 (semantic fixtures + 20x byte stability)
  - The fixtures must be independently derived (hand-written, or produced by a known-good external tool). If they're produced by the same generator, "compare to fixture" is circular and will pass under any generator that round-trips its own output.
  - 20 is a low N for byte stability. Map iteration order, parallel-write races, embedded timestamps, and locale-dependent formatting can produce non-determinism that surfaces at run 50 or 100, not run 20. Either raise N or specify that 20 is the floor and not the ceiling.
  - "Repeat 20 times" needs a definition: 20 sequential runs in the same workspace, 20 from clean checkout, or 20 in parallel. Clean-checkout reruns catch cache-related non-determinism that sequential reruns miss. Pick the one that answers the question you're actually asking.
  - Byte comparison should strip or normalize environment-embedded fields (timestamps, build IDs, hostnames) before diffing, otherwise "byte-identical" can fail on metadata that has nothing to do with generator output.
  - Semantic-fixture drift and byte-stability drift measure different things. If only one fails, what does that mean? Specify precedence: byte-stability is a necessary-but-not-sufficient signal; semantic-fixture diff is the gate.

Step 5 (edit one CSS variable, require drift failure)
  - "Edit one CSS variable" must be at a level the drift detector actually catches. If the detector only checks value equivalence (not name/structure), editing the variable name while keeping the value still passes. Define the edit class.
  - "Require drift failure" needs to be a gate, not a log line. If the harness logs "drift detected, continuing," step 5 is theater. The harness must block on this step.
  - The edit must be detected before regeneration overwrites it. If the detector runs post-regeneration, the test is meaningless.

Step 6 (inject schema validation failure, require zero publication)
  - "Zero publication" must enumerate: zero files written to the output path, zero artifacts uploaded, zero PRs opened, zero release tags, zero docs deploys. Without that enumeration, "zero" is whatever the harness happened to check.
  - Generators that buffer output and write on completion can still leak partial files to temp paths that downstream tooling watches. Need fail-closed semantics end-to-end, including temp directories.
  - The injection point matters. Injecting into the schema file exercises a different code path than injecting into a consumer fixture. Pick the path that's most likely to catch a real regression, not the one that's easiest to mock.

CROSS-CUTTING

The matrix isn't enumerated as a unit. Steps 3, 4, 5, and 6 each gate something different, and a partial set passing could be read as "matrix passed." Define "complete matrix passes" as a single named condition, not a hand-wave.

Isolation isn't demonstrated. "Isolated branch" doesn't include verification that the branch has no auto-merge hooks, no scheduled shared-CI runs, no shared cache keys, no shared scratch paths. Add an isolation-checklist step before step 1, or assert each of these in writing.

The prior mismatch isn't named. The proposal should say what the prior mismatch was (generator 0.9.0-rc1 vs. schema 2? cached vs. fresh?) and how each step prevents that specific recurrence. Without that, the mitigations could be correct in general and still miss the actual cause.

Rollback story is absent. If steps 1-6 pass and a downstream consumer fails, how is 0.8.4 kept live? Discarding the isolated branch is fine; artifacts produced during steps 3-4 that landed in shared storage are not. Add an explicit "what gets deleted on rollback" line.

Toolchain drift across days. If steps 4 and 6 run days apart, a new resolver version or a new OS package update can make byte comparisons non-reproducible for reasons unrelated to the generator. Either pin the toolchain image or run the full matrix inside a single CI job that can't drift mid-sequence.

WHAT TO ASK ANYA BEFORE THE SECOND TEAM RERUNS

  1. What specifically was the prior mismatch, and which step here prevents it?
  2. Where do the semantic fixtures come from, and who vouches they're not generator-derived?
  3. What's the single condition that defines "matrix passed"?
  4. Enumerate the publication channels and the holder for each, including docs.
  5. Confirm shared CI reads the 0.9.0 pin from this branch (not its own lockfile).
  6. Confirm the isolated branch has no auto-merge or shared-cache coupling.

If those six are answered in writing, the proposal is safe to run. If any of them is "we'll figure it out," the second team is going to reproduce a softer version of the original mismatch.

# Review: bounded-decompression PR (per submitted snippet)

You're flagging two real defects and asking for a structured review. Both your flagged items are legitimate, and there are a couple more I'd raise before acceptance. Working through the four asks in order.

## 1. Permit ordering and cleanup

**Defect: global permit leaks when tenant acquire fails or context is canceled.**

```
global.acquire(ctx)                        // (1)
if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil { // (2)
    return canceled(err)                    // (3) — leaks global
}
defer tenant.release()
defer global.release()
```

When (2) returns an error (context canceled, tenant-shedder reject, timeout), execution returns at (3) without ever registering `defer global.release()`. The global permit stays held until the context's outer lifetime expires (which on a canceled context may be soon, but is not guaranteed — the context lifecycle is not the permit lifecycle). On a hot path with frequent cancellations, this is a slow permit-pool drain.

There's also a second issue worth flagging here, even though it isn't strictly "ordering": **the defer order is LIFO but `tenant.release()` is registered before `global.release()`**, so on the happy path releases run tenant → global. That's the correct *acquisition* mirror (LIFO release of LIFO acquire) and it's fine. But it's only fine *if both defers actually run*. The current bug is precisely that `defer global.release()` doesn't get registered when tenant.acquire fails — so the LIFO symmetry is moot.

**Fix:**

```go
if err := global.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
    return canceled(err) // never held → nothing to release
}
released := false
defer func() {
    if !released {
        global.release()
    }
}()

if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
    return canceled(err) // global still held → defer fires
}
released = true
defer tenant.release()
```

Or, cleaner, acquire both into a small `release` slice at the bottom and pop on error:

```go
acquired := 0
release := func() {
    for i := acquired - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
        permits[i].release()
    }
}
defer release()

if err := global.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
    return canceled(err)
}
acquired = 1

if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
    return canceled(err) // defer release() runs the loop, releases global
}
acquired = 2
```

Either shape guarantees that every successfully-acquired permit is released exactly once on every exit path. Pick the one that matches the existing permit-pool style in this codebase — if `metrics-router` already uses the slice pattern, use it; don't introduce a third idiom.

## 2. Allocation-before-limit (append-after-check)

```
for chunk := range decoder {
    output = append(output, chunk...)    // grows the buffer
    decompressed += len(chunk)            // count goes up
    if decompressed > bodyLimit {         // check AFTER
        return bodyTooLarge()
    }
}
```

Two problems here, one obvious, one subtle.

**Obvious:** on overflow, `output` is already grown past `bodyLimit` before you return. That's wasted memory, but the bigger concern is that the comparison is *strictly greater than* and the limit check happens *after* `append`. If `bodyLimit` is, say, 10 MiB and a single chunk is 5 MiB, the first iteration reads, appends, then sees 5 MiB ≤ 10 MiB and continues — fine. But if a single chunk is itself 12 MiB, you append all 12 MiB before noticing. For a per-request cap intended to bound memory, that's a hole.

**Subtle:** `append` will grow past `bodyLimit` even when no single chunk is larger than the limit, because Go's growth strategy doubles. If `bodyLimit` is the *decompressed output* cap (which it should be — that's the DoS surface), then you also need to bound the live buffer. Using `append` without a `cap` ceiling means a single oversized output can hold many bodyLimits worth of bytes transiently.

**Fix — check first, append second, cap the buffer:**

```go
for chunk := range decoder {
    decompressed += len(chunk)
    if decompressed > bodyLimit {
        return bodyTooLarge()
    }
    // append after the check, into a length-bounded buffer
    output = append(output, chunk...)
}
```

And use a length-capped destination (e.g. preallocate `make([]byte, 0, min(chunkSize, bodyLimit))` and reject when `len(output)+len(chunk) > bodyLimit` before appending), or use a streaming writer to the response so you never materialize the full decompressed body. The streaming-to-response shape is the stronger one — it bounds memory regardless of decompressor behavior and removes the temptation for anyone to "just hold it in memory and then write" later.

Either way: **check before append, not after.**

## 3. Cancellation

Three cancellation surfaces to handle distinctly, and the snippet conflates them:

| Surface | Expected behavior |
|---|---|
| Canceled while waiting on `global.acquire` | Return 4xx (client error), do not consume any permits. Current code: correct (returns at `global.acquire`). |
| Canceled while waiting on `tenant.acquire` | Return 4xx, **release the already-held global permit**. Current code: **broken** — leaks global. |
| Canceled mid-stream (`decoder` produces after `ctx.Done()`) | Stop streaming, release both permits, return 4xx. Current code: depends on whether `decoder` honors ctx; if it does, the for-range exits cleanly and the defers fire correctly. If it doesn't (some zlib/gzip bindings don't), the request hangs until `decoder` naturally returns. |

So: fix (b) via the permit-tracking fix in §1, and verify (c) by adding a regression test that cancels mid-stream and asserts both permits are returned within a bounded time (use a semaphore test helper that counts `acquire` minus `release`).

Also: do not conflate `context.Canceled` (client went away) with `context.DeadlineExceeded` (server-side timeout). Both should release permits and return 4xx; neither should return 5xx. Pick the status code based on which one fired — `499` (client closed) if you use nginx-style codes, otherwise `408` for deadline and `429` for tenant-shedder reject. The user's note "returns without releasing" is specifically about `context.Canceled` on the tenant wait, but the same audit should be done for `DeadlineExceeded`.

## 4. Minimum regression tests

A test plan that actually exercises the three failure modes above. Each test should be deterministic and bounded by a timeout (use `t.Deadline` / `time.After`).

1. **Happy path, under limit.** 1 KiB decompressed body, assert both permits released and `output` equals expected.
2. **Overflow at single chunk.** Mock decoder emits one chunk larger than `bodyLimit`. Assert `bodyTooLarge()` returned, **no chunk written to `output`**, both permits released. (This is the one that catches the append-before-check bug.)
3. **Overflow across chunks.** Mock decoder emits many small chunks whose sum exceeds `bodyLimit`. Assert same as (2).
4. **Cancel while waiting on tenant permit.** Pre-hold the tenant permit so `tenant.acquire` blocks, cancel the context, assert global permit count returns to baseline within 100 ms. (This catches the leak.)
5. **Cancel mid-stream.** Start a request, cancel context after first chunk, assert both permits released within 100 ms and the response status reflects cancellation, not 5xx.
6. **429 path still emits randomized 1–3s `Retry-After`.** Run the overflow path N=200 times, assert every `Retry-After` value is in `[1s, 3s]` and the distribution is not degenerate (e.g. not all 1.000s). This is the regression guard for the v2.19.4 production behavior — your runbook explicitly says the rollout does not return to the pre-v2.19.4 baseline, so any PR that touches this code path needs a test that pins the behavior.
7. **Permit accounting under cancellation storm.** Fire M concurrent requests, cancel half of them mid-flight, assert `permits_in_use` returns to zero within a bounded drain window. This catches the slow-leak class of bug that unit tests on single requests miss.

For (4)–(7), wrap the permit pool with a counter-only test double so you can assert `acquired == released` after the test, not just observe absence of deadlock. Don't rely on a sleep-then-check pattern.

## Summary

- **Permit ordering/cleanup:** real bug — global leaks when tenant acquire fails. Fix via defer-guard or release-slice so every acquired permit is released on every exit path.
- **Allocation-before-limit:** real bug — `append` happens before the limit check, and `output` can transiently exceed `bodyLimit`. Check first, append second; consider streaming to the response to bound memory by construction.
- **Cancellation:** bug is the §1 leak on the tenant-wait path; verify mid-stream decoder honors ctx and add coverage for both `Canceled` and `DeadlineExceeded`.
- **Tests:** at minimum the seven above, with a counted permit pool double and a randomized-`Retry-After` distribution assertion to guard the v2.19.4 production behavior.

Reader safety: sound.

  The epoch-guard pattern is correct as written. Reader enters epoch, loads
  the active gen pointer, looks up through it, exits epoch. Writer swaps
  active and then calls epochs.Retire(old), which frees only after all
  earlier reader epochs have drained. Readers that loaded the old pointer
  see a frozen generation and complete their Lookup against matchers that
  remain reachable for the duration of their epoch. Two preconditions worth
  confirming on the file Wes actually lands:
    - the matcher objects built in BuildGeneration are fully immutable
      after construction (no lazy init, no shared mutable state across
      generations, no internal sync that touches the registry)
    - Validate does not mutate candidate.Matchers in a way readers can
      observe (it shouldn't, but if it prunes or rewrites anything, the
      post-Swap readers see a different shape than pre-Swap validators
      did)

Failed reloads: still leak. The race fix didn't touch this path.

  `generationRegistry[candidate.ID] = candidate.Matchers` runs before
  Validate. On failure, `candidate = nil` only nulls the local; the
  registry still pins candidate.Matchers and its backing storage
  (compiled regex DFAs, AST nodes, whatever BuildGeneration allocated).
  Failed candidate generations accumulate in the registry for the life
  of the process. Leak rate is bounded by reload-failure frequency ×
  per-candidate footprint, which on a hot-reloading config path is not
  a theoretical number.

  Minimal fix - delete on the failure path:

      candidate := BuildGeneration(config)
      generationRegistry[candidate.ID] = candidate.Matchers
      if err := Validate(candidate); err != nil {
          delete(generationRegistry, candidate.ID)
          candidate = nil
          return err
      }
      old := active.Swap(candidate)
      epochs.Retire(old)

  Or move the registration after Validate, if nothing in Validate (or
  anything Validate transitively calls) needs the candidate to be
  registry-visible. If there is a reason for the current order -
  concurrent-build dedup by ID, a self-check that queries the registry,
  etc. - keep the order and use the delete form, and add a one-line
  comment saying why so the next reader doesn't reorder it.

  Either way, also worth a `defer` cleanup at the top of the rebuild
  function so any non-Validate failure (panic in BuildGeneration after
  the registry write, future early-return added between the two lines)
  doesn't reintroduce the same leak.

Other things to look at while the diff is open:

  - Concurrent rebuilds with the same ID. If two goroutines can call
    this path in parallel, the current order lets the second writer
    overwrite the first's registry entry before either validates; on
    failure, the delete only removes the loser's ID and the winner's
    pre-validate entry is the one that gets pinned if it fails. Worth
    confirming rebuilds are serialized by ID upstream, or adding a
    per-ID mutex around the build/validate/register block.
  - GenerationRegistry cardinality. If this map is exposed anywhere
    (metrics, debug endpoint, another service that walks it), failed
    candidates are reported as live. That is a correctness smell even
    before the memory argument.

cleanup is in; if the build/validate/register ordering needs to stay
for a documented reason, I want that reason on the page.

================================================================
SCOPE
================================================================
In scope for this rerun (the five items you listed):
  - Cross-tenant cache reuse under (tenant_id, subject_id, resource_id, action, policy_generation)

  - Policy-generation change invalidation
  - Denial without existence leakage
  - Permitted-but-missing source -> explicit `unknown`

  - Raw-body inference leakage

  - Owner-card override path
  - Customer-preview contract surface
  - Co-wide export
  - Manager-readiness view
If rerun surfaces any of these, log as a follow-up, not as a pass condition.

================================================================
PRECONDITIONS TO CONFIRM BEFORE RUNNING (these change cell wiring)
================================================================
P1. Membership revocation channel. The candidate says cache invalidates on policy_generation change only. Confirm one of:
    (a) Membership revocation advances policy_generation atomically and observably, OR
    (b) Membership revocation is a second, explicit invalidation channel keyed on (tenant_id, subject_id, resource_id).
    If neither, Axis B is unrunnable. Pick one and wire the trace event for it.

P2. Deny envelope shape. Confirm exact body: `{ "error": "not_authorized" }` and no other keys. If additional keys exist (request_id, trace_id), they must be identical across all deny paths (D.7).

P3. `unknown` sentinel. Confirm the field-state type/tag (e.g., `{ "state": "unknown", "reason": "source_absent" }` vs string `"UNKNOWN"`). It must be distinguishable from `null`, `""`, and field-absent at the parser level. Same shape whether the field is scalar or object.

P4. Permitted-source allowlist versioning. The list of permitted external sources for a given (tenant, subject, resource, action) is itself policy-versioned. Confirm; otherwise Axis C does not exercise source-allowlist changes.

P5. Cache eviction semantics on gen bump. Confirm: bump gen N -> N+1 invalidates entries stored under N for that tenant. Confirm whether the invalidation is synchronous (request after bump never sees N entries) or best-effort.

P6. Timing-side-channel tolerance for D.6. Pick a concrete bound (e.g., p99 within 5ms of "does not exist" path) or commit to constant-time deny.

================================================================
AXIS A — CROSS-TENANT CACHE REUSE
================================================================
Key invariant: cache hit requires tuple match on ALL five key fields. tenant_id mismatch -> miss, full re-eval. No cache entry from tenant T may serve a request scoped to tenant T'.

A.1 [positive isolation, allow/allow]
  Setup: T1/S1/R1/A1/G1 -> evaluated -> allow cached.
  Request: identical tuple but tenant_id=T2.
  Expected: cache miss. Fresh eval. Result = T2 policy outcome (likely deny if T2 has no grant; allow if T2 has independent grant).
  Evidence: trace shows key build includes tenant_id; no lookup against T1's entry; re-eval path executed.

A.2 [positive isolation, deny/allow]
  Setup: T1/S1/R1/A1/G1 -> evaluated -> deny cached.
  Request: T2/S1/R1/A1/G1.
  Expected: cache miss. Not denied by T1's cached deny.
  Evidence: same as A.1.

A.3 [in-tenant hit]
  Setup: T1/S1/R1/A1/G1 -> evaluated.
  Request: repeat same tuple within T1.
  Expected: cache hit, no re-eval.
  Evidence: trace shows cache hit path, evaluator not invoked.

A.4 [negative — decomposed key without tenant_id]
  Setup: synthetic request built with key (S1, R1, A1, G1) only (no tenant_id).
  Expected: rejected as miss or as invalid key. NEVER served from T1 cache.
  Evidence: unit test on key builder rejects/ignores tenant-less lookups.

A.5 [negative — key collision attempt]
  Setup: attacker controls subject_id naming within T2 to mirror T1's subject_id string.
  Expected: cache lookup still partitioned by tenant_id; no cross-tenant hit.
  Evidence: trace shows separate cache namespaces per tenant.

================================================================
AXIS B — MEMBERSHIP REVOCATION FRESHNESS
================================================================
Depends on P1. If (a), membership revocation -> gen bump. If (b), explicit invalidation event. Cells assume (a) unless noted.

B.1 [revoke -> next request re-evaluates]
  Setup: S1 member of T1 with action A1 on R1 at gen G. Allow cached at G.
  Action: revoke S1's membership on R1 (or on T1 entirely). Gen advances to G+1.
  Request: T1/S1/R1/A1 at G+1.
  Expected: cache miss at G+1. Re-eval. Outcome = current policy (deny if no other grant).
  Evidence: trace shows gen compare, miss, re-eval; old G entry not consulted.

B.2 [negative — broken wiring]
  Setup: same as B.1 but revoke path does NOT advance gen (regression test for the wiring).
  Expected: this cell must FAIL when run. Catching the failure is the test's purpose.
  Evidence: explicit assertion; CI must flag.

B.3 [re-add after revoke]
  Setup: revoke -> gen G+1 -> re-grant -> gen G+2.
  Request: T1/S1/R1/A1 at G+2.
  Expected: miss at G+2, fresh allow.
  Evidence: trace + cached allow at G+2.

B.4 [concurrent revoke + in-flight request]
  Setup: request enters evaluator at gen G. Revoke fires before eval completes.
  Expected: response reflects post-revoke policy (gen G+1 outcome). No race-window allow.

B.5 [revocation of one resource, not all]
  Setup: S1 has grants on R1 and R2 at gen G, both cached.

  Request: T1/S1/R2/A1 at G+1.

AXIS C — POLICY GENERATION CHANGES
================================================================
C.1 [gen bump, allow -> allow]
  Setup: allow cached at gen G. Edit policy (no semantic change for S1/R1/A1), bump to G+1.
  Request: at G+1.
  Expected: miss + re-eval -> allow (matches new policy).
  Evidence: trace; cache not consulted for old gen.

C.2 [gen bump, deny -> deny]
  Setup: deny cached at G. Policy edit + bump to G+1.
  Request: at G+1.
  Expected: miss + re-eval -> deny.
  Evidence: trace; old deny not served.

C.3 [gen bump, allow -> deny via policy change]
  Setup: allow cached at G. Policy edit removes S1's grant, bump to G+1.
  Request: at G+1.
  Expected: miss + re-eval -> deny. Crucially, no stale allow served.
  Evidence: trace + cached deny at G+1 (or no cache entry if policy says don't cache denies — confirm with design).

C.4 [boundary — two requests straddle bump]
  Setup: in-flight requests R_a (pre-bump) and R_b (post-bump).
  Expected: each sees its own gen's outcome. No cross-contamination.
  Evidence: per-request gen tag in trace.

C.5 [rollback]
  Setup: G -> G+1 -> G+2; ops rolls back to G+1 (e.g., bad edit).
  Expected: cache entries under G+2 are not served; entries under G+1 (if retained) are served; entries under G are not served.
  Evidence: trace + cache state dump.

C.6 [source-allowlist versioned under same gen mechanism]
  Setup: permitted-source list for (T1, S1, R1, A1) changes at gen bump.
  Expected: new request reads the new list. Old cached decision does not serve stale source list.
  Evidence: trace; depends on P4.

================================================================
AXIS D — DENIAL WITHOUT EXISTENCE LEAKAGE
================================================================
D.1 [deny on existent resource, no leak]
  Setup: R1 exists in T1; S1 not authorized for A1.
  Request: T1/S1/R1/A1.
  Expected: status 403, body exactly `{"error":"not_authorized"}`. No field names, no values, no resource metadata, no preview payload.

D.2 [deny on nonexistent resource — indistinguishable from D.1]
  Setup: R1 does not exist in T1.
  Request: T1/S1/R1/A1.
  Expected: identical status, identical body, identical headers (modulo legitimate transport-level headers) as D.1.
  Evidence: byte-equal body diff.

D.3 [deny when R1 has rich fields]
  Setup: R1 exists with fields F1..Fn populated. S1 not authorized.
  Request: as D.1.
  Expected: body contains zero of F1..Fn, neither names nor values.
  Evidence: response body grep / schema assertion.

D.4 [partial grant — action denied, resource exists, other actions would allow]
  Setup: S1 allowed for A_allow on R1, denied for A_deny on R1.
  Request: A_deny on R1.
  Expected: 403 envelope. No field serialization. Existence of "A_allow works" not revealed.
  Evidence: response body diff vs allow-on-A_allow.

D.5 [sibling resource in same tenant, no access]
  Setup: S1 authorized for R1; R2 exists in T1; S1 has no access to R2.
  Request: T1/S1/R2/A1.
  Expected: identical 403 to D.1/D.2. No info about R2's relationship to R1.

  Setup: replay D.1 and D.2 across N=500 iterations each.

D.7 [envelope uniformity across deny paths]
  Compare body across:

    - cross-tenant deny (A.2 outcome)
  Expected: identical envelope. No path-distinguishing marker in body.

D.8 [error/log channel leakage]
  Setup: trigger each deny path.
  Expected: server-side logs may record resource_id (for ops), but client-facing response carries none. Verify log scrubbing if logs are user-visible via support tooling.
  Evidence: log capture + redaction policy.

================================================================
AXIS E — PERMITTED-BUT-MISSING SOURCE -> EXPLICIT UNKNOWN
================================================================
E.1 [single source absent]
  Setup: S1/T1 authorized for R1/A1; permitted external source Sx returns no record (or graceful timeout, not 5xx).
  Request: as authorized.
  Expected: 200. Field(s) backed by Sx carry explicit `unknown` (shape per P3). Other fields populated normally.
  Evidence: response body; field-by-field state assertion.

E.2 [mixed present/absent sources]
  Setup: Sx present, Sy absent, Sz present.
  Expected: per-field state — value for Sx/Sz, `unknown` for Sy. No field-level error, no global error.
  Evidence: response body; field-state map.

E.3 [all permitted sources absent]
  Setup: every permitted source absent.
  Expected: 200 with all fields `unknown`, OR a single envelope-level "fully unknown" indicator — confirm which with design. NOT 4xx, NOT 5xx.
  Evidence: response body + status code.

E.4 [absent source for a field whose category subject is not otherwise authorized for]
  Setup: source absent AND subject lacks category-level grant for that field.
  Expected: `unknown` (not 403). Rationale: nothing to leak if no field value is fetched.
  Evidence: response body. Flag to design if cell returns 403 — that's a leakage opportunity.

E.5 [sentinel distinguishability]
  Setup: serialize `unknown` alongside `null`, `""`, and field-absent in the same response shape.
  Expected: parser-level distinguishable. E.g., tagged union or typed sentinel, not raw null.
  Evidence: type check + parser test. Catches accidental collapse.

E.6 [source timeout vs source-absent]
  Setup: source times out vs source returns explicit empty.
  Expected: both surface as `unknown`. Source error must not bubble as 5xx or partial 200 with field omitted.
  Evidence: response body under both conditions.

E.7 [source fails after policy permits it at gen G, then gen bumps]
  Setup: Sx absent at gen G; request returns `unknown`. Policy + source-allowlist unchanged at G+1.
  Expected: still `unknown` at G+1, no false-positive population.
  Evidence: response body at both gens.

================================================================
CROSS-AXIS INTERACTION CELLS
================================================================
X.1 [A + B] T1 allows, cache hit; revoke S1 from T1 + cross-tenant request from T2 arrives concurrently.
  Expected: T2 path misses cache (A); T1 post-revoke path misses cache due to gen bump (B). No cross-tenant or stale-allow bleed.
  Evidence: paired traces.

X.2 [B + C] Revoke (gen bump) + subsequent policy edit (another gen bump) before next request.
  Expected: only the latest gen served; intermediate gen entries do not serve.
  Evidence: trace + cache dump at each bump.

X.3 [A + D] Cross-tenant request where T1 has cached deny and T2 has no record of resource.
  Expected: T2 path returns D.2-style 403, indistinguishable from T2's own D.1. T1 cache does not contribute.
  Evidence: response body + trace.

X.4 [C + E] Policy bump adds a new permitted source; existing fields stay `unknown` until source populated.
  Expected: at new gen, fresh eval reads new source list; response field states reflect actual source availability, not cached pre-bump state.
  Evidence: trace + response body.

X.5 [D + E] Subject denied for resource, but a permitted source for that resource is absent.
  Expected: 403, not 200-with-unknown. Denial takes precedence; we do not confirm absence.
  Evidence: response status + body.

================================================================
EVIDENCE BUNDLE PER AXIS (deliverables for signoff)
================================================================
For each axis A–E, the rerun produces:
  1. Test names + pass/fail (CI-runnable, not ad-hoc).
  2. Trace captures (request -> key build -> lookup -> decision -> response) for representative cells.
  3. Response body diffs vs allow baseline (D-axis especially).
  4. Latency histograms (D.6) with statistical summary.
  5. Cache state dumps at each bump (C-axis).
  6. Owner-map snapshot per Lantern provenance rule: source, generation timestamp, named maintainer (per the standing prov-fix convention).

================================================================
SIGNOFF CRITERIA
================================================================
Signoff requires:
  - All cells in A, B, C, D, E pass, OR
  - Documented exceptions with named owner, scope-narrow fix, and follow-up issue link. No open exceptions without owner.
  - P1–P6 confirmed in writing (each Precondition resolved, not deferred).
  - Evidence bundle attached to the signoff comment, not referenced by link only.
  - Re-run triggered on any subsequent change to: cache key, gen-bump wiring, deny envelope, `unknown` sentinel, source-allowlist versioning.

NOTES ON THE CANDIDATE DESIGN (what I would push back on now)
================================================================
1. "Invalidated when the policy generation changes" leaves membership revocation under-specified. Resolve via P1 before run.
2. The cache value should record the gen under which the decision was made, not just key on it, so a stale entry from a rolled-back gen cannot serve (C.5).

4. `unknown` must not be reachable from a deny path (X.5). Worth a static check, not just a runtime test.
5. Source-allowlist versioning (P4) — if this is not policy-versioned, E and C are not fully exercised and the rerun matrix understates the surface.

Violation: YES.

Window end 14:10. First completion at 14:10:31 (T+31s). Lateness allowance 90s, so completion should not fire before 14:11:40. Latest late record arrived 14:11:18 (T+78s) — inside the 90s allowance. Every record arriving between T+31s and T+90s was excluded from the initial publish by construction. The 312 records (39,033 − 38,721) landed in exactly that band. 39,033 is the correct count; 38,721 was the prematurely-finalized count.

This is not an upstream or delivery problem:
  - accepted-point count stable → upstream emitted what it should
  - route-delivery loss: none → records reached rollup-service in time
  - next compaction caught them → storage path is intact
The bug is in rollup-service's publish/completion gating, not ingest.

Gating assertions for a fix:

  1. Completion timing. For every window W:
       completion_time(W) − window_end(W) ≥ configured_lateness_allowance
     (never finalize before T+90s.)

  2. No-late-after-completion. For any W completed at C:
       no record with event_time ∈ W has arrival_time > C.
     If one does, completion was early OR delivery was late — fix must distinguish.

  3. First-publish == final-publish (modulo documented delta). For every W:
       first_published_count(W) == compaction_final_count(W)
     unless any change is via an explicit, attributable re-emission channel — not a silent overwrite.

  4. Lateness-boundary inclusion. For any record with event_time ∈ W arriving at A:
       A − window_end(W) ≤ lateness_allowance → included in W
       A − window_end(W) >  lateness_allowance → routed to W+1 or dropped per policy; never silently dropped from W.

  5. Count monotonicity post-completion. After W is marked complete, its published count must not change except through the documented re-emission path, and any delta must be attributable to downstream consumers.

Assertion 1 is the root-cause fix; 2–4 are the safety net that would have caught it; 5 protects downstream from the two-publishes-per-window pattern that just happened.

HUEVOS RANCHEROS, FASTER WAY
(for two, ~25 minutes)

ONE PAN: a 10- or 12-inch skillet (nonstick or cast iron). Plus one mixing bowl for the slaw.

THE 25-MINUTE PLAN

0:00  Shred about 2 cups of cabbage very thinly (knife or vegetable peeler gives nice thin strips). Slice 2-3 scallions, whites and greens kept separate. Halve and pit the avocado.

0:02  Heat the skillet over medium with a small pour of oil. Add the scallion whites and a pinch of salt; stir 30 seconds.

0:03  Add the black beans (drained, rinsed briefly) plus 3-4 heaping spoonfuls of salsa verde and a splash of water. Warm and roughly mash about a third of the beans so the mixture holds together but isn't refried-smooth. Salt and pepper. ~5 minutes.

0:08  While the beans cook, build the slaw in the bowl: cabbage + most of the scallion greens + a pinch of salt + a spoon of salsa verde tossed through. Add the avocado (sliced or cubed) AT THE VERY END so it stays intact.

0:10  Push the beans to one side of the pan. Crack 4 eggs into the cleared side (use the other 4 if you're hungry — you have them). Salt the whites. Cover the pan, lower heat slightly; cook 3-4 minutes until whites set and yolks are still runny. Or fry and flip for over-easy.

0:14  Warm the tortillas: 20-30 seconds per side directly over a gas flame, OR stack and microwave 30 seconds wrapped in a damp towel, OR slide them into the empty corner of the pan for the last minute.

0:16  BUILD (two plates):
  - warm tortilla
  - spoon of beans
  - 1-2 eggs on top of the beans
  - heap of raw slaw on top of the eggs (runny yolk + crunchy cabbage)
  - crumble cheddar over the warm eggs so it just softens
  - more salsa verde, remaining scallion greens

WHAT KEEPS THE CABBAGE CRISP (don't skip these)
  - The cabbage never goes near heat. It's a raw slaw, not a sauté.
  - Dress and salt the slaw at the last second, not while the eggs cook. Salt + acid + time = limp cabbage.
  - Avocado joins the slaw at the end so it doesn't get mashed into mush.
  - Slaw sits ON TOP of the eggs, not under — you want the contrast between runny yolk and cold crunchy cabbage in the same bite.

CLEANUP
One pan, one bowl, one cutting board, one knife. Done before Devika finishes setting the table.

Pantry-only moves if you want to upgrade without buying anything: a pinch of cumin or smoked paprika in the beans; a tiny splash of vinegar or pickle brine in the slaw if you've got any.

Short answer: based on what you described, this is NOT a classic overload signature — and understanding why matters for what to do next.

A GFCI outlet does not trip on overload. It trips when it senses roughly 5 mA of current leaking to ground (hot and neutral currents no longer match). A real overload would trip the breaker in your electrical panel, not the outlet on the wall. What you almost certainly had is cumulative appliance leakage: both the kettle and the toaster oven produce a small amount of normal leakage through their heating elements and insulation, and running them together pushed the total over the GFCI's threshold. That matches your observation exactly — each one alone stays under the threshold, so each runs fine by itself.

This is a nuisance trip, not a wiring fault, given the clean reset and the absence of any warning signs. The fix is to change how you use the outlet.

What to do right now
- Keep both appliances unplugged until you have somewhere safe to run them.
- The outlet is usable for single, ordinary loads (coffee maker, toaster, phone charger, lamp). It is not safe to run two high-draw appliances from it at the same time.
- Plug the kettle and toaster oven into separate receptacles, ideally on different circuits. Kitchen counters are usually split across two small-appliance circuits; the two halves of one duplex outlet are often on the same circuit, so a plain splitter or power strip will not help — and will make trips more likely, not less.
- Once you've confirmed each appliance works in its new spot, resume normal use, but never both at once on one receptacle.

Low-risk checks you can do yourself
- Look closely at both plugs and the outlet face: any darkening, scuffing, melting, or discoloration?
- After running one appliance alone for a minute, feel the plug and the outlet face — they should be cool or at most barely warm.
- Confirm the other kitchen receptacles still have power.
- Test the GFCI itself: press TEST (the RESET button should pop out and the outlet should go dead), then press RESET to restore. Do this monthly as a habit. If TEST does not trip the GFCI, the device has failed and should be replaced by an electrician.
- Try one appliance, alone, briefly in the original outlet. If it holds, the outlet is fine for single loads.

What NOT to do
- Do not run both appliances from this receptacle simultaneously again — that is what tripped it.
- Do not add a multi-plug adapter, splitter, or power strip to this outlet to "get more capacity." It does not add capacity, and it increases nuisance-trip and fire risk.
- Do not run either appliance through an extension cord. High-draw kitchen appliances plug directly into a wall receptacle.
- Do not open, replace, or attempt to bypass the GFCI outlet yourself.
- Do not keep pressing RESET on a GFCI that re-trips immediately. Stop and call for help.

Leave the circuit off and contact building maintenance or an electrician if any of these appear
- The GFCI will not reset, or trips again immediately after resetting.
- It trips with only one appliance plugged in, or with nothing plugged in at all.
- It trips when you plug in something low-draw like a lamp or phone charger.
- Burning smell, scorch marks, or discoloration at the outlet, plug, or wall around the outlet.
- Buzzing, crackling, popping, or sizzling from the outlet.
- Warmth or heat at the outlet face, wall plate, or plug.
- The outlet feels loose, plugs fall out, or the face plate is cracked.
- Sparking when you plug or unplug.
- Tingling when you touch an appliance, its cord, or the outlet.
- Water has gotten into the outlet (spill, splash, steam, leak).
- The breaker in the panel trips instead of — or in addition to — the GFCI outlet.

Bottom line: this pattern is consistent with a GFCI nuisance trip from combined appliance leakage on one protected outlet, not with a true overload and not, on the evidence you have, with a wiring fault. Separate the appliances onto different receptacles/circuits, never run both from this outlet at the same time, and stop using the circuit the moment any of the warning signs above appear.

Diagnosis
=========

This is not harmless packaging metadata. It is a real reproducibility
defect in the packaging step, and the drift-check is correctly catching
it.

The data-plane view (extracted file contents, mode 0644) matches, which
is necessary but not sufficient. The artifact-as-distributed is the ZIP
bytes, not the extracted contents. Two consequences:

  (a) Any downstream consumer that pins the package by archive hash
      (CDN cache, signed manifest, SBOM, in-toto/SLSA provenance,
      attestation) cannot rely on a single hash across rebuilders. A
      verifier running on macOS cannot validate a hash minted on Linux.

  (b) Reproducers rebuilding from the pinned schema-3 generator at
      0.9.0 cannot byte-match a canonical artifact. That breaks the
      "deterministic rebuild" property the schema is supposed to give
      you.

So: fail-closed on the archive hash. The extracted-contents match is
reassuring - it rules out content drift and confirms the generator is
correct - but it does not excuse publishing a non-byte-reproducible
package. The gate is doing its job.


Where the defect lives
======================

Timestamps:
  Linux pins to a single sentinel (13:52 UTC - looks like a pre-set
  mtime). macOS carries real wall-clock mtimes from the source files
  with sub-second spread (09:51:58 to 09:52:02 local). Almost certainly
  two different toolchains - e.g., Info-ZIP on Linux with stripped
  extras vs. macOS Archive Utility / `ditto -c -k` / Finder Compress,
  which embeds Unix extended timestamps and is non-deterministic by
  default.

Ordering:
  Linux walks as css, ios, android, json. macOS leads with json and the
  rest follow. Different glob/walk strategies. ZIP central-directory
  order is not part of the spec, so anything other than explicit sort
  is non-deterministic across tools.

Both are surface symptoms of the same root cause: two packagers, two
default configs, neither pinned.


Recommended deterministic packaging rule
=========================================

Apply in ONE place, on ONE runner. Do not let two platforms package.

  1. Single tool. Pick one. Python `zipfile.ZipFile(... 'w',
     ZIP_DEFLATED, compresslevel=6)` is the most portable and gives
     deterministic control over every byte. Pin the python version in
     the lockfile. Do not let platform defaults (`zip`, `ditto`,
     Archive Utility, Finder Compress) anywhere near the artifact.

  2. Force entry ordering: sort by relative path, UTF-8 NFC, bytewise
     (`LC_ALL=C sort`). Better: write the manifest list explicitly in
     the generator. Do not glob.

  3. Force mtime: set every entry's date_time to a pinned sentinel -
     (1980, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0), the DOS epoch floor. Do NOT write the
     extended-timestamp extra field. Python `zipfile` defaults to not
     writing it; Info-ZIP needs `zip -X` to strip extras but you also
     lose Unix mode bits, so prefer Python.

  4. Force file mode: emit 0644 in external_attr (upper 16 bits:
     0o100644 << 16). Set create_system = 3 (Unix) so mode bits
     survive. Do not let the host umask leak in.

  5. Force filename encoding: UTF-8 (general-purpose bit 11). Moot
     for ASCII paths; pin it so future non-ASCII entries don't drift.

  6. No archive comment, no extra fields on the central directory,
     no directory entries. EOCD minimal.

  7. Compression: DEFLATE level 6, fixed. No STORED-vs-DEFLATE
     branching.


Concrete Python shape (drop into the schema-3 pack step)
=========================================================

    import os, hashlib, zipfile

    PINNED_MTIME = (1980, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)   # UTC, DOS epoch floor
    MODE_FILE    = 0o100644 << 16           # external_attr for 0644
    ENTRIES = [                             # explicit, sorted, pinned
        "android/tokens.xml",
        "css/tokens.css",
        "ios/Tokens.swift",
        "json/tokens.json",
    ]

    def pack(root, out_path):
        with zipfile.ZipFile(
            out_path, "w",
            compression=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED,
            compresslevel=6,
        ) as z:
            for rel in ENTRIES:
                zi = zipfile.ZipInfo(rel, date_time=PINNED_MTIME)
                zi.compress_type = zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED
                zi.external_attr = MODE_FILE
                zi.create_system = 3      # Unix, so mode bits honored
                with open(os.path.join(root, rel), "rb") as f:
                    z.writestr(zi, f.read(), compresslevel=6)
        return hashlib.sha256(open(out_path, "rb").read()).hexdigest()

Note: do not use `ZipInfo.from_file(...)`. It reads the source mtime and
converts host-local, so the same source on Linux vs. macOS produces
different bytes. Build the ZipInfo explicitly with the pinned tuple.


Recommended comparison rule (fail-closed)
==========================================

Primary gate - BLOCKING:
    archive_sha256 == expected archive_sha256 from the pinned manifest.
    On mismatch, fail-closed. Diagnose before unblocking.

Secondary gate - BLOCKING, complementary:
    For each path in the sorted manifest:
        sha256(extracted_file) == sha256 from the canonical
        extracted-manifest.
    On mismatch, content drift - block, P0.

Diagnostic - NON-BLOCKING but recorded on every build:
    entry ordering, entry mtimes (DOS and extended if present),
    compression method per entry, extra-field summary, archive comment.
    Diff these between Linux and macOS runs.

Classification:
  - Content-hash mismatch                          -> P0, block.
  - Archive-hash mismatch, content-hash match      -> P1, block.
                                                     Do NOT bypass.
  - Diagnostic drift only, archive-hash stable     -> record,
                                                     do not block.


Specific fixes for the current run
==================================

  - Pick one runner for packaging. Linux CI is the conventional
    choice; macOS produces source files only and the published
    artifact always comes from Linux. This sidesteps cross-platform
    toolchain drift entirely.

  - If macOS must package, run the SAME Python `zipfile` script as
    Linux. Do not use `ditto -c -k`, Archive Utility, or Finder
    Compress.

  - Replace whatever is producing the 09:51:58-09:52:02 mtime spread
    with the PINNED_MTIME. The macOS run is preserving source-file
    mtimes; you want the sentinel written into the ZipInfo, not the
    host mtime.

  - Replace whatever produces the json-first ordering with a sorted
    or manifest-explicit walk.

  - Add a packaging-reproducibility log to the CI artifact so the
    next divergence shows up at the diagnostic layer, not at the
    publish gate.


Stronger-than-ZIP option
========================

If you want a guarantee ZIP cannot give you under toolchain churn,
escape ZIP entirely: ship a deterministic JSON manifest plus per-file
blobs, hash the canonical-JSON manifest, and pin that. ZIP
reproducibility is achievable but fragile; a schema-pinned token
package is exactly the kind of artifact where you want one canonical
hash with no excuses.

Good call on it staying off and unplugged. Two teaspoons is small enough to be a one-time overflow rather than a cracked pan or breached coil — those would drip continuously while running. The most likely causes for that volume are (a) the condensate slinger not keeping up during a long humid cycle, or (b) frost on the evaporator from restricted airflow that melted off when the compressor shut down. Both are user-fixable. The order below is built so you bail at any point with a partial answer and still know whether to resume.

PRE-FLIGHT (already done, just confirming the right state)
- Unit off and unplugged at the wall, not just at the panel. Good.
- Sill and plug dry before you put fingers or tools near the chassis.
- Hands and floor dry. No metal ladder leaning on the unit or the bracket.

INSPECTION ORDER — work top to bottom, exterior to interior, no-contact to contact.

1. EXTERIOR VIEW FROM OUTSIDE (or through the window, no leaning out)
  What to check:
    - Slight outward tilt of the chassis. A quarter to half inch of drop from front (indoor) to back (outdoor) lets condensate reach the slinger and rear drain slots. If the unit is level or tipped inward, condensate pools at the front lip and spills into the room.
    - Rear drain slots / drain spout at the back-bottom of the base pan. Should be clear of leaves, insect nests, fuzz. Visible without disassembly.
  Stop condition: if the chassis has visibly slid forward in its cradle, or the side fillers have shifted, or the bracket hardware looks deformed — stop, don't touch it, call the installer. The approved bracket is doing load-bearing work.

2. INDOOR-SIDE WIPE-UP PATTERN (before you clean it)
  Where the water sat tells you which way the pan overflowed.
    - Puddle spanning the full width directly under the front indoor edge → pan filled and overflowed at the front lip. Points at slinger or humidity overload.
    - Puddle offset to one side → pan is not level side to side, or one corner of the pan is lower and that's where it spilled. Note which side.
    - Puddle further inward on the sill (not directly below the unit) → condensate tracked along the sill from a higher point. Unusual; take a photo before wiping.
  Stop condition: any oily film, rainbow sheen, or sweet chemical smell — stop, ventilate the room, don't run it. That's a refrigerant issue, tech territory.

3. FILTER (safe to do, do this first if you want a fast answer)
  What to do: pop the indoor grille per the unit's manual. Slide the filter out.
  What to look for: visibly matted with dust. Hold it up to light — if almost no light passes, it's starving the evaporator of airflow, which is exactly what causes the frost-then-puddle pattern.
  Action: rinse, let it dry fully, or replace.
  Stop condition: none — this is always safe. Just don't force the grille clips.

4. CONDENSATE SLINGER (the usual culprit for two-teaspoon puddles)
  With the grille off and the filter out, you can see the evaporator coils and the fan blade / squirrel cage behind them.
  What to look for:
    - A small plastic or metal ring or scoop at the hub of the fan, sitting in the base of the pan. That's the slinger. It should be present, intact, and rotating with the shaft (you can rotate it by hand with the unit still unplugged).
    - If it's missing, cracked, or rotates freely on the shaft without the shaft turning it (slipped), the slinger isn't picking up water and the pan will overflow during long humid runs.
    - Pool of water still sitting in the base pan. If it's full and not draining, the rear slots are blocked (you checked those in step 1) or the pan is tipped wrong.
  Stop condition: anything oily, any sign of corrosion at the coil-to-pan seam, or any tubing you can't identify — stop and call service. Don't reach past the coil into territory you can't see.

5. PAN LEVEL AND CHASSIS SEAT (no bracket disturbance)
  What to do: with one hand steadying the chassis from inside, see whether you can shift the unit a fraction of an inch within the bracket cradle to correct the tilt you observed in step 1.
  What you're trying to achieve: that quarter-to-half-inch outward tilt and a level side-to-side. The bracket has a range of adjustment for exactly this.
  Stop condition: if it doesn't move easily, or moves and doesn't hold position, or you feel any shift in the bracket itself — stop. The bracket is approved hardware; don't fight it. Call the installer to re-level.

6. CORD, PLUG, OUTLET, SILL (already partially done — just complete it)
  - Cord and plug: already dry and cool. Confirm the plug prongs and the wall outlet face are dry and free of discoloration.
  - Outlet type: window units are commonly on a dedicated 15- or 20-amp circuit. Confirm the breaker is correctly sized and not shared with other loads. If the outlet is GFCI, note that — many window unit manuals call for a non-GFCI dedicated circuit because compressor leakage trips GFCI. Not a hazard, just a nuisance trip risk on resume.
  - Sill: dry. If water wicked into wood, dry it before you close up; trapped moisture under a sealed frame invites mold.

RESUME-DECISION CHECKLIST
Resume cooling only if every one of these is true:
  - Filter is clean (or replaced).
  - Tilt is outward by roughly a quarter inch or more.
  - Pan is level side to side.
  - Slinger is present and rotates with the shaft.
  - No oily residue, no chemical smell, no corrosion at the coil seam.
  - Plug, outlet, cord, and sill are dry.
  - Side fillers and sash restraints are still immobile.
  - The puddle was a one-time event, not a recurring drip while running.

If all green: plug it in, run it on a shorter cycle first (medium fan, moderate setpoint) and watch the front indoor edge for 30 to 60 minutes. Two teaspoons of condensate over a long humid cycle is within design tolerance; steady dripping is not.

CALL A TECH (don't resume) IF:
  - Oily residue or sweet smell anywhere.
  - Puddle recurs on the next short test cycle.
  - Slinger is missing or damaged and you don't want to live with periodic small puddles.
  - Bracket, sash, or side fillers have shifted.
  - You see water tracking on the interior wall rather than the sill — that means it's not condensate, it's a seal or envelope issue around the unit, different problem.

ONE THING NOT TO DO: don't drill a drain hole. Most residential window units are not designed for it, the pan material splits around the bit more often than it cuts clean, and on a unit with an internal slinger it bypasses the intended evaporation path and can starve the coil. If the slinger is the problem, the right fix is the slinger, not a new hole.

REVIEW: rollup-service completion-rule correction (90s grace)

Scope: cross-service invariant between rollup-service and shard-keeper, plus the atomicity and idempotency guarantees of the new completion transaction. Cyrus's team retains impl + ops; this specifies what must hold before approval.

1. Cross-service invariant under test

   Contract rollup-service owes to shard-keeper and its downstream consumers:

   (a) A window W is eligible for completion only when min(watermark[p] for p in assigned_partitions) >= W.end + 90s.
   (b) The rollup output row and the checkpoint row for W are written in one transaction with one compaction_id. Either both are visible or neither is.
   (c) On assignment change, a worker that picks up partitions for W reads the most recent committed checkpoint AND the current watermarks for its assigned partitions before evaluating eligibility.
   (d) Records arriving after W is committed do not mutate the committed first-pass output; they are retained for a correction pass that, if it runs, writes under a new compaction_id and atomically replaces the first-pass output.

   The patch asserts (a)–(d). Tests below pin each clause.

2. Boundary (90s grace)

   B1. Exactly at boundary.
       Setup: W.end = T; three assigned partitions with watermarks T+90s, T+90s, T+90s.
       Action: tick the completion evaluator.
       Expect: eligible. One transaction commits with effective_watermark = T+90s.

   B2. One millisecond short.
       Setup: watermarks T+89.999s, T+90s, T+90s.
       Expect: not eligible. No write. Re-evaluation at next tick where min >= T+90s succeeds.

   B3. Mixed partitions straddling boundary.
       Setup: T+89s, T+90s, T+91s.
       Expect: not eligible (min wins). No write. Re-evaluation succeeds only once the slowest partition crosses T+90s.

   B4. Watermark regression.
       Setup: partition 2 watermark regresses from T+95s back to T+80s (republish, backfill, or operator action).
       Expect: effective_watermark is the min over currently observed values. Eligibility cannot exceed the lowest current partition. This pins that watermarks are observed, not assumed monotonic.

   B5. Empty assignment.
       Setup: a worker briefly holds zero assigned partitions (all in flight to peers).
       Expect: evaluator must skip and not treat empty as immediately eligible. State the policy explicitly in the PR.

3. Partition-skew

   S1. One permanently slow partition.
       Setup: partitions 1, 3 healthy with watermark T+120s; partition 2 stuck at T+10s.
       Expect: not eligible for the duration of the test. No write. The stall is observable through existing lag metrics and is not coupled to this patch.

   S2. Slow partition recovers after the window.
       Setup: as S1, then partition 2 advances past T+90s.
       Expect: eligible on the next tick. Transaction commits with effective_watermark = partition 2's value. Output covers data from all three partitions up to the slowest partition's observed watermark.

   S3. Hot partitions must not raise the cutoff.
       Setup: partitions 1, 2 at T+200s; partition 3 at T+90s exactly.
       Expect: eligible. Output covers up to T+90s, not T+200s. Pin the documented behavior as a named test so a later reviewer does not "fix" it.

   S4. Partition disappears mid-window.
       Setup: partition 3 unassigned during W's eligibility window.
       Expect: state and pin the policy. The patch text implies "over assigned_partitions only," meaning unassigned partitions are excluded from min. Confirm and document.

4. Rebalance

   R1. Rebalance during an open window.
       Setup: worker A holds {1,2,3}, watermarks T+30s each. Rebalance reassigns partition 3 to B.
       Action: B reads checkpoint for W (none), reads its assigned partitions' watermarks ({3} only).
       Expect: B cannot complete (no global min context). A still holds 1,2 at T+30s; A cannot complete either. Both idle until the next watermark advance. No duplicate compaction attempt.

   R2. Rebalance after eligibility, before commit.
       Setup: A holds {1,2,3} at T+95s each, enters the transaction. Mid-transaction, rebalance reassigns {2,3} to B.
       Expect: A's transaction either commits atomically (B observes committed checkpoint + output, skips evaluation) or does not commit (B sees no checkpoint, re-evaluates from scratch with its assigned partitions). Never observe a half-state: checkpoint without output, or output without checkpoint.

   R3. Rebalance after commit.
       Setup: W committed by A. A dies. B takes over {1,2,3}.
       Expect: B reads the checkpoint for W, observes completion, does not re-evaluate, does not write a duplicate output. Late records that arrive for W's partitions are retained for the correction pass.

   R4. Rebalance during correction pass.
       Setup: first-pass committed for W. Late records for W flow in. Correction pass starts on A. Rebalance moves partitions to B.
       Expect: B reads the first-pass checkpoint (compaction_id, effective_watermark) and resumes or restarts the correction pass deterministically. Correction writes a NEW compaction_id and atomically replaces the first-pass output. The first-pass compaction_id is never reused.

5. Recovery

   C1. Crash between eligibility check and commit.
       Setup: worker computes eligibility, begins transaction, process killed before commit.
       Expect: on restart, no checkpoint for W exists. Worker re-evaluates from current watermarks. No half-written rollup row. Inject the kill between BEGIN and COMMIT and assert neither row is visible post-recovery.

   C2. Crash during commit (DB-level).
       Setup: kill after BEGIN, before COMMIT lands.
       Expect: DB rollback; no partial write. Restart re-evaluates and produces a fresh attempt.

   C3. Crash after commit, before downstream notification.
       Setup: commit lands, process killed before downstream is signaled.
       Expect: restart reads checkpoint, sees W completed, skips evaluation. Downstream notification must be idempotent given this scenario.

   C4. Watermark cache loss.
       Setup: worker holds watermark cache in memory only; crash drops it.
       Expect: on restart, worker re-fetches watermarks from shard-keeper (or its local store). Eligibility must not rely on cached values.

6. Duplicate-compaction

   D1. Two workers, same window, both observe eligibility.
       Setup: brief rebalance window where both A (old owner) and B (new owner) independently observe min >= T+90s for W.
       Expect: at most one transaction commits. compaction_id MUST be deterministic from inputs both workers can reproduce — e.g., hash(W, shard-keeper assignment_generation) — so a unique constraint or compare-and-set on (window, compaction_id) rejects the second. If compaction_id is chosen independently per worker, both succeed and corrupt state. This is the load-bearing question; flag it as a blocker if not pinned.

   D2. Fencing across assignment generations.
       Setup: W completed under assignment_generation G with compaction_id C1. Assignment rolls to G+1. A late record triggers a correction pass.
       Expect: correction compaction_id C2 is strictly greater than C1 and tied to G+1. Replaying an old transaction must not overwrite a newer state.

   D3. Duplicate correction triggers.
       Setup: correction pass for W in flight; same trigger fires again (two late records in quick succession, or a retry).
       Expect: idempotency keyed on the correction's compaction_id. Only one correction output per compaction_id; subsequent attempts observe the committed state and exit.

   D4. Correction must not silently mutate first-pass output.
       Setup: first-pass committed. Late record arrives. Correction runs.
       Expect: a NEW compaction_id is used; the new output atomically replaces the first-pass output. Concurrent readers of W's output see either the first-pass value or the corrected value, never a partial. Test the read-side visibility window, not just the write-side atomicity.

Open questions for Cyrus's team before approval

   - S4: policy for unassigned partitions during a window — excluded from min, or blocking? Document it.
   - D1, D2: compaction_id derivation. Deterministic from (window, assignment_generation), or per-worker? If per-worker, the duplicate-compaction defense is broken — blocker.
   - D3: correction pass trigger and rate limit. What fires it, and how is duplicate triggering suppressed?
   - D4: first-pass vs correction output visibility. Do downstream consumers read keyed on (window, compaction_id) and pick the latest, or is there a separate "latest pointer"? The atomicity model must be explicit, and the correction pass must not silently leave downstream reading stale data after the replace commits.

Once D1 (compaction_id derivation) is pinned and the four open questions above are answered in the PR text, the boundary, partition-skew, rebalance, recovery, and duplicate-compaction tests as specified are the gate.

No prior history on this AC. Based purely on what you observed and described, here's the assessment.

Can ordinary use resume? Yes — with the monitoring/escalation gate below, not as a blind yes.

The picture that fits your observations:

Your unit was tilting INWARD (the back/lower rail sitting higher than the front, so condensate pools against the chassis instead of running out the drain slot). You corrected the tilt to a slight outward pitch (~1/4 in), confirmed the drain slot is clear, the filter and evaporator coil intake are clean, and a 30-min fan + 45-min cool cycle produced exterior dripping only — no interior water, no vibration, no hot plug, no panel shift. That matches a successful "tilt + clear drain + clean coil" recovery, and you didn't introduce new risk (no drilled holes, no inserted tools).

Why I'm comfortable saying yes:

  1. Direction of tilt now matches what every manufacturer specifies for condensate drainage (slightly down toward the outside).
  2. Drain slot is unobstructed (you removed the obstruction) and the interior intake is clean, so coil runoff isn't blowing back into the pan.
  3. A combined fan + cool soak test under load is the right pass criterion — fan-only wouldn't have produced condensate, and you ran both.
  4. Exterior dripping confirms the drain path is actually flowing, not just "open."

Monitoring criteria for ordinary use (do these every time you run cooling in the next 7 days):

  - First 10 minutes after each cool-on: walk past the unit and look at the sill and the floor under the front edge — any wetness = stop and re-check tilt.
  - Every hour during the first 3 cooling cycles: glance at the exterior drip point. If it's dry during active cooling, treat that as a yellow flag (condensate has nowhere to go).
  - At end of every cooling cycle: feel the front bottom rail/pan area inside — it should be dry or just barely damp, never wet.
  - After any heavy rain or wind: re-check tilt has not shifted, and clear the exterior drain slot again (leaves, grit).
  - Keep the filter clean on the normal schedule — a dirty coil re-introduces carry-over into the pan even with a good drain.

Escalation criteria — interior condensate = STOP cooling and address:

  - Triggers (any one):
    - Any water, dampness, or staining appearing on the interior sill, front panel, floor, or wall below the unit.
    - "Plinking" or dripping sounds from inside the chassis during cool mode (water hitting the pan/fan housing instead of the drain slot).
    - Visible ice on the coil at any point (suggests restricted drain or low airflow — both can overflow).
    - Exterior drip stops while the unit is producing cold air and the air feels humid at the outlet.
    - Tilt visibly changes (rail settled, sash shifted, bracket slipped) — re-set before resuming.

  - What to do before resuming:
    - Power off at the plug, not just the controls.
    - Re-verify the ~1/4 in outward tilt with a level on the top.
    - Inspect the exterior drain slot again (the most common re-failure cause).
    - Re-run the 30-min fan + 45-min cool test. Only resume ordinary use after it passes clean.

  - Call a tech if it fails twice in a row, or if you see interior water despite correct tilt + clear drain — that points at a cracked drain pan, separated pan seal, or an internal drain routing issue, none of which are DIY fixes.

One standing constraint worth keeping in mind: the tilt is currently held by the sash and friction. If anyone opens/closes that window, re-check tilt before the next cool cycle. If you want it held more reliably, a foam-block wedge under the front rail or a bracket to the sill is the usual next step — but you didn't ask for that, and it's not required for ordinary use given how the test went.

Short version: yes, resume ordinary use, with the four monitoring checks above for the first several cycles, and stop immediately on any of the five escalation triggers.

ARTIFACT CONTRACT: HASH THE CANONICALIZED ARCHIVE, NOT THE RAW ARCHIVE

DIAGNOSIS

The 0x000a NTFS extra field (36 bytes/entry) records NTFS mtime/atime/ctime at 100-nanosecond precision, written by Windows ZIP tools because the source files have NTFS attributes. Linux/macOS runners don't write it because their source filesystems don't have those attributes. It's filesystem-provenance metadata, not content. Given your "normalized entry timestamps: equal" check, the NTFS field is either a redundant higher-precision copy of an already-normalized timestamp, or carries the un-normalized original NTFS timestamp — either way, content-invariant.

THE PRINCIPLE GAP

Right now the implicit artifact contract is "the raw archive byte stream." That entangles two things that should be separate:

  - Content: what gets shipped (entries, order, file contents, normalized timestamps)
  - Build environment: which OS produced the archive (which writes which extra fields)

Drift detection should guard content. The build environment shouldn't be part of the contract.

THE SAFE CONTRACT

The artifact is: the ZIP archive after canonicalization, identified by SHA-256 of the canonicalized bytes.

Canonicalization rules, applied identically on all platforms before hashing:

  1. Entry order: fixed (manifest order, lexicographic, or as built)
  2. Entry timestamps: normalized to a single fixed value (e.g., 1980-01-01 00:00:00) or a manifest-specified per-entry timestamp
  3. Extra fields: stripped except those explicitly whitelisted (none, for releases)
  4. Compression: deterministic per entry

One canonical form, one canonical hash. That hash is the artifact identifier.

IMPLEMENTATION PATHS, IN ORDER OF PREFERENCE

  1. Switch the Windows runner to a deterministic builder that doesn't write 0x000a: `zip -X` (strip extra fields) or Python's `zipfile` (doesn't write 0x000a by default). All three platforms then produce byte-identical archives and you don't need a canonicalization post-step.

  2. Standardize on a manifest-driven builder that writes a canonical ZIP from a single source of truth (entries, timestamps, no extra fields). Cross-platform from one place.

  3. If keeping platform-native builders, add a post-build canonicalization pass: strip 0x000a (and any other platform-specific extra fields like 0x000d Unix), then hash the canonicalized bytes. Drift detection compares the canonical hash. Raw archive hash differences across platforms become expected build-environment variation, not a publication blocker.

Path 1 is cleanest. Path 3 is the smallest change if swapping the Windows toolchain isn't on the table.

WHY THIS ISN'T WEAKENING FAIL-CLOSED DRIFT DETECTION

Drift detection still runs on the artifact's content hash. Real content changes — different file contents, missing/added entries, reordered entries, different normalized timestamps — still change the canonical hash and still trip drift detection. Only platform-derived filesystem metadata that doesn't affect extracted content is normalized away. Your three passing checks (extracted file hashes equal, entry order equal, normalized entry timestamps equal) are exactly what the canonical contract requires. The only thing the byte-for-byte hash was catching is content-invariant metadata.

WHY THIS ISN'T A PLATFORM-SPECIFIC EXCEPTION

There is no allow-list keyed on Windows. All three runners apply the same canonicalization rules and produce the same canonical bytes. The hash is computed identically on every platform. Windows is not "excused" — it's brought into the same contract as the other two. If a fourth runner appears later (FreeBSD, WSL2, etc.), the same rules apply automatically.

WHAT TO TAKE TO ANYA'S TEAM

  1. Document the canonicalization rules: fixed entry order, normalized timestamps, no extra fields. Put them in the release process so future tools and runners inherit them.
  2. Pick path 1 or path 3 above.
  3. Re-run on all three platforms. Confirm: same canonical hash (this is the artifact ID and the drift-detection key), and — as a bonus on path 1 — same raw archive hash too.
  4. Keep drift detection on the canonical hash. Optionally log the raw archive hash per platform as a build-environment trace; never gate on it.
  5. APPNOTE.TXT explicitly treats extra fields as optional and per-implementation, so normalizing them away is consistent with the spec, not a workaround.
