Decision: close the alert. No restart, no failover.

The replica's authority was never in question. Lease validity is a separate plane from replication progress. A follower can hold a perfectly valid lease — keep its epoch, keep its term, keep its acknowledged position — while temporarily falling behind on apply because its local disk is slow. That is exactly the shape of this incident.

Evidence that this is host-side, not lease-side:

  - Lease holder and epoch stable throughout. No acquisition, no relinquishment.
  - No stale-owner message, no overlapping leadership, no split-brain signature.
  - No leader-side write error, no replica restart, heartbeats normal.
  - Proximate cause was disk latency; it returned to baseline at 8:02 and lag declined continuously rather than oscillating.
  - Lag below 1s for 17 minutes, replica reentered follower reads after the 15-minute criterion, normal reads for 3 minutes since.

Why no restart:

A restart would discard the state the replica already applied and force a fresh snapshot or transfer from a peer. On a replica already recovering on its own and now serving reads correctly, restart manufactures a longer outage to fix nothing. Restart is indicated when lease validity is in question or on-disk corruption is suspected. Neither applies: epoch is intact, no stale-owner, disk subsystem recovered.

Why no failover:

Failover addresses leader-side authority failure — a leader that has lost its lease, cannot commit, or risks split-brain. The leader here was healthy for the whole window. The replica in question is a follower, not a leader candidate, and a healthy leader should not be displaced because one follower had transient disk pressure. Forcing a leader change here would manufacture an outage on a system that had none.

The distinction to keep clean:

Host-latency events produce liveness and performance symptoms — high p99 disk, apply lag, slow catch-up. They do not produce lease-safety signals. Lease-safety failures produce epoch bumps, stale-owner messages, overlapping leadership claims, write rejections, leader-side errors. You saw the first without the second. This is a blameless host issue. Treating it as a consensus problem would have made the system less safe, not more.

Acceptance for close:

  - Lease holder stable.
  - Lag below 1s for 17 continuous minutes (criterion: 15).
  - Replica reentered follower reads.
  - Normal reads for 3 minutes since reentry.
  - Disk latency back at baseline.

Close.

Effective-savings framing

1. Six months "free" framing (misleading): $720 saved ÷ 6 free months = $120 saved per "free" month. This is the headline number landlords use. It is only real if you would have left at month 12 anyway.

2. Net-out-of-pocket framing (the honest one): If you would stay past month 12 either way, Option B saves you $720 in absolute rent ($39,000 → effectively the same rent total, but spread). If you would leave at or before month 12, Option B costs you the extra six months × $3,190 = $19,140 above what Option A would have cost.

So the offer is really asking you to bet $19,140 of downside (six more months locked in) against $720 of upside. That is roughly a 27:1 risk/reward in the landlord's favor on pure numbers.

Break-even / opportunity-cost view
- Average monthly cost across the full 18 months if you commit to B: $3,190 (the rent itself).

Here's a low-risk diagnostic sequence that preserves your current config and answers each part of your question. The order matters — record evidence first, then isolate variables one at a time, then escalate.

==========================================
1. EVIDENCE TO CAPTURE BEFORE TOUCHING ANYTHING
==========================================

Do this within the first 24 hours of the problem, before any config change. It costs nothing and preserves options.

a) Wi-Fi neighborhood snapshot. Run a scanner on a laptop (WiFi Analyzer, NetSpot, inSSIDer, or `sudo iw dev wlan0 scan` on Linux). Save a screenshot of the 5 GHz band showing every neighbor AP and which channel each is on. Repeat 3-4 times across the day (morning/afternoon/evening/late night) — neighbor density changes and you want to see that.

b) Router event log. Pull the syslog / admin log from the router UI (not a reboot — just open the page). Save/export it. You're looking specifically for entries containing:
   - "radar", "DFS", "CAC" (channel availability check)
   - "channel change", "channel switch"
   - "5G" / "5 GHz" / "radio" disassoc or restart
   - temperature warnings, if the firmware logs them
   - firmware watchdog / crash / reboot lines

c) Drop timestamp log. Every time a phone or laptop loses the 5 GHz SSID, note:
   - exact time (to the minute)
   - which device dropped
   - did the wired TV keep streaming? (you said yes — confirm again, it matters)
   - did the 2.4 GHz device stay connected? (you said yes — confirm again)
   - did the SSID disappear, or did it stay visible but not associate?

d) Current 5 GHz radio settings. Screenshot the existing values for: channel, channel width (20/40/80/160 MHz), transmit power, "Auto channel" state, DFS enable/disable, MU-MIMO/beamforming toggles, band-steering / Smart Connect state. You're going to compare against these later.

e) Router placement. Photo of where it sits — open shelf vs enclosed cabinet vs stacked against a wall. Note ambient room temp.

Why this matters first: a DFS radar detection forces a 30-minute channel vacation, and in an apartment building the radar "hits" are usually false triggers from neighbor APs, cordless phones, or even weather radar. If your log shows channel-change events matching the drop timestamps, you've already localized the cause without touching config.

==========================================
2. THE FIXED NON-DFS CHANNEL + WIDTH TEST
==========================================

5 GHz channels that do NOT require DFS in the US/EU:
   - UNII-1: 36, 40, 44, 48
   - UNII-3: 149, 153, 157, 161, 165

Channels 52–64 (UNII-2A) and 100–144 (UNII-2C) are DFS — avoid them for the test. 165 is sometimes restricted on older client devices; 149 or 36 are the safe defaults.

Procedure (preserves everything else):

Step A — set channel to a fixed non-DFS value.
   - Pick the least-congested of 36 / 149 from your scanner snapshot. If unsure, use 36.
   - In the router UI, change "Channel" from Auto to that specific number.
   - If your router has a separate "DFS channels" toggle, disable it for now.
   - If the router has "Auto" + "DFS-aware" modes, switch to a manual fixed channel.

Step B — set channel width.
   - Start at 40 MHz. It's a good signal: it usually fits non-DFS in one block (36+40 or 149+153) without leaking into DFS territory, and it's more robust against interference than 80 MHz.
   - If your router only offers 20/40/80/160, pick 40. Do not pick 160 — it's almost guaranteed to touch DFS in the 5 GHz band.

Step C — leave everything else alone.
   - Don't change SSID, password, security, transmit power, 2.4 GHz, WAN, DHCP, IPv6. The point is one variable at a time.

Step D — observe 24–48 hours.
   - If drops stop: original cause was DFS event, auto-channel oscillation, or co-channel congestion. You can now try widening to 80 MHz on the same channel, and try a second non-DFS channel (e.g., 149 vs 36) to find the cleanest one.
   - If drops continue at the same 10–15 min cadence: channel isn't the cause. Move to step 3.

Step E — revert if needed.
   - Set channel back to Auto and DFS-on, width back to whatever it was. Everything else was untouched.

This test is fully reversible. It costs you nothing if it doesn't fix it, and it isolates the channel-related hypotheses cleanly.

==========================================
3. DISTINGUISHING INTERFERENCE FROM A FAILING 5 GHZ RADIO
==========================================

The signatures are different. The 2.4 GHz device staying stable while 5 GHz drops, with no WAN drop on the modem, already tells you a lot — the failure is local to the 5 GHz radio path.

INTERFERENCE / DFS signature (channel-related):
   - Drops correlate with events in the router log (channel change, radar, CAC abort).
   - Drops are more frequent at busy hours (7–11 PM) when neighbor APs are active; rarer at 3 AM.
   - Wi-Fi scanner shows your AP on a channel that has at least 2–3 strong neighbor APs (> -70 dBm), or shows your AP's channel shifting across the day.
   - Switching to a clean fixed non-DFS channel (step 2) eliminates or sharply reduces the drops.
   - Reboot "helps" briefly because it forces a fresh channel scan; the new channel happens to be cleaner for some minutes, then auto-channel logic or a DFS event re-buries it.

FAILING 5 GHZ RADIO signature (hardware/thermal):
   - Drops happen regardless of channel — even after locking to a clean non-DFS channel, even at 3 AM with no neighbor activity.
   - Drops occur at a suspiciously regular interval (every 10–15 min is a thermal-cycle hint — many radios throttle or reset on a thermal timer).
   - RSSI / link rate on clients fluctuates wildly even at the same distance, or clients report "low signal" while sitting next to the router.
   - Router log shows 5 GHz radio resets, firmware restarts, or "radio 0 restarted" entries with no DFS events.
   - Router gets noticeably warm to the touch during a drop, cooler between drops. "Warm but not hot" is borderline — feel the case during a drop and again 30 min after a drop, and compare.
   - A reboot restores service for ~10–20 min then it returns. (You saw exactly this: ~20 min restoration, then drops.) That short-recovery pattern is a hardware/thermal tell, not interference.

Quick tie-breaker test if you're uncertain:
   - Move the router to a different outlet, ideally off any power strip, and put it on a hard flat surface with 10 cm clearance on all sides. Let it run 24 hours.
   - If drops persist with the same cadence: not thermal placement, leaning toward radio failure.
   - If drops reduce or shift pattern: thermal/placement was contributing.

Another tie-breaker:
   - Set the 5 GHz transmit power to "Low" or "Medium" (instead of High) for 24 hours.
   - If drops decrease: power-amp thermal stress was the trigger.
   - If drops are unchanged: not power-related.

==========================================
4. WHEN TO STOP REBOOTING
==========================================

Rebooting is a diagnostic, not a fix. Stop when any of these are true:
   - You've rebooted twice in a row and the second restoration is shorter than the first (e.g., 20 min → 8 min). That's the radio dying faster each time, and another reboot is just burning runtime on a failing component.
   - You've rebooted three times total for the same issue without a config change in between. Three data points is enough; further reboots won't tell you anything new and they destroy the very log entries (channel changes, DFS events) that would explain the cause.
   - You need the network for something time-sensitive (call, upload, anything with a deadline). Stop and use the 2.4 GHz SSID or a wired connection instead.

Between reboots, always pull and save the log. A reboot wipes the in-memory event ring on most routers.

==========================================
5. WHEN TO CONTACT THE PROVIDER
==========================================

The modem status page showing no WAN disconnects is a strong signal that the ISP link itself is healthy. Contact the provider when:
   - After a clean non-DFS test (step 2) the drops persist AND the router log shows no DFS / channel-change events — you've ruled out the obvious local causes and the provider may want to look at line stats, SNR margins, or replace the ONT/modem if they bundle it.
   - The router is ISP-provided (most providers own the router in this case; you usually can't even log into it deeply).
   - You see WAN-side anomalies on the modem page you didn't notice before — T3 timeouts, T4 timeouts, SNR margin dropping below ~6 dB downstream, or a large count of "uncorrectable codewords" / FEC errors. These are evidence of a line problem the modem UI may not surface by default; the provider can read them remotely.
   - Multiple devices on different bands start failing — that flips the diagnosis away from "5 GHz radio" toward "whole link."

What to tell the provider: drop pattern (every 10–15 min), affected band (5 GHz only), that 2.4 GHz + wired are stable, that modem shows no WAN disconnects, and that you've already tested a fixed non-DFS channel. That last point saves them an hour of "have you tried changing the channel" script.

==========================================
6. WHEN TO REPLACE THE ROUTER
==========================================

Replace when any of these hold:
   - The failing-radio signature from section 3 is clear: drops persist on a clean fixed non-DFS channel, happen at idle hours, and the log shows radio resets rather than DFS events. At that point you've isolated the cause to the router's 5 GHz hardware.
   - The router is 4+ years old and the vendor has stopped releasing firmware updates. Old 5 GHz radios drift out of spec; outdated firmware also stops being tuned for current client behavior.
   - The router has no separate toggle to disable DFS, doesn't expose a channel-width setting, or runs a fixed non-configurable Auto-channel. You can't run the test in section 2 at all, and you can't diagnose — that's a replace signal on usability grounds alone.
   - The router is ISP-rented and the provider confirms it's the failing component; they'll swap it.
   - Warranty claim is viable — check the serial number before buying a new one; a free replacement beats any purchase.

Don't replace yet if:
   - You haven't yet run the non-DFS fixed-channel test in section 2. That test alone resolves a large fraction of apartment 5 GHz drop reports, and a replacement router inherits the same congested 5 GHz air.
   - The log shows DFS radar events matching your drop timestamps. That's a configuration problem (or a regulatory one), not a hardware problem — a new router on Auto with DFS on will hit the same wall.

==========================================
SHORT VERSION (if you only do three things)
==========================================

1. Pull and save the router log + a Wi-Fi scanner screenshot before changing anything.
2. Lock the 5 GHz channel to 36 (or 149), set width to 40 MHz, disable DFS if your router exposes that toggle, and wait 48 hours.
3. If drops continue unchanged on a clean non-DFS channel with no DFS events in the log, treat it as a 5 GHz radio failure and replace the router. If drops stop, you've found it; widen to 80 MHz and pick the cleanest non-DFS channel as your long-term config.

Is interference likely?

Consistent with it, not yet proven. Three points:

  - 75 min clean on channel 36 while neighbors cluster on 149 is the expected pattern if 149 was congested and 36 is clean. That's positive evidence for interference.
  - 75 min is short. Interference is often intermittent (neighbor streaming peaks, time-of-day patterns, occasional DFS/radar events). A clean run during a quiet window doesn't rule out a radio fault that shows up under heat or sustained load.
  - 2.4 GHz and wired staying up argues against a router-wide fault and supports a 5 GHz band-specific cause, which fits interference better than a hardware fault.

So: interference is the leading working hypothesis. Don't close it as solved yet — that would be premature.

Bounded monitoring plan

  Window: 7 days minimum, 14 if you want to catch a weekly pattern. Cover at least two weekday evenings and one weekend day of heavier use.

  Record daily (low effort):
    - Any 5 GHz disconnect or speed drop, with clock time
    - Same for 2.4 GHz and wired, so you have a comparison band
    - Approximate time of heavy local network activity that preceded problems
    - Router uptime / reboot count if visible in the admin page

  Hold constant during the window:
    - Channel 36, 40 MHz width, current power setting
    - No channel swaps, no width changes, no factory reset
    - Write down the firmware version at the start so it's not a confounder later

  Recurrence patterns that point back to a failing 5 GHz radio:
    - Disconnects on channel 36 with the same pattern as on 149. A clean channel staying clean is the test; if it doesn't, the channel wasn't the problem and the radio is suspect.
    - Disconnects that correlate with router uptime or heat (worse after the router has been on for hours, better after a reboot).
    - Disconnects only under sustained 5 GHz load, with 2.4 GHz fine at the same time. This is the harder case to distinguish from interference, but if it persists across channel changes, suspect the radio.
    - 5 GHz signal at a fixed distance noticeably worse than a phone/laptop WiFi analyzer says it should be.
    - 2.4 GHz or wired developing the same problem. That rules out a 5 GHz-specific cause and points somewhere else entirely.

  Recurrence patterns that confirm interference:
    - All quiet on channel 36 across the full window.
    - Problems return only when you re-test 149. Do one short A/B at the end of the window: a few hours on 36 vs a few hours on 149.
    - Problem times line up with neighbor usage (evenings, weekends).

  End-of-window decision:
    - 7+ days clean on 36 → interference confirmed. Either leave it on 36, or briefly A/B 149 to see whether it's still bad, then pick the best non-DFS channel from a fresh scan.
    - Problems recur on 36 → escalate to radio-failure investigation. Check Tx error / retry counters in the router admin page, watch thermal behavior, or swap the unit.

One thing worth doing now: confirm the router's 5 GHz transmit power and channel-width are set where you think they are, and write down the firmware version. Both are confounders if you ever need to compare across this window.

The external preview contract scopes what a viewer is allowed to infer from a Lantern-rendered value. Provenance metadata attached to an explicit `unknown` is treated as evidence of source-poll recency, not as freshness evidence for the value itself. Those are two different claims; collapsing them is exactly what Iris flagged.

For an explicit `unknown` incident-load value, the correct timestamp semantics are:

  - It records when Lantern last successfully polled the source for that signal.
  - It does not attest to recency of the missing value, because the value is unknown.
  - It does not let the viewer infer "the unknown was last known to be X at ts" — only "the source was polled at ts and was already unknown."

Implications for this fixture:

  - Suppress the timestamp when the value is `unknown`. Cleanest read; removes the inference path entirely.
  - If it has to stay (e.g., to show the fixture is live), relabel it as poll recency, not value freshness. The pre-review wording shift (capacity signal -> service operational load signal) is the same instinct applied to labels: scope the wording to what the data actually says.
  - Internal-only access does not weaken this. The contract is the canonical semantic; an internal fixture that lets poll recency stand in for value freshness is the same bug a customer preview could not ship.

Iris's read is correct: the timestamp as currently rendered is a misinterpretation vector. Don't fix it by writing "unknown as of <ts>" — that just states the bug in declarative form. Either drop the timestamp or relabel it so it cannot be read as freshness evidence. No new data invented, no contract clause added; just enforce the separation the contract already requires.

Assessment: yes, this violates the cross-service invariant. The transaction that prevents publication is a downstream coincidence, not the contract.

Why the transaction does not save it:
  - The watermark predicate is a property of the COMPLETE current assignment. Evaluating it against 5/6 partitions produces a transient answer that does not reflect the system's true state.
  - No commit occurred here for three contingent reasons stacked together: (1) the transaction wrapper, (2) the missing partition loading inside 280 ms, (3) no side-effecting reader observing the stale predicate result. Any one of those changing in prod (slower partition load, GC pause, a metrics-emitting reader, a future refactor that drops the transaction wrapper) surfaces the bug as a silent undercount or a premature completion signal.
  - The 280 ms window is staging-coincidence. Prod partition loads widen arbitrarily with network, GC, and disk variance.
  - The invariant belongs at the snapshot boundary, not at the commit boundary.

Minimum gating rule:

  Predicate evaluation MUST be blocked until the assignment-snapshot-ready signal has fired for every partition in the current assignment. Concretely:

    - assignment_epoch N is "ready" iff every partition p in assignment[N] has a loaded snapshot.
    - watermark/predicate evaluation against epoch N is gated on ready[N] == true.
    - if the epoch transitions mid-evaluation, abort the in-flight evaluation and start fresh against the new epoch; no incremental merge with the stale partial result.

  Implement as a per-epoch snapshot-ready latch that flips only when every partition in the assignment reports load-complete; predicate consumers wait on the latch transition (or the epoch bump, whichever comes first). The downstream transaction stays as a belt-and-suspenders guard, but the contract lives at the latch.

Regression test (must be wired into the staging drill before the patch ships):

  1. Inject a configurable per-partition snapshot load delay (set partition 5 to 500 ms–2 s, randomized per run).
  2. Drive a rebalance that adds a new partition to the assignment.
  3. Assert no predicate is evaluated and no completion signal is emitted until ALL partitions in the new assignment report snapshot-ready.
  4. Increment a counter for "premature predicate evaluations"; assert zero across the run, including during the gap window.
  5. Increment a counter for "predicates evaluated against stale epoch"; assert zero.
  6. Negative test: rebuild with the transaction wrapper stripped out; the regression test must still fail. The gating rule alone has to catch the bug, not the transaction.
  7. Run with the missing partition's load delayed past any plausible commit window (e.g., 5 s); predicate must remain blocked for the full duration, not just "eventually evaluated" once the late partition lands.

Pre-open for the drill: confirm the gating rule is in the diff and the regression test is wired and observed to fail on the unpatched build. Pre-close: confirm zero premature-evaluations logged across the staging run, then the tag can come off.

Cyrus's instinct to ask is correct — the absence of an undercount this time is not the bar; the invariant has to hold independent of the txn wrapper.

Here's safe first-aid guidance for a shallow skin flap on your finger. Based on what you describe — bleeding controlled, flap still partly attached, normal sensation/movement, no deep wound, no obvious contamination, no nail involvement — this is manageable at home with careful dressing, but watch closely for the red flags below.

CLEANING
  - You've already done the most important step. Gently rinse under clean lukewarm running water for a couple of minutes to flush chalk and grit.
  - A small amount of mild soap on the skin around (not directly in) the wound is fine. Avoid hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, or undiluted iodine on the wound itself — they damage healing tissue.
  - Pick out any visible debris you can rinse free. Don't scrub or pick at the flap.
  - Pat dry with clean gauze or a clean cloth. Don't use cotton balls — fibers stick to wounds.

TRIM OR PRESERVE
  - Preserve it. Don't trim it yourself.
  - A still-attached flap carries some of its own blood supply and acts as a natural biological dressing. It's almost always worth saving, and a clinician will normally try to preserve one.
  - Gently lay it back into its natural position. Don't stretch, fold, or bunch it.
  - Don't tape it down aggressively, and definitely don't use superglue or any industrial adhesive on the wound.
  - If part of it later turns black, dry, or leathery (clearly non-viable), a clinician can trim just that portion and close the wound properly if needed. That's not a home task.

COVERING FOR THE EVENING
  - Apply a thin layer of plain petroleum jelly (Vaseline) or an OTC antibiotic ointment (bacitracin, polysporin) over the flap. This keeps the tissue moist and prevents the bandage from sticking to it.
  - Place a non-adherent pad (Telfa, Adaptic, or any "non-stick" pad) directly over the wound. Plain gauze can adhere to the flap and rip it off when removed.
  - Cover with a gauze pad and secure with a self-adhering wrap (Coban-style), a fingertip bandage, or a tube of tubular gauze sized for a finger.
  - Change the dressing daily, or sooner if it gets wet, dirty, or soaked through. When changing, moisten the pad first if it's sticking — peel, don't rip.

ACTIVITY LIMITS
  - No climbing until the flap has clearly re-adhered and there's no raw surface exposed. A reasonable floor is one to two weeks off, longer if still tender or open.
  - Avoid submerging the finger (no swimming, no dishwashing without a waterproof glove).
  - For showers, cover with a waterproof bandage or a finger cot sealed at the base so the wound stays dry.
  - Avoid gripping, pulling, or anything that could shear the flap off — heavy bags by that hand, climbing, contact sports, even rough towel-drying.
  - If it throbs or feels warm, elevate the hand above heart level.

URGENT CARE — GO IN TODAY OR TONIGHT IF ANY OF THESE SHOW UP
  - Bleeding that doesn't stop after 10–15 minutes of firm, direct pressure.
  - Finger goes pale, blue, purple, or cold — possible circulation problem.
  - You lose sensation in the finger, or can't fully bend or straighten it — possible nerve or tendon injury.
  - Deep tissue, tendon, bone, or joint is visible.
  - Red streaks up the hand or arm, fever, rapidly spreading redness, or severe throbbing pain — spreading infection.
  - The wound is heavily contaminated and you can't get it clean.

ROUTINE MEDICAL CARE — NON-URGENT, WITHIN 24–72 HOURS
  - Tetanus booster: if your last one was more than 5 years ago, a climbing-wall / outdoor / dirt-contaminated wound is a reasonable reason to get one. A pharmacy or your PCP can handle this quickly.
  - The flap turns dark, dry, or leathery — a clinician can debride and decide whether closure is needed.
  - Increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pus, foul smell, or pain that worsens after the first day or two — possible infection.
  - The wound reopens, keeps oozing, or shows no sign of healing within 3–5 days.
  - Stiffness or loss of range of motion develops.

GENERAL CAVEAT
This is general first-aid information, not a diagnosis or a replacement for an in-person assessment. Finger wounds are awkward — high-use, easy to reinjure, close to the nail bed, and unforgiving of poor dressing technique. If anything below the flap looks off, if you're not sure it's viable, or if you just want peace of mind, a same-day or next-day clinic visit (urgent care or your primary care office) is cheap insurance. They can dress it properly, decide whether closure is needed, and update your tetanus if appropriate.

For tonight: keep it clean, moist under a non-stick pad, well-dressed, and dry. Re-check it in the morning.

Verb: RECEDE. Tense: present, third-person singular (the -S on the end is your subject agreement, not past tense — past would drop that S for "receded"). So you're looking for something like "[he/she/it] recedes." Quietly is just adverbial flavor on the clue, not a separate indicator — the whole phrase parses as one definition.

Yes, this is reasonable. Your description — dry, closed at rest, minimally tender, no redness/warmth/swelling/drainage — is the picture of a wound in early but stable epithelial closure. A day after the injury, that closure is real but mechanically fragile: the new layer will shear off more easily than the skin around it, and a direct blow or scrape can reopen it. So the activity is fine with the right cover, and the failure modes are mostly preventable.

How to cover without constricting the finger

The principle: protect from friction, dirt, sweat, and shear — but never wrap anything tight enough to act like a tourniquet on a digit. A finger is small enough that even a "snug" wrap can become constricting the moment the finger swells during exertion.

Best options, in order of preference:

  1. Hydrocolloid bandage (Band-Aid Hydroseal, CVS hydrocolloid, Duoderm thin). These are flexible, adhesive all over (not just a strip in the middle), and they self-adhere without needing to be wrapped tight. Trim to size so the adhesive sits on intact skin at least a few mm past the wound edge on every side. This is the lowest-friction, lowest-constriction option and survives a hand-plant on grass well.

  2. Non-adherent pad (Telfa) + a thin smear of petrolatum (Vaseline) on the wound + a single piece of porous adhesive tape along the length of the finger (not wrapped around). The tape goes on the dorsal (top) and volar (palm) sides only — never circumferentially. A small piece of tubular gauze (finger-net) over the whole thing holds the pad in place without compression. This is what you'd use if the wound is still slightly weepy or if hydrocolloid won't stick because of location (knuckle, fingertip pad).

  3. Plain adhesive bandage sized for the finger, applied without pulling. If the Band-Aid feels "tight" at the base when you bend the finger, it's wrong — reapply looser. The adhesive should hold it; you shouldn't need tension.

Avoid: athletic tape wrapped around the finger, "X" taping across the joint, rubber finger cots pulled on tight, anything that leaves a visible indentation when you take it off. If your fingertip looks pale, blue, or feels cold/numb within a few minutes of play, the cover is too tight — remove and reapply.

Also useful: a thin layer of petrolatum or zinc-oxide barrier on the intact skin around the wound before the hydrocolloid helps it stick through sweat and reduces the "pulling the bandage off rips the scab" risk if it does come loose.

What should make you stop

Stop immediately and re-cover or sit out if any of these happen:

  - Fresh bleeding — bright red, more than a tiny spot. Reopening has occurred; the cover failed.
  - The wound edges visibly separate, or the scab lifts/tears.
  - Pain that increases during play, especially sharp or throbbing, or pain that wasn't there before a specific impact.
  - Dirt, grass, or grit gets into the wound and you can't rinse it out cleanly on the sideline.
  - The finger becomes pale, blue, cool, numb, or tingly — this is the cover cutting off circulation, not the wound, but it's a stop either way.
  - Direct impact to the wound — someone steps on your hand, the ball jams it, you brace hard and feel a "pop" of pain at the site. Don't play through a known direct blow to a 24-hour-old closure.

After play: clean with mild soap and water or saline, pat dry, inspect the wound and the skin around it, re-dress with a clean non-adherent pad. Over the next 24-48 hours watch for the infection signs you already know — increasing redness, warmth, swelling, tenderness, drainage, red streaking — and treat any of those as a reason to have it looked at rather than waiting it out.

One last honest note: if the wound is on a fingertip pad, over a joint, or in a high-shear spot (palm side near the knuckle), the cover is much more likely to fail during soccer than if it's on the dorsal surface of the finger. If it's in one of those locations, a hydrocolloid plus a finger-net sleeve gives you the best chance of finishing the game without reopening it — but also accept that "I played one half" is a perfectly reasonable outcome if the cover starts to peel.

DECISION: The event is NOT allowed to be emitted in the proposed form. A (service, commit, deployed_at) tuple is a deploy-shaped record regardless of label. `provenance_status: partial` does not neutralize that shape — downstream readers, reviewers in adjacent rooms, and any future migration of the room boundary would treat it as a real deploy signal. "Commit is verified" is necessary but not sufficient: the pipeline run ID is the linkage that proves this commit was actually deployed via this specific pipeline invocation. Without it, we have a verified commit and a timestamp, not a verified deploy.

REASONING
- Lantern's prov discipline is prov + perm-bounded, not prov + perm-bounded + best-effort. Perm-bounded means the external-facing shape is constrained regardless of how much prov we have.
- The preview contract excludes customer preview; the failure mode you're worried about is the same one — an externally meaningful deploy event surfaced through a path the contract does not authorize.
- A reviewer-cleared exception path exists for genuine prov gaps (owner-map snapshot with source, gen ts, named maintainer). That path applies only after a deliberate reviewer decision on a held-back fixture. It does not authorize an automatic emit with a partial label.

FAIL-CLOSED EXTERNAL REPRESENTATION

Preferred — suppress:
  Do not emit any record. Hold the fixture back. Re-attempt ingestion once pipeline_run_id is available, or route through the reviewer exception path if the gap is structural rather than transient.

If suppression is not viable (e.g., the room requires some record for accounting) — redact to non-deploy shape:

    "event_type": "provenance_incomplete",
    "service": null,
    "repository": "sphere/billing-api",
    "commit": null,
    "deployed_at": null,
    "pipeline_run_id": null,
    "provenance_status": "partial",
    "reason": "missing_pipeline_run_id",
    "reviewer_required": true
  }

Hard rules either way:
  service, commit, and deployed_at MUST NOT co-appear in any externally visible record when pipeline_run_id is null.
  provenance_status must never be "partial" on a deploy-shaped record.
  The reviewer exception path may clear the gap, but cleared records carry provenance_status "cleared" (with the owner-map snapshot attached) — they do not retroactively turn "partial" into "complete".

TESTS REQUIRED

1. Egress redaction test
   For any inbound record with pipeline_run_id = null, assert the egress transform produces either (a) no record, or (b) a record with service, commit, and deployed_at all null. Specifically:
   egress(service='billing-api', commit='a8f31c2', deployed_at='2024-06-10T13:42:00Z', pipeline_run_id=null) == null_record  (or all-identifiers-redacted)

2. No partial-deploy shape test
   Assert no record can carry provenance_status='partial' together with any populated value among {service, commit, deployed_at}. This is a schema-level invariant, not a per-record check.

3. Downstream grep test
   Query downstream consumers (search index, BI export, alert source) for (service, commit) tuples originating from records where pipeline_run_id was null at ingest. Assert zero matches.

4. Re-entry vs back-fill test
   When pipeline_run_id becomes available later, the record is re-emitted as a full-provenance deploy event on its own. It does NOT merge into or back-fill the prior partial record. The prior partial record, if any, is tombstoned.

     - owner-map snapshot attached with source, gen ts, and named maintainer

     - cleared records do not flow through any customer-preview-allowed path (the contract exclusion applies post-clear too — clearing closes the prov gap, it does not widen the audience)
     - reviewer identity is captured (not anonymous)

6. Cross-room reference test
   An incomplete-provenance deploy record cannot be referenced, linked, or joined into a customer-preview-allowed room's data, even after reviewer clearance. The audience boundary and the prov boundary are independent constraints.

7. Alert-source non-trigger test

8. Cardinality / source-count test

   Replaying the proposed fixture (service=billing-api, commit=a8f31c2, deployed_at=2024-06-10T13:42:00Z, pipeline_run_id=null, provenance_status=partial) against the current build must produce either no egress record or the redacted non-deploy shape above. Yes — the team's proposal does undermine canonical identity, and I'd push back on it. Quick assessment, then the safer rule.

Does it undermine canonical identity?

Yes, in three ways:

1. The defect is in the canonical source, not the Android exporter. Two names that mean the same thing ("surface muted") is a semantic duplicate in canonical regardless of what any platform does with case. Android just happens to expose it because its normalizer is case-insensitive; iOS and web tolerate it because theirs isn't. Dormant ≠ absent.

2. A platform-only suffix is a per-platform identity exception. It breaks the "one canonical token, many platform forms" invariant: now the canonical name `surface.muted` does not identify one thing on Android, it identifies `surface_muted`. Every downstream consumer who reads tokens by name has to learn the exception. And the next ask of this shape will be "our normalizer does X, can we add an iOS-only suffix too?" — you don't want a suffix zoo.

3. It papers over a canonical bug with a downstream workaround. Future audits of the canonical layer will not show the duplicate, so reviewers can't see the real shape of the token set. That's worse than the original state, where at least the collision was visible at import time on the platform that exposed it.

The pipeline failing closed is correct and stays. "Preserve fail-closed publication" is necessary, not sufficient — the identity of what's published has to be right too.

Recommended rule

Treat this as a canonical-source defect with a canonical-side fix. No platform-only suffix.

1. Standardize on the lowercase dot-separated form. `surface.muted` is the canonical name; `Surface.Muted` is the stray/legacy entry. If the org convention is the other way, flip which one gets deprecated, but pick one.

2. Mark the loser as a canonical alias with an explicit sunset, not a co-resident token. In canonical, `Surface.Muted` becomes `legacy_alias_of: surface.muted` (or equivalent). Every platform exporter — Android included — emits the canonical name, normalized per the platform's own convention. The Android exporter doesn't change at all.

3. Add a consumer-side migration window. Grep for `Surface.Muted` usages, file replacement issues against owners, set a removal date. Past that date the alias is dropped and any reintroduction fails the canonical import.

4. Move the collision check to the canonical importer, not the Android exporter. Add a case-insensitive uniqueness check on token names at canonical import. Today the importer accepted both names because canonical treated them as distinct strings; that is the bug. The Android export step should never have been the line of defense, and the fix shouldn't depend on it being one.

5. Reject the suffix proposal to the team, with the reasons above. The alias+migration path gives them everything they actually need (publication proceeds, no consumer breaks this week) without carving a platform-only identity exception into the canonical model.

Net: fail-closed stays, canonical identity stays one-to-one across platforms, and the next case-variant duplicate gets caught at the layer where it actually exists.

Slow drain with hair and soap visible at the stopper, no leak, no odor, no
backup elsewhere — this is almost certainly a hair clogging the stopper or
the first inch or two of the drain just below it, not a deep blockage. Stay
at that level tonight; it's the highest-yield and lowest-risk fix.

Quiet / low-risk sequence (stopper area only)

1.  Pull what you can see. With the sink empty, lift out anything sitting
    on the stopper — hair, soap blob — using a paper towel or tweezers.
    Don't run water yet.

2.  Identify your stopper type:

      - Lift-rod (the rod sticking out the back of the faucet, with a
        small knob/clip under the sink): a pop-up stopper in the drain.
      - Push-pull or toe-touch (you press or twist the stopper itself):
        screws out by hand, usually counterclockwise as viewed from above.
      - Grid / mushroom (no moving part): just lifts out, or is held by a
        small setscrew underneath.

    If you're not sure after 30 seconds of looking, stop and skip to step
    4 — don't force anything.

3.  Remove the stopper. For a lift-rod style: under the sink, find the
    thin horizontal pivot rod coming out of the drain just above the P-trap.
    Pinch the spring clip and slide the rod out of the clevis, then unscrew
    the pivot nut by hand a turn or two (no tools needed for this). The
    stopper will lift straight out from above. For push-pull / toe-touch:
    unscrew by hand. Have a dry rag ready — a small amount of water sits in
    the drain and will spill out when the stopper comes free.

4.  Clean the stopper. Most of the clog is hair wound around the stopper
    shaft or the rod beneath it. Peel it off with a paper towel, rinse in
    the basin you've just emptied into a bucket. Don't use the sink to rinse
    yet — you haven't tested flow.

5.  Look into the open drain with a flashlight. If you see more hair sitting
    an inch or two down, fish it out with a plastic zip-tie cut into a
    small hook, or a bent wire coat hanger with a blunted hook. Twist
    gently, pull up, wipe, repeat. Stop at the first sign of resistance —
    the goal is the first few inches only.

6.  Reassemble. Put the stopper back, re-seat the pivot rod, re-clip the
    spring clip. Hand-tight only. Then test: a shallow basin, let it drain,
    watch the stream. Empty in 10–15 seconds = fixed.

Stop conditions — don't push past any of these tonight

    - Stopper won't free by hand, or feels corroded / stuck
    - You can't remember how it goes back together mid-step
    - You see water weeping at the pivot nut or trap joint after
      reassembly
    - Drain is still slow even though the opening looks clear from above
    - Any new symptom appears: gurgling from the tub, water in the sink
      when you run the tub, sewage odor

If any of those happen, put the stopper back (or leave the drain covered
with a towel so sewer gas doesn't rise), and call building maintenance
in the morning. State: "single fixture, slow drain only, no backup, no
leak — please send a plumber for a snake through the trap." That's their
standard ticket and won't get bumped.

Things to deliberately avoid tonight

    - No chemical drain cleaner (corrosive, bad for the chrome trap, and
      you want it clear of chemicals before maintenance works on it)
    - No plunger — the gasket on a pop-up sink can blow, and it's loud
    - No trap disassembly unless the above failed — it's the noisiest
      step and the most leak-prone if the slip nuts don't reseat
    - No boiling water — porcelain can crack and it's unnecessary at the
      stopper level

If by morning the basin still empties in a slow swirl, leave a note for
Devika ("runs slow — about 90 seconds for a basin — building maintenance
called") rather than improvising. A working-but-slow sink is fine for one
day; a chemical reaction under her morning routine is not.

A 35-minute plan with a clean hold for the walk and the soggy bottom engineered out.

PRE-DEVIKA PREP (start about 7:40 PM)

1. Oven to 500°F with a pizza steel, stone, or an inverted heavy sheet pan on the middle rack. Give it a full 20-30 min to soak heat. A screaming-hot preheated surface is the single biggest anti-soggy move — it sears the dough the instant it lands.

2. Mozzarella: tear or slice, then pat between paper towels for a few minutes. Wet fresh mozz is soggy-pizza enemy number one.

3. Cherry tomatoes: halve, set cut-side-UP on a paper towel, sprinkle lightly with salt. The salt pulls juice out before the oven ever sees them.

4. Mushrooms: slice thin. Dry-skillet over high heat, single layer, no oil, 3-4 min until the pan goes quiet and the edges brown. Pinch of salt, then onto a paper towel. Mushrooms that hit the oven pre-cooked don't dump water into the dough.

5. Olives: slice or halve. Arugula: wash, spin dry. Zest the lemon; halve it for serving.

6. Dough: stretch onto parchment (not a floured board) so the whole thing slides onto the hot surface later. Light dust of semolina or cornmeal on the parchment — adds crunch and keeps the bottom from steaming.

ASSEMBLE BEFORE SHE WALKS IN

Brush dough with olive oil, very thin smash of garlic if you have it, then: mozzarella, mushrooms, olives, cherry tomatoes cut-side-UP (juice runs into the cheese, not the dough). Salt, pepper. Skip a heavy sauce — the tomatoes are your sauce. Go light on the cheese layer; less is drier.

HOLDING POINT — KIBO WALK (8:15 to 8:30 PM)

Leave the assembled pizza on its parchment on a cutting board at room temp. 15-20 min on parchment is fine — the parchment plus the upcoming blast of heat keeps the bottom from going gummy. Walk Kibo together; that's the hold.

BAKE (back from the walk, about 8:35 PM)

Slide the parchment straight onto the preheated steel/stone/sheet. 8-10 min at 500°F. Watch the bottom first — that's where sogginess lives. Pull when the bottom is blistered and the cheese has brown spots.

FINISH (last 60 seconds)

While it bakes: toss the arugula with a squeeze of lemon, a glug of olive oil, pinch of salt, the lemon zest. Pull the pizza. Pile the arugula on top — don't bake it, it wilts and goes sad. Squeeze the remaining lemon half over the whole pie. Slice into 4, plate, eat.

CLEANUP

Short version: yes, a short easy session is reasonable. The signs you describe (fully closed, dry, pink, no tenderness or swelling, full fist, pain-free hang) line up with what you want before loading the area. The risk is that newly epithelialized skin stays fragile to friction and shear for a few weeks, so treat this as a test session, not a workout.

  Taping the healed area without constriction
- Use a thin rigid sports tape (leukotape or equivalent), about 10 to 12 mm wide. Not elastic tape, not a band-aid strip, not a circumferential wrap.
- Cut the strip about 1.5x the length of the area you want to cover, oriented along the long axis of the finger (so it lies on the palmar surface, not around it).
- Dry the skin completely before applying. Any moisture under tape lifts new epithelium - that is the main cause of a "tape took the skin off again" outcome.
- Lay the strip flat across the healed area with both ends anchored on intact healthy skin a few millimetres past the wound edges. Do not wrap it around. Do not overlap the ends. Do not stretch the tape as you apply it.
- Press it down with light thumb pressure only. You should still see skin color at the edges, and the tape should not dimple the skin or pinch anywhere along its length.
- Check capillary refill after 5 minutes: press the nail bed, count the seconds for color to return (under 2 is normal). If the finger feels cool, tingly, throbbing, or "tight," pull the tape off and reapply with a shorter strip or none at all.
- Optional second strip: a thin perpendicular cross-piece anchored only on healthy skin can keep the first from lifting during crimping. Still no circumferential wrap.
- Remove the tape at the end of the session - in the shower is easiest - peeling slowly along the direction of hair growth. Do not leave it on overnight. Overnight swelling under a non-yielding strip is the classic way finger taping turns into a constriction injury.

  How to progress the session
- Total time on the wall 30 to 45 minutes, with a hard end time set before you walk in.
- Warm up for at least 15 minutes on jugs, big slopers, and traverses. No crimps during the warm-up.
- Self-cap effort at 4 or 5 out of 10. If you feel the ring finger pad whitening, you are past the line.
- Prefer open-hand and slope grips. Avoid full or half crimps, finger pockets that lock the ring finger in flexion, and pinches that press directly on the taped area.
- Skip dynos and any move where the ring finger could peel off a hold unexpectedly - those shear events are what reopen new skin.
- Tell Ren in advance that this is a return-to-climb session, not a project session. If a hard problem gets queued at your limit, decline and step off.
- After the session: remove tape, wash gently, dry fully, and inspect the area in good light for any new redness, lifting, or weeping. If intact, leave it alone - no creams, no occlusion.

  Stop the session as soon as any of the following happens
- Any sensation in the taped area at all: warmth, throbbing, pinching, stickiness, or a sense that the tape is pulling. New skin under tape should be forgettable while you climb; the moment you notice it, you are done.
- Sharp or burning pain in the ring finger on any move.
- Loss of fine motor control in that hand - you cannot fully open or close the finger on command.
- Color change anywhere under or beyond the tape: white, dusky, or grey fingertip, or pallor showing through the strip.
- The tape lifting, peeling, or wrinkling mid-move. You may replace once and continue only if the next move is clearly easy; otherwise stop.
- You catch yourself crimping hard without intending to. That is a sign intensity has crept above where it should be for this session.

The single rule that covers everything: the moment you go from not noticing the finger to noticing the finger, stop. Reopening new epithelium resets the healing clock and adds infection and scarring risk, so a clean exit at 25 minutes beats a heroic session that ends in a fresh wound.

One follow-up worth flagging: a ring-finger skin issue that took a week to close is worth a brief look at what is underneath. If the area was over a callus that came off, or if the underlying tissue feels firmer than the surrounding skin, or if you had any sense of "something giving" when the skin originally tore, mention it to Devika or your PCP at the next convenient visit. Nothing in what you describe suggests a pulley or tendon problem - the pain-free fist and pain-free hang argue strongly against that - but a one-line check-in is cheap insurance, and the ring finger A2/A3 pulleys are the one structure you do not want to find out about the slow way.

DECISION: external contract requires explicit unknown, not stale owner.

Reasoning against Product Engineering's "stale: true" proposal:

1. The owner-map's twenty-four-hour freshness limit is a contract-level bound, not an internal hint. Once the source timestamp crosses it, the record is no longer a permitted source per the owner-map pipeline's own rules. Returning the object with `stale: true` would still mean product surfaces a named maintainer for a record whose provenance we have just declared unfit. The contract is: a permitted record's age at publication <= 24h. Outside that window, there is no record to publish.

2. Iris's read is the binding one for product-facing surfaces: the product must not imply current ownership from a stale permitted source. "Imply" is the operative word — a `stale` flag doesn't undo the implication; it annotates it. Annotating with staleness while still naming the person is exactly the misleading state we want to prevent. Permitted + past-fresh = not permitted, full stop.

3. What the fixture must test instead:

  - Authorization constraint: fixture must only publish an owner when the record was sourced from a permitted provider AND source_timestamp is within the freshness window at the moment of publication. Both predicates required. No "OR was once permitted."

  - Provenance constraint: the fixture must assert the full provenance tuple on publish — provider name, source_timestamp (gen_ts), record identifier, and the freshness window applied. If any field is missing or stale, publish must be denied. Reviewers clearing an exception require the same tuple, no shortcuts.

  - Fallback constraint (the hard one): on freshness miss, the fixture must publish `owner: unknown` with `provenance: { source: "owner-map", status: "expired", source_timestamp: <ts>, age_hours: <n> }` — and must NOT:
    - infer ownership from the stale record,
    - fall back to internal room metadata (Lantern room, importer FM room, or any other internal room) as a proxy owner,
    - fall back to recent author / last-deployer / on-call rotation / code-ownership file,
    - widen scope to look across other permitted providers to "find" an owner.

  - Error path: the unknown publish must still be a valid external response shape (same envelope, owner field present and null/unknown, provenance present and honest). No silent omission, no implicit default.

  - Negative fixtures the test must include:
    a. source_timestamp = 24h + 1s → expect unknown, not stale-named.
    b. source_timestamp exactly 24h → expect unknown (boundary is inclusive, treat as expired).
    c. permitted source but missing provider name → expect unknown.
    d. clock skew: if the publisher's local clock is behind the gen_ts by more than the window, treat as expired even if wall-clock age looks fresh — gen_ts is the reference.
    e. no permitted source at all → expect unknown (this is the existing path; keep it covered so the fallback rewrite doesn't regress it).

Quick read of what you described: single vomit containing food and grass, no blood, no foreign object, alert, non-painful abdomen, drinking water, no repeated retching. That is a low-risk presentation, and withholding the next meal is the right first move. I'm not a vet, but this is the standard monitoring and re-feeding protocol for an uncomplicated single-vomit episode.

RE-FEEDING PLAN
  - Fast about 12 hours from the vomit. Since this happened on the evening walk, an overnight fast into tomorrow morning lines up cleanly.
  - During the fast, offer water in small amounts — a few laps every 30 to 60 minutes — rather than filling the bowl. Gulping a lot of water can retrigger vomiting.
  - If he gets through the fast with no further vomiting, start a bland diet:
      - Boiled skinless chicken (no bones, no skin, no salt or seasoning) with plain white rice, roughly 1 part chicken to 2-3 parts rice. Lean ground turkey works as a substitute.
      - First meal: about 1/4 to 1/3 of his normal portion.
      - Wait 1-2 hours. If he keeps it down, offer another small portion.
      - Repeat 3-4 small bland meals through the day.
      - Over the next 2-3 meals, mix increasing amounts of his regular food back in until he's back to normal.
  - Skip rich treats, table scraps, and any new foods for a couple of days.
  - Walks tomorrow: short and calm is fine. Skip the run, off-leash, or heavy play until stools are normal and he's eating well again.

MONITORING OVER THE NEXT 12-48 HOURS
  - Appetite should come back when the bland food arrives.
  - Energy: he may be a touch quiet tonight, but should be at baseline by morning.
  - Stools: mildly loose for a day is common after grass and not alarming on its own.
  - Vomiting: ideally zero. One isolated repeat during re-feed is a yellow flag. More than that is a red flag.
  - Water intake: normal. Neither refusing everything nor suddenly drinking large amounts.

HEAD TO THE EMERGENCY VET (call the nearest 24-hour vet on the way) IF YOU SEE
  - Repeated, unproductive retching — especially the posture where he's trying to vomit and nothing comes up. This can signal bloat / GDV, a true emergency in dogs.
  - Abdomen that becomes swollen, hard, tight, or painful to the touch.
  - Pale, white, blue, or grey gums.
  - Collapse, severe weakness, or rapid / labored breathing.
  - Blood in vomit (bright red or dark / coffee-ground) or blood in stool (red streaks or black tarry stool).
  - Any suspicion he got into something toxic — xylitol (sugar-free gum, some peanut butters), grapes or raisins, chocolate, onions or garlic, ibuprofen or acetaminophen, rodenticide, antifreeze, marijuana edibles, dropped medications. Bring the packaging.
  - Suspected foreign body — sock, toy piece, corn cob, stone, bone shard — followed by vomiting, pain, or food refusal.
  - He cannot keep even small sips of water down for several hours, or signs of worsening dehydration (tacky gums, skin pinch slow to flatten back).
  - Any sudden severe behavior change that suggests significant pain.

CALL YOUR REGULAR VET (next-day or scheduled) IF
  - One more isolated vomit after the fast that resolves and he otherwise eats, drinks, and acts normally.
  - Mild intermittent loose stool without other signs.
  - Picky appetite for one meal — try a smaller bland portion; if it persists, call.
  - Grass-eating without vomiting the next day. Common dog behavior, but worth mentioning at the next checkup if it becomes a pattern.
  - You're just not sure. A quick phone call is fine; most clinics will tell you whether to come in or wait.

IF IT ESCALATES, HAND THE VET THESE FACTS
  - Time of the vomit and contents (food + grass), that it happened right after chewing grass on a walk, no blood.
  - His state right after: alert, drinking, abdomen non-painful.
  - Approximate time of his last full meal before the vomit.
  - Any recent diet changes, new treats, table scraps, medications, supplements, trash access, known toxin exposure, or contact with other dogs.

If anything changes overnight — especially repeated retching, belly swelling, or sudden lethargy — don't wait for morning, take him in.

1. Safe scheduling
   - Stable round-robin order (sorted tenant ID) so the schedule is reproducible across pods and retries.
   - Don't advance the cursor on empty tenants. No busy-wait when nothing is queued.

2. Cancellation
   - Cancelled waiting request atomically decrements the tenant's waiting count and frees its slot.
   - Cancellation must not produce a 429. If the cancel's only effect is "wake the scheduler, admit the next tenant," the cancelled request is invisible to the 429 metric.

3. Capacity sharing (borrowing)
   - Define before coding. Recommendation: a tenant with 0 waiting lends at most 1 of its own 2 active slots to another tenant at the 8-cap; the slot returns within one tick when the lender has a waiting request.
   - No cross-pod borrowing — that brings back the synchronized-retry-burst behavior the v2.19.4 randomized Retry-After was deployed to fix.
   - If borrowing is deferred from v1, say so explicitly. Undocumented emergent borrowing is worse than no borrowing.

4. Retry-After
   - v2.19.4 randomized 1–3s Retry-After is already in prod. This change must not regress it.
   - Uniform random in [1, 3]s on the waiting-cap 429, independent of position in the round-robin order.
   - Same distribution on active-limit 429s and waiting-cap 429s — clients must not be able to tell them apart.

5. Starvation
   - Round-robin bounds worst-case wait, it doesn't eliminate it. State the bound before merge: roughly (N − 1) × (max single-request decompress time) for N tenants at an 8-cap.
   - Add a per-tenant max-wait metric. No preemption rule in v1 — kicking a long-waiting tenant to the front breaks the fairness invariant. Fix starvation by lowering the per-tenant cap or raising the pod-wide active limit.

6. Focused tests required before merge

   - Waiting-cap enforcement: 9th request from a tenant at cap gets 429 with Retry-After in [1, 3]s; other tenants unaffected.

VERDICT
-------
Reject the proposal. The serving path must fail closed on lease loss within a hard bound, not within one 500ms poll. The 310ms window is not "below a polling period and therefore fine" — it is a 310ms window during which a known-non-leader served authoritative-looking routing state to clients. That is the hazard the gate exists to prevent.

WHY THE FRAMING FAILS
- A polling check is a liveness mechanism, not a safety bound. The polling interval is the maximum staleness the design tolerates, not the maximum staleness the operator can accept.
- Lease loss during failover is exactly the case the gate must react to, not the case where it is allowed to coast.
- "No writes" is not the safety argument. Read-only routing snapshots are the deliverable; serving a stale view during a rebalance is what causes hot shards, 5xx storms, and split-brain reads.
- The owner is asking us to accept the gap because the mechanism happens to be slow. That inverts the requirement: the mechanism must be fast enough to satisfy the requirement, or the requirement is wrong.

REQUIRED BEHAVIOR
- Gate close on lease loss: bounded p99 latency from "lease known invalid" to "gate closed" should be in the tens of milliseconds, not hundreds. If the current design relies on a 500ms poll for the invalidation path, the invalidation path needs to be push (lease-state watcher, revocation channel, or per-request epoch check) — not a poll.
- Snapshot stamp: every routing snapshot served must carry lease epoch / holder id so downstream checks or clients can reject stale data even if a read slips through.
- In-flight policy must be explicit: either drain or cancel on gate close. Document which and why.

FOCUSED TESTS BEFORE APPROVAL

Failover tests (partition vs kill matters):
1. DB network partition on the lease holder under steady read load. Measure "lease-known-invalid" to "last read served." Must be within the bound above. Repeat with process kill to confirm partition path is not worse than kill path.
2. Lease expiry under load: force lease TTL expiry (not revocation) and verify gate closes on expiry detection, not on the next 500ms tick.
3. Explicit revocation: deliver a lease-revocation event; gate must close within the bound, not wait for the poll.
4. Replacement race: new holder acquires lease while old holder is still inside the 500ms window. Old holder must close the gate immediately on observing the new state, not at the next poll.
5. Renewal failure while lease still valid: gate stays open until actual expiry, then closes within the bound. Confirms we are not over-closing.

Race tests:
6. Concurrent lease contenders: only one serves; the loser must close its gate before serving any read.
7. Snapshot stamping: assert every served snapshot includes epoch + holder id; assert a client-side reject path exists for stale epochs.
8. Clock skew: force the lease to be treated as expired while the local poll still believes it valid. Gate must close from the expiry signal, not the poll.
9. In-flight reads on gate close: confirm chosen policy (drain or cancel) is actually enforced and measured, not just designed.
10. Post-failover replay: new holder serves consistent state without depending on the old holder's last snapshots.

Acceptance + monitoring:
- Hard numeric bound on gate-close latency (proposed: p99 < 50ms in staging drill; tighten for prod).
- Counter + alert on "read served N ms after lease loss" — alerts must fire in this drill, not just exist.
- Drill report must show the bound held across all 10 cases, not just the happy path.

DRILL HYGIENE (per our rule)
- Pre-open: confirm the staging drill tag has a TTL and a named cleanup owner. If it does not, fix that before the drill runs.
- Pre-close: before the drill is closed out, verify the tag is removed or repointed.
- If the owner cannot produce the failover test plan with the bound above, route back to Alex/owner for resolution. Do not widen scope to "make 310ms acceptable."

RECOMMENDATION TO THE OWNER
- Either (a) move lease-loss detection off the 500ms poll onto a push / per-request epoch check, with the bound above, and re-run the drill, or (b) tighten the poll to the bound and add the alerts and tests. 
- Approval requires the drill to demonstrate the bound, not to assert it. The current proposal accepts the wrong thing for the wrong reason.

Here's a practical playbook for what you're seeing. Two tablespoons caught with towels, dry wall, far outlet, intact glass, leak above the A/C — that's a small, wind-driven envelope leak, not an A/C drain issue and not an electrical hazard. Your read is right.

CONTAINMENT (do now, no tools needed)

1. Keep the window closed and latched. Opening it during wind-driven rain pulls more water in, not less.
2. Move bedding, electronics, books, rugs, and anything absorbent off the floor within a few feet of the sill. Even small amounts wick into wood floors and drywall fast.
3. Keep towels on the sill; rotate to dry ones when saturated. Put a bowl, pot, or baking sheet under the heaviest bead point so a soaked towel can't overflow onto the wall.
4. Keep Kibo out of the room until the sill is fully dry. Good call on your part.
5. Don't aim a fan, heater, or hair dryer at the sill while water is still beading — wait until rain stops and you've toweled it, then airflow is fine and helpful.
6. Once the rain passes: towel-dry the sill and frame, then ventilate (open the window briefly once rain has stopped, or run a room fan). The goal is to dry the wood/vinyl before it sits wet for hours.

LOW-RISK OBSERVATIONS TO LOG FOR MAINTENANCE

These are all safe to check from inside, no ladders, no going out in the storm.

- Entry location: full top edge, or one corner? Top-left vs. top-center vs. top-right.
- Pattern: a single drip point, or a horizontal line of beading along the top?
- Water clarity: clear water only, or any grey/brown tint that suggests it traveled through building material before reaching the glass?
- Frame: is the frame itself wet to touch, or only the glass and sill?
- Timing: when did it start relative to peak rain/wind? Did it stop promptly when the rain eased, or keep dripping after?
- History: first time, or has it happened in past storms? Any pattern with storm direction (e.g., always with strong south wind)?
- Surroundings: any staining, peeling paint, or soft spots on the interior wall above the window? On the exterior wall above (look after the storm from a safe window)?
- Window history: any recent caulking, painting, or work on this unit?

Take phone photos now and again after the storm ends. Timestamps help a lot.

ESCALATION THRESHOLD — WHEN TO STOP WAITING AND CALL THE EMERGENCY LINE

Stay on the standard path (open a maintenance ticket, schedule a look, follow up Monday) AS LONG AS:
- Volume stays around what you've described — a few tablespoons, bead-and-drip
- It's contained to the sill with towels/bowl
- The wall and floor stay dry
- No water is anywhere near the outlet or any fixture on that wall
- The leak stops within minutes of the rain stopping

CALL THE BUILDING'S EMERGENCY / AFTER-HOURS LINE (super, on-call maintenance) NOW IF ANY OF THESE HAPPEN:
- Flow shifts from beading to a steady drip or stream
- Water crosses the sill onto the wall or floor
- Water reaches within roughly a foot of the outlet, a switch, a smoke detector, or any powered device
- You see or smell anything electrical — buzzing, warm switch plate, flickering light
- Water starts coming in around the A/C unit, from the ceiling, or from a new spot
- The ceiling above the window bulges, stains, or drips
- The storm restarts and the leak returns at noticeably higher volume

You don't need 911 unless there's an active electrical or structural danger. For everything in that second list, the building's emergency maintenance line is the right number.

One judgment call: since this is Saturday afternoon and the storm is ongoing, it's reasonable to open the ticket now and, if your building has an after-hours line, flag it as same-day rather than waiting for Monday. Even small envelope leaks into the wall cavity become mold and framing problems if they repeat — catching it today is the cheap version.

> "Do not chain pushes: even a clean outcome of that single push does not authorize a second push without re-entering Rules 1 and 2 from a fresh sample."

Wes's push was the bounded single-push resume the infra review authorized on 2024-06-18. Its outcome — retired peaked at 3 (under the Rule 1 stop of 4), largest cleanup pause 61 ms (under 100 ms), p99 returned from 49→75→49, heap back to baseline, and all six verification checks (active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload, restart — plus drain to ≤1 retired gens and baseline p99/heap) clean — qualifies it as a clean Rule 2 push, not a Rule 3 re-pause case. The "clean outcome" branch is exactly what the rule points at with the chain-pushes sentence: it confirms the single push was correctly authorized but explicitly does not roll that authorization forward.

So for Wes's question:

- "Does a clean observed push permit another push immediately?" — No.
- "Does `attempt at most one configuration push` require a fresh explicit decision before another push?" — Yes. The prior resume does not carry over (same wording in Rule 3).

Bottom line: the contract is enforceable in principle — finite allowlist, lowercase normalization, no fallback — but as written it has specific gaps I'd want closed before agreeing. The "no 4th label" guarantee holds only if rejection is enforced at every hop in the producer → router → consumer path, not just one. Walking through it.

Direct answer to the 4th-label question:
- "unknown" cannot appear as a producer fallback — good, the proposal closes that. But the contract as written binds only the producer. If rollup-service has its own default-to-"unknown" code path on unrecognized values, the 4th value appears downstream even when the producer is clean. Need a consumer-side row.
- A raw value cannot appear IF rejection is at the OTel collector AND metrics-router re-validates. Today the label shows 38–51 distinct values in 24h, so raw values are clearly flowing. Single-hop enforcement at the collector is fragile: a legacy collector, a direct emit, or the replay/mirror path can still push raw values through. Defense-in-depth re-validation at metrics-router is required.

Gaps:

1. Enforcement location is unspecified. "Reject before metrics publication" + "OTel collector producer → metrics-router → rollup-service consumer" leaves three hops where rejection could live. Pick a primary (OTel collector is right — it sees raw input first) and require re-validation at metrics-router. Cardinality Guardrails preflight applies here per the runbook: "label changes that touch metrics-router, shard-keeper, or rollup-service must run the Cardinality Guardrails checks before the change is treated as safe for production review." Replay evidence alone is not enough; live canary or representative live-path fixture is required.

2. Normalization is incomplete. Lowercase handles case but not whitespace, Unicode form, or empty-string handling. Specify trim, NFC-normalize, and what empty-string-after-trim means. Recommendation: empty/whitespace-only after normalization → omit (treat as missing). Non-allowlisted non-empty → reject. Otherwise an empty producer input becomes a noisy rejection when it should be a quiet omission — parity gap.

3. Missing vs malformed boundary. State the trigger explicitly. Producer doesn't emit the label → omit. Producer emits "" or "   " → omit (per #2). Producer emits anything else non-allowlisted → reject. Without this stated, the rejection stream and the omission stream have unclear boundaries.

4. Per-tenant budget = 3 has no stated breach action. The cap is structural (3 allowed values means anything else breaches). What's the action on breach? Reject the metric line, drop the label and emit unlabeled, or count+alert? If reject-the-line, that's a data-loss surface that needs a rejection counter (see #6). If drop-the-label, you've downgraded rejection to omission, which conflicts with the missing→omit rule (same outcome as legitimate missing). Pick one.

5. Parity with prior label name. Is this a rename? If producers were emitting `environment` or `env` previously, dashboards and alerts on the old name will go silent during the transition window. Cardinality Guardrails requires "Identify new or changed label keys and changed value-shape behavior" — the proposal should name the prior label and include a parallel-emission / dashboard-update plan, otherwise you ship a silent observability regression.

6. Alert-source attribution shift. Cardinality Guardrails rule: "Classify whether the relevant panel or alert signal is live-path, replay-source, mirror-source, or other validation-source evidence." Once rejection is live, throughput for affected tenants drops. Without a rejection counter, "throughput dropped" looks like a regression when it's the new path working. Add `metrics_router_deployment_environment_rejected_total{reason="non_allowlisted"|"malformed"|"budget_exceeded"}`. This is also the canary attribution evidence the runbook preflight requires.

7. Historical data in rollup-service. The contract covers new emissions. The 38–51 distinct values currently in storage will fail consumer-side re-validation. What's the historical-read behavior? Backfill path? Retention window during which old values still surface in dashboards? State it; otherwise the consumer-side row has undefined behavior on legacy data.

8. Consumer-side bidirectionality. Does the same allowlist apply on rollup-service → metrics-router read paths (e.g. rollup read-back)? State whether the contract is one-way or bidirectional. If one-way, say so explicitly so the consumer side doesn't accidentally re-introduce raw values via a different path.

9. Empty-string from the consumer. Same as #2 but on the consumer: if rollup-service normalizes a missing/empty label to anything at all (including ""), the metric-router ingestion can re-surface a value the producer contract tried to suppress. Consumer must also "omit on missing" with no default.

10. Review path routing. Per the runbook: "Nadia keeps alert semantics in the Cardinality Guardrails review path. Cyrus keeps the cost/cardinality angle attached to review. Rollup-service ownership remains with the Cyrus/data-platform side; this rule does not move enforcement ownership to data platform." This contract touches alert semantics (Nadia) and rollup-service consumer (Cyrus team, Alex backup). Routing through Alex alone is wrong; the proposal should explicitly route to Nadia for the alert/attribution row and Cyrus for the consumer-side row + cost/cardinality. Do not move enforcement ownership to data platform — metrics-router stays owner, rollup-service is a defined consumer contract.

11. Deploy ownership. The change touches metrics-router prod. Wes solo deploy surface is non-prod only per the runbook. Alex owns the prod deploy, Wes backup. State this in the rollout plan to avoid a Wes-solo-on-prod scope drift.

12. Pre-deploy evidence. State which evidence the producer-side change ships against: live canary on metrics-router canary path, or a representative live-path fixture. Replay alone is not enough for live-path value-shape changes per the runbook.

What I'd ask Product Engineering to add before I sign off:
  - Primary enforcement hop named (OTel collector) + metrics-router re-validation row.
  - Consumer-side row with rollup-service co-sign (Cyrus team).
  - Normalization spec: trim + NFC + lowercase; empty → omit.
  - Breach action for budget = 3; rejection counter spec.
  - Prior-label migration plan; rejection counter feeding the alert-source attribution.
  - Historical-data behavior on consumer reads.
  - Review routing: Nadia (alert semantics) + Cyrus (consumer + cost/cardinality); metrics-router ownership unchanged.
  - Deploy ownership: Alex prod / Wes backup; live canary or live-path fixture as pre-deploy evidence.

Enforceability verdict: not yet. The allowlist + reject shape is right, but with the gaps above the contract is theoretically enforceable and practically leaky in three places — the consumer side, the budget breach action, and the historical-data path. Close those and the 4th-label guarantee holds.

Sunday-night plan, two people, ~45 min of evening work. One sheet pan, one rice pot, one board, one knife. The "holding point" sits at T-5: rice covered, sheet pan tented — both hold 15+ min, so dinner waits for Devika's text without anything drying out or overcooking.

Afternoon prep (~15 min, then walk away)

- Chicken thighs: toss in a bowl with olive oil, salt, pepper, the zest of one lime, a squeeze of its juice, and the cilantro stems (save the leaves). Cover, fridge.
- Halve the cherry tomatoes.
- Cut the corn off the cob (or snap into short rounds).
- Chop the cilantro leaves; keep a small handful whole for serving.
- Halve and pit the peaches; toss with a tiny squeeze of lime, cover, fridge.
- Measure the rice.

Dinner (45 min)

- T-40 min  Preheat oven to 425°F (220°C). Rinse the rice, put it on (about 1.5 c water per 1 c rice; bring to a boil, cover, drop to low).
- T-30 min  Parchment-line a sheet pan. Chicken thighs skin-up in the center, corn and tomatoes scattered around, drizzle of oil, pinch of salt. Into the oven.
- T-15 min  Rice off the heat, lid on, leave it covered. Quick peek at the chicken.
- T-5 min   Pull the sheet pan. Tent the chicken + veg with foil. <-- holding point
- Plate when ready: rice first, chicken and veg on top, shower of cilantro, squeeze of lime.
- Dessert: peaches go straight from the bowl to the plate with a few cilantro leaves and a final squeeze of lime — no extra cooking needed.

If you want the peaches warm, nestle them cut-side down on the sheet pan at T-5 min; they'll pick up residual heat while the chicken rests.

Why the hold works

- Rice covered off-heat stays soft 15-20 min.
- Chicken thighs tented with foil stay juicy well past 15 min — they're the most forgiving cut for this.
- Tomatoes and corn just warm through from residual oven heat under the foil; no re-cooking needed.

Cleanup: parchment goes in the trash. Rice pot soaks while you eat.
