The sequence is broadly correct in principle — stop the source, let the wall dry, verify dryness, then close and paint. Painting over damp drywall or compound is one of the more common ways a leak becomes a mold problem, so the "dry before repaint" rule is right. A few things are missing from the plan as described, and there are specific conditions that should move you from "monitor" to "open the wall" or "bring in a mold assessor."

What the sequence should also include
  - A baseline moisture reading now, with a meter, taken at the patch and at an unaffected spot on the same wall for comparison. Visual "damp" is too soft a check; a pin or pinless meter gives you a number to trend.
  - Photo documentation of the wet area's footprint today, so any expansion is provable, not arguable.
  - Active drying in the room — a dehumidifier and modest airflow over the patch. Eight inches of drywall can take one to several weeks to dry depending on how deep the saturation went, ambient humidity, and whether insulation behind it is wet.
  - A check on what's behind the drywall. Fiberglass insulation that got wet is usually removed, not dried in place; closed-cell spray foam and rigid foam behave differently. If the cavity stayed wet for any length of time, the sheathing and the bottom plate are the items to worry about, not the paint.

When to escalate rather than wait for the planned rechecks
  - The patch does not shrink week over week, or moisture readings stay elevated two weeks after the exterior is fully sealed.
  - The wet footprint grows rather than contracts, or new wet spots appear below or beside the window.
  - Any musty, earthy, or "old basement" smell develops or persists after the masonry work — smell is often the earliest mold signal and does not require visible growth.
  - Visible discoloration: dark staining, greenish or black spotting, white fuzzy growth, or paint that bubbles, blisters, or peels.
  - The wall beside the outlet (or any outlet in that wall) shows dampness, warmth from a receptacle, or tripped/GFCI behavior. Wet sheathing near wiring is a separate concern.
  - Heavy rain between now and the permanent masonry work, or any sign the temporary seal has failed — don't wait for Friday if water is re-entering.
  - Anyone in the room develops persistent respiratory symptoms, sinus irritation, headaches, or unusual fatigue that improves when they're out of the home.
  - The leak turns out to have been ongoing longer than the recent episode — long-duration leaks are where hidden mold in the cavity is most likely.

A reasonable practical bar: if the source is fixed and two to three weeks of drying with a dehumidifier don't bring meter readings back to baseline and don't visibly shrink the patch, open a small inspection hole or have a mold assessor check the cavity before anyone closes the wall back up.

A timed low-cleanup dinner for three, ready right around 6:00.

THE SHAPE

  Couscous with lemon and parsley (cold-prepped, just needs boiling water)
  Sheet-pan chicken sausages + zucchini + bell peppers (oven does the work)
  Watermelon-feta salad (assembled cold, dressed at the very end)


PRE-ANYA (about 3:45 to 4:25, before she arrives)

  Line two sheet pans with parchment — no scrubbing later.
  Halve and seed the peppers, cut the zucchini into half-moons about 1 cm thick.
  Toss the veg on one pan with olive oil, salt, pepper, and the zest of one lemon.
  Prick the sausages a few times with a fork, lay them on the second pan with a little olive oil.
  Cover both pans and leave them on the counter (sausages are fine at room temp for 30 min). If your kitchen runs warm, slide them into the fridge instead.
  Cube the watermelon into bite-size pieces. Strip parsley leaves off a small bunch.
  In a wide serving bowl: watermelon, a generous handful of crumbled feta, most of the parsley, a few grinds of black pepper. Cover and refrigerate.
    Important: do NOT salt or dress the salad yet — salt and lemon pull water out of the melon and it goes soupy.
  Measure the dry couscous into your serving bowl (one less dish — the same bowl becomes the couscous bowl).
  Have a kettle or small pot ready to go for the water.
  Set the table, put out plates and forks, fill water glasses.


WHEN ANYA ARRIVES (4:30)

  The kitchen is clean. Nothing on the stove. Kibo is the main event. Greet her, hang out.


THE SHORT FINAL COOK (5:20 to 5:55, about 35 minutes)

  5:20  Preheat the oven to 425°F. Put the kettle on for the couscous.
  5:25  Slide both sheet pans into the oven.
  5:28  When the water boils, pour it over the couscous (about 1:1 by volume, or follow the package), cover the bowl with a plate, set a timer for 7 minutes.
  5:35  Fluff the couscous with a fork. Stir in a glug of olive oil, the juice of half a lemon, a pinch of salt, and most of the remaining parsley. Cover again.
  5:45  Pull the sheet pans. Veg should be charred at the edges, sausages browned and at 165°F inside. Halve the sausages on a diagonal if you like.
  5:50  Finish the watermelon salad: a small pinch of salt and a squeeze of lemon over the top, one gentle toss so the feta stays mostly on top.
  5:55  Carry everything to the table, family style — couscous in the middle, sausages and veg on a platter, salad on the side.


BY 6:00

  Eating. Fireworks can start whenever; you're inside, fed, and Kibo is the only thing that needs attention.


CLEANUP

  Toss the parchment. Soak the sheet pans while you eat. Total dishes: one cutting board, one knife, two sheet pans, two bowls (the salad bowl and the couscous bowl), one kettle or pot. That's the whole list.


A FEW NOTES

  The sausages and vegetables can sit covered on the sheet pans for the 60-ish minutes between prep and oven with no issue. If they went into the fridge, pull them 10 minutes before the oven so they don't shock the pan.

  Couscous holds fine — if you fluff it at 5:35 and don't eat until 6:00, just drape a clean kitchen towel over the bowl and leave it. It will still be light and fluffy.

  For Kibo: windows closed, one room with the three of you is the calmest setup. If the first big bang sets him off, a filled Kong or a long-lasting chew from before dinner buys you a quiet 20 minutes while you eat.

Quick read: Kibo is showing moderate noise anxiety — panting and pacing — but he's still interactive (taking treats, settling briefly), and the bathroom-with-fan setup is already the right shape. Build on it, don't rebuild it.

PLAN FOR THE REST OF THE EVENING

Now and over the next few hours
  - Stock the safe room: water bowl (refresh every couple of hours; panting dehydrates), a washable bed or towel, a familiar toy. Keep the fan on. Add a podcast, music, or TV at moderate volume layered over the pops — louder than the fireworks from inside is the target.
  - Don't force comfort, don't avoid it either. Sit nearby, speak normally, act like it's an ordinary evening. Dogs read your state. Reward calm moments with a tossed treat, casually, not a big production.
  - If you have an Adaptil diffuser, plug it in near the safe room now (takes ~30 min to start).
  - Quick 2-minute check tonight: collar tags current, microchip registration current. July 4–5 is peak lost-dog night.
  - Pre-stage: phone charger in the safe room, towel, keys and a light lead by the door. Look up the nearest 24-hour ER vet right now and save the address — don't look it up later.

When he needs to go out
  - Front-clip harness on, short leash (your usual). If he'll wear the harness calmly indoors, leave it on during outdoor trips so a sudden bang at the door can't slip the leash off.
  - One person holds the leash, the other opens the door. Shortest route, grass close to the building. No long walks, no Prospect Park tonight.
  - If he flatly refuses and hasn't urinated since the fireworks started, that's common and usually fine for one evening as long as he's drinking. Don't drag him out.

What NOT to improvise
  - Medication. No Benadryl unless your vet has previously given you a dose for him — it's mg/kg and many formulations combine it with pseudoephedrine or acetaminophen, both toxic to dogs. No human sleep aids, no CBD or melatonin gummies without vet sign-off.
  - Crating as a fix. If he's not crate-trained, a crate tonight can turn panic into broken teeth and cut gums.
  - Leaving him in the yard, even fenced. Peak escape, fence-jump, and wildlife-fight night.
  - "Let him bark it out" while you're out. Stay home through the worst of it if you can.

Call the ER vet ON THE WAY IN if you see any of these
  - Collapse, loss of consciousness, or a seizure.
  - Gums that are pale/white, gray/blue, or bright brick red instead of healthy pink.
  - Hot to the touch, panting that won't stop, or any stumbling/wobbly gait (possible heat stroke). Rectal temp ≥104°F if you can check safely.
  - Bloody vomit or stool, or persistent vomiting/diarrhea.
  - Suspected ingestion of a firework, a spent match, or any debris.
  - Bloated, hard, or distended abdomen, especially with retching.
  - Self-injury: broken tooth, cut gums, bleeding paws from frantic chewing or scratching.
  - Continuous frantic activity with no settling for 2–3+ hours even in the safe room, especially if he's starting to refuse water.

Call your regular vet (or ER after hours) for advice — not necessarily an immediate trip — if he just won't settle or is hiding and shaking for hours, or if you've used a previously-prescribed anxiolytic and aren't sure if it's helping.

Overnight
  - Most neighborhood fireworks wind down 11 PM–1 AM but can run later. Keep him in the safe room (or with you in the bedroom) until things have been quiet for 20–30 minutes. Water available, dim light, fan/audio still on low.
  - Sleep when you can — alternate with Devika if she's up. You have night-shifts ahead and tonight will be long.

Tomorrow
  - Expect residual restlessness in the morning. Walk when it's been quiet for a while; short route, harness, shorter leash.
  - If tonight was worse than prior years, book a non-urgent vet appointment in the next week or two to talk through a desensitization plan or a pre-prescribed anxiolytic for next year. Worth getting on the calendar now while it's fresh.

HAZARDS

Watermark ordering
- cache[tenant].watermark is set from maxTimestamp(rows) BEFORE the write is attempted. If write fails, the cache is now ahead of persisted state — a follower process or health check can observe a watermark that was never durably written.
- The watermark is not monotone in this code. A later batch with an older max timestamp will overwrite a newer cache watermark even if both writes succeeded. Minimum fix: max(cache.watermark, maxTimestamp(rows)). Better: derive from the store.
- Setting the cache watermark before the write means retries that fail re-run the assignment harmlessly, but retries that succeed then run it a second time with stale input — same hazard as the failure path.

Retry / idempotence
- store.write(rows) is described as if idempotent but nothing in the pseudocode makes it so. If the first attempt wrote and only the response was lost, the retry writes the same rows again. For an append-only rollup store that means double-counted aggregates; for an upsert keyed on (tenant, ts, dimension) it might be safe, but the note doesn't say.
- emitReady runs on every successful applyBatch, with no dedupe key. A retry that wrote dupes (or didn't) emits readiness a second time. Whatever sits downstream of emitReady will re-aggregate and re-fan-out. That's the load-bearing hazard.
- The watermark the second emitReady carries may differ from the first if rows are non-deterministic — so even if downstream dedupes on tenant, it can't dedupe on watermark.

Crash recovery
- "Cache survives ordinary request failures but not a process restart" — that is the worst case for this design. After restart, applyBatch for any tenant with persisted-but-not-emitted rows produces no readiness signal for those rows, because the next call's watermark is computed only from the new input.
- Even within one process, a crash between store.write and emitReady leaves data durable and readiness lost. Same gap.
- The cache gives no protection across instances either. Two replicas handling the same tenant diverge the moment one restarts.

The pattern this code violates: data-write and readiness-publish are two operations with no atomic binding, and the readiness signal carries no identity the publisher can dedupe on.

A SAFER SEQUENCE

1. Assign each batch a batch_id (UUID, or hash of (tenant, canonicalized rows)). It is the dedupe key for both the write and the readiness emission.

2. Make store.write idempotent on batch_id. If the row already exists, return the previously-stored watermark instead of re-writing. Retries become safe at the data layer.

3. In the same durable write, also persist a row in a readiness_outbox: (tenant, batch_id, watermark, status='pending'). The watermark written here is the store-derived max — authoritative by being stored, not by being recomputed in memory.

4. emitReady is no longer inline. A separate publisher loop:
   a. reads pending rows from readiness_outbox,

IF THEY DON'T WANT A FULL OUTBOX

Minimum viable: idempotent write keyed on batch_id, watermark stored alongside rows in the same write, emitReady called with (batch_id, watermark) and downstream dedupes on batch_id. Covers the duplicate-emit hazard. Does NOT cover the crash-between-write-and-emit hazard — for that you need the outbox, or a startup replay that scans for persisted rows with no matching emission log.

Quick read on what you've described: this is the classic picture of a mild-to-moderate lateral ankle sprain — inversion force, pain and swelling on the outside of the ankle, no deformity, can bear some weight, no numbness, no pinpoint bony pain. The absence of those red flags is reassuring. Nothing below replaces being looked at by a clinician, but here's a sensible plan:

IMMEDIATE CARE (next 24-48 hours — POLICE)
- Protect: avoid movements that sharply hurt; an elastic wrap or simple lace-up ankle brace from a pharmacy is worth grabbing on the way to the viewing.
- Optimal loading: don't immobilize completely. Gentle pain-tolerated walking is better than total rest after the first day.
- Ice: 15-20 minutes on, 40+ minutes off, for the first 24-48 hours. Bag of frozen peas works fine.
- Compression: figure-8 elastic bandage around the ankle, snug but not numb. Check toes for color/warmth.
- Elevation: above heart level when you're sitting — easier than it sounds, just prop it on a cushion.
- Pain relief: ibuprofen (with food) or acetaminophen per bottle directions is fine for the first couple of days if you're medically cleared for NSAIDs.

WALKING TODAY — FOR THE VIEWING
Yes, ordinary walking is reasonable given that you can already take four steps without giving way. A few practical adjustments:
- Wear a supportive closed shoe (sneaker), not a sandal or dress shoe.
- Wrap or brace the ankle before you go.
- Take ibuprofen ~30 minutes before if the walk will be longer than a few minutes.
- Plan to sit during parts of the tour if possible.
- If walking makes the pain sharply worse, you're limping badly, or the ankle feels unstable, cut the outing short — there's no version of this where pushing through helps.

URGENT EVALUATION (same-day urgent care or ED) IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR
- Cannot put any weight on the foot at all, or the ankle feels structurally unstable/buckling.
- Visible deformity, or the ankle "looks off" compared to the other side.
- Numbness, tingling, burning, or cold/blue/pale toes — circulation or nerve concern.
- Severe pinpoint tenderness directly on a bone (especially the posterior edge or tip of either ankle bone, or along the outside of the foot at the 5th metatarsal base).
- A snap or pop at the moment of injury with immediate large swelling and weakness pushing off the foot — raises suspicion for an Achilles tendon or ligament rupture.
- Swelling that balloons rapidly in the first hour, or skin that is stretched, shiny, and very tight.
- Open wound, ongoing bleeding, or suspicion of a fracture.
- Pain that is getting clearly worse (not just sore) over the next 24 hours despite POLICE.

NON-URGENT APPOINTMENT (primary care, sports med, or podiatry within a few days) IF
- Pain and swelling aren't clearly trending better after 48-72 hours of POLICE.
- You can't return to a normal walking pattern within about a week.
- Stiffness, clicking, or a feeling of the ankle "giving way" persists or recurs.
- You want a definitive diagnosis, X-ray if anything looks off, or a rehab plan — physio for ankle sprains meaningfully shortens recovery.

REALISTIC TIMELINE
Most mild lateral sprains feel markedly better in 3-7 days and return to full activity in 2-6 weeks depending on grade. The biggest predictor of a slow recovery is going back to cutting/jumping too soon, not the walking you'll do today.

One important caveat: this is general first-aid information, not an exam. If anything in the urgent list above applies, or your gut says something is wrong, get seen today. Otherwise, the plan above is a sensible starting point, and a non-urgent visit is the right move if you're not clearly better by mid-week.

REVIEW OF WES'S PROPOSED STAGING EXERCISE — metrics-router#423 cleanup correction

Scope: pre-run review only. This review does not authorize the exercise to start.

OVERALL
The proposal covers isolation, attribution, stop conditions, and recovery at a high level but leaves gaps that will blur attribution if the harness is approved as-is. Per-attempt distinction is implied but not pinned; the blocked-push invariant is named but not defined; the stop list is missing four thresholds and conflates two failure classes; the recovery line will auto-continue the harness, which is the single biggest attribution risk in the document.

PER-ATTEMPT DISTINCTION

The 600 pushes resolve to two attempt classes:

Regular pushes (588): positions 1-49, 51-99, 101-149, 151-199, 201-249, 251-299, 301-349, 351-399, 401-449, 451-499, 501-549, 551-599.

Blocked-push attempts (12): positions 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500, 550, 600. Position 600 doubles as the run's terminal attempt; record it as both the 12th special and the run-end marker.

Each attempt must be recorded with:
  a. Pre-push snapshot: retired-generation count, active-generation id, route-set hash, dropped-series count, heap, request p99.
  b. Push outcome: accepted, rejected-pre-write, or blocked-by-invariant.
  c. Post-push observation: same fields as pre, plus largest cleanup pause observed during that attempt, reload failures, restarts.
  d. Generation delta: retired-count delta and active-generation id delta scoped to the attempt only.
  e. Timestamp and attempt number.

"Dropped-series count" and "largest cleanup pause" must be recorded as deltas scoped to the triggering attempt. Cumulative counters will erase attribution across the 588 regular pushes.

BLOCKED-PUSH INVARIANT (explicit)

A push is "blocked" iff, at write time, retired_count == (max_retired - 1) AND write_path == "config-push". With "fifth retired generation" framing, max_retired == 5 and the gate fires at retired_count == 4.

Properties the invariant must hold:
  1. Rejection occurs before any active-generation mutation. The rejected push must not produce an active-generation transition.
  2. The rejection path emits a metric/log event distinguishable from reload failures and from the regular "push rejected: schema" path. Same code path must not be reused.
  3. The harness's setup of retained readers must be the only source of the 5th-generation pressure for that attempt. Cross-tenant retained-reader growth during the attempt invalidates the attempt.
  4. Cleanup-completion is observed via retired_count returning to a cap-respecting value, never via log silence.

The proposal's phrasing "arrange retained readers so the attempted push would create a fifth retired generation" must be re-stated as: "ensure retired_count == 4 at the moment the push is attempted; the push must be blocked at the retention gate; no fifth retired generation is created." The current phrasing permits a buggy implementation that creates the 5th generation and then rolls back, which is the failure the correction is meant to prevent.

STOP CONDITIONS

Proposed list (Wes): active-generation inconsistency, route-parity failure, dropped series, reload failure, restart, cleanup pause above staging limit.

Issues:
  1. "Cleanup pause above the existing staging limit" — T is not named. The run cannot start without a pinned value. Require: T set by Wes/Alex before run, derived from current production pause baseline + a tight margin so the new code path is observable.
  2. "Active-generation inconsistency" is too coarse. Enumerate: (a) active-generation id missing from in-memory state; (b) two distinct ids reported active by different replicas; (c) active-generation id changed without an accepted push; (d) active-generation id == a retired-generation id.
  3. Missing from the proposed list:
     - Retired-generation envelope: retired_count > max_retired at any snapshot. This catches the failure mode the correction is meant to prevent.
     - Heap ceiling: heap > H MB sustained > N seconds. Without this, a leak during the cleanup loop is silent until OOM.
     - p99 ceiling: request p99 > P ms sustained over the attempt window.
     - Rejection-path indistinguishability: a blocked-push attempt's rejection event not visible in logs/metrics within K seconds.
  4. Clarification: a blocked-push attempt is NOT a stop condition. It is the expected outcome at positions 50, 100, ..., 600. Stop conditions apply to (i) regular pushes, and (ii) anomalous observations during or after a blocked-push attempt that exceed thresholds (e.g., blocked push followed by unexpected restart is a stop).
  5. Paging: any single stop trigger pages Wes and Alex. Run does not resume past a stop until both have signed off in the run log with an attribution line.

RECOVERY (no auto-retry, attribution preserved)

Replace "After a blocked push, allow the harness to continue once cleanup completes" with:
  1. On a blocked push: harness records the blocked outcome, snapshots generation state, and pauses. No auto-resume.
  2. Cleanup completion is determined by harness polling retired_count and confirming it is at or below max_retired AND no in-flight cleanup worker holds a generation reference. No inference from log silence.
  3. Un-pause requires explicit human action: Wes or Alex reviews the blocked-push record, confirms the cleanup-completion snapshot, and un-pauses. The un-pause is a distinct logged event, not a timer.
  4. On a non-blocked stop trigger: harness halts; no further pushes; pages Wes and Alex. Resume only after the trigger is attributed (new cleanup path vs. pre-existing staging artifact) and a fix or waiver is recorded.
  5. Retries: a retry of an attempt is a NEW attempt with a new attempt number. Never a re-observation of the original. If the harness retries a blocked config push, log it as attempt N+1 with a "retry-of-N" tag; the original attempt's outcome must remain visible in the run log.
  6. Restart attribution: if a restart occurs during the exercise, the log must show which attempt was in flight, the pre-restart snapshot, and whether the restart was caused by the cleanup code path or something else (OOM, deploy, manual).

ISOLATION GAPS TO RESOLVE BEFORE RUN

Not in the proposal; will compound the attribution problem if left open:
  - Confirm staging has no concurrent config-push traffic from other tenants during the exercise window. If not, gate with a freeze notice or use a dedicated fixture tenant.
  - Confirm no other staging traffic mutates retained-reader state during the exercise. The "every 50th push" setup assumes the harness is the only writer of retained readers; real staging readers attaching during a blocked-push attempt invalidate invariant property #3 above.
  - Confirm no overlap with the rollup correction-import staging work already in flight — both touch the staging backend; cross-talk will corrupt snapshots.
  - Pin H, P, T, K before the run starts. No run begins without these in the exercise record.

OUT OF SCOPE — DO NOT ADD

- No production sampling, shadow-mode hooks, or canary wiring in this exercise. The proposal correctly keeps prod out of scope; do not widen it here.
- No staged rollout of the correction itself. If staging passes, that's a separate Wes + Alex decision and not part of this run.

NOT AUTHORIZED TO RUN UNTIL:
  (a) T, H, P, K are pinned in writing,
  (b) staging isolation is confirmed in writing,
  (c) the blocked-push invariant is restated per the four properties above,
  (d) the stop list is updated with the sub-enumeration and the four additions,
  (e) the auto-continue line is replaced with the explicit human-unpause rule,

Five remaining defects, then the required sequence.

Defect 1 — Lost-write window between writeWatermark and writeBatchResult.
Crash after the watermark write and before the batch-result write leaves the watermark at batch.end with no result durably stored. On retry, the watermark-only idempotency check returns already_done and the missing write is never retried. This is silent data loss, not a stall. The watermark now lies about state.

Defect 2 — Watermark is the only idempotency key.
The check `batch.end <= current` advances-or-skips based on a single scalar. It cannot distinguish three states that the protocol must distinguish:
  (a) this batch has never been attempted,
  (b) this batch was attempted and fully committed,
  (c) this batch was attempted and crashed mid-way.
Today (b) and (c) collapse into the same return path. Idempotency must be keyed on (tenant, batch.id), not on the watermark value, and writeBatchResult must be conditional on batch.id not already being present (or, if recompute is non-deterministic, on the result hash matching the prior write — but the cleanest answer is to make recompute deterministic and key on batch.id).

Defect 3 — recompute failure is masked after the watermark is written.
If recompute throws, the watermark is already at batch.end. Retry sees `batch.end <= current` and returns already_done, so the failed recompute is never re-run. The watermark write must not precede recompute-and-commit.

Defect 4 — readiness.publish from the attempted value, not a readback.
Publishing batch.end directly means a readiness signal can be emitted for a state that did not durably land (defect 1), and can be emitted more than once if recompute is non-deterministic and writeBatchResult is not guarded. Publish must follow a durable readback of (watermark, batch_result) so the published value is provably the committed one.

Defect 5 — Crash between writeBatchResult and readiness.publish.
Result and watermark are durable, but readiness is lost. Retry returns already_done and never re-publishes. Downstream sees a watermark that has advanced with no corresponding readiness signal — exactly the gap the readiness channel exists to close. This is the hardest of the five because the fix is structural, not a reorder.

Required sequence.

process(tenant, batch):
  // 1. Idempotency check on batch identity, not watermark
  if store.hasBatchResult(tenant, batch.id):
    return already_done

  // 2. Compute before any state mutation
  result = recompute(batch)

  // 3. Atomic commit: result first, watermark second, in one transaction
  //    Ordering inside the txn matters only for failure-mode reasoning;
  //    the contract is that both are visible together or neither is.
  txn = store.beginTxn()
  txn.writeBatchResult(tenant, batch.id, result)   // insert-if-absent on batch.id
  txn.writeWatermark(tenant, batch.end)             // conditional on prior watermark < batch.end
  txn.enqueueReadiness(tenant, batch.id, batch.end) // outbox row, committed atomically
  ok = txn.commit()
  if not ok:
    return retry   // nothing durably landed; safe to re-enter

  // 4. Readiness publication is driven by the outbox, not by process().
  //    A separate dispatcher reads enqueued readiness rows and publishes,
  //    retrying with at-least-once semantics until subscribers ack.
  //    Subscribers dedupe on (tenant, batch.id) or (tenant, batch.end).

  return ok

What changed and why each piece is required:

  - Idempotency moved to (tenant, batch.id) via hasBatchResult, so partial progress can never look "done."
  - recompute runs before any mutation, so a compute failure cannot strand an advanced watermark.
  - writeBatchResult and writeWatermark commit atomically. The watermark can only advance when the result is durable; the result can only be "the result" while the watermark reflects it.
  - Readiness is enqueued in the same transaction (outbox pattern). The dispatcher owns retry, backoff, and at-least-once delivery; subscribers own dedup. This resolves defect 5 without making process() responsible for cross-system publish durability.
  - If a synchronous publish is required instead of the outbox, the rule is: publish only after a readback of (watermark, batch.id) returns the expected values, with publisher-side retry and subscriber-side dedup on (tenant, batch.id, batch.end). Do not publish from the in-memory batch.end.

Two notes for the PR description:

  - recompute must be deterministic for a given (tenant, batch). If it is not, the design needs a result hash or version column on batch_result and the insert must be conditional on the absent row, otherwise a retry that races itself can silently flip the stored value.
  - The watermark write inside the txn should still be conditional on `prior_watermark < batch.end`, so two concurrent process() calls for the same tenant cannot both advance the watermark and leave a stale result row behind. The atomicity guarantee is per-key; the conditional write prevents the cross-key footgun.

This should be enough for Cyrus to write the PR. The two items I would not let past review without a written answer are (a) the outbox dispatcher's retry/ack contract and (b) what subscriber-side dedup looks like — those are where the next class of bugs will land.

Three corrections map to the three clauses of the fail-closed contract.

1. "unknown" must ERROR, not OMIT.

   The current order treats the literal string "unknown" the same as missing input. That conflates two cases the contract separates. "Missing" means the producer sent no value at all (the label is absent from the metric). "unknown" means the producer sent an explicit unsupported value, and under fail-closed the publication is rejected so the producer sees the instrumentation error and fixes it. Silently folding "unknown" into OMIT hides a known producer-side bug and is what the team avoided on build_channel 2/7 (the value was cleared from the allowlist, not silently dropped). tenant_size_class still lists "unknown" only because that label's allowlist includes it; deployment.environment's allowlist is {prod, staging, dev}, so "unknown" is out of band.

   Concrete change: drop the `if value == "unknown": return OMIT` branch. The corrected normalize is:
     if raw missing: return OMIT
     value = lowercase(trim(raw))
     if value in {"prod","staging","dev"}: return value
     return ERROR
   "unknown" then falls through to ERROR like "qa" already does.

2. Budget check must precede publication and must reject, not alert.

   Current sketch publishes first, updates the tracker second, and alerts if the count is over 3. That admits a fourth value and only notifies after the fact — the contract says "cannot admit a fourth value," so a 4th value never reaches the publication path. Alerting is the wrong verb; rejection is.

   Required shape:
     - on OMIT: publish metric without the label, return
     - on ERROR: returned to caller, no publish
     - on a normalized value:
        read distinct set for tenant
        if value already in set: publish with label
        else if |set| < 3: publish with label and add value to set, atomically
        else: return ERROR (no publish, no alert)
   The "alert if tracker exceeds 3" line is removed entirely. Exceeding the budget is not a soft signal; it is a condition that must be made unreachable.

3. The check-and-publish step has to be atomic.

   Even with the corrected order above, two concurrent publications for the same tenant can both read |set|=2, both reserve a slot, and both publish, leaving the tenant at four distinct values. The "cannot admit a fourth" guarantee requires the reserve and the publish to commit together (single transactional write, or a compare-and-set per slot). The sketch doesn't show this, so as written it expresses intent, not enforcement.

With those three changes the examples resolve as:
   "PROD"    -> "prod"   (unchanged)
   " qa "    -> ERROR    (unchanged)
   "unknown" -> ERROR    (was OMIT — correction 1)
   missing   -> OMIT     (unchanged)

The lowercase-then-trim normalization before allowlist membership is fine; it is idempotent and runs before the membership check, which is what makes "PROD" -> "prod" safe without admitting any value the allowlist would not otherwise accept.

ANKLE SELF-CHECK — Thursday bouldering decision

Context: ~96 hours post lateral ankle sprain (rolled right ankle, soccer). Tuesday status — normal walk, stairs clean, swelling decreasing, no bony tenderness or numbness. Mild lateral ache on deep squat and quick direction change points to ATFL/capsule still irritable.

Run the checks Thursday morning, ~2-3 hours before the session, after a 5-10 min easy warm-up (walk or stationary bike).

TIER 1 — Baseline (all must pass)

  1. Single-leg stand, injured side, eyes open, 30 sec — no pain, no buckling
  2. Same, eyes closed, 30 sec — no sharp pain, no loss of trust
  3. Single-leg calf raises x 10, full ROM — no lateral pain at top or through push
  4. Hop in place on injured leg x 10 — no pain, no feeling of "giving"
  5. Lateral bounds side-to-side x 6 each direction — no pain, no weakness on push-off
  6. Deep squat (as deep as you can) — lateral ache ≤ 2/10, dull only, not sharp or localized

ANY sharp lateral pain, give-way, or ache > 3/10 = go straight to RED.

TIER 2 — Climbing-specific loading (only after Tier 1 is clean)

  7. Heel hook test — hook heel on a chair back or low box, pull heel toward glute while loading the ankle into mild inversion. Mild stretch is fine; sharp lateral pain is not.
  8. Edge stand — stand on a 2x4 or stair edge on the ball of foot, shift weight lateral to medial. No pain.
  9. Low drop — step off an 8-12" box onto the injured leg, soft landing. No sharp pain, no buckling.
 10. Twist under load — knee bent, rotate torso over the planted injured foot. No lateral pain.

If Tier 2 reproduces the squat ache sharply, or causes give-way, treat as RED regardless of Tier 1.

DECISION

GREEN — easy climbing (all Tier 1 + Tier 2 pass, baseline ache 0-1/10, no new morning swelling):
  - V0-V1 only, prefer vertical and slab
  - No heel hooks, toe hooks, dynamic jumps, high steps with twist
  - Downclimb everything; never jump off
  - Stick to problems you've done before or that are well within grade
  - Stop the session if lateral ache crosses 3/10 or any move feels unstable

YELLOW — modify (Tier 1 passes, Tier 2 has mild 1-3/10 dull ache, OR baseline ache 2-3/10):
  - Same problem-grade cap as green
  - Add: no overhang, no flags or twisty sequences, no campus moves, no mantles
  - Optional: low-Dye or kinesiology tape the lateral malleolus for proprioceptive cue
  - Cut planned session in half; if first 20 min is clean, fine to extend

RED — skip (any of the following):
  - Any sharp localized lateral pain in Tier 1 or Tier 2
  - Any give-way, buckling, or "I don't trust it" sensation
  - Swelling or morning stiffness worse than Tuesday
  - Heel hook test reproduces the squat ache sharply
  - Baseline walk-through on Thursday morning > 3/10
  - Action: replace climbing with stationary bike 15-20 min, ankle alphabet ROM, single-leg balance work, isometric calf/eversion holds. Re-test Friday or Saturday; if clean, easy session Sunday.

RED FLAGS DURING CLIMBING (regardless of pre-check)

  - Sudden sharp lateral pain on a move
  - Foot slip that catches the ankle — let yourself fall, don't try to save it
  - Increasing ache that doesn't settle within 60 sec of rest
  - Feeling the ankle "roll" or "give" even without a full injury

Any of these = stop immediately, ice 15 min, reassess. Do not push through.

WHY THE SQUAT/DIRECTION-CHANGE ACHE MATTERS HERE

Deep squat is loaded dorsiflexion with a mild inversion component. Heel hooks and twisty flag moves apply the same vector under dynamic load. Tuesday's mild ache is encouraging, but Thursday's heel hook test (Tier 2 #7) is the most direct read on whether the ATFL/capsule is ready for climbing-specific stress. If Tier 2 #7 passes cleanly, the rest of the session risk is mostly landing/jump-down, which the GREEN rule (downclimb, no jumps) handles.

Dry-run finding restated for grounding

  The harness as it stands collapses two requests into one observation: the
  blocked attempt and the post-cleanup retry share a single recorded entry,
  and only the final success is kept. That fails two tests:

    - Identity: a logical push that produced a blocked attempt and a later
      successful retry is one logical push but two requests. Recording only
      the retry hides that two router calls actually happened.

    - Invariant: nothing in the recorded evidence proves that the blocked
      attempt left the active generation unchanged. A blocked response
      status is not the same as proof that state did not move.

  The recommendation below is harness design only. No production semantics
  are changed; nothing here modifies the four-rule push boundary in the
  canary runbook, it just makes that boundary observable from dry runs.

Design principles for the harness

  1. Phase-first, not request-first. The unit of record is a phase, not a
     HTTP outcome. A logical push expands into a sequence of phases; the
     record keeps all of them.

  2. Distinct identities per phase. No phase reuses another phase's
     identifiers. A retry is not a continuation of the blocked attempt;
     it is a sibling with its own identity and its own evidence.

  3. The cleanup interval is a phase. It is not idle time between phases.
     It has its own start, its own end condition, and its own evidence.

  4. Retry is gated, never automatic. The harness refuses to retry without
     an explicit decision artifact (operator token or scripted approval).
     Auto-retry-after-cleanup is the exact behavior that produced the flaw.

  5. Each phase carries an invariant check, not just an outcome. A phase
     that did not flip a status code can still have moved state, and the
     harness must be able to detect that.

Phase model (three named phases, plus optional more)

  Phase A — attempt_blocked

    Trigger: harness issues the push; router rejects it (the deliberate
    block under test).

    Required evidence captured at phase end:
      - attempt_id (unique to this attempt; never reused)
      - request_id (router-side request identifier from the rejected call)
      - pre-attempt snapshot: active-generation count per pod, retired-
        generation count per pod, route-table hash, matcher-cleanup state,
        config-reload-failure counter, drop-series counter, restart count
      - post-attempt snapshot: same fields as pre-attempt
      - diff between pre and post snapshots (must be empty for the
        active-generation, route-table, dropped-series, reload-failure,
        and restart fields; this is the proof that blocked ≠ mutation)
      - timestamp aligned with pre and post snapshots, plus the rejection
        status code and any router-side rejection reason
      - parent_logical_push_id linking this attempt to the logical push
        it belongs to

    Exit condition: invariant diff is empty AND phase evidence is on disk.
    Failure to capture either is itself a harness failure, not a router
    failure.

  Phase B — cleanup_window

    Trigger: phase A completed; harness enters the cleanup interval
    observed by the router (matcher teardown, epoch drain).

    Required evidence captured at phase end:
      - attempt_id (a new id, distinct from phase A; same
        parent_logical_push_id)
      - retired-generation count per pod at phase start and phase end
      - epoch-drain progress at phase start and phase end
      - matcher-cleanup progress at phase start and phase end
      - stop-the-world cleanup pause durations and counts over the phase
      - a heap-profile snapshot per pod (or per representative pod, with
        the selection noted), aligned to phase start and phase end
      - timestamp at phase start and phase end
      - exit reason: cleanup-complete (retired count <= 1) or
        cleanup-stalled (held; do not advance to retry gate)

    Exit condition: retired count <= 1, no Rule 1 threshold recrossed
    during the window. A stalled cleanup does not advance; the harness
    holds and surfaces that as a separate outcome from "retry succeeded."

  Phase C — retry_authorized (only after explicit decision)

    Trigger: phase B exited cleanly AND a decision artifact is presented
    to the harness (operator token or scripted approval). Without that
    artifact, the harness terminates the logical push here and records
    it as held, not retried.

    Required evidence captured at phase end:
      - attempt_id (a new id, distinct from A and B; same
        parent_logical_push_id)
      - request_id from the retry call
      - the decision artifact reference (who approved, when, on what
        evidence — at minimum a pointer to phase B's retired-drain and
        pause evidence)
      - pre-attempt snapshot (same fields as phase A)
      - post-attempt snapshot (same fields as phase A)
      - diff between pre and post snapshots
      - timestamp aligned with pre and post snapshots
      - outcome: accepted or rejected; if rejected, the rejection reason

    Exit condition: outcome recorded AND decision artifact on record AND
    phase evidence on disk. Success here does not erase phases A or B.

Identity model (one paragraph, since the flaw lives here)

  Each phase gets an attempt_id. Each HTTP call inside a phase gets its
  own request_id from the router. The logical push has a
  parent_logical_push_id that links the attempt_ids together. The
  harness must never reuse an attempt_id across phases, never collapse
  attempt_ids when reporting "the push outcome," and never let a
  successful retry_authorized phase hide the prior attempt_blocked or
  cleanup_window evidence. The record for a logical push is the
  ordered list of its phase records, not the final phase's status.

What the harness must NOT do (anti-patterns, for the review checklist)

  - Do not auto-retry after cleanup. Retry requires a decision artifact.
  - Do not collapse multiple attempt_ids into one observation when
    reporting logical-push outcomes. Two requests are two records.
  - Do not use status code as the only evidence of "blocked." Status
    code plus an active-generation invariant check is required.
  - Do not let cleanup_window be implicit. Epoch drain, matcher
    cleanup, and stop-the-world pause durations must be on record
    for that phase, with timestamps.
  - Do not let a successful retry erase the blocked attempt from the
    evidence bundle. The bundle is append-only per logical push.
  - Do not let "one logical push = one observation" be a valid output
    shape. The minimum output shape is (logical_push_id,
    ordered_phase_records, ordered_request_ids).

Mapping to the existing canary rule set

  The four-rule push boundary in the canary runbook (stop rule on
  retired > 4 or cleanup pause > 100 ms; bounded single-push resume
  only when drain, baseline p99/heap, active-generation consistency,
  route parity, dropped-series, reload, and restart are all clean;
  immediate re-pause on recross; rollback conditions unchanged) is a
  production-canary rule. The harness above is the staging dry-run
  analog: it makes Rule 1 thresholds observable in phase B, makes the
  Rule 2 preconditions checkable before phase C is allowed to start,
  and makes the Rule 4 conditions (active-generation inconsistency,
  route divergence, dropped series, reload failure, unplanned restart)
  detectable in the phase A and phase C invariant diffs. The dry run
  then rehearses those checks under staging conditions, which is what
  the extended sequence is meant to use it for.

Open question worth flagging before implementation

  Decision artifact for phase C: scripted approval token or operator
  prompt? A scripted token is easier to wire into an unattended
  dry-run; an operator prompt forces human review but slows the
  extended sequence. The right answer probably depends on whether the
  extended sequence is meant to run hands-off overnight or with a
  reviewer attached. Worth deciding before the harness is finalized,
  because changing it later means changing the gate, not the harness.

Short answer: don't climb tonight.

You separated the right things. Walking, stairs, single-leg balance, and slow calf raises are low-load, controlled, and bilateral-dominant. A forward two-foot hop and a lateral hop are the first tests that actually demand the lateral stabilizers under landing and side-to-side load. You got a 2/10 ache on the first and a clear sense of instability on the second. That's not a borderline pass — the lateral hop is the test that most directly mirrors what a slipped foothold, a heel hook, a dyno landing, or a bail off the wall does to the same ligaments and peroneals. Treating those two results as soft would be the exact "walking = ready" thinking you're trying to avoid.

Tonight instead of climbing:

  - Single-leg stance 30–60 s, eyes open → eyes closed, on a folded towel or foam pad. If the injured side is appreciably worse than the other, stay here.
  - Lateral band walks and resisted eversion (light band) for the peroneals — high rep, no pain.
  - 3 x 10 slow controlled calf raises progressing to single-leg, only if the bilateral set is fully clean.
  - Ice / elevation if there's any residual swelling. No test, no loading tonight.

Re-test criteria before you book a session (all four should be true on the same day, on the injured side):

  1. Bilateral forward hop, then single-leg forward hop for distance: pain = 0/10, no apprehension.
  2. Single-leg lateral (side-to-side) hop, 10 reps, at a pace that feels controlled: no pain, no "wobble."
  3. Single-leg calf raises to fatigue (aim ~20+ reps): no pain, no sinking on the injured side.
  4. Single-leg balance on foam, eyes closed, 30 s: roughly symmetric to the other side.

If all four clear, you can think about a return session. Plan it for a day after a rest day, with no evening plans after — you want to read how the ankle responds 12–24 hours later.

Modifications for the first one or two sessions back:

  - Indoor only. Top-rope only (no lead — a take on a small foothold is exactly the loading you don't want, and a slack catch can load the ankle unpredictably).
  - Vertical to slightly overhanging terrain on jugs and large footholds. Avoid slab on small edges — slip → inversion is the classic re-injury path.
  - No heel hooks, no toe hooks, no dynos, no long moves. If a route forces any of these, climb something else.
  - Stick to grades where your feet smear on volume/feature, not on edges. Think "feet stay planted the whole move."
  - No bouldering above mat-level without a spotter focused on your feet for the first session. Avoid any problem that ends with a rolling or drop move.
  - Cap the session: warm-up on the easiest terrain you can, 30–45 min total on the wall, stop while technique still feels deliberate. Fatigue is when form goes and ankles roll.
  - Tape or a laced ankle brace for the first session back is reasonable — it doesn't fix anything but it raises the threshold for an inversion event. Don't use it as a reason to push harder.

Stop criteria. End the session — and reassess before coming back — if any of these happen:

  - Any sharp pain or pain >1/10 on a move.
  - A sense of "giving way," hesitation before a foot placement, or a missed foothold that you would normally have caught.
  - Pain that builds during the session, not just one isolated twinge.
  - Any clicking, catching, or locking sensation on the lateral side.
  - Within 24 hours after: visible new swelling, stiffness that's worse than the day before, or pain on stairs that wasn't there before.
  - You finish the session and your honest read is "I was protecting it the whole time." That's not a return, that's a test you didn't pass.

One thing to flag: I'm working only from what you described — grade of injury, mechanism, imaging if any, and how far out from the injury you are all matter, and I don't have those. If the lateral instability persists across two re-test cycles, or if you ever felt a pop, had bruising that took more than a few days to clear, or can't recall a clear inversion mechanism, that's worth a sports-medicine or physio visit before you return. The hop tests are a good gate, but they're a gate, not a diagnosis.

That's the decision: skip tonight, run the four re-tests on a single day when the swelling is fully gone, and only book a session if all four are clean — with the modifications and stop criteria above for the return.

Short answer: a short, graded return is reasonable today given that single-leg calf raises, straight-line jogging, and forward hops are all clean, and the lateral cut produces only tightness rather than sharp pain. The tightness on hard lateral cut is still meaningful, though — that's the highest-risk demand in pickup soccer (reactive, multi-directional loading), and it should be the gating test, not just a data point you observe.

Plan below assumes you go. If at any pre-play gate you fail, you're done for the day — don't try to push through the warm-up.

WARM-UP (about 20 minutes, do not skip)

 1. 5 min easy bike or brisk walk — general warm-up, raise core temp.
 2. Double-leg calf raises, 2 x 15, slow tempo (2 sec up, 2 sec down).
 3. Single-leg calf raises, 2 x 10 each side. Confirm the previously-injured side matches the other side for height, control, and any tightness. Asymmetry here = stop.
 4. Banded ankle dorsiflexion mobilizations, 2 x 10 each side, slow.
 5. Walking lunges with a torso rotation at the top, 2 x 10 each side — opens hips, primes cut mechanics.
 6. Linear drills only, ~4 min total: high knees, butt kicks, A-skips, B-skips. Stay straight-line.
 7. Progressive jog: 50% x 60 m, 75% x 60 m, ~90% x 60 m on a straight section.
 8. Re-test small forward hops (3-5) — should still be clean.
 9. GATING CUT TEST: one slow lateral cut at ~50-60%, then 1-2 at ~75%. If tightness is gone or unchanged from baseline today, you may play. If tightness is sharper, deeper, or comes with any hesitation, you do not play today — re-evaluate next session.

PARTICIPATION LIMITS

 - First session back: cap at 30-40 minutes of actual play, not including the warm-up.
 - Position yourself in lower-demand roles for the first 15 min (central defending or central midfield rather than wing/corner duty; no goalkeeping).
 - Communicate to teammates you're on a return — first 10-15 min, avoid being the primary receiver in tight space.
 - Cap intensity at RPE 7/10. No max-effort sprints, no contested 50/50 balls, no long balls over the top in the first half of your minutes.
 - One session only this week. Do not stack a second pickup within 72 hours even if you feel fine Sunday night.

STOP CRITERIA (during play — immediate, no negotiation)

 - Sharp or stabbing pain anywhere in the calf/Achilles/ankle.
 - Tightness that increases over the course of play rather than staying steady or fading as you warm up further.
 - Any sense of "giving way," hesitation, or guarding when you plant to cut — that means the tissue isn't trusting the load.
 - Painful first-step push-off after any rest period (substitution, water break, halftime). If the next sprint is worse than the previous one, you're done.
 - Heaviness, "fullness," or visible/palpable swelling in the calf or around the Achilles within 2 hours post-session.
 - Drop in push-off strength on the affected side that you can feel mid-play.

NEXT-DAY CHECK (do this Monday morning before deciding on anything mid-week)

 - First steps out of bed: any more stiffness or pain than this morning? Should be the same or better, not worse.
 - Single-leg calf raises, 10 reps slow: should still be clean and symmetric.
 - One hard lateral cut at home or at the field: should be no tighter than today.
 - If any of these are worse than today: no second session this week, reassess Thursday.
 - If equal or better: a second, slightly longer session Wednesday or Thursday is fine, then normal load the following week.

**Sequence review — Cyrus's maintenance-backfill staging rehearsal**

Five steps as proposed:
1. Three synthetic contiguous ranges
2. Intentional crash *before* commit
3. Another crash *after* commit but *before* acknowledgement
4. Duplicate retry using the same batch identifier
5. Out-of-order range that must not advance readiness

The shape is reasonable for exercising the at-least-once-with-dedup and commit-point semantics the maintenance backfill path needs. But the sequence as stated has real coverage gaps and one ordering trap. Walking it step by step:

**Step 1 — three synthetic contiguous ranges**
Fine as a precondition. For backfill specifically, I'd want to confirm:
- The three ranges are *contiguous but non-overlapping* (no shared boundary keys), so a partial commit leaves an unambiguous "first uncommitted" cursor.
- The synthetic IDs/time-range do not collide with any in-flight live import. With a tagged maintenance window that's normally fine, but the proposal doesn't say how the window is isolated — worth adding.
- *Missing assertion:* after ingestion but before any crash, readiness watermark should be unchanged. Capture the baseline watermark and assert it hasn't moved. Otherwise later steps can't distinguish "stuck" from "advanced."

**Step 2 — crash before commit**
This is the classic uncommitted-state case. Coverage looks right. Assertions to make explicit:
- No persisted rows for any of the three ranges (no partial write leaking through).
- Dedup/journal state is *absent* — i.e., a retry of these ranges must do full work, not be silently absorbed by a half-written journal entry. If the journal writes happen before commit, a crash here can leave a journal entry that a later replay treats as "already done." That's the dangerous variant of step 2 and the proposal doesn't pin down which one is being tested.
- Idempotency key for the batch is reserved (e.g., recorded as "in-flight") but not committed — so a retry with the *same* batch id can proceed and is not blocked by a "completed" sentinel.
- Watermark unchanged.

**Step 3 — crash after commit but before acknowledgement**
This is the at-least-once critical case. Coverage looks right in principle. Assertions:
- Rows for the three ranges *are* persisted (commit succeeded).
- Acknowledgement was *not* sent — so the upstream/caller will retry.
- Watermark *has* advanced. This is the one place readiness legitimately moves, and it's the load-bearing assertion of the whole rehearsal.
- Idempotency key is now in the "committed" state, not the "in-flight" state — distinct from step 2's exit condition.

**Step 4 — duplicate retry with the same batch identifier**
This is where step 3 pays off. Coverage looks right, but it has to be tested against *both* crash exit states, or its meaning is ambiguous:
- Retry after a step-2-style exit (uncommitted): must do full work; result equivalent to a fresh attempt; no duplicate rows.
- Retry after a step-3-style exit (committed, unacked): must be a *no-op against persisted state*; result equivalent; no duplicate rows; watermark stable at the post-step-3 position.

If step 4 only exercises one of those, the other path is uncovered. The proposal reads like one retry — I'd ask Cyrus to run it twice, once after each prior crash, or at minimum confirm which prior state is the precondition. Assertions:
- Row count for each of the three ranges identical pre- and post-retry.
- Watermark identical pre- and post-retry.
- The retry returns success (or the equivalent of ack) — not a duplicate-key error and not silent silent-drop. The caller needs to make forward progress on retry, not get stuck.
- *Missing assertion:* metrics/counters. If there's a "duplicate batch observed" or "idempotent replay" counter, assert it incremented exactly once per retry path. That counter is what gives you evidence the dedup fired rather than the work silently re-executing.

**Step 5 — out-of-order range that must not advance readiness**
This is the readiness-coupling guard. Coverage intent is right, but the proposal is light on what "out-of-order" means concretely. Three plausible readings, each with a different assertion:

a. A range whose *time range* is older than the current watermark — must be rejected or held, and in neither case may the watermark move backward.
b. A range whose *batch sequence number* is older than a range already being processed — must be queued behind, watermark unchanged until the gap closes.
c. A range that *partially overlaps* a committed range — must be rejected for the overlap and accepted for the non-overlapping tail.

The first two are readiness-guard cases; the third is a design-boundary case that may belong to PR #317 if that's where the overlap policy was actually settled. *Missing assertion:* specify which form of "out-of-order" is being tested, and assert explicitly that the watermark neither advances nor regresses. If you want full coverage of the readiness coupling, you actually want one test per reading — (a), (b), and (c) all behave differently.

Also worth asserting on step 5: no error is silently swallowed. If the out-of-order range is rejected, the rejection must be visible (response code, log line, or counter) so an operator can distinguish "held pending ordering" from "lost."

**Cross-cutting gaps in the proposed sequence**

- **No assertion on idempotency-key TTL or state cleanup.** After steps 2–4 complete, is the in-flight vs. committed state for the batch id eventually reaped? If yes, when, and what's the assertion? Replay protection that never expires is a slow leak.
- **No concurrent-batch assertion.** Steps 1–4 use a single batch id. The backfill path will also receive *different* batch ids concurrently. A second batch arriving during step 3 (committed, unacked) must not be blocked by the first batch's in-flight key, and must not collide on any global lock. Worth a sixth step.
- **No acknowledgment-timeout assertion.** The whole reason step 3 is dangerous is that the caller *will* retry after a timeout. The rehearsal should pin down what that timeout is and assert the retry actually fires on that timer, not just on manual replay. Otherwise step 4 is testing manual replay, not the production retry path.
- **No readiness rollback assertion.** If step 3 advances the watermark and step 4 is then discovered to have produced a divergence, is there a defined rollback path for the watermark, or is divergence detection the only recourse? That's a runbook question, not a rehearsal assertion, but it's adjacent.
- **Order of steps 2 and 3 matters for the dedup invariant.** As written, step 2 (crash pre-commit) runs before step 3 (crash post-commit). That's the right order — you want the dedup state machine to have been observed in the "in-flight then abandoned" state before being observed in the "committed then unacked" state, because the latter is a superset of the former in terms of what the dedup table must distinguish. Good as-is; flagging because if Cyrus reorders, the rehearsal loses information.
- **Watermark observation point.** Every step should record watermark before and after. The proposal only states the expected outcome for step 5 ("must not advance"). Steps 2, 3, 4 need the same explicit before/after assertion.

**Net**

The five steps cover the right shape — pre-commit crash, post-commit-pre-ack crash, replay, out-of-order — but the rehearsal will be much stronger with:

- Step 1: capture baseline watermark.
- Step 2: assert no persisted rows, no completed-sentinel, watermark unchanged.
- Step 3: assert rows persisted, ack not sent, watermark advanced.
- Step 4: run *twice* — once after a step-2 exit, once after a step-3 exit — and assert row counts, watermark, and the idempotent-replay counter on each.
- Step 5: pick one of (a)/(b)/(c) explicitly, or run all three; assert watermark stable and rejection visible.
- Add a sixth step for a concurrent different batch id during step 3.
- Pin acknowledgment timeout and assert the retry fires on the timer.

This is a client retry defect, not an ingest-edge invariant failure.

Why the server side is clean:
- The 8-waiting ceiling is a documented throttling signal, not an invariant — hitting it is the system working as designed
- Active concurrency stays at 4/pod and 2/tenant — both invariant ceilings intact
- Low-volume tenants still receiving slots — fairness preserved
- Randomized 1/2/3s Retry-After is standard jittered backpressure, the canonical defense against synchronized retry storms
- Accepted / dropped / restart metrics clean — server is in steady state

The tell is the behavior you described: three immediate retries within the same second, "apparently before its application code can inspect the header." That's a retry path firing below the application layer — on socket reset, on a transport-level retry middleware, on a default-retry trigger that doesn't read the response. A correct client honors a 1/2/3s jitter by spacing its retries across that window; an immediate burst means it never parsed the header.

Focused evidence needed before any server change:

1. Header on the wire. A captured 429 from this path showing `Retry-After: <1|2|3>` actually present in the response — not stripped by an LB, proxy, or CDN. While you're there, confirm there's no code path that returns 429 without a `Retry-After`.

2. Client retry timing vs. header value. Exact sub-second timestamps of the three retries relative to the 429. If they fire within ~100ms of the response, the client's retry path isn't reading the response at all.

3. Client isolation. Search the access log: is this the only client showing the immediate-burst pattern at the 8-waiting cap, or are there others? Single-client behavior points to a client defect; a wider pattern points elsewhere.

4. Header-honoring baseline. Pull 2–3 well-behaved clients hitting the same cap in the same window; show their retries land at ≥1s spacing matching the jittered value. This proves the server's header is being honored by clients that bother to read it.

5. Invariant dashboard snapshot. 4/pod, 2/tenant, fairness, accepted / dropped / restart all clean across the burst window — solidifies that the server isn't in a degraded state driving the misbehavior.

6. Client fingerprint. User-agent, HTTP library, framework version, retry middleware. Known-bad default-retry behavior in common HTTP libraries (urllib3 on certain transport errors, some service-mesh sidecars) is the usual suspect.

What would shift this from "client defect" to "server change warranted":
- Header is being stripped somewhere on the wire (item 1)
- Multiple unrelated clients show the same pattern (item 3)
- The 8-waiting ceiling itself is the wrong number — that's a separate tuning question, not an invariant call, and needs product/load review

Until at least 1 and 3 land in your favor, the server is doing what it's documented to do and the fix belongs on the client. No ingest-edge code change should be on the table.

Root cause hypothesis

The single changed variable is the runtime (Node 20.15 -> 22.4). The artifact is byte-identical on iOS and Android but reordered on web, and the diff is key-order only. That points at one specific thing: V8 changed how it orders keys when a plain object is enumerated or stringified, and the web emitter is letting that order leak into the output.

Most likely emission site: somewhere in the web path the generator builds a token group object via `Object.fromEntries(map)`, `{...map}`, or `Object.assign({}, entries)`, then runs it through `JSON.stringify` (or a serializer that uses `Object.keys`/`for...in`). V8 12.x in Node 22 tightened/drifted property ordering for objects built from non-literal sources — the ~300-line delta is consistent with a top-level group map reordering itself, not a handful of stray keys.

Why only web: iOS/Android emit binary/proprietary formats where key order is canonicalized by the format itself or by the emitter. Web emits JSON or a JS module, so textual key order IS the artifact. Against the at-least-once / durable-readback shape that Cyrus described:

  Passes the parts that matter:
  - Pre-commit crash leaves neither result nor watermark — correct. The durability invariant is "nothing visible until something durable exists," and this preserves it. No phantom readiness from an in-memory state.
  - Post-commit / pre-ack crash retried under the same batch identifier returning the identical committed result — this is the right idempotency story. Same key in, same committed result out. It means the retry path does not double-apply work, and the caller can treat the duplicate as success without re-checking side effects.
  - Readiness published only after reading the durable result and watermark back — this is the correct "no readiness ahead of durability" rule. It closes the gap where readiness flips and then a crash loses the work that the readiness signal claimed was done.
  - Third range held not-ready until missing second range commits — this is the right out-of-order rule. The readiness gate is per-range and gated on the durable watermark of the prior range. If readiness for range N depended on range N-1 being durable and that holds, then readiness cannot leak across an unfinished range.

  Remaining stop conditions to state (not actions, just the set that has to remain true for this rehearsal to count as a clean pass):
  - Same-batch-id retry path must be bounded. If a post-commit / pre-ack crash loops indefinitely (caller retries, server keeps returning the same committed result because the original ack was lost), there needs to be either an upper bound on retry attempts or a max-age on the committed-batch dedupe window. Otherwise a stuck caller can pin storage on a batch the server has no other reason to keep.
  - Crash window between the two durability writes (result and watermark) must stay narrow enough that one durable and not the other is recoverable. If the crash window is the wider "watermark persisted but result not yet persisted" gap rather than the narrower "both persisted but ack lost" gap, the retry path has to be able to re-derive the result from the watermark — otherwise the idempotency story collapses. The rehearsal description doesn't tell me which crash window Cyrus was actually exercising, and the difference matters.
  - Out-of-order readiness gate needs an explicit hold, not a skip. "Third range remains not ready until the missing second range commits" only holds if readiness publication is gated on the durable watermark of the prior range, not on a stale in-memory "I think range 2 is done" signal. Confirm the gate is reading the durable watermark and not an in-process flag.
  - Readiness publication has to be monotonic. If range 3 can publish readiness, then range 2 commits late, range 3 readiness must still hold (or be re-evaluated) — a late-arriving range 2 commit must not invalidate already-published readiness for range 3.
  - Bounded batch means a hard cap on what's in one batch. Rehearsal should include at least one run at or near the cap, with a crash inside the batch, to prove the cap is enforced under failure and not just under happy-path throughput.
  - Caller-visible failure mode for a batch that fails its bounded retry window must be defined. If the bounded retry window is exhausted, does the caller see a terminal error keyed by the batch id, or does it just keep retrying? "Bounded" implies a terminal mode; the rehearsal should show one.
  - Bounded retry window needs an alerting hook, not just a stop. A batch sitting at its retry cap is exactly the kind of state that should page the mapped owner (Cyrus team on rollup-service), not just sit in a log.

  Structural pattern is correct (authorize-then-callback; resolver body does not execute when authorization denies). The boundary is established per-resolver for the two migrated paths. It is NOT established system-wide — partial migration plus no integrated readiness plus open negative-test gaps. Do not treat as a pass.

What the wrapper establishes (deployCard, ownerCard only)
  - Authorization runs before the resolver callback is invoked.
  - The denied-path tests (adapter.calls == 0) confirm the resolver body is bypassed on a clean deny.
  - This inverts the rejected resolver-local approach and removes the resolver's first-action leak window.

What the wrapper does NOT establish on its own
  - It does not prove previewLookup is the only entry. Any caller that invokes a resolver directly bypasses authorization. Per-resolver unit tests do not catch this.
  - It does not cover non-migrated resolvers. incidentSummary is still TODO; any preview path that reaches it skips the boundary entirely.
  - It does not cover the gap between authorization decision and resolver execution. If authorizePreview uses a fresh provenance snapshot but the resolver refetches owner data, a state change between decision and execution can leak preview to a non-owner. Snapshot must be captured at decision and passed into the resolver, not regenerated.
  - It does not cover authorize-throws paths. The denied tests assert adapter.calls == 0 on a clean deny result. Behavior when the authorizer throws (exception, not deny) is unspecified — the callback must not fire in that case either.

Remaining migration work
  1. Migrate incidentSummary resolver to the wrapper.
  2. Enumerate every preview-bearing lookup path across the four named rooms (Checkout API, Mobile Sync release-review, Search ingest timeout 1/25, Billing Web release-review 2/7). Any path not routed through previewLookup is a boundary bypass — confirm there are no legacy direct-resolver callers.
  3. Decide and document provenance-snapshot lifetime: capture at authorizePreview decision, pass into the resolver, do not refetch inside the resolver.

Remaining negative-test work
  1. Denied-path unit test for incidentSummary (after migration): adapter.calls == 0.
  2. Authz-throws-path test for each migrated resolver: when authorizePreview throws, the callback must not fire and adapter.calls must remain 0.
  3. Provenance-TOCTOU test: simulate an owner-map change between authorization and resolver execution; assert preview is denied, not leaked from a stale-allowed decision.
  4. Direct-invocation negative test or static guard: calling deployCard, ownerCard, or incidentSummary resolvers directly without the wrapper must be rejected (lint rule, or a test that imports them and asserts access denial).
  5. Cross-resolver atomicity: a request that triggers multiple preview fields must be denied atomically — one deny denies all, no partial preview returned.
  6. Reauthz-on-refresh (per Iris importer FM precedent 3/12): after a deny, a fresh retry must not return stale cached preview. If any preview result is cached, deny must invalidate the partial.

Integrated readiness suite
  - Not run. Per-resolver unit tests do not substitute. The four named rooms need an end-to-end run in production-equivalent config that exercises preview lookups and asserts adapter.calls == 0 on denied paths at the system level. Without it, treat the migration as in-progress regardless of per-resolver green.

Recommendation
  - Do not merge as boundary-established. Land incidentSummary migration, the provenance-snapshot lifetime decision, the negative tests above, and the integrated readiness run — then reassess. Current state: structurally correct for 2 of 3 resolvers, unverified system-wide.

Plan: sheet-pan salmon over orzo with a dill-yogurt sauce. One sheet pan, one pot, one bowl — that's it. The trick is doing all the prep now, then sliding the pan in when Devika surfaces.

ACTIVE PHASE (about 20 min, while she naps)

1. Oven to 425°F. Line a sheet pan with parchment.
2. Salt a pot of water and start it boiling. Cook orzo to al dente (about 1 min under package time). Drain, toss with a splash of olive oil, cover the pot. (Orzo holds 45 min like a champ — refresh with a spoonful of hot water when you plate.)
3. While the orzo cooks, on a cutting board: trim green beans, halve the cherry tomatoes, zest the lemon then juice half, chop a small handful of dill.
4. Yogurt sauce in a small bowl: most of the yogurt, a few spoonfuls, plus chopped dill, the lemon zest, a small squeeze of lemon juice, salt, pepper. Stir. Cover and put it in the fridge — cold sauce on hot salmon is the move.
5. Pat the salmon dry, season with salt, pepper, and a pinch of the remaining dill. Leave the fillets on a plate on the counter — they come to room temp while you wait, which is exactly what keeps them from drying out in the oven.
6. On the sheet pan: toss green beans and tomatoes with olive oil, salt, pepper. Push them to the edges and leave a clear strip down the middle for the salmon.

HOLDING POINT (up to 45 min)

- Salmon on the counter, uncovered (well within the safe window for raw fish; under 2 hr is fine).
- Sheet pan with the veg, at room temp, ready to go in.
- Orzo covered on the stove.
- Yogurt sauce chilled.
- Bread on the counter.

If the nap runs longer than 30 min and you're twitchy about it, slide the salmon plate back into the fridge and pull it 15 min before you cook — that's the only swap.

COOK PHASE (3 min active, 12 min in the oven)

1. Set the salmon in the cleared strip of the sheet pan. Slide it in. 10–12 min — pull at 125°F internal if you have a probe, or when the thickest part flakes gently but still looks translucent at the center. Carryover heat will finish it on the plate.
2. While it bakes: warm the bread, fluff the orzo with a fork (splash of hot water if it's clumped), and plate the orzo into two bowls or onto a platter.
3. Lift the salmon and veg off the pan onto the orzo. Spoon the cold yogurt sauce generously over the salmon. Tear bread, serve.

Why the salmon won't dry out: short hot roast on a room-temp fillet, with the tomatoes on the same pan releasing juice that lightly steams the fish from below, plus the cold yogurt spooned on at the end. The sauce is what most people forget — it's doing half the moisture work.

Total active time lands around 22–25 min, so you're under the 35-min budget even if something slows you down.

ASSESSMENT

A controlled, graduated return is reasonable. The current checks (jog, 10 single-leg calf raises, forward/lateral hops, figure eights, moderate cuts, no swelling or giving way for a week) clear the early-phase gate. But they are not a green light for full match play at 14 days post mild lateral sprain:

  - 10 single-leg heel raises is roughly half the typical RTP threshold in the Ankle Function Test battery (~25 reps, or >90% symmetry with the uninvolved side). Posterior-chain endurance is still under-prepared.
  - Your figure eights and cuts were "controlled" and "moderate" — reactive cutting at speed and pivoting under fatigue are not yet tested.
  - Re-injury risk is highest in the first 2-4 weeks after a sprain. Unrestricted full match at 14 days is on the aggressive end even for a Grade I.

Bottom line: enter the return, but on rails. Treat the next 7-10 days as a stepwise re-load, not a single test.

WARM-UP (10-15 min, every session before any cutting or jumping)

  1. Cardio flush, 3-5 min — bike or easy jog, RPE 3-4. Do not start cold.
  2. Mobility, 3-4 min:
     - Ankle alphabet (capital letters with the big toe), both sides, ~30 sec
     - Knee-to-wall dorsiflexion hold, 2x30 sec each
     - Straight-knee and bent-knee calf stretch, 2x30 sec each
  3. Activation, 3-4 min:
     - Single-leg balance, eyes open then closed, 2x20-30 sec each — the right side is your test
     - Single-leg calf raises, 2x15 each — if you cannot reach 25, you have not passed
     - Lateral band walks, 2x10 each direction
  4. Movement prep, 3-4 min:
     - Lateral shuffle low-to-medium, 2x20 m each direction
     - Carioca, 2x20 m each direction
     - Progressive jog, 75% then full, straight-line, 4x20 m
     - Straight-leg bounds, 4x20 m — quality over distance

INITIAL TIME CAP

First session back: 20 minutes of on-field activity with a planned rest block at 10 min. Treat the session as exposure, not fitness. Add ~10 min per session across the week; do not jump to full duration in one step. Pickup game framing: arrive early, do the warm-up, and leave the field after your cap regardless of who is still playing.

ACTIVITY LIMITS — first 7-10 days of return

  - No 11v11 match play until you have completed at least two small-sided or sub-max sessions without symptoms.
  - If pickup structure allows it, start in a half-field or small-sided game at ~70% effort, no headers, no overhead balls.
  - No reactive cutting drills in the first two sessions — only pre-planned cuts under 75% intensity.
  - Avoid hard planted pivots on the right ankle for the first 3-4 sessions. If a cut requires the right foot as plant, decelerate first.
  - If you have used an external ankle support (semi-rigid brace or low-dye tape) before, use it for the first two weeks. If you have not, do not introduce one now — too many new variables at once.
  - No new cleats, no new surface, no new position this week. One variable at a time.
  - Skip goalkeeper duties initially — the landing and lateral pivots are the wrong re-introduction.

STOP CRITERIA — any one halts the session and resets the next-day plan

  - Reproducible pain in the right ankle during or right after a rep — not mild awareness, anything that changes how you move.
  - Swelling or stiffness within 24 hours that exceeds your current baseline (compare visually and by feel to the left side).
  - A giving-way episode, a "roll," or any subjective sense of instability — even one.
  - Compensation patterns: hitching on cuts, offloading to the left, reduced push-off on the right, or visibly slower change-of-direction on the right vs. left.
  - Performance drop: hops lose height, cuts lose speed, calf raises fall below 10 reps with form breakdown.
  - Next-morning check fails: single-leg balance on the right under 30 sec, or residual soreness that alters your gait on waking.

Rule of thumb: if a session ends and you cannot tell whether you did it or not, the next session can advance. If you can tell, the next session repeats the same dose.

NEXT MILESTONE — closer to full clearance when all of the following hold

  - 25 single-leg heel raises on the right, equal to the left
  - Reactive 90° cut drill at full speed, bilaterally, no asymmetry
  - Small-sided or sub-max play at full effort for 30+ min, no symptoms during or after
  - Two consecutive practices with no stop-criterion hit

If any milestone stalls more than one session, the right move is a PT visit — not more soccer.
