KIBO — POST-ANTIBIOTIC LOOSE STOOL, HOME PLAN

Observation window: next 24-72 hours. Today's picture is mild — no red flags noted. Plan is bland food, hydration, a brief stool log, and clear escalation triggers.

DIET (next 1-3 days)
- Small, frequent meals: skinless boiled chicken + plain white rice (roughly 1:2 chicken:rice), or boiled lean ground turkey + rice.
- Optional soother: a tablespoon or two of plain canned pumpkin — pure pumpkin, NOT pie filling (no sugar/spice).
- Transition back to his normal food over 2-3 days once stools are consistently formed.

HYDRATION
- Fresh water always available.
- If he's drinking less, offer low-sodium chicken broth (no onion/garlic — read the label) or a few ice cubes.
- Quick dehydration check: gums slick and pink; skin on the back of the neck snaps back immediately when gently lifted.

DO NOT GIVE WITHOUT VET OK
- Imodium / loperamide, Pepto Bismol, or any OTC anti-diarrheal. Dose depends on weight, some formulations are unsafe for dogs, and they can mask a worsening picture.
- Unprescribed probiotics; if you want one, ask the vet which strain and dose.
- Dairy, fatty foods, table scraps, new treats, bones.
- Do not restart or extend the antibiotic on your own.

CALL REGULAR VET (non-urgent, same/next day)
- Soft stool persists past 48-72 hours, or trends worse (more frequent, looser).
- Any blood, mucus, or black/tarry stool.
- Appetite drop lasting more than ~24 hours.
- Mild lethargy or behavior change.
- Worth a brief check-in regardless: most clinics want a heads-up when a patient has GI signs during or right after a prescribed course.

SEEK URGENT / ER CARE NOW
- Repeated vomiting, or vomiting blood.
- Abdominal swelling, hard belly, or obvious pain when picked up or touched.
- Repeated unproductive straining.
- Large-volume watery diarrhea, or any significant amount of fresh blood.
- Signs of dehydration: tacky/sticky gums, skin tenting, sunken eyes.
- Pale or white gums, collapse, weakness, or shivering/panting at rest.

REPACK SEQUENCE (books under 35 lb, apartment + one shelf usable)

0.  Set up the workspace
    - Clear a path between the shelf wall and an open floor area (ideally the room you're boxing out of, not a hallway).
    - Stage the 6 small boxes, your towels/linens, a kitchen scale, and a marker in that open area.
    - Mark the one row that's staying unpacked with painter's tape on the shelf edge so nothing from it gets pulled into the repack.

1.  Inventory before you move anything
    - Weigh each medium box (or lift and rank: 48, 47, 46, 44, 43, 43, 42, 42 — exact numbers don't matter, just heaviest 3 vs lightest 5).
    - Open only the 3 heaviest. Sort each into:
        A)  Hardcovers / textbooks / coffee-table / reference (heaviest)
        B)  Standard trade hardcovers
        C)  Paperbacks (lightest)
    - Leave the other 5 medium boxes sealed for now.

2.  Split the 3 heaviest mediums into the 6 small boxes
    - Each heavy medium becomes 2 small boxes: one for category A, one for B/C.
    - Stack heaviest books on the bottom of each small box, flat, spine-in or spine-out (consistent), with no single stack taller than ~3/4 of the box height.
    - Fill remaining vertical void with a folded towel or two. The towel is doing two jobs: keeping books from shifting (which damages spines) and absorbing any last bit of weight so the box isn't top-heavy on a single stack.
    - Target 28–32 lb per small box, never above 35. Small boxes feel heavier than mediums of the same weight because of the handle geometry — that's why you want margin.

3.  Redistribute the remaining 5 mediums
    - Open and weigh each. The split in step 2 should have pulled ~10–13 lb of A-class books out of each heavy one, but the now-rebuilt small boxes absorbed that. So your 5 remaining mediums likely have lost their A-class books.
    - For any of the 5 that still reads 36–40 lb: pull 2–4 hardcovers out and add them to whichever small box has the most headroom (or swap a paperback in for a hardcover).
    - Crumple a dish towel into each remaining medium's empty corners — boxes that aren't full become dangerous when carried because the weight shifts. Towel fill keeps them rigid.
    - Reweigh. Every box, medium and small, should now be 28–35 lb.

4.  Verify and restack
    - Lift each box with two hands from the bottom (not the cut-out handles, which on medium book boxes at 30+ lb are the failure point).
    - Label each box with the weight and a category tag (e.g., "BOOKS / 32 lb / shelf 2").
    - Restack along the wall you cleared, keeping the taped "do not pack" row physically reachable without moving anything. If a bookshelf must stay usable during this, that row's contents stay on the shelf until moving day.

5.  Safety note for the actual carry
    - 35 lb of books in a small box is awkward even though it's within spec. Lift with legs, keep the box close to your body, and don't twist. If a box pushes past 35 lb during redistribution, split it again before you tape it shut — much easier now than in the stairwell.

DRYWALL ANCHOR PATCH (later-ready, no paint today)

1.  Identify the anchor type (each one may differ):
    - Plastic expansion anchor (conical, ribbed): was driven into a pre-drilled hole.
    - Threaded self-drilling anchor (EZ-anchor, looks like a fat screw with coarse threads): screwed straight into the drywall.
    - Toggle bolt or molly bolt: has a metal sleeve behind the wall — you won't be able to pull it out flush easily.
    - Two ordinary drywall anchors on one removed bookcase is almost certainly the first two types; toggle/molly bolts are uncommon for bookcases unless they're heavy-duty shelving.

2.  Remove each anchor:
    - Plastic: grip with pliers and push it into the wall cavity (don't pull — you'll tear the paper face of the drywall). The hole it leaves is what you patch.
    - Threaded self-drilling: unscrew counterclockwise with a screwdriver or pliers. It backs out cleanly and leaves a small round hole.
    - Toggle/molly: tap the head flush with a hammer to push the metal sleeve into the wall, then patch over the small dimple.

3.  Patch (lightweight spackle, e.g., DAP DryDex or similar):
    - Press a small amount of spackle into the hole with your finger or a putty knife, slightly overfilling so it's proud of the wall surface.
    - Smooth the surface flush with a flexible putty knife (1" or 2"), wiping the blade clean between passes.
    - For holes deeper than ~1/4", do this in two thin layers rather than one thick one — thick layers crack as they dry.

4.  Dry and sand:
    - Dry time: 15–30 min for shallow holes, longer for deep fills. Color-changing spackle tells you when it's ready (goes from pink to white).
    - Sand lightly with 150-grit, then 220-grit, just until the patch is flush with the surrounding wall. Don't oversand — you'll expose the paper face again.
    - Wipe with a dry cloth or barely damp rag. Done.

5.  What's left for later:
    - The patches will be off-white and visible up close but read as flat wall from a normal viewing distance. That's the "later-ready" state — no primer, no paint, no smell, no mess for today.
    - When you do paint (one afternoon, before handoff), a single light prime + one finish coat over the patches with a small foam roller will disappear them. Keep a few tablespoons of the wall paint labeled with the room and date if you have any; if not, take a chip to a paint store for a match.

Order of operations for the rest of today: finish the repack before touching the anchors. The dust from drilling anchors out and sanding spackle will land on everything if you do it first, and you don't want to re-clean book boxes.

One small thing worth flagging while the bookcase is still detached: photograph the wall behind where it was mounted, in case the handoff inspection notices any discoloration or anchor holes beyond the two you already spotted. Easier to plan a touch-up now than on handoff day.

Kibo's behavior is mild adjustment stress, not pathology — and importantly, his coping mechanism (bed anchor) is working. The setup below protects that anchor.

SAFE AREA
- Pick one room or corner that stays unboxed across every packing block. Kitchen or a bedroom away from the staging zone.
- Bed and water stay in their current corner. Do NOT rotate them into a "designated safe area" — he'll gravitate to the familiar spot, not a designated one. If you move the anchor, you break the only thing that's working.
- Add a worn t-shirt or blanket with your or Devika's scent on the bed.
- Run a fan or low music to mask tape, box shuffling, and door slams.
- If he has a crate he already uses, treat it as the den. Otherwise, baby-gate the safe area so no one wanders in with a box.

TIMING AROUND BLOCKS
- 20–30 min before each block: a brisk walk with a sniff-heavy stretch. Let him lead; drain the cortisol before the noise starts.
- 5 min before: stuffed Kong, lick mat with peanut butter or wet food, or a long-lasting chew in the safe area. Licking and chewing drop heart rate fast.
- During the block: someone with him in the safe area, OR gate him in with the chew item. Do NOT carry him room-to-room — the following and pacing you're seeing is the response to that shuffle. Reduce the shuttle, not the dog.
- Right after each block: 10-min decompression walk before the next block. Even a short one counts.
- Avoid stacking two blocks back-to-back without a 60–90 min reset.

VET WARMANTS (call your vet or an urgent-care line)
- Food refusal past 24h, or water refusal past 12h
- Repeated vomiting or diarrhea, or any blood in stool
- Trembling or panting at rest that doesn't resolve within ~30 min of being back in the safe area
- Hiding and refusing to come out past 2–3 hours
- Sudden reactivity he doesn't normally show — growl, snap, freeze. That's stress overflow, not a training issue.
- Housetraining regression (indoor accidents when previously clean)
- Self-directed behavior: paw-licking to raw, tail chase, flank-sucking
- Lethargy that persists past one good night's sleep after a block

NOT TO DO
- No sedatives. A sedated dog can't communicate stress, so real signs get masked right when you'd most want to see them.
- No bed or food relocation before the move itself.
- No correction for following or pacing. He's not misbehaving — he's asking for proximity. Reduce the trigger (room-to-room shuttling), don't suppress the signal.
- Skip the "let him get used to boxes" idea. That's novelty on top of novelty.

One thing worth keeping in mind for the rest of the day: both the following and the pacing stop the moment his bed is back in its usual corner. That's a clean read — the anchor works. Hold that corner untouched through every block and he'll most likely ride the rest of packing out without escalating past what you saw this morning.

Strategy: one-pot chickpea + rice + wilted-spinach pilaf. Everything in it is fully cooked at 7:15, so it holds safely covered for 2 hours with no perishability concerns. Eggs cook to-order the moment Devika walks in. Yogurt stays in the fridge until plating.

Times assume white rice (~15 min). If you've only got brown, start the rice at 6:35 and push everything else back 15 min.

TIMELINE

6:50  Start rice. Rinse 1 cup rice into the pot with 1.75 cups water and a pinch of salt. Boil, cover, drop to low.

7:05  Rice done. Add 1 tbsp oil to the same pot, then 1 drained can of chickpeas, ~1 tsp cumin, ~1/2 tsp coriander, black pepper. Stir 1 min to season and warm the chickpeas.

7:10  Pile a big handful of roughly chopped spinach (stems ok) on top of the chickpeas. Cover. Steam 2 min.

7:12  Uncover, stir the wilted spinach through the chickpeas, then fold the cooked rice back in. Squeeze in ~1 tbsp lemon. Taste for salt.

7:15  Plate YOUR portion. Dollop of yogurt on top, extra lemon if you want it. Eat now — you have 30 min before the walk.

7:30  Tidy and hold. Wipe the pot rim, lid back on, leave it on the now-off burner. Fully cooked rice + legumes + cooked-down greens holds 2 hours at warm room temp under a lid with no issue. If you'd rather be belt-and-suspenders, slide the covered pot into a 170 F oven.

7:45  Walk Kibo. 25-30 min loop. (Prospect Park West side tends to be quieter on the skateboard/skate front — gentler on him.)

8:15  Back. Do the easy wash now while the pot wipes clean: pot, cutting board, knife. Leave the small skillet for Devika's egg.

9:25  Heat a small non-stick skillet, medium-low. Crack 2 eggs, fry sunny-side or soft-scramble with salt. ~3 min.

9:30  Plate Devika's pilaf (60-90 sec in the microwave with a splash of water and a loose cover, or straight from the pot if still warm), eggs on top, cold yogurt on the side, lemon wedge.

WHY THE HOLD IS SAFE

    Eggs: not cooked yet at 7:30. They come in fresh at 9:25.
    Spinach: wilted INTO the hot pilaf at 7:10 — already heat-treated and bound in starch. It can't go slimy the way raw leaves left sitting in a bowl would.
    Yogurt: stays sealed in the fridge until plating.

CLEANUP

    One pot, one small skillet, one cutting board, one knife, two plates/forks. Total active cooking window: ~25 min, mostly before the walk.

Your self-check (no red flags, just mechanical stiffness from loaded forward flexion over the weekend) is the right frame: a session that loads the back gently, avoids lumbar compression and deep flexion under load, and stops the moment the dull stiffness shifts toward anything sharper. Plan below for ~60 min total.

PRE-SESSION GATE (cancel or scale down further if any apply right now):
  - Stiffness has worsened since this morning, or forward-bending to mid-shin is sharply painful
  - You slept poorly or are unusually worn down (recovery debt = injury risk on a managed back)
  - You took ibuprofen before climbing (you want to hear your back today, not mute it)
  - Pain at rest has appeared since you wrote this

WARM-UP (~15 min, do this before pulling on the wall):

General (5 min) - easy cycling, brisk walk, or jumping jacks to a light sweat

Spine and hips (8-10 min, slow, nasal breathing):
  - Cat-cow: 2 x 8
  - Prone press-ups (cobra press): 2 x 6, hold 2 sec at top - directly counteracts the forward-flexion load the back has had
  - World's greatest stretch: 2 each side
  - 90/90 hip switches: 2 x 8
  - Glute bridges: 2 x 10, pause 2 sec at top
  - Dead bugs: 2 x 6 each side, slow

Easy on-wall (5 min) - 3-4 easy problems or a traverse; smooth footwork, hips in, no long reaches

SESSION (~35-40 min):

Pick problems that:
  - Are steep or vertical with good feet so you can keep hips close to the wall
  - Sit at or below ~70-80% effort. Nothing you have to work for today.
  - Skip: slab, compression sequences, heel-hook cruxes, deep crouch starts, twisty moves that load the lumbar
  - 3-5 problems total; rotate > crank

Volume rule:
  - 3-4 attempts per problem, then move on
  - 3-5 min rest between burns (longer than usual)
  - Total attempts today: roughly half a normal session

Movement limits:
  - Static and controlled. No dynos. No jumping for the top.
  - Downclimb everything; no falls from height onto the pad
  - No high steps with a loaded, rounded spine
  - Let the wall hold weight; don't muscle through with the back
  - If a move forces deep spinal flexion under load, skip the problem entirely

STOP CRITERIA (end the session on any one of these - do not push through):
  - Pain radiating down the leg or into the buttock
  - Numbness, tingling, or pins-and-needles in leg or foot
  - Any new sharp or focal pain (different from the current dull stiffness)
  - Pain climbing past 3-4/10 that doesn't return to baseline after a 5-min rest
  - Pain appearing at rest (currently absent - its appearance is itself a signal)
  - Leg weakness, or a foot that doesn't track normally
  - Back "locking up" or visibly guarding; you're moving asymmetrically or breath-holding
  Stretching won't undo any of those. The session is over.

COOL-DOWN (~5 min):
  - Cat-cow: 2 x 8
  - Child's pose with arms long: 60 sec
  - Figure-4 stretch each side: 60 sec
  - 2-3 min easy walking

AFTER - signals to actually act on, not just note:
  - New symptoms tonight or tomorrow morning that weren't there before
  - 24 hours later, stiffness is worse than it was this morning instead of better
  - Any stop-criterion sign appears post-session

If tomorrow morning is the same or slightly better, you're cleared for Saturday's main packing block as planned. If it's meaningfully worse, shift Saturday to sorting/labeling and keep heavy lifting minimal for 48 hours.

If Ren asks what you're working with: "Mild back stiffness from the move, keeping today low-volume and easy, no projects."

The service stays on the post-push state with health at baseline; the breach is a window-boundary event, not a service-health event.

RECOVERY EVIDENCE REQUIRED BEFORE ANY NEXT PUSH
================================================

The rule states: "Recovery = 1 fully-observed push per fresh decision; new window needs decision after baseline."

A fully-observed push is one in which every per-push invariant is confirmed simultaneously:

  1. Preflight passes.
  2. Retired generations peak ≤ 4.
  3. Cleanup pause ≤ 100ms.
  4. Full health set returns to baseline.
  5. No rollback condition fires (consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, restart).

If the new window's first push fails any one of these — including cleanup >100ms — it is not fully observed and recovery is not established, regardless of how the other signals land. Recovery is binary on the full set, not partial-credit. A breach on any one invariant re-closes the window.

FRESH-DECISION BOUNDARY BEFORE ANY NEXT PUSH
=============================================

A new window is not a continuation of yesterday's. To open one:

  (a) Baseline must be re-established on the post-breach metrics-router state. "New window needs decision after baseline" means the owner decides only after seeing a clean baseline, not on the heels of the 103ms breach. The eventual 7-minute return-to-baseline from push 2 is a fact about yesterday's push, not a substitute for a deliberate current-state baseline observation taken as the precondition for the new decision.

  (b) The fresh decision must come from the primary owner. Owner map is unchanged: Alex is primary; Wes is backup-not-primary. Wes can halt on a breach (he did) and can report the result, but he cannot self-authorize a new window. An owner-led fresh decision from Alex is required before any next push.

  (c) Once Alex's decision opens the window, the first push in that new window is the recovery push and must be fully observed against all five invariants above before any further push is permitted inside the window.

Summary: 103ms is a cleanup breach that stops the window, not a rollback condition. No rollback required; service stays on the post-push state with health at baseline. Next push requires (i) a current clean baseline reading on metrics-router, (ii) Alex's owner-led fresh decision opening a new window, and (iii) a fully-observed first push inside that window. Wes alone cannot satisfy (ii), and a push that breaches any single invariant — including cleanup >100ms — does not satisfy (iii).

  optional, and stop the moment anything feels wrong.

  Attempt order, lowest risk first (one try each before moving on):

  1. Rubber band in the socket. Lay a flat rubber band across the hex
     recess, press the correct-size bit into it, and turn slowly with
     firm down-pressure. The rubber fills the stripped voids and can
     give the bit fresh purchase. If it slips, do not force — go to 2.

  2. Painter's tape in the socket. Same idea, thinner material. Fold a
     strip of tape onto itself 2-3x so it is stiff, lay it over the
     recess, press the bit in, and turn. Sometimes works where rubber
     does not, sometimes vice versa.

  3. Next-size-up hex bit, ONE size only. Press straight down with your
     palm and try a quarter-turn by hand. If the bit does not bite in
     the first 1/8 turn, stop. A larger bit that does not immediately
     engage will only flare the metal and crush the surrounding wood.

  4. Locking pliers clamped on the bit shaft (not in the socket). Clamp
     the pliers onto the hex bit about an inch above the screw head,
     then use the pliers as a short cheater bar to turn. Keeps the bit
     from popping out of the socket under load. Light, steady force.

  5. Flat-blade manual screwdriver wedged into one corner of the hex and
     turned like a pry. Last household option. Expect to deform the
     recess further; this is the last cheap try before bracing.

  Stop and brace if any of these happens:
  - the screw head deforms further or you feel metal flaring
  - the wood around it creaks, the panel flexes, or finish cracks
  - you have spent about 5 focused minutes across all attempts
  - any single attempt needs more force than a firm hand-turn

  Bracing plan, do this as soon as you decide to stop:
  - Wrap the outside of the joint with 3-4 rounds of painter's tape.
    Partly vibration insurance, mostly a bright visual flag.
  - Cut a cardboard L-brace: fold a piece of cardboard into a 4-6 inch
    L and tape it across the INSIDE corner where the side panel meets
    the frame. If the screw lets go in transit, the L holds the joint
    square.
  - Write "1 SCREW / GENTLE" on the tape in marker so it reads from
    outside.
  - Tell the mover in person: this corner is held by one screw, keep
    the piece upright, do not lay it on that side.

  Post-move extraction, no rush: a real extractor bit or a left-handed
  drill bit will pull this in under a minute on a workbench with the
  panel unclamped. Leave it for then.

Recommendation: start with the hallway shelf.

Comparison
                     Media wall   Hallway shelf   Delta
Second room          410 Mbps     386 Mbps        -24 (-6%)
Bedroom              365 Mbps     342 Mbps        -23 (-6%)
Kitchen               92 Mbps     228 Mbps       +136 (+148%)
Spread (max - min)   318 Mbps     158 Mbps        halved
Kitchen / peak        22%          59%            much better

The kitchen is the deciding number. 92 Mbps on the media wall is the kind of reading where one interior wall plus a fridge/microwave path is killing 5 GHz, and it leaves the room as a slow outlier - fine for a phone, rough for a video call or a streaming device. The hallway shelf more than doubles that and roughly halves the spread between your best and worst rooms, which is exactly the "even coverage" target.

The tradeoff
The media wall gives you ~6% higher peaks in the two rooms that already had a clear path to it. That's a small win on rooms that were already strong, paid for by leaving the kitchen well behind. The hallway shelf gives up that small peak in the well-served rooms to lift the weak room out of the borderline zone. Net: a slightly lower ceiling, a much higher floor.

Why this is the right starting point
- Both placements are temporary until furniture lands, so you don't yet know which room will be the heavy-use one. Starting from even coverage means you learn real usage patterns instead of discovering a weak spot after you've committed.
- The hallway shelf has nearby power and doesn't obstruct the hall, so it costs you nothing operationally to pick it.
- If a couple of weeks in the second room turns out to be the one that needs every Mbps (gaming console, work-from-home desk, big TV), swapping back to the media wall is a 5-minute move - the trade is reversible. The reverse move (discovering the kitchen is the bottleneck after the furniture is in) is the annoying one.

So: hallway shelf now, revisit once you know which room actually carries the load.

Recommendation: certified check.

Reasoning:

1. The fee-versus-risk trade only matters if the check option carries real closeout risk. It doesn't here. You can obtain the check Thursday, so it is in hand before Friday's unload begins. Handover at completion is instantaneous — no Friday-morning scramble, no terminal, no network, no processor. The "payment problem delaying closeout" scenario you want to hedge against effectively cannot happen with a pre-obtained certified check.

2. The card's only genuine advantage over a check you already hold is speed of confirmation, and a signed completion receipt from the crew lead covers that on the check path too (per your note).

3. $55.80 is a meaningful cost — ~3% of $1,860 — and you're paying it purely to insure against a risk you've already neutralized on the check path.

4. Caveat: keep the check secure between Thursday and Friday (don't leave it in a car, etc.). That's the residual risk and it's routine.

Bottom line: the card fee buys you protection against a problem you don't have. Take the check.

One small thing worth doing Thursday: confirm with the mover's office that the certified check is still acceptable and made out to the exact payee name on the contract — last-minute surprises on payee name are the one way a perfectly good check can stall closeout.

COOLER-PACKING AND TRANSPORT PLAN
Friday Park Slope load-out, separate late-morning food trip to South Slope

UP-FRONT RECOMMENDATION

Take the separate late-morning food trip to South Slope. The cooler stays in
your car (AC, cabin shade) for maybe 30-60 minutes, then goes straight into
the fridge. The Park Slope truck route is slower, often sits in sun, and
gives you no guarantee of shade or AC for the cooler. The food trip is the
lower-risk path.

If you ever do send the cooler on the truck instead: keep it in the cab,
not the truck bed. A late-September NYC truck bed in sun can hit 120 F+.
Cab stays cooler and the cooler is in your line of sight.

PRE-COOL THE NIGHT BEFORE (Thursday)

  - Freeze the 4 packs solid. 12+ hours; they should be rock hard, not
    slushy.
  - Pre-chill the empty cooler: drop the 4 packs inside, close the lid,
    leave overnight in the coldest spot you have (garage floor near the
    freezer, or a cold basement).
  - Pre-chill the food containers in the fridge on the coldest shelf
    (back, bottom). Move milk and yogurt to the back overnight.
  - Wash and thoroughly dry the spinach. Wet greens wilt and spoil fastest.
    Wrap loosely in a dry paper towel inside a partially closed bag.

FRIDAY MORNING — PACK ORDER

Pack from coldest and most-perishable to least. Bottom of the cooler
listed first.

  1. Two of the four frozen packs on the bottom, one on each long side.
  2. Frozen berries — packed tight on the bottom; they double as cold mass.
  3. Cooked lentils (both portions) — already-cooked food spoils fastest.
     Keep sealed tight so juices can't migrate.
  4. Unopened milk — coldest dairy first, in its carton.
  5. Yogurt.
  6. Eggs — keep in the original carton (cushions them and blocks light).
  7. Spinach — bag with the paper towel, on top so it isn't crushed.
  8. Remaining frozen packs — tucked along the top and one end.
  9. Condiments — only put in the cooler if they've been opened recently
     or the label says "refrigerate after opening." Most shelf-stable
     condiments (mustard, many hot sauces, soy sauce, ketchup packets,
     sealed jams) are fine at ambient for a day.

Slide the thermometer probe into the middle of the cooler, somewhere
between the lentils and the milk. Close the lid.

TARGET TEMPERATURE

  - 32-40 F (0-4 C) is the safe zone.
  - USDA rule: perishables in the danger zone (40-140 F) for less than
    2 hours total is fine; above 90 F ambient, cut that to 1 hour.
  - If the cooler reads above 40 F at any point, eat the most perishable
    items (lentils, then spinach, then dairy) that night, not the next
    day. When in doubt, throw it out for the cooked lentils specifically,
    since cooked starches in the danger zone are the highest-risk item in
    your cooler.

TRANSPORT RULES

  - Keep cooler in the AC cabin, not the trunk. Trunks in late-September
    NYC sun can hit 130 F+.
  - Open the cooler only when you have to.
  - Direct trip to South Slope, straight into the fridge. If fridge space
    is tight, the frozen berries refreeze immediately; lentils go on the
    coldest shelf.

EAT-BY ORDER (minimizes waste across the first week)

  - Day 1-2: cooked lentils. Already-cooked food has the shortest window
    (USDA: 3-4 days from cook date).
  - Day 1-3: spinach. Wilts fastest.
  - Day 1-7+: yogurt, milk, eggs. Standard fridge life.
  - Day 1-2 weeks: berries. Refreeze if you won't use them in 2 days.
  - Flexible: condiments.

FIRST-NIGHT MEAL

Lentils + wilted spinach + fried egg, with yogurt and berries on the side.

  - Warm one portion of lentils in a small pot with a splash of water.
    Salt, pepper, any warm spice you have (cumin, smoked paprika, or
    garam masala all work).
  - In a separate pan, sauté a big handful of spinach with a little oil
    or butter until just wilted, 2-3 minutes. Salt.
  - Fry an egg in the same pan (or a fresh pan) — runny yolk is fine, the
    rest of the plate is already cooked.
  - Plate: lentils, spinach on top, fried egg on top of that.
  - Side: a few spoonfuls of cold yogurt and a small bowl of berries.

Why this works:
  - Uses the perishables with the shortest remaining life (lentils and
    spinach) first.
  - One pot, one pan. Minimal cleanup on moving night.
  - Hot food after a load-out; cold yogurt and berries as a refresher.
  - Eggs fully cooked, lentils reheated to steaming — safe even if the

No panting/trembling/GI signs/escape attempt/treat refusal. That's a well-adjusted dog doing a first-night territory scan in a new building, not a dog in distress. The plan below is mostly about not accidentally teaching him that the door is the interesting spot.

TONIGHT'S PLAN

- Move the bed off the door's sightline if it isn't already. Anchor it against an interior wall or in a corner where he can see the room but the entry isn't the main view. Same familiar bed, new geography; reduces the "post" feel.

- Pre-bed decompression, not pre-bed arousal. A 10-15 min sniffy walk or low-energy scatter-feeding 1-2 hours before sleep. Avoid rough play or training right at bedtime — you want his nervous system coming down, not going up.

- Frozen toppl / stuffed Kong at lights-out. Licking and chewing are physiologically incompatible with door-patrol. Wet food + kibble + a splash of bone broth, frozen. Give it on the bed, not near the door.

- Mask the hallway. Fan on medium or a white-noise machine. NYC building sounds (elevator chime, neighbor doors, radiator ticks) lose their novelty when they're not the loudest thing in the room. This is the single biggest helper for apartment dogs on night 1.

- Cover any peephole / sidelight / door window. Visual triggers are what pull him back to the door. Remove the channel and the patrol impulse drops on its own.

- When he barks at a hallway sound: do not go to the door, do not verbally soothe, do not look at him at the door. Wait for the bark-burst to end (his are already short, ~3, which is good). After one beat of quiet, calmly go sit by the bed yourself — exactly what you did tonight. You're reinforcing "quiet → bed → you" without making the door part of the loop.

- When he returns to the bed on his own (especially after a door check), drop one small treat quietly on the bed. No fanfare. You're paying the choice, not the door-check.

- One normal last potty trip, then lights low, then you do your actual bedtime. Don't get up repeatedly to "let him check the hall" or reassure him mid-sleep. Repeated rising teaches restless → door opens → you appear.

- Keep your own energy flat near the door: low voices, no phone calls in the hallway, no excited comings-and-goings for the first few nights.

Expect 20-40 minutes of intermittent alert-then-settle on night 1, roughly halving by night 3-4. What you're describing is the lower end of that range.

WHAT WOULD WARRANT A CALL TO HIS VET

Behavior changes (escalation over nights, not persistence on night 1):
- Barking that grows in frequency or duration across several nights instead of decreasing
- Panting at rest that doesn't resolve once he settles (and isn't heat/exercise related)
- Trembling or shaking when not cold
- Refusing food or water for more than 24 hours
- Repeated, focused attempts to escape — scratching the door, pawing the frame, chewing the threshold
- Pacing that won't stop, or inability to settle for stretches beyond 1-2 hours despite the plan above
- Hiding and refusing to come out, or a sudden withdrawal from you (he currently seeks you out — that's the anchor, watch for the opposite)
- Growling, snapping, or freezing when anyone approaches the door

Physical signs:
- Vomiting, especially more than once or with bile/blood
- Diarrhea, especially bloody, black, or with straining
- Any house-soaking urination or straining to pee (could be stress cystitis, could be a UTI — both worth a same-day call)
- Excessive drooling or lip-licking paired with restlessness
- Lethargy beyond normal sleepy settling — won't get up for you, won't take a high-value treat
- Limping, stiffness, or flinching when lifted or touched
- Coughing, sneezing, or nasal discharge
- Pale gums, rapid breathing at rest, or resting respiratory rate you can count consistently above ~30/min while he's sleeping

Recommendation, least disruptive first:

1. SHADE (primary, do this first). During 2:30–4:00 PM on sunny days, lower the existing light-filtering shade on the side where the afternoon sun is hitting. Light-filtering shades cut direct beam glare while keeping the view, so the room still gets daylight elsewhere. No layout change, fully reversible, costs nothing. If a hotspot still lands on the right monitor, slip a sheet of paper or cardstock against the window-side bezel as a quick monitor hood.

2. RIGHT-MONITOR ANGLE (secondary). Rotate the right monitor on its stand so its right edge angles slightly away from the window and its left edge swings toward the center. A 5–10° horizontal yaw is enough — the screen normal no longer points into the window's reflection path, so the specular highlight slides off your line of sight. Most stands allow this with no tools and no height change. Leave the left monitor where it is.

3. LAMP REPOSITION (tertiary, for comfort). Move the movable lamp to sit just behind and slightly toward the window-side of the right monitor. Switch it on during the glare window. The added ambient behind the screen narrows the brightness gap between window and monitor, which is what actually drives eye fatigue even after the on-screen glare is gone.

4. DESK ROTATION (only if 1–3 don't fully fix it). Rotate the desk 5–10° clockwise — right side angles away from the window, left side angles toward the interior wall. You keep the interior-wall anchor and the unobstructed window; only the Ethernet run shifts a few inches along the baseboard. Test before committing to the new position.

Things to avoid:
- Anything in front of the window: tall plants, monitor arms reaching past the sill, a freestanding screen. The shade handles the sun; the room needs the daylight everywhere else.
- Tilting the right monitor vertically (top edge back). That won't redirect a roughly horizontal reflection from a side window — you want the horizontal yaw described above.

Monday check: sit down at 2:30 next week, spend five minutes on each monitor, confirm the right side is glare-free. If the hotspot persists, escalate to step 4.

The pattern you describe — bilateral, symmetric, worse with stairs, better with warmth, no focal findings — fits delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) from the move rather than an injury. Devika's call to stop lifting is the right one. Plan below is conservative and assumes that's what it is.

EVENING RECOVERY PLAN
- No more lifting. Done for the day.
- Keep moving gently: short easy walk, or a few slow trips up and down one flight of stairs, then stop. Light motion reduces next-day stiffness; full bed rest makes it worse.
- Hydrate steadily through the evening, normal dinner with protein (repair substrate).
- Heat is fine — the warm shower worked because it relaxes tight muscle and increases local flow. A heating pad on shoulders or thighs, 15-20 min on/off, is equivalent.
- Gentle stretching only: slow, no bouncing, hold to a mild pull — quad, hamstring, hip flexor, chest/shoulder. Stop at any sharp sensation.
- Pain relief: acetaminophen first (up to ~3 g/day for an adult, less if any liver issue). NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) help but can irritate stomach/kidneys after heavy exertion and may blunt recovery — fine for a dose or two if you need it, but acetaminophen is the safer default for tonight.
- Sleep 7-9 h. Pillow under/between knees if thighs are tight; pillow under the armpit if shoulders are pulling.
- Avoid: more lifting, alcohol (dehydration + worse sleep), aggressive deep-tissue massage tonight (can flare DOMS).

SUNDAY PICKUP SOCCER
Default recommendation: skip or play significantly modified — walking/jogging only, no sprints, no hard cuts, no max-effort shooting. Goalest, or half-field at half speed. If you go, a 10-15 min warm-up (easy jog + dynamic mobility) and stop at the first sharp pull.

If you want a morning self-check before deciding:
- Stairs feel normal
- A bodyweight squat and a lunge are pain-free and full-depth
- A 5-minute light jog doesn't bring the soreness back

If all three are yes, light play is reasonable but still no all-out sprinting. If any is no, walk-jog only or skip. DOMS from the move should be on the downslope by Sunday morning, but "should be" isn't "is" — re-injury on the first sprint back is the actual risk here.

WARNING SIGNS — WHEN TO GET EVALUATED
ER tonight or tomorrow:
- Dark, tea- or cola-colored urine, or noticeably decreased urine output — possible rhabdomyolysis after heavy exertion; this is the one I'd watch for most carefully given how sore you are.
- Sudden severe focal pain, especially in the calf or thigh, with swelling, warmth, or redness — concern for DVT or muscle tear.
- Chest pain, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, coughing blood — possible pulmonary embolism; 911.
- A "pop" you heard or felt, then sharp pain and weakness in one specific muscle — likely a partial tear.
- Numbness, tingling, or pain radiating down an arm or leg — nerve, not DOMS.
- A focal area that's hot, very tight, and increasingly painful, especially worse with stretch — possible compartment syndrome.
- Fever, chills, or a hot red streak on a limb.

Call Devika / primary care / urgent care within 24 h:
- Soreness still worsening after 3-4 days, or not substantially better by day 5-7.
- Asymmetric weakness (one shoulder or one thigh clearly weaker than the other).
- Joint swelling, locking, or inability to bear weight on a leg.
- Expanding bruise or a hard lump in a muscle.

Devika is in the best position to triage anything borderline tonight, and the picture you've described doesn't sound like any of the above — these are the pre-cautions to know, not the predictions. Reassess the soccer call in the morning against the self-check.

Concrete shape for the next couple of weeks:

- Timing: if you want truck noise in his life at all, do it at low-traffic times (mid-morning, after the school rush, before evening deliveries). Same block, fewer variables.

Most likely the freezing fades on its own once he has a few weeks of uneventful walks as the baseline. If it doesn't loosen up in 3–4 weeks, that's the point where a short round of structured desensitization (recorded truck sound at low volume, paired with food, gradual increase) is worth adding — but that's a later decision, not this week.

Subject: Re: sample import (1,237 points) — do not rewrite `qa` to `staging`

Product Engineering,

The proposal to silently rewrite `qa` → `staging` so those 17 points produce series is a no-go. It would fabricate a deployment classification at ingest and publish it downstream as if the producer had asserted it. We don't classify on the producer's behalf, especially into a higher-stakes tier than the source label warranted.

Contract (unchanged):

  - Allowed environment values are `prod`, `staging`, `dev`. Mixed-case inputs are normalized on accept (e.g. `Prod`, `STAGING`, `DeV` → canonical).
  - If the producer has no environment to report, the label is omitted. Omission is a first-class signal, not a missing field to be guessed.
  - `qa` is not in the allowed set. Points carrying `qa` are rejected by the collector before publication. No series is created, no rewrite is attempted.

For your sample import:

  - 1,237 total → 1,220 accepted (mixed-case-normalized or unlabeled), 17 rejected (`qa`).
  - The 17 rejections are correct behavior, not a defect. Re-pointing them at `staging` would manufacture staging traffic that does not exist.

What producers must do instead:

  - Send `prod`, `staging`, or `dev` (any case) when one of those is the true environment.
  - Omit the label entirely when none of the three applies (e.g. ephemeral QA, local dev, ad-hoc investigation).
  - Do not introduce new label values to bypass validation — `qa` included — without a contract change.

If we genuinely need `qa` data in the platform, that is a contract question: extend the allowed set intentionally, with a documented purpose and owner, rather than papering over it in the ingest path. Happy to take that discussion in a follow-up if there is real demand.

Top-line: yes, `Not reported` stays presentation-only. The CASE is a display transform on a clearly renamed column, the underlying NULL semantics in the source are untouched, and no write-back or new metric is introduced. No correction is needed for the query itself.

Contract point-by-point:

  1. Allowed values preserved.
     The WHERE clause restricts `deployment_environment` to `('prod', 'staging', 'dev')` OR `IS NULL`. The ELSE branch of the CASE passes the original label through unchanged when it is one of those three values. No new value is introduced into the `deployment_environment` label set; `Not reported` exists only inside the derived column.

  2. Missing input still means the label is absent.
     The CASE only renames NULL for the legend column. In `deployment_request_rate`, rows with missing `deployment_environment` are still rows with NULL `deployment_environment`. The transform does not promote NULL into a real label — the source table's contract is untouched. Any join, alert, or export that reads the source directly still sees NULL where input was missing.

  3. Display text is not written back, not queried as a metric, not used by alerts.
     - Write-back: this is a SELECT. Nothing is inserted or updated.
     - Metric value: the queried metric is `request_rate`. `environment_legend` is a string label column, not a measurement; the CASE does not alter the metric value at all.
     - Alerts: alerts would have to be configured separately against this query's output. The query gives them nothing to grab onto as a metric — the only numeric column is `request_rate`, and the only string column is `environment_legend`, which is clearly named as a legend.

Why the alias carries the load:

  Naming the CASE output `environment_legend` (not `deployment_environment`) is what makes the presentation-only nature enforceable by inspection. If it had been aliased back to `deployment_environment`, downstream tools could plausibly treat `Not reported` as a fourth label value. The current alias prevents that conflation at the schema-of-output level, which is the right place to enforce it.

Things to verify outside the query (not corrections to the query, just confirmation):

  - Alerts on request rate are configured against the source table with `deployment_environment IS NULL` for the missing-input case, not against this dashboard's output or `environment_legend`.
  - Any export of this dashboard carries the `environment_legend` string, which is expected — but no consumer re-ingests that string as a label.
  - If the dashboard is later wired into automated pipelines, the column name `environment_legend` (not `deployment_environment`) is what those pipelines should key off of.

Optional hardening (not required, just nice-to-have):

  - Add a one-line SQL comment above the CASE: `/* environment_legend is presentation-only; do not persist, alert on, or join as deployment_environment. */`. Cheap insurance against future edits that might rename the column or add an INSERT path.
  - If Product Eng wants belt-and-suspenders, the alias could be tightened to `deployment_environment_legend` to mirror the source column name and make the relationship obvious. This is a naming preference, not a contract fix.

Right now, this is a low-battery chirp, not an active alarm. The "LOW BATTERY" display, the once-per-minute cadence, the absence of symptoms in both of you, and the separate plug-in CO monitor reading zero all point the same way. You have today to fix it on your schedule — but a chirping unit is not protecting you, so handle it today rather than ignoring it for a week.

1. Immediate safe response

  a. Get a replacement. If the unit has a battery door, a standard 9V (or AA, per the label inside the door) is fine. If it is a sealed 10-year lithium model with no battery door, the whole alarm is replaced, not the battery — don't try to pry it open.
  b. Stand on a stable step stool, twist the alarm off its mount, swap the battery or the unit, reinstall.
  c. Press and hold TEST for the full cycle (5–10 seconds) to confirm it sounds the alarm pattern end-to-end.
  d. Read the manufacture date on the back. Replace combo units on the schedule printed on that sticker — typically 10 years from manufacture for the smoke side and 5–7 years for the CO sensor side of a combo unit. If it's past the date, what you have is an end-of-life chirp, not a low-battery chirp, and the fix is a new unit, not a new battery.

2. How to tell a low-battery chirp apart from an active alarm

  a. Low-battery / end-of-life chirp: one short beep about every 30 to 60 seconds, no voice, no rapid flashing, display reads LOW BATTERY or END OF LIFE or ERR. Does not speed up, does not run in groups.
  b. Active smoke alarm (fire): three beeps in rapid succession, pause, three beeps, pause, repeating. Voice models say "Fire!" continuously. Red LED flashes in sync.
  c. Active CO alarm: four beeps in rapid succession, pause, four beeps, pause, repeating. Voice models say "Warning! Carbon Monoxide!" continuously. Many units show a ppm number on the display.
  d. Test or hush mode: a single short beep or a brief run of the alarm pattern after you pressed TEST or HUSH — that's normal and stops on its own.

3. When to leave or call 911 instead of troubleshooting

  Stop troubleshooting and get out — Devika, Kibo, you — then call 911 from outside or a neighbor's, if any of these is true:

  a. The unit switches from a single chirp to the three-beep or four-beep pattern, or starts a voice announcement of "Fire" or "Carbon Monoxide."
  b. Anyone in the apartment develops headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, or flu-like symptoms, especially if more than one person feels it at once. CO exposure often looks like the flu and can incapacitate before you realize what's happening.
  c. Your plug-in CO monitor shows anything above ~35 ppm sustained or any reading above 70 ppm, even if the combo unit is still just chirping. Trust the CO reading, not the silence of the wired unit.
  d. You smell smoke, gas, or vehicle exhaust pooling in the hallway. In a South Slope row house, exhaust from a neighbor's attached garage or a car idling in an attached garage can back up into shared space — that is a real risk the moment cold weather starts and heaters come on.
  e. The alarm will not stop after a fresh battery, a reset, and a TEST, or you cannot reach it safely to silence it.

A few notes specific to your situation:

  The "no symptoms + plug-in monitor at zero" picture is reassuring but is not proof of nothing. Plug-in monitors are a second line of defense, not the primary sensor — do the battery swap regardless.

  South Slope row-house geometry means CO from an attached garage, a basement furnace, or a neighbor's appliance can migrate between units. The first cold night when you fire up a gas oven, space heater, or the building's heating for the season is the higher-risk moment for a real CO event — not tonight.

  If you confirm the manufacture date on the back is recent and the unit is a sealed 10-year model, the chirp means end of life or a defective unit — file the warranty if it's a known brand rather than buying a replacement out of pocket. Kidde, First Alert, and BRK all have straightforward warranty claim flows.

One-line summary: chirp once a minute, "LOW BATTERY" on the display, no symptoms, separate monitor at zero → swap the battery (or replace the unit) today; any switch to rapid repeated beeps, any symptoms, or any sustained CO reading on the plug-in monitor is a real emergency — leave first, call 911 second.

First-pass interpretation

The fingerprint is single-client, large-payload-scoped — not system-wide:

- Error rate flat (0.18% vs 0.17%): not a throwing/panicking code path; just slow. No correctness blast radius.
- Zero duplicate IDs, zero retries, zero accepted/rejected accounting gap: rules out client retry doubling, server double-ack, and sharded-ack inconsistency. This is a latency story, not a counting story.
- Other client classes within 7% of baseline: the regression is scoped to one identifier's traffic, not the fleet.
- 91% of >8k requests come from that one identifier: the tail is large in absolute terms because the payloads are big AND that client supplies most of them.
- Overall p99 is being pulled up by this client's tail; the unaffected fleet sits near baseline.

Net read: client-side change in batch sizing, or a per-client processing path (slow tenant schema, dedicated shard/route, upstream aggregator that slowed them). A general ingest-edge regression is unlikely on this fingerprint alone — those typically move multiple clients AND the error rate.

Smallest evidence request

A 2x2 cross-cut on p99 latency:

  rows:    affected client | other clients (aggregate)
  cols:    <8k points      | >=8k points
  window:  alert (since 08:31) vs. pre-08:31 baseline

The single decisive cell is OTHER CLIENTS in the >=8k BAND during the alert window. Your 7% baseline check is for other-client classes overall, not their >=8k subset — if other clients barely send >=8k traffic, that 7% figure does not actually rule out a regression in the large-batch code path. That one cell is what cleanly separates the two hypotheses.

Decision tree on the result

- Other >=8k normal AND affected <8k normal
    → oversized-client-batch change. Confirm by checking that client's batch-size distribution since ~08:00 (median points/request, p95 points/request, request count). Likely cause: client batching change, new tenant from that client with a different shape, or upstream cadence change.

- Other >=8k elevated (comparable to or worse than affected client)
    → general ingest-edge regression in the large-batch path. Then look at per-stage latency, queue depth, GC, CPU, and recent PRs/config touching the large-batch handler. Affected client was just the loudest because they send the most >=8k traffic.

- Other >=8k normal BUT affected <8k also elevated
    → not a batch-size story; it's a per-client route/schema/config story. Look at per-route and per-tenant latency plus any recent config diffs scoped to that client identifier.

Action posture

No rollback, no permanent guardrail — fingerprint doesn't support either yet, and a 91% concentration in one identifier is a strong prior for client-side. Get the cross-cut, then decide. HOLDING SEQUENCE — START NOW (~7:06 PM)

1. Cool the rice, fast.

   - Spinach: cold. Wash and spin-dry now if you want; otherwise wash at finish.
   - Yogurt: fridge. Whisk with a pinch of salt and a small squeeze of lemon right before plating; keep lidded in the fridge.
   - Lemon: counter is fine.

3. A 10-minute head start (~10:00 PM).

TEN-MINUTE FINISH (starts ~10:05 PM)

Pan, medium-high, glug of olive oil.

  0:00 — Wilt the spinach with a pinch of salt, 60-90 sec. Push to the side or pull it out into a bowl.
  0:02 — Lentils in, splash of water (1-2 Tbsp), warm through, 90 sec.
  0:03 — Rice in. Break up clumps with the spatula. Splash another Tbsp of water. Press flat, cover, 60 sec — the steam rehydrates and heats the rice evenly without drying it out.
  0:04 — Uncover, toss, taste for salt.
  0:05 — Plate. Big squeeze of lemon over everything. Spoon of yogurt on top. Black pepper if you have it.

- Rice went danger-zone → fridge within ~30-45 min of now, well inside the 2-hour cooling window.
- Reheating to steaming hot (above 165°F) at the end handles any vegetative bacteria.
- Yogurt and spinach never left the cold chain.

QUICK SNIFF CHECK AT THE END

WEEKEND CONTAINMENT (bounded, reversible)

Primary path: have PE ask the client to revert max_batch_points to 1000 and flush_interval_seconds to 1. Smallest change, restores prior SLO, requires no ingest-edge action. Set a named deadline — if no revert by 12:00 Sunday, escalate to backup.

  - config-loader change, not a deploy — house rule (no prod deploys Fri PM/weekend) is preserved
  - Nadia's config-loader supports reload; reject-on-bad-config leaves active cfg + watcher untouched, so a misconfigured cap is safe
  - tenant-scoped if the loader supports per-tenant overrides; otherwise broad cap with documented impact list

Containment must NOT:
  - change retention, indexing, storage, or queue topology
  - introduce new code paths

Watch while contained:

  - per-tenant ingest rate (look for the affected client's traffic reshaping)
  - queue depth and worker saturation (catch any shared-resource exposure)
Page Alex on any deviation from baseline while contained.

EVIDENCE BEFORE PERMANENT GUARDRAIL

The decision is between (a) PE-driven client-side guidance, (b) hard server-side cap in ingest-edge, (c) do nothing. Gather these before picking:

1. Latency-vs-batch-size curve. Replay at 1000, 2500, 5000, 7500, 10000 points. Linear → cap is well-defined; super-linear above a knee → that knee is the natural cap.
2. Confounder check. Replay at 10000 points with flush_interval=1s vs 10s. The client changed both knobs in one shot — isolate which one drives the p99. Guardrail must cover both axes if both matter.
3. Multi-tenant exposure. Compare other tenants' p99 in the 08:30-09:30 window vs their week baseline. If neighbors were affected, the case for a server-side cap is strong (noisy-neighbor defense). If only this client suffered, PE guidance is sufficient.
4. Internal saturation. Queue depth, GC pause, worker pool utilization during the window. Bounded systems fail fast — tail-latency stretching without saturation means the curve is the story; saturation means we had real shared risk.
5. Legitimate-use ceiling. 99th percentile of max_batch_points across all tenants in the last 30 days. A cap should sit comfortably above legitimate use (e.g., 2x p99) and below the failure knee.
6. Client motivation. PE asks: why did they change it? Throughput target, cost, backpressure? Their reason determines whether they'll accept a cap or push back. PE owns this conversation; we don't guess.
7. Production accounting check. Controlled replay showed gap=0, dup=0. Confirm the live window showed the same at the moment of the change and the recovery. Any non-zero real-world reading escalates severity.
8. Population check. How many other clients run this high? If only this outlier, guidance; if several, pattern → cap.
9. Downstream propagation. Did the p99 surface in customer-facing API latency, downstream consumer lag, or shard-keeper pressure? Cross-service exposure changes who else signs off.
10. Incident cost. Hours of elevated p99, SLO breach minutes, support tickets, on-call pages. That is the engineering budget for building the guardrail.

DECISION RULE

  - curve well-behaved AND multi-tenant exposure → server-side cap in ingest-edge, config-loader path, promoted from the weekend safety net
  - curve well-behaved AND no multi-tenant exposure AND single client → PE-driven guidance + ingest-edge runbook entry noting the pattern; no code change
  - curve not predictable → keep incident open past Monday, gather more data, do not ship a guardrail yet; revisit after one more week of observations

PRE-CHECKS (before driving any fastener)
  Verify the replacement connector matches: same depth, same orientation, seats flush in the pocket without forcing. A proud connector racks the panel as the case goes together.
  Dry-fit the repaired joint by hand first — start the dowels/connector, confirm the seam closes with no daylight at the edge, then take it apart before any glue/final drive. This is your chance to catch a misaligned hole while panels are flat.
  Lay everything out on carpet or a blanket. Tall panels stay flat until step 4.
  Have a 90° square, a straightedge, and a tape on hand for the checks below.

REASSEMBLY ORDER (panels flat until the case is a U)
  1. Bottom panel + one side panel, both flat on the floor. Drive the connector with both panels horizontal — a side panel can't twist if it's lying down.
  2. Second side panel onto the bottom, same flat setup. You now have a U-shaped base with the bottom shelf pinned between the two sides.
  3. Square the base before adding height. Measure both diagonals of the bottom rectangle; they must match within 1–2 mm. If they don't, loosen the bottom connectors, re-seat, re-tighten. Do not proceed out-of-square.
  4. Stand the assembly upright (helper if the sides are tall). Add the top panel and any fixed mid-shelves. Square the inside corner at each new seam before driving its fastener.
  5. Back panel next. If it's thin hardboard or MDF, nail/staple it flush with the case squared on the diagonals. A back panel that's bowed or not seated flat will pull the case out of square over time. Re-measure front-face diagonals after the back is fastened.
  6. Adjustable shelves last — they aren't structural, so they go in once the case is true.

ALIGNMENT CHECKS AT EACH STAGE
  Inside corner: 90° square at top and bottom of every seam.
  Outside faces flush: edges of both panels coplanar at the outside. A stepped seam means a dowel is misaligned — back it out and re-seat before tightening.
  Connector line flush: no proud edges along the dowel/connector line. If the seam is flush but a dowel sits high, the hole drifted; address it now, not after glue sets.

STABILITY CHECKS BEFORE LOADING ANY SHELF
  Rock test: push each top corner diagonally toward the centerline. Zero movement at the repaired joint and at every other corner.
  Diagonals: front face and back face diagonals equal, top to bottom.
  Fastener audit: every connector snug, none over-driven (over-driving splits wood invisibly). Run a finger along each dowel line — no give, no soft wood.
  Floor check: case doesn't rock. If it does, shim the feet before loading — a rocking case multiplies stress on every joint every time a door is opened or the case is bumped.
  Anti-tip: if the case is taller than it is deep, attach a wall anchor now. Loaded shelves raise the center of gravity; a fully repaired joint doesn't make a tall case tip-proof.

NOTES SPECIFIC TO NOT TWISTING THE TALL SIDE
  Never use a tall side as a lever to seat a connector. If a connector won't start by hand, the hole is wrong — ream gently or adjust, don't muscle it.
  Drive fasteners in a star pattern across the case (bottom-left, top-right, bottom-right, top-left), not sequentially around one face. Sequential tightening racks the case.
  If the dowel holes took any stress during extraction, probe each with a finger. Any softness means the joint needs a glue-and-dowel rebuild, not just a connector swap.
  If the replacement connector differs from the rest of the case in depth or angle, the repaired joint will sit slightly proud or recessed even when "tight." Check seam flush before declaring it done.

One last flag: you said none of the dowel holes are loose, but verify the hole that held the stripped connector didn't get ovaled during extraction. If the wood around it crushes under a fingernail, that hole needs a glue-and-dowel fill before you reinstall the new connector — otherwise the new one will strip too.

The two numbers driving the call are your 50°F air reading and your 2h40m duration. Both put the interior above the 40°F (4°C) safety line for longer than the 2-hour window USDA uses for perishable food, and your instant-read food temperatures are above 40°F too — which is the more important number than the air display. The "nothing smells or looks off" check is not reliable: most pathogens and their toxins (Salmonella, Listeria, Staph aureus enterotoxin, Bacillus cereus emetic toxin) do not produce detectable odor or visual change at dangerous levels. Item-by-item below.

MILK (48°F) — DISCARD
Liquid dairy is high-water-activity, near-neutral pH, and an excellent bacterial growth medium. Clear discard under the 2-hour rule. Do not taste-test.

COOKED CHICKEN (49°F) — DISCARD
Poultry is the highest-risk category, and cooked poultry is riskier than raw: cooking has already selected for spore-formers and any post-cook contamination multiplies fast in the danger zone. Reheating will not neutralize heat-stable toxins (Staph enterotoxin, B. cereus emetic toxin) that may already have formed. Discard.

YOGURT (47°F) — DISCARD
Commercial yogurt's cultures and acidity offer some buffer but not enough to override the 2-hour rule at 47°F. Discard. (Strongly home-fermented, very high-acid styles are a marginal exception; standard grocery-store yogurt is not.)

EGGS (48°F) — DISCARD, with a caveat by type
  - Raw eggs in shell: discard. Interior is high-protein, neutral-pH; shells are not a reliable Listeria/Salmonella barrier once contents have warmed above 40°F for over two hours.
  - Hard-boiled eggs (peeled or in shell): discard — actually riskier than raw in shell, since cooking removes protective cuticle defenses and contamination has no competition.
If you have a large carton, the only borderline case is raw in-shell eggs that spent only a portion of the 2h40m above 40°F — but at a 48°F interior reading the safe call is still discard.

SEALED BLOCK OF HARD CHEESE (44°F) — KEEP
Hard cheese (cheddar, parmesan, aged gouda, gruyère, etc.) is low-water-activity, low-pH after aging, and dense — which is why yours read 44°F while everything else read 47–49°F. The sealed wax or vacuum layer adds protection. USDA and most food-safety guidance treat hard cheese as recoverable from a temperature-abuse event when soft cheeses must be discarded. When you use it, cut and inspect the outer ~1/4 inch; if anything looks or smells off in the cut face, discard that portion. Soft cheeses (brie, ricotta, cream cheese, fresh mozzarella, cottage cheese) would all be DISCARD in the same situation — you didn't list any, flagging in case they were in there.

RECOVERY STEPS
1. Close the door firmly and confirm the latch and gasket are fully engaged. Run your hand around the seal feeling for cool-air leaks — that confirms it's sealed now.
2. Don't open the fridge for the next 2–3 hours. Every door opening slows recovery; the compressor needs uninterrupted run time.
3. Place a thermometer in the middle of the fridge (not against a wall, not in the door) and wait until it reads 40°F or below before trusting it again for perishable storage. If you don't have a dedicated fridge thermometer, get one — door-ajar events are exactly the failure mode they catch, and built-in displays drift.
4. If after 4 hours of closed-door operation the interior still hasn't dropped below 40°F, there's a mechanical problem (often a failed door switch that kept the compressor off, or a degraded gasket). Stop using it for perishables and call service.
5. Wipe up any condensation or spills now with hot soapy water, or a dilute bleach solution (1 tbsp unscented liquid bleach per gallon of water). Warm interior + moisture = mold on surfaces even when no food is involved.
6. Once back at 40°F, restock with fresh perishables. Do not refreeze anything that thawed, and do not re-taste any of the discarded items above to "see if they're okay" — tasting contaminated food gives you no useful information.

ONE ADDITIONAL CHECK
If anyone in your household is pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly, or very young, apply the discard rules more strictly for that person. Listeria monocytogenes can grow at refrigerator temperatures and is especially dangerous to those groups; the 40°F threshold exists largely because of it.

Both options produce the four metrics you listed, but they differ in what they touch, what they measure, and what they leave unknown. Here's the comparison and recommendation.

Comparison

Option A — client cap at 2,000 + 1s flush
- Blast radius: production behavior change for the affected client class only. Their SDK ships the new behavior; they'll notice if anyone looks at client logs or dashboards.
- What you learn: how the system behaves when this client is hard-capped at 2,000. You do not learn how often they would have exceeded 2,000, 4,000, 8,000, etc. — the natural distribution is destroyed the moment you cap.
- What you don't learn: whether 2,000 is the right number, or whether their traffic pattern would have produced occasional larger bursts you'd want to allow.
- Reversal: client change. Rollback is a new SDK version; slow and visible.
- Evidence quality: low for choosing a cap; fine for validating that a 2k cap keeps things stable.

Option B — ingest-edge soft rejection above 8,000
- "Soft" is the swing term. Two interpretations:
  - Soft = observe only (count/log, no drop): zero customer impact, full natural distribution visible across every threshold you want to evaluate post-hoc. Reversible by removing the metric; no rollback needed.
  - Soft = reject with diagnostic (4xx, count, log): behavior change for any tenant >8k. You'd need to confirm no other tenant currently sends that size, or accept that you'll measure them too.
- Blast radius: ingest-edge only — service Alex owns, with established deploy/canary paths.
- What you learn: the actual size distribution from this client and anyone else over 8k, plus accepted/rejected accounting and duplicate-request behavior, all under real traffic.
- Reversal: config or single commit revert on ingest-edge.
- Evidence quality: high — you can pick the right threshold after seeing the data.

Recommendation

Option B, scoped as observation-only on ingest-edge (count + log above 8k, no drop). It's lower-risk on every axis that matters for decision-quality evidence:

1. Zero customer-visible behavior change. The affected client and any other tenants are unaffected. No SDK coordination, no escalation risk from a client noticing a cap appear.
2. The metric you actually need is the natural size distribution. Capping the client at 2,000 destroys that signal and forces you to pick a number before you have evidence. Observation at 8,000 lets you read the distribution and pick the right cap after the fact — at 2k, 4k, 6k, whatever the data supports.
3. Reversal is a config flip or commit revert, not a client release. If the metric turns out to be noisy or the deploy exposes a bug, you walk it back in minutes.
4. Deploy timing fits the constraint. Today is Thursday; ingest-edge can ship under your normal window and you have the full 7 days by Wednesday. Option A's client change has its own release cadence outside your control and you'd be negotiating that window, not running the experiment.
5. Consistent with established pattern. Your metrics-router already treats below-threshold slices as release-validation/annotation-only rather than enforcement — same idea, applied to batch size.

Caveats / things to confirm before recommending to the owner

- Pin down "soft" in writing. If the owner means actual rejection, Option B still wins on blast radius (one service vs. a client SDK) and evidence quality, but you should know whether any tenant currently sends >8k and whether a 4xx for that case is acceptable. My strong preference is observation-only; if the owner wants enforcement, push for the smallest possible reject window first.
- Make the 8k threshold a configuration value, not a hardcoded constant, so you can re-bin the data post-hoc without redeploying. The whole point of the experiment is to choose the threshold — don't bake one choice into the measurement.
- Decide the interim read cadence now. Owner chooses Monday; a Friday + Monday interim cut (even partial) gives you a sanity check before the full 7-day window closes.
- Verify the duplicate-request-identifier signal is captured at ingest-edge, not just at the client. If it's only visible client-side, Option A's instrumentation may be the only way to surface it for this specific client — in which case the experiment pair becomes "A for the dup-IDs, B for everything else," and that's a different recommendation. Worth checking with the owner before Monday.

Net: Option B as a pure measurement on ingest-edge is the lower-risk path to evidence the owner can actually decide from. Option A answers "does a 2k cap work" — useful, but it's not the question on the table.

Phishing indicators in the email:
  1.  Urgency + fear tactic: "expires in 30 minutes" combined with "Failure... will lock your account" is textbook pressure to bypass critical thinking. Legit IT almost never combines a 30-minute countdown with a credential-collection link.
  2.  Sender / link domain mismatch. The "From" address is @sphere-login.example but the link goes to sphere-access.example — two different lookalike domains for one supposedly trusted message. A real corporate notice uses one domain, the one you already trust.
  3.  Reserved ".example" TLD on both addresses (RFC 2606). This is the TLD reserved for documentation and tests. Either this is a drill, or the attacker used a domain that no real corporate system would use.
  4.  Generic greeting: "Dear Sphere User" — not your name, not your handle. Legitimate account-targeted mail is personalized.
  5.  Wrong mechanism. VPN certificates are renewed by the VPN client / MDM or your IT pushes a new profile. They are not "verified" by you typing credentials into a web form. Asking the user to "verify credentials" to renew a cert is the credential-harvesting pattern, not a cert workflow.
  6.  Vague, mismatched threat. A VPN cert expiring blocks VPN access — it does not "lock your account." The threat is wrong on the mechanics, which is a tell.
  7.  "ACTION REQUIRED" all-caps subject + countdown = pressure pattern. Combine with #1 and it's a social-engineering template.

  - Do not click the link.
  - Do not reply (it confirms the mailbox is live and monitored).
  - Do not forward to colleagues in a way they might auto-click; if you do forward, prefix the subject with "[EXTERNAL PHISH — DO NOT CLICK]".

Load = 2 × 90 W + 180 W + 12 W = 180 + 180 + 12 = 372 W. Rating = 1,875 W, so headroom ≈ 1,503 W (≈ 80% unused). At 120 V that draws ~3.1 A against a 15 A / 1,875 W rating — well within spec, and continuous-load headroom is fine.

Nothing you described is a red flag: no odor, discoloration, buzzing, sparking, intermittent power; cord/wall plug/strip body cool; brick warm but holdable (normal for a USB-C PD brick under load).

Unplug-now / call-electrician signs (any of these, stop using the strip and have it inspected):
- Smell of hot plastic, ozone, or melting; any discoloration, scorch marks, or melted/bubbled areas on the strip, plug, cord, or outlet
- Buzzing, crackling, hissing, or sparking from the strip, plug, or outlet
- Outlets feel loose (plug falls out or slides), or the plug face is warm/hot to the touch (a warm plug under heavy load is borderline; hot is not)
- Breaker trips or the strip's own breaker/switch keeps tripping or won't reset; any blown fuses on the strip
- Intermittent power, flickering, or a device that reboots when something else turns on (points to a failing connection, not the load)
- Cord that's cracked, frayed, pinched, or has exposed wire; plug prongs bent, loose, or discolored
- Strip is hot to the touch anywhere on its body (warm is OK, hot is not)
- Any sign of water, rust, or corrosion in/near the strip or outlet
- Lights dimming noticeably when the dock or monitors power up (suggests the circuit, not the strip, is marginal)

For the brick specifically: warm under load is expected; unplug and replace if it becomes too hot to hold, makes any noise, smells sweet/burnt, or the laptop stops charging reliably.

Practical note: a 15 A / 1,875 W strip is overkill for 372 W — the listed gear is fine. The actual risks to watch on a work-room strip are condition and connection quality, not aggregate watts.

The cadence (once per revolution) is the strongest clue. It tells you the issue is either (a) a high spot on a rotating part passing a fixed reference, or (b) a fixed reference (caliper/pad) offset to one side while the rotor's normal lateral runout swings through it. The diagnostic order below separates those without guesswork.

SAFE DIAGNOSTIC ORDER

1. Confirm rotor lateral runout, separately from rim true.
   - Spin the wheel slowly and watch the rotor pass through the caliper window. Look for a visible side-to-side weave as it crosses the pads.
   - Bring a finger (carefully, no pinch) just outside the rotor edge near the caliper. You should feel the rotor pass within ~1 mm of your finger with even clearance. A localized "push" at one spot = rotor high spot.
   - Better: dial-indicator or a phone-macro close-up. Spec for most road/mtb rotors is lateral runout <= 0.10-0.15 mm. Past ~0.2 mm you can usually both see and hear it.

2. Mark and localize the scrape.
   - Put a small piece of tape or a Sharpie dot on the rotor at the exact spot where the scrape is loudest (you'll hear/feel it).
   - Spin again. If the scrape moves with the dot (the dot returns to the same azimuth each rev) the rotor itself is the high spot -> bent or warped rotor.
   - If the scrape is constant regardless of rotor position, suspect caliper/pad.

3. Inspect pad wear pattern before touching anything else.
   - Pull the wheel (or just look past the pads with a flashlight and mirror).
   - Both pads should show a uniform wear band across the swept area. Tapered, heel-toe wear, or glazing on one pad only = caliper is offset, not the rotor.

4. Inspect rotor surface.
   - Look for a shiny blue/purple heat tint patch, a polished groove, oil smear, or pad transfer. A single shiny high spot that lines up with your tape mark confirms a bent rotor.
   - Run a clean gloved finger across the braking surface. Any oily/greasy feel = contamination; do not ride even if alignment is fixed (see criteria below).

5. Re-center the caliper (only after 1-4 point at misalignment, not a bent rotor).
   - Loosen the caliper mounting bolts just enough for the caliper body to float.
   - Squeeze and hold the brake lever firmly. This pushes the pistons out and recenters the caliper around the rotor.
   - While still holding the lever, retighten the caliper bolts evenly to spec.
   - Release the lever, spin the wheel. The scrape should be gone or symmetric (small tick from rotor runout is normal and safe).

6. Re-test under load, still off-bike.
   - With the wheel off the ground, spin and brake hard a few times. Listen/feel for pulsing through the lever and judder in the wheel. Pulsing under load means the rotor is bent beyond what braking can tolerate -> do not ride.

NOT-RIDE CRITERIA (any one of these means don't ride, fix first)

- Rotor lateral runout you can see (visible weave passing the pads), or measured > ~0.2 mm.
- A localized shiny high spot or heat-tint patch on the rotor that aligns with the scrape.
- Any oil/grease contamination on rotor or pads (including fingerprints you can't fully clean off). Clean with isopropyl alcohol or dedicated disc brake cleaner only; if a pad is saturated, replace it.
- Tapered or uneven pad wear, or pad material worn below the backing-plate indicator.
- Pulsing lever, judder, or vibration under braking even after caliper recentering.
- Any clicking, ticking, or scrape that does not change at all when you squeeze and release the brake lever while spinning (means a pad is dragging, not just the rotor's natural runout).
- Lever pulls to the bar, spongy feel, or any hydraulic seep at the caliper/lever/hose.

In your described situation (firm lever, no rim wobble, no visible damage, only ridden slowly) the most likely cause by a wide margin is a caliper that drifted out of center when the wheel went back in. Step 5 fixes that in under two minutes. If the scrape still tracks a single spot on the rotor after recentering, you have a bent rotor and should replace or true it (rotor truing is doable with a purpose-built tool but is the kind of job where "good enough" is not good enough for a front brake).
