Sounds like a textbook "flapper" — annoying, not dangerous. Here's how to handle it:

Wound care
- You've already done the right first step (clean with soap and water, pressure to stop bleeding).
- Once dry, apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment (bacitracin/Neosporin). Keeping it moist heals faster and with less scarring than letting it dry and scab.
- Cover with a non-stick pad (Telfa) or just a plain bandage. Change the dressing daily and any time it gets wet or dirty. Re-apply the ointment at each change.
- After 2–3 days, you can leave it uncovered and just moisturize (overnight heavy cream or Bag Balm). Air exposure at that point is fine.
- Avoid hydrogen peroxide or alcohol on an open wound — it damages new tissue and slows healing.

The loose skin flap
- Default: leave it. It acts as a natural biologic dressing; trimming it removes protection from the new skin underneath.
- Trim it only if it's clearly non-viable (gray/white, paper-thin, dangling, or snagging on everything). Use clean sharp scissors wiped with alcohol, and cut flush with the healthy skin edge — don't pull it off and don't cut into live tissue.
- If it's still pink/red and well-attached, just lay it back over the wound and bandage it down. It'll either re-adhere or fall off on its own.

Get it evaluated if you notice any of these
- Bleeding that doesn't stop after 10–15 minutes of firm, direct pressure
- Wound edges that gape and won't approximate (you can't close it with a Steri-Strip or tape)
- Increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaks up the finger, or fever
- Numbness, tingling, pallor, or bluish color in the fingertip (circulation or nerve concern)
- Visible deeper tissue — fat, tendon, or bone
- Wound that extends under the nail or into the joint crease
- Dirt/grit you can't rinse out
- Tetanus: if your booster is more than ~10 years old (5 years for dirty wounds), this is a reasonable reason to get one, especially since holds and skin contact in a gym can carry bacteria. Worth mentioning at your next visit.

None of those appear to apply based on what you described.

Return to climbing
- This isn't a "rest until perfect" injury — skin splits heal quickly if you protect them.
- Minimum: keep it covered and dry for 24–48 hours, no climbing.
- Then test: if the wound is closed (no open gap, no oozing, no pain on light pressure), you can climb with tape.
- Taping protocol that works for most climbers:
    - Cover the wound with a thin layer of ointment and a small non-stick pad or a piece of climbing tape placed adhesive-side-out so it doesn't stick to the wound.
    - Wrap the finger with 2–3 rounds of athletic or climbing tape, snug but not tight enough to cut circulation. Check capillary refill after taping.
    - Avoid full crimp on that finger for the first session back. Half-crimp or open-hand on the affected hand. Jug holds and big edges are fine.
    - Re-tape if the tape gets sweaty or shifts.
- If it reopens, oozes, or hurts under load: stop, clean, re-dress, give it another 2–3 days.
- Typical timeline for a 6mm superficial split: closed and climbable with tape in 3–5 days; fully remodeled (no scab, no tenderness) in 10–14 days. Don't try to "tough through" the first day back — if the flap tears again it's worse than the original.

Two small extra notes for next time
- A small tube of tincture of benzoin on the surrounding skin before taping makes tape stick dramatically better through sweat.
- Liquid skin bandages (New-Skin, Band-Aid Liquid) work well on flappers — they seal the wound and let you climb sooner without a bulky dressing.

Heal up and get back on the wall.

Here's the correct sequence. The order matters because each step depends on the one before it being solid — you don't want to anchor a leaning case, and you don't want to reload a case that isn't anchored.

1. Unload the lower shelves too. You can shim under a lightly-loaded case more safely and you get a clean read on whether the case itself is still truly square before adding any load. Pull books off in roughly the reverse order you'd put them back.

2. Find the slope direction. Put a level (or a marble) on top of the empty case and watch which way it drifts, then confirm by laying the level on the floor on each side. Mark the lowest corner — that's where shims go. In your setup the top leans away from the wall, which means the floor is lower on the room side, so the low feet are the ones farthest from the wall (gravity pulls the top toward the low side).

3. Shim the low side. With someone steadying the top, pry the low corner up just enough to slide a composite shim under the foot (or under the base if it's continuous). Tap it in flush, recheck the level on top both directions, and add a second shim if you need more lift. Avoid stacking more than two short shims — a single longer shim is stiffer. The goal is level on top AND plumb front-to-back; the 1/4" lean should be gone. If your floor is hardwood, stick a small rubber furniture pad under each shim so they don't creep under load.

4. Check stability before anchoring. Press each side at the top with flat hands — no rock, no rack, no shift. All four feet (or the full base) should sit firmly with no shim half-compressed. If anything moves, adjust shims and re-level before going further. The anti-tip strap is for tipping, not for steadying a wobbly case.

5. Locate a stud at the back-rail height. Run a stud finder along the wall behind where the top back rail of the case will sit, and mark the stud center. Drywall anchors won't hold a tipped bookcase — it has to be a stud. If the case's position doesn't line up with a stud, slide the case left or right until it does.

6. Install the anti-tip strap per the manufacturer's instructions — typically a lag screw into the stud and a smaller screw into the back rail. Snug, not over-torqued. For a tall unit, two straps (one near each end of the top rail) are safer than a single centered one.

7. Test the anchor. Push the top of the case forward with steady hand pressure. The case should not lift, tip, or shift at all.

8. Reload from the bottom up, heaviest books on the lowest shelves and lighter items higher. Don't fill the top shelf with anything you wouldn't want on a kid's head — and in your case, on Kibo's head. A startled dog (you've mentioned the skateboard/skate startle before) leaning into a tall case is exactly the failure mode the strap is there to prevent.

9. Final push test with the full load. Same as step 7, but now the case is loaded. If it passes, you're done.

What you described last cycle — three knocks at warm-up, then quiet, even heating, dry valve and floor, setpoint reached — fits the benign pattern most consistent with a steam system where steam pushes past pooled condensate at startup, then settles into steady flow. A few structured observations over the next 2–3 cycles will let you confirm it's staying benign without touching the building's valve.

OBSERVATIONS TO RECORD PER CYCLE

Use one note per cycle (phone note is fine). Don't touch the valve.

  1.  Cycle start time (when the thermostat first calls or you first hear it begin to warm).
  2.  Opening noises — count and type:
        -   sharp knocks (one, two, or three)
        -   ticks or pings
        -   hissing (note which end of the radiator)
        -   gurgling
  3.  When each noise stops (10 seconds? 2 minutes? 5 minutes? persists?).
  4.  Heat-up pattern — even, or does one end clearly lead?
  5.  Which end is the supply valve (where the pipe enters) and which is the air vent (the small fitting, often a brass cylinder or cap, at the opposite end)?
  6.  Air vent behavior — brief hiss at start that stops once the radiator is hot, or continuous?
  7.  Time from cycle start to room reaching thermostat setpoint.
  8.  Steady-state — any ticking, creaking, or knocking that continues past the first few minutes.
  9.  Cool-down — any ticks as the metal contracts. Note yes/no and type.
  10. End-of-cycle damp check — run a finger or piece of toilet paper along the valve stem, each pipe joint, the floor directly under the radiator, and along the visible pipe run. Any dampness, even slight, record the spot.
  11. Smell — toasty/burning-dust (normal first 1–2 cycles of the season), metallic, sweet (ethylene glycol), or sulfur/rotten-egg (gas).

WHAT HARMLESS EXPANSION NOISE CAN SOUND LIKE

  Single tick or two the instant heat first arrives.
  Cast iron sections and supply pipes expand faster than wood brackets and floorboards. The bracket clip at the radiator's feet, or the pipe where it passes through a hole in the floor or wall, ticks as it slips against the wood. Stops once temperatures equalize.

  Two or three sharp knocks at the moment steam first enters a cool radiator.
  The most likely explanation for what you heard. Steam pushes past condensate pooled from the previous cycle, the slug shifts and knocks against internal baffles or section walls, then flow steadies. Common in one-pipe steam systems; not a fault.

  Brief hiss from the fitting at the FAR end of the radiator from the supply valve.
  That's the air vent doing its job — releasing air as steam enters, then closing once steam reaches it. Short hiss (a few minutes) is correct operation, not a leak.

  Slow creak from the floor or wall near the radiator.
  Building structure expanding as the riser in the wall heats. Irregular, sounds like wood moving.

  Soft gurgle for the first minute or two of a steam cycle.
  Air finishing its escape. Different from continuous gurgling.

  Burning-dust smell on the first 1–2 cycles of the season.
  Dust on the fins burns off. Toasty, not electrical or chemical. Goes away after a cycle or two.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT A (NON-EMERGENCY) MAINTENANCE REQUEST

  Air vent hissing more than ~10 minutes after the radiator is fully hot, or loud enough to hear across the room.
  Vent has likely failed open. Wastes steam and shortens valve life; not dangerous.

  Radiator heats at the supply end but stays cool or only lukewarm at the vent end.
  Steam isn't reaching the far end. Could be a stuck vent, wrong pitch, or internal blockage. The room won't fully heat.

  Persistent banging throughout the cycle, not just at startup — once a minute or more.
  Water hammer. Building-side issue (pipe support or valve type).

  Valve handle that won't fully close when cool, or no longer aligns with its original position.

  Any of the above patterns repeating across 2–3 cycles with no improvement.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT IMMEDIATE SHUTDOWN AND EMERGENCY CALL

If any of these appear during a cycle, close the supply valve on the radiator (the one where the pipe enters — turn the handle/wheel clockwise to close) and call the building's emergency line. Do not touch the boiler.

  Active water discharge — drip, stream, or forming puddle — anywhere on the radiator, valve stem, or pipe joints. Towels under the leak, isolate the radiator, call.

  Visible steam coming from anywhere except the small air-vent fitting at the far end. Steam from a pipe joint, the valve stem, or the radiator body means a failed gasket or a cracked section.

  Sweet, slightly syrupy smell.
  Ethylene glycol leak in a hydronic (hot water) system. Toxic to pets, damages flooring. Close both supply and return valves if you can identify them, ventilate, call.

  Sulfur or rotten-egg smell.
  Gas leak from the boiler — different problem. Leave the apartment, call from outside or 911 / building emergency.

  Radiator with a visible bulge, crack, or seam separation, or one that's hot on one side and completely cold on the other with hissing.
  Failing-section rupture risk.

  Valve that spins freely without resistance, or a handle that comes off in your hand.
  Cannot isolate if a leak develops.

ONE PRACTICAL NOTE ON THE SUPPLY VALVE

If you ever need to close it for an emergency, the supply valve is the one where the pipe enters the radiator (usually a wooden handle or metal wheel). Clockwise closes. Never force — if it resists, stop and call. After an emergency close, let maintenance reopen it so they can verify the system before repressurizing.

Two cycles of consistent quiet, even heating, dry floor, and setpoint reached is the baseline you want to confirm. Last cycle already met three of those four, which is a good sign; the checklist above just makes sure it stays that way.

Three findings rule out a wiring fault and point to overload:

  - Cool outlet and plug faces (no resistive heating at the terminations).
  - No odor, discoloration, buzzing, or moisture (no arcing, tracking, or leakage path).
  - GFCI resets cleanly and holds on a phone-charger load (no latent ground fault).

If it had been a real ground fault or insulation breakdown, you'd typically see at least one of: a warm receptacle, scorch marks, a smell, repeated trips on reset, or a trip under low load. A trip at the moment you stacked a 1,500 W dryer and a 750 W heater (about 2,250 W combined) is what you'd expect from a residential bathroom circuit hitting its limit.

Why 2,250 W is a problem on the circuits bathrooms typically have:

  - 15 A circuit: 1,800 W rated; continuous-load ceiling = 1,440 W.
  - 20 A circuit: 2,400 W rated; continuous-load ceiling = 1,920 W.

A hair dryer used for several minutes is treated as a continuous load; so is a ceramic/space heater. Stacking them pushes almost any bathroom circuit past its continuous rating, and on a 15 A circuit it exceeds the rated capacity outright.

Safe use on that circuit right now:

  - Phone charger and similarly light loads (toothbrush charger, LED vanity light): fine.
  - One high-draw appliance at a time is generally fine, with two caveats:
    - If this is a 15 A circuit, even a 1,500 W dryer alone is about 83% of rated capacity. Brief, attentive use is OK; do not pair it with anything else on the same circuit (bathroom lights, exhaust fan, hallway outlets that share the breaker — easy to miss).
    - If it is a 20 A circuit (more common in buildings rewired in the last ~20 years; current NEC requires it for new bathroom receptacle circuits), a single 1,500 W device is comfortably within limits.
    - A 750 W heater alone is fine on either.
  - Do not reintroduce both together; the trip is your warning that combined draw is not tolerated.

If you can identify the breaker and it says 20 A, you have more headroom. If it is 15 A, or unlabeled/old, treat it as the conservative case.

Stop using the circuit (leave it off, contact management or an electrician) if any of these recur:

  - The GFCI trips with only one device running, or with low loads (charger + light).
  - It trips again immediately on reset, or will not hold reset at all.
  - Any heat, odor, discoloration, buzzing, crackling, or visible damage at the outlet, plug faces, or breaker.
  - Tripping coincides with an appliance turning on elsewhere in the apartment (shared/overloaded branch circuit beyond the bathroom).
  - The GFCI test button stops functioning, or the device feels mechanically loose in the wall.

None of those apply to what you observed, so overload remains the best fit. Leave both high-load devices unplugged when not in use, run one at a time if needed, and note the breaker amperage so you know your real ceiling.

Since the split is closed, dry, and shows no infection signs with full painless motion, re-epithelialization is done. The new skin is still functionally fragile though — tensile strength at this stage is roughly a quarter to a third of mature skin, reaching about 80 percent by 6–8 weeks, with full collagen remodeling taking much longer. So protection during the first few sessions back isn't optional.

PROTECT THE HEALED AREA

In order of usual preference:

  1. Liquid bandage film (New-Skin, Band-Aid Liquid Bandage, similar). A flexible film that tolerates light friction and lets you watch the skin. Reapply between burns. Best first line because it doesn't change grip geometry.

  2. Climbing-specific tape (Metolius, Trango, Black Diamond, etc.). Thinner and stickier than generic athletic tape. Use an H-tape:
       - a strip across the pad covering the split and ~5 mm around
       - two anchor strips wrapped circumferentially, loose enough to slide a fingernail under
       - check capillary refill in the fingertip within 2 seconds after taping
       - smooth the pad strip so it doesn't bunch under load
       - replace if it lifts, rolls, or soaks through

  3. Tegaderm (clear occlusive dressing) under the tape. Adds a low-friction glide layer so peeling the tape off later doesn't shear the new epithelium.

Avoid generic leukotape or rigid athletic tape directly on the fingertip. Too thick, can blister adjacent skin from friction, and tends to lift new skin when removed.

Stick to open-hand and three-finger drag grips at first. Full crimp puts shear directly across the pad where the split was — that's the last grip to reintroduce.

CAUTIOUS RETURN PROGRESSION

Start on rope (top-rope or autobelay), not bouldering. You want controlled, low-consequence loads first. Tape the finger every session. Stop while form is still clean.

  Days 7–9 from injury, 1st session back:
    - slab to vertical, large holds (jugs, big edges, pockets you can sink fingers into)
    - open-hand or three-finger drag only
    - no dynos, no falls, no campusing
    - 30–40 min
    - inspect the finger under good light at the end

  Days 10–14, sessions 2–3:
    - add gentle overhang on jugs
    - same grip rules
    - lengthen sessions only if no issues

  Week 3:
    - moderate-size edges and crimps, open-hand first
    - then half-crimp on positive holds
    - begin testing full crimp on large, positive crimps only

  Week 4 and beyond:
    - full crimp on progressively smaller holds
    - return to bouldering only after a full crimp on small edges with the taped finger is uneventful

Plan on a 3–4 week runway for a 6-day-healed superficial split. If anything reopens, drop back two stages and pause 3–5 days.

STOP THE SESSION — OR DON'T START — IF

  - skin reopens, cracks, or bleeds, even a pinpoint
  - gripping produces pain that wasn't there at rest
  - new redness, warmth, swelling, or any drainage (could be infection or re-injury — see a clinician promptly)
  - numbness, tingling, or color change in the fingertip (loosen tape right away; circulation issue)
  - blistering under or next to the tape (means the tape is bunching or too thick — change method)
  - the tape lifts mid-session — stop, replace, or call it done

When in doubt, end the session. A 6-week-old healed split is a non-event. A 8-day-old reopened split costs you another 2–3 weeks.

Two practical checks before session 1: under a strong light, look for any thin pink or slightly raised line on the pad, and gently press it against a tabletop edge to confirm there's no tenderness on loaded contact. You already said both are clean, so you should be good to start the progression above on day 7 from the injury.

If you want a sanity check from a clinician before loading it, a hand therapist or a sports-medicine doctor familiar with climbing finger injuries is the right call — I'm an AI assistant, not a substitute for that.

Here's how I'd frame it, given what you've described (and noting up front: I'm not a clinician, so treat this as a reasoned lay summary, not medical advice):

Recommendation: MODIFY, with a tight exit criterion — do not play at full intensity today.

Reasoning from the picture you gave:
- No red flags at rest: no pop, no swelling, no bruising, no focal tenderness, no weakness, no numbness, no pain walking.
- Pain-free on a gentle calf raise (slow, low load).
- Tightness only surfaces under faster / more dynamic load (lateral shuffle = more eccentric demand on the gastroc/soleus, plus faster stretch-shortening).

That pattern fits a low-grade calf strain or simple tightness far better than a complete tear or DVT, but a strain that surfaces during warmup is already telling you the tissue is irritable. Going to max-effort sprints in a pickup game is the textbook way to turn a Grade I into a Grade II and put you out for weeks. Pickup soccer is also exactly the context where "I'll just loosen up as I play" backfires — there's no controlled ramp, and the first hard sprint is sudden.

Concrete plan for tonight:
1. Extend the warmup: 5–10 min easy jog/ride, then progressive calf raises (slow -> faster), then a few low-intensity shuffles. If tightness is unchanged or better at the end, you can play.
2. If you play: limit minutes, avoid max sprints and long accelerations, sub yourself out at the first sign of a sharp/acute change. No "play through and see" — if it sharpens, you're done for the night.
3. If tightness worsens during the extended warmup, or a gentle calf raise starts to hurt, sit out. No negotiation.

Warning signs that mean STOP and seek medical evaluation (same session or urgent care / ER depending):
- A sudden "pop" or sharp stabbing pain in the calf.
- New swelling, bruising, or skin color change in the calf or ankle.
- A tender knot, depression, or gap you can feel in the muscle.
- Pain at rest, or pain when walking / bearing weight.
- Weakness on a single-leg calf raise, or a feeling of giving way pushing off.
- Calf warmth/redness with swelling, especially after travel, prolonged sitting, or if you're on hormones or have other clot risk — that's a DDT/ED concern for a DVT; go to ER.
- Numbness, tingling, or color change in the foot.
- Symptoms that haven't resolved within 3–5 days of relative rest, or that recur every time you return to running.

Post-session, whether you played or not: ice 15–20 min on/off for the first 24–48h only if it's bothersome, gentle pain-free mobility, and avoid aggressive stretching of a hot, tight calf — that often makes a low-grade strain angrier. If anything on the warning-sign list shows up, get it checked rather than waiting it out.

Your hesitation is the right instinct — a coarse-thread wood screw driven into light-gauge cold-formed steel will hold initially and then strip out under cyclic or shock load (dog bump, kid climb, light seismic event). That's exactly the load pattern an anti-tip strap exists to resist. Interim measure of keeping Kibo clear of the bookcase is sensible while you work this out.

SAFE ATTACHMENT OPTIONS (strongest to most renter-friendly)

All of these assume a single-sided installation into a hollow metal-stud wall:

1. Rivet nut / threaded insert ("nutsert") through the stud. Drill a properly sized clearance hole through the stud flange, install a blind-side threaded insert with the right tool, and bolt the strap to it. Full clamping load across the stud wall, room-side access only. Cleanest answer if you want it done once. About $20-40 for a rivet-nut tool and an assortment; 1/4-20 or M6 inserts are plenty.

2. Through-bolt with access to the back side. Drill clearance for a machine bolt (1/4-20), pass it through with a washer and nylock nut. Stronger than a rivet nut (true clamping force), but you need open access behind the wall — not common in an apartment.

3. Fine-thread Type A or Type AB self-tapping sheet-metal screw, #10 or larger, into the stud. This is what metal framing is designed to accept and will hold meaningfully better than the supplied wood screw. Still only as strong as the steel gauge and the threads it cuts — acceptable for a strap, not ideal as the sole restraint on a heavily loaded bookcase.

4. Heavy-duty hollow-wall anchor at the stud cavity (Snaptoggle, Toggler, or equivalent). Carries real shear load through a metal channel bearing on the inside face of the drywall, so the drywall becomes part of the load path. Fine as a secondary measure; less fine as the only attachment.

5. Plywood blocking between two studs. Cut a small drywall opening, fit a plywood panel spanning stud-to-stud fastened into each stud with multiple self-tapping screws, then attach the strap to the plywood with the supplied wood screws. Strongest result; drywall repair afterward.

Drilling-free alternatives worth considering:
- Tension/anti-tip braces that press between floor and ceiling (Quakehold-style and similar). They use the ceiling as the anchor instead of the wall. Work well for tip prevention on furniture that isn't top-heavy; verify the ceiling above the bookcase is structural (not a drop tile).
- Reposition the strap to a wood stud if one exists in range. Metal-stud apartments almost always have wood studs at corners, doorways, or plumbing walls — worth probing for before committing to the metal-stud path.

CONFIRMING YOU ACTUALLY HAVE METAL FRAMING

A stud finder plus a magnet indicating metal is consistent with a real metal stud, but the magnet will also stick to the black-phosphate drywall screws fastening drywall to either a wood or a metal stud. Slide the magnet horizontally a few inches in each direction: continuous attraction means metal stud; attraction that breaks into discrete points roughly 12-16" apart with weak attraction in between means you're hitting drywall screws on a wood stud, in which case the supplied fastener is correct as-is. Two minutes of probing before you buy different hardware.

WHEN TO STOP AND INVOLVE BUILDING MANAGEMENT OR A PROFESSIONAL

Stop and contact the landlord / building management if:
- Your lease restricts wall penetrations, requires written approval, or limits fasteners to picture-hangers. Most multi-family leases do, and metal-stud framing is more common in exactly this kind of building.
- The wall is a shared wall between units or between your unit and a corridor. Those assemblies are typically fire- or sound-rated; any penetration generally has to be sealed with fire-rated caulk to preserve the rating. That is the building's responsibility, not a DIY patch.
- You can't verify what's behind the drywall. Plumbing, electrical, data, sprinkler, and HVAC lines run through metal-stud knockouts, sometimes horizontally. A handyman with a multi-scan stud finder that detects live AC and metal will spend ten minutes saving you from a very bad afternoon.
- The bookcase is tall, heavily loaded, or positioned such that a tip would put a person or Kibo at real risk. At that point a handyman can install blocking or a proper anchor in well under an hour for under $200, and "good enough" isn't the right bar.
- You're not confident in the installation. A loose anchor that pulls out under load is worse than no anchor, because it gives a false sense of security.

Net: metal studs aren't a reason to skip the strap — they're a reason to pick the right fastener (rivet nut, self-tapping screw into the stud, or plywood blocking), confirm you're actually on metal rather than missing a wood stud, and check your lease before you drill.

WHAT IT IS, IN ONE LINE
The pulse is almost certainly mechanical and tied to the rotor — the only thing rotating once per wheel revolution that touches the pads. Your "lever never approaches the bar" tells you the hydraulic system is sealed and functional, so this is geometry/thickness, not a fading system. Ten-minute low-speed test in a traffic-free area was the right call — that's exactly how you separate a real fault from a parking-lot rub.

MOST LIKELY CULPRITS, IN ORDER
  1. Rotor thickness variation — a thin high spot or a faint ridge on the braking track. Easiest to miss visually, single biggest cause of once-per-rev pulses.
  2. Rotor twist / single high spot — not a full bend, just a small geometric anomaly the recenter masked.
  3. Caliper or adapter bolts not actually torqued (snugged by feel during the recenter). The caliper can micro-rock under braking.
  4. Pad surface unevenness — new pads bedding, or contamination (chain lube, sweat, degreaser splash, even fingerprint oil after handling).
  5. Loose rotor bolts / Centerlock ring not fully seated.
  6. Hub bearing play — you've ruled it out visually, but worth re-checking with the wheel off.

DIAGNOSTIC ORDER — DO THESE IN SEQUENCE
Tier 1: No tools, bike on a stand or flipped

  1. Spin the wheel slowly and look at the rotor through the caliper slot from behind the saddle. Note any side-to-side wobble and the position of any high spot relative to the caliper.

  2. Sight along the rotor's edge against a plain background. A thickness high spot shows as a shiny stripe or a faint ridge. A clean fingernail dragged across the surface will catch on a lip.

  3. Pull the wheel and inspect both pads under a strong raking light. Look for:
       - uneven wear (one pad loaded more than the other)
       - glazing (mirror-like surface)
       - oily sheen — contamination
       - pad not sitting flat in the caliper bore

  4. Check torque on:
       - caliper-to-fork/frame bolts (typically 6-8 Nm)
       - adapter bolts if separate
       - rotor bolts (6-bolt: ~6 Nm, star pattern; Centerlock: ring fully seated + lockring)
     Rock the caliper by hand. If anything moves, that's likely your bug.

  5. Rotate the wheel slowly under a strong light and look for hairline cracks at the braking track, around bolt holes, and at the spider / Centerlock interface. Hairlines hide — change angles.

Tier 2: Minimal tools

  6. Rotor truing. If you find a high spot, use a proper rotor truing fork. In a pinch, a clean adjustable wrench with painter's tape on the jaws works — brake-track surface only, never the painted spider or the aluminum spider arms. Work in 0.1 mm increments, re-check after each nudge. Small corrections only; over-bending cracks rotors.

  7. Pad re-bed. Light scuff of the pad face on 120-grit on a flat surface (do not round the leading edge), reinstall, then 20-30 progressive stops from low speed with cooling walks between sets. New pads sometimes inherit a flatness error from packaging.

  8. Clean the rotor if contamination is suspected: 90%+ isopropyl alcohol, lint-free wipe, both sides, full surface. Re-bed afterward.

Tier 3: Substitution (the discriminating test)

  9. Swap in a known-good rotor. If the pulse disappears, the rotor is bad. If it persists with a fresh rotor on the same wheel/hub, the issue is upstream — bearings, axle, hub shell.

  10. Swap in a known-good pad set. Same logic.

Tier 4: Shop-level

  11. Dial indicator: >0.15 mm lateral runout or >0.02 mm thickness variation at the track = replace the rotor.
  12. Hub overhaul if bearings show play with the wheel off.

RIDE-vs-REPAIR THRESHOLD

OK to ride — short, low-risk only ("ride to the shop, not to the trail"):
  - Pulse remains light and does not grow with firmer braking
  - Lever feel is firm, lever-to-bar distance unchanged from before the symptom appeared
  - No new noise during braking (grinding, metallic scrape, click)
  - No visible rotor damage growing on re-inspection
  - Dry conditions, low gradient, low speed
  - No cargo, no child seat, no passenger

Do NOT ride:
  - Pulse grows under firm braking — that's the front of a feedback loop: uneven contact → glazing → less bite → lever travel grows → more heat → more uneven wear
  - Lever feel softens, lever travels farther toward the bar, or the bite point migrates
  - Any new noise during braking
  - Any crack, deep scoring, or blue heat discoloration appears on the rotor
  - Pulse becomes judder you can feel in the bars or fork — it's starting to deform your steering geometry
  - Pulse appears on the rear brake too — rules out a fork/tab-specific issue and points at hub or wheel
  - You're carrying weight (kid, cargo, passenger) or riding wet

Bring to a shop (don't DIY further) if:
  - You find any crack on the rotor
  - Rotor is at or below minimum thickness (stamped on the rotor — usually 1.5 mm road, 1.8-2.0 mm MTB)
  - Hub bearings show play with the wheel off and you don't have spare cones/ bearings
  - The hydraulic lever is going to the bar at all (separate system issue, not this pulse)
  - Pulse survives both rotor AND pad substitution — the fault is upstream and you're guessing

BOTTOM LINE
Once-per-rev signature on the lever, with firm lever feel and no play, is almost always rotor-side after a recenter. You're allowed to ride carefully to a shop only if you stay inside the "OK to ride" list. Any trigger on the "do not ride" list parks the bike.

Exposure assessment

The 4 MiB compressed cap bounds attacker-controlled input bytes, but it does not bound the bytes the gateway then allocates, processes, or forwards. Decompression ratio is content-dependent and attacker-controlled: pathological content (uniform bytes, repeated patterns) reaches 1000:1 easily, and OTLP-shaped JSON commonly lands at 10:1–100:1. From a single 4 MiB compressed input, worst-case fan-out is multi-GiB into the gateway's decompressor buffer and into the forwarded payload on the private path.

What this lets a sender do at the gateway, in the abstract:
  - force large transient allocations in the decompressor (memory pressure, GC pauses)
  - hold connections longer while inflating (slowloris-style)
  - push oversized traffic into the private path (collector bandwidth, processing, downstream)

What this is NOT, per your framing:
  - the advisory is not evidence of an active exploit against this deployment; the 4 MiB input cap is real and the worst cases above are theoretical fan-outs from a constrained input
  - the private collector is not directly internet-exposed per your setup; the residual surface is bounded to senders who can reach the public gateway (legitimate clients, any internal service that can route there, future code paths you don't yet know about)

Smallest bounded mitigation

Add an explicit post-decompression byte cap at the gateway, in addition to (not instead of) the existing 4 MiB compressed cap. Reject with 413 on exceed; do not silently truncate.

Why this is the minimum:
  - it is one new bound at the existing public-ingress control point, not a redesign
  - the guidance you've cited already names the gateway as the public-ingress control; the limit belongs there
  - it does not require content inspection, per-sender rate limits, or any change to OTLP or the collector

Sizing the cap:
  - pick a value above your observed maximum legitimate decompressed payload, with margin, and well below what would strain the gateway. For typical OTLP ingest this lands in the 16–64 MiB range; the right number is yours to set from your own telemetry.
  - sanity floor: a few MiB minimum, or legitimate batched exports start failing.

Enforcement shape:
  - cap is enforced after full decompression but before forwarding, so the collector never sees the oversized payload
  - 413 (Payload Too Large) on exceed, not silent truncation — truncated OTLP can look valid enough to slip past monitoring while breaking downstream parses

Optional second-order tightening (NOT required for the smallest version):
  - hard ratio cap (compressed/decompressed) as a backstop in case the absolute cap is misconfigured
  - per-source concurrency / rate limits
  - canary the cap in observe-only mode before enforcing

These are defense-in-depth, not the smallest mitigation.

One-line summary: the residual exposure is the decompression fan-out from the 4 MiB compressed cap; the smallest bounded mitigation is a post-decompression byte cap enforced at the gateway, rejecting 413 on exceed.

Title: Metrics-router batch policy — second 14-day evidence run (3 clients)
Folder: Eng
URL: https://docs.mock/doc_1789289956995

The doc captures the agreed bounded configuration:
- Three participating Product Engineering clients (the original single client plus two additional ones).
- Per-client temporary settings: 2,000-point maximum batch, 1-second flush interval.
- Ingest-edge admission behavior unchanged for the duration of the run.
- 14-day duration.
- Recorded metrics: per-client and aggregate p99, overall error rate, accepted-versus-rejected point accounting, duplicate request identifiers, and client-side backpressure.

The permanent disposition is explicitly marked pending after this run concludes.

WHAT THIS EVIDENCE SUPPORTS

1. Atomic-handoff correctness. "Old gate closed before later routing in every trace" across 1,200 transfers is the canonical safe-handoff invariant. No observed split-brain window, no observed both-closed window on the success path.

2. Single-holder invariant. "Exactly one holder served throughout" rules out double-serve for the full sample. Combined with (1), the correctness story is strong where measured.

3. Cache freshness. "No stale responses" confirms the new holder had usable state before serving — prefetch is doing what it claims.

4. Bounded, predictable warmup cost. p99 2.2s, max 3.4s, total transfer capped at 4.1s. Tight spread suggests prefetch is payload-bound, not contention- or retry-bound, at observed load.

5. Low user-visible error rate. 3 / 1,200 = 0.25% got transient 503 during warmup. Small but non-zero. Retry behavior is the open question.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SUPPORT

1. Peak-load behavior. 50 transfers/hour average; peak hour is plausibly 5–10× that. Concurrent-prefetch contention, source-side pressure, and p99 under burst are untested.

2. Failure paths. The observation is success-path only. Partial prefetch, source unreachable mid-transfer, payload corruption, new-holder unhealthy post-prefetch — none exercised.

3. Holdover / fallback. If the new holder fails after prefetch completes, does the old holder reopen? What's the user-visible window?

4. Long-window stability. 24h is one observation. Doesn't cover GC cycles, deploys, network events, weekday/weekend delta, dependency blips.

5. Source-side blast radius. No signal on CPU / memory / network cost on the source holder during prefetch. A heavy prefetch can regress existing traffic sharing that host.

6. Cold-start prefetch. Routine transfers vs. first-time handoff may behave differently.

7. Client-side impact of the 3 × 503s. Did they retry successfully? Any downstream amplification?

SAFEGUARDS FOR A GUARDED ROLLOUT

A. Contract invariants the data platform must guarantee and expose as metrics:
   - atomic-handoff violation count (page on > 0)
   - double-serve count (page on > 0)
   - stale-serve count (page on > 0)
   - both-gates-closed window duration (page on any non-zero measurement)
   These four are the canary set. Everything else is secondary.

B. Per-transfer timeout with circuit breaker, derived from observed max + margin. Observed total max 4.1s; a hard ceiling around 6–8s with abort-and-fallback-to-lazy on breach is defensible. Anything tighter is unsupported by the data.

C. Fallback path stays live. Lazy / on-demand fetch must be the default-when-disabled path, not removed. Rollback is a config flip, not a code change.

D. Kill switch exercisable per-tenant or globally within seconds. Authority for the kill switch needs explicit naming — given the ownership constraint, see the closing section.

E. Concurrency cap on simultaneous prefetches per source holder, with backpressure to the transfer queue. Cap chosen from observed peak; revisit quarterly.

F. Source-side resource budget during prefetch (CPU, memory, egress) with alerting if the source holder's own SLO is at risk. This protects the existing traffic on the same host.

G. Gradual ramp with hold-points. Suggested: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% of eligible transfers, each with a 24–72h soak and an explicit go/no-go review against the canary metrics.

H. Synthetic canary. Scheduled test that exercises the handoff path on a non-critical key/tenant so failure modes are observable even when production traffic doesn't naturally trigger them.

I. Documented rollback procedure with a target time-to-disable. Given ownership, the decision-right must be named, not implied.

J. Prefetch success-rate SLO. The 99.75% (1,197 / 1,200) observation is the starting number; tightening requires either absorbing the 503s in retries or removing them at the source.

REMAINING EVIDENCE BEFORE BROADER ROLLOUT

1. Peak-hour observation: same metrics during the worst-hour-in-last-30-days window. Goal — p99 ≤ observed, atomic-handoff holds, source SLO unaffected.

2. Concurrent-prefetch test: drive 5 / 10 / 20 simultaneous prefetches on one source. Measure transfer latency tail, source resource use, queue depth.

3. Failure-injection matrix:
   - source killed mid-prefetch
   - network partition mid-prefetch
   - prefetch payload corruption (truncated, checksum fail)
   - new-holder crash post-prefetch
   For each: confirm no stale serve, no double-serve, fallback engages, atomic invariant holds.

4. 503 retry analysis on the 3 observed cases. Client retry success rate, downstream amplification, user-visible impact. If retries absorb cleanly, tolerable; if not, fix before ramp.

5. Source-side resource profile during prefetch at production load. Verify no regression on existing traffic sharing the host.

6. Extended-window observation (1–2 weeks): cover deploys, GC, network events, weekday/weekend. Confirm metrics hold outside the original 24h.

7. Baseline comparison: current warmup p99 without prefetch. If 2.2s is not better than baseline, the rollout's value proposition needs re-examination before any ramp.

8. Rollback dry-run: time the disable path end-to-end. If it can't be done in < 5 minutes, that's a blocker on calling this "guarded."

ON THE OWNERSHIP CONSTRAINT

"Without changing service ownership" should be made explicit in the rollout doc, not assumed. Concrete assignments:

- Data platform owns the prefetch mechanism, its deploys, and verification of the contract invariants (atomic handoff, no stale serve, fallback path).

- The kill-switch authority and rollback decision-right need a named owner. Recommend co-owned: data platform executes, your side can request via a documented paging path. Neither team should be blocked waiting on the other during an incident.

- Your services consume the contract. If the contract breaks, your services must have an independently exercisable path to disable prefetch without waiting for a data platform deploy.

That last point is the one most often glossed over. The whole case for "guarded" lives or dies on whether your side can actually stop the bleed without a data platform deploy in the loop. If the answer today is "we have to file a ticket," the rollout isn't actually guarded — it's gated on the other team's deploy cadence.

Direction-wise, Cyrus's pivot is sound: timeout reduction tries to make the slow path faster (more failures), prefetch tries to eliminate the slow path. The 24h observation supports the success-path case for the pivot but does not yet support a broad rollout. With the canary metrics in place, the failure-injection matrix run, and a named kill-switch authority, a 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% ramp becomes defensible. Without those, the right move is to keep the proposal at "observation extended, not yet rolling."

Short answer: USE IT. The meds are fine.

Why the crushed carton doesn't matter
- The foil blister is the actual integrity barrier — it keeps out moisture, oxygen, light, and contamination. The outer carton is just a shipping shell and label carrier.
- Your blister is flat (no swelling = no moisture/temp abuse), unpunctured (no barrier breach), and every tablet is intact and dry. That's the test that matters.
- Lot expires Aug 2026 (~20 months out — comfortably within date) and the printed name/dose matches his existing Rx, so you also have identity + dating confirmed.

Quick pre-dose habit (still worth doing each fill)
- Look each tablet over before giving: no chipping, discoloration, softness, stickiness, or off odor. Should look identical to his previous fills.

Packaging defects that mean HOLD + call the pharmacy
Hold the shipment and contact the pharmacy (or manufacturer) if you see any of these:

1. Blister breach — punctured, torn, peeled, or delaminated foil (even a pinhole)
2. Blister deformed — swollen, bulging, or warped pockets (can signal temp abuse or gas formation)
3. Loose tablets in the blister cavity — suggests the heat-seal failed
4. Visible moisture, condensation, or liquid inside a pocket
5. Tablets cracked, chipped, broken, crumbly, or stuck together
6. Discoloration, unusual mottling, or any unexpected color vs. prior fills
7. Soft, sticky, or powdery tablets (moisture ingress)
8. Off or unexpected odor
9. Foreign material in the blister (debris, white powder, residue, insects)
10. Missing or unreadable lot number or expiration date anywhere on the unit
11. Printed name, strength, or tablet count doesn't match his prescription
12. Tamper-evident features broken in a way that suggests prior opening (e.g., a peel-push tab that's already been depressed)

Practical note: most pharmacies will replace a damaged shipment on the spot when you call, often without requiring you to bring it in. Have the lot number and a photo of the crushed carton ready when you call — it speeds the replacement if you want one anyway, but you do not need to wait on a replacement to use this fill.

One caveat that's not a defect but worth flagging: if Kibo's dose, formulation, or manufacturer changed from his last fill (e.g., new generic supplier, scored vs. unscored), confirm with his vet before the first dose — but that's an "ask the prescriber" item, not a "hold the shipment" item.

  - If kept down for a full hour: offer 1/4–1/2 cup at a time, hourly.
  - If he vomits water: withhold 1–2 hours, then restart with ice chips or
    1 teaspoon amounts at a time.
  - Free-choice water is fine once he has tolerated small frequent sips for
    several hours and is clearly interested in food.
  - Goal: hydration without gastric distension that retriggers vomiting.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. FEEDING REINTRODUCTION (bland, low-fat, small + frequent)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Good bland options:
    - Boiled skinless chicken breast (no salt/oil/skin/bones) + plain white
      rice, ~50/50, well-cooked.
    - Boiled lean ground turkey (rinsed after cooking) + plain white rice.
    - Plain canned pumpkin (not pie filling), 1 tbsp per meal, if stool goes
      loose later.

  Schedule:
    - First meal: 1–2 tablespoons only. If kept down 1–2 hours, proceed.
    - Hours 0–12 post-fast: small meals every 3–4 hours (a few tablespoons
      each, scaled to his size).
    - Hours 12–24: slightly larger bland meals, 3x/day.
    - Day 2: continue bland, 3 meals.
    - Day 3: 50/50 blend of bland + normal food.
    - Day 4: back to normal food if stools are normal and no further vomit.
  Hold treats, fatty food, dairy, and table scraps until day 4.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. MONITORING (next 24–48 hours)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - Every few hours: energy, gum color (should be pink and moist), appetite,
    posture, breathing.
  - After each meal: kept down or not? Stool at next potty break.
  - Keep a quick log (time / what offered / vomit or stool / behavior). It
    pays for itself if anything changes and you need to call the vet.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. CALL THE VET DURING BUSINESS HOURS (non-emergency, but don't wait)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - One more vomit in the next 12–24 hours, even if he otherwise looks fine.
  - Appetite not fully back within 24 hours.
  - Soft stool or diarrhea developing.
  - Mild lethargy that doesn't resolve with rest.
  - Repeated grass-eating on walks — worth mentioning; rule out GI upset,
    dietary deficiency, or behavioral cause.
  - Wanting reassurance. That is a valid reason to call.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. URGENT / EMERGENCY — GO TO ER OR CALL IMMEDIATELY
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - Repeated vomiting (2+ more episodes, or vomiting that won't stop).
  - Vomit with fresh blood, coffee-ground appearance, or foreign material.
  - Non-productive retching — pacing, dry heaving, swollen or tight belly.
    In deep-chested breeds this is bloat/GDV until proven otherwise and is
    time-critical.
  - Abdomen becomes hard, distended, or painful to touch.
  - Gums pale, white, blue, yellow, or sticky/tacky instead of pink and wet.
  - Severe lethargy, collapse, weakness, or sudden behavior change.
  - Trouble breathing, persistent panting at rest, or restlessness that
    won't settle.
  - Cannot keep any water down (vomits every drink).
  - Dehydration signs: skin tenting, dry gums, sunken eyes, no urine 8+ hrs.
  - Black tarry stool, bloody diarrhea, or vomiting + diarrhea together.
  - Suspected ingestion of toxin, medication, plant, mushroom, or foreign
    object — even if he "seems fine" right now.
  - Shivering, fever, or cold ears/paws (low temperature).
  - Anything that just feels wrong. Gut instinct is a legitimate trigger.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. CONTEXT WORTH NOTING
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Grass-induced vomiting is very common. Two practical follow-ups regardless
  of how today goes:
    - Check whether the grass he gets into is treated (fertilizer, pesticide)
      or in foxtail / grass-awn territory for your region/season.
    - If grass-eating is becoming a pattern, mention it at his next wellness
      visit — sometimes it's behavioral, sometimes it points to GI irritation
      or a dietary gap.

Below is a traffic-free sequence that follows the manufacturer's two phases, adds a real-world cool-down, and gives you a clear abort list. Assumes the shop-yard baseline (firm lever, no pulse, runout under 0.05 mm, no rub) still holds when you arrive at the site.

Pre-flight at the site
  Rotor lateral runout still under 0.05 mm cold (heat from the ride over can shift a marginal rotor).
  Caliper bolts and axle (QR skewer or thru-axle) at the correct torque; wheel seated.
  Tires inflated; quick-release or thru-axle fully engaged.
  Helmet on; gloves and clear eyewear recommended for the Phase 2 stops.
  No headwind strong enough to mask a grabby lever or to push you off line.

Site
  Paved, level, traffic-free, dry. Empty parking lot, school lot on a weekend, closed service road, or a wide bike path with no pedestrians. No camber, no slope - a slope biases decel effort and pad load.
  Sweep leaves and pine needles off the line (wet leaves are slick enough to lock a wheel without you braking).
  Long enough straight to coast back to entry speed between reps; budget roughly 150-200 m of clean straight per cycle.
  Midday light if possible so you can see rotor discoloration (blue or purple tint = overheating) and pad face condition.

Phase 1 - moderate decels, 15 mph to 5 mph, 20 reps
  Build to about 15 mph under pedaling or a gentle downhill. Use a bike computer, GPS, or a timed measured distance (15 mph is roughly 6.7 m/s, so 100 m takes about 15 s).
  Pull each lever firmly but not hard. Body cues: bike slows noticeably, your weight shifts forward onto the bars, lever travels about half to two-thirds of its range, and no wheel locks.
  Exit each rep near 5 mph, then coast back to speed with no braking.
  Do not roll to a complete stop. The card is explicit: a hot stationary clamp lays down uneven pad transfer (a glaze patch, not a uniform film).
  Do not lock either wheel. If the front starts to skid, ease off immediately - that means the interface is hotter than the transfer layer can tolerate.
  Space reps about 10-15 s apart by riding a small recovery loop so the rotor stays in a controlled heat band rather than running red-hot.

Inter-phase cool-down
  Ride easy and brake-free for 2-3 minutes. Airflow over a spinning, unclamped rotor sheds heat much faster than a clamped one.
  Target: rotor barely warm to the touch. If you cannot hold a finger on it for 1-2 seconds, it is still too hot for Phase 2.
  Do not splash water on the rotor to speed this up - the thermal shock can warp a rotor that just left Phase 1.

Phase 2 - firm decels, 20 mph to 5 mph, 10 reps
  Same line, same surface.
  Entry speed about 20 mph; lever pull firm - full-finger grip, weight forward, lever two-thirds to nearly full travel.
  Same no-lock, no-stop rule; exit near 5 mph and coast back to speed.
  After rep 10, ride easy and brake-free for several minutes until the rotor is cool to the touch.
  For the next 10-15 minutes avoid any hard stops - let the transfer film set before it sees another thermal shock.

Stop criteria (abort, let everything cool, then diagnose)
  Lever goes soft, spongy, or bottoms out at the bar - possible hydraulic issue, not just air. Stop riding and inspect before continuing.
  Pulsation develops that was not in the shop-yard test - rotor is heat-warping, or pad transfer is uneven. Stop, cool fully, re-measure runout cold.
  Wheel locks under moderate lever force - pads are glazing or the rotor has a hot spot. Stop, cool, then either lightly scuff the pad faces with fine sandpaper and re-bed, or replace the rotor.
  Burning smell, visible smoke, or any blue or purple tint on the rotor - the rotor is overheated and at risk of heat-checking. Replace it.
  Any new rub or scrape the shop test did not show - pad sticking in the caliper, a caliper bolt loosening from heat, or rotor warping. Stop and inspect.
  Any handling change - wobble, pull to one side, inconsistent lever stroke - stop and check axle, caliper alignment, and pad retraction.

After the bed-in
  Cold rotor runout should still be under 0.05 mm lateral. If it has grown, the rotor heat-warped and should be replaced rather than re-bedded.
  Lever feel should match the shop-yard reading: firm, no pulse, consistent through the stroke.
  Pad face: even gray transfer film across the full contact area, no shiny glaze patches, no uneven coloration.
  One short low-speed stop in the same traffic-free area to confirm bite and modulation before you head onto public roads.

On later rides
  Full bite typically settles in over the next few heat cycles in normal use.
  Avoid prolonged dragging braking (long descents) for the first ride or two so the transfer film has time to stabilize.

Do not mount or load the arm. Return it as-is.

Why:

  The clamp body is the primary load-bearing structural element — it resists the bending moment from the arm and monitor cantilevered off the desk. A hairline crack in cast metal sitting next to the desk-tightening bolt boss is in exactly the worst place: a stress concentration that sees cyclic load every time the arm is moved, bumped, or adjusted. Cast metal (vs. forged/wrought) is particularly vulnerable to crack growth from casting porosity, and there is no consumer-repair path for a cracked structural casting. The 14.2 lb vs. 22 lb rating is a red herring — the rating assumes an intact part. Failure mode here is the arm and monitor dropping onto the desk, floor, or a person.

Evidence to include in the return request:

  1. Photos (you already have most of these — add a scale reference):
     - Close-up of the crack with a ruler or coin in frame so the ~18 mm size is verifiable.
     - A second angle with raking light to show the crack is a real fracture, not a scratch or casting seam.
     - Wide shot of the whole clamp with the crack visible, for context.
     - Model label, readable.
     - Serial number, readable.
     - Packaging: outer carton (all sides), inner foam/molding, any plastic wrap, shipping label with tracking.

  2. Short unedited video (10–30 s): pan from the model/serial label to the crack in one continuous take. This ties unit identity to defect in a way a photo series can't be argued with.

  3. Text in the request itself:
     - Order number, purchase date, receipt date.
     - Seller/listing (SKU, product page URL).
     - One-paragraph description: where the crack is, approximate length, what component it sits on, that the unit was never installed or loaded.
     - Explicit note that the outer shipping carton arrived intact — this shifts the defect to manufacture or to whoever handled an unopened carton, not to you.
     - Monitor weight (14.2 lb) and arm rating (22 lb), to preempt any "used outside spec" objection.

Process tips:

  - Open the RMA with the seller first; a clearly defective unit with this evidence is usually accepted without argument.
  - If the seller pushes back, the combination of intact carton on arrival + defect present at unboxing + photos taken before any use + never mounted is strong credit-card chargeback material.
  - For a manufacturer warranty claim, the photos plus serial number are usually enough; don't ship the unit until they ask.
  - Keep the cracked arm and all packaging in the same condition until the claim is resolved — don't repack it, and don't throw anything out.

Pre-rain setup (one-time, before the next forecasted rain)

Allow ~45-60 minutes for this; do it once and reuse the same points every time.

1. Mark interior observation points with painter's tape so readings are repeatable:
   - Point A: lower-left window return (where the inspector's reading was elevated)
   - Point B: control area (where the inspector's reading was lower — same spot they used)
   - Point C: 1-2 ft up the same wall, away from the window
   - Point D: opposite side of the same wall, mid-height, away from the window
2. Baseline at each point with the same meter in the same mode:
   - Record date, time, indoor temp, indoor RH (if you have a hygrometer), meter reading, meter units
   - Take three readings per point 30 seconds apart to capture drift
   - Photograph each point with the meter visible in frame so the number is on record
3. Photograph the exterior seal joint gap from the window view:
   - One wide shot, one close-up with a coin or ruler for scale
   - Note compass direction the window faces and the gap's location in the joint (top, side, bottom)
   - While you're outside the view, photograph any adjacent cracks in cladding or trim
4. Log the forecast: predicted rain start, expected duration, intensity, wind direction
5. Log current indoor ambient: temp, RH

During the rain (fixed schedule, not ad hoc)

Adjust intervals if the rain is brief; the rule is same points, same meter, same mode.

- T+0 (within 15 min of rain start): full sweep A/B/C/D, photo of A
- T+30 min: A and B, photo of A
- T+60 min: A and B, photo of A
- T+120 min: full sweep A/B/C/D, photo of A
- Rain stops: full sweep, photo of A
- T+30 min post-rain: full sweep
- T+60 min post-rain: full sweep

At each reading: record time, reading, any visible change (staining darkening, sheen, condensation, efflorescence). If you can see the exterior seal joint from inside, note whether the gap appears to be taking on water or whether water is tracking down.

Do NOT during this period: open the wall, apply sealant of any kind, probe the surface, drill, run fans or dehumidifiers aimed at the wall, or move stored items away from point A. The goal is to let the wall respond to the rain undisturbed so the data is interpretable.

Post-rain monitoring (24-72 hours after rain ends)

- Hourly readings at A and B for the first 4 hours
- Then A and B every 4-6 hours through the next day
- Single readings at A and B at 24h, 48h, and 72h post-rain
- Goal: capture the drying curve — does A return to baseline, asymptote above it (reservoir), or stay flat?

How to read what you get:

- A rises during rain, B does not → A is responding to the event; the gap is a consistent contributor (not proven, but supported)
- A and B move together → the gap is less likely the dominant source
- A does not rise during rain but started elevated → the moisture is from an earlier event, drying slowly; the rain event is not currently adding to it

What to send management after the event

A short packet, not a novel:

- Baseline table (date, time, points, readings, ambient)
- During-rain time series (just A and B is enough if C and D were flat)
- Drying curve (post-rain)
- 3-5 photos: pre-rain exterior seal joint with scale, during-rain exterior seal joint if safely visible, interior point A at peak reading, interior point A at 24h, any visible change
- One-paragraph note stating: what you observed, what you did not do (no sealant, no wall opening, no fixture disturbance), and the request — exterior contractor assessment with a scheduled date

Urgent escalation — contact management the same day, do not wait for the rain window to close, if any of the following occur:

- Active drip into living space (water reaching a surface, not just an elevated meter reading)
- Visible staining that appears or expands during the rain
- Meter at A climbs to within roughly 10% of the meter's stated maximum or holds pinned at the high end
- Softening plaster, bubbling paint, peeling surface, or swelling drywall at A or the surrounding area
- Moisture appears at or near any electrical outlet, switch, light fixture, or visible wiring
- Visible mold growth (fuzzy or textured dark spots, not just discoloration)
- Water reaches the baseboard, floor, or any adjacent unit
- Occupant develops respiratory, eye, or skin symptoms they associate with the area
- Rapid (not gradual) change in readings during the rain — can indicate a pressurized leak
- Sound of running water inside the wall when no plumbing fixtures are in use

For each escalation, message management with: what was observed, when, a photo if obtainable, and the ask — same-day or next-business-day response from the exterior contractor, or a qualified interior investigator if exterior cannot respond in that window.

What this checklist is not

- It does not locate the source definitively. It builds a defensible, time-stamped record.
- It does not replace the contractor assessment — it gives the contractor better data when they arrive.
- It does not justify delaying escalation if any trigger above fires. Escalation overrides the observation schedule.
- It is bounded: setup once, one rain event, 72 hours of follow-up, then stop and reassess based on what the data and the contractor's response show.

Short answer: this is a client-interpretation problem, not accounting loss. Every point the SDK put on the wire is accounted for in Sphere's response — the client's dashboard is just reading the wrong field.

Why it's not accounting loss
- Attempted (what your SDK sent): 12,000
- Server-side totals: accepted 11,760 + rejected 240 = 12,000
- No duplicate request IDs, no retries, no partial drops in transit
The two sides reconcile exactly. If there were real loss, accepted + rejected would be strictly less than attempted (e.g. a 5xx mid-stream, a truncated body, a network reset before the server wrote its reply). That signature isn't present here. The 240 missing points aren't missing from the system — they're sitting in the `rejected` field of the partial-success response that the client's "sent" counter is ignoring.

The 240 are not duplicates either. OTLP partial success reports rejection of valid payload entries the server chose not to ingest (in your case: invalid attributes). Retries/duplicates would show up as the same point ID appearing on the wire twice or as a retried request ID; you confirmed neither.

How the client should represent the three numbers
A correct client view splits the partial-success response into three distinct counters, not two:

1. Attempted — 12,000
   Source: SDK send side, or the request body's point count. Represents what the client tried to export. Always equal to the points in the original OTLP request body.

2. Accepted — 11,760
   Source: the ExportMetricsPartialSuccess / ExportLogsPartialSuccess / ExportTracesPartialSuccess message's `accepted` field returned by ingest-edge. Represents points the server persisted and is queryable as telemetry.

3. Rejected — 240
   Source: the same partial-success message's `rejected` field, plus `error_message` for reasons. Represents points the server explicitly refused to ingest. These need a separate counter, not a subtraction from "sent".

The dashboard invariant the client should enforce is:
   attempted == accepted + rejected  (+/- transport loss, which is a distinct bucket)

In your case that invariant holds with zero transport loss, which is itself evidence that nothing was dropped silently. The client's current "sent" view is a renamed "attempted" view that treats the gap to "accepted" as a mystery; once it surfaces `rejected` explicitly, the 240-point gap disappears and the dashboard reads 12,000 attempted = 11,760 accepted + 240 rejected, matching Sphere's counters.

Practical fix on the client side
- On every partial-success reply, increment three counters, not one: `otlp_points_attempted`, `otlp_points_accepted`, `otlp_points_rejected`.
- Surface `rejected` with the server's `error_message` breakdown so the 240 are actionable (in your case: invalid attributes — likely a schema/semconv change in the new SDK version).
- Do not subtract `rejected` from `attempted` to derive a "delivered" number silently — that hides the rejection signal that triggered the partial success in the first place.
- Don't retry the rejected 240 blindly. Partial success means the server looked at them and refused; retrying sends the same invalid attributes and produces the same rejection. The fix is on the producer (SDK upgrade validation / attribute sanitization), not on the transport.

So: the accounting is sound, the partial-success response is doing exactly what OTLP designed it to do, and the 240 are an interpretation bug on the dashboard side — specifically, conflating attempted with accepted.

2. Single-holder telemetry during the window. If one holder served, did that holder see elevated latency / queue depth / errors tied to prefetch pressure, or normal traffic? "One holder served" reads the same way for "rollout is contained" and "rollout is concentrating load" -- the holder's own telemetry disambiguates.

  Smoke machines (some blocks) — cross early.

  Duration rule: if he offers any avoidance posture — ears back, low head, tail tuck, whale eye, scanning — turn around immediately and head home. Don't push through it; the goal of this walk is a neutral-to-positive 20–25 min, not distance.

INDOOR: DOOR + SOUND

  Stop answering entirely. Put a bowl of wrapped candy on a chair just outside the front door with a small sign ("please take one — happy Halloween"). Lights on inside still look like a participating household; door stays closed.

    Chocolate, especially dark and baking chocolate — toxic (theobromine). Even a small amount of dark chocolate per kg is a problem.

    Xylitol (sugar-free candy, gum, mints, peanut butter cups labeled "sugar-free") — very small amounts cause rapid hypoglycemia and can cause liver failure. This is the single most dangerous category on Halloween.

    Raisins and certain trail-mix candies — kidney toxic.

    Macadamia nuts — neurological signs.

    Wrappers — foil, plastic, sticks — can cause obstruction even if the candy itself was small.

    Glow sticks and glow jewelry — the liquid inside is intensely bitter; dogs who chew them usually drool profusely and may vomit. Usually self-limiting but call your vet if he chews one.

Below is a conservative, graded protocol built around the principle you already named: symptom-free walking is necessary but not sufficient. Two weeks out with full ADL clearance is a good baseline, not a clearance for acceleration and change-of-direction. Use the order below, don't skip stages, and stop at the first stage that reproduces the original sensation.

PRE-FIELD SELF-SCREEN
Do this tonight and again 60-90 min before kickoff. ~10 minutes.

1. Single-leg heel raises: 20 slow reps each leg, full range, controlled eccentric ("down" as slow as the "up"). Note last-rep pain or cramping and reps-to-fatigue. If the right side fails below 15 reps or lags the left by more than 3 reps, do not pass go.

2. Single-leg forward hops: 10 each leg, mark and compare landing distance. Pain on landing, knee/trunk compensation, or more than ~10% distance deficit on the right is a stop.

3. Knee-to-wall (weight-bearing dorsiflexion): measure toe-to-wall distance with heel down. More than ~1.5 cm deficit on the right is a caution flag.

4. Palpation: medial gastrocnemius belly, musculotendinous junction, lateral soleus line, Achilles insertion. Any focal tenderness, knot, palpable defect, or "different from the other side" sensation is a stop.

5. Sub-maximal pogos: 2 sets of 15-20 double-leg pogos, then a 30-second quick-feet drill. Re-check for the original tightness. If it shows up here, skip the field test.

ON-FIELD GRADED TEST
~20 minutes, in order, 2-3 minutes of walking between stages.

A. Easy jog, 5 minutes, conversational pace.
B. 4-6 x 40 m progressive accelerations, last 1-2 at roughly 80%.
C. 4-6 x 20 m near-sprint strides, full calf push-off, full recovery between.
D. 4-6 x 10-15 m lateral shuffles each direction, athletic stance.
E. 4-6 x 45-degree plant-and-drive cuts at moderate speed.
F. 10 single-leg hops each leg, then 6-8 bounding strides.
G. Re-check block: 10 slow single-leg raises on the right, a 200 m easy jog, then 5 minutes of walking.

DECISION CRITERIA

PLAY FULL
- All stages A through G completed without the original tightness, pain, swelling, or new asymmetry.
- Right calf feels quiet and equal to the left at G.
- No tightness returns during the 10 minutes after cool-down.

MODIFY
Play, but with a constrained first 30 minutes: first 15 minutes conservative, no max sprints or hard cuts for the first 30, planned sub at the first sign of tightness, warm down fully after. Acceptable only if:
- Tightness appeared only at stage E or F and fully cleared within 2-3 minutes of easy jogging.
- Mild awareness (not pain) that did not progress with continued movement.
- No warmth, swelling, or visible change.

STOP FOR THE DAY
- Tightness returns at any stage and persists more than 5 minutes into easy activity.
- Any pain, even 1-2 out of 10.
- Sensation of managing the calf, holding back, or favoring the leg.
- New warmth, visible swelling, or a bruise that appears during the session.
- Anything that feels like the original tightness, even briefly.

DO NOT PLAY NEXT WEEK WITHOUT EVALUATION
Schedule with PCP or sports med within 1-2 weeks if any of the following:
- Tightness reappears at stages B or C (i.e., low load).
- Asymmetric heel-raise endurance or hop distance persists.
- A second recurrence inside two weeks.
- Palpable tenderness that does not fully clear after warm-up.

URGENT EVALUATION TODAY
ER or urgent care, not the field, if any of the following:
- Sudden pop or sharp pain during test or play.
- Calf swelling with redness or warmth, especially with DVT risk factors (recent long travel, immobility, dehydration, hormonal medications, prior clot, family history, recent illness).
- Pain at rest, particularly with ankle dorsiflexion.
- New inability to do a single-leg raise on the right.
- Foot color change, numbness, or tingling.

CLOSING NOTES
- Eccentric calf control (the controlled "down" of every raise) is the most protective single factor — make sure the lowering phase is fully controlled and pain-free, not just the push.
- If you play Sunday, expect the calf to be quiet for the first 10-15 minutes; do not chase the first ball at 100%. If it speaks, pull out cleanly rather than test through it.
- Two weeks of rest plus symptom-free daily activity is a reasonable starting point, not a clearance. Calf strain recurrence is common when graded exposure is skipped, especially the acceleration and cutting stages.
- A brief sports medicine or PCP visit (not urgent, but worth scheduling in the next week or two) is reasonable given that the original tightness was enough to make you skip a game — particularly to rule out soleus strain, early Achilles or gastroc tendinopathy, or a vascular contributor. Devika's clinical eye is useful as a sounding board but is not a substitute for your own evaluation.

This is a conservative self-management framework, not a diagnosis or a replacement for clinical evaluation. When in doubt, default to stop and seek evaluation rather than treating the absence of walking symptoms as clearance.

Quick framing first, since it makes the rest obvious: a typical kitchen microwave oven radiates around 2.45 GHz to heat food. That sits right in the middle of the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band (channels 1–11/13 in the US, centered 2.412–2.472 GHz). The magnetron's Faraday cage is imperfect, so a small amount of that energy leaks out the door seal and viewport. 5 GHz Wi-Fi (5.18–5.85 GHz) and any wired link are far enough away in frequency or out of the RF path entirely that they're unaffected — which matches what you're seeing exactly. So the symptom is consistent with leakage, not a provider or modem issue; no outage page check needed.

VERIFY (least disruptive, no moves, no purchases):

  1. Reproduce on demand. From the work-room laptop on 2.4 GHz, run a continuous ping to the router gateway (or any LAN host) for 60 seconds. Start a microwave cycle partway through (a mug of water is the cleanest load — more leakage than empty, less than a frozen burrito). Watch for loss spikes. Repeat on the 5 GHz SSID as a control; it should stay clean. That single comparison isolates the microwave as the cause.

  2. Visualize. On a phone, install a Wi-Fi analyzer (WiFi Analyzer on Android, Net Analyzer or similar on iOS). Stand near the work-room laptop, watch the 2.4 GHz signal/noise graph. Run the microwave for ~30 seconds. You should see the noise floor jump or the RSSI for your AP drop during the cycle, then recover. This is the most convincing piece of evidence and costs nothing.

  3. Channel test (also doubles as the fix). The 2.45 GHz leak hits channels 6–9 hardest; channels 1 (2.412 GHz) and 11 (2.462 GHz) sit at the band edges and are usually clean even with a leaky oven. In the router admin page, manually set the 2.4 GHz channel to 1, retest the ping-during-microwave. Then try 11. If channel 1 or 11 is clean and 6–9 is not, you've both confirmed interference and found a zero-cost workaround.

  4. Quick physical check (optional, borderline-disruptive). With the microwave off and cool, close the door on a slip of paper and tug gently. If it pulls out easily, the door seal is degraded and leakage is higher than normal — useful context, not required to act on the result.

STABLE SETUP, no moves, no purchases:

  - First choice: wired. You already have it landed in the work room per the Sphere IT setup, and it sidesteps the entire problem class. Use it as the default for the work-room laptop whenever the laptop is at the desk. This is the only option that is immune to microwave leakage, neighbor APs, and 2.4 GHz noise in general.

  - Second choice: 5 GHz only on the work-room laptop. In the OS Wi-Fi settings (or the Intel/Realtek adapter advanced properties: Preferred Band = 5 GHz, or set roaming aggressiveness to favor 5 GHz), force the laptop onto the 5 GHz SSID. 5 GHz is outside the microwave's emission band, so it's stable by physics. Keep both SSIDs broadcast for other devices; only the laptop needs the band preference.

  - Third choice: pin 2.4 GHz to channel 1 or 11 on the router (whichever the analyzer shows as cleaner in your unit). Avoid Auto — many routers auto-pick 6, which is the worst-case channel for a 2.45 GHz interferer. Channel 1/11 is the lowest-cost fix for any 2.4 GHz-only device that can't move to 5 GHz.

WHEN TO ESCALATE (only if the above isn't enough):

  - If channel 1/11 still drops, the leakage is unusually strong and the microwave itself is the next thing to address — door seal, or replace the unit. Don't start here; it's the most disruptive move and is unneeded for a typical leak.
  - If 5 GHz coverage to the work room is marginal, that's a separate coverage problem, not a microwave problem, and the right fix there is router placement or a wired backhaul — but only after the microwave question is closed.

Net: confirm with a ping-during-microwave + analyzer snapshot, then default the work-room laptop to wired, with 5 GHz as the wireless fallback and channel 1 or 11 pinned if any 2.4 GHz-only device needs to stay on Wi-Fi. Nothing moves, nothing gets bought until the verification actually says it's required.

Two questions, two answers. General NYC Board of Elections practice — not a substitute for what your specific site's coordinator tells you.

WHICH PATH AFTER TWO REJECTIONS

In NYC, the standard sequence after a scanner rejection is:

  1. You may SPOIL the ballot — hand it back to an inspector (folded, in the privacy sleeve), they seal it in a "spoiled ballot" envelope without examining your marks, and they issue you a replacement blank ballot from a sealed book.
  2. After up to two spoilage events (i.e., third total attempt), if a ballot is still rejected OR if you ask, you move to an AFFIDAVIT BALLOT — that's the "emergency ballot" the worker described. You mark it, seal it in an affidavit envelope with your signed affidavit, and it goes into a separate, secured box.

Which is "safer ordinary" depends on what failure mode worries you more:

  - Third replacement, fresh marks: if the scanner accepts it, it counts exactly like any other ballot on election night — no extra review. The risk is another rejection; depending on the site's reading of the rule, that may put you on affidavit anyway.
  - Affidavit now: guaranteed to be cast (you won't be turned away), but it's counted later by BOE staff after they verify your registration against the poll book. Affidavit ballots in NYC have a real non-count rate driven by registration/signature/style mismatches that wouldn't affect a normally-scanned ballot.

A practical rule: if you can guess what tripped the scanner (oval not fully filled, stray mark in the write-in row, an X or check instead of a filled oval, faint pencil that the scanner reads as ambiguous), the third replacement is usually the cleaner outcome. If you genuinely don't know and are worried you'll repeat the error, switching to affidavit is the conservative path.

KEEPING SELECTIONS PRIVATE WHILE ASKING FOR HELP

  - Use the privacy sleeve/folder the site is required to provide. Mark and re-feed inside it.
  - When returning a rejected ballot, fold it marks-in; inspectors handle the physical ballot but are not authorized to read its marks — only to confirm it is a ballot and, if you ask, to re-feed it.
  - Ask about the SCANNER'S MESSAGE, not your marks. The display tells you the rejection reason ("ambiguous mark," "overvote," etc.). "What does the screen say?" and "Which oval is it complaining about?" do not require showing marks.
  - An inspector may watch you re-feed to give verbal pointers; that's allowed without them seeing your face. If anyone tries to look at the ballot content, that's outside their role — you can politely decline.
  - For affidavit ballot: the affidavit form asks for name/address/signature, never selections. The ballot is sealed inside the envelope; only BOE staff later open it, under confidentiality rules.

ONE SUGGESTION BEFORE YOU DECIDE

Ask the inspector to let you look at the scanner screen on the next re-feed attempt before the ballot is returned to you. That tells you the specific rejection reason and usually clarifies whether the next mark-up can fix it.

If anything feels off — a worker won't explain the screen, is steering you toward one path, or wants to see your marks — ask to speak with the site's coordinator. Every NYC poll site has one on duty on Election Day. You can also call 311 or the NYC BOE voter protection line for procedural clarification while you remain at the site.
