  Why the evidence supports a 5% canary (not a full rollout):

  - Root cause is mechanistic, not correlational. All five temp 503s traced to the same lease-acceptance → cache-ready visibility gap. That is the kind of finding a targeted patch can close.
  - The patch closes the exact gap (cache readiness published before request admission), not a correlated symptom.
  - Staging validation covered the four failure modes that matter — temp 503s, stale responses, overlapping holders, data-loss indicators. A multi-dimensional pass is stronger than a single-metric pass.
  - Production is currently paused. The canary is additive risk, not compounding risk.

  Caveats the 10k staging run does not cover:

  - 10k is bounded. Without the population the five 503s came from in prod, we don't know the pressure the staging run actually applied. If those five came from a much larger prod sample, 10k is comfortable; if they came from roughly 10k of traffic, the staging pass is one-zero and statistically thin.
  - Staging typically does not reproduce the timing characteristics that produced the original gap — lease grant latency, cache-fill latency under production traffic mix, concurrent lease transitions. That is precisely what the canary is for.
  - "No data-loss indicators" in staging is good, but staging rarely exercises the write/read patterns that surface staleness. This is the failure mode most likely to need prod timing to surface.

  Safeguards the data platform team should retain:

  - Cap at 5% with no auto-promotion. Promotion is a separate decision after canary observation.
  - Pre-declare the observation window and pass criteria before the canary starts, not after.
  - Run a parallel control comparison: canary shards vs. non-canary shards over the same window, so the read is differential rather than absolute.
  - Watch the lease → cache-ready interval specifically. Flag (not page) if it trends above the original 180–240 ms on canary shards.
  - Keep the previous shard-keeper version hot-rollbackable. A clean canary should not erase the rollback path.
  - Do not expand to a second tranche until the first has cleared the original 180–240 ms window at production timing.

  Rollback signals (auto-trigger, no human judgment required):

  - Any temp 503 inside the original 180–240 ms post-lease-acceptance window on a canary shard. That is the original failure signature; one is enough.
  - Any case where cache-ready publishes after request admission — i.e., the patch's gating logic fails open.
  - Overlapping holders detected by the lease tracker.
  - Data-loss indicators: write skew, missing entries on read-after-write, or any inconsistency the shard's consistency check flags.
  - Latency spike localized to the cache-warm boundary on canary shards but not on control shards.

  Three things I'd ask Cyrus's team to confirm before the canary starts:

  1. The population the original five 503s came from, so the staging pass gets its statistical weight.
  2. Whether the cache-ready publish path in prod is the same code path staging validated, or whether there is a production-only branch.

Yes — the `unless` clause suppresses the actionable signal in exactly the scenario the annotation calls out. The intent is reasonable (don't page about a backlog we can't observe cleanly), but the implementation creates a coverage gap on the wrong side of the dependency. Two independent problems with what's proposed:

(1) The PromQL is structurally broken, not just risky.

`unless on()` with an empty label list requires the two vectors to have identical label sets. `up{job="metrics-router"}` carries `job="metrics-router"` plus an instance label; `rollup_queue_age_seconds` carries `job="rollup-service"` plus its own instance. Those label sets differ, so the `unless` comparator almost never matches — meaning the suppression clause is effectively a no-op regardless of metrics-router state. To actually pair the series you'd want something like `unless on(instance) up{job="metrics-router"} == 0` (and even then, see (2)). So the alert as drafted behaves differently from its annotation: it says "suppressed when metrics-router is unavailable," but the expression either always fires or fires unpredictably.

(2) Even if the vector matching is fixed, suppression is the wrong shape.

When metrics-router is fully down and unscrapable, Prometheus has no `up` sample for it — the series is absent, not 0. `up == 0` returns nothing, `unless` does not match, and the alert fires anyway. So suppression only works in the partial/flake case, not the hard outage. That's the worst of both worlds: it hides the backlog in the ambiguous middle, and pages on it (without the context it actually needs) in the full outage.

The conceptual problem: rollup backlog is data platform's owned, independently actionable condition. Whether or not metrics-router is up does not change the fact that the queue is aging — and treating upstream health as a gate makes the rollup backlog signal exactly the thing that disappears when the upstream relationship is most strained. The right pattern is to treat upstream health as correlation or severity modulation, not a gate.

Suggested safer formulation. Alert stays owned by data platform; no Infra ownership transfer.

```
ALERT: RollupQueueBacklog
  expr: max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: page
    owner: data-platform
  annotations:
    summary: "Rollup queue age > 5m on {{ $labels.instance }}"
    description: >
      Investigate rollup-service ingestion path. If metrics-router is also
      unreachable, treat upstream boundary evidence (logs, dependency map)
      as corroborating context, not a precondition for this alert.
```

Then a separate, Infra-owned alert for metrics-router availability — lives in our rules, not theirs:

```
ALERT: MetricsRouterDown
  expr: up{job="metrics-router"} == 0
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: page
    owner: infra
  annotations:
    summary: "metrics-router target unreachable"
```

If data platform wants to escalate the rollup alert based on whether the upstream is also down, do that as severity modulation — a second rule with `severity: ticket` (not page) that fires when both backlog AND upstream-down are true — rather than suppression. That preserves the rollup backlog signal at all times and keeps data platform as the owner of the backlog alert. Infra can supply the metrics-router target as context — for example a recording rule exposing `up{job="metrics-router"}` that the rollup alert annotations reference — but the gating decision stays with the backlog metric.

Two notes for Cyrus:

- Fixing the vector matching alone won't make this safe; removing the `unless` is the actual change.
- If the concern is paging on rollup backlog during planned upstream maintenance, the right mechanism is a maintenance window / silence tagged with a `suppress_until` timestamp, not an `unless` clause in the expression. Maintenance silences are auditable; expression-level suppression is silent. This is also consistent with the precedent you and I already locked in for the rollup correction-import flow (6/14) — narrow, tagged suppression with explicit re-arm, not blanket upstream-availability gating.

Worth raising in the review: ask whether the upstream-scrape concern came from a specific incident, or from a general "don't double-page." If the former, the right fix is a targeted correlation; if the latter, the right fix is just better annotation and routing, not suppression.

When the backlog traced back to the compaction-worker flag, his team rolled it back themselves rather than redirecting the incident — and the backlog cleared on the right cause. Given the pattern (hot weak at kitchen only, cold fine at kitchen, hot and cold both normal at bathroom sink and shower) combined with today's upstream plumbing work, the most likely cause is sediment/debris that the building work dislodged and that lodged at the first narrow point downstream on the hot branch — typically the aerator, the sprayer diverter, or the under-sink hot angle stop. The fact that other fixtures are normal rules out a building-wide hot-side issue, and the absence of leaks, odor, discoloration, and water hammer rules out active supply problems.

SAFE TENANT-LEVEL DIAGNOSTIC SEQUENCE
(No supply line disconnection at any step. Move to the next step only if the previous one did not resolve the issue.)

Step 1 — Reproduce and characterize
  - Fully open hot alone, then fully open cold alone. Do a quick cup-fill test (time how long each takes to fill a fixed container).
  - For a single-handle faucet, confirm "fully hot" really is the hot extreme — a partially-positioned handle can masquerade as weak flow.
  - Note whether hot flow is weak from the instant you open it, or weak only for the first second and then catches up. Weak-from-the-start supports a blockage; brief-then-normal supports a small air or debris slug that often clears itself.

Step 2 — Remove the aerator and retest (the single most common cause)
  - The aerator is the small threaded screen at the spout tip. Most unscrew by hand; if stuck, grip with pliers wrapped in a rag to avoid scratching the finish.
  - With the aerator off, re-run the cup-fill test on hot and cold.
  - If hot flow is now normal: the aerator is clogged. Rinse the screen, brush gently with an old toothbrush, soak in white vinegar 10-15 minutes if you see chalky scale, then reinstall.
  - If hot flow is still weak without the aerator: the restriction is downstream of the spout — go to Step 3.

Step 3 — If you have a pull-out or pull-down sprayer, bypass it
  - Disengage the sprayer head from its dock and let the hose hang freely. Run the faucet.
  - If hot flow is now normal: the diverter or check valve at the sprayer base is restricting hot flow. You can leave the sprayer undocked and use the spout normally until management replaces that assembly.

Step 4 — Inspect (do not force) the under-sink hot angle stop
  - Look at the small valve on the hot supply line where it exits the wall or floor. Two common types:
      - 1/4-turn lever (ball valve): lever parallel to the pipe = open, perpendicular = closed.
      - Multi-turn oval handle (compression stop): handle backed out counter-clockwise all the way = open; do not crank past the stop.
  - Confirm it is actually fully open. Do not force a stuck, corroded, or crusty handle.
  - If it is partially closed and turns easily to fully open: open it, retest, then watch the valve stem and supply line for several minutes for any moisture. If any appears, close it back to its original position and stop.

Step 5 — Gently cycle the angle stop (still no line disconnection)
  - With a towel ready, slowly turn the hot angle stop fully closed, then slowly back to fully open. This can sometimes clear a tiny bit of debris sitting at the valve seat.
  - Immediately retest the faucet, then watch the angle stop and supply line for 5-10 minutes for any seep or drip.
  - If you see any moisture: close it back, dry the area, stop. Do not retry.

Step 6 — Confirm the problem is still localized
  - Recheck hot at the bathroom sink and shower after the building work has wrapped up — they should still be normal.
  - Time how long hot water takes to arrive at the kitchen versus the bathroom sink. If the kitchen's hot-water arrival is dramatically delayed relative to the bathroom, the hot branch serving the kitchen likely has a deeper restriction, which is past tenant scope.

STOP AND CONTACT MANAGEMENT IF ANY OF THE FOLLOWING:
  - After Steps 2 through 5, hot flow is still noticeably weak at the kitchen.
  - The angle stop is stuck, corroded, leaking from the stem when touched, or you cannot confidently tell whether it is fully open.
  - Any moisture, drip, corrosion, or green/white crusty deposit appears at the angle stop, supply line, or any under-sink connection at any point during testing.
  - Hot-side flow at the bathroom sink also becomes weak — the issue is no longer localized, and this is a building hot-side problem.
  - The water heater starts making new noises, hot water disappears from any fixture, or you see temperature swings toward scalding at other taps.
  - You are not confident identifying any of the parts above — guessing with valves can turn a small inconvenience into a leak emergency.

WHAT TO TELL MANAGEMENT (gives the tech a fast, accurate handoff)
  - Exact symptom: hot weak at kitchen only; cold normal at kitchen; hot and cold both normal at bathroom sink and shower. No leaks, odor, discoloration, or water hammer.
  - That building plumbing work occurred earlier today upstream of the unit.
  - The diagnostic steps you ran and what each showed (e.g., "aerator removed, hot still weak"; or "angle stop was partially closed, fully opened it, no change").
  - That no supply lines were disconnected.

This framing points the technician straight at the likely repair — aerator or cartridge replacement, sprayer-diverter replacement, or a hot-side branch flush — rather than spending the visit on diagnosis you have already done.

Yes - what you described is consistent with normal wet disc-brake behavior, especially on a freshly installed rotor. Here is the breakdown and what to do next.

WHY WET-ONLY SQUEAL HAPPENS

A thin film of water on the rotor changes the friction interface between pad and rotor. The pad and rotor form a coupled vibration system; the water film shifts the resonant frequency of that system into the audible range, producing the high-pitched squeal for the first few stops. Once braking heat and airflow dry the rotor, the resonance stops, the coefficient of friction returns to its normal value, and the brakes go quiet. The same thing happens on cars after a wash or rain.

WHY YOUR SPECIFIC READING IS REASSURING

The other indicators rule out the conditions that would make this concerning:

  Lever firm          = no air in the hydraulic system, no fluid loss
  Straight pull       = caliper aligned, no sticking piston
  No pulse            = rotor is not warped or thickness-variant
  No scraping         = pads have material left, no metal-on-metal
  No discoloration    = no overheating and no oil/grease glazing
  Dries to quiet      = consistent with water film, not contamination

The only thing worth confirming is that the new rotor and pads were properly cleaned and bedded in when installed, because a residue or unbedded rotor can also squeal - but it would typically be loud in the dry too, and you would usually see a shiny glaze on the rotor or pad face. You saw neither.

CLEANING AND TEST SEQUENCE BEFORE THE NEXT RIDE

  1. Inspect the rotor. Hold a light behind it and look down the braking surface; reject anything with a visible bend, a deep blue/purple heat tint, or grooves you can catch a fingernail in.
  2. Wipe the rotor with a clean lint-free cloth dampened with 90%+ isopropyl alcohol. Apply to the cloth, not by spraying, so overspray does not reach the pads or caliper piston seals. Rotate the wheel while wiping so the entire swept arc is cleaned. Use one cloth per wipe so you are not redepositing residue.
  3. Inspect the pads through the caliper window. The face should be uniform in color, with even wear across both pads, and at least 1.5-2 mm of friction material remaining. If either pad looks shiny black, oily, or has metal flakes, replace the pads as a set.
  4. Re-bed if anything felt marginal. From a quiet stretch, do 20 to 30 progressive stops starting at low effort (roughly walking-pace speed, gentle lever) and building to moderate speed with firmer lever. Coast between stops long enough for the rotor to cool to the touch. This rebuilds an even transfer layer on the rotor face and quiets new hardware. Avoid any single hard stop until the bed-in set is finished - a hot, unbedded rotor can hot-spot and then warp.
  5. Test ride on dry pavement. Confirm the lever feels the same as before, the bike tracks straight under firm braking from both levers, and there is no rub, click, or pulse. The first wet ride after a clean-and-bed should still squeal briefly and then go quiet - that is the expected pattern.

SIGNS THAT MEAN STOP RIDING IMMEDIATELY

  - Lever goes soft, sinks to the bar, or requires pumping to build pressure (air in the line, fluid leak, or a failing seal).
  - The front wheel pulls left or right under braking (misaligned caliper or a sticking piston on one side).
  - A pulsing or rhythmic thump through the lever or fork (warped rotor; this can progress to a lock-up if the warp is severe).
  - A continuous grinding, metallic scraping, or howl that does not stop when the brakes are released (pads worn to backing plate, or contamination that has destroyed pad material).
  - Visible rotor cracks, deep scoring, a blue or rainbow heat tint across a wide area, or a hotspot you can feel as a raised ridge with a fingernail.
  - Any fluid on the caliper, hose, or lever body (hydraulic leak).
  - Loss of stopping power relative to your baseline - especially if the lever feels fine but the bike does not slow as expected.
  - Burning smell, smoke from the caliper area, or a rotor too hot to touch after a stop (glazed pads, seized piston, or stuck rub).

If any of those appear, do not ride the bike until the issue is resolved. For the first two (soft lever, pulling) and the fluid leak, the bike should not be ridden even to a shop - that is a flatbed situation.

Honest note on method: this environment doesn't expose a shell or code-execution tool to me (only the work apps and session search), so I can't run the sum through a calculator. The arithmetic is simple enough to do reliably by hand, and I'm showing every step.

Calculation (US 120 V circuit):

  Strip rating:  15 A x 120 V = 1800 W

  Existing load:
    Monitor          120 W
    Laptop adapter   140 W
    Network switch    30 W
    Desk charger      10 W
                   -----
    Subtotal         300 W

  + Task light       90 W
                   -----
  TOTAL with light  390 W

That's 390 / 1800 = ~22% of the strip's stated capacity (about 3.25 A on a 15 A breaker/strip). Comfortably within the rating on paper.

Practical caveats worth knowing (these are why "stated" load isn't the whole story):

  - The strip and breaker are thermal/magnetic, not wattage-limited; they trip on overcurrent, and UL also treats 1800 W as a hard ceiling for the receptacle.
  - Continuous loads (>3 hrs) are conventionally capped at 80% = 1440 W; a task light on a workday can be continuous. 390 W is still far below that.
  - "Stated watts" on adapters/monitors is often the maximum, not steady-state draw. Real draw is usually lower, so the load is even smaller than the math says.
  - Each outlet on a residential circuit is usually daisy-chained with others on the same 15 A breaker; the strip's 15 A is only as good as the wall circuit feeding it. If other heavy loads share that circuit (space heater, microwave, hair dryer, etc.), the breaker, not the strip, is the real limit.

Warning signs - unplug the task light (and the strip) immediately if you notice any of these:

  - Warm-to-hot plug, outlet faceplate, strip housing, or any device brick
  - Discoloration, scorch marks, or melting on the strip, plug, or wall outlet
  - Buzzing, crackling, sizzling, or a burning/ozone/plastic smell
  - Flickering lights on the strip or in the room when the light turns on
  - Tripped breaker or any GFCI/AFCI reset popping after you add the load
  - Loose fit (plug slides in/out easily, or falls out)
  - The strip is daisy-chained off another strip or an extension cord
  - Any sign of liquid near the strip

Your pre-plug check (cool, undamaged, no buzz/odor, no daisy-chain) already cleared the main physical hazards. At 390 W / ~3.25 A on a 15 A strip with nothing else wrong, the task light is safe to plug in - just stay attentive for the warning signs above during the first hour or so of use, and again any time the strip is under continuous load.

# Sphere collector exposure: assessment and bounded staging plan

## 1. What's actually exposed right now

Two OTLP ingress paths on `0.95.0-sphere.12`, both behind edge-gateway, both still reachable:

- **OTLP/HTTP receiver with `Accept-Encoding: gzip` decoding.** This is the path the upstream advisory is about. A peer that can negotiate gzip and send a malformed compressed payload can drive the receiver into the decompression failure mode the advisory describes.
- **OTLP/gRPC.** gRPC framing has its own compression negotiation (`grpc-accept-encoding: gzip`), and on a collector that's vulnerable to the same defect class, a malformed gzipped stream on the gRPC port is a separate, independent reach path. The advisory text focuses on HTTP, but I would not assume the gRPC path is safe on 0.95 just because the HTML writeup says "OTLP/HTTP." Until I see a diff confirming otherwise, treat both receivers as in-scope.

The gateway gives you two things, and only two things:

- A `decompressed_size` cap on the HTTP body before it gets handed to the collector.
- A `compression_ratio` cap on the expansion factor between compressed and decompressed bytes.

Both reduce the *reachable* set of malformed inputs. They do not eliminate the class, because:

- A malformed gzip stream can trigger the failure mode at sub-cap sizes — the issue is malformedness of the compressed payload, not its inflated size.
- The gRPC path goes through the same gateway only at L4; gateway-level body decompression checks are typically not applied to the gRPC port. Even if they are, the gRPC compression negotiates inside the HTTP/2 stream, after gateway handoff.

So the honest framing for Hema is: gateway cuts the surface area meaningfully for the HTTP path, but it is **not** the fix. The fix is the collector version.

## 2. Where Sphere sits vs. the fixed line

- Deployed (staging + prod, both envs): `otel-collector 0.95.0-sphere.12` — vulnerable.
- Fix line: upstream `0.96.0`.
- Candidate built and unit-passed in your environment: `otel-collector 0.96.2-sphere.7`. 0.96.2 includes the fix plus any 0.96.x backports, and the `.sphere.7` is your internal patch surface (which is why it has to go through Infra, not a vanilla bump).

There is no authorization yet for any rollout. That is the entire gap: there's a known-vulnerable deployment in prod, no approved path off it.

## 3. What I'm explicitly not claiming

- I'm not claiming the gateway *eliminates* the issue. It reduces reachable inputs on HTTP; gRPC is a separate question.
- I'm not claiming `0.96.2-sphere.7` is production-ready because build + unit pass. Build + unit covers correctness in isolation. It does not cover: receiver behavior under real OTLP/gRPC + HTTP traffic parity, processor pipeline equivalence, exporter backpressure under staging load, metric/log/traces cardinality regression, or memory and goroutine profiles at staging scale.
- I'm not claiming a deadline. The advisory doesn't (in what you described) name an active in-the-wild campaign, so urgency is "patch on the normal cadence, don't sit on it," not "emergency."

## 4. Bounded staging validation sequence for `0.96.2-sphere.7`

Goal: prove receiver + pipeline equivalence against staging traffic at non-zero load, with a rollback path that's been exercised, *before* anyone asks Infra to schedule prod.

### Phase 0 — Pre-flight (no traffic change)
- Confirm with Infra which collector config(s) staging runs. There may be a single file or split (receivers / processors / exporters). Capture the rendered config from the current `0.95.0-sphere.12` deployment as the diff baseline.
- Confirm the receiver list and ports are unchanged across the bump: OTLP/HTTP, OTLP/gRPC, any host metrics / kubelet receivers present on staging today. If `.sphere.7` adds or removes a receiver, that's a config diff, not just a version diff.
- Confirm the build artifact includes both the HTTP and gRPC patch. If your internal patch only covers the HTTP path, the gRPC validation steps below are also the validation that gRPC is still vulnerable, and you need to flag that to Infra before going further.
- Identify the staging canary slot. Per your standing rule (Mon AM staging cutover, no Fri-PM/weekend deploys), this lands on a Monday morning.

### Phase 1 — Config-parity smoke (single replica, off the load balancer)
- Roll `0.96.2-sphere.7` to a single staging replica, **not** receiving production-shaped traffic.
- Feed it a fixed synthetic OTLP fixture: HTTP POST with a valid gzip-compressed payload; gRPC unary export with `grpc-accept-encoding: gzip`. Assert the receiver accepts both and the expected processors/exporters fire.
- Feed it the **advisory's reproducer** (a malformed gzip body that would crash 0.95). Assert: receiver returns 4xx (HTTP) or `INVALID_ARGUMENT` (gRPC), no panic, no goroutine leak. This is the "fix is in" check.

### Phase 2 — Shadow / canary at 5% for 60 minutes
- Shift 5% of staging OTLP traffic to the `0.96.2-sphere.7` instance using whatever weight/shift knob staging uses (one weighted upstream, one canary upstream — don't try to do this at the receiver level).
- Watch for 60 minutes:
  - **Receiver parity:** per-reporter counts (OTLP/HTTP, OTLP/gRPC) within ±5% of the 0.95 baseline for the same window.
  - **Pipeline parity:** `dropped` counters on processors, `send_failed` on exporters, retry queue depths — none of these should move.
  - **The specific fix's symptoms:** receiver goroutine count flat, no new panic/restart lines, no spike in `decompression_error` or equivalent.
  - **Memory:** RSS within the band you've previously observed; collector restart count = 0.
- Promote decision rule: green on all four. If any one is off, hold and post a doc comment on the staging runbook entry before promoting.

### Phase 3 — 50% for 4 hours, then 100% for the rest of the day
- Same panels, but with the collector now serving half of staging volume. At 100%, leave it on staging for the remainder of the business day so it sees the late-afternoon and early-evening traffic mix (cardinality peaks, batch flushes, exporter backpressure cycles).
- Capture a `pprof` goroutine + heap snapshot at 100% soak and diff against a `0.95.0-sphere.12` baseline at the same hour-of-day. Internal patch surfaces tend to leak goroutines or hold memory differently; this is where you'd see it.

### Phase 4 — Rollback rehearsal (do this, don't assume it)
- On staging, *before* declaring staging green, execute one rollback: shift 100% back to `0.95.0-sphere.12`, confirm collector comes back clean and traffic resumes. If the rollback path isn't actually exercised in staging, the prod rollback isn't proven — it's just hoped for.

### Phase 5 — Sign-off, then ask Infra
Only after Phase 0–4 are green:
- Staging soak duration at 100%: ≥ 1 full business day with the panels above flat.
- A staging runbook entry that captures the four panels, the rollback command, and the on-call escalation if a panel moves post-rollout.
- Then take it to Hema with: "staging at 100% for X hours, four panels flat, rollback rehearsed, request Infra schedule prod."

## 5. What I want from Hema, framed concretely

1. Authorization to run Phase 1–3 in staging on the next Mon AM cutover window.
2. Infra confirmed for the prod scheduling conversation (don't let the staging soak slip into the following week without a prod date).
3. A named decision-maker for the gRPC fix status. If `.sphere.7` only patches HTTP, gRPC stays vulnerable at the same version, and "upgrade to 0.96.2-sphere.7" doesn't close the exposure you described — that's worth knowing before the staging window opens.

Good news first: a building valve replacement almost never triggers a boil-water advisory, and what you saw (brief sputtering + light brown water clearing within seconds, no smell, no sediment after clearing) is the textbook signature of dislodged pipe sediment — iron, manganese, and mineral scale that gets shaken loose whenever flow is restored. That's an aesthetic problem, not a contamination problem, and your caution about not running appliances yet is the right instinct. Here's how to finish safely.

STEP 0 — STOP-NOW RED FLAGS
Stop flushing and contact management before running anything else if any of these appear at any point during the sequence below:
  - A fixture fails to clear after 5 minutes of continuous cold running, or keeps cycling clear → brown → clear → brown
  - Any smell other than faint chlorine: sulfur / rotten egg (possible bacteria or sewage), sewage, gasoline, chemical, or earthy/musty that persists after flushing
  - Visible particles, flakes, or grit that don't clear (sediment looks like dissolved color; particles are different)
  - Milky water that doesn't clear in a glass after sitting 1–2 minutes (small air bubbles are normal and rise; persistent cloudiness is not)
  - Hot water stays discolored after cold is fully clear and you've run hot taps 10+ minutes → likely water-heater sediment; if the heater is building-owned, management handles
  - Low pressure, no pressure, or new leaks/moisture anywhere near fixtures (valve work can dislodge seals upstream of you)
  - Management or your utility issues a boil-water, do-not-drink, or do-not-use notice at any point
  - Anyone in the household develops GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever) within a day or two of exposure — call a doctor AND notify management

STEP 1 — PREP (5 minutes)
  - Remove the aerator screens from the kitchen and bathroom faucets. They trap sediment and will keep re-staining the flow even after the line is clear. Put them in a bowl, rinse, set aside.
  - If you have a refrigerator water/ice line, pull the fridge out enough to access the supply saddle valve or tee; you'll flush this in step 5.

STEP 2 — FLUSH COLD LINES, LOWEST-RISK FIXTURE FIRST
Order matters: start where contamination would matter least so you're not pulling more sediment past the fixtures you'll drink from.
  1. Toilet — flush 3–4 times; each refill pulls cold water through the branch.
  2. Bathtub cold tap — open fully, run 2–3 minutes (cold only). The tub gives you the highest flow, which clears lines fastest.
  3. Bathroom sink cold tap — 2–3 minutes.
  4. Utility sink or washing-machine cold taps (if accessible) — 2–3 minutes.
  5. Kitchen cold tap — 2–3 minutes. This is the one that discolored first, so it may take the longest; if it sputters again, that's just trapped air, not a problem.

At each step: water should be crystal clear, no smell, no particles. Move to the next fixture only when the current one is and stays clear.

STEP 3 — FLUSH HOT LINES (only after cold is fully clear everywhere)
Sediment that entered the cold inlet during the work settles in the bottom of the water heater, and the heater held stagnant water the whole outage, so the hot side needs longer.
  - Kitchen hot tap: 5+ minutes
  - Bathroom hot tap: 5+ minutes
  - If your water heater is in-unit: after the taps run clear, you can also open the heater's drain valve at the bottom into a bucket for a minute or two to flush tank sediment directly. If it's building-owned, don't touch it — that's management's job.

STEP 4 — APPLIANCES (only after steps 2 and 3 are fully clear)
  - Dishwasher: run an empty rinse cycle with no detergent. Most machines have a "rinse only" or a normal cycle with the detergent cup open and empty.
  - Washing machine: run an empty hot/cold rinse-and-spin cycle, no detergent. Or do a small dark-load wash (old towels) first as a sacrificial run.
  - Don't add detergent to either until the rinse cycle came out visibly clean.

STEP 5 — DRINKING-WATER FILTERS
Filters and their housings sat full of stagnant water during the outage; sediment and biofilm risk concentrate here.
  - Refrigerator dispenser/ice maker: discard any ice currently in the bin, then run 2–3 gallons through the dispenser (about 5–8 minutes). Replace the filter cartridge if it's near its rated lifespan.
  - Under-sink filter (reverse osmosis, etc.): open the dedicated faucet and run 3–5 gallons; replace the cartridge if it's old or sat unused for more than a day or two.
  - Pitcher filter (Brita, Pur, etc.): toss the current cartridge regardless of age, install fresh, then run two full pitchers through and discard.
  - If any filter sat dry or with stagnant water for the whole outage, replace the cartridge — don't try to flush it clean.

STEP 6 — REASSEMBLE
  - Reinstall aerators on both faucets.
  - Run each fixture for 30 seconds one more time to confirm everything is clear.

WHAT "NORMAL" LOOKS LIKE GOING FORWARD
  - No discoloration at any fixture for 24 hours
  - No return of sputtering (occasional air bursts in the first day are fine; persistent sputtering is not)
  - No odor, no leaks, pressure back to normal

If everything above holds, you're done. If something discolors again later, especially intermittently, that's a sign the building's valve or a section of pipe upstream is still shedding sediment or wasn't fully reopened — call management and ask them to verify the valve is fully open and to run a building-side flush from a hose bib if your building has one.

Sources behind the recommendations above: standard post-outage / post-maintenance guidance from CDC, EPA, and municipal water utilities (e.g., AWWA), and water-heater manufacturer instructions on flushing after stagnation. No tools were needed for this answer — it's a pure-knowledge question.

**Option A — hard 2,000-point client cap**

Failure modes:
- Peak local queue at 88% on the burstiest client. The cap turns the 0.4% tail into a binary accept/reject boundary at exactly 2,000, so the burstiest client sees essentially all of its 0.4% become rejections while the other two clients see close to zero.
- Preserves point accounting, but forces every burst to split into N x 2,000 requests. Each split adds connection overhead, request-handling state, and a partial-batch failure mode (some chunks accepted, one rejected).
- 88% is a single-client peak. Aggregate impact across the three clients is not stated, so we can't tell whether the cap creates an isolation problem (burstiest client's split traffic affecting others) or a contention problem (the splits themselves adding load).

Evidence gaps:
- The burstiest client's position inside 2,001-9,600 is not given. If their burst mode is 2,001-2,200, the cap creates ~5x more requests per burst; if it's 8,000-9,600, it creates 3-5x. Different magnitudes, different operational consequence.
- Retry and partial-batch behavior at the boundary is not modeled. We don't know whether the SDK batches-and-retries, batches-and-fails, or fails-open with over-the-limit single requests.
- The reproduced latency path that Option B is meant to leave open — does Option A actually close it? It closes it for the burstiest client only, and only above 2,000. The 2,001-9,600 band is exactly where the latency path was reproduced, so Option A's closure is mechanical (rejection) rather than evidentiary (we measured no latency there).

**Option B — documentation-only guidance**

Failure modes:
- The reproduced latency path remains possible. This option changes nothing in code or protocol; it depends on client teams choosing to batch smaller.
- No enforcement signal, so post-hoc we cannot tell whether the guidance is working, whether the 0.4% would have tapered anyway, or whether the latency path is even being exercised under current load.
- SDK drift across the three clients is uncontrolled. Pin-to-old-SDK behavior is invisible to us.

Evidence gaps:
- We do not know whether any of the three clients is willing or structurally able to honor a soft guidance. The 30-day distribution was measured against current behavior; it does not tell us what fraction of those bursts were deliberate (client knowingly batching above 2,000) vs. accidental (a single misconfigured producer).
- We cannot measure the latency path without instrumentation that docs-only does not add. The path itself remains unobservable in the new state.
- We cannot distinguish "guidance is followed" from "bursts are rare" from "path is dormant."

**Option C — soft rejection above 8,000**

Failure modes:
- 0.03% of recorded requests are rejected. But the 2,001-8,000 band — most of the 0.4% tail, roughly 0.37% of all requests — still goes through and presumably still triggers the latency path.
- Introduces explicit client retry and partial-delivery semantics as new contract surfaces. The risk isn't just SDK update lag; it's partial-state failure modes (some points committed, some rejected) where the client's responsibility for replay is underspecified.
- The 0.03% number is a count, not a temporal rate. If those rejections are correlated (one client in retry storm at one moment), the impact at that moment is higher than the average suggests.
- Retry storms: if a client retries an 8,500-point batch without backoff, soft rejection amplifies load instead of bounding it. SDK-side retry-with-backoff is not established.

Evidence gaps:
- The split between 2,001-8,000 and 8,001-9,600 inside the 0.4% tail is not given. If most of the tail is below 8,000 (plausible from the framing), Option C rejects a small fraction of the actual latency-incurring traffic.
- Partial-delivery semantics have not been tested across the three clients. Each will likely interpret "explicit retry" differently.
- The 8,000 threshold is not justified by data — it is a round number, not a measured queue-utilization knee.
- We have no evidence that the latency path is bounded by point count alone. If it is also driven by point-type composition, payload size, or per-point cost, an 8,000-point threshold does not directly address it.

**Cross-option comparison**

A (hard 2k cap):
  - rejected: 0% of all requests (0% of 0.4% tail)
  - latency-tail still served: 0%
  - new contract surface: none
  - failure mode introduced: burst fragmentation, partial-batch failures
  - enforcement signal: measurable
  - evidence for closing latency path: mechanical (rejection), not measured

B (docs only):
  - rejected: 0%
  - latency-tail still served: 100%
  - new contract surface: none
  - failure mode introduced: drift, ignored guidance, unmeasurable state
  - enforcement signal: none
  - evidence for closing latency path: none

C (soft reject >8k):
  - rejected: 0.03% of all requests (~7.5% of the 0.4% tail)
  - latency-tail still served: ~92.5% of the 0.4% tail (~0.37% of all)
  - new contract surface: retry + partial-delivery
  - failure mode introduced: partial-state, retry storms
  - enforcement signal: measurable but only on reject events
  - evidence for closing latency path: partial — bounded only above 8,000

The honest read: the temporary experiment setting is being treated as a candidate for permanence, but the 30-day distribution does not by itself endorse any of the three. Each option leaves a different shape of the 0.4% tail in place, and none of them is supported by evidence that fully closes the reproduced latency path. Option A moves closure to a hard boundary; Option B does not close it; Option C closes it only above 8,000.

Which option is defensible depends on which evidence gap is cheapest to close next:

- Option A becomes defensible once we can measure the other two clients' queue utilization under the cap and model split-burst retry behavior. Without that, we are approving a 5x request-multiplier on one client on the strength of one peak number.
- Option C becomes defensible once we have client commitment on retry-with-backoff and partial-delivery semantics, plus evidence that the latency path is actually bounded above 8,000 (which the distribution does not establish — we only know 0.4% sits in 2,001-9,600, not that anything inside 2,001-8,000 is benign).
- Option B is defensible only if the latency path is acceptable as-is, in which case the 30-day analysis is informative but not actionable and the right answer is to do nothing rather than document.

The non-obvious finding is that Option C, the most operationally cautious-looking of the three, actually serves the largest fraction of the latency-incurring tail (~92.5% of the 0.4%) and so does the least to close the original failure. If the disposition is meant to address the reproduced latency path, the analysis has to acknowledge that none of the three options closes it on the evidence given.

A few thoughts, mostly confirmations of what you're already doing, plus a couple of small concrete moves.

You've already set the right shape: she asked for a shower and a quiet hour, and you're honoring it without making her justify the request. The hardest thing tonight is going to be resisting the urge to make it better through conversation. She'll come back to you when she's ready, and if she doesn't come back tonight at all, that's fine.

Things you can do in the next hour without her having to engage:

  - Warm the apartment if it's cool, and put a glass of water on the bathroom counter or just outside the door. No comment required.
  - Have something warm and easy to eat available. Soup, toast, tea. The point isn't that she eats; it's that deciding to eat costs her zero effort. "There's soup if you want it" is enough. Don't watch her eat.
  - Stay in the apartment, doing something low-demand. Dishes, a book, your phone. Be present, not hovering. She said she didn't want to be alone. The version of "not alone" she usually means at this hour is someone in the next room, not someone asking questions.
  - Take Kibo out for a short walk if his timing works. Brief, calm route, front-clip harness, short leash. You know his triggers. This isn't you retreating; it's giving her the apartment to herself for twenty minutes, which is often its own form of company.

When she comes out of the shower:

  - A small physical gesture if she moves into it. Hand on her back, a brief hug, sitting next to her on the couch. Don't hold on longer than she's holding on. Don't initiate a long embrace that requires her to decide whether to cry.
  - One low-key sentence that doesn't need a reply. "I'm glad you're home." Or just "Hi." Then let her set the next move.
  - Do not ask what happened, who the patient was, whether she did everything right, or whether she's okay. You already know the answers to the first three, and "are you okay" puts her in the position of having to reassure you.

If she talks:

  - Listen. Don't ask clinical follow-ups. Don't say "that must have been so hard" more than once if at all. Mirroring ("yeah," "mm") and silence are more useful than commentary. She doesn't need you to understand the case. She needs you to be the person who isn't the case.
  - If she cries, stay. If she's angry, stay. If she's flat and matter-of-fact, stay. The flat version is often the one that needs the most steadiness from you, because it'll feel like she's fine and your instinct will be to relax. Don't.

If she doesn't talk:

  - Don't fill the silence. Sit with her. Something low-stakes on in the background is fine, a show you've both seen, music she likes, but don't make small talk to prove everything's normal. Let the evening be quiet. The quiet is the support.

One thing to flag for yourself, gently: you're running night shifts and you're probably depleted too. Supporting someone through a hard shift while you're running on empty is its own kind of work. If there's a window tonight where she's settled, even asleep, protect thirty minutes for yourself. You being okay tomorrow is part of how you keep being useful to her the day after.

The line you're trying not to cross, between honoring the grief and pathologizing it, is the right line to stay on. An attending losing a patient is the human cost of the job, not a clinical event. She knows every resource, every framework, every hotline number. What she doesn't get at work is someone who treats her like a person and not a case. That's what tonight is for.

If a few days from now she's not sleeping, she's shut down in a way that feels new, or she's talking about not going back, that's a different conversation, and it can wait. Tonight is just tonight.

The 240 points did not disappear in transport. They were rejected at the collector's content-validation stage after the request body had already been fully accepted. The four-minute dashboard gap is real, but its origin sits between HTTP success and series persistence.

Where the loss actually occurred

  Client -> Edge-gateway -> Collector
    600 requests emitted (client)
    600 forwarded (edge-gateway counts requests, not points)
    600 received (collector request count)
    240 points rejected inside those requests (timestamp validation:
        +7 min future exceeds the configured tolerance window)
    HTTP 200 returned with a partial-success body (OTLP semantics)
    Client logs only the status code -> infers "all good"

The transport layer delivered every byte. The collector's ingest pipeline then evaluated each point and dropped the out-of-skew ones before they were batched/exported. So:

  Transport success = bytes arrived and an HTTP response was issued (200).
  Point acceptance = the point passed validation, was attributed to a series,
                    and was persisted/exported.

These are orthogonal. HTTP 200 in OTLP guarantees only that the collector parsed and considered the payload, not that every point inside was retained. A response with partial_success.rejected_points > 0 is the explicit signal that some points were dropped while the request itself still returned 200. That is by design in the OTLP spec -- partial success is a first-class response, not an error.

Why 240 points, and why a 4-minute dashboard gap

The client clock is producing timestamps roughly 7 minutes ahead of the collector's wall clock. The collector's timestamp tolerance (commonly configured around 5 minutes, sometimes per-signal) refuses anything beyond that window. The 4-minute gap on the dashboard is not arbitrary -- it is the points in the most recent ~4 minutes whose timestamps were rejected, leaving a hole on the read path even though the request that "contained" them succeeded at HTTP.

Smallest diagnostic corrections

  1. Pull collector-side rejection metrics / logs: otelcol_exporter_sent_failed_points
     and the collector log line for rejected points with reason = "timestamp too far
     in future" (or equivalent). This is the ground truth for which points were
     dropped and why.
  2. Read the response body on a sample of the 600 client requests -- confirm
     partial_success.rejected_points is non-zero and inspect the error message.
     If it is empty/zero, the cause is elsewhere; if it is populated, the
     rejection is happening at the collector.
  3. Compare client wall-clock, collector wall-clock, and an NTP reference. A
     7-minute skew is far beyond normal NTP drift and almost always means the
     client host's clock is wrong (VM clock not synced, container clock not
     inheriting host time, manual override, frozen VM after suspend, etc.).
  4. Check the collector's timestamp-tolerance configuration. If tolerance is
     tighter than the team's actual clock drift, every drift event becomes a
     silent drop.

Smallest client-accounting corrections

  1. Stop logging only HTTP status. The client must parse the OTLP response body
     and surface partial_success -- at minimum, count rejected points per
     request and emit them as a client-side metric/log line. HTTP 200 with
     rejected_points > 0 is a partial-failure outcome, not a clean success.
  2. The client's "sent vs. accepted" reconciliation must compare against the
     sum of rejected points, not the count of 200 responses. Today the client
     equates 600 requests with 600 successful requests; that is the bug.
  3. Fix the client clock. Until timestamps are within tolerance, the collector
     will keep rejecting. NTP, container/VM clock inheritance -- verify and
     lock it.
  4. Cheap addition: record the rejection reason string per request so future
     skew events are diagnosable from the client side without a separate
     collector-log dive.

Why this is not an ingest transport failure

  - Edge-gateway forwarded all 600 requests.
  - The collector received and parsed all 600.
  - The HTTP response was 200 in every case.
  - The OTLP protocol contract was honored -- the collector reported exactly
    which points it refused and why.
  - The transport path performed correctly; the loss is in point-level
    validation against a clock-skew tolerance, and the visibility gap is in
    the client's accounting.

Remediation belongs to (a) the client's clock and (b) the client's response-body logging, not to the edge-gateway, the collector's receiver, or the wire path. Labeling this a transport failure would route investigation and fixes to layers that already did their job correctly.

Verdict: high-confidence phishing. The email has too many independent red flags to be a legitimate hospital benefits notice, and Devika's instinct not to click is correct.

Phishing indicators (matched to what was in the message):

1. High-pressure deadline tied to immediate action ("tonight at 11:59 PM"). Real benefits notices give weeks of lead time and don't threaten same-day suspension over an incomplete form.

2. Sender domain `benefits-manhattanhealth.co` is not the hospital's real domain. Real hospital benefits traffic comes from the hospital's own domain (e.g. `*.<hospital>.org` or `*.hospital-name.org`), not a lookalike or generic third-party "benefits-" domain. The `.co` TLD is also unusual for a U.S. hospital benefits vendor.

3. Shortened URL (bit.ly) in a credential/identity request. Legitimate benefits portals never ask you to click a shortener to verify identity. They tell you to log in through your normal portal.

4. Asks for hospital password and DOB together. A legitimate benefits site already has her DOB on file and never asks for a password via an emailed link. This is the classic "harvest credentials + PII" combo for credential-stuffing or identity fraud.

5. Missing personalization and identifiers. No employee ID, no plan name, no HR contact, no case/ticket number. Real benefits notices reference her by name and include verifiable specifics.

6. Generic salutation ("Your 2025 benefits verification") instead of her name.

7. Tone and layout of a "final notice" from a vendor — designed to short-circuit careful reading.

What Devika already did right: did not click, opened the real portal from her saved bookmark, and saw no matching alert. That is the correct pattern — the bookmark is the trusted path, the email is not.

Safe reporting steps (run in this order):

1. Report to the hospital's security/IT team, not to the sender. Most hospitals have one of:
   - A "Report Phish" button in Outlook/OWA (preferred — preserves full headers).
   - A reporting address like `phishing@<hospital>.org` or `security@<hospital>.org`.
   If she doesn't know which, the IT helpdesk number on the hospital intranet is the right starting point.

2. Forward the message as an attachment (not just forwarded body) so headers survive. In Outlook: Home > More > Forward as Attachment. This preserves the `Return-Path`, `Received`, and authentication results that IT needs to block the sender at the gateway.

3. After IT confirms they have it, delete the email from Inbox and Deleted Items so a tap on a phone notification later can't accidentally open the link.

4. Do not reply, do not click, do not call any phone number in the email. Any phone number in a phishing email is part of the lure.

5. If her hospital SSO is reused anywhere (personal email, banking, etc.), treat the email as confirmation that her hospital address is being targeted and consider whether any password reuse needs to be tightened — but do this from a trusted device, not in response to anything in the email.

Independent verification — confirm there is no real action needed:

1. The bookmarked portal showing no alert is strong evidence the email is bogus, but she should still confirm in one more trusted channel:

2. Call the hospital's HR/Benefits office using a number from the official hospital intranet directory or her own badge/ID card — never a number from the email. Ask whether any 2025 verification is actually open for her and what the deadline is.

3. If she has an HR/Benefines representative by name, email them directly using the address in her hospital address book (not a reply to this message) to double-check.

4. Optional but useful: report the sender domain to the hospital's abuse contact and to the registrar of `benefits-manhattanhealth.co` (via `abuse@<registrar>` found in a WHOIS lookup from a trusted device) so the lookalike can be taken down before other staff get the same lure.

One operational note: since she is an attending at a hospital, this kind of phishing against clinical staff is common and frequently used as a foothold for business-email-compromise or to pivot into clinical systems. Reporting it quickly (today, not Monday) is worth it even if it feels routine.

Bottom line up front: with the described findings — 4 mm surface cut, no casing threads visible, no tube visible, no sidewall damage, no bulge, pressure stable after 30 minutes — the tire is in the "rideable locally with a boot, replace at the next convenient interval" category. The case for that call, plus the inspection sequence to confirm it before you roll, is below.

INSPECTION SEQUENCE (do these in order; each one tightens or overturns the conclusion of the one before)

1. Visual, with raking light
   Hold a flashlight or phone light nearly parallel to the tread so it rakes across the cut. Look for:
   - Embedded fragments. Glass rarely exits cleanly. The chunk you pulled is often one of several.
   - Casing threads — fine black/dark woven fibers. "No threads visible" at straight-on angles can still mean threads visible at a raking angle.
   - Inner liner — the matte black butyl/latex surface under the casing. If you can see this, the cut is full-thickness and the tube is exposed.
   - Cut geometry. A clean linear slit behaves very differently from a star, flap, or wedge. Flaps flex open under load and propagate; slits stay closed.

2. Probe
   Use a fingertip or a rounded toothpick (not a sharp pick — you don't want to drive glass deeper). Press the cut edges toward each other and gently rotate the tire so the cut is at the contact patch against the floor:
   - Firm floor under the cut, edges meet cleanly, no inward "give" → casing structurally intact.
   - Soft floor, edges separate, you can feel the tube through the cut → casing compromised regardless of whether threads are visually obvious.

3. Inside-out check (most informative single step)
   Deflate, unseat one bead on the cut side, push the tire wall inward, and run a finger inside opposite the cut. You're checking:
   - Inner liner condition at that spot — smooth and continuous means the cut has not penetrated.
   - Any remaining glass or debris on the inside surface.
   - Whether the casing felt "spongy" from the inside, which would indicate partial damage invisible from the outside.
   This takes about a minute and resolves most of the residual uncertainty from steps 1 and 2.

4. Pressure hold
   You already have 30 minutes at stable pressure. That's a strong negative for an active leak. For full confidence, re-inflate to spec and re-check at 2 hours and again next morning before the first ride. A real puncture through the casing loses over hours, not minutes. Optional but definitive: lower the cut section into a basin of water and look for bubbles.

5. Load test before committing to a ride
   Re-inflate. With the wheel back on the bike, sit on the saddle with the cut at the contact patch. Have someone watch the cut from behind the bike:
   - Cut stays closed, no gap opens → riding is acceptable.
   - Cut gapes, edges separate, or you hear/feel a "pop" → casing failed under load, do not ride.

DECISION MATRIX

- Casing threads visible at any point → replace before riding.
- Inner liner or tube visible → replace before riding.
- Slow leak (pressure drops between checks) → replace before riding.
- Bulge anywhere, or any sidewall involvement → replace before riding.
- Clean surface cut, no threads, no liner exposure, firm floor on probe, smooth liner from inside, pressure holds, no gape under load → ride locally with a boot; replace at next opportunity.

WHAT TO DO BEFORE YOU ROLL, GIVEN YOUR DESCRIBED FINDINGS

1. Run step 3 (inside-out check). It's the single highest-yield action and tells you more than everything else combined.
2. Mount a tire boot from the inside. A vulcanizing patch (Park Tool VP-1 / equivalent) cut to cover the cut with margin, or a purpose-made tire boot, or in a pinch a folded section of tough material. The boot does two things: it stops the cut from propagating under road flex, and it shields the tube from any glass fragments still embedded in the casing.
3. Re-inflate to spec, ride 1–2 km at low effort, then re-check pressure and visually re-inspect the cut. If unchanged, you have your answer for that day.
4. Order a replacement tire. The boot makes the cut safe for now, but the casing in that area has been compromised and is the most likely spot for the next failure. Don't wait for the next piece of glass.

RIDE PROTOCOL WHILE BOOTED

- Check pressure before every ride for the first week; every ride is fine after that.
- Stay off curb hits, potholes, and hard braking on the cut — anything that loads the tire at an angle tends to flex cuts open.
- Local-only range (your Prospect Park loops, neighborhood errands) is reasonable. Longer rides with no spare tube and no boot material along are not, until the tire is replaced.

STOP IMMEDIATELY AND DO NOT RIDE IF

- Pressure drops more than ~5 psi between checks.
- The cut visibly grows, opens under load, or develops a flap.
- A new bulge appears anywhere on the tire.
- Any casing threads become visible, or the inner liner becomes visible.
- Sidewall damage appears — sidewall cuts are a different risk class and the same call does not apply.

If step 3 turns up something the outside view didn't — a rough spot on the liner, embedded glass still inside, a soft floor on the probe — the answer flips to replace before riding. Until that step is done, the call above is provisional rather than final.

This is written so Devika and you can run it without re-reading. Bounded = active monitoring closes once defined exit conditions are met, not "until it feels fine."

----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. CURING PERIOD — next 48 hours (do not extend)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Do not touch:
  - The exterior joint (no probing, no caulk additions, no painting over)
  - The interior paint at and below the repair zone (no spot-painting)
  - The window trim / sill in that quadrant

Maintain stable interior conditions where reasonable:
  - Keep room temp roughly steady (large swings drive moisture in/out of plaster and confuse the meter readings)
  - Avoid draping fabric or mounting anything against the affected wall section
  - Keep the outlet cover undisturbed; do not unplug/replug the bedroom outlet in that wall

Daily photo log (same angle, same lighting):
  - Interior: wide shot of wall + close-up of repair zone + outlet
  - Exterior: close-up of the joint (lower-left return)
  - Note time of day on each photo

----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. BASELINE — record today, before any more weather
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Moisture meter:
  - Affected spot: ___ (current reading)
  - Control area (same wall, untouched zone): ___
  - Delta: ___
  - Meter model + setting (pin/pinless, wood/drywall mode): matters, write it down

Ambient:
  - Indoor temp and relative humidity if you have a hygrometer
  - Outdoor temp and conditions at time of reading

This baseline is the reference for everything that follows. Without it, "the meter went up" is unfalsifiable.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. "MEANINGFUL RAIN" — define it before you wait for it
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Treat as meaningful (and trigger the protocol):
  - Forecast or observed accumulation of ~0.1 in / 2.5 mm or more, OR
  - Sustained rain for 2+ hours at any intensity, OR
  - Wind-driven rain from the quadrant facing the window (this is the one that actually stresses the joint)

Do not treat as meaningful:
  - Brief drizzle, condensation on the glass, fog, or snow without melt

----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. POST-RAIN MONITORING — one rain event is enough; you do not need three
----------------------------------------------------------------------
T-0 (just before or at rain start):
  - Photo interior + exterior
  - Meter reading at affected spot and control

T+1h (during or right after rain ends):
  - Visual check of joint and interior wall
  - Note any new discoloration, damp feel, drip, or odor

T+24h:
  - Meter reading at affected spot and control
  - Compare to baseline

T+72h:
  - Meter reading at affected spot and control
  - Compare to baseline

Resolution = affected spot within ~1-2 points of control on the same meter setting, no new visual moisture, no odor, after one meaningful rain. If those hold, monitoring closes.

If a second meaningful rain comes before you close out, repeat the T+24h and T+72h readings. Two clean events is stronger than one, but you do not need to wait for a third.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
5. ESCALATION — call management, do not wait for the next scheduled check
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Escalate promptly (same day) if any of these appear:
  - Any new visible moisture on interior wall, trim, sill, or window interior face
  - Any moisture, discoloration, or warmth at the outlet (electrical + water = not a wait-and-see)
  - Meter reading at affected spot RISING after the 48h cure (cured plaster should be flat or falling, not climbing)
  - Meter reading at 72h post-rain not trending toward the control reading (gap not closing)
  - Joint shows a new crack, gap, separation, or missing sealant on inspection
  - Paint bubbling, peeling, or softening anywhere in the repair zone
  - White/chalky mineral deposits (efflorescence) appearing on interior — means water passed through and is drying, even if no wet stain is visible
  - Musty or earthy odor developing in the room
  - Water appearing on a different part of the wall or ceiling than before (path changed, problem may have redirected, not resolved)

A dry workday is not proof. Proof requires the rain event. The above list is what tells you the rain event failed.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
6. CLOSE-OUT
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Send management:
  - Baseline readings
  - Pre-rain, T+24h, T+72h readings
  - Photo set (interior + exterior)
  - One-line statement: "Reading at affected spot is X, control is Y, no visible moisture / odor / outlet issue after one meaningful rain — closing monitoring" OR an escalation note if criteria in §5 triggered.

If the joint or interior paint is going to be painted over as part of finishing, do that only after §5 is clean and the 72h post-rain reading is at control. Painting over a still-moist wall traps the problem.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Two things worth flagging that are not in your ask but matter for this plan
----------------------------------------------------------------------
  - "Slightly above control" after a fresh reseal is expected; what matters is the direction over the next 48-72h, not the absolute number today.
  - The window return is a common failure point precisely because wind-driven rain hits it at an angle a flat joint never sees. When you document the first rain, note wind direction, not just total accumulation — that is what tests the actual repair.

WEDNESDAY EVENING PREP (Nov 27)

Thaw the chicken
  - Preferred: 4-5 lb whole bird on a rimmed plate in the fridge since Tuesday night — USDA allows roughly 24 hr per 4-5 lb. Fully thawed by Wednesday evening.
  - Backup if it isn't in the fridge yet: cold-water thaw Thursday morning. Submerge sealed bird in cold water, change water every 30 min. Allow about 30 min per lb, so about 2.25 hr.

Vegetables (store covered in the fridge)
  - Potatoes: peel, cut into even ~1.5" chunks, submerge in cold water in a sealed container. Or parboil 8 min, drain, toss with butter, and refrigerate (saves stovetop time on Thursday).
  - Carrots: peel, cut on the bias or into sticks, store in a sealed container with a splash of water.
  - Green beans: trim ends, store whole in a container lined with a damp paper towel.
  - Cranberry relish: keep refrigerated. If making it from scratch, do it tonight.
  - Gravy: stage flour, butter, stock, salt, pepper. If using a pre-made base, refrigerate.

Pie (refrigerated, unbaked)
  - Bake tonight while the oven is free. Most fruit, pumpkin, or pecan pies need 50-70 min at 375°F. Cool fully on a rack, cover loosely, leave at room temp overnight. Reheat 10 min at 325°F Thursday before serving if you want it warm.


THURSDAY SEQUENCE (Nov 28)

Targets: chicken thigh hits 165°F by 4:25-4:30 PM; rests 15 min while sides finish; serve at 5:00 PM. The trick to keeping sides out of the danger zone is to cook them at the very end and hold potatoes and gravy on the lowest burner.

 1:00 PM    Oven to 375°F. If the pie wasn't baked Wednesday, bake it now (done ~2:15).
 2:45 PM    Pull chicken from fridge. Pat dry, salt inside and out, leave on counter to lose chill (15-20 min — more even cooking).
 3:00 PM    Chicken in at 375°F, breast-up on a rack in the roasting pan. (Anya arrives — keep her out of the kitchen a few minutes.) Target 165°F in the thigh around 4:25-4:30 PM.
 3:00 PM    Big pot of salted water on a front burner for potatoes.
 3:15 PM    Potatoes in, simmer 12-15 min until just tender. Drain, return to pot with 4 tbsp butter, cover. Hold covered on the stove.
 4:00 PM    Oven down to 200°F (warm-hold) for the serving platter and any side you want to park.
 4:15 PM    Carrots on a burner: 1 tbsp butter + splash of water in a covered pan, medium-low, 8-10 min until just tender. Cover and pull off the heat.
 4:25 PM    Check thigh with an instant-read thermometer. Pull the chicken at 165°F, move to a warm platter, tent loosely with foil, rest 15 min. Put the roasting pan with drippings on a back burner for gravy.
 4:30 PM    Rewarm potatoes on the lowest burner, lid on, stir in 1/4 cup warm milk. Hold above 140°F.
            Green beans on a second burner: 1 tbsp butter, sauté 5-7 min with a pinch of salt, cover off heat.
            Gravy on a third burner: 2 tbsp drippings fat + 2 tbsp flour, whisk 1 min, whisk in 2 cups stock, simmer 3-5 min.
 4:45 PM    Carve the chicken (or carve at the table).
 4:55 PM    Pull the cranberry relish from the fridge into a small bowl.
 5:00 PM    Serve.

The four burners map cleanly: potatoes (low/re-warm), carrots, green beans, gravy. Nothing sits at room temp — sides come off the burner at serving, potatoes and gravy hold covered on low, and the resting chicken stays tented under foil plus a clean kitchen towel (still well above 140°F after 15 min).


SAFE TEMPERATURES (USDA reference)

  - Poultry safe internal: 165°F in the thickest part of the thigh, not touching bone.
  - Hot holding minimum: 140°F.
  - Cold holding maximum: 40°F (relish, pie at room temp is fine for under 2 hr).
  - Danger zone (40-140°F): no more than 2 hr total, 1 hr if the room is above 90°F.
  - Reheating cooled sides: bring to 165°F or hold at 140°F+ until served.


WHAT TO WATCH

  - An instant-read thermometer is the only reliable way to know the chicken is done at 4:25 PM. Start checking at 4:15 PM if you're unsure of your oven.
  - If Anya is late or conversation runs long, the oven at 200°F becomes the holding cabinet: covered potatoes and a covered pan of beans can ride there safely while you wait.

The whole bird can stay together, but you don't want it to — the breast will overcook badly while the thigh catches up. The clean fix is to separate them now while the breast is at its peak.

The chicken

1. Pull both breasts off the carcass right now at 162°F. Don't slice all the way through if you want presentation; just lift them off the keel bone, keeping each breast as one piece with the wing attached or detached, your call.
2. Wrap the breasts in foil with a spoon or two of pan juices and a pat of butter. Seal the foil loosely so steam doesn't build up and keep cooking them. They'll coast to about 167–170°F and stay there on the counter for 30+ minutes without drying out — the foil and juices are doing the work. Carryover is basically your insurance.
3. Put the rest of the bird (thighs, drumsticks, back) back in a 400–425°F oven (375 convection). 151°F is too far below 165°F for carryover alone to finish safely — that gap needs real heat.
4. Roast until the deepest part of the thigh reads 165°F on an instant-read. From 151°F that's usually 15–22 minutes depending on size. If you have a probe, clip it in and watch.
5. Pull at 165°F, tent loosely with foil, rest 5–8 minutes. Carve at service.

Why this is safe: 162°F breast is past the USDA instant-read target; foil-wrapped carryover doesn't drop it below safe, it just preserves moisture. Thigh finishing at 165°F in the oven meets the standard. No raw-side risk because the carcass never went back to room temp.

Sides holding sequence

Potatoes (mashed): transfer to a slow cooker on "warm" or hold covered in the pot on the smallest burner with a diffuser. Stir every 10 minutes; add a tablespoon of warm cream or stock if they stiffen. They hold for an hour+ this way. If neither option exists, a covered bowl over a pot of simmering water (bain-marie) works.

Carrots: covered pot on the lowest burner, or sheet pan covered with foil in a 200°F oven. A splash of butter in the pan keeps them glossy.

Gravy: small saucepan on the lowest possible heat, stir every 10 minutes. If it looks like it will sit longer than 30 minutes, transfer to a thermos or an insulated carafe — it holds for an hour with no scorching and stirs back smooth.

Green beans: do the prep now during the thigh cook. Blanch in salted water 3–4 minutes, ice-shock to stop the cooking, drain, toss with butter, hold on a sheet pan at room temp or in a 200°F oven. At service, give them a 60-second sauté in a hot pan with a knob of butter and a pinch of salt to wake them up — finishing to order is what keeps them green and snappy instead of mushy.

Timing sketch
- 0–5 min: separate breast, foil-wrap breast, dark meat back in at 425°F.
- 5–22 min: thigh cooks to 165°F.
- 22–30 min: rest dark meat, blanch/shock green beans, move sides into holding config.
- 30–40 min: everything on warm hold; carve and plate.

One safety note: if the thigh ever stalls in the 150s and the oven is clearly not catching up, that's a sign it's a thicker thigh than expected — go to 170°F to give yourself margin, or pull and slice the thigh meat off the bone and finish it in a hot pan with butter so you can verify doneness visually. Don't serve dark meat at 151°F; the risk isn't worth the carryover math.

Short version: nothing needs to be frozen. From Thursday dinner to Sunday is roughly 2 to 2.5 days at 38°F, which is well inside the 3–4 day safe window for cooked poultry, gravy, potatoes, and cooked vegetables. Your real job is portioning so each container is reheated exactly once.

PORTIONING (the key to "no repeated reheating")
  - Divide everything now, while still cold from the fridge, into meal-sized containers.
  - Friday containers: enough for today's meal for you and Devika. If you eat together, one family-style container that gets reheated once and finished is fine.
  - Sunday containers: pre-portion Sunday's plates now — two servings, sealed, set aside at the back of the fridge where the temp is most stable.
  - Anya's container: already with her; not your responsibility past pickup.
  - Anything left over beyond Friday + Sunday: portion and freeze today (see below).

REFRIGERATION
  - 38°F is correct. Keep the door closed as much as possible; airflow matters, so don't pack containers tight against each other or the back wall.
  - Anything still in a deep pot or thick layer: move to a shallow container (≤2–3 inches deep) so it cools through quickly. Lid loose until cold, then tight.
  - Don't add warm food on top of already-cold food.

FREEZING (only if there is surplus beyond Sunday)
  - Use rigid freezer containers or freezer bags pressed flat with air squeezed out.
  - Label each with contents + date (2024-11-28).
  - Freeze at 0°F or below.
  - Notes by item: chicken freezes very well; gravy freezes well; carrots and green beans freeze acceptably; potatoes can go slightly mealy when thawed — best frozen mashed with extra butter/cream or submerged in gravy.

THAWING (anything frozen)
  - Preferred: refrigerator, overnight for a typical portion. Plan ahead.
  - Faster: sealed bag submerged in cold water, change water every 30 min, cook immediately after.
  - Fastest: microwave defrost, then cook immediately.
  - Never thaw on the counter.

REHEATING
  - Bring everything to 165°F internal — spot-check with a thermometer, especially chicken and gravy.
  - Reheat only what you'll eat in that sitting. Don't reheat a whole container to eat half and save half.
  - Cover to keep moisture in; stir halfway through.
  - Eat within about 1–2 hours of pulling from the fridge.
  - Rule: a container is reheated once. If it's not finished, toss the rest.

CHECKLIST
  - [ ] Portion today's servings; refrigerate, eat, done.
  - [ ] Portion Sunday's servings into a separate container; refrigerate.
  - [ ] Portion + freeze anything that won't be eaten by Sunday (if any).
  - [ ] Anya's portion is with her.
  - [ ] Sunday: pull Sunday container, reheat once to 165°F, eat.

One safety note worth flagging: the 90-minute-to-fridge and 38°F both check out. If for any reason anything was left at room temperature past 2 hours (1 hour if your kitchen was over 90°F), or if anything smells off at any point, throw it out — don't try to rescue it with extra reheating.

DECISIONS (item by item; temperature and time only)

  RAW CHICKEN (surface 44°F)
    The surface reading is above the 40°F safety threshold, and how long
    the package spent in the 40-140°F danger zone is unknown. Raw poultry
    is the highest-risk category (Salmonella, Campylobacter). Cooking to
    165°F internal will kill the bacteria but will NOT destroy heat-stable
    toxins that some bacteria produce once they have grown in the danger
    zone, so "just cook it" is not a safe rescue here.
    Verdict: DISCARD.

  MILK (43°F, refrigerator compartment)
    43°F is above the 40°F refrigerator threshold, and the duration above
    40°F is unknown. The whole fridge compartment has been compromised,
    not just this carton. Pathogens don't change the smell or flavor of
    milk reliably.
    Verdict: DISCARD this milk, AND audit the rest of the fridge (see
    "other perishables" below).

  ICE CREAM (liquid around edges)
    The center presumably still has ice (you would have said so otherwise);
    refreezing is safe from a pathogen standpoint because the cold mass
    never reached danger-zone temperatures. Texture after refreezing will
    be icy and possibly separated — quality loss, not a safety loss.
    Verdict: KEEP if you accept degraded texture. DISCARD if you want the
    original mouthfeel. Don't taste-test it to decide; decide on the
    quality-vs-waste tradeoff.

  FROZEN PEAS (hard, ice crystals visible)
    Visible ice crystals and a hard texture mean this package stayed at
    or below ~32°F, well under 40°F. It never entered the danger zone.
    Verdict: KEEP. Refreeze or cook directly. Quality unaffected.

  OTHER PERISHABLES IN THE FRIDGE (not listed, but worth checking)
    Anything in the refrigerator compartment that read above 40°F when you
    checked: discard raw fish, raw ground meat, deli meats, soft cheeses,
    cooked leftovers, opened condiments with dairy/eggs. Whole uncut
    hard cheese, butter, intact unpeeled vegetables, and unopened
    shelf-stable items in the fridge door are lower risk and likely fine.

RECOVERY AND CLEANUP

  1. Confirm the door is fully closed and the latch has engaged. Listen
     for the click.

  2. Stop opening both compartments. A half-full freezer with the door
     open for ~2.5 hours typically needs 6-8 hours of closed-door time to
     return to 0°F; a full one, 2-4 hours. Plan on leaving the freezer
     shut overnight.

  3. Verify recovery with the appliance thermometer. Wait for a stable
     0°F or below before restocking with previously-frozen items or
     trusting the unit again. If the temperature drifts back up after the
     door is closed, the seal is leaking (see step 6).

  4. Clean now, while everything is still cold. Warm soapy water on
     interior walls, shelves, and the gasket; rinse with a damp cloth;
     dry. Pull and wash drawers and bins. Melted ice cream and meat
     juices become harder to clean once they dry onto surfaces, and
     spills are the actual cross-contamination risk you want to remove.

  5. Clean the refrigerator compartment with the same protocol. It was
     also at 43°F, so the failure mode crosses compartments.

  6. Diagnose why the door ended up partly open. The usual causes:
       - Something leaning against the door (a bag, ice cube tray, box)
       - A worn or torn door gasket
       - A misaligned door (level the unit or check hinge screws)
       - A weak or broken latch
     Quick test: close the door on a piece of paper and pull. If the
     paper slides out with no resistance, the gasket has failed and
     needs replacement. Also run your palm along the closed seal feeling
     for cold-air leaks.

  7. After both compartments return to safe temperatures (freezer ≤ 0°F,
     fridge ≤ 40°F), restock and resume normal use. Keep the appliance
     thermometer in place — it is the only objective signal you have,
     and you used it correctly here.

WHY THIS APPROACH (since you asked without smell or taste)

  The actual safety variable is time spent in the danger zone (40-140°F),
  not how long the door was open. Door-open time is only an upper bound,
  and the thermometer readings are what narrow it down. Items that stayed
  at or below freezing are unaffected. Items whose temperature crossed
  40°F — even briefly — have entered the danger zone, and from there
  duration is the only remaining question. Without duration data, the
  conservative call is discard for high-risk items and keep for items
  whose temperature clearly never crossed 40°F.

  The authoritative wording for the same temperature-and-time logic,
  applied to door-open incidents, is in USDA FSIS's "Food Safety During
  Power Outages" guidance at foodsafety.gov.
