Quick read on the numbers: 7.4 kg is 82% of the arm's 9 kg ceiling — within range with a healthy margin, not over-built. A 28 mm solid-wood top is actually a favorable surface (solid wood grips far better than MDF/particleboard). 28 mm is near the low end of the clamp's 20–60 mm range, which means the screw has less travel — do not chase "tighter" past the point of full contact.

PRE-INSTALL CHECKS
  - Unplug/cable-route the desk area first. Nothing must sit in the clamp's footprint on top or underneath (cables, USB hubs, mat edges, papers).
  - Inspect the top surface where the clamp will sit: no finish damage, no knots within ~3 cm of the clamp footprint, no pre-existing cracks running with the grain under the clamp path. A pre-existing crack under the clamp = stop and pick a new location.
  - Inspect the underside where the lower plate will bear: flat (you said it is), clean, no cable trays, no screw heads, no standoff brackets in the footprint.
  - Confirm the VESA plate on the monitor is fully seated: all 4 screws present, correct length (too long can crater into the panel), flush against the monitor back. Re-torque to the plate maker's spec — usually 0.5–0.8 Nm for the M4 screws; a quarter-turn past snug is the typical failure point for stripped monitor threads.
  - Confirm arm's tilt/pivot tension rings/screws are at manufacturer default — adjust AFTER mounting, not before.

CLAMP INSTALLATION
  - Orient the arm so the post sits at the back edge of the desk (or as the arm's manual specifies). The clamp's upper jaw on top, lower plate flat against the underside — the two contact surfaces must be parallel to the desk surfaces. A tilted lower plate = the clamp binds on one edge and the wood gets stressed unevenly.
  - Slide the clamp on so its back lip (the "stopper" that prevents the desk from sliding out the front of the clamp under load) is hard against the back edge of the desk. This lip is your primary anti-slip feature; it is more important than clamp tightness.
  - Hand-tighten the clamp screw. Stop when:
      (a) the upper jaw stops wobbling,
      (b) the lower plate is fully flush against the underside — no daylight anywhere along its perimeter,
      (c) the wood has not begun to compress (no creaking from the wood itself).
    Do NOT use a wrench, pliers, or extension for extra leverage. Do NOT chase a "firmer" feel by another quarter-turn once (a)+(b)+(c) are met — solid wood crushes before it feels obviously tight.
  - Confirm by trying to slide the clamp forward/back along the desk with moderate hand force — should be immovable. If it slides, the back lip is not engaged correctly; reposition, do not over-tighten to compensate.

STAGED LOAD TEST (do these in order; do not skip stages)

Stage 0 — Empty-arm clamp integrity
  - Push and pull the post horizontally in all directions with firm hand force. Expect zero movement, no creak.
  - Rotate the post (if it has a swivel collar) through its full range — smooth resistance, no grind.
  - Extend the arm to its full horizontal reach with no monitor attached. This is the worst moment the empty clamp will see. Hold it there for 15 seconds; the clamp must not rotate forward (the front edge lifting away from the desk). Any forward rotation = stop, the clamp is sliding and the monitor will fall.

Stage 1 — Mount with the arm tucked in
  - Support the monitor's full weight with one hand. Do not let it hang from the VESA head during engagement.
  - Click the VESA head onto the plate; confirm the locking tab/latch is fully closed (most have a visible red/green indicator or audible click — check the arm's manual for which).
  - With the monitor close to the post and arm at low extension, hold it steady for 30 seconds. Look for any sag, drift, or creak from the clamp area.

Stage 2 — Move to your primary working position
  - One hand on the monitor while repositioning. Do not let the arm articulate under full load without a guiding hand.
  - Release. Watch for 60 seconds. Note any audible creak from the clamp or any slow drift of the monitor's position.
  - Place a small mark on the desk at the front edge of the clamp with a pencil. Any forward migration of the clamp will show as a gap appearing between this mark and the clamp front.

Stage 3 — Worst-case position
  - Full horizontal extension AND full height adjustment (if your arm supports it). This is the maximum moment the clamp will ever see.
  - Hold the monitor while moving into position. Release. Hold for 60 seconds.
  - This is the stage where an under-spec clamp fails first. If it survives this, it will survive normal use.

Stage 4 — Articulation under load
  - Slow full tilt up and down (3 cycles).
  - Slow full swivel left and right (3 cycles).
  - Listen for any new creak that wasn't there in Stage 0. A new creak under load typically means the clamp is micro-slipping — stop and re-evaluate clamp position/torque.

Stage 5 — Static soak
  - Leave the monitor in your primary working position, undisturbed, for 15 minutes.
  - Re-check the clamp bolt (still snug, not loosened), the desk surface at the clamp (no fresh compression marks), and the underside plate (still flush).
  - Re-check after 24 hours. Wood can creep slightly under sustained load; a small re-snug at the 24-hour mark is normal and expected.

STOP SIGNS — any one of these means stop, unload the monitor, and address before continuing
  - Any audible creak, pop, or tick from the clamp area at any stage. Silence is the success criterion.
  - Any visible movement of the clamp on the desk surface — forward rotation of the clamp front edge is the classic failure mode and means the back lip is not doing its job.
  - A gap opening between the upper jaw and the desk top, or between the lower plate and the underside. This means the wood is crushing or the clamp is bending.
  - Fresh compression marks, finish bruising, or any visible crushing of the wood at the clamp contact points.
  - A pencil-mark gap appearing at the front of the clamp (forward slip).
  - Monitor sag > ~2–3 mm at full extension that wasn't present empty.
  - Slow drift of the monitor's position when left static for 30+ seconds.
  - Wobble, resonance, or a "loose" feel when you lightly tap the desk near the clamp.
  - Sudden stiffness or binding during articulation that wasn't there empty — usually indicates the clamp has shifted and is now binding the post.

AFTER SUCCESSFUL TEST
  - Mark the clamp's final position on the desk with a light pencil outline at the front and back. A future slip will be visible immediately.
  - Re-check bolt torque at 24 hours and again at one week.
  - Do not push the arm into positions that exceed the monitor's center-of-gravity envelope — the VESA plate should sit centered on the monitor back; a plate offset toward one edge multiplies the effective load the clamp sees and can push the system past 9 kg effective even with a 7.4 kg monitor.

If you want, send me the arm brand/model and I can flag any known failure modes specific to it (some C-clamp designs have a notorious back-lip geometry that doesn't actually engage on thinner tops).

What this proves about the deterministic rejection path

  The bounded replay demonstrates a clean, exact-boundary rejection with
  no accounting ambiguity. Concretely:

    - Threshold is sharp one-directional: 25,000/25,000 oversized requests
      returned 413; none slipped to 200 and none returned 429. The path
      is unambiguously the rejection path, not throttling.
    - Accounting is lossless on reject: accepted = 0 and rejected =
      submitted count for every request. No partial ingestion, and no
      double-counting via a silent-retry path that could re-inject the
      same payload.
    - Reason is structured: oversized_batch is machine-readable, not
      opaque. Clients can branch on it deterministically rather than
      probe.
    - Boundary is not over-eager: the same payload split into compliant
      requests was fully accepted with totals reconciling. The guard is
      not clamping too low.
    - Boundary is not leaky downward: the control set at <= 8,000 points
      stayed at baseline latency and error rate. The new path did not
      introduce collateral slowdown for compliant traffic.
    - Client-side visibility: the test client's no-unchanged-retries
      behavior confirms the 413 surfaces the failure to the caller; the
      rejection is not hidden behind a successful-looking response.

  Net: the rejection mechanism is deterministic at > 8,000, with exact
  accounting, a structured signal, and no contamination of the compliant
  path. The path itself is proven; what remains is policy.

What still belongs to the owners' permanent-disposition decision

  The replay proves the mechanism under bounded conditions; it does not
  decide production posture. Items that remain owner-owned:

    - Threshold permanence: whether 8,000 stays the long-term cutoff, or
      is a calibration point, and what production evidence would justify
      changing it.
    - Observability policy: whether sustained oversized sends alert,
      page, or log only. Bounded-replay silence is not the same as a
      decision; the owners still need to set the alert/no-alert line
      (e.g. the invariant-violation vs. backlog-only framing used
      elsewhere on the ingest path).
    - Rejected-payload metadata disposition: what is recorded per
      rejection (size, tenant, source, count), retention, and whether
      any of it surfaces to customer-preview surfaces or owner-card
      overrides.
    - Client-impact policy: what callers are expected to do at the
      boundary (docs, SDK guidance, response headers) and how this
      interacts with batching clients that cannot trivially split.
    - Rollback / runbook criteria: under what production signal the
      owners would reverse the path, and who owns that call during a
      live incident.
    - Cross-team propagation: whether the disposition needs to
      coordinate with ingest-edge or shard-keeper given adjacency to
      the write path.
    - Bounded -> permanent scope conversion: the replay ran under an
      agreed bounded scope (excluding raw bodies, query-volume
      inference, owner-card overrides, customer preview, co-wide
      export, mgr-readiness). Owners still need to convert that
      exclusion list into a permanent scope statement, or decide which
      exclusions carry forward.

  Mechanism: provable. Disposition: still owner-owned.

Here's the safest sequence. The core principle: go to the wallet operator first (they have the cleanest fix and lowest risk to the legitimate load), and never let anyone "reverse and re-post" — only an additive refund/correction.

1. Preserve evidence before contacting anyone
   - Screenshot the full card statement page showing both $34 charges, with the exact timestamp and full merchant descriptor visible (no cropping, no markup over the original).
   - Screenshot the transit-wallet history showing the single $34 load, with its timestamp and any confirmation/reference number.
   - Save both to a folder with filenames that include the date you captured them. If your phone's gallery stamps metadata, leave it intact; otherwise add a brief note ("captured 2024-12-06, prior to any dispute action").
   - Pull any email/SMS confirmations from the wallet for the load and save those too. Check spam for a duplicate-load notice.
   - Note the descriptor exactly as posted — disputes are often lost on a "merchant name didn't match" technicality.

2. Identify which charge is the orphan before you talk to anyone
   - Match by timestamp: the card charge whose time aligns with the wallet load is the legitimate one.
   - If the wallet load has a confirmation/reference number, the matching card charge usually carries it in the descriptor or in a linked transaction detail. The charge without a matching wallet entry is the duplicate.
   - Write down: legitimate charge timestamp, duplicate charge timestamp, wallet load timestamp, wallet confirmation number, and the descriptor verbatim. This is your "do not touch" anchor for the legitimate charge.

3. Open a written case with the transit-wallet operator FIRST (not the bank)
   - Why operator-first: they can see exactly which inbound payment credited the wallet and can refund the orphan from their side in days, not 30–90. A bank chargeback can drag the merchant into reconciliation that claws back the legitimate load.
   - In-app support chat or email is preferable to phone because you get a written transcript automatically. If you must call, note the agent's name and ask them to follow up by email.
   - Tell them: "Two $34 card authorizations posted with the same timestamp and descriptor; only one load is reflected in my wallet history. Please confirm which transaction ID credited the wallet, confirm the second is an uncredited duplicate, and issue a refund to the original payment method."
   - Get a case/ticket number and an expected resolution date in writing before you hang up or close the chat.

4. Wait for the operator's written confirmation before doing anything else
   - You want an explicit statement that charge A is the one tied to your load and charge B is the duplicate they're refunding.
   - If they say "we'll just void one and re-run the other," say no — you want an additive refund on the duplicate, not a reversal-and-rebook of the legitimate one. Re-runs can fail and leave you with neither load nor refund while the dispute is open.

5. Only escalate to the bank/card issuer if the operator stalls or refuses
   - File the dispute against the orphan charge only. In the dispute narrative, explicitly name the legitimate charge by timestamp/descriptor and state you are NOT disputing it. Example wording: "Two identical $34 charges posted on [date] from [descriptor]. Only one corresponds to a wallet load (confirmation [#]). I am disputing only the charge at [exact timestamp]; the other charge at [exact timestamp] is a legitimate load and must remain posted."
   - Attach the screenshots and the operator's case number/confirmation. Reference the operator's finding that the disputed charge is an uncredited duplicate.
   - Do not file a blanket "duplicate transaction" dispute — issuers sometimes auto-reverse both when the merchant's response lumps them together.

6. Safeguards against accidentally reversing the legitimate load
   - Never authorize a "cancel and re-post" of either charge. Only accept an additive credit for the duplicate.
   - If the operator or bank asks for permission to "clean up by reversing both," decline and ask for a partial refund tied to the orphan only.
   - Keep a single running log (paper notebook or a dedicated note): date, time, channel, agent, reference number, what was said, what was promised.
   - After each step, check the wallet balance and your card statement to confirm the legitimate load is still intact and untouched.
   - If at any point the legitimate charge is reversed, stop all other actions and contact the operator and issuer the same day to have it restored before the wallet's reconciliation window closes.

7. Follow-up and closure
   - When the refund posts on the card statement, screenshot it next to the original duplicate charge and save with your case file.
   - Close the bank dispute only after the refund is fully posted (not just "issued") and matches the duplicate amount exactly.
   - Keep all of the above for at least one full statement cycle after resolution — disputes can be re-opened.

Short version of the rationale: the wallet operator has the cleanest, lowest-risk fix because they control both the credit side and the refund side. Going to the bank first works, but chargebacks routinely drag the legitimate sibling charge into the merchant's reversal, which is the exact failure mode you're trying to avoid.

Salvage sequence — keep everything wet and cold, and do not let anything hit heat until the pink is gone.

1. Hold position. The shirts are still wet and cool, which is the favorable state — dye is loosely held on the fiber right now. Do not run them through a dryer even on low; a single hot cycle can lock the pink in permanently.

2. Sort the red sock out. Inspect it: if it still looks deeply red it will bleed again in any future mixed load — isolate it or retire it.

3. Oxygen-bleach soak (this is the workhorse, and it's the one your labels explicitly permit). Use sodium percarbonate (OxiClean free, Biokleen Oxygen Bleach, generic "oxygen bleach" powder, or hydrogen peroxide 3% as a weaker alternative). In a basin or back in the washer on a cold fill:
   - Fully dissolve the powder in cold water before the shirts touch it, so you don't get concentrated spots on the fabric.
   - Dose per the product label; a typical working bath is roughly 1/4 to 1/2 cup of sodium percarbonate per gallon of cold water, or the labeled scoop for a load.
   - Submerge the shirts, agitate briefly, then let them soak 6–8 hours or overnight at room temperature or cooler. Stir/squeeze the fabric a few times during the soak.
   - Keep the bath cold throughout. If your ambient is warm, refresh with cold water and a little more oxygen bleach rather than letting it warm up.

4. Drain and rinse in cold water until the rinse runs clear.

5. Flush wash. Run a normal cycle in cold water with your regular detergent only — no bleach this time — to carry away the oxidized dye. Again, cold, and the smallest agitation your machine offers is fine.

6. Inspect while still wet. Hold each shirt up to good light. If any pink remains, repeat steps 3–5; two or three rounds is normal for a fresh transfer. Do not proceed to drying until the wet shirts look white.

7. First dry should be air-dry, flat or on a line. Heat is what you're still avoiding. Once fully dry, check again in daylight — a faint tint that wasn't visible wet can show up dry. If anything is still off-tint, do another cold oxygen-bleach round; do not tumble dry.

8. If after 2–3 oxygen rounds a shadow of pink persists, escalate to a true dye remover — Rit Color Remover or any sodium hydrosulfite product. That chemically reduces the dye instead of oxidizing it, and it works where oxygen bleach stalls, but it is more aggressive on fibers and trims. Test one shirt first, follow package directions exactly, and treat it as a single last shot before accepting the tint.

9. Prevention for next time: keep reds and darks out of white loads, wash new reds separately for the first three or four cycles, and toss in a color-catcher sheet (Shout Color Catcher) when you have to mix.

Two hard rules to keep in front of you for the next several hours: cold at every step, and nothing goes in the dryer until a wet inspection shows white.

Below is a ready-to-send dispute package. The main artifact is the letter to your card issuer; the second item is a short request to the transit-wallet operator for written confirmation, which you should have before (or alongside) the bank filing. A consolidated evidence checklist follows.

I left two placeholders for you to fill in, because the card statement doesn't tell you on its face which of C-7712 or C-7713 actually funded TW-884190:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. DUPLICATE-CHARGE DISPUTE — TO CARD ISSUER
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

To: [Card Issuer] — Billing Disputes / Chargeback Department
From: [Your full legal name], cardholder
Card account: [last 4 digits]
Subject: Duplicate charge dispute — single $34 merchant credit posted twice

Dear Dispute Resolution Team,

I am writing to dispute a duplicate $34.00 charge posted to my card on [date] at [timestamp, with timezone]. My card statement shows two charges of identical amount, merchant descriptor, and timestamp:

  • [LEGITIMATE CARD REF]  — $34.00  — [date, timestamp]  — [merchant descriptor as it appears on statement]
  • [DUPLICATE CARD REF]   — $34.00  — [date, timestamp]  — [same merchant descriptor]

Only one of these card charges corresponds to a service I actually received. The merchant of record, [transit-wallet operator legal name], has confirmed in writing (see Attachment A) that my account received exactly one $34 load at this timestamp under their transaction reference TW-884190, and that no second wallet credit was issued. The merchant explicitly states it cannot reverse a charge it did not record.

Reconciliation:
  • One $34 card charge = one $34 wallet load (TW-884190). Legitimate. Retain.
  • One $34 card charge = no corresponding wallet credit. Unmatched. Dispute.

Requested remedy:
  1. Reverse only the [DUPLICATE CARD REF] charge of $34.00 posted on [date].
  2. Leave the [LEGITIMATE CARD REF] charge of $34.00 and the underlying TW-884190 wallet load intact, as both reflect a transaction I authorized and received.
  3. Confirm in writing once the reversal posts, with the credit date and any associated reference number.

This is not a request for a refund of the legitimate transaction, nor an allegation of unauthorized card use — both charges were initiated by me as part of the same intended load. The issue is a posting/settlement duplicate by the merchant or its processor, for which the merchant has acknowledged it has no offsetting record.

Please respond within 10 business days. I can be reached at [phone] or [email]. Supporting documents are attached and indexed below.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Signature, if submitting on paper]

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. REQUEST FOR WRITTEN CONFIRMATION — TO TRANSIT-WALLET OPERATOR
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Send this only if the operator's "one load only" statement is currently verbal, in-app, or in a non-portable chat. You want a letter or email you can attach to the bank dispute.

To: [Transit-wallet operator] — Customer Support / Records
From: [Your full legal name], account holder
Account: [your wallet account ID or email]
Subject: Written confirmation of single load — TW-884190 on [date]

Hello,

On [date, time] I initiated a $34.00 load to my wallet from my card ending [last 4]. My card was charged twice for that load (references [LEGITIMATE CARD REF] and [DUPLICATE CARD REF]), but my wallet shows only one credit under your reference TW-884190.

A representative has informed me that only one load was applied to my account and that you cannot reverse or refund a second charge you did not record. To support my dispute with my card issuer, please reply to this email (or send a letter on letterhead) confirming, in writing:

  1. Exactly one $34.00 load was credited to my account on [date, time] under transaction reference TW-884190.
  2. No second $34.00 load exists in your records for my account at that timestamp.
  3. Your payment processor or acquiring bank handled the card authorization and capture for TW-884190.

Please include the name and contact details of your payments/records department so my issuer can verify if needed.

Thank you,
[Your name]
[Phone] · [Email]

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. EVIDENCE TO ATTACH (INDEXED)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Label these and attach in a single PDF or packet in the order below. Banks process disputes faster when the paper trail is clean and labeled.

  A. Card statement excerpt — full-page view of the two $34.00 transactions with timestamp, merchant descriptor, posted date, and references C-7712 and C-7713 circled or highlighted. Both lines must be on one page so the duplicate is visible at a glance.
  B. Transit-wallet transaction record — screenshot or PDF export showing the single TW-884190 credit of $34.00 at the same timestamp, with no second credit at that time.
  C. Written confirmation from the transit-wallet operator (Attachment A from §1) — letterhead email, signed letter, or chat export with the representative's name, date, and the "exactly one load, no second wallet credit" statement. If the operator will only confirm by phone, follow up immediately with an email: "Per our call on [date], confirming that only one $34 load was applied under TW-884190…" and save their reply.
  D. Load intent / authorization receipt — the original app confirmation, email receipt, SMS, or push notification you received when initiating the $34 load. This shows you authorized one load, supporting the "posting duplicate, not user error" framing.
  E. Card-on-file link — screenshot from the wallet app's payment methods page showing the specific card used (last 4, expiry), proving the two card charges originated from the same wallet account and the same intended load.
  F. Account profile snapshot — your name, wallet account ID, and the card last 4, so the dispute reviewer can link the parties without back-and-forth.
  G. Timeline note (one page, optional but useful) — a short written summary: "[date, time] — initiated $34 load → card charged twice (C-7712, C-7713) → wallet credited once (TW-884190) → operator confirmed single load on [date] → dispute filed on [date]." This pre-digests the story for the reviewer.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
NOTES BEFORE YOU FILE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  • Match the merchant descriptor exactly as printed on your statement in the letter — issuers keyword-search the descriptor and a paraphrase can route your dispute to the wrong queue.
  • Most issuers let you file a duplicate-transaction dispute online; upload the packet as a single PDF with the index above. Keep the originals.
  • Note the dispute filing date and any reference number the issuer gives you. Card networks generally give provisional credit within 1–2 business days while they investigate; final resolution typically takes 30–45 days.
  • Do not close the wallet account or remove the card on file until the dispute is resolved — if the issuer needs to trace the second authorization back to the merchant's processor, the link must still exist.
  • If the operator's reply in §2 is delayed, file the bank dispute now with everything except Attachment A and supplement it when the written confirmation arrives. Most banks accept supplemental evidence mid-investigation.

Good news up front: no pop, no swelling, no bruising, no neuro signs, full ROM, and normal grip on a 2/10 ache is a textbook mild muscular overload pattern from overgripping (flexor mass did more work than it's adapted to). Nothing here points to a tear that needs urgent care. Plan accordingly.

TONIGHT

- Don't immobilize; gentle movement is fine and helpful.
- Warmth if it feels good — warm shower or heating pad 15-20 minutes on the sore area. Skip ice unless it specifically feels better; there's no real swelling to chase.
- Skip aggressive stretching, deep massage, foam rolling, or a percussion gun directly on the forearm flexors tonight. They irritate an already-loaded tissue.
- Light pain-free ROM only: open/close hand, slow wrist circles, gentle prayer stretch (palms together, lower hands until you feel comfortable tension, not pain).
- Avoid heavy gripping tonight: tight jar lids, one-handed grocery carry, yanking the leash, etc.
- Sleep is the biggest recovery lever. Hydrate, eat normally.
- Skip NSAIDs unless the ache is meaningfully bothersome. A 2/10 doesn't warrant them, and routine NSAIDs blunt training adaptation. If you do take one, with food, and stop after a day or two.

GRADED SELF-CHECK (next morning, before any session)

Run these in order, compare to the other side.

1.  Pain at rest in the forearm? (0 = clean; anything > 0 = flag)
2.  Pain with light grip — coffee mug, door handle, toothbrush?
3.  Resisted wrist flexion: palm up, curl hand toward forearm against your other hand's resistance. Pain or notable weakness vs. the other side?
4.  Resisted finger flexion: hook fingertips into your other palm and try to curl them in. Sore?
5.  Passive wrist extension: other hand gently pulls the back of your hand toward you until you feel a stretch. Sore in the belly of the forearm (not just at the elbow)?
6.  Hang test, only if 1-5 are clean: dead-hang from a pull-up bar or edge for 10-15 seconds, then a few easy pull-ups. Any sharp pain or pulling sensation?

RETURN-TO-CLIMB CRITERIA

GREEN — climb normally:
- All six checks clean or essentially so.
- Warm-up climbs feel fine, no pain returning at the same intensity.
- You can self-correct overgripping mid-route.

YELLOW — modify the session:
- Mild awareness/soreness on checks 2-5 but no sharp pain, hang test feels okay.
- Drop 1-2 grades below your usual max on bouldering, or about a letter on routes.
- Avoid full crimp and heavy pinch; favor open-hand, slopers, and bigger holds.
- Halve your normal volume; stop well short of failure.
- Use the session as a technique rep — footwork, hip position, breathing. The fix to overgripping is technical, not grip-strength.
- If the same awareness is still there at the end of the session, that's information: next session stays yellow, or drops to red.

RED — skip the session:
- Pain at rest, or with typing / coffee mug / door handle.
- Pain or clear weakness on the resisted tests.
- Pain that shows up in the warm-up and doesn't settle within 10-15 minutes of easy climbing.
- Return of any red flag from tonight: swelling, bruising, numbness/tingling, focal sharp spot, sudden pop, or grip that suddenly gives way.
- Persistent soreness for more than 7-10 days despite modified training — that's the threshold to book an in-person eval. A climber-specialized PT or a sports-medicine clinician who climbs is the right call; they'll know the difference between flexor strain, medial epicondyle irritation, and pulley stuff without you having to explain the sport.

TRAJECTORY

This pattern typically clears in 2-5 days with normal training modifications. The fastest path back to hard climbing is restating it briefly when it asks for it, not muscling through. If you're still grumbling after a week of modified sessions, don't escalate — get it looked at.

- The mismatch is a unit mismatch: `rejected_points` is in *points*, `request_count` is in *requests*. A request contains ~21 points on average (4,000,000 / 190,000 = 21.05). So 4,000 rejected points are spread across ~190,000 requests — the ratio of "requests that had any rejection" (or "fraction of total points rejected") is being conflated with "fraction of requests rejected."
- Correct point-rejection rate = rejected_points / attempted_points = 4,000 / 4,000,000 = 0.001 = 0.1%.
- Per-request view (requests that experienced at least one rejected point) could in principle approach 100% if rejections are well-distributed, or stay at ~2.1% if only ~4,000 distinct requests had a single-point rejection; the raw counters don't disambiguate. The headline number to publish is the point-level rate.

---

Diagnosis

- Not data loss. Counters reconcile exactly: accepted_points (3,996,000) + rejected_points (4,000) = attempted_points (4,000,000). The 4,000 rejected points are fully accounted for; nothing is missing or duplicated.
- It is a unit mismatch in the dashboard formula. The numerator `rejected_points` is measured in points (the unit the ingest pipeline batches and validates), while the denominator `request_count` is measured in requests. With ~21 points/request on average (4,000,000 ÷ 190,000), the two counters describe different things, so their ratio is dimensionally nonsensical — it answers neither "what fraction of points did we reject?" nor "what fraction of requests did we reject?" It answers a hybrid that happens to print as 2.1%.

Correct point-rejection rate (the metric a release-review actually wants):

  rejected_points / attempted_points = 4,000 / 4,000,000 = 0.001 = 0.10%

  Equivalently, acceptance = 3,996,000 / 4,000,000 = 99.90%.

The 2.1% figure should not be retired as "wrong, ignore it" — it is a real signal in a different unit. It means: rejections occurred in the same order of magnitude as ~2% of request volume, i.e. rejections are *spread across* requests, not concentrated in a few. Useful, but not a rejection *rate*.

How to correct the dashboard query and annotation

1. Fix the numerator/denominator pairing. Use the same unit in both:
   - For point-level health (recommended headline): rejected_points / attempted_points. This is the metric that matches the SLO the team actually cares about (did the pipeline drop user data?). Result: 0.10%.
   - For request-level health (secondary): requests_with_any_rejection / request_count — only meaningful if you instrument a per-request flag. Without that flag, do not compute a per-request rate from these counters; you'll reproduce today's mistake.

2. Stop the mixed-unit formula from rendering anywhere. Either delete the panel or rename it explicitly: "rejected points per request volume (unit-mixed, do not interpret as a rate)." Do not let it sit next to the corrected rate with the same axis label — reviewers will average them in their heads and get the wrong number.

3. Preserve, don't bury, the 4,000. Annotation on the corrected 0.10% panel should read approximately:

   "Point-rejection rate: 0.10% (4,000 / 4,000,000 points). Counters reconcile: accepted_points (3,996,000) + rejected_points (4,000) = attempted_points. Average payload size ≈21 points/request; rejections are spread thinly across request volume, not concentrated. No data loss — this is a unit-correction, not a recovery."

4. Cross-link the old panel. If the old 2.1% number must stay visible during the transition (e.g. someone has a screenshot in a review doc), annotate it with the same point count and the explicit unit-mismatch callout, so the 4,000 rejected points are not silently re-read as 4,000 rejected requests. The real fact — "we rejected 0.1% of points, all accounted for" — must be the headline; the 4,000 is the numerator that makes it auditable, not a number to hide behind the rate.

ASSESSMENT

This is almost certainly ordinary charger waste heat, not a fault. A 65W laptop brick under sustained load typically runs 100-115°F (38-46°C) on its case, which is well inside its thermal design envelope. The most important signal is the heat distribution you measured: brick at 104°F, plug body and outlet face at 76-77°F, room at 70°F. That pattern means the heat is being generated inside the brick (normal AC-to-DC conversion losses) and dumped out through the case. A failing connection concentrates heat at the plug/outlet interface instead — the outlet ends up hotter than the brick. You have the opposite, which is the safe signature.

WHY 104°F ON THE BRICK IS NOT ALARMING

  - 104°F is below body temperature (98.6°F). It will feel "warm phone," not "hot pan."
  - Modern 65W GaN bricks are rated for case temps up to roughly 158-176°F (70-80°C) before thermal protection kicks in. You are nowhere near that.
  - Heat scales with how hard the laptop is drawing. Charting + browser + EHR can keep a system busy enough to hold the charger near full output for hours at a time.
  - The 70°F ambient is actually helping — cooler room = more headroom for the brick's passive convection cooling.

WHAT YOUR CHECKLIST CONFIRMS (you ran the right checks)

  No discoloration, no odor, no buzzing/hissing/crackling, no sparking, no looseness, no cable damage, no breaker trip, laptop charging normally, plug and outlet face cool relative to brick. All eight line up with "healthy."

MONITORING (no action needed, just baseline these)

  1. Touch-test with the BACK of your hand (more heat-sensitive than the palm). The brick should feel "noticeably warm but holdable for 5+ seconds comfortably." The moment it crosses to "pull away," that is an unplug signal — see below.
  2. Re-measure the brick temp under the same workload in 1-2 weeks. Stable within roughly ±5°F is reassuring. A climbing trend (104 → 115 → 125°F over weeks) means degrading efficiency, usually aging capacitors, and the brick should be replaced before it gets worse.
  3. Spot-check the plug body and outlet face each time. They should stay within a few degrees of ambient. If those start climbing, the contact interface is becoming the problem, not the brick.
  4. After Devika finishes a heavy session and the laptop idles 30-60 minutes, the brick should cool substantially back toward ambient. If it stays hot at idle, something is wrong.
  5. Feel along the cable. It should be barely above room temp everywhere except the strain reliefs at the brick end and the laptop end. Any hot spots along the jacket = internal damage, replace.

UNPLUG-NOW CRITERIA (any one of these, stop using the brick immediately)

  - Brick case too hot to keep your hand on it (back-of-hand test = "ouch, pull away"), or sustained above ~130°F / 54°C
  - Plug body OR outlet face climbs above ~110-115°F / 43-46°C — that is the contact-resistance failure signature and the wall side is now the problem, not the brick
  - Any smell at all: sweet (capacitor electrolyte), ozone or "electrical" (arcing), burning plastic (insulation breakdown)
  - Any discoloration: yellowing, browning, scorch marks on the brick case, plug prongs, outlet face, or wall plate
  - Buzzing, hissing, crackling, or popping from the brick, plug, or outlet
  - Plug feels loose in the outlet — wiggles, drops partway out, no firm grip. Worn outlet contacts arc under load even if everything looks fine in daylight.
  - Cable jacket is stiff, cracked, bulging, sticky, or hot along its length, or any conductor is exposed
  - Laptop stops charging or charges intermittently — the brick is failing under load
  - Brick cuts out and comes back on its own — thermal protection cycling means degraded cooling, replace soon
  - Visible swelling of the brick case, or any wetness or residue on it

ELECTRICIAN OR MANAGEMENT ESCALATION (the wall side, not the charger)

Call an electrician if:

  - The outlet is warm or hot to touch even with the charger unplugged (the wiring behind the wall is the problem)
  - Outlet feels loose, plugs fall out, or the faceplate wiggles
  - Burning smell comes from the outlet itself, with or without the charger in it
  - Scorch marks, melting, or discoloration on the outlet or wall plate
  - Repeated breaker trips on that circuit, especially with only modest load on it
  - Buzzing from the outlet
  - Lights on the same circuit flicker or dim noticeably when the charger is under heavy load (circuit undersized or a voltage-drop problem upstream)

Notify building management (if applicable to your lease) if:

  - Any of the electrician criteria appear and the outlet is in a managed or shared space
  - Multiple outlets in the unit show similar symptoms (panel-level issue, not a single device)

REPLACEMENT GUIDANCE (for whenever, not urgent today)

  - Match or exceed 65W. A 65W brick running at 90-100W peak load is what generates the most heat.
  - GaN (gallium nitride) bricks run cooler and lighter than older silicon designs at the same wattage.
  - Stick with the laptop OEM brick or a reputable USB-PD certified third party (Anker, Ugreen, Baseus, Apple for MacBooks). Cheap no-name bricks often skip the safety capacitors and thermal protection.
  - A genuine UL or ETL listed mark on the brick is non-negotiable.

OPTIONAL COMFORT MOVES (while it stays in the safe range)

  - Don't bury the brick under papers, books, or fabric. It cools by passive convection off the case and needs airflow.
  - Don't rest it on a soft surface (cushion, bedding, rug) — those insulate the bottom and trap heat.
  - A small stand, a laptop riser, or even a hardcover book under the brick keeps air circulating around it.
  - The separately routed outlet you set up for Devika is exactly the right topology — keeping it off your desk power strip means no shared-circuit interaction and no ambiguity if something ever does trip.

BOTTOM LINE

104°F on the brick with everything else normal and the plug/outlet staying close to ambient is normal GaN-charger behavior under sustained charting load. Nothing to do today. Keep the monitoring checklist and you will catch any real problem weeks before it becomes a hazard.

Rule of thumb: don't delete a single byte until the backup is verified. 5-6 weeks of unbacked-up work on a near-full drive is exactly the failure mode where a careless pre-backup delete becomes permanently lost data.

Target free space before the update
- Aim for 30-40 GB free minimum, ideally 50 GB+.
- A feature update (Windows) or major macOS update needs 15-30 GB just to unpack and stage.
- The installer keeps a rollback copy for ~10 days post-install, another 10-15 GB.
- 9 GB is well below the floor; she will bottleneck the installer even with a clean backup.

Step 1 - connect the drive and confirm it
- Plug in the external drive.
- Confirm it shows up in Finder/Explorer and has free space >= 1.5x the used space on the laptop (for ~480 GB used, 750+ GB on the backup drive is comfortable).
- If old backups are on the drive, that's fine - the tool will append/increment.

Step 2 - run the backup with the right tool
- macOS: Time Machine (System Settings -> Time Machine -> Select Disk). First full backup may take hours; let it finish in one pass.
- Windows: File History alone won't cover a full restore. Use Windows' "Backup and Restore (Windows 7)" -> System Image, or a free full-image tool (Macrium Reflect, Veeam Agent Free, or the drive manufacturer's tool).
- Third-party: whatever she was already using (Backblaze, Acronis, etc.).

Step 3 - verify the backup before any destructive cleanup
This is the step most people skip, and the one that prevents disaster.
- The tool reports "successful" with a real timestamp matching today.
- Backup size looks right: if the laptop's used space is ~480 GB and the backup is 5 GB, something is wrong - stop and investigate.
- Spot-check 3-5 files from different folders: open a recent document, view a recent photo, confirm a project folder is intact.
- For a Windows system image: confirm the .vhdx/.wim exists and is non-zero.
- For Time Machine: enter Time Machine from any folder and confirm you can browse today's snapshot.
- For cloud sync: confirm the cloud client shows "up to date" and the green/synced indicator on key folders.

Only after verification passes -> proceed to cleanup.

Step 4 - inventory the disk
- macOS: Apple menu -> About This Mac -> Storage -> Manage. Shows categories (Documents, Apps, Mail, Photos, System, Other) and safe recommendations.
- Windows: Settings -> System -> Storage -> Storage recommendations; or TreeSize Free / WinDirStat for folder-level breakdown.
- Goal: identify the 50-100 GB of safe-to-remove items, not nibble around the edges.

Step 5 - safe deletions (do these first; all reversible from backup)
- Empty Trash / Recycle Bin (often 5-20 GB on its own).
- Clear the Downloads folder after reviewing it - installers, old exports, forgotten archives.
- Clear browser caches (Chrome/Firefox/Safari -> Clear browsing data -> Cached images/files only; keep passwords and history).
- Clear Mail caches and old attachments (macOS Mail: Mailbox -> Rebuild; Outlook: clear the OST cache; or just remove old attachments from inside Mail itself).
- Run OS-native cleanup:
  - macOS: "Reduce Clutter" from the Storage pane - auto-empties Trash, removes old Apple TV episodes and Mail attachments.
  - Windows: Disk Cleanup -> "Clean up system files" - this is where old Windows Update files live (usually 5-15 GB), plus Delivery Optimization cache and temporary files.
- Uninstall apps she genuinely doesn't use, via the proper uninstaller (Settings -> Apps, or the app's own uninstaller), not by dragging to Trash.

Step 6 - offload large media
- Photos and videos are usually the single largest reclaim. Move (don't copy-then-delete) old years to the backup drive or a cloud archive.
- iCloud Photos / Google Photos / OneDrive can move originals to the cloud and leave thumbnails on the laptop, reclaiming tens of GB.
- Music libraries: point Music/Spotify cache folders at the backup drive.

Step 7 - what NOT to delete manually
Tempting-looking targets that break the system or lose data the backup tool may not have captured cleanly:
- Anything inside C:\Windows, C:\Program Files, /Library, /Applications, /System, /usr - never touch these.
- C:\Windows\WinSxS, hidden $Recycle.Bin, /private/var - managed by the OS, not by you.
- AppData (Windows) and Library (macOS) folders - hold app settings, Mail data, browser profiles, keychains, game saves, font caches. Don't delete to free space; clear caches only via the app itself.
- Virtual machine disks (.vdi, .vmdk, .vhdx) - only delete after confirming the VM is no longer needed; these are usually huge.
- The OS update staging folder if one exists (C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download or /Library/Updates) - Disk Cleanup / a dedicated tool clears these safely; manual deletion can corrupt an in-progress update.
- Mail databases (Outlook .ost/.pst, Apple Mail envelopes.db) - unless mail is on IMAP/Exchange/iCloud, the local database is the only copy; deletion without backup = lost email.
- Original installers she no longer has license keys for, raw photo/video originals not in cloud, scanned documents, tax records, source code not in version control.
- Browser profile folders (Chrome User Data, Firefox profiles, Safari containers) - bookmarks, history, saved logins, extensions all live here.
- The backup drive itself - never use it as scratch space; one accidental format and both laptop and backup are gone.

Step 8 - final space check, then update
- Confirm free space >= 30 GB (more is better).
- Start the update with the laptop plugged in; don't interrupt it.
- After the update completes and she's confirmed everything works for a day, the rollback partition frees itself automatically (~10-15 GB back).

If free space is still short after Step 7
- Check whether OneDrive / iCloud / Google Drive is set to mirror folders back to the laptop - that can re-fill the drive.
- Windows: disable hibernation (powercfg /hibernate off) to remove hiberfil.sys, which equals RAM size (often 8-16 GB).
- macOS: /private/var/folders/* holds user caches; "Reduce Clutter" plus a reboot usually clears them safely.
- Last resort: replace the boot drive with a larger SSD - that's beyond cleanup but is the long-term fix for a 512 GB laptop that regularly gets near-full.

One more thing
November 5 was the last backup - 5-6 weeks of unbacked-up work. Treat "backup, verify, then cleanup" as the standing rule. Drives that run near-full also fail sooner, and the next near-full event will not have a backup tool already configured.

WHY THIS BILL IS HARD TO READ AT FACE VALUE

The prior period ended on an *estimated* meter reading (Nov 11). The current period ends on an *actual* reading (Dec 12). That transition is doing a lot of hidden work in your numbers — the 286 kWh figure may be sitting next to a one-time reconciliation line that settles what the Nov 11 estimate missed. Until you isolate that adjustment, the kWh comparison is contaminated and any dispute is premature.

QUICK MATH FROM THE EXCERPT

Per-kWh rates (current bill only):
- Supply:  $34.32 / 286 kWh = $0.1200 / kWh  (exact)
- Delivery: $56.20 / 286 kWh = $0.1965 / kWh
- Blended: $90.52 / 286 kWh = $0.3165 / kWh
- Daily cost: $90.52 / 31 days = $2.92 / day

Daily usage:
- Current period: 286 / 31 = 9.23 kWh/day
- Prior period:   252 / 30 = 8.40 kWh/day
- Delta: +0.83 kWh/day, about +9.9%

Dollar counterfactual (assumes prior-period rates were identical to current):
- 252 kWh × $0.3165 = $79.76 implied prior-period total
- $90.52 − $79.76 = $10.76 delta

So the upper bound on the bill increase is ~$10.76 if rates were flat. If supply or delivery rates moved between the two periods, some or all of that delta is rate, not usage.

THE FOUR THINGS THAT COULD BE HAPPENING (alone or mixed)

1. Real usage increase. Nov 11 → Dec 12 is when NYC heating loads start showing up in residential bills. Holiday cooking and lights add a measurable slice too.
2. Estimate reconciliation against you. The Nov 11 estimate was *lower* than the meter's actual reading on Dec 12's back-calculation, so this bill catches up the under-billed kWh. Look for a line item like "estimated usage adjustment," "true-up," or "prior period correction" — a positive number.
3. Estimate reconciliation in your favor. The Nov 11 estimate was *higher* than actual — same line item, but as a credit.
4. Rate change. Supply rates often reset in late autumn; delivery rates reset on a different cycle. Either can shift $0.01–$0.03/kWh between bills without any usage change.

BEFORE YOU CALL, COLLECT THESE FROM THE BILL OR ONLINE ACCOUNT

- Full line items for the current bill. Specifically: any adjustment/true-up line, any rider or surcharge, the fixed customer charge, and any tax line.
- Meter reading history with dates and readings: roughly the Oct read (start of prior period), the Nov 11 read (was it actual or estimated, and what value was used if estimated), and the Dec 12 actual read.
- Rate schedule effective for each of the two periods — supply $/kWh and delivery $/kWh separately, not just a blended number.
- Same period one year ago (Dec → Dec). This is the strongest baseline because it strips out weather and rate-season effects.
- The prior bill's full dollar breakdown, so you can back out the prior-period per-kWh rate if the utility doesn't publish it.

COMPARISONS TO RUN (in this order)

1. kWh/day normalized. 9.23 vs 8.40. A ~10% rise is plausible for early heating season. Not alarming on its own.

2. Per-kWh rate check. Confirm $0.1200 supply and $0.1965 delivery were the same in the prior period. Quick sensitivity:
   - If supply rose $0.015/kWh (e.g., $0.120 → $0.135), that's $4.29 of the $10.76 delta with zero usage change.
   - If delivery rose $0.01/kWh, that's $2.86 more.
   So a 1–2 cent rate move can explain a third to a half of the dollar increase.

3. Estimate adjustment isolation. If the bill carries a +30 kWh adjustment line, real period usage was 286 − 30 = 256 kWh. Then 256 / 31 = 8.26 kWh/day — basically flat with the prior 8.40. The "increase" was a one-time correction, not a behavior change. This is the single most important number to extract.

4. Year-over-year same-period. If last year's comparable 31-day span was 320 kWh, your 286 is *below* baseline and there is nothing to dispute. If it was 240 kWh, you have a real conversation to have about weather, a new load, or a sticky estimate.

5. Household events. New space heater, window AC still running, holiday guests, new appliance, EV charging at home. Any one of these can plausibly add 1–3 kWh/day.

WHEN TO DISPUTE VS WHEN TO JUST ASK

- Ask, don't dispute, once you find an adjustment line. Most utilities will explain it in two minutes. You're verifying, not fighting.
- Dispute if (a) the math doesn't reconcile after they explain the adjustment, (b) the per-kWh rate moved without a posted notice and you want it on the record, (c) the Nov 11 estimate was wildly off and you want a confirmed read every cycle going forward, or (d) the year-over-year comparison shows this bill as a clear outlier.
- Don't dispute the ~10% kWh rise by itself. It's inside normal heating-season variation; the utility won't adjust a bill just because you used more electricity.

ONE THING WORTH DOING EITHER WAY

Ask the utility to lock in an actual read every cycle going forward (or request a smart meter if the building supports one). Estimated readings on a recently-opened account are common in the first few months and tend to recur if the meter is behind a locked closet or the building super isn't reliably granting access. Solving it once now means you never have to do this reconciliation again.

The compatibility evidence is solid and supports the layered design; the SDK error text gap is real but small, and I'd correct it before owners lock in the permanent disposition rather than after.

Compatibility evidence — what it shows:

  Local pre-flight at SDK: 100,000 oversized attempts (50k per SDK), all rejected before network. The candidate's first layer is doing its job — oversized batches are kept off ingest-edge entirely by current SDK paths. Zero network-load contribution from this layer.

  Server-side 413 at ingest-edge: 10,000 direct oversized attempts (the older / no-local-SDK path), every one validated, no unchanged retry, recovery via split succeeded for all. Second layer works, and clients do not loop on it.

  Splitting recovers complete point accounting — no truncation, no point loss. The reject-then-split contract is honest: a rejected batch is not a partially-accepted batch.

  Programmatic error codes are correct in both SDKs, so automation branches correctly even where the human-facing string is weak.

The signal across these is consistent: the layered oversized-batch candidate behaves as intended at every layer it can be observed, and the recovery path is clean.

The error-text gap:

  "batch too large" without the 8,000-point threshold is technically correct but diagnostically thin. A developer hitting it in logs has to look the limit up rather than reading it off the message. Programmatic code is right, so this is a discoverability / support-friction issue, not a correctness one. It is also a one-line SDK text change in the same release.

Should it block the disposition? My read: fix it before, not because the layered design depends on it, but because the SDK message is part of the surface the design will be known by. A few reasons to bundle it now rather than defer:

  Once the layered design is declared permanent, the SDK error string is part of the contract. Changing it later costs a deprecation note or a versioning decision; changing it as part of the same release that adopts the design permanently is essentially free.

  The two layers should give equivalent diagnostic value. Today the server returns 413 with the limit observable to the operator path; the SDK returns "batch too large" without it. Aligning them is a quality fix in the same spirit as the layered design itself.

  It is small and scoped. Deferring it would just turn it into a follow-up ticket on the same owners with the same release-cost profile.

If the owners want to keep the disposition decision itself free of UX nits, the workable alternative is to acknowledge the gap, lock in the layered design, and commit to a paired SDK text fix in the same change-set — which is roughly the same outcome, since the text change is on the critical path either way.

Net: compatibility evidence is good enough to recommend permanent adoption of the layered oversized-batch design; the SDK error text should be corrected in the same release that adopts it permanently, not as a separate later change.

  a. Burrs: any chipped, bent, or discolored teeth? A chip on an outer tooth is cosmetic. A chip on the inner cutting surface, or scoring that visibly changes the gap profile, is not.
  b. Burr seat and threads: no scoring, no metallic swarf, no black streaks (carbon tracking).
  c. Chamber wall: no warping, bubbling, or brown scorch marks on the plastic.
  d. Stone: keep it on the tray.

STEP 5 — HAND-ROTATE THE BURR SHAFT

  - With hopper and upper burr removed, turn the rotating burr by hand.
  - It should spin freely for several rotations with no rub, no binding, no gritty feel.
  - Listen: scraping, ticking, or rubbing = bearing or burr-seat issue. Out of service.
  - Smell: waft air from the chamber toward your face. Any residual hot-electrical or sharp ozone smell = out of service.

STEP 6 — INSPECT FOR ELECTRICAL CLUES

  - Smell near the motor housing vents (don't touch). Lingering hot-insulation or ozone = out of service.
  - Look at switch, plug prongs, and cord at the strain relief. No discoloration, no deformation.
  - If your grinder uses a wall-wart adapter, inspect the brick for bulging, cracked casing, or discoloration on the AC plug side. Any of those = replace the adapter before considering any test, and even then the grinder is suspect.

DECISION POINT

DO NOT TEST — leave out of service if ANY of these is true:

  - Residual hot-electrical or ozone smell at Step 5 or 6
  - Burr shaft binds, rubs, or sounds wrong when hand-rotated
  - Visible chip on an inner cutting surface, or any scoring that changes burr gap geometry
  - Scorch, carbon track, warping, or discoloration anywhere in chamber, switch, plug, cord, or adapter
  - Stone was larger than ~3 mm, or you found metallic debris alongside it (something else broke)
  - Any unresolved uncertainty

MAY TEST ONCE — only if every inspection above was clean:

  Test A (no-load, 5 seconds):
    - Reassemble. Hopper empty, no beans.
    - Plug into a different outlet than the one you used previously (rules that outlet out).
    - Stand back, hand on plug (not on grinder body).
    - Power on for 5 seconds, then off.
    - Acceptable: brief hum, slight vibration, no smell, no sparking, no smoke, no pitch change.
    - Stop and retire if: any smell at all, any sparking, any hum-pitch change, any smoke, any roughness you feel through the body.

  Test B (small dose, after Test A passes):
    - ~10 g fresh beans. Discard the grounds — do not drink them; they may carry contamination from the stall.
    - Listen for a steady, even burr tone. Any rattle, ticking, or "missing tooth" sound = out of service.
    - Smell the grounds: any plasticky/electrical note = out of service.
    - Inspect the grounds: any visible metal flecks = out of service (suggests a tooth chipped during the stall).

RETIREMENT TRIGGERS — stop using, replace or send for service, if:

  - Smell returns during any test
  - Any noise change persists between doses
  - Grind distribution no longer matches the dial setting (boulders, fines, or inconsistent pour-over vs. espresso)
  - Stall recurs with a normal bean
  - The adapter brick showed any heat or deformation

In short: if the stone comes out clean, the burrs and shaft are mechanically fine, and there's no residual smell or visible electrical damage, one short no-load test is reasonable. Any of those checks failing means the grinder stays out of service, and a stall with hot-electrical smell alone is enough reason to retire a grinder that has been run hard for years.

Right forearm — recurrent 3/10 on the first undercling 12/21, ordinary use pain-free since the mild ache after 12/10. Stopping the session was the right call. The pattern (open-hand fine, undercling symptomatic) reads as flexor-side tissue (finger/wrist flexors or their common origin) — useful as a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.

LOADING PAUSE — next 7–10 days
  Goal: a clean window where the undercling-specific pain does not reappear in any daily task.
  Avoid entirely:
    - Undercling, any crimp (full or half), pinch, side-pull, gaston
    - Wrist curls / extensions / rice bucket / grip trainers
    - Heavy deadlifts, rows, pull-ups, anything that pre-fatigues the flexors
  Allowed / encouraged:
    - Cardio without grip load — bike, walk, easy run
    - Lower-body work; if upper-body, use straps so grip is removed
    - Climbing on easy open-hand jugs is technically OK if completely pain-free, but cleaner to skip climbing entirely until the pause is done and start the progression fresh
  Track one number each evening: pain at rest / with ordinary grip on 0–10. Should stay at 0.

RETURN-TO-CLIMBING PROGRESSION — gated by symptoms, not the calendar
  Stage 0 — Baseline. Ordinary use pain-free ≥ 7 days, full motion, normal grip, no swelling.
  Stage 1 — Re-introduction. Easy problems on jugs / large open-hand holds, low volume (3–5 moves), long rests. No undercling, crimp, pinch, wrist-loaded positions. Stop the session at the first twinge. Two clean sessions before progressing.
  Stage 2 — Expand hold variety. Add open-hand slopers and moderate pinches held with an open grip. Brief, easy underclings on large holds permitted once 1 is clean, short moves only.
  Stage 3 — Undercling re-exposure, graduated. Easy undercling problems, full recovery between attempts, total undercling moves per session capped below the warmup count from 12/21. Watch for the same 3/10 character.
  Stage 4 — Normal variety with volume guardrails. Resume full grip variety but cap total attempts and add an extra rest day for the first 1–2 weeks.
  Rule across all stages: any recurrence of the specific pain → drop back one stage and hold ≥ 5–7 more days at the lower stage before retrying.

NON-URGENT EVAL — schedule sports medicine / PT within 1–2 weeks if any of these
  - Same-character pain (3/10 undercling) recurs after two full passes through Stage 3 with proper rest
  - Pain does not resolve to 0 in ordinary use within 2–3 weeks of the pause
  - Grip strength becomes noticeably reduced vs. the other side
  - Pain begins to localize more sharply or spread (forearm → elbow / wrist)
  - Mild pain lingers > 24 hours after any climbing session
  - "Warms up, worse after" pattern appears

SAME-DAY / URGENT EVAL — stop the plan and get seen if any one of these
  - New numbness, tingling, or color/temperature change in hand or fingers
  - New swelling, bruising, or visible deformity
  - Sudden sharp pain with a specific mechanism (pop, snap, twist)
  - Pain at rest or that wakes you from sleep
  - Loss of wrist or finger motion you don't already have

If the progression stays clean, expect a full return to normal variety in roughly 3–4 weeks. If it doesn't, the eval is the right next move — one PT visit to confirm flexor tendon vs. something else beats grinding through a slow recurrence.

First-pass classification: bounded convergence during a planned shard-keeper node replacement, consistent with the expected lease handoff window. Not an incident on the evidence you described, conditional on the fence/audit checks below.

Why it reads as bounded:

  22s is short. If shard-keeper's lease TTL is in the tens of seconds, the alert interval sits inside the design envelope, not above it.

  12 of 480 (2.5%) is the signature of node-locality — primaries that happened to live on the replaced node. A scattered distribution would have been the surprise, and would point elsewhere.

  Zero write errors + zero stale writes + baseline latency is the signature of fencing holding and clients not retry-storming through the handoff. Those three together are the strongest single signal you get that the system re-stabilized cleanly.

  All 480 converged without manual intervention.

What would flip the classification to an incident:

  A write bearing the old generation number landing at the storage layer after the new generation acquired the lease (fence failed).

  Client retry rate on the affected shards spiking above baseline even if it didn't move the latency floor — that means clients were blind to the new gen, not just briefly out of date.

  Any single shard's two-generation overlap exceeding its lease TTL.

  Even one affected shard whose primary was not on the replaced node.

Checks needed before signing off as bounded convergence. Of these, 1–3 are load-bearing; the rest are due-diligence:

1. Window vs. TTL, per shard. Confirm the 22s was inside the configured lease TTL on every one of the 12, not just the cluster average. The right comparison is per-shard max overlap vs. per-shard TTL. A single shard over TTL is the only finding that, by itself, re-classifies the event.

2. Fence integrity on each affected shard. For each of the 12: timestamp the new generation acquired the lease, timestamp the old generation's lease was revoked/expired, and whether any write bearing the old generation was accepted at the storage layer between those two. "No stale write recorded" needs to be provable from the write-ahead log, not just from the absence of an error metric. This is the single check I'd not skip.

3. Client retry behavior on the affected shards during the window vs. that shard's baseline over the prior 7 days. Zero retries = strongest signal. Small non-zero bump = normal fencing rejection, clients learned the new gen, fine. Large bump = clients were looping on the old gen, not fine even if write errors stayed zero.

4. Locality. Confirm all 12 primaries were on the replaced node. If even one was unrelated, that's a coordination/clock/lease-renewal signal, not a node-local handoff.

5. Read-your-writes for in-flight multi-shard transactions during the window. No stale writes doesn't rule out a write-then-read-on-different-shard race that returned pre-write state. Small population to check, worth checking.

6. Alert threshold vs. runbook expectation. Was the runbook expecting this alert for a planned replacement, or did it fire on a window the runbook considers routine? If routine, the alert is over-paging and that's a separate ticket.

7. Replacement procedure conformance. Confirm the runbook sequence (pre-revoke → drain → replace → re-acquire) ran end-to-end on the replaced node. A skipped drain would have made the 22s window possible but would also have changed the risk profile — worth knowing even if everything else checks out.

8. Replayability. For each of the 12, can you reconstruct which clients saw which generation, what writes landed in the window, and what reads served from which generation? If yes, the event is fully understood. If any shard's timeline has gaps, that's where I'd hold off on signing off as bounded.

Sign-off criterion (my version): 1–3 clean, 4–5 clean, 6 and 7 routine, 8 complete. Anything short of that, I'd treat it as incident-pending and have Cyrus close the gaps rather than declaring bounded and moving on.

ROAST CHICKEN TIMELINE — service at 6:30 PM
4-lb unstuffed chicken | separate-pan potatoes | quick-sauté green beans

OVEN: 425°F the whole time. Two rack positions: lower-middle for the chicken, upper-middle for the potatoes when both are in together.

4:15 PM — Pull chicken from fridge, place on a plate. Pat dry inside and out with paper towels. Letting it lose fridge chill for ~40 minutes = more even roasting.

4:30 PM — Season inside and out with salt, pepper, any rub. Truss or tie legs, tuck wing tips behind. (Aromatics like a halved lemon or garlic cloves in the cavity are fine — that is not "stuffing"; do not fill with a bread-based stuffing since you said unstuffed.)

4:55 PM — Chicken into the oven, breast-side UP, on a rack set in a roasting pan. Start a 75-minute timer but begin probing temperature at the 60-minute mark.

4:45 PM (overlap) — Prep potatoes: peel and cut into ~1.5-inch chunks, toss with oil, salt, pepper, spread in a single layer on a sheet pan (do not crowd or they steam).

5:15 PM — Potatoes into the oven. At 425°F in 1.5-inch chunks, expect 45-55 minutes. Toss once at the 30-minute mark. They finish close to when the chicken does, which is the point: potatoes do NOT hold well once covered, so timing them to end with the chicken is what keeps them crisp instead of soggy.

6:00 PM — Start checking the chicken every 3-5 minutes with an instant-read thermometer. Two checks are what make this safe:

  - Thickest part of the BREAST: must read 165°F.
  - Thickest part of the THIGH: must read 165°F, inserting from the outside near the leg joint or from the inner thigh near the body cavity, NOT touching bone (bone contact reads false-high).

  Pull the bird the moment BOTH spots read 165°F. If the breast hits 165°F first, pull immediately — do not wait for the thigh to "catch up," because the breast will overcook and dry out. (For a 4-lb unstuffed bird at 425°F, both spots usually hit 165°F together between 65 and 80 minutes.)

6:05 PM — Potatoes out when browned and crisp at the edges. Tent LOOSELY with foil and set aside. They will hold 10-15 minutes this way without going soggy; longer than that and they soften, so do not start them any earlier.

6:10 PM — Chicken out. Transfer to a carving board. Tent LOOSELY with foil (loose tent = steam escapes, skin stays crisp; a tight tent = skin turns rubbery). Rest 15-20 minutes. Internal temperature will rise another 5-10°F during rest (carryover cooking) — that is normal and expected.

6:20 PM — Start the green beans. They are the only component that cannot be held, so they go in last:
  - Large skillet, high heat, splash of oil, optional minced garlic.
  - 6:22 PM — add beans, constant tossing, salt and pepper.
  - 6:24 PM — if they need a bit more cooking, splash of water or broth, cover for 30 seconds.
  - 6:27 PM — kill the heat when they are bright green, just tender, with a few charred spots.
  - Hold in the pan off the heat with a lid on for at most 2-3 minutes while you carve.

6:28 PM — Carve the rested chicken.

6:30 PM — Plate and serve. Everything hits the table at the same time and hot.

FALLBACKS

  - Chicken reading cold at 75 min: bump to 450°F, recheck every 2 min — a 4-lb bird only needs a few more minutes.
  - Chicken reading 165°F by 55 min: pull early, rest as planned, everything else still works.
  - Potatoes finishing 10+ min early: leave them on the counter uncovered for 5 min, or hold in a 200°F oven. Do not tent and hold past 6:20 PM or they will lose crispness.

ONE-LINE SUMMARY
  4:15 out of fridge -> 4:30 season -> 4:55 chicken in -> 5:15 potatoes in -> 6:00 start probing -> 6:05 potatoes out -> 6:10 chicken out (165°F in breast AND thigh) -> 6:20 beans on -> 6:30 serve.

  - No upstream distress (the burst is genuine accepted load, not a misbehavior upstream)
  - Queue drained on its own (queue max retention vs burst duration is the only capacity lever that matters here)

What would NOT be consistent with that classification (red flags to rule out):

  - Throughput dropping while errors = 0 ............... suggests stall/hang rather than saturation
  - Queue depth not returning to pre-burst baseline ... suggests leak or backpressure elsewhere
  - Metric emission gaps during the window ............ data may be silently lost even if errors are 0
  - DLQ or retry-topic growth ........................ invisible to rollup-error counter
  - Lag/SLO breach on downstream consumers ............ backpressure propagating past rollup

CHECKS NEEDED BEFORE CLOSING AS BOUNDED CONSUMER-CAPACITY BACKLOG
==================================================================

Run these in order; any failure changes the classification:

  1. Queue depth, not just queue age: confirm depth returned to pre-burst baseline (age can fall while depth is still elevated if drain is incomplete)
  2. Lag against SLO during the window: was end-to-end lag ever past the alert threshold, or did it merely brush the warning band
  3. DLQ / retry-topic / parked-message counters: confirm zero growth even when rollup-error counter is zero
  4. Metric emission continuity for the burst window: spot-check a representative series for gaps or flatlines that would indicate silent drop
  5. Consumer instance count vs concurrency config: confirm consumers were at expected replica count (a missing replica during a burst looks identical to saturation in the throughput-flat signal)
  6. Broker/queue max retention vs burst duration: confirm 6m of age did not approach retention ceiling (if it did, this is no longer bounded; it is one burst away from data loss)
  7. Dependency-side lag for anything rollup feeds: confirm backpressure did not push lag into downstream consumers
  8. Pattern check: is this the same shape as prior holiday bursts, or new behavior? New shape = treat as preliminary, not closeable

If 1-8 all clear: bounded consumer-capacity backlog is a defensible close. Anything else: reclassify before closing.

DATA PLATFORM FOLLOW-UP (Cyrus's lane)
======================================

These are pacing/capacity/scaling questions; they belong with shard-keeper:

  - Consumer capacity sizing vs expected holiday burst envelope (+31% is mild; the real question is what the design point is and how far above it the burst went)
  - Auto-scale trigger thresholds and cooldown; whether consumers can scale up fast enough that age never reaches 6m on a normal-shape burst
  - Whether there is a documented burst-absorption target (e.g., "age < 2m at +50% sustained") that this event did or did not meet
  - Alert tuning: queue-age alerts that fire on a self-draining bounded backlog during known-burst windows produce noise without signal; paging policy during tagged import windows is already handled per the correction-import rule, but holiday bursts are a different tag

Cyrus owns pacing + alerts; these items go to him. They do not change who owns rollup.

INFRA CONCERN (narrow, kept narrow on purpose)
==============================================

The only thing here that is plausibly Infra rather than rollup-or-Data-Platform:

  - Broker/queue sizing or partition layout, if the queue's max retention or partition count is the binding constraint rather than consumer compute
  - Broker-side throttling or connection limits, only if metric evidence points there

This is a sizing question about the substrate the rollup queue runs on. It does not pull rollup itself into Infra; the queue substrate is Infra's, rollup consumer behavior is not.

WHY ROLLUP OWNERSHIP DOES NOT MOVE
==================================

The classification "bounded consumer-capacity backlog" puts the fix squarely on consumer capacity, which is a rollup-side decision (replicas, concurrency, partition assignment, scaling policy). Those decisions live with whoever owns rollup today. Surfacing "broker substrate is undersized" to Infra is an Infra ticket, not a transfer of rollup. The two stay separate:

  - Rollup (current owner): consumer config, scaling policy, alert tuning, SLO definition
  - Data Platform (Cyrus): pacing envelope, burst design point, capacity roadmap
  - Infra (if any): broker/queue sizing, only as a substrate ticket

CLOSING-FRIENDLY SUMMARY FOR CYRUS
==================================

If checks 1-8 pass:

  Classification: bounded consumer-capacity backlog during a +31% accepted-points burst over the holiday window. Consumer healthy (throughput flat, errors zero), upstream healthy (router + edge at baseline), queue self-drained once input normalized. No data loss indicated.

  Close conditions: depth returned to baseline, lag stayed within SLO, DLQ/retry growth = 0, metric emission continuous, replica count nominal, retention ceiling not approached, downstream lag not pushed, pattern matches prior bursts.

  Hand back to Cyrus (Data Platform): consumer capacity sizing vs burst envelope; auto-scale triggers; burst-absorption target definition.

  Open as Infra only if: broker/queue sizing is the binding constraint, evidenced by retention-ceiling proximity or partition saturation, not consumer compute.

  Rollup ownership: unchanged.

  - "Kinda-owns, unowned in practice" is the actual risk here. A bounded-backlog close without a named owner for the consumer-capacity follow-up means the fix does not happen and the next holiday burst reproduces the same 6m age. If you want this to actually close cleanly, name the owner on the rollup side before closing, even if that owner is you.
  - The +31% / 6m / self-drain pattern is the kind of evidence that gets used to argue "no action needed" forever. It is bounded *this time*. Whether it stays bounded as bursts grow is a Data Platform capacity question, not an alert question; do not let the alert close substitute for the capacity answer.

Yes — the combined load fully explains the trip, and your description (clean reset, no heat / odor / discoloration / buzzing / sparking / loose receptacle) is consistent with an overload, not a wiring fault.

The math:

  15 A circuit × 120 V = 1,800 W nameplate capacity
  NEC continuous-load limit = 1,800 × 0.75 = 1,350 W (for loads expected >3 hrs)
  Kettle alone:        1,500 W  (~83% of nameplate)
  Toaster alone:       1,450 W  (~81% of nameplate)
  Both together:       2,950 W  (~164% of nameplate, ~218% of continuous limit)

Either appliance on its own is already running near the edge of a 15 A circuit; together they push the circuit well past its trip curve. A standard 15 A breaker will hold around 1,800 W indefinitely and will trip somewhere in the 1,875–2,100 W range over the few seconds it takes to heat — which is what you saw. Nothing in the trip suggests a fault. It's the breaker doing exactly its job.

How to reuse both appliances safely on a 15 A circuit:

  1. Never run them simultaneously on the same circuit, not even briefly.
  2. Map what else is on that breaker — the other countertop receptacles, fridge, microwave, disposer, dishwasher, dining-room outlets, kitchen lights. Their draw is the silent extra that pushes you over the edge. A fridge compressor kicking in mid-toast is a common culprit.
  3. Run the kettle first, finish / unplug, then the toaster — or use them on different circuits. Most kitchens have at least two small-appliance branches; try the other receptacle across the sink to confirm it is on a separate breaker.
  4. No power strips, no extension cords, no daisy-chains for these loads.
  5. Unplug after each use. A kettle left plugged in can leak standby current or cycle.

If you actually want both running at once (e.g., a regular breakfast routine), the proper fix is a dedicated 20 A small-appliance circuit — not upsizing the breaker on the existing wire. NEC 210.11(C)(1) and 210.52(B) require two 20 A small-appliance circuits serving kitchen / dining countertops, so older kitchens wired with 15 A branches are common and worth upgrading. That is an electrician's job.

When to stop and call someone:

  - The breaker trips with only one appliance running and that appliance alone is well under ~1,350 W continuous. (Note: the 1,450 W toaster is right at the edge on its own — if it trips solo, the circuit may already be marginal and should be looked at.)
  - Repeated trips after you've gone back to single-appliance use.
  - Any of the warning signs you already checked for come back: warm faceplate, buzzing, scorch marks, melted-plastic smell, plugs that fall out, lights on the circuit dimming or flickering.
  - The breaker won't reset, or trips again with nothing plugged in.
  - You can't reliably identify what's on the circuit, or the panel labeling is unclear / wrong.

If you rent, contact management for any of the above and request an electrician — don't ask them to just swap a bigger breaker onto the existing wire. If you own, call a licensed electrician directly for a circuit-trace and a 20 A branch if you want both appliances concurrently.

Bottom line: your read is correct. This is a load-management problem, not a wiring problem. One appliance at a time on that circuit, map the rest of the loads on the breaker, and don't paper over it by upsizing the breaker.
