INTERPRETATION

This crossing is almost certainly not a real failure signal. Two
compounding artefacts converge in the same 5-minute bucket:

1.  Denominator collapse. Decision volume of 420 against a baseline of
    tens of thousands is roughly 1-2% of normal. At N=420, the 1%
    threshold fires on the fifth error (1.19%), so any unrelated blip
    becomes an automatic page. Rate-based SLOs without a minimum
    sample floor are unreliable in near-idle traffic, and the holiday-
    evening timing makes the exposure worse.

2.  Single-identifier clustering. Seven 500s sharing one synthetic
    request_id means the metric layer observed seven HTTP 500
    responses, not seven distinct failing requests. Plausible shapes:
      a.  One canary probe that internally retries or fans out to N
          decision paths and each leg returns 500 — counted as N.
      b.  A fanout miscount where one real decision emits one error
          per downstream egress and is double-counted at the route-
          decision plane.
      c.  A synthetic probe whose identifier was reused across
          attempts (probe loop, probe-mid-rollover).
    In all three shapes the right unit-of-analysis is "one synthetic
    probe failing," not "seven user-impacting failures."

The corroborating evidence supports the benign read:
  -  Adjacent intervals are zero-error, so the failure is contained
     to a single bucket.
  -  Latency is normal — the failure mode is not a slow/stuck path
     degrading into 500s.
  -  Egress reconciliation is normal — the decision plane still
     agrees with egress counts and the expected policy-deny envelope;
     no decision is being made and then dropped or misrouted.
  -  Synthetic-ID concentration rules out organic user traffic,
     because independent users produce independent request_ids.

Bottom line: the canary-panel SLO has been tripped by a synthetic
artefact in a near-idle bucket, not by a real fault in the routing
plane.

WHY IT STILL LOOKS LIKE A PAGE

The current rule is two standard alert anti-patterns stacked: low-N
rate volatility and request-burst inflation. Together they convert
one probe failure into a page. That is a rules problem, not a
routing problem.

IMMEDIATE EVIDENCE CHECKS (in priority order)

1.  Resolve the shared request_id. Pull metrics-router logs and
    canary-emitter logs for that identifier across the 21:15-21:20
    ET window. Confirm:
      -  it is synthetic/canary, not a real-user trace;
      -  whether the seven 500s are seven HTTP responses or one
         response retried/counted seven times;
      -  which downstream or internal decision path produced them.
    This single check decides whether to close the page or escalate.

2.  Cross-check real-user traffic in the same bucket. Filter
    metrics-router decisions to non-synthetic request_ids in the
    same 5-minute window. A non-zero real-user 500 count changes
    the read entirely; zero confirms the artefact hypothesis.

3.  Confirm canary pool volume. Look at the canary-emitter's
    emit-rate at 21:15. Was the pool throttled, paused, or
    emitting at a reduced cadence? Was a config canary mid-rollout
    (e.g., a new decision path under probe)? A pool-throttle
    explains the 420.

4.  Verify egress reconciliation in detail. Reconciliation is
    normal at the aggregate, but check whether the seven 500s map
    to a specific egress and whether that egress had any rate-
    limit / timeout / connection-reset in the same window. If
    reconciliation is clean at egress granularity too, the failures
    are not at the boundary.

5.  Probe-side logs. If the canary probe has its own client logs,
    check whether it recorded a successful outcome elsewhere (it
    usually has multi-step assertions) or whether metrics-router
    was the only failing leg.

6.  Counter-staleness sanity check. A counter that emits once and
    then re-emits on a retry, or a metric with a non-idempotent
    increment, can inflate count without corresponding traffic.
    Cheap to verify, and rules out a metrics-layer bug masquerading
    as a routing failure.

Decision rule: if checks 1 and 2 confirm synthetic + no real-user
impact, close as a benign canary blip and file the alert-rule
follow-up. If check 2 surfaces any real-user 500s, treat as a real
incident and engage the on-call runbook.

ON-CALL POSTURE

Weeknight off-duty, re-engage only if paged. This scenario lands
during a holiday evening — it should produce a page under the
current rule, which is itself part of the problem the new
formulation is meant to solve. If the page does fire, the checks
above are small enough to run from a laptop; if it doesn't fire
because of the floor, that is the new formulation working as
intended.

A SAFER ALERT FORMULATION

The current rule (error_rate > 1% over 5m, no floor, no de-
duplication) is wrong on two axes. A better rule expresses two
things separately: "is real user traffic failing?" and "is a
synthetic probe failing?"

Layer 1 — primary user-traffic page rule:

    distinct_failed_request_count >= K
    AND error_rate > 1%
    over 5m,
    where request_ids are de-duplicated and synthetic traffic is
    excluded from this rule entirely.

    Choose K from the smallest real incident you want to catch.
    For a routing service at this traffic scale, K = 25 over 5m
    is a reasonable default: at the holiday trough (~420
    decisions / 5m) even a fully-failing bucket de-dupes to a
    handful of probes and will not trip; at normal volume
    (~30k / 5m) 1% is 300 errors and any real incident clears
    K trivially. K = 25 sits between "page on a single probe"
    and "miss a real 0.5% degradation," which is the right
    neighbourhood.

Layer 2 — rate-only safety net for very low traffic:

    error_rate > 10%
    AND decision_count >= 100
    over 5m,
    excluding synthetic.

    This catches "everything is broken" even when K is not yet
    reached, while still ignoring the N=420 holiday trough's
    normal noise.

Layer 3 — synthetic-probe panel (separate, no paging by default):

    synthetic_probe_outcome = "fail" over 5m,
    routed to a canary-health dashboard, not the on-call pager.

    A single probe failing on metrics-router is information, not
    a page. Aggregate synthetic failure rate becomes a weekly-
    review metric, not a paging metric.

Optional refinement — fanout-aware counting:

    If the metric layer can attribute a 500 to a (request_id,
    egress) pair, count distinct (request_id, egress) pairs as
    the unit instead of raw 500 responses. This collapses the
    "one probe, N legs" shape into one failure and makes Layer 1's
    K directly meaningful.

What this preserves:
  -  Sensitivity to a real incident: at normal volume, 1% rate plus
     25 distinct failures still trips immediately.
  -  Resistance to near-idle traffic: at N=420, neither Layer 1
     nor Layer 2 trips on a single synthetic probe.
  -  Separation of concerns: synthetic health is observable
     without polluting the on-call page budget.

What this gives up:
  -  A very small real incident that produces exactly K-1 distinct
     failures in 5 minutes will not page. That is the right trade
     for a routing service in this position — the adjacent-interval
     zero state plus egress reconciliation will surface it on the
     next bucket, and the synthetic panel will continue to flag
     probe health independently.

   Best containment, if you have it: a metal bucket or ammo can part-filled with clean dry sand or unused kitty litter, with the power bank nestled in so it can't shift. Sand smothers and cools. A loose metal lid is fine; airtight plastic is wrong (pressure can build). Do not refrigerate or freeze it — thermal shock and condensation make things worse.


2. HANDLE AND TRANSPORT IT

   Before moving:
     - Tape over the USB ports and any button with electrical tape so nothing can short
     - Wear nitrile or work gloves (electrolyte is corrosive); eye protection is sensible
     - Lift it as a unit, don't squeeze the case

   Carry it in the sand-filled metal container, lid on but not sealed airtight, so it can't roll, slide, or get bumped. In the car: trunk or wedged into the footwell with towels so it can't shift under braking. Passenger seat or your lap is wrong. Don't ride a bike or subway with it loose; if you must take transit, the metal sand-can padded inside a backpack so nothing moves is the loosest acceptable — driving yourself is better. Crack a window for ventilation. Go straight to the drop-off; don't leave it in a hot car.


3. DISPOSAL — NOT HOUSEHOLD TRASH

   A swollen cell is treated as a damaged Class 9 lithium battery. Garbage trucks, transfer stations, and recycling facilities have burned because of exactly this. Use a route that handles damaged cells:

     - Your city or county household hazardous waste (HHW) facility. Most US cities take swollen lithium batteries free. Search "[your city] household hazardous waste" or call 311 / 211
     - Call2Recycle locator at call2recycle.org — but call ahead. Many retail drop-offs (Home Depot, Lowe's, Best Buy, Staples) will refuse a visibly swollen cell; ask before you drive over
     - The manufacturer (Anker, RAVPower, Aukey, Belkin, etc.) — most have a mail-back or support email that will arrange return for damaged cells
     - A dedicated e-waste or battery recycler (Redwood Materials, Battery Solutions, an e-Stewards recycler near you) — they routinely accept damaged Li-ion if you call first
     - Your local fire station — some will take it for disposal, others will just tell you where to go

   When you hand it off, say it is swollen/damaged so they bag it in a fireproof container on their end.


4. EMERGENCY SIGNS — STOP DIY, CALL 911

   Any of these means it is going into or already in thermal runaway. Evacuate the room, close the door behind you, call 911, and tell the dispatcher "swollen lithium battery, possible thermal runaway":

     - Hissing, popping, crackling, whistling
     - Smoke, vapor, or a white-to-gray plume (toxic — do not breathe)
     - Sweet solvent or nail-polish-remover smell (electrolyte venting)
     - Any warmth to the touch — it should be room temperature; warm is a red flag
     - Visible swelling getting worse, the case cracking open, or electrolyte leaking
     - Discoloration, charring, melted plastic
     - Sparks, flame, or nearby material catching fire

   If it ignites and you can do so without approaching the plume:
     - A standard ABC dry-chemical extinguisher knocks down flame but the cell can re-ignite repeatedly
     - Large amounts of water actually work on lithium-ION (different from lithium metal — your power bank is Li-ion, water is correct). Douse generously and keep it cool
     - A bucket of sand smothered over it works well
     - Leave the room once flame is suppressed and let the fire department handle re-ignition

   Do not try to move a smoking or burning cell — it can flare in your hands.


5. TIMING

   It is fine to leave it isolated in the sand-filled metal container on a hard floor for a day or two while you arrange disposal — but don't leave it next to the bed "to deal with tomorrow." If you don't have a metal container tonight, a ceramic baking dish on a concrete balcony floor, away from anything flammable, is an acceptable overnight stopgap.

What you're describing is a textbook fear response — mobile, taking treats, breathing normally between bangs means he's tracking you and not in medical distress. He's already doing half the work by picking the closet. Here's the plan for solo NYE night.

DO THESE IN THE NEXT 30 MINUTES, BEFORE DEVIKA LEAVES:

Stage the safe retreat. He's chosen the closet — honor it. Move his bed in if it isn't already. Add an unwashed t-shirt with your scent (and hers, if she can leave one). White noise machine on, plus a fan if you have one — steady hum beats random bangs. Dim the lights. Close the door. If the closet feels too tight at any point, the interior bathroom is the second-best option (no exterior walls, smaller volume). Don't force a crate unless he's crate-trained.

Stage the door kit. Front-clip harness + short leash on a hook by the door. High-value treats (cheese, hot dog, whatever he'd work for) in a pouch by the door. Poop bags. His collar with current ID tags on him or right next to the harness.

Save the numbers NOW while she's still home. Your regular vet's after-hours line. Your nearest 24-hour vet ER — Animal Medical Center in Manhattan is 212-838-8100 and 24/7; VERG has Brooklyn locations. Put both in your phone with one-tap dialing.

FOOD AND WATER:

Light dinner, nothing rich or new — keep his normal schedule. Don't worry if he picks at it; stress suppresses appetite. Fresh water in the retreat and near you. The single best calming tool tonight is a lick mat with frozen xylitol-free peanut butter or wet food — licking releases endorphins and occupies his mouth. Stage it in the freezer now.

Skip any new treats or chews. Nothing that could upset his stomach on top of stress.

BATHROOM SCHEDULE:

Harness goes on before you open any door. Short leash, no retractable, phone away, calm energy — he reads you.

  6:30-7:00 PM — go now, while Devika's still there to help and bangs are still sporadic. Brief curb, then straight back to the retreat.

  9:30-10:00 PM — one more brief trip before the main ramp.

  11:00 PM-ish — brief trip, or skip if it's continuous; your call based on how he's holding up.

  12:30-1:00 AM — the one to prioritize if you can only do two more. Activity drops fast after midnight in NYC.

If he freezes or tries to bolt back inside at any point, let him. Don't drag.

IF HE GETS OUT (low odds, plan anyway):

Do NOT chase. Sit or kneel, call his name once, bait with a high-value treat. Most panicked dogs circle back within a block or two. ID tag on, microchip registered to your current number — anyone who finds him can scan. Skip the chase-and-panic loop; sit still and call.

RECOGNIZING DISTRESS THAT NEEDS URGENT HELP:

Manageable at home tonight — these are normal fear response:
  Panting, pacing, trembling, ears back, lip-licking, hiding, whining, picking at food, clinging to you. He can still take treats and respond — that's a good sign.

Call your vet or go to the ER now:
  Self-injury — cuts from trying to break through door, window, or crate. Dogs damage their teeth and paws badly in panic.
  Collapse or brief unresponsiveness, even if he pops back.
  Gums pale, white, blue, or tacky instead of pink and moist.
  Real breathing trouble — ribs heaving, neck extended, gums going blue. Not pant-from-stress; this is heatstroke or respiratory crisis.
  Repeated vomiting, or any blood in vomit.
  Bloody diarrhea.
  A seizure.

Three pieces of evidence, ordered by cost (cheap first), each ruling in or out exactly one hypothesis. No edits to the iOS file at any point.

Step 1 - What did the iOS generator actually consume?
Hash the canonical package version the iOS project pins to (lockfile / resolved version), not the version you intended. Inspect those exact bytes for the new spacing value.
- If the pinned package does not contain the new value -> canonical-package problem (C). The fix is upstream: republish or bump the pin. The iOS file cannot regenerate correctly until then.
- If the pinned package does contain it -> C is provisionally out.

Step 2 - Was the iOS run the same generator as the web run?
Capture the generator version (commit SHA, release tag, or binary hash) for the iOS invocation and for the web invocation that produced the correct output. Diff the invocations: command, flags, inputs, generator version.
- If iOS used a different or older generator, or different flags/inputs -> generator-version drift (B). Align the iOS generator with web (or upgrade it if web's is the correct newer one), then re-run.
- If identical -> B is provisionally out.

Step 3 - Force a clean iOS regeneration.
Bypass every cache layer (generator cache, build cache, copy/derived-data step). Re-run iOS generation from the pinned canonical package with the same generator as step 2.
- If the iOS output now matches -> stale generated output (A). The fix is in the build/refresh/copy step that should have picked up the new file, not in the file itself.
- If it still does not match -> a subtler case remains: either an iOS-specific generator bug (per-platform config, template, transform) which is a subset of B, or the iOS path is reading from a non-canonical override that shadows the package, which is a subset of C. Next move: dump what the generator actually read at runtime vs the pinned package contents. That resolves which one.

End state for Anya, in every branch: the iOS file gets corrected by regenerating, never by hand. Whichever hypothesis lands, the fix is upstream (canonical, generator, or build) and the regenerated file is the proof.

Two anti-patterns to flag if she has to escalate: do not "fix" the iOS file by editing it (it will be overwritten and masks the real fault); do not assume "web matched so the package is fine" without checking what iOS actually pinned to - the asymmetry you observed is the entire diagnostic, and web being correct is what makes iOS's failure isolable in three steps.

OFF-BIKE INSPECTION SEQUENCE

The "skip only in smallest cog under hard pedaling" pattern is classic for chain/cog wear mismatch (small cog wears fastest, has the thinnest profile, and the fewest teeth sharing torque), but the four causes you named each have their own checks. Work through them in order — what you rule out sharpens what remains.

PRE-INSPECTION

  Move the bike to a stand or flip it upside-down on the bars and saddle (put a rag under the bar tape/saddle to protect them). If neither works, lean it drivetrain-side-out against a wall.
  Degrease and wipe the chain and cassette before you start. Skipping this step is how people miss worn teeth.

1. INDEXING CHECK (rules out cable tension / limit screw / hanger alignment)

  Shift into the smallest cog, hand-pedal slowly, and listen for the chain wanting to upshift on its own — that's mis-indexing toward an easier gear.
  Click one cog at a time up and back down. Every click should be a clean shift with no hesitation or chain rub in adjacent gears.
  In the smallest cog, look at the rear derailleur from behind: the upper jockey wheel should sit directly under the smallest cog, not past it. Overshoot = high-limit screw problem.
  Cable tension: with the chain in the smallest cog, the cable should have just taken up slack. If the barrel adjuster has more than ~2 turns of room either way, indexing drift is plausible.
  Indexing problems usually misbehave under hand-pedaling too. Clean shifts by hand + skipping only under load = indexing is probably not the sole cause.

2. STIFF LINK CHECK (rules out a seized link)

  Shift into the small/big combo (smallest chainring + largest cog). This slackens the chain.
  Hold the chain against a straight edge (ruler works). A clean line = no stiff link; a bow = the culprit.
  Flex each pair of links by hand. Most should pivot freely with no grinding or stiffness. Note any that bind or feel gritty.
  Decisive test: lift the chain off the small cog at the rear derailleur and hold it vertically with one link between thumb and forefinger on each side; flex. Every link should hinge smoothly.
  A stiff link usually causes skipping at whatever cog position it happens to land at, which changes as you pedal. Skipping only in the smallest cog is less suggestive of a stiff link — but worth ruling out.

3. CHAIN WEAR CHECK (rules out elongation past the cog teeth's ability to engage)

  Best: use a chain wear tool (Park CC-3.2 or similar) with 0.5% and 0.75% notches. Modern 9/10/11/12-speed chains should be replaced at 0.5% to preserve the cassette; 0.75% is almost always "replace chain AND inspect cassette."
  No tool: measure pin-to-pin across 12 complete inner+outer link pairs with a ruler. New = exactly 304.8 mm. Each 0.1% of stretch adds 0.3 mm. 306.3 mm = 0.5%; 307.1 mm = 0.75%.
  Chain past 0.75% with skipping in the smallest cog is your smoking gun. Even if the chain measures OK, the cog may be the weak link — go to step 4.

4. CASSETTE / COG WEAR CHECK (rules out hooked "shark-fin" teeth on the smallest cog)

  With the chain on the smallest cog, lift the chain off the leading face of a tooth and look at the tooth profile from the side.
  New teeth: symmetric trapezoid, flat top, even sides.
  Worn teeth: asymmetric, hooked toward the drive direction, often with a visible pointed tip — the classic shark fin. They grab and slip under peak torque.
  Compare the smallest cog to a middle cog (4th or 5th from smallest). If the small one looks visibly more hooked, more polished, or sharper, it's past the chain's ability to engage.
  Smallest cog wears first because it has fewer teeth sharing the load and is aluminum on most cassettes; steel/nickel-plated larger cogs last longer.

5. REAR WHEEL + CASSETTE SECURITY CHECK (rules out loose axle/bearings or a cassette shifting on the freehub)

  Wheel bearing play: grip the tire at 3 and 9 o'clock and rock side to side. Any clicking/clunking/felt movement = loose cone or cartridge bearing issue (spoke flex isn't movement; bearing play is). Repeat at 12 and 6 for axle-direction play.
  Axle security:
    - QR: closing the lever should require firm hand pressure and leave a visible imprint in your palm. Snap-shut with no resistance = loose.
    - Thru-axle: should be torqued to spec (typically 5–15 Nm — model-specific). Use a torque wrench if you have one.
  Cassette on freehub: with the wheel in the frame and the chain on any cog, grab the largest cog and try to rotate it against the freehub direction. It should not turn independently. Any rotational play means the lockring (or the cassette, depending on the system) is loose; under peak torque the whole cassette can momentarily unindex on the spline and cause a skip. A loose lockring can be re-torqued; a cassette that moves freely on the spline usually means worn splines — that's a shop job.

DIAGNOSTIC SUMMARY — which finding matches which cause

  Indexing only (shifts sloppy by hand, no cog wear): cable tension, limit screw, or hanger. Adjustable at home.
  Stiff link (chain bows when slack, one hinge binds): free with chain lube + flex, or replace the chain.
  Chain + cog wear (chain past 0.5%, smallest cog teeth hooked): replace the chain AND the cassette; new chain on worn cogs = the skip returns within a few rides.
  Loose wheel (rocking play at bearings/axle): tighten axle, then service bearings — cup-and-cone vs. cartridge is different work, may be a shop job depending on your tools.
  Loose cassette (rotational play on the freehub): lockring torque; if the splines are already worn, replace the freehub or wheel.

CRITERIA FOR LEAVING IT UNRIDDEN AND TAKING IT TO A SHOP

  Stop home work and take it in if any of the following is true:
    - Chain wear is at or past 0.75%.
    - Smallest cog teeth show visible hooking or shark-fin shape, regardless of what the chain measures.
    - Cassette has rotational play on the freehub, or the lockring is visibly loose.
    - Wheel has bearing play you can't diagnose or confidently adjust.
    - A stiff link won't free with chain lube and careful flexing.
    - Indexing is clean, chain is in spec, cog teeth look fine, and the skip still isn't explained. There's a fifth cause (chainring wear, hanger bent despite looking straight, or a damaged tooth hidden under the chain) that needs hands-on inspection.

A skip under hard pedaling means the drivetrain momentarily lost engagement. A chain that comes off or a pedal that kicks back at speed is the failure mode you're preventing by not riding it under load — your call to stop the ride and park the bike is the right one until the cause is identified or corrected.

Diagnostic sequence for the modem-to-router Ethernet link

Premise: the modem's optical-status light stayed solid, so the upstream fiber/coax side looks fine. The signature you saw (1 Gbps → 100 Mbps renegotiation) is the classic fingerprint of a degraded physical link — 1000BASE-T needs all four pairs, 100BASE-TX only uses two, so the router is telling you that at least one pair is marginal. That almost always points at the patch cable or a connector-seating issue; a failed modem Ethernet port is rarer but possible. Order below is least to most disruptive.

1. Capture a clean baseline (zero disruption)
   - Router admin page → WAN/internet status. Record negotiated speed/duplex (expect 1000 / Full) and any interface counters it exposes (CRC errors, input errors, runts).
   - Copy or screenshot the router log so you have a reference before the next failure.

2. Visual and tactile inspection of the existing patch cable and jacks (no swaps)
   - Look at the jacket for kinks, crushed sections, sharp bends, or a stretched run.
   - Look at both RJ45 connectors: bent pins, loose latch, oxidised/gold-discoloured contacts, debris in the jack.
   - Confirm cable category: must be Cat 5e or Cat 6. CCA (copper-clad aluminium) patch cables are a known failure mode — they negotiate gigabit at first then drop under thermal or load changes.
   - Reseat both ends firmly until the latch clicks.

3. Watch and capture the next failure (no change yet, just observation)
   - When it renegotiates again, grab: timestamp, the exact log line that names the speed transition, the WAN port counter deltas (especially CRC and input errors), and what the modem's own link light does at that moment. Don't reseat immediately — let one or two cycles happen so you have real data to work with.

4. Substitute a known-good cable (one disruption, the most informative single step)
   - Swap in a different Cat 5e or Cat 6 patch cable of the same length or shorter. A cable you've used elsewhere is fine as a temporary.
   - Leave it in place for several days. If the link stays at 1 Gbps and CRC counters stay flat, the original cable is the failure — replace it permanently. If the fallback recurs, the cable wasn't the only problem; continue.

5. Try alternate ports if step 4 doesn't stabilise the link
   - Some routers let you move the WAN to a different port; otherwise just reseat firmly into the same WAN port and inspect the pins with a flashlight.
   - If the modem has more than one Ethernet jack, try the second one. If it has only one, leave the port swap to the ISP step.

6. Re-check the modem's own diagnostics (zero disruption once you're in its admin UI)
   - Modem status page (often 192.168.100.1 or printed on the label). Look at the WAN Ethernet port counters and the upstream line stats. Errors on the modem-side WAN counters with a clean router-side cable point at the modem's Ethernet port. Errors on the upstream line counters point at the ISP feed — and the solid optical light doesn't rule that out, it just means the optical link itself is up.

Evidence that justifies contacting the ISP:
- A known-good cable and reseated jacks still produce recurring renegotiation to 100 Mbps, link flaps, or climbing CRC/input errors on the router WAN interface.
- The modem's own WAN-Ethernet page shows port errors, or the modem's upstream line stats show errors/retries/retrains while the optical light stays solid.
- The same failure reproduces when you connect a different router to the modem with a known-good cable — i.e., the router is ruled out.
- You have captured timestamps and log excerpts showing the pattern. One or two cycles is enough.

What to ask the ISP for: a modem swap (suspect the modem's Ethernet port) and a line test from their side. Tell them the optical light is solid so they don't waste time on the fiber run, and hand them the renegotiation timestamps plus your speed and CRC observations — that saves a truck roll when they have to escalate.

Optional follow-up once things are stable on a new cable: label the run and add a small strain relief so the connector isn't tugged, and check whether the cable sits near a heat source or under furniture that could be slowly deforming the jacket.

Short answer: yes — a clasp whose gate won't return fully closed on its own is not safe to use with Kibo, unless the sequence below restores it to crisp, fully self-closing behavior afterward. Cleaning is the diagnostic to find out which case you're in. If the post-clean tests don't all pass, retire it.

Why the bar is that high: the spring force is the safety mechanism. A gate that hangs partway open has either debris adding friction, a weakened spring, or both. Cleaning fixes the first and not the second. The consequence of a clasp popping open during a walk — a startled Kibo loose near traffic while you're rebuilding the truck-intersection work — isn't a risk worth running on a marginal piece of hardware.

Cleaning sequence (unloaded, Kibo already on the backup leash):
1. Move Kibo onto the backup leash first. Don't clean the suspect clasp while it's anywhere near him.
2. Lukewarm water rinse. No hot water — slush is already melted, and heat is bad for spring temper.
3. Under the rinse, work the gate open and closed 20–30 times to flush salt, sand, and grit from the pivot pin and spring channel.
4. Optional: one drop of light machine oil (3-in-1 or sewing-machine oil) on the pivot, then work the gate many times to work it in. Do not use WD-40 — it's a solvent that strips the spring's lubrication and dries out the mechanism.
5. Wipe dry, then air-dry fully before testing.

Unloaded test sequence (hold the clasp with the gate opening facing away from you the whole time — a spring release under tension can snap hard):
1. Visual: with the gate released, does it sit fully flush in the body's catch with a clear "click"?
2. Repeat-open test: open and release the gate 10 times in a row. Every time, it must snap fully closed under spring force alone, with the same snappy return. Any mushiness, hesitation, or need to nudge it = fail.
3. Side-load test: hook the closed clasp to a fixed point (doorknob, fence ring, the backup leash's loop) and try to pull the gate open sideways with finger pressure. If your fingers open it, a lunging dog will absolutely pop it.
4. Shock-load test: hook the clasp to something fixed at waist height and give the leash body a firm, quick jerk — the kind of snap a startled dog produces. If the gate opens, retire immediately.
5. Static load test: hook the clasp to a fixed point and hang roughly Kibo's weight from it for a minute. Any gate creep or partial-disengagement click = retire.

Decision rule:
  - Pre-clean, partial self-closure is a strong signal but not definitive (could be debris). Clean first, then retest.
  - Post-clean, partial self-closure on any of the five tests = retire. Don't use it with Kibo. It's still fine for tying up a pack strap or a non-safety use where failure has no consequence.
  - Post-clean, all five pass crisply = likely debris-related, and the clasp is fine to return to service. Watch it over the next several walks; any return of mushiness means retire.

Replacement note worth mentioning: a forged brass or stainless bolt-snap from a marine/hardware supplier is a few dollars and gives a real safety margin over a stamped pot-metal clasp. Worth picking up as a permanent backup even if this one passes — salt and slush will eventually get the better of any clasp on a Brooklyn winter routine.

Account containment sequence

Premise: the password is unique, MFA is on, and you see no unfamiliar orders, payment changes, recovery-email changes, or active sessions. So the goal is to invalidate the disclosed credential, close any session the credential may have opened before MFA was challenged, and audit the recovery surface. Card rotation is reserved for actual-use signals, not the breach notification alone.

1. Independent sign-in
   - Open the retailer by typing the domain or using your own bookmark. Treat the alert link as evidence, not as a route.
   - Confirm HTTPS and that the certificate matches the canonical domain; the password manager's stored URL is the reference.
   - Sign in directly. If the login page copy, branding, or fields look off, stop and re-verify the URL before entering anything.

2. Password replacement
   - Generate a new password through your password manager: long, random, unique.
   - Replace the password manager entry. The old value stays out of reuse.
   - Where the site imposes composition rules, prefer the manager-generated value and store any constraint with the entry; don't downgrade to a memorable variant.

3. Session revocation
   - Open the account security / devices / active-sessions page.
   - Sign out every session, or use "sign out everywhere" if offered.
   - Revoke any third-party app authorizations, OAuth tokens, or linked accounts you don't recognize.

4. MFA and recovery audit
   - Confirm MFA is still on and that every listed factor is yours. Authenticator app and hardware key beat SMS; SMS is acceptable but not preferred.
   - Regenerate backup / recovery codes; store the new set with the password manager or other safe store, retire the old.
   - Verify recovery phone and recovery email: both should be yours, unchanged, and reachable.
   - Remove any factor, app password, or paired device you don't recognize. A factor you didn't add is a takeover signal — treat it as compromise and go to step 6.

5. Saved-payment review
   - List cards and payment methods on file. Compare last four, brand, and expiration against what you actually have.
   - Remove tokens, wallets, or cards you don't recognize.
   - You don't need to rotate the card yet — see step 6 for triggers.

6. Conditions that justify broader action

Rotate the card / request a new number from the issuer if any of:
   - A charge you don't recognize appears, including small test charges.
   - A saved card or wallet token you didn't add.
   - A shipping or billing address you didn't add.
   - Gift-card balance activity that doesn't match your history.

Widen credential rotation if:
   - The disclosed password was used elsewhere — re-confirm "no" by searching the password manager for it; an indexed dump may predate your memory of reuse.
   - Any recovery email or factor on another account matches this account's email.
   - The breach metadata indicates plaintext or weakly-hashed passwords rather than modern salted hashes.

Treat the account as compromised and contact the retailer's security / fraud team if:
   - You can't sign in (password or recovery changed under you).
   - Recovery email or phone on file is no longer yours.
   - An MFA factor appears that you didn't add.
   - Active sessions reappear after step 3.
   - Orders, addresses, gift balances, or loyalty redemptions changed since your last look.

Posture notes
   - "No signs yet" and "no compromise" are not the same. Re-check the account in 24-48 hours; a clean review today doesn't rule out slow-burn activity.
   - MFA materially reduces takeover risk from a credential dump but doesn't remove it (SIM swap, MFA-fatigue prompts, recovery-flow abuse, mailbox compromise of the recovery email all remain live paths).
   - Because the password is unique, the blast radius is the one account. The whole reason the sequence can stay proportionate is that this assumption holds; if it doesn't, the scope widens immediately.

The preservation-first principle: do not delete or shrink anything in iCloud until a verified encrypted local copy exists on your computer. Here is the ordered sequence.

0.  Confirm what you have. The path differs slightly between macOS (Finder, since Catalina) and Windows (iTunes, or the new Apple Devices app on Windows 10/11). The procedure below covers both.

1.  Confirm space on the destination volume.
    -   Rule of thumb: free space should be at least 1.5x to 2x the phone's Used storage (Settings → General → iPhone Storage). A backup is usually larger than the source data it represents.
    -   Put the backup on a stable internal volume, not an external drive that may be disconnected later. A backup on a drive that disappears is functionally lost.
    -   If iCloud Photos is fully synced (which you said it is), the backup will not contain the full photo library — it stores references to iCloud Photos. So the backup will be smaller than you might expect. That is normal, not a sign the backup failed.

2.  Set up the backup password BEFORE you click Encrypt.
    -   The password cannot be recovered by Apple or by you. If you lose it, the backup file is unusable even if intact.
    -   Save it in your password manager under a clearly named entry. Optionally print it and keep the printout somewhere physically safe. Do not email it to yourself.

3.  Pre-connect conditions.
    -   Phone on power, or battery well above 50 percent.
    -   Computer awake and not on a sleep timer.
    -   Known-good cable, or both devices on the same Wi-Fi if you intend to back up over Wi-Fi. Note: wireless sync has to be enabled during a prior wired session, so the first run is normally wired.
    -   Unlock the phone. When the Trust this computer prompt appears, tap Trust and enter the passcode. If you have ever tapped Don't Trust on this computer, you must trust again before any backup can proceed.

4.  Create the encrypted local backup.
    -   macOS: connect the phone, open Finder, select the iPhone in the sidebar. Under Backups, pick Back up all of the data on your iPhone to this Mac and check Encrypt local backup. Enter and confirm the password.
    -   Windows: open iTunes or the Apple Devices app, click the phone icon, choose This computer under Backups, check Encrypt local backup, enter and confirm the password.
    -   Click Back Up Now. Do not disconnect until the progress completes and the reported timestamp matches the moment you started.

5.  Verify the backup. Three levels, increasing strength. Do not skip this.

    Level 1, surface check.
    -   macOS: in Finder, with the iPhone selected, click Manage Backups. The new entry should show today's date and a size in the multi-gigabyte range. A backup that finished instantly and is only kilobytes did not capture anything — do not trust it.
    -   Windows: in iTunes, Edit → Preferences → Devices. Same check: today's date, meaningful size.

    Level 2, structural check.
    -   A third-party reader can list the backup's domains. iMazing, iBackup Extractor, or the open-source iphone-backup-tools all work. Confirm the domains you care about are present, especially:
        -   MessageDomain (Messages, iMessage attachments)
        -   SettingsDomain, PreferencesDomain (device settings)
        -   HomeDomain, KeychainDomain, NoteDomain, CalendarDomain
        -   CameraRollDomain or PhotoData (photo library metadata, not full photos)

    Level 3, restore test. The only definitive proof.
    -   Restore the backup to a second compatible device. If you do not have one, the practical strongest check you can do at home is Level 1 plus Level 2, plus taking a second backup immediately afterward and confirming the two backups differ only in the time window between them (a structural diff). If the second backup is identical down to the byte, both are probably stale or the backup is being silently skipped.

6.  STOP HERE. Do not touch iCloud yet. The 12/26 stale backup stays put until your local copy is verified.

7.  Only after verification, decide on iCloud.
    -   To free space: Settings → [your name] → iCloud → Manage Account Storage → Backups. The stale 12/26 entry is a candidate for deletion. Delete it only after the local backup is verified AND you have a second backup taken on a different day — that way one corrupt file cannot strand you.
    -   To shrink future backups: in iCloud Backup options, toggle off apps whose data you do not need in a full restore (large chat apps, offline game data). Backups then stop carrying that data forward.
    -   Independent of backups, consider turning on Messages in iCloud (Settings → [your name] → iCloud → Messages). With it on, iMessage/SMS history lives in iCloud continuously and is not solely dependent on a periodic full backup. This is the single biggest reason cloud device backups grow large.

8.  Recovery posture going forward.
    -   Pattern: local copy first, then cloud edit, never the reverse. Any time you intend to delete or rotate cloud data, take and verify a local encrypted backup first.
    -   Rotate local backups every few months — old ones accumulate app data that no longer matches your current phone.

Minimum bar before you touch the 12/26 backup: Level 1 verification (correct date, multi-GB size) plus Level 2 verification (Messages and Settings domains present) plus a second backup taken on a later day that is structurally different from the first.

  - Symptoms settle back to baseline within roughly 30 minutes — yours settled within 10

Goal: free ~8 GB by deleting ONLY the obsolete device backup, verify the resulting headroom, then refresh the current encrypted cloud backup. Nothing else in your iCloud account is touched in this pass.

PRE-FLIGHT (read-only — no changes yet)

2.  Locate the Backups list and identify the obsolete one.

    - Mac (older): Apple menu > System Preferences > Apple ID > iCloud > Manage.
    - iPhone / iPad: Settings > [your name] > iCloud > Manage Storage > Backups.
    - For each entry, confirm device name, iOS version, and "Last Backup" date. The obsolete one will:
        * have a device name that is NOT your current phone,

3.  Confirm what must NOT be touched in this pass.
    - iCloud Photos: synced/complete — leave status alone.
    - Messages in iCloud (if enabled): do not toggle off (would delete synced messages from the cloud copy).
    - iCloud Drive contents: do not delete.

DELETE ONLY THE OBSOLETE BACKUP

4.  Select the obsolete backup from the list.

    - Used space should drop by ~8 GB (expected ~41.7 GB used of 50).
    - Free space should be ~8–8.3 GB, which is enough for one fresh encrypted cloud backup.
9.  If the size did not drop as expected (Apple sometimes rounds the displayed backup size, or another item shares quota), STOP here. Do not start a new backup until you understand the discrepancy.

REFRESH THE CURRENT ENCRYPTED CLOUD BACKUP

Lock the card now through the issuer's app (toggle the lock/freeze — reversible, blocks new authorizations instantly, doesn't affect recurring bills or the pending $1.00 which will either post or drop off on its own). Lock is the proportionate immediate move; replacement is the second step, not a substitute for locking.

Why this is almost certainly card-testing: a $1.00 authorization from a generic-sounding merchant ("NORTHSTAR DIGITAL") at an odd hour, with the physical card in your possession and no other activity, is the classic pattern of a fraudster confirming a stolen card number is "live" before selling it or running a larger charge. Treat the card number as known to a third party whether or not a bigger charge ever appears.

Issuer contact and verification — independent channel only

- Use the issuer's app or the number printed on the back of the physical card you hold. Do not use any phone number, URL, or email address that appeared in the transaction details or in any text/email about the charge — those can be set by the fraudster or a follow-on scammer.
- Through the app first: you can usually view merchant category, terminal ID, and full descriptor; dispute the charge; lock/unlock the card; and order a replacement — all on a written trail without a phone call.
- Phone the issuer only if the app can't show the merchant details you want, or if you want to file a verbal fraud report on top of the in-app dispute. Confirm identity with the usual prompts; an issuer will never ask for your full card number, CVV, or online-banking password on an inbound call they initiated.
- Decline any inbound call claiming to be the issuer about this charge; if you want to act on what they say, hang up and call the number on the card yourself.

Evidence to preserve before anything ages out

- Screenshot, with timestamps visible: the pending transaction line (amount, merchant name as shown, date/time, pending vs. posted), the full transaction details screen, any merchant category code or terminal info the app exposes, and the lock confirmation.
- Screenshot any push notification, email, or SMS from the issuer about the charge — exactly as received.
- The merchant descriptor string verbatim ("NORTHSTAR DIGITAL") and any associated phone/URL the app shows. Do not call the number or visit the URL.
- Your recent transactions list as of right now (to show no other unfamiliar activity) and the device/session list on the card account.
- A short note: date/time you first saw the auth, where the physical card is (with you), and that you have not contacted any number from a text/email about it. Useful if you later file a police report or an IRS identity-theft affidavit.
- The pending $1.00 will typically drop off in 1–7 business days if not captured, or post. Either outcome is fine; the screenshot is what matters.

Criteria for replacing the card

- Replace, don't just lock, if any of the following holds (and in your case the first one alone is enough): the PAN has demonstrably been exposed to a third party (the $1.00 test confirms that, even if no further charge appears); you use the card at online merchants where a stored number could be the breach vector; you want recurring charges to automatically fail and force you to re-enroll them on the new number (often a feature, not a bug); you don't want to manually unlock the card for every legitimate future purchase.
- Lock-only is reasonable if the card is rarely used, you can tolerate the friction of unlocking per purchase, and you want to avoid re-entering the new number across many recurring merchants. Lock-only does not change the PAN, so the next test charge on the old number will still land if you unlock by accident.
- Recommendation for your situation: lock immediately (already done above), then order the replacement today. The recurring-bill update cost is small; the residual risk of leaving a known-bad PAN alive is not.

Other proportionate hygiene

- Turn on transaction alerts (push or SMS) for any future charge above a low threshold, if not already on.
- Review the issuer's list of stored merchant tokens / digital wallet entries (Apple Pay, Google Pay, merchant-saved cards); remove anything you don't recognize. These survive a card lock but will need re-enrollment on the new card.
- Don't pre-emptively delete saved cards on shopping sites until you've decided whether to investigate a specific breach vector — replacing the card number accomplishes the same goal and is easier to roll back if you guess wrong.
- If a real (non-$1.00) charge ever posts, dispute via the app and request provisional credit; under federal law the issuer must investigate and typically credits within ~10 business days, and you'll get a written fraud affidavit to keep.
- If anyone contacts you demanding payment for the $1.00, or asking you to "verify" the card to reverse the block, that's the next-stage scam — hang up and call the number on the card.

Net: lock now, screenshot everything, contact the issuer only through the app or the number on the physical card, and order a replacement card today rather than gambling that no larger charge will follow.

## Aligned thresholds (reference session, 2024-10-07, Alex + Wes)

A canary push window is in force only while every observed push meets all of the following:

- Retired generations remain at **four or fewer** at every observation.
- Cleanup pauses remain **at or below 100 ms** at every observation.
- The **full health set returns to baseline** after every push.

Any push that exceeds either ceiling (retired generations > 4, or cleanup pause > 100 ms) **stops the window immediately**. A health-set baseline that fails to return after a push also stops the window.

## Recovery sequence

1. Window is stopped by a ceiling breach.
2. Health set is brought back to baseline and held there.
3. A **fresh decision** (re-confirmation of the push authorization by the owner of record) is recorded.
4. That fresh decision permits **exactly one fully observed recovery push**.
5. The recovery push is **not** a reopened multi-push window. After the single observed recovery push, a new window requires another fresh decision.
6. Health baseline is re-established after the recovery push before any further authorization is considered.

## Standing rollback conditions (unchanged)

The following conditions remain in force and trigger rollback independent of the canary thresholds:

- Consistency violations
- Parity violations
- Dropped-series regressions
- Reload failures
- Restart failures

## Recorded case — second September push (correctly classified)

- Intended change: single file.
- Retired generations: peaked at **4** (at ceiling, not over).
- Cleanup pause: **103 ms** (over the 100 ms ceiling).
- Window action: **stopped immediately**.
- Health set: full baseline returned **7 minutes** after stop.
- Additional pushes in the window: **none**.
- Classification by Wes: **stopped window** — explicitly *not* a completed safe push and *not* a reopened window.

The 103 ms cleanup pause is the binding breach in this case. Retired generations sitting at the 4 ceiling is consistent with the rule; the cleanup-pause ceiling is what stopped the window.

## Recorded case — 94 ms recovery-push exercise (2024-10-08, Alex + Wes, accepted by Hema)

- Authorization: the *** fully observed recovery push permitted by Alex's fresh post-recovery decision following the 103 ms stop above. Not a reopened multi-push window.
- Intended change: single file.

- Cleanup pause: **94 ms** (under the 100 ms ceiling).
- Health set: **full health set returned to baseline** after the push.
- Window action: recovery push observed in full; window closed after the single observed push per the recovery sequence.
- Classification by Wes: **the one fully observed push authorized by the fresh decision**, verified against the retired-generations and full-health-set conditions above. Explicitly *not* described as a reopened window.
- Hema's acceptance: accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators.

Here is a prioritized checklist, ordered by what protects you soonest vs. what can wait for the new card.

TIER 1 — TODAY: preserve the record and take inventory

  1. Preserve the issuer case record
     - Screenshot or download the case number, the closure date, the Jan 27 replacement ETA, the confirmation that the $1.00 NORTHSTAR DIGITAL auth will not post, and the statement that no other unfamiliar pending or posted activity exists.
     - Save any chat/email transcript with the issuer into a dated folder (e.g. "card-fraud-closure-2025-01-22").
     - Why first: this is your timestamped proof that you reported and resolved the issue. If anything else surfaces later, it establishes the boundary of what was known when.

  2. Inventory every recurring charge on the closed card
     - Pull the last 2–3 statements (or use the issuer app).
     - For each merchant, note: amount, next billing date, and whether they have another payment method on file.
     - You cannot triage what you have not enumerated.

TIER 2 — TODAY / TOMORROW: move only the critical recurring payments

  3. Tier the recurring list by harm-of-miss
     - Critical (move today): rent/mortgage, heating/electric (it's January in NYC — heat matters), health insurance premium, auto insurance if paid monthly, phone, anything with a hard cutoff.
     - Important but flexible: internet, car payment, transit pass, gym.
     - Deferrable: streaming services, subscription boxes, anything that charges monthly and won't cause harm if delayed.

  4. For each Tier-1 critical charge, switch the payment method off the closed card
     - Preferred: another card, or ACH from your bank account.
     - If the closed card is the only one on file, call the merchant, explain the replacement is in transit, and ask for a one-time extension or alternate payment (bank transfer, check).
     - Do this BEFORE the next billing date, not after.

  5. For Tier-2/3 charges, decide case-by-case: switch now, or let them fail and fix once the new card arrives
     - A failed charge you correct within a billing cycle usually costs nothing.
     - Switch now only if the merchant has no grace period or you actively depend on the service.

TIER 3 — BETWEEN NOW AND JAN 27: receive the new card

  6. Activate the replacement card the day it arrives; set/confirm the PIN if your issuer uses one.

  7. Move the remaining (Tier-3) recurring charges to the new card and keep a written log of what you changed and when.

  8. Destroy the old card after all critical charges are confirmed running on the new card — cut through the chip and magnetic stripe. The account is closed but the physical card still carries the cancelled number.

TIER 4 — AFTER ACTIVATION

  9. Verify the first statement on the new card is clean (same merchants, expected amounts, no surprises). Your Tier 1 record is the reference if anything looks off.

  10. Optional belt-and-suspenders: pull a free report at annualcreditreport.com 30–60 days from now to confirm nothing else was opened in your name. Cheap to do, rarely needed.

One note on the $1.00 auth pattern: small "card-testing" authorizations are a standard fraud probe — someone verifies a stolen card number is live before attempting larger charges. The issuer catching it quickly and closing the card is the right outcome, and the absence of other unfamiliar activity means the probe was rejected or stopped before anything larger was attempted. Residual risk is low; the value of Tier 1 is that you now have a dated record if anything does surface later.

No — don't silently map `qa` → `staging`. Three reasons:

1. The bounded contract lists `qa` in the rejection set deliberately, on the same line as `unknown`, malformed, and arbitrary raw strings. Silent mapping is label laundering: the submitter never learns their config is wrong, downstream consumers see `staging` and act on it without knowing the source used `qa`. That's exactly the failure mode the pre-publication rejection exists to prevent.

2. The rejection was a safe outcome, not an incident. Zero series published, accepted-traffic error and latency at baseline — the contract did what it was designed to do. There is nothing to "fix" on the normalization side.

3. The owner's framing is wrong. "Workload is non-production" is not the criterion the label encodes; the label encodes the environment the telemetry originates from. If this is a staging environment, the right answer is for the owner to resubmit with `staging` (or `dev` if it really is dev). Both are in the allowed set — it's a one-line config edit on their side.

What to tell the owner: re-submit with `staging`. If they genuinely think `qa` should be an accepted value going forward, that's a contract-change request to the contract owner (separate conversation, not a per-release exception). Don't carve a one-off mapping — that becomes the precedent everyone then cites, and the bounded set stops being bounded.

Under the deployed contract, the `env` field on a deploy is a bounded enum that accepts exactly three values: `dev`, `staging`, `prod` (verbatim, lowercase — that's what the contract on `deploy_service` enumerates; anything else returns an `{error: invalid env}` response and the deploy is not performed).

Classification of the rejected `QA` value
- Out-of-vocabulary / not a valid environment label under the current contract.
- Not a coercion target. There is no alias, mapping, or case-fold rule that turns `QA` into any accepted value — the rejection is the contract behaving correctly, not a transient or upstream failure.
- Not "staging-with-a-QA-tag." QA is treated as a distinct label space the bounded contract does not recognize; passing it through silently would be exactly the kind of scope-creep the bounded contract is designed to prevent.

Correct producer action
1. Do not retry with `QA` and do not substitute a guess.
2. Determine the actual intended deployment target from context and re-issue the call with the correct in-contract label (`dev`, `staging`, or `prod`).
3. If the producer genuinely needs a `QA` target, that is a contract-extension request — raise it with the contract owner before calling `deploy_service` again. The bounded contract is not the place to negotiate new labels inline.

Plan for mild salt irritation on Kibo's right front paw:

TONIGHT (already started)
  - Finish the rinse with lukewarm (not hot) water; 30-second soak on the affected paw, gently work water between the pads with your fingers. Plain water is fine; if you have dilute chlorhexidine (0.05%) or a mild unscented dog paw cleanser, that adds margin.
  - Pat dry thoroughly, especially between the pads. Residual moisture there prolongs irritation and invites a bacterial/fungal issue.
  - Apply a thin layer of paw balm between and on the pads: plain petroleum jelly, Musher's Secret, Bag Balm, or similar. This both soothes and starts a barrier habit.
  - Recheck the area in good light: look for any small crack, splinter of ice/crystal, or spot you may have missed. If you find anything sharp, do not dig - that's a vet visit.

INTERRUPT THE LICKING
  - Licking is both a sign and a perpetuator - saliva macerates already-irritated skin. After the rinse and balm, redirect for 10-15 min (frozen Kong, short sniff game). If he returns to the paw persistently, use an e-collar for short stretches or a sock secured above the dewclaw with a small strip of vet wrap (not tight, two-finger check). Take it off when supervised.
  - Avoid zinc-oxide creams, essential oils, perfumed lotions, hydrogen peroxide - all can worsen a chemical-type irritation or are toxic if licked.

FOR THE NEXT SEVERAL DAYS WHILE SALT IS ON THE GROUND
  - Pre-walk: thin balm layer between pads and on pads. Wait a minute before heading out so it sets.
  - Mid/post-walk: wipe each paw with a damp cloth or rinse in a shallow tub at the door before he can lick. Do not let salt sit on the skin.
  - Prospect Park paths are usually less aggressively salted than city sidewalks; if your usual loop has a route with less treated pavement, prefer it for a few days.
  - Booties are the gold-standard barrier, but given Kibo's startle response to skateboards/skates near the curb, I'd skip them on busy Prospect Park paths - a surprise + unfamiliar pawgear is a bad combination. Stick with balm + wipe routine unless you can desensitize booties on quiet sidewalks first.

WHEN TO CALL THE VET (same-day, not emergent unless noted)
  - Limping, toe-touching only, or refusing to bear weight
  - Swelling of toes or the whole paw
  - Heat in that paw compared to the others
  - Any discharge - pus, blood, foul smell from between the pads
  - Visible erosion, raw spot, open crack, or ulcer between pads (salt chemical burns can progress from pink to open quickly)
  - Repeated vomiting, lethargy, or marked appetite drop (heavy paw-licking can mean meaningful salt ingestion; rare but worth flagging)
  - Color change - pale, white, blue, or purple anywhere on the paw (circulation, not just irritation)

CALL THE VET FOR ADVICE (not emergent, but don't sit on it)
  - Pinkness is unchanged or worse after 48-72 hours of the rinse + balm + wipe routine
  - Redness spreads to other pads or up the leg
  - Between the pads looks moist, macerated, or "weeping"
  - He keeps licking the paw more than 24 hours after the rinse, or you catch him licking other paws too
  - Subtle behavior change - less interested in walks, picking the paw up occasionally, slower on stairs

TIMING CHECKS
  - Before bed tonight: pinkness should look stable or improved after the rinse.
  - Tomorrow morning: if the area looks raw, has spread, or he's licking on/off, that's a within-24h vet call.
  - 48-72 hours: normal mild salt irritation should be clearly trending better by then. If it isn't, that's the line for vet advice - salt irritation that lingers can mask or evolve into a chemical burn or interdigital infection.

Kibo's otherwise-normal behavior tonight is a good sign. The routine that gets you to a clean recovery is: rinse + dry + balm tonight, then pre-walk balm and post-walk wipe for as long as sidewalks stay salted, with recheck at 24h and 72h against the red flags above.

Good news on the pinkness clearing - that suggests the interpad irritation from the previous walk is resolved. The 4 mm rough patch is small enough to manage conservatively, but a few things make it worth being deliberate about.

What the rough patch likely is
A shallow, non-bleeding, non-painful rough spot on a single pad in winter, on a dog who walks treated Brooklyn pavement, is most often a mild abrasion or a healing scab from contact with de-icer residue or gritty treated surfaces. Less commonly it can be the early stage of a cracked pad or a small focal callus. None of those are urgent on their own.

On your three questions:

1. Rinsing and a short route - yes, reasonable.
Lukewarm water rinse or a damp cloth wipe right after the walk is still the right move, especially while treated sections remain. A short route reduces total contact time. If it's well below freezing and a full rinse feels harsh, a wipe-down with a damp cloth plus a quick rinse once you're home is fine. Drying the paw afterward matters - lingering moisture between pads is what drove the original irritation.

2. Dog-safe paw balm - appropriate here.
A thin layer on the pad once or twice a day is reasonable for a rough patch of this size. What to look for:
  - Labeled specifically for dogs
  - Non-toxic if licked (they will lick)
  - Simple ingredients: beeswax, shea butter, coconut oil, vitamin E
  - Avoid zinc oxide and avoid essential-oil-heavy formulas (tea tree, citrus, wintergreen are toxic to dogs even in small amounts)
  - A balm or paw wax also works as a pre-walk barrier on treated sections, which is the more useful role for it long-term.

3. When to call the vet - clear thresholds.
Reach out if any of these appear:
  - The rough patch is still there or worse after 7-10 days of rinse + balm
  - It deepens, cracks open, bleeds, or starts to spread
  - New heat, swelling, discharge, or odor from that paw
  - Kibo starts favoring the leg, licking becomes constant rather than occasional, or you get a pain response on gentle handling
  - Any sudden lameness, even brief

A rough patch that holds steady or improves over the next week is not concerning on its own. The combination of "no pain, no limp, otherwise normal, pinkness already resolved" is the reassuring picture right now - the bar to call is change in that picture, not its persistence alone.

One small habit worth keeping: a quick visual check of all four pads after each walk through the end of winter. Treated-section irritation tends to recur on the same paw until either the route changes or you start using a pre-walk barrier.

Bottom line
The pattern you describe — lamp flickers twice and drops out, a known-good lamp fails the same way at the same outlet, the first lamp is fine in another room — points to a problem at the receptacle or upstream on that branch circuit, not the lamps. The "flickered, then died" signature is the classic early behavior of a loose or overheating connection (backstabbed termination, worn contact, or a loose splice upstream in the wall) and is one of the patterns NYC fire investigators flag as a precursor to residential electrical fires. Treat the outlet as out of service until a licensed electrician has looked at it.

One permitted reset, with conditions
- Look at the breaker panel without touching anything yet. Some breakers do not move to a clearly "off" position when they trip — they sit partway between on and off, or look almost-on. If one breaker is in a different position from the rest of the row, that is your candidate.
- Reset rule: flip it fully OFF, then fully ON, once. This is the standard diagnostic step.
- What you learn matters:
  - Outlet returns and breaker holds 24+ hours under ordinary lamp load: the underlying fault is still there. The connection opened for a reason, and the loose/overheating joint hasn't been fixed. Still report it.
  - Breaker trips again immediately, or within minutes: stop, leave the breaker OFF, do not keep resetting. Repeated resets on a real fault is exactly the duty cycle that turns a loose connection into an arc event.
- Do not reset a breaker that clearly matches the rest of the row (still ON). The fault is downstream, not at the panel.

Check for a tripped GFCI elsewhere in the apartment
Bedroom circuits in NYC apartments are often protected by a GFCI device located in another room — bathroom, kitchen, sometimes a hallway, laundry, or outdoor outlet. Press TEST then RESET on every GFCI you can find. If one was tripped, resetting it may restore the bedroom outlet. If it restores, the bedroom still needs reporting — a GFCI that trips under ordinary lamp load indicates leakage or a failing connection, not normal behavior.

Do not do these
- Do not open the faceplate. Even with the breaker off, a renter should not be opening an energized-looking device; miswired receptacles can backfeed, and "off" at the panel is not a guarantee on a shared neutral or multi-wire branch.
- Do not keep plugging things into that outlet, even briefly, to "test" it.
- Do not run a heavy load (space heater, hair dryer, vacuum, window AC) on any other outlet on that same circuit in the meantime — they share the same failing joint.
- Do not ignore it because the plate looks fine. The hazard is internal to the box or upstream in the wall.

Report to building management — yes, this is the correct path
This is a maintenance issue under NYC Housing Maintenance Code and the Multiple Dwelling Law: the owner is responsible for the electrical system, and an intermittent receptacle failure is a recognized fire-risk pattern. Report it tonight and in writing:
- Tonight: call the super's emergency line if your building has one. Most NYC managed buildings maintain a 24-hour line for conditions "likely to cause or lead to fire" — a flickering-then-dead outlet qualifies.
- Within 24 hours, in writing: email or the building portal, with the facts (date, time, both lamps failed, you have de-energized by unplugging). A written record matters if the building is slow.
- Ask specifically for a licensed electrician (not just the super) to inspect the receptacle and trace the circuit back to the panel. If the building only sends the super, say so in writing.

If management is unresponsive
- File with NYC 311 (online or by phone) — "electrical defect / defective outlet." HPD will log it and can dispatch an inspection. The online complaint keeps a paper trail.
- For an active fire-risk concern with no response, FDNY non-emergency line. Call 911 only for visible smoke, sparking, or odor — none of which you are reporting.

One more thing tonight
Verify the bedroom and hallway smoke and CO detectors respond to the test button. The failure mode you described is the kind that, in a worse case, can precede a fire. Working detectors are the right backstop while you wait for the electrician.

Quick recap
- GFCI scan elsewhere in the apartment: do it.
- Single breaker reset, only if you can identify a clearly tripped breaker: permitted once.
- Open the outlet: no.
- Keep using the outlet: no.
- Report to building management and request a licensed electrician: yes, by phone tonight, in writing within 24 hours.

Yes — retire the shorter leash now. Don't trim, don't tape.

A leash is safety equipment, not a fabric item you patch. The frayed fibers are a stress-concentration zone: once a bundle of fibers has been cut, the remaining fibers carry more load per strand, and the next failure happens without warning, usually at peak load — exactly when Kibo startles and lunges. Tape is cosmetic; it doesn't restore strength. Trimming moves the weak point but doesn't eliminate it, and on a leash that's already intentionally short, you can't afford to lose length. Set it aside for recycling and order a replacement of the same length and rating.

For the longer leash near Prospect Park entrances until the replacement arrives:

- Coil the excess and hold it in your off-hand (or clip the loop to the D-ring on the harness if your leash has one). Only let the length out once you're past the entrance plaza into an open path. The goal is to keep effective length close to what the short leash gave you in congested zones.
- Stick with the front-clip harness — unchanged. The harness does the pulling-control work, not the leash.
- Give the skate/skateboard approaches extra clearance. That's Kibo's known trigger, and a longer leash gives you less recovery margin if he lunges. Cross wider, wait for the path to clear, or use a quieter side entrance.
- Off-peak timing helps. The longer leash is easier to manage when the entrance isn't dense with dogs, joggers, and kids.

If at any point the longer leash feels unmanageable in a particular entrance, leave the park from a different side or shorten the walk — don't push through a setup that's working against you.

The short version up front, because this is the part Anya needs to be able to defend if the migration script's author pushes back:

The canonical package is the source; the generated iOS file is a derived artifact. "Newer-looking timestamps in the derived artifact" is not evidence that the source is wrong. Writing derived values back into the source inverts the trust boundary that all three teams agreed on, and it should not happen until source-level evidence (a real diff in values against a pinned (package commit, generator version) pair, with a known-good baseline) says it should.

Bounded verification sequence

Run these in order. Each step has a specific failure mode it's designed to surface. Stop and report — don't proceed past a failure — when a step doesn't match expectations.

1. Pin the generator version
   - Identify the exact generator version (tag or commit SHA) used to produce the iOS file in question. Was it a released version, or a working tree? If the generator has moved since the artifact was generated, the "drift" may simply be new generator behavior, not a source problem. The artifact is only meaningful relative to the generator that produced it.

2. Pin the package commit
   - Identify the exact commit SHA of the canonical package that was the generator's input. The artifact is reproducible from a (package commit, generator version) pair. If the package commit has advanced since the artifact was generated, the artifact doesn't represent the current canonical state at all — comparing its timestamps to current canonical is apples-to-oranges.

3. Read the generation logs
   - Find the CI / build run that produced this specific iOS file. Capture: who/what invoked the generator, against which package commit, with which flags, and what post-processing ran afterward. The "two newer-looking timestamps" pattern is a classic signature of post-generation tooling — a Swift formatter, a header injector, a code-signing or packaging step that rewrites mtime without touching values. If post-processing is the cause, the drift is in metadata, not in the token values, and the migration script's premise is wrong.

4. Drift check on values, not on files
   - Resolve token names end-to-end on both sides and compare values, not raw file contents. If values are identical and only timestamps or file metadata differ, there is no source drift — the artifact is correct and the migration should be rejected. If values genuinely differ, the question becomes which (commit, generator version) pair each side came from, and whether the generator's output for the current canonical input reproduces the artifact's values. A real value-level divergence is a generator bug or a stale artifact, and the fix is to fix the generator or regenerate — not to overwrite the source.

Why generated iOS output should not be written back into canonical without source-level evidence

- Inverts the agreed source of truth. Three teams consume generated outputs from a canonical source. Letting one team's generated file rewrite that source silently moves the source of truth into a derived artifact that the other two teams don't independently audit.
- Destroys provenance. The canonical package's git history is the audit trail. A migration that writes values into it from outside that history leaves future readers seeing a value change with no record of why, who approved it, or what produced it.
- Conflates metadata with semantics. Newer-looking timestamps in a generated file are usually a post-processing artifact, not a signal about the values. Writing timestamps-as-values back into canonical propagates build-tool non-determinism into the source of truth.
- Hides the actual bug. If the values really do diverge, the cause is almost always in the generator or in a stale artifact against an old commit. Rebasing canonical on the artifact papers over the bug; the next regeneration against the now-mutated canonical will produce a different artifact than the one Anya just trusted, and no one will know why.
- "No evidence canonical is wrong" is the stronger claim. The migration script's heuristic is "the generated file looks newer." That isn't evidence; it's a timestamp comparison. Until step 4 shows a real value-level divergence with a known-good baseline, there is no source-level reason to touch canonical.

Recommended posture for Anya: reject the migration script's write-back path. If steps 1–4 produce no value-level divergence, the script is solving a non-problem and should be closed. If they do produce a divergence, the right fix is in the generator or the regeneration pipeline, with the canonical package unchanged until that fix lands.

The hair and soap residue at the stopper is the most useful clue — this is almost certainly a clog right at the pop-up assembly, not a deep drain problem. The 90-second clear time with everything else normal is consistent with that.

Renter-level sequence, lowest to highest effort:

1. Pull and clean the stopper.
   Most pop-up stoppers lift straight out. If it doesn't pull free, look under the sink for a small nut on the back of the drain pipe (the pivot rod) — loosening it a turn or two releases the rod and the stopper comes out. Pull off the hair mat with gloves or a paper towel, scrub the post and stopper with dish soap and an old toothbrush, rinse. This single step fixes most slow bathroom sink drains.

2. Hot water flush.
   Heat a kettle to just-off-boil. Don't pour truly boiling water straight into a cold porcelain basin — thermal shock risk on a chilled sink. Pour slowly in 2–3 stages with 30 seconds between pours.

3. Plastic hair snake / zip tool.
   The $2–3 plastic barbed strip from a hardware store. Push 6–10 inches down the drain, twist, pull. Repeats usually pull up a second hair wad. Safe for porcelain and pipes; gentler than a wire hanger.

4. Baking soda + vinegar.
   1/2 cup baking soda down the drain, then 1 cup white vinegar. Cover the drain with a wet rag so the reaction pushes downward, not back up. Wait 30 minutes, flush with very hot water. Best for soap residue; marginal on hair.

5. Cup plunger (last resort before calling).
   Use a cup plunger, not a toilet flange plunger. Seal the overflow opening with a wet rag first — without that seal you won't build pressure. A few gentle plunges, then test the drain.

If still slow after steps 1–4 (or 5), stop and call management.

Stop and call management if any of these appear:
  - Water backs up into the tub, shower, or toilet when you run the sink
  - More than one fixture slows at the same time (signals the branch or stack, not your sink)
  - Gurgling from other fixtures while the sink drains (vent issue)
  - Sewage odor anywhere in the bathroom or from the sink
  - Any water on the floor, under the cabinet, or at the P-trap
  - Visible corrosion, cracked pipes, or shut-off valves under the sink that don't fully close when tested
  - You live below another unit and the building has a shared history of drain issues

Don't use chemical drain cleaners (Drano, Liquid-Plumr, etc.) in a rental. They can damage the older galvanized or thin-walled pipes common in South Slope buildings, and they'll show up on a move-out damage deduction. If the clog turns out to need a P-trap removal or a snake past the trap, that's management's call to make.
