The drop is well beyond normal permeation. A butyl tube at that pressure typically loses 1–3 psi per day from seepage alone; 18 psi in 20 hours confirms an active leak, not overnight cooling or gauge drift. Because the front is fine, the loss is localized to the rear wheel, which makes a methodical search worthwhile before opening anything up.

Non-destructive leak-check sequence

Do these in order; each step either pinpoints the leak or rules out a region.

1. Re-baseline both tires with the same gauge, in the same ambient temperature, before doing anything else. Confirms the 18 psi loss was real and tells you whether the front is also drifting (if so, the gauge or temperature is partly to blame, and you recalibrate expectations).

2. Reinflate the rear to 68 psi and do a quiet-room sweep. With the bike on the ground and the wheel unloaded:
   - Listen at the valve stem, face 5–10 cm away.
   - Slowly pass an open palm 1–2 cm from the tread and both sidewalls, feeling for cold air movement. A bare hand will catch hissing leaks; tiny seep leaks need soapy water (next step).
   - Roll the bike forward a few inches at a time and repeat, so you cover the full circumference.

3. Valve check with soapy water (mix dish soap with water, roughly 1:4 in a spray bottle or small cup). Apply to:
   - The valve opening and cap threads
   - Where the valve stem enters the rim
   - The valve core (visible brass piece on a Schrader, accessible under the cap on a Presta after unscrewing the locknut)
   Look for slow-forming bubbles. Anything here is a fast, free fix — reseat the valve core, replace the core, or snug the Presta locknut. No tire removal needed.

4. Soapy-water wash of the whole tire. Sponge or spray generously over:
   - Center tread (most debris lives here)
   - Both shoulders and both sidewalls, including the inside-facing sidewall you cannot see until you rotate the wheel
   - The bead line where the tire meets the rim
   - The spoke/rim area visible between the spokes
   Wait 30–60 seconds per section. Slow leaks take a moment to grow a bubble. Note the wheel position when you see one — you will need it later to align tube-to-tire.

5. Mechanical listening for sub-audible leaks. A mechanic's stethoscope on the rim, or a length of 8–10 mm hose / rolled paper tube with one end at your ear, sweeping slowly along the tire and rim. Catches leaks so slow that soap doesn't bead up, especially rim-tape seepage.

6. Overnight re-pressurization test if steps 1–5 found nothing. Inflate to 68 psi, record the value and the time, leave the wheel untouched for 8+ hours, re-measure. A healthy tube should lose under 2 psi in that window. Anything more is a confirmed leak that step 4 missed (rim-tape seepage is the usual culprit).

7. Submersion test as a last resort without disassembly. If you have a stock tank, large tub, or a kiddie pool the wheel can fit in, inflate to 68 and roll the wheel through the water section by section while watching for bubbles. Most home bathtubs are too narrow for a 700c wheel; do not force it.

If a leak is found inside the tire or under the bead, the tube still needs to come out. Before any patch or replacement, do this once the wheel is off:

   - Inflate the tube (still off the rim) and listen/feel for the leak. Patches go on the tube, not the tire.
   - Mark the hole position on the tube, then line the tube up against the tire using the valve as a reference. Inspect that exact spot on the tire inside and out. Pull out whatever punctured it. Skip this and the new tube inherits the same hole.
   - Run a fingertip carefully around the inside of the tire. Look for the debris you just pulled, and for casing slivers, exposed belt edges, or a bulge you missed from outside.
   - Inspect the rim tape end-to-end. Spoke nipples that poke through torn or shifted rim tape are a common silent killer — the tire and tube look perfect and you lose air anyway. If you see daylight through the rim, the tape is the leak source and the tube was a victim.

Decision criteria

Patch the tube yourself when:
   - The hole is in the tube body (not at or within ~2 cm of the valve stem).
   - The puncture is small (under about 5 mm), single, and from a recognizable small sharp (thorn, glass shard, wire) — not a pinch, snake-bite, or tear.
   - The tube is in good shape otherwise: not dried out or cracked, not previously patched in the same area, not so old that vulcanizing cement won't bond.
   - You are comfortable removing the wheel, breaking one bead, pulling and patching the tube, and re-seating the tire. A glueless plug patch is fine for tread punctures while riding; a vulcanizing patch is the durable shop-style fix.

Replace the tube yourself when:
   - The hole is at the base of the valve stem or in the valve stem itself — patches don't hold here reliably.
   - There are two or more holes (snake-bite from a rim strike, or two separate punctures).
   - The hole is a tear or slash longer than ~5 mm, or the tube has any visible thinning/bulge around it.
   - The tube is several years old, has multiple existing patches, or has been stored inflated and creased.
   - You find that the rim tape is the actual leak source — patch the tube and the air still escapes through the spoke hole. Fix the tape first, then decide on a fresh tube while you are in there.

Take it to a shop when:
   - Step 6 confirmed a leak but steps 1–5 found nothing — the leak is rim-tape or spoke-related and the shop has the tools (and a spare tube and rim tape on hand) to diagnose and fix in one visit.
   - The tire itself shows damage you didn't catch on visual inspection: sidewall bulge or scuff that exposes casing threads, deep cut, deformed bead that won't reseat, or the tire is so old that the casing is hardening and cracking.
   - You find a tubeless or tubeless-converted setup with sealant that won't hold — sealant-clogged valves and porous-rim repairs are shop territory.
   - The wheel is a hydraulic-disc setup and you would rather not reindex the caliper / reset pad spacing yourself after re-installing the wheel — not a leak issue, just a service-bundle reason to let a shop handle the whole job.
   - You simply want it done right and back in service without owning the process; a flat repair plus a new tube and a fresh rim-tape is usually under an hour of shop labor.

Replace the tire along with the tube when:
   - Sidewall damage of any meaningful depth, a bulge anywhere, exposed casing threads, or a cut that you can see into.
   - The tire has been run flat or very low for any distance — the sidewalls can crease and fail later even if they look okay now. You already kept it off the road, which is the right call.
   - The tread is worn to the casing on a tire you trust for fast road or loaded-touring use.
   - The bead is deformed from whatever caused the loss.

Two cross-cutting points worth flagging now:

   - Tube material matters for expectations. Latex tubes (common on high-end road bikes for lower rolling resistance) lose 5–10 psi per day as a baseline; an 18 psi overnight drop on latex is normal permeation plus a small leak, and the search needs to be sharper. Butyl tubes lose far less, so the same drop on butyl is essentially all leak.
   - Whatever you decide, do not reinflate and ride on the rear before locating the source. A small leak that is bearable on a short ride can turn into a blowout-style deflation if the tire has hidden damage you haven't found yet — exactly the failure mode you are protecting against by holding the bike pending inspection.

Short version: do not pay the $85. The EOB wins.

The hospital portal balance is almost certainly a stale or pre-adjudication figure that never got reconciled when the insurer processed the claim. A finalized EOB showing in-network and $0 patient responsibility is the authoritative determination; the portal is just a ledger view, not a legal statement of what you owe.

What it likely means mechanically: the hospital billed full charges, the insurer applied the in-network contractual adjustment and paid the allowed amount, and the portal is still showing the original $85 difference between charge and allowed amount as a "patient balance" without realizing the EOB already zeroed it out. The fact that the portal shows no adjustment or denial is consistent with this — no denial happened, the claim was just adjudicated and the portal didn't catch up.

Before March 28:

1. Call hospital billing (number on the statement, not the portal message). Reference the EOB by its document/claim control number and date. Ask them to: (a) pull the claim, (b) confirm they have the EOB on file, (c) post the in-network adjustment, (d) zero out the $85.
2. Do it as a written dispute if the first call doesn't fix it. A short dispute letter / portal dispute message referencing the EOB control number creates a paper trail and starts the clock on their response time.
3. Ask for written confirmation (email or letter) that the patient balance is $0. You want proof, not just a phone rep saying "we'll fix it."
4. If they push back or stall, call the insurer back, reference the EOB, and ask them to intervene with the provider — in-network providers are contractually obligated to honor the EOB, and the insurer's provider-relations team will apply pressure fast.

Things to avoid: paying the $85 and trying to get a refund later (slower, more friction), or waiting past 3/28 hoping it resolves (it won't, and you may get dunning letters).

One thing worth checking on your end: confirm the date of service on the EOB matches this claim and that the provider NPI on the EOB is actually the hospital you were billed by — those two are usually fine but it's the one scenario where the portal could be right and the EOB could be misapplied.

Safe to handle at home — Kibo is stable, skin looks clean, and you have the right tools. The shoulder is an easy-access site. Procedure:

Removal
  1. Gloves on.
  2. Part the fur so you can see the bite clearly.
  3. Grasp the tick with the fine-tipped tweezers as close to the skin as possible — at the mouthparts, not the body.
  4. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. No twisting, no jerking, no squeezing the body. Slow and steady beats a quick yank.
  5. If mouthparts stay embedded in the skin, don't dig for them. Clean the area with antiseptic and let it work its way out; see a vet only if it becomes red/swollen/painful over the next few days.

After removal
  - Photograph the tick (dorsal view, next to a ruler or coin for scale) before disposal. Useful for vet ID if symptoms develop.
  - Wipe the bite site with antiseptic.
  - Drop the tick in the sealed container. Label with date and body location. Keep it for ~30 days in case you need it; fridge is fine.
  - Wash hands + disinfect tweezers.

Avoid
  Heat, petroleum jelly, nail polish, essential oils, "twist-and-pull," and squeezing the body. All of these can cause the tick to regurgitate into the wound, raising infection risk.

Monitoring window: 2–4 weeks. Watch for:
  - Lethargy, fever, off food
  - Stiffness, joint pain, reluctance to move
  - Bull's-eye rash (anywhere on body, not just bite site)
  - Vomiting or behavior change
  - Increasing redness/swelling at the bite itself

If any of those appear, vet visit and mention the bite + date. NYC / Prospect Park is in the Lyme-endemic range, so the species matters for treatment — that's the main reason to keep the specimen.

If he's wiggly, the fur is matted around the bite, or you'd rather not do it yourself, a vet or groomer can remove it in seconds. Otherwise, at-home removal is the right call for a small, recently attached tick with no skin reaction.

TICK REMOVAL + MONITORING — KIBO
Context: Sat 2025-03-22, late morning. Northeast / NYC = Lyme-endemic; deer ticks are active in Prospect Park margins. Many regular vets have Saturday hours; if anything acute develops Sun, plan for an emergency clinic (Animal Medical Center on the Upper East Side, BluePearl locations in Manhattan/Brooklyn/Queens) rather than waiting for Monday.

1. GATHER BEFORE YOU TOUCH THE TICK
- Fine-tipped tweezers, or a tick removal tool (Tick Twister / Tick Key). Avoid household blunt tweezers.
- Nitrile gloves.
- Antiseptic: chlorhexidine 2–4% or povidone-iodine (Betadine), diluted per label.
- Small sealed zip-bag or pill vial, plus a moist paper towel or rubbing alcohol.
- Treats and a helper if Kibo wiggles.

2. REMOVE
- Gloves on. Part the fur so you can see the mouthparts meeting the skin.
- Grasp the tick at the head, as close to the skin as possible. Never squeeze the body.
- Pull straight up with steady, even pressure — slow and constant beats fast yanks.
- Do NOT twist, jerk, burn, smother, or apply oils / petroleum / soap / alcohol to an attached tick. Those make it regurgitate into the bite and raise infection risk.

3. IF MOUTHPARTS BREAK OFF
- Don't dig. Clean with antiseptic; a small retained fragment usually sloughs in a few days. Note it for the vet.

4. WOUND CARE
- Clean the bite with antiseptic, pat dry. Wash your hands.

5. PRESERVE THE TICK (do this even if you think you won't need it)
- Sealed bag or vial with a damp paper towel, or submerge in rubbing alcohol.
- Label: date, location on Kibo's body, your name.
- Why: species ID drives risk. In NYC parks: deer tick (Ixodes) = Lyme + anaplasma; lone star = ehrlichia/STARI; American dog tick = Rocky Mountain spotted fever (rare here but possible). The vet may want the actual tick to test, or to decide whether to test Kibo.
- Keep it ~30 days in case symptoms appear, then discard.

6. DOCUMENT
- Photograph the bite site now. Re-photo at the same angle daily for ~7 days — an expanding red ring is the key signal, and timestamped photos beat memory.
- Note: engorgement (size), estimated attachment duration, any current Kibo symptoms.

7. MONITOR — 30-DAY WINDOW
- Bite site, daily for 14 days: expanding redness, rash, swelling, drainage.
- Whole dog, daily for 30 days: lethargy, warm ears/paws (fever), shifting-leg lameness or stiff gait (classic Lyme sign in dogs, often 2–5 weeks post-bite), loss of appetite, vomiting, swollen lymph nodes, behavioral change.
- Important: dogs rarely show the human "bullseye" rash. Don't wait for one.

8. CONTACT YOUR VET — DECISION TREE
Same-day or next-open-day call:
- Tick was engorged (plump, gray, larger than a sesame seed).
- You can't tell the species.
- Mouthparts retained in skin.
- Bite is on face, ear, near eye, genitals, or in a skin fold.
- Kibo is not currently on a tick preventive, or a preventive was missed.
- Site still irritated >48 h, or any discharge/lump.

Urgent / emergency clinic:
- Sudden lethargy, fever, or vomiting within hours–days.
- Acute lameness, joint swelling, or pain on movement.
- Any neurologic sign (wobbliness, head tilt, facial droop, seizures).

9. WORTH ASKING YOUR VET TODAY (even by phone)
- For a confirmed deer-tick attachment >24–48 h in a Lyme-endemic area, some vets prescribe a 4-week course of doxycycline as prophylaxis. Practice varies — your vet decides based on tick ID, engorgement, and Kibo's history.

10. WEEKEND PLAN

A few practical notes for the record:

- Musty odor without visible moisture often points to one of: a slow leak behind the back panel/wall, residual moisture from a prior leak, or simply stagnant air in an enclosed cabinet (less common in a frequently-used kitchen sink base). Worth ruling out the first two.
- Since everything accessible is dry, the leak source — if there is one — is likely on the supply side behind the wall (sprayer line, shutoff, or a fitting in the wall cavity) rather than the drain/trap side. A moisture meter at the back panel and wall can confirm; management's inspector should bring one.
- Watch for: odor intensifying after running the sprayer or dishwasher, any dampness returning at the base of the back panel, or the smell migrating to the adjacent wall/cabinet. If any of those appear, escalate from "inspect" to "active leak suspected."
- Cabinet staying empty is the right call — stored items would mask early signs and could be damaged if a slow leak is present.

If you want, I can draft a short maintenance request email — something like: location, observed odor, areas already inspected dry, cabinet cleared pending inspection, request for moisture check behind panel and wall. Just say the word.

Here's a tight, non-destructive approach plus a clear urgency threshold.

WHY DRY-BUT-MUSTY IS WORTH TAKING SERIOUSLY

  A musty smell without visible wetness usually means one of:
  - past moisture that never fully dried (residual mold/mildew)
  - a slow leak feeding hidden evaporation (supply line, P-trap, dishwasher
    hose, shutoff valve)
  - chronic high humidity in an unventilated, dark space (mold colonizing
    cabinet back/floor without free water)
  Particleboard cabinet floors are especially vulnerable - they absorb and
  hide moisture and grow mold internally even when the surface feels dry.

NON-DESTRUCTIVE DOCUMENTATION (one-time, ~30 min)

  1. Empty the cabinet. Photograph interior before touching anything - this
     is your visual baseline.
  2. Smell-map with cabinet door closed, then open:
     - where is odor strongest? back wall corners, floor seam, front edge,
       under P-trap?
  3. Pinless moisture meter at 5+ points if you have one:
     - both back-wall corners, floor near P-trap, both side walls near the
       base, front lip, and a known-dry reference (e.g. a kitchen shelf) for
     - particleboard: <12% normal, 12-15% watch, 15-20% wet, >20% saturated
     - solid wood / plywood: roughly 2-3 points lower across the board
  4. Visual sweep with a flashlight held FLAT against surfaces (raking light
     reveals staining and fuzz that overhead light hides). Look for:
     - discoloration, dark spots, white powdery deposits (efflorescence =
       past water movement)
     - bubbling or peeling of laminate/veneer
     - swelling along the cabinet floor edge
  5. Dry-paper-towel test: press a fresh paper towel around P-trap unions,
     supply line connections, dishwasher hose connection, and the cabinet
     floor seam against the back wall. Hold 10 seconds. Any damp transfer
     = active slow leak even if you can't see water.
  6. Note cabinet floor material: particleboard vs plywood vs solid wood.
     Particleboard that has been wet is the highest-risk substrate.

WATER-USE CORRELATION TEST (run once)

  - Run the faucet (and dishwasher, if applicable) at full flow for 5 min.
  - Close the cabinet door and leave it closed for 30 min, then re-smell.
  - Re-check the cabinet at 1h, 4h, and the next morning before any water use.
  - Smell clearly worse after running water = active leak feeding mold.
  - Smell unchanged = likely residual colonization or humidity, not an active leak.

TIME-SERIES MONITORING (10-14 days)

  Same time daily, record:
  - smell intensity (1-5)
  - meter reading at the same 5 points (same sequence each day)
  - weather note (rainy/humid/dry day)
  - whether water was used heavily that day
  - weekly photo from the same angle as your baseline

  Patterns to look for:
  - smell/meter spikes after rain = possible envelope or venting issue
  - smell/meter spikes after heavy water use = active leak
  - steady readings with no correlation = residual colonization, lower urgency

LOW-COST VENTILATION WHILE MONITORING

  - Leave cabinet doors cracked overnight
  - Place a small calcium-chloride moisture absorber inside; weigh it weekly -
    a sudden weight jump means the cabinet is producing moisture
  - If it's a bathroom cabinet, run the exhaust fan during and 20 min after
    showers

URGENT THRESHOLD - CALL PLUMBER OR MOLD PRO WITHIN 24-48 HOURS

  - any visible mold growth, regardless of color or size
  - moisture meter reading rising week-over-week, or any reading >20% on
    wood / >15% on particleboard
  - cabinet floor feels soft, spongy, or visibly warped/swollen
  - active drip, even intermittent, or fresh/wet paper-towel transfer
  - water staining that appears fresh or is expanding
  - musty smell clearly intensifies during or within hours of water use
    (active leak feeding mold)
  - smell spreading out of the cabinet into living space, or any household
    member developing respiratory symptoms, headaches, or allergic reactions
    since the smell started
  - sewage smell rather than musty smell - that's a drain-trap or venting
    failure, different urgency, same-day plumber call
  - any flooding or spill into the cabinet within the past 48 hours that
    wasn't fully dried with fans/dehumidifier

ORDINARY INSPECTION - MONITOR FIRST 1-2 WEEKS

  - stable mild musty smell with no visible moisture
  - low and stable meter readings (wood <15%, particleboard <12%)
  - no change after the water-use test
  - smell stays localized to the cabinet
  - no household health symptoms
  - no matching moisture-correlated pattern in the daily log

If after 2 weeks of monitoring it stays in the "ordinary" column but the
smell doesn't fade, the next non-destructive step is having a mold inspector
do an air sample or surface swab - still no demolition, but it tells you
whether professional remediation is warranted or whether you're dealing with
a benign residual.

[00:00 — OPENING — 1 min]

This is a fifteen-minute readout on what we learned from March's exception-routing sheet. Three examples, one lesson. I want to lead with the examples and end with the lesson, because the lesson is small and the examples carry it.

The sheet itself is one page. It says: here's an invariant, here's what counts as an exception to it, here's where the exception routes, here's who decides. That's the whole shape. What it isn't is also part of the design — it isn't a review queue, it isn't a sign-off path, it isn't a calendar someone else owns.

[01:00 — THE LESSON — 2 min]

The lesson from March is straightforward, and it's not new. It's just sometimes hard to hold in practice. Define the box, not the contents.

An invariant is a thing that must always be true about a service or a path, with a named failure mode if it stops being true. An exception path is the documented route when something falls outside normal flow — who gets paged, what gets logged, what gets deferred to owner judgment. A routine decision is everything else, and it stays with the owner.

The trap — and we hit it in three different places this month — is to write the sheet as if the boundary is the decision. It's not. The boundary is what tells an owner, "this is yours" versus "this needs to go through an exception path." The decision inside the boundary still belongs to whoever owns the service. Writing the sheet as if it centralized decisions is how you accidentally build a review board.

[03:00 — EXAMPLE 1: PARITY-GATE — 4 min]

The parity-gate in metrics-router is the cleanest example.

The invariant: when the recovery path engages, the signal shape and freshness must match the primary path within a defined budget. The 94-millisecond recovery-push we validated back in October is the reference. That's the invariant — it isn't "the recovery path works," it's "the recovery path produces a signal the rest of the system can treat as equivalent to the primary."

The March exception: we saw a recovery-push come through with the right shape but stale provenance on one of the trace fields. The signal was functionally usable, but the gate condition wasn't met. The question the sheet answered cleanly was: who owns this?

It routed to me. Not because metrics-router is the only service that touches the trace, but because the gate condition — parity — is defined against metrics-router's behavior. The exception was: parity didn't hold on one field. That's my service's invariant. I made the call, in the standard way, without anyone needing to convene anything. The parity-gate didn't ask for a meeting. It asked for an owner.

The lesson: had parity been implicit — "the recovery path generally works" — three teams could have reasonably argued about whose problem the stale-provenance case was. With the gate explicit, the exception routed. No escalation, no committee, just an owner acting within a defined scope.

[07:00 — EXAMPLE 2: LANTERN INTERPRETATION — 4 min]

The Lantern interpretation case is more subtle because the failure was about reading a signal, not about a service misbehaving.

The Lantern rerun structure — three synthetic cases, tenant-safe paging, matching traces required, internal exercise env only — gives us a fixed pattern for distinguishing real anomalies from interpretive noise. The invariant the sheet records isn't "the rerun passes." It's: a synthetic anomaly is real only if it produces both a tenant-safe page and a matching trace. Both. Not one or the other.

The March exception: we saw a signal that looked like the stale-provenance class from the Lantern synthetic set. It paged correctly. It didn't produce a matching trace.

The temptation in the room — and I include myself in this — was to treat it as a real anomaly and act on it. The sheet's value here is that it doesn't tell us what to do. It tells us what counts. A page without a matching trace doesn't meet the gate. We didn't act on it as if it were real. We treated it as an interpretation question for the on-call — and that's a routine owner-decision category, not an exception, because the on-call rotation owns interpretation within the defined gate.

The lesson: the sheet doesn't centralize triage. It defines what two people must agree on before a signal is treated as real. After that, it stays with the owner of the rotation. The Lantern exercise is what makes the gate stable across rotations. The sheet is what makes it explicit so the next on-call doesn't have to reinvent it.

[11:00 — EXAMPLE 3: AN ORDINARY OWNER-DECISION — 3 min]

The third example is a non-example, and it's the most important one.

In March I made roughly a dozen routine calls inside metrics-router and ingest-edge: a config change, two staging rollback drills, an adjustment to a canary window. None of these touched the exception-routing sheet. None of them should have. They were within the boundary of my owner-decision scope.

This is the part that's easy to lose when you're documenting exceptions. Most decisions are like this. They're ordinary, they're within scope, they belong to the owner. The sheet exists for the boundary cases, not to wrap everything. If we end up routing every config change through the sheet, we've built a review board. If we end up treating every routine decision as if it needed an exception path, we've centralized what should stay distributed.

The sheet's test for whether it's working: most decisions don't touch it. The ones that do, route cleanly. That's the bar.

[14:00 — CLOSING — 1 min]

What this isn't: a new central review board. A bid to manage release calendars. A sign-off queue. An escalation process in disguise.

What it is: a boundary document. It says what must always be true, what counts as falling outside that, and where that goes. The decisions inside the boundary still belong to owners. The decisions at the boundary have a documented path. That's it.

What comes next: keep the sheet. Revisit it quarterly — Hema has already adopted it as a step in the quarterly infra-rotation onboarding, which means it gets stress-tested by every new on-call. No new process. No new gate. No new meeting.

Thanks.

YES — the canonical-encoding + repeated-reload evidence closes the nondeterministic-provenance-digest concern on the current representation; no alternative canonicalization is required.

Why it closes (mapped to what a nondeterministic digest would actually break):

1. Order-independence is enforced at the input boundary, not the output. Sorting by configured integer priority + normalized pattern before serialization means the byte sequence is a function of the logical config, not the order fields happened to arrive in. This kills the most common source of reload-to-reload churn — config files that get re-emitted in different orders on reload, or in-memory maps that iterate non-deterministically.

2. Serialization is made structural, not pretty. Explicit length-delimited fields replace whatever the language/serializer default is (JSON map ordering, struct field ordering, whitespace). Two parallel implementations writing "the same" logical record can no longer disagree on bytes, so the hash is a property of the data, not the writer.

3. The 1000-reload empirical bound on a 500-route config is the right test. It's large enough that any non-determinism with non-trivial probability would have surfaced; one digest across 1000 runs is strong evidence the canonicalization is closed under reload, not just stable on a few samples.

4. Generation stability is the operational payoff. One active generation means downstream consumers (cache keys, staleness checks, owner-card comparisons) won't see a digest flip on a no-op reload and trigger spurious refresh/invalidation. That's the user-visible cost the concern was really about.

5. Sensitivity (one target edit → digest change) confirms the canonicalization isn't over-aggressive — it's not collapsing distinct configs to the same digest. That's the failure mode you'd worry about with a too-coarse canonical form.

6. Routing invariance confirms the digest change is decoupled from evaluation. The digest is observational metadata, not a routing input, so changing how it's computed can't have changed which route a request lands on.

- Pin the canonicalization in a unit test that hashes a known 500-route fixture and asserts the digest matches a golden value. The 1000-reload run proves stability in distribution; a golden test proves stability for a specific config across versions and platforms.

- Treat the sort key (priority + normalized pattern) and the field set fed to the serializer as the API surface. Any change to either is a digest-format change and should be versioned, not landed silently.

- Keep the sensitivity test (one-target-edit) in CI so a future "optimization" that drops a field from the canonical byte sequence fails loudly.

Raw refusal strings are unsafe as metric labels for four distinct failure modes, each of which breaks bounded-cardinality assumptions in a different way. The design below treats metrics as an aggregated, finite-cardinality surface and pushes all freeform detail down into structured logs and traces that are joined back via trace_id.

Why raw refusal strings are unsafe as labels

  1. Cardinality blowup. A refusal string is usually a formatted error: it embeds request parameters, IDs, free-form messages, and stack fragments. Each unique value creates a new time series in the TSDB. Even modest traffic plus a handful of refusal shapes can multiply active series by 10x-1000x in a single deploy. The failure is silent at first (memory grows, scrape latency creeps), then catastrophic (OOM in the TSDB, dropped scrapes, lost alerting). It also costs real money: most TSDBs bill per active series.

  2. Non-aggregability. If labels differ per request, you cannot compute aggregate rates meaningfully. Sum-of-refusals returns a sum over an arbitrary subset; rate-by-refusal-class returns one series per unique string. You lose the operation a counter is supposed to support.

  3. Privacy and tenancy leakage. Refusal strings frequently include user/tenant/request identifiers, internal hostnames, policy-rule text, or auth-related context. Lifting these into shared label space puts them on dashboards, in alert payloads, and on any external metric export path (status pages, vendor backends). A Grafana snapshot of a shared dashboard can become a disclosure vector.

  4. Label instability. The format of an error string changes whenever a library upgrades or a developer rewords a message. Once that string is in dashboards and alerts, you have an undeclared dependency on the exact text. Schema churn breaks alerts and SLO calculations retroactively.

The bounded design I would require

Principle: metrics describe categories, not instances. Anything that varies per request - IDs, free text, parameters, paths with variables - belongs in logs and traces, joined back to the metric via trace_id and request_id.

  a) Closed enum for refusal_reason. A small, documented set of codes (target: under 30 values, ideally under 15): policy_deny, policy_deny_tenant_scope, auth_missing, auth_invalid, rate_limited, quota_exceeded, budget_exceeded, validation_failed, validation_required_field, upstream_timeout, upstream_5xx, upstream_circuit_open, dependency_unavailable, internal_error, not_found, unsupported_version. Each entry has a runbook stub - owner, common cause, first action.

  b) Sub-bucketing goes to logs, not metrics. If you need to break down policy_deny further (which rule fired), that is a log field (policy_rule_id, policy_version) and a log query, not a metric label. The metric only knows "policy_deny happened."

  c) Hashed quanta only when you genuinely need cardinality. If you must count by something high-cardinality, do not lift it to a label. Bucket it. Examples: tenant_tier (free/pro/enterprise) instead of tenant_id; route_group (catalog of bounded classes) instead of raw path; first 4 hex chars of a hash of the detail string when the detail really is the dimension you care about, capped at a known bucket count.

  d) Schema-versioned, allowlisted at the client. The metrics client validates every label value against the enum at emission time. Off-enum values are coerced to "other" and the original string is dumped to logs, with refusal_unknown_total incremented. This makes the design self-healing when a new refusal type ships before the enum is updated.

  e) Tenant safety by construction. Tenant-scoped metrics live under tenant-scoped metric namespaces; shared (cross-tenant) metrics never carry raw tenant_id labels. Per-tenant breakdowns happen through tenant-scoped metric streams with explicit access control, not by lifting tenant_id into the shared label set.

  f) Three-layer correlation.
     - Metric: refusal_reason, service, route_group, tenant_tier, policy_version, env. Aggregatable, finite cardinality, dashboardable.
     - Log: full refusal detail, structured fields (request_id, tenant_id, refusal_reason, refusal_detail, policy_rule_id, trace_id), PII-scrubbed at the logger, capped message length.
     - Trace: a span event marking the refusal with the same refusal_reason code, so a single trace explains one point on the metric.

  g) Backpressure on unknown classes. A dedicated refusal_unknown_total counter, alerted on rate. If anything is being coerced to "other," you want to know in the same hour, not after the next on-call rotation.

  h) Documented and reviewed. Each enum entry is in the runbook, owned by a named service. Adding a new entry requires a review of the metric surface (cardinality, tenant safety, alert impact) - the same gate as adding a new label today.

What this gets you

  - Bounded, predictable active-series count. The set of possible label values is enumerable; you can prove cardinality in CI.
  - Alerts that do not rot when error messages get reworded.
  - Cross-tenant metric surfaces that cannot leak.
  - A clean handoff from a dashboard spike to the offending request: dashboard -> metric series -> log query by refusal_reason + time window -> trace_id -> single trace.

Mental model: metrics answer "how often, by category, with what rate"; logs answer "show me this one"; traces answer "what did it do." If a label is doing more than category-bucketing, it is in the wrong layer.

Recommendation: single counter `card_combination_outcomes_total` on the `card` service, with a required label `outcome` that takes exactly one of three values.

Why one counter, three labels: the three states are mutually exclusive on a per-card basis (a given attempt either was ineligible, or was eligible and succeeded, or was eligible and failed), and the same downstream tooling — dashboards, alerts, ratios — works on all three with no extra joins.

Why this exact name and value set:

- `card_combination_outcomes_total` — counter (monotonic `_total`), service-scoped (`card_`), describes the decision point (`combination_outcomes`). "Combination" is the canonical term from the 3/27 card design (multi-card responder-card combination); "outcome" covers both attempts that failed because they were never combinable and attempts that actually rendered.
- Label `outcome` with values `{ineligible_unknown, ineligible_separated, renderer_failure}`. The two `ineligible_*` values are the corrective additions — without them, an "ineligible" bucket silently swallows both "we don't know what these employees' roles are" and "we know but they aren't on the same response" as one indistinguishable mass, which is exactly the conflation the 3/27 schema change is meant to break.

Counts to publish alongside it:

- `card_combination_ineligible_unknown_total{reason="missing_employee_id"|"stale_provenance"|"ambiguous_role"}` — fired when the card-side check can't determine combinability because of the 3/27 schema-rejected fields (`primary_responder_name`, comparison fields). Reasons are mutually exclusive per card; pick one canonical reason, don't double-count.
- `card_combination_ineligible_separated_total{reason="different_response"|"different_room_horizon"}` — fired when combinability is known but the rule rejects it. The "different response" sub-reason is the dominant production case (separate incidents; do not combine into a responder card); "different room/horizon" is the secondary case.
- `card_combination_renderer_failure_total{kind="template_miss"|"layout_invalid"|"comparison_field_dropped"}` — fired only when the card reached the renderer and the renderer could not produce a valid combined artifact. `comparison_field_dropped` is specifically the 3/27 regression case (renderer used to consume the comparison fields that the schema now rejects); `template_miss` and `layout_invalid` are the pre-existing failure modes.
- `card_combination_attempts_total` — denominator. Sum of all three outcome counters above. Publish it explicitly so consumers can compute rates without re-deriving the sum.
- `card_combination_renderer_attempts_total` — denominator for renderer-failure rate (`renderer_failure / renderer_attempts`). This is intentionally separate from `attempts_total` so that an "ineligible" surge doesn't dilute the renderer health signal.

Why the split matters (the corrective part, since the question called it out):

The pre-existing metric, whatever it was called, almost certainly had a single `card_combination_failure_total` that lumped "renderer threw" with "we never tried because the inputs weren't combinable." Under the 3/27 schema change — which drops `primary_responder_name` and the comparison fields — the unknown-eligible share rises naturally: more cards now have missing/ambiguous employee identity, so the *eligibility* failure rate goes up even if the renderer is fine. Without this label split, a renderer that is healthy will look like it's regressing, and a renderer that genuinely broke will look like an eligibility problem. The three-value label preserves the diagnostic:

- Eligibility ratio = `(ineligible_unknown + ineligible_separated) / attempts`. Watch this for input/schema drift.
- Renderer health = `renderer_failure / renderer_attempts`. Watch this for the renderer itself.
- Combined-success rate = `1 - sum(outcomes) / attempts`. Watch this for end-to-end SLO.

- Emit `card_combination_attempts_total{outcome=...}` incrementing in the same code path that decides the outcome, *before* returning. The unknown/separated decisions must be recorded even though no renderer call happens — otherwise the denominators won't reconcile.

Timestamp alone is insufficient provenance because it answers only "when" and leaves four blind spots the candidate-scan cannot recover from:

  1. Source identity. A timestamp does not identify which component emitted the record, under what authority, or which version of its schema/policy applied. Two publishers with skewed clocks can produce indistinguishable timestamps for fundamentally different events.

  2. Content identity. A timestamp does not bind the record to the payload that was emitted. Without a content hash or canonical record-id, you cannot tell whether two records at the same instant are duplicates, a replay of an older observation, or genuinely independent emissions.

  3. Causality. A timestamp does not say what observation or decision produced the record. Without a causal token (parent event id, decision id, ingestion-source id), "freshness" is unverifiable: an old record re-published at a recent timestamp still looks fresh on timestamp alone.

  4. Replay resistance. Timestamps are monotonic only on a single trusted clock. Once a record leaves the publisher's clock domain, a misconfigured retry or an adversary can re-stamp it; staleness checks become a knob, not a guard.

For the stale-provenance synthetic in the 1/6 10:00 Lantern rerun, the publisher must emit, at minimum:

  - record_id (publisher-scoped monotonic or uuid)
  - source (component + schema_version + config_version_hash)
  - observed_at (event-time, distinct from emit-time)
  - emit_at (wall-clock at the publisher boundary)
  - causal_parent (id of the observation/decision that produced this record)
  - tenant_scope (or explicit "internal" sentinel)
  - content_hash (over the canonical payload)

The candidate-scan regression must then enforce, per record:

  a) All seven fields present; missing/empty is "malformed," not "stale."
  b) source.schema_version and source.config_version_hash match the publisher's currently-declared version. A record whose source config no longer corresponds to live policy is stale by definition, regardless of how recent emit_at looks.
  c) causal_parent resolves to a known live observation. Orphan causal tokens are stale-by-definition regardless of timestamp recency.
  d) record_id not seen earlier in the scan window. Replay is rejected before staleness is evaluated.
  e) emit_at within the freshness window AND observed_at >= the publisher's last-known ingestion horizon for that source (catches clock skew and back-dated replays).
  f) tenant_scope matches the scan's permitted scope; internal-only sources leaking tenant labels — and tenant sources missing scope — fail before staleness is checked.

Net: timestamp is a freshness signal, not a provenance one. Provenance is identity + authority + causality + content-binding; the scan must require all four and treat the timestamp as a derived check, never the primary one.

Anya's proposal drops designer_account_id and engineer_account_id from the adoption export and keeps only team-level data plus four counts. Here's a design that makes that output verifiable without re-introducing member identifiers.

Goals
- One row per team_id, no member identifiers anywhere in the export payload.
- Counts are deduplicated correctly within the 6-week window.
- An auditor can verify the counts match a re-aggregation against the underlying raw event log, without the export itself containing member data.
- Output is bounded in size and shape (one row per team, four integer counts, fixed audit block).

Bounded aggregation

Inputs (kept inside the aggregation environment, never exported)
- team_id, event_type (drift_catch / platform_exception_request / platform_exception_accept / post_gen_correction)
- member_id (designer_account_id or engineer_account_id, depending on event type)
- event_id (stable id from the source system: drift_id, exception_request_id, exception_accept_id, correction_id)
- event_timestamp

Window
- Fixed 6-week window, pinned in UTC, recorded in every export row. No sliding or live tail.

Grouping
- Group by team_id, then by event_type. Member IDs never appear in any output, log line, or intermediate file that leaves the aggregation environment.

Deduplication (this is the part member IDs are needed for, so it must be done before redaction)
- Primary dedup key is event_id. Source system retries that produce duplicate event_ids collapse to one.
- Secondary dedup, where the source system does not already collapse retries, uses a salted, truncated per-export hash:
    dedup_key=HMAC-S...t_S, member_id || ":" || event_id), truncated to 16 bytes
    Keep a transient in-memory table (dedup_key -> first_seen) inside the aggregation environment. The table is discarded when the export is finalized; S is destroyed.
- Result: two retries from the same member for the same event_id count once; two different events from the same member count separately; the same event from two different members counts once (event_id primary dedup wins). No member_id ever crosses the boundary.

Counts (per team_id)
- drift_catches_count            = unique event_ids with type=drift_catch, after dedup
- requested_platform_exception_count = unique event_ids with type=platform_exception_request, after dedup
- accepted_platform_exception_count  = unique event_ids with type=platform_exception_accept, after dedup
- post_gen_corrections_count     = unique event_ids with type=post_gen_correction, after dedup

Suppression for small teams (k-anonymity guardrail)
- If a team has fewer than k members who contributed any event in the window, omit that team's row entirely. Recommended k = 5. This prevents trivial re-identification by exclusion in very small teams. Surface this in the proposal as a documented guardrail, not a hidden rule.

Audit design

Two-track audit so the export itself stays member-free but a small, separately-authorized group can still verify counts.

Track 1: what the export carries (member-free, safe to publish broadly)
- Per team_id: window_start, window_end, four counts, plus an audit block:
    aggregation_id (UUID)
    merkle_root_per_measure: {drift, request, accept, corrections}
    event_count_per_measure: {pre-dedup totals}
    dedup_dropped_per_measure: {counts that dedup removed}
    aggregation_input_sha256 (over the redacted intermediate: list of (event_id, event_type, timestamp) with no member_id)

Track 2: what stays behind the aggregation boundary (small-auditor access only)
- Raw event log for the window (still has member_id) is retained under existing data-access controls.
- per_export_secret_S is discarded after the export is sealed; it is never persisted.
- A signed manifest from the aggregation service binds (aggregation_id, window, team list, merkle roots). Auditors verify the signature.

Verification flow (auditor side, with raw-event access)
- Re-run the aggregation in the secure environment using the same window and rules.
- Recompute the four Merkle roots:
    leaf_hash = BLAKE3( team_id || event_type || event_id || HMAC-SHA256(S, member_id) )
    S is the same per-export secret used originally (auditor must replay deterministically; this is why the raw log + window are needed).
- Confirm the recomputed roots equal the ones in the exported audit block, and the recomputed counts match.
- The published export alone (no S, no raw log) is not enough to reverse any leaf hash, because S is destroyed and member_id space is small enough that unsalted or weakly-salted hashes would be reversible.

What this gets you
- The export payload cannot be used to identify any specific member. Even if an attacker knows the team roster, they only learn aggregate counts, not which member contributed.
- Counts are verifiable. A dispute ("our drift_catches_count is wrong") has a concrete resolution path: an auditor re-runs aggregation and compares Merkle roots.
- Deduplication is correct. Same-member retries collapse; different members contributing to the same event still collapse to one via event_id dedup.
- Output is bounded. One row per qualifying team_id, four integer counts, one audit block. No event-level rows in the export.

Output schema (per team_id, one JSON object per row)

{
  "team_id": "<id>",
  "window_start": "<UTC ISO8601>",
  "window_end":   "<UTC ISO8601>",
  "drift_catches_count": <int>,
  "requested_platform_exception_count": <int>,
  "accepted_platform_exception_count":  <int>,
  "post_gen_corrections_count": <int>,
  "audit": {
    "aggregation_id": "<uuid>",
    "merkle_root_per_measure": {
      "drift":       "<hex>",
      "request":     "<hex>",
      "accept":      "<hex>",
      "corrections": "<hex>"
    },
    "event_count_per_measure": {
      "drift":       <int>, "request": <int>, "accept": <int>, "corrections": <int>
    },
    "dedup_dropped_per_measure": {
      "drift":       <int>, "request": <int>, "accept": <int>, "corrections": <int>
    },
    "aggregation_input_sha256": "<hex>",
    "small_team_suppressed": <bool>
  }
}

Operational notes
- Run aggregation once per window, not streaming. Streaming would force keeping member-linked state alive longer than needed.
- Treat the aggregation environment as the privacy boundary: logs, crash dumps, and metrics from it must be scrubbed of member_id before they leave.
- Publish the k-anonymity threshold (k) and the suppression rule alongside the proposal, so the consumer of the export knows why some teams are missing.
- If a stronger privacy posture is later required, swap the Merkle-root verifier for a DP-noised release with a noise budget calibrated to the four counts; that is a follow-up, not part of this proposal.

Why elapsed instants, not local dates, must drive the 24-hour spread:

1. A local "24-hour day" is not 24 elapsed hours. DST makes it 23 or 25 wall-clock hours; zones occasionally change offset for political reasons. Anything denominated as "events per local day" is silently mis-denominated on those boundaries — rates, throughput, SLOs, percentiles all skew without any alarm firing.

2. Local-date labels are undefined across DST. Spring forward creates a non-existent wall-clock hour (e.g., 02:00–03:00 in the US); fall back creates an ambiguous hour that occurs twice. "2025-03-09 02:30 local" can resolve to two distinct elapsed instants or to none. Every event must have exactly one elapsed instant; a local-date label is a presentation projection of that instant, not the source of truth.

3. Cross-zone aggregation. Tenants, sources, and replicas span zones. Summing per-local-date buckets is meaningless — two zones' "Tuesday" overlap by only a partial interval. Only an elapsed-instant axis is comparable.

4. Audit and replay determinism. Given an instant, the 24-hour window is identical on every machine and every replay. Given a local-date label, two readers can disagree on which instants fall in the window depending on which zone interpretation is loaded.

5. Late-arriving and backfilled data. Reassignment belongs to event_time (the instant), not to arrival_date or wall-clock date. Otherwise a backfill produces different numbers than live ingestion.

6. Storage correctness. A local date without an offset is information-lossy. Store the instant; derive the local date for display. Buckets should be indexed as floor((instant - epoch) / 86400), not parsed from a wall-clock string.

Boundary regressions the refactor needs:

A. DST spring-forward. A 24-hour spread anchored at an instant straddling the skipped hour still measures exactly 86400 elapsed seconds; the spread does not stretch and does not skip.

B. DST fall-back. The duplicated hour produces two distinct elapsed instants; both are included or excluded by anchor, not by local-time parsing. Test: events at 01:30 PDT and 01:30 PST in a fall-back zone land in the correct bucket by instant, with no double-count and no loss.

C. Non-DST offset changes. Spread remains 86400 elapsed seconds regardless of an offset shift during the window.

D. Calendar-rollover boundaries. Feb 28 / Feb 29 / Mar 1 and Dec 31 / Jan 1 — the spread is invariant in elapsed seconds; only the local-date label changes.

E. Leap-second boundary. The 24-hour spread remains 86400 SI seconds even when POSIX time smears or skips the leap second. Do not assume 86401.

F. Tenant-cross-zone. Aggregating two tenants in different zones over the same anchor instant returns one coherent 86400-second interval, not the union of two local-day buckets.

G. Anchor-vs-edge. Where the legacy code used "00:00 local" as the bucket edge, freeze and assert the offset from the desired anchor instant; the refactor should make the anchor explicit (instant-based) rather than implicit (parsed local midnight).

H. Late-arriving placement. An event with event_time 23:59:58 local on day N, ingested at 00:01:00 local on day N+1, is placed in the day-N bucket by its event_time instant. Arrival local date is irrelevant.

I. Replay determinism. Replaying the same instant-timestamped events through the new bucketing yields byte-identical bucket assignments across runs and across machines. This is the strongest gate.

J. Zone-invariance. elapsed_seconds(spread_at_instant_T_in_zone_Z) is the same constant for every IANA zone Z, given a fixed anchor T. Property-test across a corpus of real zones rather than spot-checking.

Request-level and point-level accounting for a multi-point system (one request carries N points):

REQUEST-LEVEL

  N_r            = total requests in window
  N_r_ok         = requests that completed with no point-level errors
  N_r_partial    = requests where some points succeeded and some failed
  N_r_err        = requests that errored before any points were emitted
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  N_r            = N_r_ok + N_r_partial + N_r_err

POINT-LEVEL

  N_p            = total points observed in window
  N_p_ok         = points that succeeded
  N_p_err        = points that failed
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  N_p            = N_p_ok + N_p_err

RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE TWO

  N_p            = Σ over r of points_in_request(r)
  N_p_ok         = Σ over r of ok_points_in_request(r)
  N_p_err        = Σ over r of err_points_in_request(r)

  avg_points_per_request = N_p / N_r

  A request in N_r_partial contributes to BOTH N_p_ok and N_p_err.
  A request in N_r_ok can still contain err_points if "ok" is defined
  by HTTP/transport status rather than per-point success — pick one
  definition and pin it on the dashboard.

COUNTERS THE DASHBOARD MUST NOT MIX

  1. Request success rate vs point success rate
       R_r = N_r_ok / N_r
       R_p = N_p_ok / N_p
     These diverge whenever N_r_partial > 0. Plotted on the same
     axis they will lie on top of each other and tell different
     stories.

  2. Request latency vs point latency
       L_r is end-to-end (queue + parse + all points + serialize).
       L_p is per-point work. L_r ≥ max(L_p) + overhead.
     A p99 latency chart that mixes the two is meaningless.

  3. Error counts at the two granularities
       request_errors = N_r_err (+ optionally N_r_partial)
       point_errors   = N_p_err
     A spike in point_errors with no spike in request_errors means
     the system is degrading silently inside otherwise-200 responses.

  4. Tenant counters at the two granularities
       tenants_at_request_level = distinct tenants seen on a request
       tenants_at_point_level   = distinct tenants seen on a point
     The same tenant appearing in 50 points of one query = 1 at
     request level, 50 at point level. Summing them across panels
     double-counts.

  5. Throughput denominators
       requests/sec = N_r / window
       points/sec   = N_p / window
     Off by exactly avg_points_per_request. If the panel label says
     "rps" the denominator must be N_r, never N_p.

Rule of thumb: every panel must declare its grain (request or point)
in the title or legend, and the two grains never share an axis, a
ratio, or a denominator on the same chart.

The duplication defect and the required guarantees, with the SDK kept on the auto-split path:

The duplication defect

The convenience split + generic retry path violates the layering contract in two places at once:

  1. Silent duplication after partial transport success. Chunk A (8,000 points) is durably ingested by the server before chunk B times out. The generic retry path stores the *logical* batch and resends *both* chunks on retry, so the 8,000 already-acked points are transmitted a second time alongside chunk B's 1,000 points. The fixture's "18,000 total transmitted" expectation is documenting the bug, not the contract. Each of those 8,000 points now exists twice on the server side, indistinguishable from legitimate traffic by any downstream consumer. The logical batch ends up marked "successful" while 8,000 points have been double-counted.

  2. The SDK is not authorized to invent retry splitting. Per the deployed layered design, oversized callers are responsible for splitting before they call, and the server's whole-batch rejection (HTTP 413 with `oversized_batch`) for non-splitting clients is deterministic and intended. This PR's auto-split moves a server-side invariant into a client-side retry heuristic, which means callers that already pre-split (older clients) keep getting the deterministic 413 path while callers that don't pre-split get a different, duplicating path the server can't tell apart from a legitimate retry of an un-acked batch. Two client populations, two different on-the-wire behaviors for the same logical input — a divergence, not an improvement.

Retry-state guarantees required if auto-splitting is kept

If the SDK is going to retain automatic splitting, the retry state has to be designed around per-chunk ack tracking, not around replaying the logical batch. Concretely:

  - Per-chunk idempotency key generated once at split time and retained for the lifetime of the logical batch. The server-side dedupe window is what makes re-sending a chunk that already crossed the wire safe; without that key on every retry, the server cannot distinguish "duplicate from a buggy retry" from "duplicate from a buggy caller" and cannot reject the resend. The key must be stable across retries, not regenerated.

  - Ack-state map for the logical batch: {chunk_id -> pending | acked | failed | terminal_failure}. Retry decisions consult this map, not the original logical-batch contents. A chunk in `acked` state is never re-sent. A chunk in `pending` or `failed` is eligible for retry. A chunk in `terminal_failure` (e.g. oversize server rejection of a sub-chunk, schema rejection) is not retried — that failure surfaces to the caller.

  - The retry path must be the *only* code that decides what goes on the wire next, and it must read from the ack-state map. The current defect is that the generic retry path replays the logical batch independently of which chunks the server already acked. That coupling has to be broken.

  - State persistence boundary. Ack-state must survive transient network failures (timeouts, connection resets, 5xx) but must be cleared on logical-batch completion (all chunks acked) or terminal logical-batch failure. Leaving stale `acked` state around indefinitely risks later re-sends if the caller re-uses an idempotency key by mistake; not clearing `failed` state promptly risks the retry path giving up on a chunk the caller would have wanted retried.

  - No "logical batch replay" code path. If any code path can re-send a chunk that has already been marked `acked` — for example, a fallback retry, an outer retry around the split-aware retry, a queue replay — the defect recurs. The retry-state design has to make this structurally impossible, not just discouraged.

Caller-visible-result guarantees required if auto-splitting is kept

The caller must observe a single logical batch behaving like a single logical batch, regardless of how it was split internally:

  - No silent inflation of on-the-wire point count. The cumulative points transmitted across all chunks and all retries must be <= the unique points in the logical batch. A 9,000-point batch can produce 9,000 transmitted points (possibly fewer if the server dedupes; never more). The fixture's 18,000 is the bug shape; the guarantee is "<= original, deduplicated by idempotency key."

  - Logical-batch success means all chunks acked. The caller must not observe a successful logical batch while any chunk is still pending, failed, or in retry. The current defect's "marked successful after the retry" line is wrong even on its own terms — it claims success while the retry may not have actually delivered chunk B's 1,000 points (or worse, delivered it with 8,000 duplicates already on the server).

  - Reconciliation invariant on every terminal result: accepted_points + rejected_points == submitted_points for the logical batch. With auto-splitting, this means the SDK must aggregate per-chunk accept/reject counts back into a single logical-batch result. The caller must not have to add up chunk results themselves to know whether anything was lost or duplicated.

  - No duplication of accepted data. From the caller's perspective, the contract is "I submitted 9,000 unique points, I will observe them exactly once in the accepted stream." The SDK must guarantee this — and the only way to guarantee it is the per-chunk idempotency key + ack-state design above, not a post-hoc reconciliation check.

  - Splitting is opt-in or at least visible to the caller. Auto-splitting silently changes the on-the-wire point count and the on-the-wire request shape for callers who did not ask for splitting. Either (a) the caller explicitly opts into "split my oversized batches and retry per-chunk," or (b) the caller is informed — via return value, log line, or documented behavior — that the SDK has split and may retry per-chunk. Silent splitting violates the principle of least surprise and makes the on-the-wire behavior of "oversized + transient failure" divergent across SDK versions.

  - Synchronous surface of chunk-level failure. If a chunk fails terminally (oversize sub-rejection, schema rejection, exhausted retries), the SDK must surface that failure to the caller with enough context to identify which points failed, not just "logical batch failed." Otherwise the caller cannot correct or split — which defeats the purpose of the layered design that puts the caller in charge of splitting in the first place.

  - Determinism for the same logical batch. Same input + same split policy must produce the same per-chunk mapping across retries, so that the server-side dedupe window and the caller's retry expectations are both stable.

Bottom line

If the SDK keeps automatic splitting, the auto-split has to be paired with per-chunk idempotency keys and an ack-state-driven retry path; otherwise the duplication defect is inherent to the design, not a bug in the implementation. And the caller-facing surface has to aggregate back to a single non-duplicating, fully-reconciled logical-batch result — anything less means the SDK is exporting a server-side invariant violation (duplication) under a "successful batch" label, which the layered design explicitly does not authorize.

What I'd still flag before this lands: the auto-split itself is the second-layer problem (callers should pre-split, per the deployed design). The guarantees above make auto-splitting *safe* if it stays, but the cleanest fix is still to remove the auto-split on the retry path and require callers to split before submission — that is what the layered design intended and what the rollout evidence already validated. If the team wants to keep the convenience path anyway, the guarantees above are the minimum bar; anything less reproduces the defect.

Overnight Safety & Monitoring — Kibo

HARD RULES (do not deviate)
- Do not remove, reposition, or pull at any equipment (drain, packing, sutures, tube). Note changes; do not fix.
- Do not rinse, swab, pack, or apply anything to the cavity.
- Do not give food, meds, or supplements beyond what is already prescribed and due.
- Keep the e-collar on at all times if one was prescribed.

Separation & Environment
- Confine to a single quiet room or crate, no furniture access, no stairs.
- Separate from other pets, children, and visitors for the night.
- Lights low, noise low, temperature comfortable; nothing to chew or mouth.
- Water available in small amounts only (lick, not gulp) unless otherwise directed.

Monitoring Cadence
- Quick visual check every 2–3 hours; hands-off unless something is wrong.
- Note time of each check and what you saw; do not wake Kibo for a check.

What to Track (note, don't intervene)
- Breathing: rate and effort at rest; any noise or open-mouth panting at rest.
- Gum color: pink is normal; pale, white, blue, yellow, or mottled = urgent.
- Bleeding: minor spotting/ooze expected; active dripping, pooling, or soaked gauze is not.
- Swelling: compare both sides; rapid increase, especially toward face/throat, is urgent.
- Pain signs: restlessness, hiding, panting, guarding the area, refusal to settle, whimpering.
- Nausea: lip-licking, drooling, retching, vomiting.
- Elimination: should pass urine overnight; straining, blood, or no urine in 12+ h is urgent.
- Mentation: should rouse and recognize you; dull, disoriented, or non-responsive is urgent.
- Equipment: still in place, intact, no fresh discharge around it. If displaced, do NOT reinsert — secure Kibo and call.

Contact the clinic / on-call line (do not wait until morning) if:
- Active bleeding that drips, pools, or soaks through gauze.
- Rapidly increasing swelling, swelling spreading toward the throat, or asymmetry that worsens.
- Difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, choking, or sustained panting at rest.
- Repeated vomiting or inability to keep prescribed meds/water down.
- Gums pale, white, blue, yellow, or tacky.
- Collapse, fainting, severe lethargy, or non-responsiveness.
- Seizure, tremors, or any sudden behavior change (confusion, head press, circling).
- Equipment visibly dislodged, broken, or missing — leave it alone, call immediately.
- Severe pain not relieved by the prescribed dose on the schedule given.
- No urine in 12+ hours, or blood in urine/stool.
- Suspected ingestion of anything not approved (food, toy piece, meds).

Morning handoff — tell the clinic
- Last med dose and time.
- Number and timing of any concerning signs from the list above.
- Whether Kibo ate or drank, and how much.
- Whether the equipment looked unchanged at every check.

What NOT to put in the log:
- Suspected unit, floor, or neighbor name
- Any pattern interpretation that pre-supposes a source
- Anything you couldn't directly observe

2. Tiered escalation (each step is a request for action by management, not an accusation)

Tier 1 — log and wait (already in motion)
After each episode: row added to the log, no contact initiated.

Tier 2 — ask management to review the pattern (no source attribution)
Trigger: any new episode. After ~3 logged episodes, send management a short note: "Here's the log since 4/5 — X episodes, here's the timing pattern. Can you take another look?" Attach the log. No unit named.

Tier 3 — ask management to escalate to a building-wide quiet-hours reminder (not a complaint against a unit)
Trigger: pattern persists across 2+ weeks of episodes. Frame as a request for general quiet-hours reinforcement, not a complaint about a specific neighbor. This protects the no-accusation boundary while still creating a paper trail with management.

Tier 4 — formal management investigation request
See threshold below.

3. Evidence that justifies requesting a formal management investigation

Any ONE of these is enough — they're independently sufficient:

- Direct observation: you or Devika see/hear the source clearly enough to identify the unit (e.g., sound becomes unmistakably louder from one direction when you stand at a specific wall, or you hear a door/voice track tied to the music from inside a unit). Note: low-frequency sound travels through structure, so this bar is high — don't claim it casually.
- Corroboration: another resident in the stack independently reports the same pattern to management and is willing to be identified alongside you.
- Management's own diagnostics: super or staff hears it during a visit and confirms it from a common area or unit.
- Frequency/density threshold: a sustained pattern (e.g., 6+ episodes over 4+ weeks) where the timing pattern strongly points to one stack, even without a unit pin — at this point management has enough to do a structured sweep (floor-by-floor listening at the same hour as a logged episode).
- A single episode so loud or prolonged that it crosses into objective disturbance (e.g., sustained for hours past quiet hours, or at a level that rattles fixtures).

- Reference to the log (by doc), not a re-telling.
- The specific trigger from section 3 that you're citing.
- The specific ask: a structured sweep, a quiet-hours enforcement review, or whatever you think fits.
- An explicit note that the request is based on the documented pattern, not on identification of a unit.

- Don't knock on doors. That's the line management drew at 4/5 and it still holds.
- Don't interpret the pattern for management ("we think it's 4F") — present the data, let them source it.
- If either of you ever does get a direct read on the source, that becomes a Tier 4 trigger automatically and goes straight to management in writing.

The bug: the integer is in milliseconds, but `Retry-After` is a seconds header.

`Retry-After` (RFC 9110 §10.2.3) takes either an HTTP-date or `delay-seconds`, where `delay-seconds = 1*DIGIT`. The integer form is whole seconds — no sub-second granularity on the wire. So:

  - Wire contract: 1200 → wait 1200 s (20 min); 3000 → wait 3000 s (50 min).
  - Implementation intent: 1200 ms → 1.2 s; 3000 ms → 3.0 s. Matches the "randomized 1–3 s" goal.
  - Fixture: reads the value as milliseconds, so it agrees with the implementation and disagrees with every spec-conforming SDK.

The fixture is hiding the bug from CI while real SDKs honoring the header will sit on retries for 20–50 minutes per response. This is a wire-contract violation, not a test problem.

Fix the implementation, not just the fixture:

  1. Pick the integer in seconds. To keep the same 1.2–3.0 s distribution, use a random integer in [1, 3] for integer-second Retry-After, or use a finer delay mechanism (e.g. a `retry_after_ms` field in a JSON body / a vendor extension) rather than overloading the standard header.
  2. Update the fixture to interpret the header value as seconds, per RFC. The test should assert the same thing a real SDK asserts.
  3. If sub-second precision is genuinely required on the wire, use HTTP-date (`Retry-After: <now + random_delay>` formatted via IMF-fixdate). Don't ship non-standard units in `delay-seconds`.

Also worth a follow-up: any existing clients that have been parsing this header as milliseconds — either internal services or out-of-tree SDKs — are operating on the buggy contract. Once the header is corrected to seconds, those consumers will see a much shorter delay than before; if that's load-bearing behavior (e.g. backpressure tuning), flag it in the changelog.

Net: the implementation is writing ms into a seconds slot; the fixture is rubber-stamping it. Tighten the implementation to the spec and let the fixture enforce the spec.

`Retry-After` is specified in RFC 9110 §10.2.3 (formerly RFC 7231 §7.1.3). The header field has exactly two valid wire forms:

    Retry-After    = HTTP-date / delay-seconds
    delay-seconds  = 1*DIGIT          ; decimal integer

That is the entire unit contract: a bare integer is **seconds**, full stop. No `unit=` parameter, no fractional-seconds ABNF alternative, no platform-native escape hatch. The integer grammar *is* the spec on that branch.

A millisecond integer violates the contract on two independent axes:

  1. Unit. `Retry-After: 1500` is parsed by every conformant client as 1500 seconds (~25 minutes), not 1.5 seconds. A randomized 1–3 s delay encoded as ms (1000–3000) would be honored by clients as 16–50 minutes — a silent, catastrophic misread with no warning.
  2. Sanity. The ABNF permits any non-negative integer, but the operational assumption is "seconds a client should wait." Values in the thousands parse fine but are nonsensical as a retry hint, and several intermediaries clamp, log, or warn on out-of-band magnitudes.

Compliant wire-format options that preserve a randomized 1–3 s delay:

  a. **Ceiling-rounded integer seconds.** Pick t uniformly in [1000, 3000] ms and emit `Retry-After: ceil(t/1000)` — i.e. `1`, `2`, or `3`. Safe (advertised wait is never less than the actual unavailable window), trivially parseable by every stack, and requires zero client or intermediary changes. The uniform-ms → ceiling-seconds mapping shifts the distribution very slightly toward the upper bucket but stays inside the intended band.
  b. **HTTP-date.** Emit `Retry-After: <IMF-fixdate>` computed as `now() + delay`. Same second-resolution dynamics as (a); slightly more bytes, no behavioral upside.
  c. **Custom side-channel.** Add `Retry-After-Ms` (or a JSON body field) for sub-second fidelity to advanced clients. This is *not* a substitute for fixing the canonical header — it is an additive opt-in. Keep `Retry-After` RFC-compliant regardless.

Recommended path is (a): no spec change, no ecosystem coordination, no risk of misread. Floor is unsafe (advertised wait shorter than actual unavailability → immediate re-429 / thundering herd); ceiling is the only honest direction.

Interoperability tests required before the change can proceed:

  1. Parser matrix. Confirm each of these parses `Retry-After: 1|2|3` and `Retry-After: <HTTP-date>` correctly, and — critically — that `Retry-After: 1500` is honored as 1500 s, not 1500 ms. The large-integer case is the regression sentinel; flag any library that "helpfully" reinterprets it:
     - Browser fetch + native handling on 503/429 (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit)
     - Node: undici, node-fetch, axios, got
     - Python: requests, urllib3, httpx
     - Go: net/http client
     - Java: java.net.http.HttpClient, OkHttp
     - .NET HttpClient
     - curl (end users run it directly; misreads here are user-visible)
  2. Intermediary matrix. Verify CDNs and gateways forward integer-seconds values verbatim and do not re-interpret, clamp, or strip them:
     - nginx (proxy_next_upstream, limit_req)
     - Cloudflare / Fastly / Akamai (Retry-After propagation on rate-limit responses)
     - AWS API Gateway, GCP API Gateway, Kong, Envoy
  3. Status-code matrix. Confirm the header is consumed on 429 *and* 503; some stacks only honor it on one of the two.
  4. Boundary cases. `Retry-After: 0` → retry-immediately behavior on the relevant stacks; `1`, `2`, `3` produce waits within ~100 ms of the integer; HTTP-dates in the near-past behave predictably (treated as 0 or ignored, not negative).
  5. End-to-end behavioral test. A black-box retry client that respects `Retry-After` is fired at a server injecting a known random delay; recorded wait distribution must be ≥ the injected delay, mean in [1.5 s, 3 s], and no observations past ~5 s.
  6. Schema pin. Regex `^(0|[1-9][0-9]*)$|IMF-fixdate` enforced on every code path that sets the header, so a future change cannot reintroduce ms values without breaking CI.
  7. Distribution pin. Statistical check on the RNG output: uniform-ms → ceiling-seconds should land at roughly 1/3 each in {1, 2, 3}, with the small upward bias from ceiling explicitly modeled in the test.

Ship only after 1–7 all pass; the parser sentinel (1) and the distribution pin (7) are the load-bearing ones — the parser sentinel proves the new format is read correctly across the ecosystem, and the distribution pin proves the randomized-delay intent is actually preserved through the ceiling.
