The readiness transition is a contract about the future, not a retraction of the past. When a service declares itself ready and admits work into its queue, it has accepted a duty of care toward that work and toward the sender that released it. Flipping readiness to "not ready" stops new admissions; it does not retroactively un-accept what was already admitted. Allowing accepted work to be silently abandoned breaks that contract and produces four concrete harms: the sender gets no signal to retry or escalate (silent loss), the sender's own accounting becomes inconsistent because it stopped retrying on the strength of your acceptance, downstream consumers waiting on a result block forever (cascading stall), and the audit trail shows neither success nor failure (compliance and debuggability gap). For a system that handles tenant or customer work, the last two become user-visible.

The owner's obligation is therefore that every accepted work item reaches a known fate before the readiness boundary closes, regardless of which path is taken to get there. The contract has five named guarantees:

    Quiesce. After readiness transitions to "not accepting new work," no
    new work items cross the admission boundary. The service closes its
    doors. Readiness is the only mechanism that needs to enforce this;
    everything below concerns work that was already admitted.

    Drain-or-explicit-rejection. Every admitted item must reach one of two
    terminal fates, and the owner picks a single policy and applies it
    uniformly across the population. Either: drain — the item is processed
    to completion, however long that takes; or: explicit rejection — the
    item is returned to its source with enough context (identifier,
    reason, retry guidance) for the source to act. Per-item mixing, or
    partial abandonment of the tail, is not permitted. The owner declares
    which policy the service follows, and the rest of the system can rely
    on that declaration.

    Terminal-response. Each admitted item's terminal state must be
    observable to the source. "Still in queue," "draining," "shutting
    down" are not terminal — they are intermediate states that leave the
    source unable to tell whether action is needed. Terminal means:
    completed (with the result delivered), or rejected (with the reason
    delivered). No item may be left in a state where the source cannot
    distinguish "still working" from "lost."

    Accounting. Every admitted item's lifecycle must be recorded: an
    identifier, accepted-at, terminal-at, terminal status, and rejection
    reason when applicable. Records must be durable before the readiness
    boundary closes — either flushed locally to a store the shutdown
    sequence is guaranteed to flush, or written to an external system the
    service does not own. Accounting is what makes the other guarantees
    auditable; without it, "drained successfully" and "silently lost"
    are indistinguishable after the fact.

    Regression-test. Automated tests must simulate the readiness
    transition under representative load — queue depth, admission rate,
    item-size mix — and assert four properties: zero new admissions
    after the signal fires; every admitted identifier reaches a terminal
    state within the declared window; accounting contains an entry for
    every admitted identifier with a valid terminal status; and no item
    is reported with an "unknown" or missing terminal state. The test
    must cover whichever policy (drain or explicit-rejection) the owner
    declared. A runbook entry, design doc, or operational procedure
    that claims these guarantees without this test is unverified.

These five are obligations on the owner, not mechanisms. How the service quiesces, how it drains, how it constructs a rejection, where it stores accounting, and how it stages the regression test are all implementation choices the owner makes within these constraints. A reviewer should be able to read the guarantees, inspect the test, and confirm the contract holds without needing to know which shutdown primitive was used.

I have the full context from the 2025-04-16 review. Restating the defect and laying out the tests that have to pass before this optimization can ship.

THE DEFECT

The proposed predicate `lease_owned == true` is necessary but not sufficient. The new holder acquires the lease at 14:03:11 (passes the predicate, returns HTTP 200) but its serving gate stays closed until snapshot catch-up finishes at 14:03:23. Anything routed to it during that 12-second window receives HTTP 503. Readiness is therefore advertising a node that is actively erroring on every request it accepts. The old holder's gate is already closed by then, so there is no split-brain and no state divergence — but the readiness probe is a false positive during exactly the window you most care about (real failover).

The defect is that the readiness signal and the serving gate are now answering different questions. They have to answer the same one. Readiness has to mean "I will serve this request without erroring," not "I have authority to serve." Cyrus's predicate is the second one.

The corrected predicate is the conjunction:

  lease_owned == true AND serving_gate == open

(Plus whatever snapshot-caught-up signal SK uses, assuming the serving gate already implies it — which it should.)

TESTS REQUIRED BEFORE THIS CAN PROCEED

The framing is: readiness must track actual serving eligibility. Every test below is a check that readiness never diverges from "this node will return non-error to a real request."

1. Serving-gate tests (readiness is downstream of the gate, not the lease)

a. Invariant: `ready(T) → gate_open(T)` at every instant T. Equivalently, `gate_closed(T) → ¬ready(T)`. The current proposed predicate violates this during the 14:03:11–14:03:23 window — this is the primary test that fails today.

b. Invariant: `gate_open(T) → lease_owned(T)`. The gate cannot open without the lease. Lease is necessary; never sufficient on its own.

c. Gate-close atomicity: when the serving gate closes (e.g., drain begins, snapshot stall detected), readiness flips to false in the same observable transition, with no intermediate HTTP 200.

d. No gate flapping under partial catch-up: at 50%, 90%, 99% snapshot progress during handoff, the gate remains closed and readiness remains false. The gate opens exactly once, at the end of catch-up.

e. Gate re-open requires re-acquire: if the gate closes mid-handoff (forced failover, snapshot stall), readiness does not return true on stale state — the new holder must re-acquire lease AND re-complete catch-up before readiness returns true.

2. Routing tests (nothing sends traffic to an unready node)

a. End-to-end during the 12s window: with the corrected predicate in place, zero routed requests to the new holder during catch-up. Measured by request logs / LB destination counters across the full handoff window. Today's behavior (with the proposed predicate) is non-zero — that's the regression we're guarding against.

b. Health-check propagation: any consumer of the readiness signal (LB pool, sidecar, ingress) must observe the false state within its poll interval. Default test budget: propagation latency < 2× health-check interval. Anything slower means the 12s window effectively widens.

c. Cache invalidation: any system caching readiness (envoy clusters, service-mesh data planes, sidecar caches) must invalidate on lease-change / serving-gate-change events, not on TTL alone. Test by forcing a stale cache and verifying a forced failover still produces zero routed 503s.

d. Connection draining on the old holder: after the old holder's gate closes, in-flight requests drain; new connection attempts fail. Readiness on the old holder must be false before its last in-flight request completes, so no new request is admitted under a soon-to-be-closed gate.

e. 503 budget during handoff: under normal failover, total externally-observed 503s attributable to the handoff window must equal zero. Under forced failover (kill -9 on old holder mid-handoff), the 503 budget is whatever is required by clients that haven't yet observed readiness=false; assert it stays bounded and is not amplified by a stale-true readiness signal.

3. Handoff tests (the window itself)

a. Boundedness: measure the catch-up window's latency distribution across N staging failovers. The 12s observation is one sample; the test asserts the distribution is bounded and the predicate's correctness holds across the full distribution, not just the median. If catch-up can take 60s+ under load, that's the window the predicate has to cover.

b. No split-brain (this was already correct, must remain correct): across the full handoff timeline, the interval `[old_gate_close, new_gate_open]` is non-empty (gap exists) — i.e., there is no instant where both holders are serving. Asserted via the gate-state log, not via readiness.

c. Readiness false throughout the entire catch-up interval: at no sample point during [lease_acquired, catchup_complete] does readiness return true. Sample at lease_acquired, 25%, 50%, 75%, 99%, catchup_complete. All must be false until the last.

d. Lease release ordering: when the old holder releases the lease, its readiness must already be false (gate already closed). Asserted via paired events: lease_release_T ≥ gate_close_T (old) and readiness_false_T ≥ gate_close_T (old).

e. Forced-failover behavior: kill the old holder mid-handoff (between its gate close and the new holder's catch-up complete). Verify the new holder does not flip readiness true prematurely due to lease-change detection; readiness remains false until catch-up completes. This is the case where Cyrus's "handoff is usually fast" defense collapses — the test pins the predicate under the worst-case path.

f. Partial-failure handling: if snapshot catch-up fails partway (network blip, source shard unavailable), the gate stays closed, readiness stays false, and a retry path is observable. Readiness must not latch true on stale partial state.

FRAMING FOR CYRUS

The reason "lease is usually fast, only matters on real failover" is the wrong defense: the whole point of this change is to be correct during real failover, where the window is twelve seconds and the new holder is a 503 generator advertising itself healthy. The predicate has to hold across the distribution, not at the median. And the predicate has to be a sufficient condition for serving, not just an authorization signal — because that's what readiness consumers assume it is.

One clean line to bring back: readiness and the serving gate must answer the same question. Today they answer different ones, and the difference is exactly the 12-second window that matters most.

The cursor must be cryptographically AND semantically bound to the authorized tenant because these two bindings defend against different attacks, and either one alone leaves a gap.


WHY: CRYPTOGRAPHIC BINDING

  The cursor must carry (or be derived from) an unforgeable proof of the
  (tenant, scope) pair it was issued for. Without this, the cursor is a
  self-asserted string and any client can claim to be any tenant. A
  signature, keyed on a server-only secret, covers the payload fields:
  tenant_id, scope_version, position, expiry. Verification happens BEFORE
  any cursor field is trusted.

  This defends against:
    - Cursor forgery (no key, no valid cursor)
    - Field tampering (a valid tenant editing their own cursor's position
      or tenant_id to peek elsewhere)
    - Stolen cursor reuse (a cursor leaked via logs/traces/MITM is useless
      against any session other than the issuer's)
    - Replay after expiry (expiry is covered by the signature)


WHY: SEMANTIC BINDING

  The cursor must MEAN "this tenant's view of the data, at this position,
  under this scope, at this snapshot." This is separate from crypto.
  Three sub-requirements:

    1. Scope-version binding — a cursor issued under preview_v3 must NOT
       be honored under preview_v4 or stable. A scope upgrade or downgrade
       invalidates outstanding cursors.
    2. Snapshot binding — the position field refers to a specific
       snapshot of the data, not a live mutable view. A cursor must not
       silently include rows added between page requests that fall
       outside the issued snapshot.
    3. Tenant identity at request time — even with a valid signature,
       the tenant_id embedded in the cursor must match the authenticated
       subject of the CURRENT request.

  Why this matters: a validly-signed but stale cursor could expose rows
  from a broader or narrower scope than the tenant is currently
  authorized for. Crypto proves who it was issued to; semantic binding
  is the runtime check that the current session still matches.


WHY BOTH ARE NEEDED

  Cryptographic binding alone is insufficient because it does not
  prevent a validly-signed cursor from being used under a different
  scope, after a snapshot shift, or by a tenant whose access was revoked.

  Semantic binding alone is insufficient because anyone with knowledge of
  the cursor format could self-issue cursors.

  Together they ensure the only way to read tenant T's data at position
  P under scope S is for the requester to be tenant T, currently
  authorized for scope S, with a cursor specifically issued for that
  (tenant, scope, position, snapshot) tuple.


TEST 1 — CROSS-TENANT CURSOR REPLAY

  Setup:
    - Two synthetic tenants: tenant-A and tenant-B, both at preview scope.
    - tenant-A paginates, consumes page 1, captures the cursor from the
      response.
    - tenant-B sends the next request, with tenant-A's cursor attached
      and tenant-B's own credentials.

  Assertions:
    1. Response denied (HTTP 403 or equivalent); no page-2 data returned.
    2. Server-side deny reason recorded as tenant_binding_mismatch.
       Reason is NOT returned in the response body.
    3. Adapter-call counter for the request is exactly 0. Verified via
       tracing — no DB query, no shard-keeper call, no downstream
       dispatch.
    4. Error response leaks no tenant IDs, no cursor structure, no
       information about whether the cursor's signature was valid.
    5. tenant-B's own valid cursor (separately issued under tenant-B's
       own session) still works — the rejection is targeted at the
       replay, not the tenant.

  Variations (each must pass assertions 1-4):
    - Valid signature, replaced tenant_id field (semantic mismatch only).
    - Valid tenant_id, tampered position field.
    - Cursor from a different scope_version (e.g., preview cursor used
      by a stable tenant, or vice versa).
    - Valid everything, but tenant-B's access was revoked after the
      cursor was issued.


TEST 2 — ZERO-ADAPTER-CALL-AFTER-DENIAL

  Setup:
    - Every denial code path instrumented with an adapter-invocation
      counter that starts at 0 and increments only on downstream calls.
    - Fixtures cover every denial condition:

      Fixture              | Trigger
      ---------------------+------------------------------------------
      missing_cursor       | No cursor where one is required
      malformed_cursor     | Cursor present, unparsable
      bad_signature        | Cursor parsed, signature fails verify
      expired_cursor       | Expiry field in the past
      tenant_mismatch      | Cursor tenant_id != request subject
      scope_mismatch       | Cursor scope_version != authorized scope
      revoked_tenant       | Tenant access revoked after issuance
      snapshot_drift       | Cursor references a snapshot no longer held

  Assertions:
    - For each fixture: response denied AND adapter-call counter == 0.
    - Aggregate: deny rate 100% under fixtures; adapter-call rate 0%
      under deny.
    - p99 deny latency bounded (e.g., <5ms) — no slow paths caused by
      signature verification or attempted DB lookups.
    - Logs capture the deny reason per fixture; no PII or cursor
      payload data is logged.


CONSTRAINT: AUTHORIZED PREVIEW SCOPE UNCHANGED

  Assertions:
    - A preview-authorized tenant, sending a cursor issued under the
      same preview scope_version, matching tenant_id, valid signature,
      and unexpired, returns 200 with identical data shape and row set
      to the pre-correction path.
    - The fix tightens cursor VALIDATION only. It does NOT:
      * Add or remove fields from the visible row set
      * Change the snapshot boundary or pagination semantics
      * Restrict which tenants are in the preview allowlist
    - Regression: row counts and field projections on a fixed fixture
      set must be identical pre- and post-correction. Diff must be
      empty for legitimate requests.

  Implication for the fix: tests 1 and 2 above are the negative-path
  tests; this constraint is the positive-path guard that the fix did
  not over-correct and shrink the visible preview.


PERSISTENCE

  This is design rationale plus test specs — the kind of artifact that
  should live next to the corrected-path implementation. If you want it
  written to a doc (or a runbook entry for the synthetic fixtures),
  tell me the doc_id/title and I'll post it. Per my standing rule I
  won't guess a doc title or pick a doc_id from internal_search_v2

================================================================
Why a missing generation report cannot satisfy the fail-closed rejoin gate
================================================================

The rejoin gate in `rb_metrics_router_canary` ("Host-maintenance rejoin gate (durable rule, 2025-04-15)") is fail-closed by construction. It requires two conditions, *both* of which must hold before isolation is released on an instance returning from host maintenance:

1. The rejoining instance positively reports the **current active generation**.
2. Only then, the full ordinary check set passes — consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health.

The gate treats a missing generation report as not-healthy by definition. That is the point of "fail-closed": silence, staleness, a stale generation value, a heartbeat without a generation field, or any report whose generation does not match the live active generation are all equivalent to "no valid current-generation report." None of them release isolation.

The reason is structural, not procedural:

- The active generation is the single coordinate the rest of the check set is anchored to. Parity compares this instance's series against the live set at generation G; dropped-series uses G as the partition key; the route check uses G as the version the router's config-loader compiled against; the health check reads the per-generation health-set baseline. A report that does not identify a generation cannot be anchored, and the checks cannot be performed coherently against an unanchored instance. Running them anyway would compare against the wrong cohort and silently let a stale instance back in.

- A missing report is indistinguishable from the failure mode the gate exists to prevent. After the Apr 12 stale-generation debrief, the specific hazard was an instance returning from maintenance believing it was on the current generation when it was not. "No report" is the same hazard with one fewer data point than "stale report" — it has strictly less evidence that the instance is on G. Fail-closed says: when evidence is missing, do not advance the state machine.

- The Apr 12 incident confirmed the cost of advancing without positive evidence. The instance that re-emerged from maintenance without a current-generation report was the proximate cause of the cross-instance inconsistency. The 2025-04-15 durable rule is the codified response: the gate must not advance on absence of evidence, and the operator must not have to *prove* the instance is stale in order to keep it isolated — the operator must only have to *not see* a current-generation report.

- The gate's "until both hold" phrasing is intentional. Passing any subset of the five ordinary checks before the current-generation report is in does not weaken isolation; it does not earn partial credit. The full check set is gated on condition 1, not parallel to it. This forecloses the operator shortcut of "consistency and parity are clean, release the instance" when the generation report is still missing.

In one sentence: the gate fails closed because the generation report is the precondition that makes every other check meaningful, and a missing report is not a passing precondition.

================================================================
Tests proving isolation remains until a valid current-generation report arrives AND the full check set passes
================================================================

Each test below is a unit/integration test against the rejoin-state-machine and the metrics-router control plane. The first set (A) holds the gate closed at the generation-report precondition. The second set (B) holds the gate closed against partial passes of the ordinary check set. The third set (C) holds the gate closed against bypass attempts. The fourth set (D) is the positive control: the gate releases only when both conditions hold simultaneously.

The tests are scoped to the **monitor correction** (the rejoin-state-machine and the check-set gating) — they do not exercise the deployment pipeline, do not authorize a push, and do not revisit the Apr 12 root-cause analysis.

----------------------------------------------------------------
A. Current-generation report precondition
----------------------------------------------------------------

A1. No report → isolation remains.
- Setup: a metrics-router instance returns from host maintenance. The instance does not emit a generation report within the configured report window (default: one full heartbeat interval past the rejoin deadline).
- Assertion: the rejoin state machine stays in `isolated_pending_generation_report` indefinitely. The instance is not added to the live set. The metrics-router control plane logs `rejoin_hold: missing_generation_report` at every subsequent observation tick.

A2. Stale generation report → isolation remains.
- Setup: instance returns from maintenance and reports generation G-1 (the previous generation; the live active generation is G).
- Assertion: state machine transitions to `isolated_stale_generation`. Instance is not added to the live set. Log: `rejoin_hold: stale_generation G-1 active_G=G`. The ordinary check set is not evaluated for this instance.

A3. Heartbeat without generation field → isolation remains.
- Setup: instance returns and emits liveness heartbeats, but the heartbeats do not carry a generation field.
- Assertion: state machine treats this as A1 (missing generation report). Log: `rejoin_hold: heartbeat_without_generation`. Liveness alone does not advance the gate.

A4. Current-generation report, then subsequent staleness before full check set → isolation remains.
- Setup: instance reports current generation G at T+0, but before the full check set completes (within the check-set evaluation window) the instance's report drops to G-1 or is missing.
- Assertion: state machine re-enters `isolated_pending_generation_report` (or `isolated_stale_generation`). The partial pass of the check set does not carry over; the check set must restart against a stable current-generation report. Log: `rejoin_hold: generation_report_unstable_during_check_set`.

A5. Generation report across the report-window boundary.
- Setup: instance is configured with report window W. The first valid current-generation report arrives at W+epsilon.
- Assertion: gate advances to `isolated_running_check_set` only at the moment the first valid current-generation report is observed. Before that moment (including the entire window W), state remains `isolated_pending_generation_report`.

----------------------------------------------------------------
B. Full ordinary check set gating
----------------------------------------------------------------

The ordinary check set, in evaluation order: **consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, health.** The gate does not release on a subset.

B1. Generation report in, no checks evaluated → isolation remains.
- Setup: instance reports current generation G. The check scheduler is suspended (operator holds the instance for an unrelated reason, or the check scheduler is down).
- Assertion: state machine is in `isolated_running_check_set`. Instance is not in the live set. No check has been skipped; the gate has not advanced.

B2. Generation report in, consistency and parity pass, dropped-series fails → isolation remains.
- Setup: instance reports G; consistency passes; parity passes; dropped-series regresses (a previously observed series is missing on this instance).
- Assertion: state machine is in `isolated_check_set_failed:dropped_series`. Log carries the specific regressed series IDs. The instance is not in the live set. The gate does not advance.

B3. Generation report in, consistency, parity, dropped-series pass; route fails → isolation remains.
- Assertion: state machine is in `isolated_check_set_failed:route`. Log carries the route-table diff. Gate does not advance.

B4. Generation report in, consistency/parity/dropped-series/route pass; health fails → isolation remains.
- Assertion: state machine is in `isolated_check_set_failed:health`. Log carries the failing health-set components. Gate does not advance.

B5. All five checks pass, but generation report is not current at the moment of release → isolation remains.
- Setup: instance reports G at T+0. Check set begins. By the time all five pass at T+30s, the instance's report is now stale (G-1) because a generation advance occurred during the check window.
- Assertion: gate does not release. State machine re-enters `isolated_pending_generation_report`. Log: `rejoin_hold: generation_advanced_during_check_set`. The check-set pass is invalidated because the anchor changed mid-evaluation.

B6. Order-independence.
- Setup: same conditions as B2-B4, but the check scheduler runs parity first, then dropped-series, then route.
- Assertion: failure of any single check holds the gate. Order does not matter.

----------------------------------------------------------------
C. Bypass attempts (negative controls)
----------------------------------------------------------------

C1. Operator override on missing generation report.
- Setup: operator issues a manual release command while the instance is in `isolated_pending_generation_report`.
- Assertion: command is rejected. Audit log: `rejoin_release_rejected: precondition_not_met (missing_generation_report)`. The owner-of-record is paged (per the rejoin-state-machine audit policy). This is a durable-rule violation regardless of operator authority on the instance.

C2. Operator override on stale generation report.
- Assertion: rejected with `precondition_not_met (stale_generation)`.

C3. Release on a partial check-set pass.
- Setup: operator issues release after consistency + parity + dropped-series pass but before route or health.
- Assertion: rejected with `precondition_not_met (check_set_incomplete)`. Log enumerates the checks that have not yet passed.

C4. Force-add to live set via the config-loader path.
- Setup: operator edits the config-loader to add the instance to the live set directly, bypassing the rejoin state machine.
- Assertion: config-loader rejects the edit because the instance is not in `released` state. Audit log: `config_loader_reject: instance_not_released`.

C5. Canary-window conflation.
- Setup: a metrics-router canary window is in force (per `rb_metrics_router_canary`'s canary-thresholds section). Operator attempts to release a rejoin during the canary window by referencing the canary's recovery sequence.
- Assertion: rejected. The rejoin gate is independent of the canary recovery sequence; a rejoin is not a push and does not consume a canary decision. Log: `rejoin_release_rejected: rejoin_is_not_canary_push`.

C6. Deploy-pipeline conflation.
- Setup: a deploy is in flight. Operator attempts to use the deploy pipeline to "carry" the rejoining instance into the live set.
- Assertion: rejected. The rejoin gate is independent of the deploy pipeline. Log: `rejoin_release_rejected: rejoin_is_not_deploy`.

----------------------------------------------------------------
D. Positive control: gate releases only when both conditions hold simultaneously
----------------------------------------------------------------

D1. Happy path.
- Setup: instance returns from host maintenance. At T+0, instance reports current generation G. The check set begins. Consistency passes at T+5. Parity passes at T+8. Dropped-series passes at T+12. Route passes at T+15. Health passes at T+18. Throughout, the generation report remains G.
- Assertion: at T+18, state machine transitions to `released`. Instance enters the live set. Log: `rejoin_released: generation=G, checks={consistency,parity,dropped-series,route,health}`. Audit log records the timestamp at which each check passed.

D2. Generation-anchored check evaluation.
- Setup: as D1, but a generation advance occurs at T+10 (between dropped-series pass and route pass). The new active generation is G+1. The instance's report remains G.
- Assertion: gate does not release. State machine re-enters `isolated_pending_generation_report` (the report is now stale relative to the new active generation). The instance must report G+1 and the check set must re-run anchored to G+1 before release.

D3. Idempotence of release.
- Setup: as D1, the instance is released at T+18. The state machine receives a duplicate release command at T+19.
- Assertion: no-op. State remains `released`. Log: `rejoin_release_idempotent: already_released`. The instance is not double-added to the live set.

----------------------------------------------------------------
E. Audit and observability
----------------------------------------------------------------

E1. Every isolated-tick must be observable.
- Assertion: for every state-machine tick where the instance is in any `isolated_*` state, the metrics-router control plane emits a state observation with the holding reason. An operator can answer "why is this instance still isolated?" from the metrics alone, without reading code.

E2. Re-hold on regression.
- Setup: an instance that was previously released regresses (e.g., drops a series) and is re-isolated.
- Assertion: the re-isolation uses the same rejoin state machine. The instance cannot return to the live set without satisfying both conditions again. Log: `rejoin_re_isolated: reason=...`.

E3. No silent state transitions.
- Assertion: every transition in the rejoin state machine is logged with a monotonic sequence number and an operator-or-scheduler origin. There is no transition path that bypasses the audit log.

FOOD SAFETY TRIAGE: ~55-MIN PARTIAL DOOR OPEN, FRIDGE AT 44°F

Quick frame
------------
USDA rule of thumb: perishable food held above 40°F for more than 2 hours (1 hour if above 90°F) should be discarded. Your 55 minutes is under that hard line, but the thermometer reading itself is informative — the fridge air doesn't drift from ~38°F to 44°F in minutes; reaching 44°F means the door was probably open longer than you noticed, or opened more fully at some earlier point. Treat 55 minutes as a floor, not the full picture.

Also: "felt cold" is unreliable. Hand temperature perception can't distinguish 38°F from 48°F. Use the rule and the checks below, not the touch test.

Per-item triage (conservative order)
------------------------------------
1. RAW CHICKEN — highest risk
   Poultry is the main vehicle for Salmonella and Campylobacter. Two defensible options:
   - COOK NOW to 165°F internal with a calibrated probe (color is not enough). Once cooked, it's safe.
   - DISCARD if you don't want to commit to cooking it within the next hour.
   Don't just push it to the back and "use it later" — that's where most foodborne illness comes from.

2. COOKED RICE — high risk, different mechanism
   Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and germinate between 40–140°F. The emetic toxin they produce is HEAT-STABLE — reheating does not neutralize it. The classic outbreak story is cooked rice left in a warm pot. With a confirmed air temp of 44°F, the conservative call is DISCARD. If you cooked it within the last few hours and it was rapidly chilled originally, risk is lower — but rice is the one item where "just cook it again" doesn't fix anything.

3. MILK — moderate risk
   Pasteurized, sealed cartons are reasonably resilient at 44°F for ~1 hour. Re-chill it, then after 30+ minutes back in the cold, smell it and taste a small sip. If anything seems off (sour, yeasty, "not right"), discard. Hard cheese is more forgiving than soft cheese or yogurt.

4. EGGS — moderate risk, depends on form
   Raw shell eggs: safer — shell provides barrier. Re-chill, then crack and sniff. If off, discard.
   Hard-boiled or peeled/cut eggs: more exposed surface; eat within 24 hours or discard.
   Pasteurized liquid egg: most resilient.

5. CUT VEGETABLES — lowest risk, but variable
   Hard veg (carrots, celery, peppers): safest. Leafy greens, cut melon, mushrooms: more exposed wet surface, faster bacterial growth. Re-chill, then visually inspect for slime, discoloration, or off smell before using.

Immediate steps (next 1–2 hours)
---------------------------------
- Don't open the door again for at least 30–60 minutes. Let it recover.
- Re-check the thermometer at 30 and 60 minutes. If it doesn't drop back under 40°F, your conservative moves need to happen faster.
- Sanitize the door gaskets and any shelves where raw chicken juices could have dripped.
- Decide cook-now vs. discard on the chicken and rice before your next meal — don't let them sit another full day.

What to check promptly
----------------------
- THERMOMETER ACCURACY. Put your fridge thermometer in a glass of ice water for 2 minutes — it should read 32°F. If it's off by 3°F, your "44°F" might really be 47°F, which changes the calculus.
- DOOR GASKET. "Partly open" — does it actually seal and latch when closed? A weak gasket will keep the fridge warm and undermine everything else.
- FREEZER AT 4°F. That's not zero, and worth flagging — your freezer thermometer may also be off, or the whole unit was struggling. Anything still frozen solid is fine; just note it.
- ITEM POSITION. Anything near the door or front of shelves warmed more than things deep in the back.

Evidence that means "discard, don't guess"
------------------------------------------
Trust these over the clock:
- SMELL: sour, yeasty, ammonia, or any odor that wasn't there before. Bacterial growth often produces detectable compounds before anything is visibly wrong.
- VISUAL: slime on vegetables, cloudiness in milk that doesn't clear, pink or iridescent sheen on chicken, dark spots, unusual liquid pooling.
- TEXTURE: chicken sticky or tacky; rice unusually clumped or gummy; vegetables limp past normal.
- PROBE TEMP: an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part of the chicken ≥45°F and held ≥2 hours cumulatively → discard. Same for any dairy/egg dish.
- AMBIGUITY: if you can't reliably fix the 55-minute window or trust the thermometer reading, err toward discard on the high-risk items (chicken, rice).

If anyone in the household is in a higher-risk group (pregnant, elderly, immunocompromised, under 5), apply the stricter version: cook the chicken now to 165°F, discard the rice, use everything else within 24 hours after a smell/visual pass.

The FSIS "Ask Karen" database (fsis.usda.gov) has the official guidance by food type.

The blocking-write-lock-around-compile pattern is the real problem here. Three concrete issues:

  1. All serving freezes for the compile window. Once routeMu is held by the writer in write mode, sync.RWMutex semantics block new RLock acquisitions too (otherwise writer starvation would never resolve). So while compile runs at 284-337 ms, every in-flight request plus every newly-arriving request sits waiting. That's not "tail latency" — it's a sustained multi-hundred-ms freeze of the routing path on every reload. If your p99 request budget is anywhere near 50-100 ms, this will surface as timeouts and 5xx during reloads.

  2. The failure path is strictly worse than the success path in terms of benefit-to-cost. A malformed candidate currently blocks serving for the entire parse+compile duration and produces zero useful state change. Easiest way to trigger a serving-grade stall becomes "push a config with a typo." That should be a near-zero-impact event, not the worst-case reload.

  3. Compile work doesn't need shared state. The candidate is built from a single config blob; it doesn't read activeGeneration, doesn't touch the serving state. There's no correctness reason for routeMu to be held during compile.

The standard shape for generation-based config reload is two-stage with a pointer swap:

  - Parse + compile the candidate with no lock held. If it errors, return immediately — readers see zero impact, and that fix alone makes the typo case a non-event.
  - On success, take routeMu only long enough to publish (activeGeneration = candidate under a brief write lock, or atomic.Pointer.Store if you want to retire the lock from the read hot path entirely).
  - Readers grab the current generation once at request entry — under a brief RLock, or via atomic.Pointer.Load() if you go that route — and operate on that snapshot. Either way the read critical section collapses from "entire request" to "one pointer copy."

A few adjacent things worth checking while you're in there:

  - Reload-during-reload. With the lock-free compile, two near-simultaneous reloads will both run full compiles and the later one wins on swap. Probably want single-flight or "latest-wins" coalescing so a burst of config pushes doesn't trigger parallel compiles.
  - During the swap window both old and new generations are live. 12k routes is fine; just confirm GC isn't going to be unpleasant.
  - The 284/311/337 ms itself — if this is regex/DFA compilation there's usually 5-10x headroom, but that's a separate change and not required for correctness.

Safety on this change is fine — the write lock does cover the swap, and the failure path correctly preserves the active generation. The issue is that liveness is being traded for safety in a way that's avoidable. Two-stage with a pointer swap is the conventional fix and shouldn't require touching the request handler logic beyond changing where it acquires its generation reference.

Verdict: the fixture is encoding the bug, not the spec. On retry, source_timestamp should preserve the original observation time (10:02), not be reset to clock.Now() (10:19). The fact that retry_attempt_at already exists as a separate field is the giveaway — you've already invented the right field for retry-side timing; the question is whether anything downstream still reads source_timestamp as if it were origin time.

Why resetting source_timestamp on retry is wrong:

  - End-to-end latency (observation -> ingestion) is inflated by every retry. A 17-min retry becomes a 17-min source_timestamp skew. Dashboards and SLO windows keyed on source_timestamp stop being real.
  - Reordering across retries: observation A (10:02) retries while B (10:05) goes through clean. A's envelope now timestamps 10:19, B's stays 10:05. Downstream timeline reconstruction sees A arriving after B even though A was observed first.
  - OTel convention: source_timestamp is the origin time of the data point, not when the envelope happened to be re-emitted. Retries are pipeline metadata, not new observations.
  - Clock skew across collector nodes during retry fan-out: source_timestamp preservation across hops is what keeps aggregation coherent. Resetting on each hop is exactly what you don't want.
  - Very-late retries (hours/days after origin) silently hide staleness instead of letting you measure and act on it.

Recommended change in the retry path:

  - Carry the original source_timestamp forward onto the new ExportEnvelope. Do not call clock.Now() for it.
  - Keep retry_attempt_at as the wall-clock at retry (already correct).
  - If you want a "first export attempt at" or "enqueued at" available downstream, add it as its own field. Do not repurpose source_timestamp.

Fixture update:

  - Expected source_timestamp should be 10:02, not 10:19.
  - Assert retry_attempt_at == 10:19.
  - Assert the two fields are distinct (the whole point of having both is that they diverge on retry).

Edge cases worth a sentence in the PR description:

  - Partial-batch retries (some succeeded, some failed): per-observation source_timestamp preservation inside a mixed envelope matters even more; a reset smears the batch's actual time profile.
  - Stale-retry policy (drop after N hours?): that decision is easier to make and audit when origin time is intact rather than hidden behind the retry clock.

Before approving, confirm that every downstream consumer (rollup, ingest-edge, shard-keeper, anything reading the envelope) treats source_timestamp as origin time and retry_attempt_at as the retry-side timestamp. If anything reads source_timestamp and assumes "this is when the data was observed," the current code is silently lying to it on every retried envelope — which, given the FD-leak cancel-handler work you have in flight on the rollup side, is exactly the kind of latent skew that turns into a paging incident later.

Failure-mode read on the SK lease-maintenance candidate (for Cyrus, before DP proceeds):

What the candidate does
- At acquisition: expiresAt = wallClock.Now() + remainingLease (absolute wall-clock deadline, cached).
- At serving: gate open while wallClock.Now() < expiresAt.
- Trades a coordinator check per serving decision for a single absolute timestamp.

What the test is actually demonstrating
- 90s backward wall-clock jump after acquisition.
- expiresAt unchanged; wallClock.Now() now reads ~T - 90s, so the gate stays open.
- Test deliberately isolates the no-second-holder case to show this is intrinsic to wall-clock-based expiry, not contingent on a concurrent acquirer. That's the right framing — the bug is the design, not a concurrency corner.

Failure modes, ordered by severity

1. Backward clock extension (the test case)
   - Any backward wall-clock adjustment extends the lease silently, up to the magnitude of the jump.
   - Sources: NTP step corrections, VM suspend/resume, container/cgroup freezer, manual date changes, live-migration.
   - Even without a second holder, lease TTL is violated — the holder is serving beyond its contractual duration. Operational cost depends on what SK leases gate (shard ownership / recovery eligibility / failover timing); an over-extended lease delays rebalancing and prolongs unavailability windows after a real failure.

2. Split-brain with a plausible second holder
   - Test excludes this; production doesn't.
   - Another acquirer using correct time, a quorum grantor, or any external coordinator that enforces the original deadline can take the lease at the wall-clock expiresAt.
   - Original holder's wall-clock still says "valid" → both serve.
   - For shard ownership this is the worst case: duplicate authority, divergent state. The optimization is correct only if no other acquirer path can ever disagree on the deadline — which is not a property you can guarantee by omission.

3. Forward clock jump
   - Lease silently expires early. Holder stops serving before the intended window; recovery path fires unnecessarily.
   - Not a correctness violation, but it's an availability blip the optimization is introducing where it didn't exist before.

4. Inter-process clock skew
   - If grantor and holder NTP independently, the TTL granted at issue time may already be wrong. The candidate doesn't defend against it — it implicitly trusts wallClock.Now() on both sides. This is the failure mode that bites teams who assume "wall-clock" means "the same wall-clock."

5. Long suspend / large discontinuity
   - Suspend/resume is effectively an unbounded backward jump. A 5-minute VM suspend means a 5-minute lease extension. There is no ceiling.

Recommendation

The wall-clock absolute-deadline design is unsafe for lease maintenance. The fix is mechanical and well-known:

  - Hybrid (preferred): keep expiresAt as wall-clock for observability and external coordination, but drive the serving check from a monotonic clock — monotonic_now - monotonic_at_acquisition < lease_duration. Monotonic is immune to wall-clock jumps in both directions. The cached wall-clock field becomes a derived/reporting value rather than the gate.
  - Monotonic-only: simpler, loses wall-clock observability of "real" deadline.
  - Coordinator-enforced: don't trust holder-side clock at all; have the grantor renew/refuse per tick. Higher latency, eliminates holder-side clock dependency, but is a bigger redesign.

The test as written only surfaces (1) in isolation. Before this is approved, the same harness should also cover:

  - A second holder attempting acquisition after the original deadline (split-brain surface).
  - Forward clock jump of comparable magnitude (early-expiry).
  - Suspend/resume simulation, including >lease-duration pauses.
  - Independent NTP skew between grantor and holder (issue path and serve path on different hosts with divergent clocks).

Bottom line for Cyrus / DP: this is not a threshold-tuning problem. The candidate's correctness model is broken; the optimization trades the property that lease maintenance is supposed to provide. Either the design switches to a monotonic-driven check, or the leases stop doing the job they're named for. I'd hold it.

Review of the bucket-layout change for `rollup_queue_age_seconds`.

Bottom line: block as proposed. The "same metric name, dashboard sums the bucket series" combination is a contract the rollout plan breaks the moment both layouts are in scrape together. Per-bucket `rate()` is no longer comparable across replicas, and `histogram_quantile()` interpolates against a CDF that's measuring different populations on different intervals.

Why the sum breaks:

  1. Per-bucket counts no longer mean the same thing across replicas.
     Old replicas emit bucket{le="5"} = observations with 1s < age <= 5s.
     New replicas emit bucket{le="3"} = observations with 1s < age <= 3s,
     and bucket{le="10"} = observations with 1s < age <= 10s (which
     subsumes the 3-5s range that the old "5" bucket exclusively held).
     sum(rate(bucket[5m])) by (le) gives a series where each le no longer
     corresponds to a coherent "everyone <= X" range.

  2. histogram_quantile() output is undefined.
     It interpolates against the union of boundaries {1,3,5,10,30,60,120,
     300,600,900,1800,+Inf}, but on the 3-5 interval only old replicas
     contribute, and on the 5-10 interval only new replicas contribute
     (in the <=10 sense). The interpolated value is not biased in a
     known direction; it's noise around the true value, with magnitude
     depending on where observations land relative to the old/new edges.

  3. Specific boundaries that will mislead:
     - 5 -> 3: anything alerting on the "fast path" share changes meaning.
     - 60 -> 120: doubles what was probably an SLO upper bucket.
     - 900 -> 1800: max observable tail doubles; "exceeded old max"
       consumers were almost certainly not re-evaluated.
     - 30 is the only stable boundary. Anything written against
       bucket{le="30"} keeps working by coincidence, not by design.

  4. Recording rules amplify the damage.
     If there's a rule caching p50/p95/p99 over 30s/5m/1h windows, it
     gets fed mixed buckets during the overlap, emits nonsense, and
     that nonsense is then cached and referenced by alerts/dashboards
     for the rule's TTL. The bad data outlives the rollout window.

Secondary observations:

  A. The layout change itself encodes an interpretation shift:
     dense resolution below 15s -> sparser resolution below 30s plus
     a 30-min tail. Either the SLO target range moved (and other
     consumers weren't notified) or the new layout drops visibility
     on sub-15s ranges something downstream uses. Worth asking Cyrus
     what drove it before debating deploy mechanics.

  B. Cardinality is not the concern (7 buckets either way). The
     concern is semantic equivalence under sum, not scrape cost.

  C. The +Inf bucket presumably still exists on both sides; total
     observation counts via sum without (le) keep working. Everything
     bucket-keyed is broken during overlap.

Safe rollout options, roughly in order of preference:

  1. Atomic cutover. Drain old replicas, deploy new, never have both
     layouts in a single scrape. Cleanest; works if deploy windows
     or single-replica deploys are tolerable.

  2. Dual emission during migration. New replicas emit the old-layout
     histogram under the original name AND a new-layout histogram
     under a new name (rollup_queue_age_seconds_v2 or similar). Old
     replicas keep emitting the old layout. Dashboard switches to
     the new metric only after full cutover. Preserves summed
     semantics on each side.

  3. Per-replica aggregation in the dashboard. Stop summing bucket
     series directly; compute quantile per replica, then merge
     (weighted merge of per-replica quantile sketches, or max-of-p99
     if you only need an upper bound). Consumer-side change, not
     producer-side.

  4. Native histograms. Switch to Prometheus native histograms
     (sparse exponential buckets, mergeable across replicas with
     different layouts). Bigger change; solves the underlying class
     of problem.

What I'd say in the review:

  "Block. Same metric name + dashboard sum + different bucket
  boundaries = silently broken quantiles for the duration of the
  overlap. Need one of: (a) coordinated cutover with no overlap
  window, (b) dual emission with a new metric name, or (c) dashboard
  changed to merge per-replica before the new layout ships. Also:
  why is the layout changing? If it's an SLO range shift, that
  should be a separately announced change with consumer review, not
  bundled into a telemetry PR. And: are there recording rules /
  alerts / dashboards keyed on specific old boundaries (5, 15, 60,
  300, 900 in particular)? Those need to be updated in the same
  change set, not discovered in production."

If you want, I can also sketch what the dual-emission patch would look like for the rollup service so you can attach it to the review.

The preflight can't return `pass` here — the violation at record 12,001 is real, and the optimization is blind to it.

What's happening:

The candidate stops at 10,000 of 12,400 records. That's not a defensible sampling strategy — it's deterministic truncation at a fixed boundary. Two failure modes follow:

  1. The coverage gap is structural. Any violation at index > 10,000 is invisible to the preflight by construction. The fixture isn't unlucky; the truncation guarantees it misses tail-positioned bad records.

  2. The "optimization" behaves like two different checks depending on input shape. On a 10K fixture it's effectively a full scan and reports correctly. On a 12.4K fixture it silently downgrades to a partial scan and reports `pass`. The two answers disagree on the same logical question, and the caller has no signal telling them which one they got.

Why this matters more than a slow-path complaint:

  - Bounded-set violations on caller-supplied labels are exactly the class Cardinality Guardrails exists to catch. If the preflight green-lights proposals the full scan would reject, downstream consumers (rollup, adapter) inherit unbounded cardinality. The blast radius shows up in the next budget cycle, not in this PR.

  - The 12,001 position looks deliberate. Whoever wrote the fixture knew where to put the bad record — past the truncation boundary, inside the file. That reads as a regression test, not an accident.

What I'd want before this lands:

  - Full scan remains the only mode, and the actual optimization is orthogonal — memoize the bounded-set lookup, parallelize across records, short-circuit only after a complete pass.

  - Or, if sampling is genuinely the goal, it has to be randomized over the full record range with a documented confidence floor, and the fixture's bad record must be in-sample under a seeded RNG. Otherwise the test is theater.

Summary of what I checked:

  - open PRs on ingest-edge: only `ingest-edge#221` (Wes's OTel 0.91 bump, unrelated)
  - runbook entries: the bounded-decompression principle is already on the books in the tenant-fair queue section ("no unbounded backlog build-up behind a noisy tenant"), and the 8,000-point / 413 oversized-batch rule is a parallel cap on the post-decode side. Neither of those binds the decode itself.
  - no production traffic touched, per your note — no paging, no incident, no rollback.

Review take:

  1. The order of operations is the bug. `io.ReadAll(gzipReader)` materializes the full decoded payload before any post-decode validation runs. A 217× expansion ratio (6.2 MiB → 1.34 GiB) on a single request is a textbook decompression bomb, and gzip's nominal max ratio is ~1000× so there's plenty of headroom for worse fixtures. The fact that the 7,640 points are syntactically valid and that the fixture happens to be rejected on some post-decode criterion doesn't matter — the 1.34 GiB allocation happens regardless of the eventual verdict, and the verdict can't change that cost.

  2. The fixture's point count (7,640) is under the 8,000-point per-batch ceiling in the 413 runbook, so point-count rejection wouldn't fire here. Whatever the rejection criterion is, it's strictly downstream of a full decode. That's the wrong place to draw the line.

  3. Fix shape I'd want to see before merge (in this PR, not a follow-up):

      a. Bound the *compressed* request body with `http.MaxBytesReader` before handing it to `gzip.NewReader`. Cap on the order of a few MiB — well above any legitimate batch, well below anything that could expand dangerously.

      b. Bound the *decompressed* stream by wrapping the gzip reader with a counting reader or `io.LimitReader` set against a per-request decompressed-byte budget. The budget should be sized to legitimate traffic with margin — e.g. 8,000 points × a generous per-point byte ceiling — not "infinity until validation runs."

      c. Treat an early termination from the limit reader as a hard reject (413 / `oversized_batch` or equivalent), surfaced before any point-level work. Don't let the gzip decoder surface a confusing `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` from a truncated trailer.

      d. Reject responses in this path should carry `Retry-After` to stay aligned with the v2.19.4 randomized `Retry-After` behavior already in production. The 413 runbook doesn't currently bind that, but the queue-cap rule does, and the shape is the same.

  4. Runbook linkage: the bounded-decompression principle in the tenant-fair queue section talks about queue depth, not per-request decode. After this lands, an explicit runbook entry on the per-request decompression bound would be worth adding — what the cap is, what response code it returns, and that it's the line of defense between the network and the decode path. Not a blocker for the PR; a follow-up.

  5. Memory-slope canary stop rule: not directly applicable here (this isn't a canary rollout yet), but if this change ever reaches a staged cohort, the rule's "compare cache-key uniqueness against the prior version, inspect the allocation profile for an unbounded type" guidance is the right lens for this exact class of regression. Worth flagging in the PR description so the next reviewer doesn't have to dig for it.

  6. Staging fixture: keep it. It's doing real work — it caught a pattern that wouldn't have surfaced from a syntactically-valid but small fixture. If anything, add a second fixture at ~9× compression ratio (a few MiB compressed → mid-GiB decoded, no invalid points at all) to prove the cap fires on the decode path before any point-level validation could reject.

  7. Rejection criterion itself isn't my call to make here — that's the author's design. The review point is independent of which post-decode rule fires: the cap must run *before* the decode completes, not after.

Bottom line: request changes. The decode-path bound is the actual fix; everything else is framing.

Parse-before-lock is the right shape — pushes the expensive work outside the critical section, so publication reduces to an atomic pointer swap. The 0.7-1.1 ms critical section tracks that.

The two correctness properties are exactly what readers need:

  - Malformed candidate leaves old gen unchanged: compile-before-swap catches parse/compile failures before publish, so a bad candidate never becomes active.
  - Complete old OR complete new, never partial: atomic swap, readers hold a generation ref, no torn read.

The +3.4 ms p99 during construction is bounded to the candidate-build window — one-time per route update, not steady-state. Relative impact depends on baseline: ~10% if baseline is ~35 ms, 30%+ if baseline is under ~12 ms. Worth checking the baseline against the SLO before merging.

The once-per-revolution pattern is itself diagnostic: it means something on the wheel is meeting a fixed reference once per turn. That points to a rotor or rim high spot, a stuck foreign object, a misaligned pad, a loose pad spring, a tire bulge, a loose spoke, or something on the fork/fender brushing the tire.

Inspection sequence (non-destructive, in order, no tools required):

1. Lift and free-spin. Lift the front, spin by hand slowly. Confirm the sound really is locked to wheel rotation (not random ambient noise). Mentally note where in the rotation the scrape peaks.

2. Localize the origin. Get your eye level with the wheel while it spins. Identify which zone makes the sound: rotor and caliper area (disc brake), rim and pad area, tire surface, or hub center.

3. Rotor and pads (disc brakes). Look edge-on through the caliper window while spinning. A bent rotor shows as a gap that visibly closes once per revolution; a stone or metal shard between pad and rotor shows as a visible interruption. Confirm both pads are parallel to the rotor with even gap, the retaining pin/screw is seated, and the pad spring clip is straight and not touching the rotor.

4. Rim and pads (rim brakes). With the lever released, both pads should sit fully in the brake track and release cleanly off the rim. Check pad thickness — if you see metal or the holder is touching the rim, pads are spent. Lightly run a finger along the rim track to feel for a burr or embedded grit.

5. Tire and rim surface. Carefully feel the tread and both sidewalls for embedded glass, wire, or a bulge. Look at the rim sidewalls for dents and at the rim strip for a tear exposing a spoke nipple.

6. Hub and spokes. With the wheel lifted, the axle should spin silently for many revolutions. Pluck each spoke — they should all ring at a similar tension and not flex visibly. A spoke that goes "thunk" instead of "ting," or moves under light finger pressure, is loose.

7. Clearance check. With the wheel reinstalled and the QR (or thru-axle) firmly clamped — firm palm pressure on the lever should leave a clear imprint on your palm when opened — spin slowly and watch the gap between tire and fork, fender, or fender strut. Any contact there is your scrape.

Do not ride, walk or take the train to a shop, if you find any of these:

- Visible rotor bend (the gap to a pad visibly closes at one spot while spinning).
- Pad worn to metal, pad loose in its slot, or pad spring missing/bent and contacting the rotor or rim.
- Any crack anywhere: rim, spoke, hub flange, fork leg, brake mount, or dropout.
- Tire bulge, cut exposing casing threads, or embedded debris you cannot flick out with a fingernail.
- Hub that grinds, catches, or has side-to-side play you can feel by hand.
- Any spoke that pings loose, flexes under finger pressure, or visibly moves.
- Wheel wobble you can see at the rim without a gauge (lateral runout you notice by eye).
- Brake lever bottoms out against the bar with little resistance, or any wet film near a hydraulic line or caliper.
- Heat, smell of burning, or any smoke.
- QR or thru-axle that will not hold firm after a clean re-clamp.

If the noise traces to a single pad kissing the rotor and clears when you gently flex the caliper body sideways (or, on rim brakes, releases cleanly off the rim), it is most likely pad rub — acceptable to ride gently to a shop, not acceptable to leave for next time. Any other once-per-revolution sound means the wheel or brake needs a truing stand, proper pad alignment, or parts before the next ride, not on this one.

Overcount confirmed: 50 unique IDs vs 56 HTTP rows = 6 retries. Sample clean otherwise (no auth/tenant-isolation/exclusion/read-only concerns), so this is the only signal to act on.

Root cause is row-grain vs request-grain. The query treats HTTP response rows as explanation requests, but each retry reuses the same `explanation_request_id`, so retries inflate the count by one per retried ID. The fact that attempt rows keep separate timestamps and outcomes means dedup is straightforward — ID is the stable key.

Fix shape depends on what the metric is contracted to mean:

  COUNT(DISTINCT explanation_request_id)        -> 50. Cleanest match for "explanation requests served/authorized."
  First-attempt semantics (MIN(timestamp) per ID) -> if you also need one outcome per request; earliest attempt's outcome.
  Last-attempt semantics  (MAX(timestamp) per ID) -> if final outcome is what matters (a retry can succeed where the first failed).

Recommendation: distinct-ID count for the headline explanation-request number; keep row-grain for attempt-level metrics (latency, error rate). Document the dedup rule next to the query so the next person doesn't re-introduce the overcount.

The defect

Logical requests and attempts are two different things, but the current accounting collapses them into one counter — typically `requests_total` is incremented on every dispatch (including retries, timeouts that re-fire, and idempotent replays). The consequences:

  - Logical volume is inflated. A single user action that retries 3× counts as 3 requests, so dashboards over-report load and rate limits fire on phantom traffic.
  - Success rate is wrong in two directions at once. Per-attempt success looks artificially low (network blips look like user failures), while per-logical-request success is not measurable at all because the denominator is attempts.
  - Authorization is conflated. The dedupe key has to come from an authorized request identity (the caller's stable ID for this logical operation), not from a transport-level correlation ID — otherwise a retry with a fresh transport ID bypasses dedupe, and a different caller's reuse of the same transport ID merges unrelated logical requests.
  - Audit trail gaps. If attempts are dropped to "fix" the count, retry storms and timeout loops become invisible post-hoc; if duplicates are kept, the audit log becomes unreliable for incident reconstruction.

The correction (concise)

Define two distinct counters, both labeled by the same `request_id` (stable, authorized, caller-supplied or gateway-issued at authorization time — not regenerated per attempt):

  1. `logical_request_total{request_id, tenant, route, outcome}` — incremented exactly once per authorized logical request, after dedupe on `request_id` within a dedupe window (recommend 24h, sliding). Outcome is the terminal result of the logical request: `success | client_error | server_error | timeout | canceled`.
  2. `attempt_total{request_id, tenant, route, attempt_number, outcome}` — incremented on every dispatch, including retries. Carries `attempt_number` so retry storms are visible.

Rules:

  - Dedup happens at the authorized boundary, before attempt accounting. The first observation of a `request_id` within the window creates the logical record; subsequent observations with the same `request_id` and same `(route, payload-hash)` are merged into the existing logical request and only contribute to `attempt_total`.
  - If a retry arrives with the same `request_id` but a divergent payload hash, that is treated as a new logical request sharing the ID and flagged (`payload_hash_mismatch=true`) — not silently merged, not silently double-counted.
  - The audit log records every attempt with `request_id`, `attempt_number`, `timestamp`, `outcome`, and the `logical_request_id` it rolled up to. Attempts are never dropped from the audit trail.
  - SLOs compute against `logical_request_total`. Rate limits and capacity alerts compute against `attempt_total`. Retry/backoff health alerts compute against `attempt_total / logical_request_total` (the retry ratio).

Regression-test requirement

The fix ships with tests that fail on the current code and must pass on the corrected code. Each test asserts on both counters independently:

  1. Single logical request, N retries → `logical_request_total` increases by exactly 1; `attempt_total` increases by exactly N; `attempt_total / logical_request_total` for that route = N.
  2. N distinct logical requests, each with 1 attempt → both counters increase by exactly N; retry ratio = 1.
  3. Retry storm (one logical request, 50 attempts within 1s) → logical counter +1; attempt counter +50; retry-ratio alert fires; no rate-limit false positive on the logical-request panel.
  4. Divergent payload hash on same `request_id` → logical counter +2 (second carries `payload_hash_mismatch=true`); attempt counter includes both dispatches; audit log records the mismatch.
  5. Replay after dedupe window expires (same `request_id`, 25h later) → treated as new logical request; both counters increment; audit log notes the late replay.
  6. Authorization rejection at the gateway (no `request_id` ever issued) → no entry in either counter; appears only in `auth_reject_total` — confirms dedupe does not leak into pre-auth traffic.
  7. Concurrent in-flight retries for the same `request_id` → exactly one logical record created under contention (test with 100 concurrent dispatches sharing one ID; assert logical counter = 1, attempt counter = 100, no duplicate logical rows).
  8. SLO recomputation check: feeding the corrected counters into the existing SLO eval must change the success-rate number for any route with non-zero retry traffic — proves the fix is actually moving the metric the SLO is supposed to measure.

Tests 3, 4, 7, and 8 are the load-bearing ones — 1/2/5/6 are guards against the most likely "fix" that just renames a counter.

Diagnosis

Single-point pad contact with a laterally true wheel that does not respond to centering the quick release is consistent with brake caliper/pad misalignment, not a wheel or hub issue. The rim is not wobbling toward the pad; the pad (or caliper) is sitting a hair too close to the rim at one rotational point, usually from an off-angle pad face, unequal pad-spring tension, or a caliper that has drifted off-center. None of what you described indicates that finding.

Short cautious ride

Yes, compatible with a short cautious ride given what you have reported. The contact is light and intermittent, no heat on lift, braking is firm, no visible pad damage, wheel is laterally true and free-spinning. The actual risks of riding it like this are noise and accelerated pad/rim wear at the contact point, not loss of control. Caveats:

  - Keep it short and low-speed; avoid leaning hard on the front brake.
  - Re-check immediately after: lever firmness unchanged, no new rubbing, no warmth at the caliper or rim, no change in tracking.
  - Address it before any longer ride, descent, wet roads, or higher-speed riding.

Findings that would make it unsafe to ride

Do not ride if any of the following is true. Each one is a standalone reason, not a combination.

  - Pad material missing, cracked, delaminated, or metal backing showing through; pad contacting the tire sidewall instead of the rim.
  - A groove on the braking surface you can catch a fingernail in, or any visible rim dent/crack at or near the scrape point.
  - Lever pulls to the bar, feels spongy, or requires much more hand force than usual (cable stretch, contamination, or pad material effectively gone).
  - Brake pads contaminated with oil, grease, chain lube, or tire sealant; this often looks clean but drastically reduces friction and won't show as visible pad damage.
  - Wheel does not spin freely when lifted — any binding, gritty feel, or rubbing that persists all the way around (not just at the one point).
  - Clicking, popping, or roughness from the hub when spun, or any lateral play at the axle.
  - Quick release not fully clamped under firm hand force, or any looseness at the dropouts / axle seating.
  - Caliper, pad, or mounting bolt shifts when you squeeze and release the lever.
  - Visible spoke damage, loose spokes, or rim hop when spun slowly.
  - Heat at the caliper, pad, or rim after even a short roll; this means real dragging under load, not just a cosmetic touch.
  - Fork flex, steering wobble, or any change in tracking under braking.

What a shop would do (for context, in case you decide not to DIY)

The standard non-destructive fix is a caliper centering adjustment (the conical bolt on most sidepull calipers, or a pad-spring bend) plus a pad re-seat with a small amount of toe-in. Typical time is 10-20 minutes, often free or minimal cost with a tune-up. None of that requires loosening the wheel, the cable, or the brake mount. If you want to attempt it yourself, the safest first move is the caliper centering screw if yours has one — squeeze the lever, tighten the screw a quarter turn at a time, release, and re-check the gap on both sides. If you'd rather not touch it, a shop visit is reasonable insurance but not required before a short cautious ride given your current findings.

Short version: block this change. The dedup_key derivation is unsafe by construction, and the fixture is documenting the bug, not catching it.

What the change does
  request_id[:32] collapses all requests that share the same 32-char prefix into one dedup entry. The key space is whatever the upstream chooses to put in the first 32 characters of request_id, which on most ingest flows (timestamped UUIDs, ULID-style, or anything with a tenant/shard prefix) is far smaller than 128 bits and is correlated across requests.

What the fixture shows
  Two distinct, valid request_ids that differ only after char 32. The fixture you described is exactly the failure mode: 1,200 - 800 = 400 points silently dropped, and the client gets a success that refers to data it never sent. From the client side this looks like a successful 800-point ingest that doesn't match what they submitted — which is the worst shape of correctness bug, because nothing logs an error.

Why this is not a "tight fixture, working as designed" case
  Idempotency on a content-bearing ingest means: same logical write, return the prior outcome. Here the bodies differ, so this is two different writes. Returning the prior outcome for the second one is data loss, not idempotency. If the design intent was "merge by prefix," that's a different feature and it needs a different name and explicit semantics, not a dedup_key truncation.

Concrete things to flag in review
  - The dedup_key must be derived from the full request_id (or a hash of it), not a truncated prefix. A SHA-256 of the full request_id is a fine fixed-size key if storage size is the motivation behind [:32].

RECOMMENDATION — FROZEN-SNAPSHOT + AMENDMENT-TAIL MODEL

For North Pier's quarterly DS health review, treat the quarter-end publish as an immutable v1 snapshot and every post-close correction as a versioned amendment (v1.1, v1.2, ...) attached to the original deduped observation. The dedup key — (team, release_candidate, canonical_package_version) — defines a stable observation identity. Amendments edit field values on that identity; they never create a new observation, so they cannot inflate adoption or failure counts for the frozen quarter.

TWO LAYERS, ONE IDENTITY

  Layer 1 — Frozen snapshot (v1, v2, ...):
    - Generated at quarter-close from a deterministic build of the observation store.
    - Stored as read-only artifacts with a content hash (SHA-256 over the serialized observations + aggregate rollups).
    - The published review cites the hash; the hash is the canonical reference for "what the quarter said."
    - Never rewritten. If you need a different view of the quarter, you publish a new version (a v1.x amendment rollup, or — for a structural change — the next quarter's v2).

  Layer 2 — Living observation store:
    - One row per (team, release_candidate, canonical_package_version) per quarter, keyed by a stable observation_id (hash of those fields + quarter_id).
    - Each row carries: current_field_values (mutable), field_value_history (append-only), amendment_log (append-only).
    - Recomputes aggregates on demand. Every aggregate answer is labeled "as of <timestamp> from snapshot v1" or "as of <timestamp> with amendments v1.x applied" — never ambiguous.

VERSIONING RULES (BOUNDED)

  - v1 = quarter-close snapshot. Immutable.
  - v1.1, v1.2, ... = amendment batches. Each has its own hash and is published as an addendum to v1, not a replacement.
  - v2 = next quarter's snapshot. Re-versioning inside a closed quarter is not allowed; only amendment tails.
  - Amendment batches edit field values of existing observations only. They never change the observation set, the dedup key, or the quarter boundary.
  - Codify a soft cap on amendment batches per quarter up front (e.g., 5). Above the cap, the team must either decline the correction or trigger a structural re-publish with a new hash.

AMENDMENT RECORD SCHEMA (MINIMUM FIELDS)

  - amendment_id (ULID/UUID, monotonic)
  - target_snapshot_version (always v1 for the closed quarter)
  - target_observation_id (the stable dedup-key hash)
  - field_corrected (e.g., adoption_count, failure_count, attribution)
  - prior_value, corrected_value
  - correction_received_at (UTC, ISO 8601)
  - correction_source (system + reporter + ticket/ref)
  - reason (categorical + free text: ingestion bug, late-reported adoption, misattribution, etc.)
  - applied_at, applied_by
  - resulting_snapshot_version (v1.1, v1.2, ...)
  - resulting_content_hash

HOW DEDUP HOLDS UNDER AMENDMENTS

  The dedup key never changes. An amendment that says "this team actually adopted 1.4.0, not 1.3.7" is NOT a value edit on the 1.3.7 observation; it is a re-attribution. Treat re-attributions as a higher-bar, two-step operation: close the misattributed observation with reason "source misattribution, see amendment #N" (preserved in v1 with its original value), and open a new observation under the correct canonical_package_version starting at v1.1. Never silently rewrite the canonical_package_version — it breaks downstream tooling keyed on it.

HOW AGGREGATES BEHAVE

  - The published aggregates in v1 are the historical record; they are never recomputed in v1.
  - "Current best-known" aggregates are computed live from the observation store and labeled with the amendment version they reflect (e.g., "as of v1.3, 2025-08-12").
  - Dashboards and downstream consumers must declare which version they read. Default for backward compatibility: read v1. New analyses opt in to v1.x explicitly.
  - Adoption/failure counts are never summed across an amendment boundary as if they were independent observations; they are the same observation with a new field value.

PROCESS

  1. Quarter closes → run deterministic build → freeze v1 → record content hash → publish review citing the hash.
  2. Correction arrives → file as an amendment ticket; require source (system, reporter, ticket) and the specific observation it touches.
  3. Lightweight validation: confirm the correction targets an existing observation, that the proposed change does not silently change the dedup key, and that the reason matches a predefined category.
  4. Apply amendment → mutate current_field_values, append to field_value_history and amendment_log, compute new content hash, publish as v1.x addendum.
  5. Notify stakeholders that the published review has been amended; link the addendum.
  6. Original v1 remains downloadable, hash-verifiable, and citable.

EDGE CASES TO PRE-DECIDE BEFORE THE FIRST QUARTER ENDS

  - Re-attribution vs. value edit: codified above as a two-step close+open, never a silent edit.
  - Late-reported new team adoption in the closed quarter: do not add as a new observation. Pick one rule — either drop from the closed quarter's adoption count (with the amendment log noting the late report) or carry as a back-dated observation in the NEXT quarter. Write the rule down.
  - Amendment window: define how long after quarter-close amendments count as in-quarter vs. next-quarter backfill. A common split: 2 weeks in-quarter; after that it is a backfill into the next quarter.
  - Who can apply amendments: at least two sets of eyes, or a single approver with the system logging the actor and timestamp on every change.
  - Retention: keep v1 and every v1.x addendum (and their hashes) for at least as long as the quarter's review is referenced — typically several years.

WHY THIS MEETS ANYA'S CONSTRAINTS

  - Frozen quarter is preserved: v1 hash and artifact are immutable; cited as the canonical record.
  - Correction is not lost: it lives in the amendment log with full provenance and is queryable from any current value back to the original v1 observation.
  - No double-counting: the dedup key is stable; amendments edit, never insert; aggregates are versioned so consumers cannot accidentally sum v1 and v1.x as if they were independent observations.
  - Auditability: every field change carries prior_value, corrected_value, timestamp, source, reason, actor, and resulting hash.

This shape scales to subsequent quarters cleanly: each quarter is a new v2/v3/... snapshot with its own amendment tail, and the same machinery applies without re-design.
