KEY GROUND RULES
- Bedroom unit stays OFF. Don't run it even briefly until the drain-channel assembly is installed — running it without that part can worsen the leak or damage.
- Use the working AC (presumably living room) as the cool zone.
- Strategy: cool the apartment overnight when outdoor air is cooler, then hold that cool through the day.

APARTMENT — KEEPING IT COOL

Daytime (charge held + heat blocked):
- Close blinds/curtains on south- and west-facing windows; reflective/light-colored backing helps most.
- Keep windows and exterior doors shut during the day.
- Run the working AC at a steady temp (don't oscillate on/off — steady is more efficient).
- Use a fan to circulate inside the AC room; one fan moving air across the room beats a still room every time.
- If you have a box fan, point it OUT a window on the leeward side overnight to pull cooler air through. During the day, point a fan IN at floor level so cool air pools low.
- No oven, stove, or toaster oven during peak heat — microwave, slow-cooker, no-cook meals only. Run the dishwasher overnight.
- LED lights only during the day. Skip vacuuming, heavy laundry, anything that generates heat and humidity.
- Keep interior doors open so the AC reaches all rooms; close off only rooms you don't need.

Overnight (recharge the apartment):
- Open windows only when outdoor temp has fallen below indoor temp (typically after sunset).
- Run the working AC through the night to "charge" walls, floors, and furniture with cool.
- Close windows before sunrise to trap the cool.

SLEEP SETUP

- Sleep in the room with the working AC. If you're on a night-shift block, that means daytime sleep — pre-cool the room 1–2 hours before bed.
- Cooling aids (stack a couple):
  - Damp cotton sheet over legs (lightly wrung, not dripping).
  - Ice-water bottle in a pillowcase at the feet or behind the neck; rotate.
  - Cooling mattress pad or chill pillow if you have one.
  - Loose cotton or minimal sleepwear.
- Glass of water + electrolytes on the nightstand.
- If the bedroom is needed for storage/storage-of-stuff, leave the door open and a fan pulling air in from the AC room.

HUMAN HYDRATION & HEALTH

- Drink on a schedule, not on thirst: roughly 1 cup per waking hour during the advisory; more if sweating.
- Add electrolytes (tablets or Pedialyte). Plain water alone during heavy sweating dilutes sodium.
- Cut caffeine and alcohol — both dehydrating and alcohol disrupts temperature regulation.

Heat exhaustion (warning): heavy sweating, weakness, cold/clammy skin, fast weak pulse, nausea, dizziness.
  → Stop activity, move to the cool room, wet cloths + fan on neck/underarms, sip water. Resolve in 30 min = OK. If it doesn't, call a doctor.

Heat stroke (EMERGENCY — 911): skin hot and dry or very damp, body temp 103°F+, confusion, slurred speech, loss of consciousness, fast strong pulse.
  → Call 911, then cool with ice water and cold packs on neck, underarms, groin while waiting.

KIBO — KEEPING HIM SAFE

Indoor setup:
- Cool spot = bathroom tile, a cooling mat, or a damp towel in the shade of the AC room.
- Multiple water bowls; refresh with ice cubes 2–3× a day.
- Hydration treats: frozen Kong, ice cubes, wet food.
- Keep him in the AC room during peak afternoon heat (roughly noon–6 PM).

Walk timing (the big lever):
- EARLY walk: before ~8 AM, before pavement heats. In 90°F+ sun, asphalt can hit 140°F+ even when air is 90°F.
- LATE walk: after ~9 PM, once pavement has radiated its heat back out.
- 5-second test every time: back of hand flat to pavement for 5 seconds. If you can't hold it, his paws can't either.
- Stick to grass, dirt, and shaded Prospect Park paths; avoid full-sun asphalt.
- Cut duration — short sniff walks, not power walks. No fetch or ball-chasing in this window.
- Skip the truck-intersection practice in heat; default to the quiet loop. Front-clip harness + short leash still apply.
- Mid-walk cooling: pause in shade, offer water, wet his belly and paw pads if he's panting hard.

Dog heat-stress signs (EMERGENCY vet if seen):
- Heavy panting that doesn't ease within a minute of stopping
- Thick or stringy drool
- Bright red gums or tongue
- Glazed eyes, stumbling, vomiting, collapse
- Action: wet him with COOL (not ice-cold) water on belly, paws, armpits, groin; get to the nearest emergency vet immediately; call ahead.

THRESHOLDS — LEAVE THE APARTMENT

Head somewhere cooler (NYC opens cooling centers during advisories — NYC.gov/cooling or 311; libraries and most malls are also AC) if:
- Indoor temp in the AC room stays above 82°F for several hours and won't come down.
- You, Devika, or Kibo show heat-stress signs that don't ease within 30 minutes of active cooling.
- Kibo is panting hard even while at rest in the coolest room.

Don't leave Kibo in the car — even a few minutes in 90°F+ is lethal.

THRESHOLDS — SEEK URGENT HELP

- Human: any heat-stroke sign, chest pain, fainting, confusion, vomiting that won't stop, or measured temp 103°F+ → 911.
- Kibo: any of the emergency signs above (especially collapse, vomiting, or bright red gums) → emergency vet, call ahead.

WATCH FOR
- NWS updates on the advisory — it can be upgraded or extended. If a higher heat-index warning (105°F+) gets issued, the "leave the apartment" thresholds tighten and a cooling center becomes the safer call.
- Kibo's paws: check pads nightly this week for cracks or tenderness from the heat.

Wes's draft pairs the wrong classification + recovery with the negative-age signal for the June 11 case. What actually happened — current generation, no route/config change, host-clock jump, recovery via deploy-pipeline instance replacement — is a clock-skew event, not a route-generation mismatch, and the fix is replace-instance, not roll-back-config.

Worth noting on the metric itself: if route_snapshot_age_seconds is computed as (now − snapshot_ts) on the receiving host, a negative value can only come from a clock offset between emitter and receiver, not from a stale local generation. If it's defined the other way (expected_age − actual_age), the negative could instead mean a stale snapshot. Either way, the runbook should disambiguate on host-clock trend and generation parity before picking a recovery action — the current draft skips that and jumps straight to "route-generation mismatch → roll back config," which is what makes it wrong for June 11.

Proposed replacement for the runbook / doc line:

  If route_snapshot_age_seconds is negative:
    1. Check the instance's host-clock trend (NTP offset, last sync, any >60s
       jumps in the last 10 min). If a host-clock jump is observed AND the
       instance is on the current generation with no recent route/config
       change, classify as host-clock skew and replace the instance via
       deploy pipeline. Do not roll back configuration.
    2. If the host clock is stable AND the instance is on an older generation
       than its peers, classify as a route-generation mismatch and roll back
       active configuration to the previous known-good generation.

Good move removing the stinger with a scraping motion (pinching or tweezers can squeeze residual venom from the sac). What you're describing — a pink, mildly swollen spot with full weight-bearing and no systemic signs — is a localized sting reaction, not anaphylaxis, right now. The risk window is the next 6–24 hours for any delayed reaction, and the next 1–3 days for the local site.

Immediate home care

  Cleaning. The rinse you did is fine. If you want, a gentle wash with mild dog-safe soap (or just lukewarm water) once more today is enough. Pat dry, don't rub.

  Cold compress. Wrap a bag of frozen peas or ice cubes in a thin towel — never apply ice directly to the pad. Hold on the swollen spot for 5–10 minutes at a time, then off for at least 10 minutes. You can repeat a few times today. Purpose: reduce swelling and the throbbing/itchy ache. If Kibo fusses or the skin looks blanched or mottled when you lift the compress, stop and give him a longer break.

  Prevent licking. This matters more than it sounds. A paw he keeps fussing at can become a lick granuloma or a secondary bacterial infection in 24–48 hours. Options:
    - A sock or lightweight breathable dog bootie taped above the dewclaw (not tight around the leg)
    - A cone/e-collar if he'll tolerate it
    - Distraction + a short lead inside so he can't sneak a lick

  Activity limits for the next 24 hours.
    - Shorter walks only — just potty trips, on flat ground, not hot pavement (the pad is already tender)
    - No running, jumping on/off furniture, stairs, or rough play
    - Skip the truck-intersection and skateboard-exposed routes until the paw is back to normal — startles plus a sore paw is a bad combination
    - Front-clip harness + short leash already gives you good control, which is helpful here

What to avoid giving him

  Human pain or anti-inflammatory meds. All of these are problematic in dogs and several are toxic:
    - Ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) — toxic, GI ulceration and kidney injury
    - Naproxen (Aleve) — toxic
    - Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — toxic to dogs (liver damage, red-blood-cell injury); do NOT use even though it's "not an NSAID"
    - Aspirin — can be given in some situations but interacts with any future vet treatment and isn't appropriate without vet dosing
    - Any leftover dog NSAID you might have (carprofen, meloxicam, etc.) — only on a vet's instruction for this specific case

  Topicals he can lick off.
    - Neosporin / triple-antibiotic ointment — generally low-risk in tiny amounts, but dogs lick it and ingestion can cause GI upset; if you use any, cover with a sock
    - Hydrocortisone cream — ingestion causes problems and steroid absorption on an open/licked area is unpredictable
    - Lidocaine / "pain-relief" gels — not dosed for dogs
    - Essential oils, tea tree, or Benadryl cream

  Oral diphenhydramine (Benadryl) without vet dosing. The canine dose is weight-based (roughly 1 mg/lb), and giving it on your own can both under-dose and mask early signs of a real allergic reaction (making it harder to tell if something is brewing). If a vet recommends it for Kibo specifically, fine — but don't start it on your own.

  Heat on the site for the first 24 hours. Cold is right early; heat can worsen swelling.

  Squeezing, massaging, or trying to "drain" the spot. It isn't an abscess yet; let it settle.

Signs that mean urgent veterinary care

  Treat any of these as "go now" rather than "watch and wait":

    Allergic / anaphylactic signs (these can come on within minutes or up to several hours later):
      - Facial swelling — muzzle, eyelids, lips, ear flaps
      - Hives or raised welts anywhere on the body (often the belly, groin, or armpits)
      - Sudden vomiting or diarrhea
      - Restlessness, agitation, or sudden withdrawn/listless behavior
      - Difficulty breathing, exaggerated or noisy panting, gums that look pale, blue, or very red
      - Weakness, wobbliness, collapse
      - Trembling or shaking that's not just cold/excited
      - Multiple stings anywhere on the body (much higher venom load)

    Worsening local injury / secondary infection (worry if these develop over 24–72 hours):
      - Swelling that expands beyond the original spot, or a firm, hot, painful swelling
      - Pus, crusting, or an open wound
      - Limping that gets worse instead of better after 24–48 hours, or Kibo refusing to bear weight
      - Repeated, obsessive licking or chewing at the paw despite a sock/cone
      - Fever-ish signs: warm ears, low energy, loss of appetite for more than a day
      - Any retained foreign body suspicion — if you only saw "a small visible stinger" and a fragment might still be in the pad (often shows as a tiny dark dot with ongoing drainage), get it looked at

    The combination to take most seriously is facial swelling + vomiting, or any breathing change, or sudden collapse — those can move fast and an ER visit is appropriate even if it's middle of the night.

A practical monitoring schedule

    Next 2 hours: behavior, breathing, gums (should be pink and moist), and any new swelling on the face or body. This is the highest-risk window for anaphylaxis.
    Tonight and tomorrow morning: appetite, energy, and the paw itself.
    48 hours: paw swelling and weight-bearing should be clearly trending better. If it's flat, that's when I'd call the vet to be safe.
    7 days: full resolution typical. If the pad still looks pink or he's intermittently licking it past a week, a vet check is reasonable.

If you'd like, I can also draft a short note in your profile (Kibo's sting date, location, and that he had a localized-only reaction) so future incidents have context — useful if he ever gets stung again and you're trying to spot a pattern. Just say the word.

JULY 4 PREVENTIVE PLAN — KIBO
=============================

You noted he currently has no distress, breathing problem, vomiting, collapse, or escape attempt, so this is a wellness/prevention day, not an emergency response. Keep your regular vet's number and the nearest 24h emergency clinic's address/phone visible all evening. ASPCA Animal Poison Control: 888-426-4435 (fee may apply) for any ingestion question.


1. EARLIER LONG WALK
--------------------
- Aim for late morning to early afternoon (e.g., 11 AM – 2 PM) — well before late-afternoon intermittent bangs start in NYC neighborhoods.
- Use his usual front-clip harness (he's comfortable in it) with a standard 4–6 ft leash. Skip the long line today so you can redirect him instantly if a bang catches him off guard.
- Pick the quiet, predictable Prospect Park loop you'd default to anyway. Avoid skateboards/skates since he startles at them.
- Aim ~15–30 min longer than a normal walk — brisk enough to take the edge off, not strenuous. No off-leash, no dog parks.
- Bring a collapsible bowl and water if it's warm.
- If he plants or pulls toward home early, take the short way back. Don't push it.


2. WINDOWS AND CURTAINS
-----------------------
- Close all windows by mid-to-late afternoon, before intermittent bangs begin.
- Draw curtains/blinds fully closed in every room he has access to — both for sound dampening and to block flashes.
- Block window perches: don't let him station on the sill watching flashes; remove or block furniture he jumps on near windows.
- Run a fan, white-noise machine, or low-volume TV/radio in his main rooms. Steady ambient sound softens sharp bangs.
- Prefer rooms with double-pane or storm windows today if you have them.
- No balcony time after late afternoon.


3. QUIET INTERIOR RESTING AREA
------------------------------
- Pick one room with no exterior wall if possible — interior bedroom, hallway nook, large closet, or bathroom.
- Set up his bed or crate with a familiar blanket and an unwashed t-shirt of yours or Devika's (scent anchors).
- Keep water available in the room.
- Background noise (fan or low music) running continuously.
- Door closed, baby gate, or exercise pen so he can't pace the apartment and bark at hallway sounds.
- If he's crate-trained, the covered crate is often the best den today — dark and dampened.
- Don't drag him there. Let him explore it on his own this afternoon; drop treats so he associates it positively.
- Rotate who is with him through the evening — your presence is the most reliable calmer.


4. FOOD AND BATHROOM TIMING
---------------------------
- Feed his normal meal at his normal time. No diet changes today.
- A small, easy-to-digest snack a couple hours before his final outing is fine if he gets hungry; nothing rich or new.
- Pick up the water bowl ~2 hours before the expected peak (often 9–11 PM in NYC neighborhoods) so he doesn't need a midnight bathroom break into the bangs. Refill in the morning.
- Don't restrict water aggressively — just shift the timing.
- Final bathroom outing: 30–60 min before bangs are expected to intensify. Short, on-leash, front-clip harness, quiet route. Keep it calm.
- Don't walk him again late at night — even if he asks — until bangs have quieted for the night.


5. HUMAN MEDICATIONS — DO NOT IMPROVISE
---------------------------------------
I'm not a vet and won't dose anything. If your vet has previously prescribed a noise-aversion med (trazodone, gabapentin, Sileo/dexmedetomidine gel, alprazolam, clomipramine), use it exactly as directed. Do not increase, redose early, or substitute.

Never improvise with these:
- Ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) — toxic; GI bleeding, kidney damage.
- Naproxen (Aleve) — same risks, longer duration, more dangerous.
- Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — toxic; liver and red blood cell damage.
- Aspirin — only with explicit vet guidance; wrong dose = GI bleed.
- Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — vet dosing only. Overdose = agitation, seizures, or dangerous sedation. Many formulations contain pseudoephedrine, which is toxic.
- Melatonin — vet guidance only; some formulations contain xylitol (toxic).
- Alcohol in any form — toxic.
- THC/CBD products — unpredictable dosing; severe sedation or agitation.
- "Calming" essential oil diffusers — many are toxic to dogs, especially concentrated.
- Any new supplement, calming chew, or CBD he hasn't had before — don't debut it today.

If he gets into anything by accident, call your vet or ASPCA Animal Poison Control (888-426-4435) right away. Don't wait for symptoms.


6. URGENT VETERINARY SIGNS
--------------------------
None of these are present now. Watch through the evening and overnight for:

Respiratory / cardiovascular:
- Difficulty breathing, exaggerated rib movement, blue/purple/white or pale gums, open-mouth breathing while at rest.
- Collapse, weakness, inability to stand or walk, sudden stumbling.
- Resting heart rate that feels very fast or very irregular.

Gastrointestinal:
- Repeated vomiting, especially with blood.
- Diarrhea with blood or black/tarry stool.
- Hard, swollen, painful abdomen (possible bloat).
- Repeated retching producing nothing.

Neurological:
- Any seizure — loss of consciousness with paddling or convulsions.
- Trembling that doesn't stop and won't resolve with calm.
- Sudden disorientation, head pressing.

Other urgent signs:
- Excessive drooling + panting + restlessness (pain or heat stress).
- Heat stroke signs: heavy panting, bright red gums, drooling, vomiting, collapse. Heat + stress = real risk today.
- Bleeding that doesn't stop within a few minutes.
- Suspected ingestion of anything toxic.
- Escape attempt that produced an injury (cut paw, broken nail, laceration).
- No water intake for 12+ hours with dehydration signs (skin tenting, sticky gums).
- Unresponsive, won't recognize you.

Psychological signs that warrant a vet call (not always ER):
- Severe unrelenting panic that doesn't ease with reassurance, crate, or quiet.
- Self-injury — licking or biting one spot raw.

When in doubt, call. Vets prefer a "false alarm" call to a late ER visit.

Here is the analysis and the drafted blocking comment.

——————————————————————————————————
1. Analysis of the missed-reload defect
——————————————————————————————————

The class of bug you're describing has a familiar shape. The loader is almost certainly doing one of these:

  a. In-place rewrite of the live config file (e.g. open(path, "w") + write). A writer that truncates and rewrites in place creates a window where the file is empty/partial on disk; a reader polling mtime or inotify can fire while the file is mid-rewrite and either error out (silently swallowed → no reload) or read a half-written config. The "missed reload" symptom is the reader seeing no change and the writer thinking it succeeded.

  b. Rename-style atomic swap (write temp + os.Rename / rename(2)) on top of a watcher that only watches the *final* path. The atomic guarantee only holds on POSIX when temp and target are on the same filesystem and the rename target is a single inode. If the loader is watching the *directory* with IN_MOVED_TO, fine — but if it's watching the file by inode/inotify watch descriptor, an IN_DELETE_SELF on the temp is normal and the *new* inode is the live config, which is exactly what the watcher must pick up. Many implementations get this subtly wrong (e.g. they key cache by path and never re-resolve the inode).

  c. Content-equal short-circuit. The reload path checks "did the content change?" before publishing a new generation, and uses a fast hash or a string compare that doesn't normalize whitespace/comments. Same on-disk bytes → "no change" → loader returns success without publishing. The caller thinks they reloaded; nothing happened. This is the most insidious variant because every layer above the loader reports success.

  d. Missing file-create handling. The very first time the config appears on a fresh host, the file doesn't exist yet; many loaders only watch for inotify IN_MODIFY / IN_CLOSE_WRITE and never see IN_CREATE. The operator drops the file in place, the loader never picks it up, and the only signal is "serving defaults forever."

The unifying failure: the reload pipeline has no observable ground truth. There is no signal that distinguishes "reload attempted and produced a new validated generation" from "reload attempted but the new generation was rejected and the old one is still live." Stale serving is silent.

What the fix has to do, in concrete terms:

  - Treat create (IN_CREATE / first-seen path) the same as modify. A missing-then-present transition is a reload trigger.
  - Treat rename (IN_MOVED_FROM + IN_MOVED_TO into the watched directory) the same as modify. Editors and deploys that write-temp-then-rename must be observable.
  - Detection must be content-based, not just event-based. Compute a stable hash of the parsed/normalized config (not the raw bytes if the writer tolerates reformatting) and only suppress publish when the hash matches the current generation.
  - The publish step must be transactional: validate the new generation fully *before* swapping the pointer that readers see, and either commit (new generation live) or fail loudly (old generation still live, with a `failed_reload` signal + the reason). The current code appears to leak the intermediate state, which is how you end up serving a half-validated config or the previous generation without anyone noticing.
  - Every reload attempt must produce one of: published(new_generation=N) | failed_reload(reason=…). No silent success.

The regressions you need to demand:

  R1. Create-on-empty: start the loader with the config file absent, drop it in, assert the new generation is live (no restart).
  R2. Rename-into-place: write a sibling file and atomically rename it over the live path; assert the new generation is live and the watcher fired exactly once.
  R3. Content-equal no-op: write bytes that hash-equal the current config; assert no spurious publish, no version bump, no spurious failed_reload.
  R4. Content-changed-but-malformed: write a syntactically invalid file (rename-into-place, so it's atomic); assert the old generation is *still* live, the swap was rejected, and a failed_reload signal was emitted with the parse error.
  R5. Mid-write crash: kill the writer between write-to-temp and rename; assert the live config is untouched (either the previous generation or a fresh empty-state default, but never half-written) and the loader emits failed_reload, not silent success.
  R6. Generation monotonicity: across a sequence of (create, modify, rename, modify, equal-content), the served generation must be strictly non-decreasing, never skip a number, and the latest served must match the latest successfully published.

The blocking review turns on (1)–(3) above plus regressions R1–R6. Anything less leaves the silent-stale-config failure mode in place.

THE DEFECT

The system tracks queue depth (or work-in-progress) through two views that should
agree: an authoritative view — the actual contents of the queue, the lease
records, the ownership map, whatever the system's source of truth is — and a
telemetry view, derived from emitted events: enqueued, dequeued, acked, etc.

A single-decrement semantics says: every terminal event for a logical item
(ack, completion, dead-letter, abandonment) produces exactly one unit of removal
in the authoritative view, and exactly one matching decrement in the telemetry
view, and these are correlated 1:1.

The double-decrement defect is the loss of that 1:1 correlation. Terminal
events flow through more than one path that the telemetry pipeline listens to
and treats as independent decrements. Common shapes:

  - The producer emits a "I committed the removal" signal AND the consumer
    emits an "I observed completion" signal; the pipeline counts both, so the
    counter falls twice per item.

  - A retry/requeue path emits a terminal event for a half-completed item and
    then a second terminal event when the requeued work finally drains. The
    item only existed once in authoritative state; telemetry counted two exits.

  - A crash or rollback path causes the same logical item to be re-claimed and
    re-terminated by a different actor, and that second termination is counted
    as if it were a fresh item's exit.

  - A lease-handoff or ownership-transfer emits terminal-shaped events from
    both the old owner (on disconnect) and the new owner (on claim), and both
    decrement.

Why it matters: dashboards, alerts, saturation logic, the legacy-aggregator
back-pressure, and the rollup queue-age calculations all consume the telemetry
view. Once the telemetry view under-counts exits, the system appears healthier
than it is (work silently accumulating), and once it over-counts, alerts trip
spuriously. The authoritative view is what really counts for correctness; the
defect's harm is the gap opening between the two.

The defect is hard to catch by inspection because in normal operation each
shape above is rare and small. The signal is statistical: telemetry's
"total removed" diverges from authoritative "total removed" by more than the
in-flight slack, in a direction consistent with the bias introduced above.

EVIDENCE REQUIRED BEFORE THIS PROCEEDS

1. QUEUE-OCCUPANCY EVIDENCE

  The telemetry-derived "items remaining" / queue-depth gauge must agree with
  the authoritative count of items currently in the queue (or owned by
  workers) within the in-flight slack at all sampled times.

  What to demonstrate, end to end:
    - telemetry_removed_total(t) - telemetry_added_total(t0)
        == authoritative_removed(t) - authoritative_added(t0)
        + items-still-in-flight-at(t)
    - Under steady load, sustained burst, sudden drain, and idle (empty queue),
      the residual drift at the moment the system is fully drained must be
      zero, not "small."
    - The gauge derived from telemetry must equal the gauge derived from a
      direct queue-state probe at a sample rate that would expose any
      sustained divergence (i.e., drift that persists longer than one item's
      residence time is real drift, not measurement noise).

  What this catches: silent long-term drift between the two views that
  accumulates with throughput.

2. TERMINAL-ACCOUNTING EVIDENCE

  Every item that is admitted to the system must produce exactly one terminal
  event, observable from both the authoritative and the telemetry views, and
  referenced to the same logical item.

  What to demonstrate:
    - A per-item lifecycle trace from admission through every state it visits
      (claimed, retried, requeued, acked, dead-lettered, abandoned) to final
      exit. Each lifecycle must terminate in exactly one event that both
      views count.
    - In tests that deliberately exercise requeue, processing-timeout, crash-
      mid-process, retry-with-backoff, and dead-letter paths, the count of
      terminal events emitted equals the count of items removed from the
      authoritative state, with no item producing two terminals and no item
      producing zero.
    - The terminal-event stream must be reconcilable against the authoritative
      log: every terminal event has a matching "item removed" record, and
      every "item removed" record has a matching terminal event.

  What this catches: requeue paths and crash-recovery paths that emit
  terminal-shaped signals without a corresponding authoritative removal, or
  vice versa.

3. SINGLE-DECREMENT OWNERSHIP EVIDENCE

  For each terminal event, exactly one actor (worker, consumer process, or
  lease-holder) must be the emitter, and no other actor may emit a terminal
  for the same logical item.

  What to demonstrate:
    - In a multi-actor test where two actors are deliberately raced against
      the same item — overlapping claim attempts, late-arriving claims from
      stale owners, claims issued after lease expiry — exactly one actor's
      claim is honored, exactly one terminal event is emitted, and the others
      are rejected without producing telemetry decrements.
    - The ownership-transfer protocol preserves a clear single-actor property
      across handoff: the old owner's disconnect signal is not a terminal
      event for telemetry, and the new owner's successful claim emits exactly
      one.
    - After a fencing-token or lease-expiry event, any actor holding a stale
      grant cannot produce a telemetry-counted terminal, even if it reaches
      the commit step.

  What this catches: dual-claim races, lease-handoff double-counting,
  fencing-token bypass, and stale-owner terminal emission.

4. END-STATE REGRESSION EVIDENCE

  After every exercised failure scenario, with all work fully flushed and no
  in-flight items remaining, the two views must agree exactly.

  What to demonstrate:
    - For each scenario — normal drain, consumer crash mid-process, consumer
      crash after partial commit, forced restart, rollback, scale-out, scale-
      in, controlled disconnect — run a post-condition: telemetry_remaining
      == authoritative_remaining, telemetry_total_removed ==
      authoritative_total_removed, and every item ever admitted is in one of
      {still present, counted as removed exactly once}.
    - The regression suite runs the scenarios in mixed sequences (not just
      isolated), because some defects only surface when a crash follows a
      partial commit follows a requeue, etc.
    - The post-condition holds at the end of the run regardless of which
      failure path was exercised. The end state is the same state the system
      would be in if all the work had completed normally through the
      single-actor terminal path.

  What this catches: defects that are masked while work is in flight and only
  visible once the system is at rest; defects that compound across multiple
  failure paths.

THRESHOLD FOR PROCEEDING

All four must hold simultaneously and reproducibly across the failure-mode
matrix. Drift bounded by in-flight slack is acceptable during operation; drift
that persists past drain, terminal events that do not reconcile 1:1 against
authoritative removals, multiple actors emitting terminals for the same item,
or end states where the two views disagree, are individually and collectively
blocking. None of this requires choosing an implementation — it specifies
what the system must be able to demonstrate about itself, and leaves open how
it gets there.

HOSTING AT SOUTH SLOPE

Low coordination: Mixed. You're trading cooking labor for setup/planning labor — shopping, a menu that's manageable for your kitchen (probably one oven round + stovetop), plates and glasses for 8. Devika's hours make that a real cost the day of.

Time with your mother: Highest. Casual atmosphere, no host-closing pressure, spills into the living room after. She stays in the visit rather than at the venue. This is the strongest pull for hosting.

Kibo logistics: Most controllable but real. Doorbell = bark, dog underfoot during plating, some guests less comfortable with dogs. Plan: pre-dinner walk on the loop (not the truck routes), crate or back room during serving, gate the bedroom overnight. Doable, but it has to be on the checklist.

Cleanup: Higher. Dishes, counters, vacuum next morning. Spreads over hours rather than disappears.

Weekday possibility: Irrelevant — your apartment is yours Mon through Sun.

NEARBY RESTAURANT

Low coordination: Lower active coordination (no cooking, no grocery runs) but external coordination: an 8-top reservation inside the Nov 10–14 window, dietary prefs, transit. Many South Slope / 5th-Ave-area sit-downs won't take a group of 8 midweek or only at off-peak slots.

Time with your mother: Moderate. You're at a venue; closing time is the upper bound. Easier to keep short, harder to extend. If her visit is short, you may want that time at home, not at a table.

Kibo logistics: Simplest. Dog stays home. If she's staying with you, transit is a walk or short cab.

Cleanup: Zero — it's their problem.

Weekday possibility: Harder. If the ceremony lands Mon/Tue/Wed, a weeknight 8-top often means an early (5:30/6:00) or late (8:30+) slot. Early cuts into post-ceremony wind-down; late is a long day for your mother and for Devika after a ceremony. Sat/Sun opens up normal dinner timing.

WHAT THE WEIGHTING ACTUALLY SUGGESTS

If ceremony lands Mon–Wed → hosting clearly favored. Restaurant availability tightens, you don't want a late table after a weekday, and you lose the lingering evening at home.

If ceremony lands Thu–Fri → closer call. Restaurant works, especially with a 7:00/7:30. Hosting still wins on mother-time and Kibo control but the cost (your night, Devika's night, next-day cleanup) is real.

If ceremony lands Sat–Sun → hosting still probably wins on your stated priorities, but a short low-key restaurant dinner becomes reasonable. You may also want to save the home-cooked evening for a separate night during her visit, with the post-ceremony dinner kept short and easy.

OPEN QUESTIONS BEFORE EITHER PATH
- Which nights is your mother actually in town? If she's only there Thu–Sun, the weekday factor matters less.
- Is the dinner the same evening as the ceremony, or a separate night? (You said "after," but worth confirming.)
- Any dietary restrictions among the 8 to plan around now vs later?
- Walkable in South Slope, or open to a short cab (Park Slope / Gowanus / Greenwood)?
- Is Devika on or off the day of, and how early does she need to be done?

Short answer: no, do not flip it to implementation-ready yet.

Reasoning on the case as you described it:

- The handoff defines three things on its face: the team, the release candidate, and the canonical-package version. "Implementation-ready" means downstream consumers can build on it without further intervention.
- The handoff also enumerates required generated platform outputs. Two completed; one failed after the canonical was published. That third output is, by the handoff's own definition, required — not optional.
- "Canonical source is valid" is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. Validity of the source tells you the artifact you're generating from is correct; it tells you nothing about whether the derived/generated artifacts actually exist in the artifacts store / registry / whatever surface downstream pulls from.
- Marking it ready while a required generator is failed will misroute downstream work. Someone will consume the missing artifact, hit a 404 or a stale fallback, and the failure will surface as a confusing consumer-side bug instead of an obvious handoff gap. That is worse than holding the flag.

Practical moves:

1. Keep the handoff out of implementation-ready. If your process has a "ready-with-known-gap" or "blocked-on-generator-X" state, use that — but it is a different flag from implementation-ready.
2. Re-run the failed generator (or fix whatever made it fail post-publish — versioning race, registry auth, signing key, etc.) and confirm the artifact is actually present, not just that the job exited.
3. Only then flip to implementation-ready.

One caveat I'd flag honestly: I don't have the North Pier handoff doc loaded in this session — no ID or link was provided, and my notes don't carry it. The above is on the merits of the situation you described. If your handoff defines a specific readiness gate (e.g., "2 of 3 generators sufficient" or a documented waiver path), that overrides the general reasoning — but I'd want to see that written down before accepting the coworker's framing.

Short answer for you first: no — not as a single assertion. Implementation readiness is two layered checks, not one. The canonical source (spec, IDL, schema) being valid, complete, and stable is one assertion, and it stands on its own. The generated-output set (clients, server stubs, docs, mocks, anything derived from the source) being fully regenerated and present is a separate assertion. A required generated output is part of the deliverable surface even though it's derived, so its absence breaks the second assertion regardless of how clean the canonical source is. So you can assert canonical readiness; you cannot assert overall implementation readiness while a required generated output is still missing — those don't collapse into one.

Reading your timeline:
  t=0.0    accepted, caller deadline=5.0s (remaining=5.0)
  t=4.8    dispatched from tenant queue (remaining=0.2s)
  t=4.8    handler starts a *fresh* 5s budget (remaining=5.0 again)
  t=9.2    handler returns; metric = 4.4s

By t=5.0 the caller has already given up. The handler runs 4.2 more seconds doing work no one reads, then reports "finished in 4.4s, under budget." The 4.4s isn't wrong about the handler — it's just measuring the wrong slice for the upstream contract.

Three things are wrong:

  1. Deadline model. The candidate resets the budget at dispatch instead of subtracting queue wait from it. End-to-end the request took 9.2s against a 5s budget; the handler just doesn't see that.

  2. Wasted post-deadline work. Fine when queues are shallow. Under load or with a hot tenant — exactly the regime the fairness/quota work is shaping — the handler burns capacity on responses the caller already dropped.

  3. Misleading metric. handler_latency_seconds (assuming that's what it is) reads healthy while callers are timing out. Any SLO dashboard built off it will lie, including during an incident.

What it should be, depending on what the candidate actually intended:
  - Pass the remaining budget (or absolute deadline) into the handler at dispatch. Handler short-circuits fast when remaining < min_processing. Metric reports e2e from acceptance.
  - Or, if there's a deliberate queue-SLA + handler-SLA split: queue wait becomes a first-class metric with its own SLO, the handler's 5s is subtracted from whatever the caller still has (not added on top), and that contract is exposed upstream — callers can't set a 5s total deadline if the queue can eat 4.8s of it.
  - Either way, queue wait can't disappear from the reported number.

Other things worth checking before approval:
  - What does the caller do on its own deadline expiry — cancel, drop, or just log? If it cancels, the handler is racing a cancellation signal and the metric should exclude the post-cancel tail.
  - Is there a cap on tenant queue depth? A misbehaving tenant pushing everyone else's wait to 4.8s+ is exactly the scenario that flips this from latent to visible. (Ties to the bucket-distro / no-tenant-label work — relevant if this PR sits near it.)
  - What's the handler's behavior when queue wait = 2.5s? Same fresh 5s on top, total 7.5s? If yes, the contract is even more broken than your one scenario shows.

A useful way to frame this: that 4 mm patch isn't the question. The question is whether the patch is surface-only cosmetic fuzzing or the visible tip of structural damage. Here's how to tell:

Tells that point to cosmetic (Kibo can wear it, with monitoring):
- The fuzz balls back when you brush it, and the underlying webbing looks smooth and full
- Webbing thickness at the spot feels the same as an adjacent unworn spot when you pinch them side by side
- Fibers don't break off when you tug a few individually
- The spot is isolated — no other wear points, no stiffness, no discoloration
- The patch sits on the surface of a weave that's otherwise crisp, not matted

Tells that point to retire-it-now:
- The webbing feels measurably thinner or softer at that spot (pinch test against clean webbing)
- Fibers pull out or snap with light tug — that means the plies underneath have lost tenacity
- The area feels stiffer than the surrounding strap when you bend it sharply (stiffness = heat, UV, or chemical damage to the fibers)
- You can see through to a different texture underneath, or the weave has gone flat/matted
- There's a wear pattern repeating in the same spot (suggests a rubbing contact that's actively working the webbing)
- The fuzzing extends onto or under the D-ring stitch line, even slightly — that stitch row is the load path

Why the location matters: the front-clip chest strap carries the leash force during a surprise pull. Kibo startles at skateboards, and you've graduated truck-intersection work, so sudden loads aren't hypothetical. A chest strap with structural damage fails at the worst possible moment and without warning — there is no "almost held."

My read on the facts you've already given me: webbing uncut, D-ring solid, buckle locks, stitches intact — those are the four checks that, if any of them failed, would settle this immediately. None failed. That's consistent with cosmetic, but it doesn't rule out structural, because structural damage at this stage hides under intact-looking surface fibers until you actually load-test the spot.

Concrete next step before you put it on him: do the pinch-and-bend comparison between the fuzzing spot and a clean section of the same strap, and tug a few fibers at the spot. If everything matches the clean webbing — same thickness, same flexibility, fibers hold — I'd call it cosmetic, put him in it, and recheck the spot weekly until you replace the harness on its normal schedule. If any of those three checks come back different, retire it; a chest strap is not the place to be charitable.

Short answer: it depends almost entirely on the fare rules and how fast the appointment slots go.

The decision tree:

**Buy tonight if any of these are true:**
- The fare is fully refundable or has free cancellation within 24h (then risk is near-zero, lock the price).
- You know from experience that slots fill in minutes when inventory opens (then waiting itself is the risky move).
- The fare is non-refundable and you're reasonably confident she can get the slot — the upside of locking a known-good price beats the small chance she eats the ticket.

**Wait until after 9 AM if:**
- The fare is non-refundable basic economy, AND
- Slots typically stay open for hours/days (not seconds), AND
- The fare is likely stable overnight or you can re-shop from the same carrier at a comparable price.

**Three things I'd want to know before answering firmly:**
1. Refundable / changeable fare, or basic economy?
2. How fast did the last cohort of slots go when inventory opened?
3. Is there a backup date window (e.g., she'd take Nov 10–16 if Nov 9 doesn't work), or is Nov 9–15 firm?

If the fare is refundable or changeable without penalty, the answer is almost always "buy tonight" — you remove fare risk without taking on appointment risk. If it's basic economy non-refundable and slots historically go in the first 10 minutes, also "buy tonight" and accept the small chance of needing to eat or change the ticket. The "wait" answer only really wins when the fare is locked-in expensive AND slots are slow-moving.

  Audience: Wes — Thursday 8/14

  Status: Teaching material only. Not production authorization. No change

§1 — Two kinds of opening (the one distinction)

  The walkthrough is mostly about telling these apart on the record:

    Fresh opening decision
      - Who opens it:  canary-response owner, explicit go
      - Pushes allowed: exactly ONE fully-observed push
      - Counts as the one? yes
      - Resets the count? yes

    Reopened window (in-window)
      - Who opens it:  already open
      - Pushes allowed: multiple, while guards hold
      - Counts as the one? no
      - Resets the count? no

  If the record can't tell you which kind you're looking at, stop and ask.
  Don't infer from guard values alone.

§2 — In-window guards (checked after every push)

  Mapped operators may keep pushing while ALL of these hold:
    - Push shape:        single-file only.
    - Retired gens:      stays at four or fewer.
    - Cleanup pause:     stays at or below 100 ms.
    - Health set:        the full health set returns to baseline after
                         every push.

  If retired gens exceeds 4 OR cleanup pause exceeds 100 ms, the window
  STOPS. A push that doesn't return the health set to baseline is handled
  under §3.

§3 — Rollback conditions (unchanged)

  Any of these requires rollback, fresh or reopened:
    - consistency
    - parity
    - dropped-series
    - reload
    - restart

§4 — Re-entry after a stop or rollback

    1. Recovery completes.
    2. A FRESH opening decision permits exactly one fully-observed push.
    3. After that push returns the full health set to baseline, a LATER
       window requires a SEPARATE fresh decision. You do not chain
       reopened windows off a fully-observed push.

  This is where confusion usually lands. The fully-observed push is the
  boundary object — it has to be visible as such in the record.

§5 — Worked example (Wes's reference)

  Use the 10/8 94 ms recovery-push as the canonical case. It is the

    2. Where is the fresh-decision artifact? (owner's explicit go)

    4. What did the health set look like immediately after?
       (returned to baseline)

  protocol. If he can't, the gap is record-readiness, not thresholds.

§6 — Discussion prompts (run in order)

Good — you've already done the most important thing (stopped using it). The "won't reset, breaker looks fine, lights still on" pattern almost always means the GFCI device itself has latched off (or a different, upstream GFCI has tripped), not a breaker issue. Here's a safe isolation sequence.

1.  Confirm the tripped device is on the receptacle itself.
    A GFCI receptacle has two buttons on its face: TEST and RESET. Look at the dead outlet — if you don't see TEST/RESET there, it isn't the GFCI; it's a plain receptacle being protected from somewhere else. In that case, skip to step 2.

2.  Hunt for the actual GFCI that has tripped. This is the single most common reason a kitchen outlet "won't reset."
    -  Press RESET firmly on the dead outlet. If nothing clicks, leave it.
    -  Walk the kitchen and press TEST, then RESET, on every other receptacle that has TEST/RESET buttons (other counters, peninsula, island, behind the sink). One of them is likely the protecting GFCI, and its RESET button may be popped out. Press it firmly until it clicks and latches.
    -  Check bathrooms, the garage, any outdoor outlet, and the laundry area — older and retrofit kitchens are sometimes cross-wired off a GFCI in an unexpected room.
    -  Check the breaker panel for a GFCI breaker: it looks like a normal breaker but has a TEST button on it. If found, press its RESET (the breaker toggle should also be fully ON — flip it fully OFF, then fully ON, to be sure it isn't in a half-tripped middle position that "looks fine").

    If you find an upstream GFCI that resets and the kitchen outlet now has power, you're done — just leave the blender unplugged from that circuit and test it elsewhere (step 5).

3.  If the dead outlet does have TEST/RESET and no upstream reset fixes it, do one orderly reset attempt.
    -  Unplug everything from the dead receptacle and from every other receptacle on the same kitchen counter circuit.
    -  Press RESET firmly (some need a deliberate push). It should click and stay in.
    -  Three outcomes:
        a.  Resets and latches — circuit is usable; proceed to step 5.
        b.  Clicks then immediately pops back out — there's still a ground fault on the wiring or a load. Do not keep mashing it. Stop here.
        c.  Won't click at all — the GFCI itself has likely failed internally, or it has no line-side power. Stop here.

4.  The breaker question.
    -  Since your lights still work, the panel breaker for that circuit is almost certainly fine and does not need to be reset. A one-time breaker reset (flip fully OFF, then fully ON) is non-destructive and reasonable as a single diagnostic move if you want to be thorough, especially if you suspect the breaker itself is a GFCI breaker that may be in a half-tripped state. Do it once. If the kitchen outlet still won't reset afterward, the breaker is not the problem.

5.  Isolate the blender.
    -  Plug the blender into a known-good outlet on a different circuit (a bathroom GFCI, for example). Run it briefly.
    -  If the blender trips that other GFCI, the blender has an internal ground fault — discard or have the blender serviced; the receptacle is fine.
    -  If the blender runs fine elsewhere, the blender is innocent and the fault is in the kitchen circuit.

Stop and contact your building management / an electrician (do not continue troubleshooting) if any of the following is true:

-  The GFCI will not click/latch at all on reset, and no other upstream GFCI restores power. In a rental this is a maintenance call — the GFCI device itself has likely failed and needs replacement, which is the landlord's job, not the tenant's.
-  The GFCI trips immediately on reset with nothing plugged in anywhere on the circuit. That points to a wiring fault (moisture in a box, a failed splice, a nail through a cable) and needs a licensed electrician.
-  Any new sign of heat, buzzing, a burning smell, scorch marks, discoloration around the outlet face, or moisture in the outlet box. Leave the breaker OFF if you've already touched it and call.
-  Power is out at multiple receptacles across the kitchen and you cannot locate an upstream GFCI or a tripped GFCI breaker.
-  The blender is confirmed to trip other GFCIs — stop using the blender regardless of what you find on the circuit.

Until you get a clean reset or a professional has looked at it, leave the receptacle alone, leave the panel breaker in whatever position you found it (don't flip it off "just in case" unless you smell heat or see damage — there's no benefit and it could mask the fault for whoever responds), and don't use that circuit for anything. If you need counter power for cooking tonight, use a different circuit entirely (a different kitchen counter receptacle that's working, or a bathroom circuit) and plug the blender in there first to test it.

**Four-month cost difference**
$148 − $130 = $18/month extra pre-tax
$18 × 4 = **$72** of additional pre-tax contributions over 4 months

**Tax savings on that $72 (33%)**
$72 × 0.33 = **$23.76** of federal tax shielded over 4 months
(≈ $5.94/month)

So the four-month out-of-pocket cost is roughly $72 pre-tax, which saves about $23.76 in federal tax — net economic cost ≈ $48.24 if 33% is your full marginal rate.

**Is increasing the election to expected use sensible, assuming you won't travel?**

No — the economics work against it.

The "use it or lose it" rule is the binding constraint. Pre-tax transit/commuter benefits are governed-use-it-or-lose-it at the IRS level: any amount above your actual commuting expenses over the runout window provides no tax benefit because there's no expense to offset — you're just deferring payroll tax on money you can't recover. That $48.24 net cost becomes pure loss if your actual transit spend over those 4 months comes in below the higher election.

A smaller bump (say $135–$140 to cover a realistic buffer for things like subway-to-bus transfers, occasional rideshare when the L is down, or transit you genuinely already use) keeps the buffer without material risk of forfeiture. The breakeven test is: *over the 4-month window, will I actually spend $148/month on qualifying commuting?* If the honest answer is "no, $130 already covers my real pattern," then $148 is a small but real guaranteed loss, not a savings.

If your transit use is genuinely going to be higher over the next 4 months for known reasons (e.g., a commute pattern change), then raising closer to expected use is fine — just don't raise based on a hoped-for travel uptick that you said to exclude.

Short version: that's not drift. The hash is operating on the wrong representation.

What you're seeing is **serialization drift, not semantic drift.** You confirmed this yourself — the parsed token maps are identical, and only key ordering + line endings differ. Neither of those carries meaning. A byte-for-byte hash on raw file contents is a serialization check; it tells you "the text differs," not "the tokens differ." The verdict is technically correct and operationally wrong.

Don't suppress the symptom. Two common bad fixes worth naming so you don't reach for them:

1. Rewriting the generator to emit LF so it matches the canonical. Silences the alert until someone regenerates from a different OS/CI, then it comes back. You'll be chasing line endings forever.
2. Adding `* text=auto` / `.gitattributes` to force LF on the iOS file. Same problem — fixes the tracked copy, not the generator output, and masks the real defect in the comparison layer.

Quick diagnostics to pin it down before you change anything:

- `file canonical.* generated.*` — one of them will report "with CRLF line terminators"
- `git config core.autocrlf` and `git config core.autefcrlf` on the repo that emits the iOS file — autocrlf=true on Windows or a misconfigured repo is the usual culprit
- `xxd | head` on both to confirm `0d 0a` vs `0a`
- Check whether the generator does a JSON round-trip anywhere in the pipeline (loses insertion order if it goes through anything unordered) or iterates a dict loaded from a plist/Set/NSUserDefaults-style source
- Check the generator's emitter — if it's templating or doing `for k in dict` in a language without ordered maps, that's the ordering culprit

The right fix is in the **comparison layer**, not the generator:

- Parse both artifacts into token maps (name → {type, value, version, ...}).
- Compare maps order-independently.
- Normalize values before comparing (color hex case, `1.0` vs `1`, string vs number, etc. — whatever your token spec calls equivalent).
- Treat semantic diffs (name/value/type/version) as the only thing that constitutes drift. Serialization differences (line endings, key order, whitespace, comments) should not page anyone.

If you also want a **stable content fingerprint** for caching/downstream change detection (separate from the drift alarm), compute it on a canonicalized serialization: sort keys, normalize to LF, strip trailing whitespace, then hash. That's a fingerprint of the semantic content, not the bytes. Just keep it clearly distinct from the drift check — never let a fingerprint hash be the thing deciding whether tokens drifted.

One more thing worth asking: who owns the byte-hash check? If it's downstream of token generation (e.g., a release gate or a cache invalidator), it was probably designed assuming the generator is byte-deterministic. That's a fine assumption for *its* purpose, but it shouldn't be wired into the drift alarm. If the same component is doing both jobs, split them — drift detection needs semantic comparison, content fingerprinting can stay byte-based but on canonicalized output.

If you want, I can sketch what the semantic comparator should look like for your token schema (Swift codable side vs whatever the canonical package emits).

The right way to frame it: the **pass/fail check is a semantic comparison over the canonical inputs**, and the **original artifacts stay as evidence on the side**, never folded into the comparison.

What should be canonicalized for pass/fail
  - `commit_sha` — the comparison is "what did this exact code produce." Any of Anya's hash-binding arguments only hold if the diff under review is the unit being judged; otherwise the cache pass is for a different binary.
  - `fixture_digest` — the input space being exercised (events, label set, cardinality distribution). Semantic, not byte-equal: a fixture that's been re-emitted with identical event IDs, identical label set, and identical distribution is the same fixture even if the on-disk bytes changed (e.g. wrapping format, field ordering). What matters is "same logical input," not "same file blob."
  - `rule_set_digest` — which policy is being applied. This is where the 100 → 80 limit change lives. The pass/fail is "under the rule set currently in force, does this commit stay under the limit." If the rule set changes, the prior pass is invalidated — that's exactly what `a81c4e2` proved, and it's the behavior you want to preserve.
  - The **active policy** (current limit value) is what the pass/fail evaluates against, not the policy that was in force when the cache entry was written. Same principle: today's rules judge today's run.

What should remain as evidence, not be canonicalized
  - Original raw fixture files (whatever bytes Anya captured) — kept verbatim so a reviewer can reproduce byte-for-byte if the semantic digest is ever questioned.
  - The exact error output from the failing run under limit 80 — that string is evidence, not a comparison input.
  - The cached prior-pass record (under limit 100) — kept so the *delta* "this pass existed under rule v1 and not under rule v2" is auditable. It's evidence that the cache correctly invalidated; it's not the thing being compared.
  - Tooling/version metadata (loadgen version, rule-loader version) — useful for forensic reproduction; doesn't change pass/fail.

Boundary, stated crisply
  - **Compare (canonicalize):** `(commit_sha, semantic fixture digest, rule_set_digest)` against the *active* policy. Pass = "this commit, under today's rules, on this fixture, stays within the active limit."
  - **Don't compare (preserve as evidence):** raw fixture bytes, prior cache entries, the textual failure output, infra/tool versions. These answer "what happened" — they do not decide "did it pass."

Why this matters for Anya's two regressions specifically
  - Fixture-only regression reruns because the new fixture's logical input differs — the canonical digest changes, the pass invalidates. Raw bytes may or may not differ; that's not what gates the rerun.
  - Policy-only regression (`a81c4e2`, limit 100 → 80) fails because the active rule set now rejects what the older rule set accepted. The prior pass stays in the cache as evidence; it does not transfer. That's the correct behavior, and it's the one that would be silently broken if byte-equality were substituted for semantic-equality somewhere upstream (e.g. if "same fixture" started meaning "same file path" rather than "same logical input," a re-emitted fixture could inherit a stale pass).

The line you asked me to hold: I'm describing where the semantic boundary belongs and what stays as evidence. I'm not specifying the digest algorithm, the cache invalidation trigger, or the rerun policy — those are Anya's calls as implementer, and Wes/whoever as routine reviewer. If you want, the natural next thing for whoever owns the routine review is to confirm that the cache key actually contains all three components (not, say, just `commit_sha` and a file-hash), since that's the only thing that prevents the silent regression where a rule change inherits a stale pass.

Safe normalizations for semantic comparison

  Only normalizations you can justify from the schema/spec, not from "looks similar":
  - Encoding canonicalization (e.g., NFC for UTF-8 sources) when the spec pins an encoding.
  - Field-separator trimming (delimiters, surrounding quotes) per the parser's own contract.
  - Sorting/dedup by a canonical key, with the key defined and versioned — not by raw string equality.
  - Case folding only where the schema explicitly says case-insensitive (e.g., HTTP method names, header names); never by default.
  - Numeric/date parsing where the schema declares the type; keep the raw token alongside the parsed value so you can re-derive.

  Anything not pinned by the schema stays as-is: zero-width chars, BOMs, internal whitespace runs, ordering of equivalent-looking delimiters, trailing punctuation. If two records look identical but differ in any of these, they are not semantically equal until the schema says they are.

Why token-value whitespace must not be silently normalized unless the schema defines it as insignificant

  - Tokens (auth tokens, chunk IDs, source-event IDs, audit IDs) are typically defined by a format spec that treats the full byte sequence as significant. A leading space, a trailing \r, an internal \t can all be part of the value, and stripping them creates collisions between distinct tokens or splits a single token into phantom matches.
  - "Looks the same" is not the same as "is the same." A trim that silently drops a byte is a write — it changes the identity of the value — and any downstream equality check, replay, or audit link will now resolve differently than the producer intended.
  - The only legitimate authority for "whitespace is insignificant here" is the schema or RFC that defines the token. Examples where it is explicit: HTTP header field-value OWS folding (with documented semantics), PEM whitespace-insensitive block decoders. In every other case, especially for audit/chunk tokens you have not pinned to a format doc, whitespace is significant by default.
  - If the schema is ambiguous or missing, the safe move is to preserve the original and surface the ambiguity, not to pick a normalization that makes the data "work."

Original artifacts to retain as evidence

  - The raw CSV bytes as received, with a content hash (sha256) and the ingestion timestamp/source recorded alongside. Do not overwrite or "clean" the source.
  - The schema/spec version referenced for every normalization decision, including the rule that authorized each step (or the explicit "no rule, preserved verbatim" note).
  - The parser/normalizer source and version that produced the comparison keys, plus the parameters it was invoked with.
  - Side-by-side samples: a few records in their raw form and the same records after each normalization stage, so a reviewer can replay the decisions.
  - The set of records flagged as differing only by characters the schema does not address (whitespace runs, BOMs, casing) — these are the cases where your policy choice is visible and auditable.
  - Any audit/chunk token format doc or excerpt that informed the "whitespace significant" call, so the next reviewer can verify the rule against the source.

Boundary

  This is the engineering frame — which normalizations are defensible, why whitespace in tokens is not yours to relax, and what to keep so the decisions are replayable. The choice of which specific steps to apply, how to version the canonical key, and how to surface the flagged cases is her implementation.

The race is the validate/publish window. "Consumed post-publish" means there's a TOCTOU gap between checking `unused` and flipping the marker — both workers can pass the unused check before either reaches publish. Two publishes on the same grant, and the second isn't blocked downstream unless the publish target is itself idempotent on audit_id (which doesn't sound like the case here, since "both complete the rollback path").

Clean fix: collapse validate-and-mark into one atomic conditional update (unused → in-flight) that returns success to one worker and a clear "already in-flight" to the other. Then publish. Then flip in-flight → consumed as the audit trail. The in-flight state is the actual gate; the post-publish mark is bookkeeping. Audit-id idempotency at the publish target stays as a backstop, not the primary defense. Two things worth deciding alongside: (1) what the loser-worker error path looks like — does it surface as a rollback failure to the operator, or is it swallowed since "someone did it"? and (2) expiry semantics — if a worker holds the grant in-flight and crashes, does the grant auto-expire out of in-flight, or does it stick and block future use until an operator clears it?

Distance & pacing
  LGA's Terminal B in particular has long concourses. Gate-to-baggage can run 10–20 minutes of continuous walking, plus standing at the carousel. Energy cost
  Walking: sustained lower-body effort and standing at baggage claim. Wheelchair: near-zero energy cost to you — you arrive at the carousel fresh.

Carry-on handling
  Walking: you manage your bag the whole way. Wheelchair: porter typically takes carry-on on the chair or beside you.

Crowd navigation
  Walking: weaving through other passengers, slow zones at security re-routes and food courts. Wheelchair: wider lanes, often against the main foot-traffic flow.

Wait at the gate
  Walking: just go. Wheelchair: a short wait for the porter (usually 5–15 minutes after deplaning; airline staff radio them).

Visibility / self-consciousness
  Walking: looks "normal" — no one is judging either way. Wheelchair: porters assist travelers of all kinds; it's unremarkable in an airport.

Cost
  Both are free to the passenger — it's an airline-provided service.

Practical takeaway
  This is less a mobility question than an energy-management question. The service is designed for anyone who'd rather not spend 20+ minutes on their feet after a flight.

The expression is structurally computing "non-received minus estimated refused" — it only equals the exact refused counter when the errored/lost bucket coincidentally equals the (actual − estimated) refused drift.

Walking Replay A:
- received_points = 920,000 (otherwise the arithmetic doesn't close), so non-received = 80,000
- refused_requests × avg = 4 × 10,000 = 40,000
- expression = 80,000 − 40,000 = 40,000 ✓ matches exact refused

Decompose non-received: refused (40,000) + errored (40,000). So the expression is actually:

  refused + errored − estimated_refused = 40,000 + (40,000 − 40,000) = 40,000

The errored bucket (40,000) coincidentally equals the drift (0 in A). Two cancellations stack.

Replay B: smaller batches → actual refused drops (say to X), but estimated stays at 4 × 10,000 = 40,000, so drift goes positive. Expression becomes X + errored − 40,000. That equals X only when errored == drift, which won't hold in general.

Cleanest fix: the collector already emits an exact refused-point counter. Wire PR 309 to that and drop the `refused_requests × average_points_per_request` term entirely. The formula as labeled doesn't compute what the PR claims — it computes "errored points beyond the refused-drift estimate," which is a different (and less useful) signal. If a drift metric is what's actually wanted, name it that; if refused is what's wanted, use the exact counter.

Here's a 15-minute substitute that keeps the longer forearm ramp via floor mobility → traversing → low open-hand routes, with a first-attempt progression after. Step-back thresholds you listed apply to the whole block.

0:00–4:30  FLOOR MOBILITY (wrists, forearms, shoulders)
  - Wrist circles both directions × 15 each wrist
  - Floor wrist flexion/extension (palm flat, then back of hand flat) × 8 each side, slow
  - Prayer stretch (palms together, lower) × 30s × 2
  - Reverse prayer / extensor stretch × 25s × 2
  - Forearm extensor self-massage with opposite thumb × 60s each arm — find tender spots, slow pressure
  - Scapular CARs × 5 each direction
  - Wall slides × 8 — keep lower ribs down, no shrug
  Goal: open up the wrist and forearm extensor chain without any load yet. Forearms should feel warm, not pumped.

4:30–10:00  EASY TRAVERSING (low, open-hand only)
  Pick the wall with the biggest, most positive holds. Stay low (feet within ~1 m of the floor is fine).
  Rules:
  - Open-hand contact only — no pinch, no full crimp, no thumb-over
  - If a sequence isn't obvious in a second, skip the hold and keep moving
  - Traverse both directions to balance shoulder loading
  - ~3 min per direction with a 30 s shake-out between
  - Breathing easy. If forearms pump before the 6 min mark, the holds are too small or you're squeezing — switch to bigger holds or load feet harder

10:00–15:00  LOWEST OPEN-HAND ROUTES
  Pick the two easiest open-hand lines in the gym (typical V0–V1), big holds, feet-on style.
  - Route A (easiest): slow, deliberate, every move controlled. Flash without ever closing to crimp or pinch — if a move forces it, pick a different line
  - Shake out 60–90 s
  - Route B (next easiest open-hand): same rules
  - Close the block with a 60 s dead-hang on a large open jug to consolidate, then shake out

FIRST-ATTEMPT PROGRESSION (after the warmup, next ~30–40 min)
  1. Pick a route ~half a grade above what you just did. Still open-hand, no dyno, no sequency crux that demands a crimp. If you can't read it from the ground in 30 s, downgrade.
  2. Full rest 3–4 min between burns.
  3. Second attempt: another route of similar grade; vary the wall angle if available to spread load across shoulder positions.
  4. From here, steeper lines and projects are fair game if forearms and shoulders feel clean. Keep the step-back thresholds live.

STEP-BACK TRIGGERS (apply to all of the above, not just climbing)
  - Pain ≥ 2/10 in wrist, forearm, elbow, or shoulder during any of this
  - Symptoms still present 30 min after stopping
  - Anything noticeable the next morning (stiffness, soreness, weakness)

If a trigger fires: stop the session, note what you were doing, and message Devika with the route angle, hold type, grade attempted, when the symptom started, and current level.

For a high-stimulus maintenance day (fair in the usual loop, Devika on a long block), the side-street detour is the safer base. It keeps you in the low-traffic environment Kibo's training defaults to, and treats the fair as something to pass around, not through. The truck-heavy route is workable but it's a training-exposure pattern, not the default, and today isn't a training day.

Structure for roughly 30 minutes (allowing about 10 minutes of detour overhead):

  Outbound: front-clip harness, normal-length leash, quiet residential.

  Before any block adjacent to the fair perimeter: switch to the shorter leash for one to two blocks. This is where the spillover risk lives — skateboards, skaters, strollers, flexi-lead dogs heading to or from the fair. Step a little further from the curb than usual. Have treats accessible but don't pre-offer.

  Past the perimeter: back to normal leash on quiet side streets for the middle of the walk. This is the rest portion.

  Loop-closure block, if detour geometry forces it: if one truck-heavy block is unavoidable to get home, cap it at one block. Short leash through, treat visible and ready, step off the curb where there's a buffer, walk briskly. The instant you're past it, return to quiet. Do not extend to a second truck block just to make the loop prettier.

  Return leg: quiet streets, easy pace.

Turn back instead of forcing the longer detour if any of these show up:

  - Kibo freezes, hard-stares, or pulls hard toward home for more than a block — he's at capacity, shorten the walk.

  - A skate or skater triggers a startle that doesn't resolve in roughly 10 seconds — reverse to the last quiet block.

  - A fair-adjacent side street turns out busier than expected (food trucks, music spillover, crowd overflow) — find a different cross street, or end the walk early.

  - Cumulative stimulus (fair noise plus any truck traffic) makes him hard to read — a 20-minute easy walk beats a 30-minute stressful one.

Two anchors for the call in the moment:

  If the detour pushes the walk past roughly 40 minutes and any single stress signal has shown up, end it. Walk again at sunset when the fair's still up but the crowds thin.

  If the detour starts to feel forced — you'd be navigating two truck blocks or fair-perimeter chaos — just take the shorter loop in the other direction and call it 20 minutes. Don't manufacture distance.

General principle for days like this: comfortable movement over coverage. He doesn't need the full loop today.

Reading the sketch against your IC scope (invariants + failure modes). Three points worth raising with Wes, plus a few open questions.

  Atomicity of the read-then-reserve
  The check `tenant_pending < 64` followed by an increment is two operations. Under concurrent arrivals to the same tenant, two callers can both pass the check and both increment and push past the cap. Same concern on the global counter, with sharper blast radius — single hot spot at 2,048.

  Worth asking Wes: CAS, per-tenant lock, or single global lock? If per-tenant, what's the contention story when one tenant dominates ingress?

  "Exactly once" release — caller crash and retry
  The sketch covers cancellation and enqueue-failure paths, but not:
    - caller process crash between reservation and enqueue (or after enqueue before "accepted" is observed by the caller)
    - caller retry: client timed out but server actually succeeded -> second attempt double-releases

  Either the caller needs an idempotency key, or the server needs a lease/timeout so abandoned reservations get reaped. Without one of those, "exactly once" is a happy-path property, not a system property — and the cap stops being a real cap once a stuck reservation can't be recovered.

  Tenant vs. global ordering — churn and visibility
  In the contended regime (global near 2,047, many tenants near 63), every incoming batch does tenant-reserve + global-reject + tenant-release. Two follow-ups:
    - do we surface this tenant-counter churn as a metric? It's invisible today and that's a gap.

    - is the recovery-push path from the 10/8 canary covered by this sketch, or a separate code path that also needs the same release discipline?

**Baseline scenario (4 primary + 1 specialist, no procedures)**

PPO: $3,848 premium + (4 × $25) + (1 × $45) = $3,848 + $100 + $45 = **$3,993**

HDHP: $2,392 premium + visit costs until $2,200 deductible met + 10% coinsurance on remainder, minus $900 HSA
- The deductible is the key driver. If negotiated primary visits average ~$180–$200 and specialist ~$350–$450 (typical NYC in-network rates), 4 PCPs + 1 spec ≈ $1,000–$1,500 — entirely within the deductible, so you pay the full negotiated amount.

- HDHP net cost: ~$2,392 + ~$1,300 − $900 ≈ **~$2,800**

**Tax angle (the big multiplier)**
- The $1,456 premium savings on HDHP is paid pre-tax via payroll deduction. NYC resident at Alex's bracket (likely ~32% federal + ~6.85% NY + ~3.876% NYC = ~42-43% combined marginal), tax saved ≈ $610–$625/year.

- PPO: $3,993 + 15% × ($10,000 − $500) = $3,993 + $1,425 = **$5,418**
- HDHP: $2,392 + min($10,000, $2,200) deductible + 10% × remainder − $900 HSA = $2,392 + $2,200 + $780 − $900 = **$4,472**
- HDHP still saves ~$950. If visits push you over $2,200 deductible, all the better for HDHP because every dollar above is only 10%.

**Verdict**

1. ~$1,200/year cheaper on the expected scenario at these cost ratios
2. ~$610+ in additional tax savings from the premium differential alone
3. The $900 employer HSA is essentially a guaranteed $900 (plus ~$380 tax savings)

Recommendation: blind plain hem with a slight break.

Why it wins on your criteria:

Lower maintenance. A slight break drapes naturally over the shoe — no precision length-matching to a specific heel. If your ceremony shoes are even slightly different from what you wear day-to-day, the trouser still looks right. A visible machine hem with no break has to hit a single exact length; any shoe-height mismatch reads as either too short (ankle flashing) or too long (pooling), and you feel it through the day.

Intentional with ceremony shoes. Slight break is the classic considered finish for a charcoal suit — it reads as deliberate, not as "I forgot to get these hemmed." A visible machine hem with no break can look great but reads more fashion-editorial; for a City Clerk visit + dinner it's slightly louder than the moment calls for.

Comfort through the visit + dinner. A slight break means the trouser falls over the shoe without binding; no break means the hem sits right at the top of the shoe and can feel like it's tugging or catching when you walk, especially through a long day of standing and moving around.

Doesn't turn into a project. This is the big one. Blind hem = set-and-forget. The stitching is invisible, so even if the fold shifts slightly between wears or after cleaning, nothing reads as wrong. A visible machine hem with no break is a precision choice: once it's done, you're locked into that exact shoe + that exact length, and any future alteration (letting out, re-cutting) is much harder because there's no hidden fold to release.

Small bonus: the hidden fold in a blind hem means a tailor can let the trouser out later if you want a different break or a different shoe — a visible cut hem can't easily be lengthened.

The Oct 4 completion gives you about two weeks of buffer before the Oct 17 license appointment, which is comfortable. Once you confirm with the shop, I can update the wedding line in memory so "trouser alt pending" becomes "trouser alt: blind hem, slight break, pickup by Oct 4."
